I'd been aware of the XCOM series for some time, but it never interested me until I tried the demo for Enemy Unknown, but even that wasn't enough. It took a love for Darkest Dungeon and a realization that there were a number of turn-based games I'd enjoyed over the years, when I had previously just told people that I don't like them. So I waited for a sale and grabbed the complete pack. Coming from DD, XCOM is both more forgiving (especially if you use the Save Scum modifier) and significantly more tactically complex. I had some experience with squad-based tactics from Dawn of War II, though this is on a smaller scale: You are limited to a single squad and control each soldier individually. It also uses small, often single digit numbers for damage and health, something it has in common with DD, combined with visual bar sections, making it very easy at a glance to see where you're at tactically. There are certain tactical shortcomings that I'm told are addressed in the sequel, such as not knowing wether a position you are moving a soldier to will give them a view on potential targets until they get there- but i've also heard its much harder to get a guarenteed hit in the sequel, even if your trooper is pressing a gun to an enemy's face. Ups and downs, I suppose.
Enemy Unknown has layers of complexity that few other games have, though series veterans will still tell you its "dumbed down." Individual soldiers are highly customizable both in their abilities and appearance, especially if you have all the DLCs. You can name them, give them medals, and arm them with a variety of extra goodies. They start out as pathetic FNGs with the accuracy of the on-screen Stormtroopers of Star Wars, and dont even have a class, which they are assigned the first time they rank up: Assaults, Heavies, Snipers or Supports. These four classes are further split by players into two subclasses based on perk choices, though you may mix and match perks to your liking. However, you CANNOT respec your soldiers: choose perks carefully. With some planning, luck and maybe a few reloaded saves, they become apex examples of what human warriors can do- some of them may even become psychics. Then you can take them beyond that in Enemy Within, granting them genetic enhancements or cybernetic augmentation. XCOM resonated with me very strongly in this regard: Evolution is a powerful weapon indeed. One of my very first recruits from the post-tutorial mission, my first Support, went on to be my Volunteer. These are not just random grunts. They are your disciples. Their stories are yours.
Combat can go very smoothly or completely sideways, and the difference can be as subtle as the positioning of a single trooper, or which soldier you place on "Overwatch" (Which causes them to fire upon the first enemy that moves within their vison during their turn) You must take into account flanking, elevation, line of sight and variety of other factors. This variety increases as you level your soldiers and their capabilities expand, as do the variety of enemies you face. One of the most useful such capabilities in my experience has been a perk for Snipers called Squadsight, which permits them to fire on any target visibile to another XCOM soldier, so long as they also would have line of sight to that enemy. Properly positioned, this enables the Sniper to hit targets from across the map: as my first Sniper did when he saved the afforementioned Support from a Chryssalid on the now-infamous "Site Recon" mission. When things go right in XCOM, it is immensly satisfying. When they don't... oh boy, do they not.
But you don't just manage your troops in combat: You are responsible for XCOM operations at every level. You must build facilities to build at XCOM HQ to expand your capabilities, launch satillites over various countries to observe alien activity, respond to alerts and requests from XCOM's financial backers, conduct autopsies and interrogations on the aliens to learn their secrets and advance XCOM's technology base, intercept UFOs with your own aircraft which themselves must be built and maintained... and all of this with a continuous running timer. You will often find yourself pressed for time, funds or both, to my eternal consternation. To make matters worse, alien activity raises a "panic meter" in the various nations backing XCOM and if it goes too high for too long, those nations will pull their support for XCOM. Lose too many nations and you immediately lose the entire campaign. In Enemy Within, there's the added headache of a human terrorist group called EXALT conducting clandestine operations seemingly in support of the invaders. They can raise panic and interfere with your research. You must launch "covert ops" against them, requring you to temporarily remove a soldier from your roster while they go undercover, and then extract them later. EXALT operatives mirror the behaviors and tactics of your own troops, but they often have inferior hardware.
XCOM is an incredible, in-depth experience and I enjoyed it from the first mission to the very last. It is easily one of the finest games of this decade. It permits you control of your characters in a manner that would be more common in a traditional RPG, and the random elements become less of a hassle as you progress, as the time and effort you put into your soldiers' development pays off as they become nigh-unstoppable post-human super-warriors that puts EDF's Storm Team to shame and would give Commander Shepard's crew a run for their money. I found myself with the same fondness for them that I had for my heroes in Darkest Dungeon. It is clear that an uncommon degree of care and respect went in to Enemy Unknown's creation, with its purely asthetic "highlight camera" when making a killing shot and its excellent soundtrack. More big-budget releases could benefit from its example, and it can be played as casually or as intensively as one prefers, thanks to its range of difficulties and modifiers. If you enjoy squad tactics games, turn-based RPGs, or strategy games of any kind, I encourage you to try the demo. I understand that it offends the sensibilities of XCOM purists, and as such a person as regards to other series I totally get where they're coming from: but Xenonauts exists, and from what I can tell they should just play that.

After spending >100 hours (it’s sad, I admit) on this game, you start realising little things:
If you destroy a system, its ‘hit points’ is at zero. But if you cause a hull breach, you can effectively make a system’s hit points go below zero (since you have to repair breaches before you can repair a system). Therefore, destroying a system and then nuking it with heavy lasers (killing the crew trying to repair it, and causing hull breaches) is still effective!

THE Best Star Wars shooter ever made. For it's age, the graphics are fantastic. No dreaded shading lag, or lag from tree foliage that the newer games have. I run a very average computer and I have my graphics set pretty high and have 32 vs. 32 battles at 50-60 FPS. The base game is great, but one of it's best aspects is the modding ability, it makes the game truly amazing. The space battles are somewhat good, but mods make it much much better. Galactic Conquest mode is truly unique, showing how good of a strategist you are as well as how good of a ground soldier you are. The maps are incredible, with none being lazily copy/ pasted, they look fantastic, and each one requires a new strategie. Each faction has great modelling for their soldiers, and each standard soldier of the factions has different rifle stats, such as: Clone Troopers have good rate of fire and accuracy, but slightly lower damage; CIS has the slowest rate of fire, but are very powerful; Rebels have the best accuracy, but lowest damage; and the Stormtroopers have the fastest rate of fire, and very high damage, but low accuracy (keeping with the theme that Stormtroopers can't hit anything). Overall, this is my favourite Grand Scale Shooter that I have ever played (over CoD and even Battlefield) 10/10 would kill rebel scum again.

This game falls just a little bit short of the 3rd game, which makes it overall the 2nd best Naruto game (along with the 4th) and there's 2 reasons for that:
1. Combat is better in the 3rd game (and also 4th), because by then the devs figured out better way to do the Substition jutsu (which is a really key part of the combat). Both in this and the first game it's rather random whether you manage to activate it or not. I've seen people use turbo controllers just so that they can spam the block button really fast when getting attacked. That way they're more likely to land a substitution. It's really dumb.
2. While this game's story mode is a massive improvement from the 1st game, they still don't go quite as deep into detail with the story and explenatiosn as in the 3rd game. They didn't leave anything too important out unlike in the first game, but a lot of times they... simplified things. You'll notice it right away in the prologue when you have to steal the bells from Kakashi - it happens a bit differently. Meanwhile the 3rd game has 10+ minute long carefully animated cutscenes that closely follow the manga and actually managed to make me cry (though chapter 6 did get my eyes to sweat a bit) too. The point is, you can play the 3rd game and understand the story without reading the manga/watching the anime. This game's story mode is not quite sufficient for that.
Overall, well worth buying, whoever you are. A must have if you're a fan. BELIEVE IT!

It is the 41st Millennium. For more than a hundred centuries the Emperor of Mankind has sat immobile on the Golden Throne of Earth. He is the master of mankind by the will of the gods and master of a million worlds by the might of his inexhaustible armies. He is a rotting carcass writhing invisibly with power from the Dark Age of Technology. He is the Carrion Lord of the vast Imperium of Man for whom a thousand souls are sacrificed every day so that he may never truly die.
Yet even in his deathless state, the Emperor continues his eternal vigilance. Mighty battlefleets cross the daemon-infested miasma of the Warp, the only route between distant stars, their way lit by the Astronomican, the psychic manifestation of the Emperor's will. Vast armies give battle in His name on uncounted worlds. Greatest amongst his soldiers are the Adeptus Astartes, the Space Marines, bio-engineered super-warriors. Their comrades in arms are legion: the Imperial Guard and countless planetary defence forces, the ever-vigilant Inquisition and the tech-priests of the Adeptus Mechanicus to name only a few. But for all their multitudes, they are barely enough to hold off the ever-present threat to humanity from aliens, heretics, mutants -- and far, far worse.
To be a man in such times is to be one amongst untold billions. It is to live in the cruelest and most bloody regime imaginable. These are the tales of those times. Forget the power of technology and science, for so much has been forgotten, never to be relearned. Forget the promise of progress and understanding, for in the grim dark future there is only war. There is no peace amongst the stars, only an eternity of carnage and slaughter, and the laughter of thirsting gods.

This game really is a diamond in the rough (fantasy version of ARK with dragons & magic) – At first as with all survival games it can be a tough environment to start in but once you’ve settled down with the basics – you will be learning plenty of new skills and seeing more of the game world which has some fantastic designs and vistas to see, explore and build from (Waterfalls, Volcanoes, Snow Mountains, Jungles),
Quick Newbie List
* Hunger – Gather berries from wild bushes / kill sheep with sword – cook meat in campfires.
* Thirst – Dive into your nearest river / push e to drink while standing – later aim for glass bottles to refill / use whenever it rains.
* Focus (Mind/Mana) – You will not be able to sleep until lv10 when you can craft a bedroll – use a sword to cut grass and eat flowers. (There is no /sleep command)
* If you’re really lazy just head back to the main city – (escape / main menu) trigger death and you can respawn with full hunger / thirst / focus – just make sure to retrieve your belongings quickly.
For solo / Casual players / world building – Official PvE servers work great – The most notable downsides/cons though are base building and taming can be very restricted if players have any structures nearby which cannot be destroyed and chests(storage) can be looted by other players – set pin codes and build chests/crafting stations within a secure house (with a roof!).
For PvP avoid official PvP servers – These are typically over run with Chinese / Russian teams with no anti-cheat protection. Can be killed anywhere / bases fully destroyed overnight and PvP dominated by higher levels / Gear + Zerg gameplay. Do not expect any balance whatsoever – players can kill each other in the same faction as all players are hostile to each other – Free for All – Full Loot on death.
I would only advise joining unofficial PvP servers with good/active Server Admins/GM to police the server against abuse and again only if part of a large gaming team/clan – solo is just a complete waste of time.
Building your first house, castle, fortress is going to be a key goal when playing this game. Before building always check for any meteor spawns nearby – as these will send out skeletons / reapers etc. which will demolish any undefended bases very quickly.
Taming your first flying mount – Vrock (2 headed flying bird) can really open up the world in this game and should be one of your mid to longterm goals to achieve while playing this game – later on you can go for Wyverns, Griffins, Snow/Fire Dragons (all these mounts require more and more expensive saddles the more advanced the mount is).
Taming can take a very long time (several real-life hours) – Be prepared for the tamed mount being killed / disappearing etc. That mount you spent hours taming can be killed within seconds – just prepare for the worst – retrieve your saddle if you can – one of these days and with further progress in the game you will be able to use a pool of revival (currently bugged) to revive your mount.
If the idea of spending hours taming sounds like your idea of hell – focus on your beast/lycanthropy magic and you can eventually transform into a Wyvern (useful mostly as a transport skill) – this does cost some expensive/rare materials but so much easier and faster to collect.
Early Access – Expect bugs! (very long loadtimes to get into the world) You will die and lose everything – you will fall through terrain / your mounts will get trapped etc. There is no bank in-game but you can try renting a simple house/hovel (30g for 2days) within your faction city for gold coins – these rented houses provide up to 300 spaces of storage. Try not to move around with all your live savings! – store some backup gear so you can quickly regather / rebuild.
Try to have fun – this game does have some amazing potential - just one final word for all you keen adventurers never travel far from home without a Stone of Recall – that moment you are truly lost in the world it can be an absolute live saver.

Somebody get B.A Barracuda, Sly Rocko and Willis Kiyay out of retirement, because those evil-doers, Black Duck, are back up to their old tricks once more! In Orange Pixel’s Gunslugs 2 you will  be reprising those roles, including many more, and teaching those evil Black Duck dudes a lesson they won’t soon forget……again!
Gunslugs 2 is a straightforward sequel to the first entry in the series that has you and your comrades travelling across the Earth, and outer space,  on the heels of the evil Black Duck army.  The game pays heavy respects to SNK’s Metal Slug series, with its hectic run ‘n’ gun action, powerful vehicles, goliath bosses, and a cast of loveable meatheads. As a sequel,’slugs 2 makes great steps forward for the series, as well as a few steps back.
The action remains, largely, unchanged, and, like Metal Slug, you travel from one side of the screen to the other, killing everything in sight. Each level also has a number of Black Duck beacon towers that you will need to destroy before a rescue chopper can swoop in and transport you away to safety. The coins you collect during gameplay can still be spent in the many shops dotted around each level, which sell a modest rotation of buff items like shields that make you look like Batman or Robocop, and health upgrades. Sadly, Gunslugs 2 dispenses with some of the humour seen in the first game, and it, seemingly, no longer has the random mini game rooms, nor the funny cameos from other game series characters.  In return for those little ommissions  you are given a campaign that is longer than the first game’s, and that is every bit as hectic, if not more so.
On your dangerous♥♥♥♥♥kicking mission you’ll  rescue your buddies from the first game, all of whom are cute pixelated send-ups of  80s action movie heroes. Some of them seem to miraculously find themselves taken prisoner on every level, but I’m not complaining, after all once you rescue them you can assume control of them and refill your health bar, which is vitally handy in some later levels when the action really ramps up.
Gunslugs 2 turns the action-o-meter up to 11, throwing scores of enemies, vehicles and a hail of bullets your way, in a relentless barrage of fast-paced run-n-gun mayhem. There is no let up in the formula, save for boss battles where enemy count is vastly reduced to make things more manageable. Boss battles are simple and formulaic, tasking you with dodging projectiles, killing mob enemies and replenishing your health and ammo.  Whilst they are fun, they couldn’t be described as challenging.
You will most likely cakewalk most of the game, as we did until we came to the Black Duck base levels. This part of the game brings a sharp increase in difficulty with it, but it doesn’t feel all that fair or congruous with the rest of the game. Whereas, for most of the action, you’ll be running and gunning at a fast pace, if you want to stay alive in the Black Duck base you will  need to be careful as you move. Puddles of green alien ooze are dotted around the place and will damage you if you step on them, meaning you will be required to suddenly adjust your play style.  In beacon towers you will have no choice but to take a hit by running through these puddles, draining your life bar – which is much bigger deal towards the end of the game than it is at the beginning.
The game further annoys by placing ooze puddles at the top and bottom of step ladders, and even adds pairs of wall mounted cannons into the mix which deal massive damage and are almost impossible to dodge. These bad design choices bring the game’s rapid pace to a screeching halt, and really grated on my nerves. Despite those issues it is hard not to see how far Gunslugs has come, from a technical and design point of view. The whole game feels just a little bit more refined than the first entry, and it is graphically better than ever.
Even with its slight missteps Gunslugs 2 is an impressive sequel. Orange Pixel have kicked the action up a notch, making for a satisfying and exhilarating Metal Slug wannabe, and while it never quite reaches the same lofty heights it makes for an admirable impersonation.

Verdict: A highly recommended joystick classic.
Arguably the single greatest combat space simulator of Star Wars' joystick era titles, X-Wing Alliance perfected the formula seen in X-Wing, TIE Fighter and X-Wing vs. TIE Fighter. Although this title can be rather difficult it offers many hours of intense combat. Whether it be fighting through swarms of enemy starfighters, helping to ambush Imperial convoys or daring rescue and escort missions. You won't be disappointed in picking up this classic which, surprisingly, has aged very well.
The graphics are antiquated but due to the nature of the game you typically won't even notice awkward textures at close range to other ships and static objects. Voice acting is a low point as well but nothing that cannot be overlooked when you're neck deep in the action. A controller or joystick is needed to play this game as well as a bit of quick thinking as you will need to periodically adjust your ship's power levels to get an edge over your competition.
Features of note include a 'combat simulator' where you may create your own rudimentary battles and fly one of dozens of available ships alone or with a few friends through IP connections. There is also a training room where you may test your skills in various 'races' where crack shots are needed to disable obstacles.
All in all this is a solid title which holds a special place in many a gamer. For the $9.99 price tag as of the time of this review it's well worth the investment and I highly recommend it for players new or old.

Blender is one of the most full-featured and expandable DCC programs available, and is extremely competitive with a wide range of software ranging from Maya/3dsmax to Premiere. From a technical standpoint it can be complicated to learn, but this is an issue with every 3D package. Giving an artist the tools they need to go from concept to model to a final rendered scene is challenging, and every package has its own way of managing the breadth of tools needed.
What helps push Blender beyond novelty is the quality of the tools and the speed of use once an artist is accustomed to them. It's a heavily shortcut-centered workflow, so it benefits from gaming keyboards and mice - I personally use the Logitech G910 and G700s. This gives me a huge amount of easily accessible macro keys for my most used functions, so I'm able to work faster (and therefore make more money!).
The interface is also unique; instead of floating windows, it uses a panel-based setup that is entirely customizable.
Want another 3D view? Drag the existing one to split it. Have multiple monitors? Create workspaces for each one, set up exactly how you need. You can save these workspaces as well, and by arranging Blender to how you like then using "Save Startup File", you can guarantee every time you start a new file it's got the layout, objects, and settings you need.
The functionality of the core Blender program is amazing too. It's modeling tools are second to none, it's sculpting tools are very good (not quite zbrush level, but extremely usable), the node-based material/compositing workflow is easy to use and very expandable, and the primary rendering engine, Cycles, is outstanding. It's entirely possible (and has been done many times) to create photoreal images/videos in Blender. Or, non-photoreal! It's entirely up to you!
And if you need more, Blender's addon system is wholly unique. There are hundreds of incredible addons out there, ranging from quality of life improvements such as the Layer Manager, to entirely new renderers (Pixar's Renderman, AMD's ProRender, LuxRender, Mitsuba, etc.).
My must-have addon list is as follows:
Like I mentioned above, 3D content creation is not an easy skill. It can take years of practice to get to a marketable level, and there's an even higher level of skill needed to do 3D as a career. It's not just the quality of the art; the speed at which it's done is another key element, and the organization and naming of the meshes/textures/assets/workspace/etc. is just as important. Since most games, movies and TV shows are hugely collaborative efforts, an artist needs to generate work that anyone else can pick up and understand without much effort.
This is one area where Blender is lacking, though it's starting to get better. Currently, there are only 20 available layers, so very large scenes with dozens of different types of assets can get complicated to manage. For example, if you have a city that has buildings, cars, lights, people, flags/banners, props, trash, etc. in foreground, midground and background, it's very easy to hit that 20-layer limit.
The organization of hierarchy is also behind. There's no way to sort the outliner by different properties so you can't sort by visible or render enabled assets, and parenting doesn't work quite as expected; when you select a parent mesh, it doesn't select its children, for example.
And my third caveat is less about Blender itself, and more about the structure of the Foundation and how features get added. Some of the choices made regarding what to add are odd, to say the least. Certain features critical to professional workflows were missing for many years, and it's only very recently that they've been added, thanks to the dedication of a handful of talented coders. And it's not like the BF was unaware that these features were requested; they just didn't see how they could be useful, so they languished in the ether.
I'm aware that the goal of Blender isn't to be the best professional DCC around, so there's not as much drive to cater to the industry crowds. But, the benefits of having a good working relationship with studios are many. From giving hobbyist artists a better chance of monetizing their skills (once you get good, where do you go?), to giving Blender more exposure and leading to more donations to the Foundation. It's getting better though, and I think the more usage Blender gets in games/animation/VFX, the more open the Foundation will become.
But, those issues are minor in the scale of what this program can do, and are all actively being worked on. Which brings me to my last note about Blender - it's open source! Besides being entirely free to use for any and all purposes (you can make money with this; I'm not sure why some people seem to think you can't get paid for work made in Blender), anyone can go in there and modify it, make addons, rip out unneeded functionality, etc. There's a large community that contributes, so Blender is constantly getting huge improvements. And this is a
plus to studios - Blender can be easily incorporated into proprietary workflows, and with a decent python coder, bugs can be fixed and features can be added in a previously unheard-of timescale.
It's not like a small studio could email Autodesk and say "hey, could you add full UDIM support to 3dsmax by tomorrow evening?". Well, they could, but it would invariably be thrown away and ignored. But with Blender, if the programmer knows what he's doing, it can be done (and has ;-) ).
In the past, while there wasn't much that used Blender in the professional sphere to point to, this has started to change. Here's a small sampling of some of the recent projects that have used Blender, including one that was Emmy-nominated for the VFX work done in this little program. And this is only covering the visible side of things; Blender has gotten a ton of use for previz, which could be its own list:
What are my credentials (i.e. what makes me think I can review Blender)? I use Blender professionally full-time for work in VFX and animation, and have for almost 2 years. My primary focus is on shading (i.e. texturing and materials), but I'm familiar with every step of the process, from concept/previz/modeling all the way to compositing and grading for final delivery. I've given talks and presentations on its use in VFX, and work closely with many of the Blender developers to help make it better. And moving past Blender, 3D art has been a hobby of mine for over 20 years. I started on 3D Studio Max 1.2 back in 1996, and have used nearly every major software package since then.

Braid is a curious game for a lot of reasons, despite it's impressive art style and legacy it actually isn't as enjoyable as it appears.
As the trailer suggests you are capable of turning back time, thus you never officially die. Despite this the leaning curve is quite steep and not always fair.
If anyone has heard of the Infamous Goat puzzle in Broken Sword this may make a bit more sense. But basically in the point and click adventure game Broken Sword there is a puzzle that requires quick timing. But you the player have never used it before, so what makes it so difficult is your lack of understanding and knowledge of a gaming mechanic. You are unaware that you are even capable of doing what the game expects you to do.
This is how Braid often feels. Although it is a very clever game many of puzzles require you to use your powers in unconventional ways to meet your goal. Although I never cared for tutorials or hand holding, the way it expects you to use your new abilities can often seem ridiculous and are incredibly specific.
As an example there's a part in the game that requires you to let an enemy kill you, by doing this you see that when the enemy kills you it jumps back upward as it falls on top of you. Similarly to how Mario would when killing a goomba.
But lets say you rewind too fast to realize this is something that can happen or you've never had an enemy kill you from above.
Because there's not really an oppuninity in the game dedicated to this very specific mechanic you might not know you're able to do this.
Since you don't know all the mechanics the game can feel as if it's cheating you. It's not that you didn't understand the puzzle but rather you didn't understand a mechanic that was never revealed properly in the first place.
Braid does this multiple times, which is where I find the most difficulty in the game.
As for the story? It's interesting but for lack of better words leaves you feeling empty of confused. Even when you do research into theories or see the ending of the game you just never feel as if you knew the whole experience. And that's not always bad but a lot of games can hold a sense of mystery while satisfying the player. This game just didn't satisfy me with it's conclusion.
Furthermore to complete the game in it's entirety you are required to collect stars. Many of which you as the player would never have even known were in the game. The first star in world 2 takes about an hour and a half to collect by standing on top of a cloud.
Let that sink in, how is the player expected to wait that long at the beginning of the game?
Perhaps later in the game a challenge like that is realistic after the player is aware that there are actual collectables. But for the completing the game it felt unfair. There is a star map at the intro but I was unaware that I could actually collect items for it as well.
Furthermore despite how interesting the story is the creator Johnathan Brow is rather pretentious in his attitude towards those theorizing or reviewing his game.
If you'd like to play it I'd suggest to avoid reading his lengthy interviews as they just leave a sour taste in your mouth and ruin the experience of a decent game.
It's normal for an artist to be protective of his work and to have a specific outlook or belief. Brow often justifies parts of critiques and mistakes as being intentional or experimental. Yet as an artist regardless of if an element is intentional or not that does not make the game improve in quality if it wont translate to the player. A game element needs to make sense not just in the eyes of the creator but the audience.
Furthermore the soundtrack is pretty but incredibly repetitive and many levels don't suit the soundtrack. Plus, a world in the game requires you to listen to the majority of it in slow motion or backwards and trust me when I say it gets irritating quickly.
The enemies feel uncreative, but I'm sure they serve some purpose in terms of appearance besides being a reference to Mario. Although the sound effects for the rabbits and goomba looking enemies are annoying.
So please before purchasing this game for 15 dollars just know that although it isn't a bad game it is overhyped. It might be a enjoyable use of your time but I don't believe it's worth the 15 dollar price tag.

Rusty, dark dirty and most of all mutant infested tunnels are in front of you if you plan on playing Metro 2033. Add a nuclear poisened overworld known as Moscow to the mix and bam you have a horror survival game that creeps the hell out of you. If you like that stuff then read on, if not nod, turn around and leave :P
As said above, Metro 2033 is set in a apocalyptic moscow which was devastated by a nuclear war a few years back. You play as Artyom. A somewhat silent guy who is set to stop attacks of the Nosalis, mutants that were created by the fallout of the nuclear winter in moscow.
In fear of said fallout, the survivors of the war went into the Metro tunnels and build makeshift camps at the bigger stations.
I don't want to spoil too much, but the rest of the plot is pretty interesting. Very dark and desperate, but yet very good.
The gameplay is very simple. Run, sneak, flee and shoot things. It is totally up to you how you play the game. You can sneak around or shoot your way through. It depends on the difficulty. In survival mode you probably want to sneak since ammo is very rare and the enemies are pretty strong.
Speaking off ammo. It isn't only rare to find, it is also currency in the game. You have two types of ammo. Military grade or normal. You can shoot with both. The military grade is stronger, but remember that you shoot your money at your enemies. So it is totally up to you what ammo you use.
One very important tool is your gas mask. Which you need half of the game. You find filters which you need to extend the time you can survive in biohazard atmospheres. But don't forget to swich filters or else you might die.
The fact that you have no HUD makes the game very immersive. Everything what a HUD would usually show you, you see on some equipment Artyom wears. The HUD you basically have is a crosshair, but it is possible to disable it too.
The sneaking system is a basic one but it works pretty good. You have to watch for sound traps and light plays a big role.
The enemies are varying. You have the Nosalis in different kinds, Each has its own flaws and strengths. Well more strenghts than weaknesses. You also fight humans. The AI is pretty good i would say. Especially on harder difficulties they aim pretty good ;) The Nosalis are jumping at walls and come through holes and try to flank you.
The weapons are, lets say very interesting, Shotguns, revolvers, Assault Rifles. Sounds pretty basic. It isn't. Except the AK, you have freaky weapons. Mostly build by weapon smiths after the war. So you have weapons consisting of old bicycle parts. A Sniper rifle using Gas pressure. You have to charge it first for example. Although the weapons look a bit strange they still work like you would expect it.
Each weapon can be upgraded with different optics a laserpointer and a silencer.
Next to the weapons you have 3 different grenade types and throwing knives. Especially the knives are pretty strong.
Well the graphics. I played both versions. The redux does have better effects and looks better yea. Since it is mostly dark the sometimes wek textures don't play such a big part. The lightning is pretty good i would say. Well just look at screenshots i guess ;)
So overall i recommend the game. It is a bit short maybe. Has replayability, but not that much. In the end it is still worth it a few bucks. It creeps you at some point and the story and plot is very interesting. No bugs i encountered so you can enjoy it fully.
One last thing. Never let the librarians escape your eyes :)

*Beat the game several times on Xbox 360 upon initial release.
Hand drawn, inspired, perceptive, and creative. All of these descriptions are fitting and directly apply to the experience. And that's exactly what this is. An experience. A journey. The finely crafted hub exploration experience, though a small area, feels like a dream to navigate. Likewise, the indiviadual levels all exhibit fantastic storybook appeal and cultivates curiousity. Complimenting the excellent visual appeal is the equally (if not more) pleasing audio. From the satisfying door stop flick that results from bobbing enemies over the head to the musical moods that build throughout the adventure, it all synchs very nicely to the artistic side of things.
This is, in all senses, a puzzle game. Solving the problem of choices already made is complicated, and involves precise timing, not to mention the very control of the flow of time. As the game progresses, these challenges increase the mental prowess required of the player, forcing them to analyze and re-analyze situations in different ways, which I believe is this games major strength. While not overly difficult, most of the later puzzles will require complete understanding of the mechanics involved.
The puzzles don't stop there. As "puzzling" as the gameplay can be, behind it is a narrative, explored between worlds, that explores deep ideas. Anyone wanting "more" in a game will truly appreciate the thought Jonathan Blow put into this aspect, all the way up to the conclusion.
Longevity of this title isnt its strong suit, but the experience sticks with you well after completing it. Which why I came here to write this review YEARS after its release. It really is that good. And it isn't just one aspect that makes it impressive. All these parts come together and form a brilliant, cohesive, and thoughtful experience that I very very rarely experience in games these days.
I cant recommend it enough.

I grew up playing games like this, and clearly so did the developer because they managed to replicate the style and feel perfectly. It's a pretty straightforward game design, a metroidvania platformer where you explore the map, shoot enemies, collect cubes to buy items from shops, find other items hidden in crates, and take on a number of bosses. Items and upgrades enable you to access areas that you couldn't reach or navigate earlier on. You've probably played this kind of thing before.
It works, though, because it's a tight game design, and because the basic mechanics of jumping and shooting feel great. Each upgrade makes a noticeable difference, and so progress feels satisfying and rapid. It's not a long game (took me around five hours, but I'm a completitionist and you can certainly do it in less) but then it only costs a couple of bucks. For that, not only do you get this great little game, you also get a surprisingly robust level and character editor, the results of which you can share on the Steam Workshop. For two bucks it's a steal, and if you want more then try this game's big brother (well actually, sister), Ghost 1.0.

Overall this was a fairly good game, with stunningly beautiful graphics and a rich narrative, world and atmosphere. A few problems would make me rank it beneath Cinders (other game by this dev), and I didn't feel all that compelled to play through all endings obsessively.
The main problem I have with this game is construction. Cinders wrapped a simple-yet-intense story around a fairytale almost everyone knows by heart; this meant we knew the story beats already and could concentrate on the actual crucial choices and the heart of the nuanced, achingly real and complex characters (well, the female characters at any rate). Also, Cinders is by her nature boxed in - that's the whole point of her story, her desire to break free from control. The reason there are only a few - but crucial - decisions to make is thus transformed from a potential flaw into being an important part of the story's concept. They also impact on the outcome a lot.
By contrast, Solstice is based around a mystery....which we are not allowed to solve, because that would derail the ending. Our supposedly intelligent protagonists either fail to do some pretty obvious things, or are occasionally allowed to try something smart only to have it fail in a contrived way. I understand this is not a Sherlock Holmes game, but then it should not have been based around a murder mystery, should it. The world was rich enough to give us lots to think about without adding a whole level of Nancy Drew, especially since it turns out we can't do much about it. Seriously, out of the dozens of decisions you can make, only four or five seem to have an actual impact on the ending - two of which are virtually random, ie, choose the blue pill or the red pill but we won't tell you which does what - and the only impact even those decisions have is on how boned everybody ends up being.
It was also a mistake to have two protagonists, IMO. It means repetition in narrative, loss of focus, and gives us twice the amount of "supposedly very smart person who had every reason to prepare for this trip...who doesn't know the first thing about the situation they walked into because that allows the player to get exposition". This happens again and again, and really loses the connection wth the characters as a result.
It's a pity, because compared to many other games of this sort, the characters are rich and very complex, nuanced, and beautifully rendered. The story is rich and complex too, but that very complexity probably explains why the rails are so strict, and thus I can't enjoy it quite as much. I would have preferred having a lot of the world building done in a series of notes - avoiding "stupid, unprepared protag" syndrome and allowing them to be skipped on playthroughs - and a story that wasn't quite so convoluted if it gave us greater agency over it.
I'd recomend the game on sale for people who like fantasy/sci-fi novels, and who will read it as such, not so much for gameplay. Would still recommend it though, it's an interesting experience.

A nice, retro Metroidvania with graphics reminiscent of the old Apple ][ era.
You're a troubleshooter sent into a dangerous maze to destroy a haywire computer. At the start of your adventure you kind of suck; you blast enemies, collect "cubes," and use them to buy combat upgrades. Scattered throughout the maze are crates that contain either nothing (usually), more cubes, or unique items that give you advantages or make you able to reach new areas. Your goal is to defeat bosses, opening up new areas, and eventually reach and destroy the computer.
Ghost controls really well, the graphics are bright and colorful, and the design of the maze is pretty clever. This isn't one of the all-time great Metroidvanias, but it's definitely a good one.
What makes the game so interesting is the presence of several software editors. You can create new skins for Ghost or even entire new maps, then upload them to the Steam Workshop for others to play with. The inclusion of this kind of feature in a game this cheap is amazing, and upgrades this to a "must buy."
If you don't use the editor features, Mini Ghost probably offers 3-5 hours of platforming action, which is damn good for the price. If you do, there's theoretically no limit (but I'm betting you'd probably start hankering for some more features around hour 20).

This game is absolutely amazing! And I say this with 100% certainty knowing all too well that I can't get my game to save. So, sure I can't actually play it with a single campaign, and I can't save or load games, but damn is this game phenominal. I spent two hours playing (before realizing the predicament I had) and absolutely fell in love with it. I had gotten my dream squad together consisting of 4 actual characters, and one soldier I would let die if one had to go. The sacrificial soldier so-to-speak. And of course, I customized my 4 actual characters which made me grow closer to each one of them. There was Javier Soto, the heavy weapons specialist, Igor Makarovich and Diego Vega were the ones to rush in and take the first blows (assualt), and my favorite of my characters was Naoki Hashimoto, the japanese sniper. This game allowed me to name my soldiers and customize them to look how I imagined them. This sort of freedom then made me start to think how their lives were before the alien invasion. Which, of course, connected me to them even more. In every battle, every time one of these four soldiers got injured, I cringed at the thought it could be their last battle. Not only that, but I was constantly forced to make unwanted decisions to try to help a civilian I was escorting or to make sure one of my soldiers was not attacked and possibly on the verge of death. This game has made me love fictional characters in a way not too many games have done. And I only had two hours with them! Speaking of which, when I found out I could not save, I realized I would never see them again. It was a sad moment, and I actually felt tears run down my cheeks. I had finally closed out of the game to see if the game had actually not saved and when I went to reload, it was gone. Everyhting was gone. Hashimoto, Makarovich, Vega, and Soto, all gone. And sure, at first I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but after I let the frustration out, I began researching how to fix my problem. I may not have fixed it, and may never be able to fix it, but it is one hell of a game. Even though my initial playthrough is forever gone, those four soldiers are legends in my eyes, and war heros, even if their "world" is non-existant.
As one more side note, I love this game more than Civilizaiton 5, and I put over 400 hours into that game within one year. If I can ever fix my problem with this game, I know for a fact that way more hours will be put into this game than Civ 5 will ever have.

Solstice is a well-written fantasy mystery game. The diverse cast of characters is fantastic, and as the story progresses, you uncover how complex each character can be.
I think the variants of each ending are what makes this game shine. Though it is tedious to restart the game to get each variant, the epilogues for each character are shaped by the decisions you make and the personalities you give the protagonists. At first my goal was to foil the saboteur and fully save the city, but after uncovering its secrets, I started to change my mind and question what was really the "best" ending. That's some good writing.
The romance parts weren't that interesting to me and felt a bit thrown in just for kicks. But romance wasn't an aspect that I really cared for anyways, so it was just a minor grievance.
And not to mention the art, music, and game interface! The aesthetics of the game are absolutely stunning, from background and character art to the smooth menus. A nice change from the clunky menus I'm used to in most other visual novels. I was also pleased with the music - each piece blended in well with the scenes, and I didn't find it too repetitive or annoying (as with some other visual novels). In fact, there are some tracks that I especially like.
Overall, I highly recommend Solstice if you like a good story with grey endings. It's not a life-changing visual novel, but it's a high-quality piece of art that is worth a pretty penny. Thanks so much for creating a lovely game.

So, many people here are against it because it was "free" long ago. And let me say that Steam did it a good deal by taking it over, all together removing subscriptions for 'premium' which only gave maps. And only maps. As well as a private server. So by taking away a crippling payment system for the F2P on steam, they made it P2P for those who didn't switch and kept it for those who did, simply because it was in their library.  However, the only negative effect was on the Game Mode, making you pick up weapons instead of getting the full onslaught at spawn with one to pick from. But the updates brought VAC, Code Patches, and updated UI that didn't rely on web-pages, Unicode goods, and many more improvements by Valve which are overlooked for a measly 10$. And for what? Because a child can't ask ma for something?
Things that are free aren't always going to remain that way, and I enjoyed this a lot, even with a few negatives, the positives outweigh them immensely.
So let me explain this:
It isn't hat fortress 2. It isn't Half Life. It isn't Any CSGO, it's equal.
No money,
No bomb,
No class loadouts,
No classes,
No added buffs, nerfs, or differntiations of the SAME WEAPONS.
Now let me be even more blunt: This is a game where you die. And you survive. You spawn, pick up your gun, and focus as hard as you can to kill your opponents, and take top score. And here's a trick: They're all gods. They've mastered the game. I played Quake 2 and 3 when I was little, and they couldnt prepare me for the head to head, player armed combat this has. Rocket Jumping, Rail lodging, and painstaking, rage inducing hours lie ahead of you. And if you want to even be remotely good, practice with the gods. Die, take the fall, and keep going. This game is all about knowing who your opponent is. Listening to each movement, sound, and shot. From Shotguns, to Plasma Guns, to the infamous "Sniper's Wet Dream," The Railgun, and even the classic Rocket Launcher, you're at no excuse to say "They're cheating" or "They have better weapons" because they're just like yours. It's YOU who sucks in this case.
So put down that stupid little credit card you used for TF2 and CS:GO, and get on equal playing grounds. It's time that you boast your skills by doing two things:
Nut up,
Or Shut up.
That's what you get with Quake Live.
Your move.

This game, from the 17 minutes I've played it, has been overwhelmingly good. The primary objective of the game is to murder your sister. Sounds simple, doesn't it? Wait until you play the game.
The first thing that really jumped at me was the atmosphere. The game has a really old and musky feel to it, which is great for this particular game. It seems to pull off the atmoshpere that it tries to create, and I really did get involved in the game/
Secondly, there are numerous dialogues in which you choose what to speak, and they seem to offer great choice honestly. I, of course, could not help but make lewd comments at the maid. Which was a lot of fun. The dialogue with the police guy was extremely well done
Thirdly, the gameplay itself is entertaining. The characters may look a bit blocky and walk funnily. But overall, with all the various items and murder weapons, the game was great.
The only con that I can think about is that if I finish the game, and succeed in murdering the protagnist's sister, I probably would not play this game. So the most I will play the game is approximately 2 to 3 hours. But hey, I got it on sale, and bought by trading steam cards, so it was a win-win situation.
If you can muster up the money, which isn't a lot really, I highly recommend this game. It is a fresh game with quite an impressive atmosphere.

Interesting game. It's a novel premise with a lot of potential and a good atmosphere brought by the writing and the graphics (which are simple, but have a very well-realized aesthetic). The characterization is solid, and the tone is dark as it should be.
It's fun to try the different ways to get away with "the deed", and the game uses the choice it gives you in a good way. It's extremely short the first time, but you can try different things for a much longer time until getting bored. Unfortunately, you have to repeat dialogue you have already seen, and there's not that much variation at certain times. After a while, the system behind framing and getting caught becomes more obvious, and if you try to 100% the game, it can become a monotonous task by the end.
All in all, it's very cheap and gave me a reasonable time of entertainment, so I reccomend it without reservations. I just wish the developer makes a more fleshed-out sequel, with more options and more variables.

I am somewhat split on this game. I play mostly story mode or single player because i feel the game design could be rage inducing vs humans. And i refuse to play games that make me mad. So keep that in mind when you read this.
Most of the games i have played are against Chaos. And the tactics used by them are just frustrating. They outpace Imperial ships by a vast margin, to the point where i avoid Data Recovery missons and Assassination missions where im the attacker because i just wont be able to catch the ship in question, and if i do it takes soo long and is soo frustrating to try and keep up and deal out enough dammage..... just not that much fun. At least the Eldar have to close the distance to shoot at you, so as long as you dont have to catch them, they are not as "rage inducing" as everyone says. Actually playing a defender Assassination misson vs Eldar is usually very comical. But im off point.
The main problem is that the main difference in this game from the tabletop game is the potential DPS. A good broadside from a cruiser with some lucky rolls could criple another cruiser, or dammage it and leave it covered in blast markers. Making it hard to shoot back or even safely move away. So when one fleet had a speed advantage, it was not a huge deal, because you could do heavy dammage with a single broadside. And in the computer version, your battleship will peck away at light cruisers and slowly take hp away as the ship darts away to safety. Its just something that will grind away at your paitence. Sometimes a full broadside from a Retrubuition class battleship can kill an escort in one shot, but more often than not, the escort will take more than one broadside to kill.
So overall, its good, i think. Right now this game makes me mad more often than i have fun with it. And im pretty sure its got a lot to do with the extremely low DPS compared to the tabletop version and the speed is just not balanced for it.
Also on my first playthrough of the story mode i chose the "Ironman" save mode so i could not go back to an old save and redo a failed misson. I figured it would add some tension to the choices i had to make, and i was right. Had a great time right untill it crashed in the final battle and counted the misson as a loss. and for some reason, no matter how many more turns i played, the last misson would not re-trigger. So that was about 30 hours of my time wasted.
So right now i cant recomend it. It might be for you, but not what i wanted. I wanted ships that hit harder.

The game is ridiculous, hilarious, and a lot of fun, but I'm not as fond of it as I am of SR3. I often feel as I'm playing like the simulated reality is an excuse for lazy graphic errors. There are a lot of clipping issues and weird glitches that are not part of the scripted simulation glitches.
I appreciate that in the mini-games/activities of this game there are tiers for completion (bronze, silver, gold) which makes the difficult things a relief just to finish, but other activities that I love fun to strive harder to get the gold scores. There are also specific co-op activities, which I haven't done yet, which is kind of nice to have acknowledged.
The high points of this game are definitely the meta dialogue and amusing commentary on games, pop culture, and fandom. Also, super-powers are a blast if you want to sprint, jump, glide, and stomp around the world (sometimes that's all I want to do, and this is the game for that).
I wasn't impressed by the minor expansion of customization choices (though there are costume nods to Star Wars which is fun, and most of the guns are very customizable). I was disappointed that the female voice I used in SR3 wasn't available in 4. Also, I'm having weird issues with incorrect subtitles coming up for my voice.
In all, I'm highly enjoying the game and pursuing the achievements, but I don't feel like I've been as immersed in it as I was with SR3. The story isn't the strong point in these games, but I feel a little less involved in this one than Third. Make of that what you will.

One of my Favoritt games in the entire tactical combat / Management games.
A tactical RPG in some sense with a great story that even uses the mid to end of the second UFO game as referance for this third installment of the series. Overall a great game for those that enjoy the UFO or X-Com inspired games and series.
the graphics are nice and enjoyable, with funny characters as well as a rarther challenging combat/management system if you increase it so. It also have the option to modifiy whats hard: so in a sense you can make the combat impossible but management easy or opposite to suit your taste,
Single Base with automated stations
You have 1 base where your characters live, they can improve the base, train, manufacture items and research new technology. However you need to build Automated Stations, Terraforming Plants and more to increase your Sphere of Influence on the map, enemies can attack these stations if they succede you lose your area or even die if it is a vital location like water.
Enviromental Threat
The planet is very hostile to human life and the humans need Suits, Light or Heavy armors to surive. The Enviromental threat is very important if this threat is higher than your suit or armor has in enviromental protection the suit will break and you will take damage over time. Either you abort the mission or you hurry to compleat the mission. In the start of the game my suggestion is to get metal 3 and get the first heavy armor as it has great enviromental protection, overall combat survivability the only downside is that it requires a total of 3 soldier talent points to learn how to wear it.
Economy
The game has no income of money or possibility to buy like other x-com or ufo inspired games, however instead you build automated mining stations that give you the resources you need. To build items you require a set level of the resource, so if you have Metal 3 you can make Heavy Armors that are great to face trouble at a higher enviromental threat.
Diplomacy
The game has a very easy diplomacy system and several factions, some are constantly hostile, others require the proper research or being hostile to a rival faction. Having Alliances will give you access to non-human allies that can among otherthings use Psionic Powers that can stun enemies for easy capture, but so can the stun grenade so it isnt the end of the world.
Class System
The classes are divided in 3, The Soldier, The Scientist and The Engineer. Some characters has 2 classes.
To use in combat they have to be soldiers, It is important to quickly take a Soldier Scientist and Soldier Engineer into your main party to make them have a good soldier level for later. The Scientist Soldier is the only one that can heal in combat with the First Aid tool and the engineer gets access to powerful weapons that no one else can use aka Warp Cannon, this weapon has a wooping 999 in damage output and anything standing infront of that blast is dead. In addition the engineers can repair suits or armors (and droids if you choose to use them)
Pure Scientist or Scientist/Engineer are used to research tech and construct some of the various overworld buildings.
Pure Engineer or Scientist/Engineer are used to produce weapons, armors and ammo, overworld resource buildings and base buildings. Scientist/Engineers work best as scientist in the start and get used for manufacture and such later in the game when you are done researching or lacking things to research.

I've been a space(craft) sim fan for ages (from the very first ELITE through Freespace series to Starlaner / Freelancer and the like) and this old one is perhaps my favourite. I played the box version a lot back in its time. For me it sums up all the attributes why I liked X-Wing and Tie Fighter and also it has a great variety of both imperial and rebel ships, and some more. I must add that the predecessors had harder missions in general but don't think XWA is a walk in the park. The main difference that it added some colour and fun to it as you play a role (don't think RPG) of a young pilot whose family got pulled into the war, not just "pliot: whatever".
The control system is based on the older Star Wars space sims and it evolved quite much I think, feels like a familiar tool. If you think you can rely on your conroller only, you're sort of wrong as you'll have to use nearly all the keyboard to completely control all the functions of the ship. You don't have to use all of them for all the ships but there are some missions that make your fingers a celtic dancer on the keyboard. That's not a bad thing, it's just a fact.
In my opinion it's one of the Star Wars games that completely nailed the feel of the SW universe, like KOTOR I+II, Galactic Battlegrounds (Age of Empires 2 with laser blasters, so what it was fun) and Jedi Knight (all of them really). Aww, LEGO Star Wars too. It feels so much more Star Wars and alive than the latest Beetlefront for example.
It is not an easy game. You keep on chasing multiple goals and diverse use of tactics even during one mission while you have to keep your attention on timing and see the battlefield as a whole (that is inherited from the predecessors).
It is a timeless classic of a space sim. I hope one day game designers will take the challenge to create a new Star Wars game like this one. Until that, X-Wing Alliance has a whole lot of universe of its own mods to discover thanks to the faithful fanbase community who keep this great classic game alive.

A relaxing and zero stress game; perfect for shy people as well.
Besides the gorgeous and unique graphics and dedicated team who supply us with constant content updates, and the overall atmosphere of the game, one of the most striking features of the game is the lack of chat. There is no way to communicate with others except for a few select actions and emoticons. This brings forth a certain sort of unique... 'culture' to Meadow. You'll learn that certain facial combinations equal someone signing off, or saying goodbye. Or you'll learn how it's customary to greet people with a wave. Or you can greet those you’ve met before by jumping frantically around them; they’ll get the point. You will get the hang of it quickly.
This game has no survival feature, and is purely simple socialization and exploration. It makes for a very wholesome experience. Truthfully, I believe a survival mode would crush the spirit of the game. There are plenty of other games in the Shelter series however which cater to a survival experience, if you are so interested. :) The graphics remain gorgeous throughout.
I can't recommend Meadow enough. It's a very fulfilling and wholesome experience. Everyone is so kind. It's nice to take a break from your busy life or hard gaming to just relax and run around with kind strangers as an animal.

Meadow is a game where you can explore a vast habitat and make friends. The look of the game is charming and sometimes  a bit Psychedelic. The critters are fun to run around with while you gather items and eat food. The landscape is dotted with mysterious obelisks that can be opened with a group of friends by using your animals call. Some are opened by just 2 critters working as a team. While some require a larger group or specific animals within the group. This aspect encourages players to join up and explore in packs to achieve your goals and unlock your rewards faster. But you can still explore and gain rewards if you would rather go it alone. Through exploring and collecting you gain different skins, emotes and voices for your animals. The game is very casual and its main theme is exploration and team work. Their are no health bars or need for leveling your critters. Just join a server explore and meet others doing the same. The communication between players is based on a series of Icons or emotes. This is the only aspect of the game that takes some getting used to. But is easy enough for any age to get the hang of in no time. If you enjoy exploring a large colorful landscape and collecting items as you go. Or just looking for a relaxing time roaming the wilds. Meadow may be just what you are looking for in a game.

X-Wing Alliance - Oh me, oh my. This is a top notch space sim, and one that in my youth I played a LOT. I was never fortunate enough to have played the original X-Wing, or Tie Fighter, or even X-Wing VS Tie Fighter, though I've heard nothing but praise, but this one here? The last one they made before the X-Wing series sort of disappeared? This was the game I brought a flightstick especially to play. Mostly because you couldn't play it without a flightstick... I tried and the game itself slapped me upside the head and refused to even load up without a flightstick.
Starting from just after the Battle of Hoth, you start this game, not as an ace Rebel pilot, or even a dreaded Imperial pilot, but as the youngest son of a family of civilians just trying to get by, maybe offering a little support to the rebels on the side, as you do. Of course, evens in the game eventually force your hand, and naturally an alliance with the Rebels is made, but it felt very natural to me. Won't give anything more away... other than that this game's climax, which is revealed on the box art so it's not much of a spoiler, is that the finale involves the Battle of Endor.
That's right, you get to take part in that finale, epic space battle and even, as an added bonus, get to try your hand and traversing the bowels of the second Death Star. Are you the next Wedge Antiles? Or Lando? Or are you one of those nameless mooks who died before you got to reach the core? Naturally, I was such an ace pilot that I reached the core and escaped, cementing my name in the halls of fame... actually I slowed down too much to make a turn and was rammed into from behind. Sad thing was... I don't think it was a Tie pilot that rammed into me, I think it was one of the other X-Wing pilots. -_- Well, that's my humorous story of the past.

Braid is a platformer puzzle game. You play as a man called Tim as he traverses across various worlds to find his 'Princess'. The game uses the concept of bending time to create platforming paths for the players to collect pieces puzzles throughout the different worlds. Each world has a certain theme or a mechanic around which the puzzle is designed. The puzzles are very well made and will surely itch parts of your brain which may have gone untouched for far too long.
That is not all what Braid is all about. Underneath this gameplay, Braid tells a story. Players can solve the different worlds and their puzzles in order to piece them together to fit an overall picture of what happened between Tim and the Princess. I don't want to spoil the ending, however I just want to say it will surely turn some heads.
Braid is a perfect example on how gameplay can act as a powerful storytelling device which other media simply cannot replicate.

UFO is the cheap homage to the classic X-COM series, and it plays that way. In this one, we enter a story where the original game was lost; instead of kicking our enemies off Earth, for some reason we allowed our enemies to take over our planet and cover it with some kind of mutant biomass. That's a part of the over-arching story you'll be briefly introduced to as you march your little soldiers over the surface of Mars, cutting yourself out a new home after having been dispossessed of your old one.
The graphics are a little old, but each weapon, including the customizations, can be seen in their tiny form during battles, and your soldiers' faces appear clearly behind their helms. The game's tutorials can be annoying, and the constant reminders by the helpers in each screen, giving you information you can't really use, is downright frustrating.
Unlike most X-COM clones, this game feels like it's especially built to be played in small bites. Battles are intense, but brief, and the whole thing consists of a lot of peaceful waiting, or tense waiting, as the rampaging beastman hordes threaten to swallow everyone whole.
Overall, I like the game. Fun, keeps you occupied for enough hours, and you get to watch your characters improve more significantly than in the original series' entries. There are also a lot of nifty, hidden entries and situations that require a bit of caution, planning, or just dumb luck, and getting a new character under better circumstances than your last playthrough is extremely rewarding.

I really love the idea of these types of games--telling a story, making choices that change future scenarios, following your gut and seeing the results of those decisions. But his game, for me, fell flat. :-\ I played for about an hour. My running theme for why I didn't really care for this game is that I didn't feel invested in it. Following are the three main issues I had with my experience:
My first issue with the game is that it's difficult to play from the perspective of two diferent characters when you don't know what either of their motivations are. I'm not sure how to play them, without really knowing what their goals are. It means that I can't invest as much in them as characters, and that means that the choices I make don't mean as much. Part of what is fun when you play a character is that they might be different than you, so you make the choices they would make (as opposed to the ones you would make) and get to see the outcomes of that. As an example, maybe I'm pretty level-headed, but I'm playing a character with a bit of a temper. So when an NPC throws an insult at me, I would have just let it slide, but the character would have exploded back. I felt like I didn't really know too much about the characters I was playing, so it was hard to try to get into their headspace. Took away from my experience to play two different people both kind of just as myself.
My second issue with the game is that the switches between when I am playing these two characters are unclear. They both write in the same journal in the same font. I only noticed later that the small amount of BG that shows behind the paper changes. That's not really enough to make it extremely obvious. A change of font and color in the text would have been a small detail that would have gone a long way to me realizing that now it's actually the other character writing, suddenly.
My third issue with the game is that the illusion of player choice (which is, of course, a good tool for designers of these types of games to use!) was not much of an illusion. There were a number of times where I picked an option, but the response was clearly "intended" for one of the other (very different) choices, and didn't really make sense with the option that I had chosen. Really made me feel like it didn't matter that I tried to go in a certain direction--I got bullied into the option they wanted. Again, makes me feel less invested since it's going to go the way it wants no matter what I pick, but on top of that, it doesn't even FEEL like I chose where we were going with it.
So while I enjoy these types of games, I don't recommend this particular one. For me, it was just too hard to get invested in it, so it became less fun. After an hour of playing, I unfortunately didn't really care about either of my player characters. (I really wanted to!)
Major kudos, though, for player diversity. Thanks for not making another game with white male PCs. A+
Hopefully this review sheds a little light for the developers on some aspects of the game that perhaps they did not focus on. It's a lot of work to make a game and it is difficult to keep an eye on everything and it is really easy to get sucked into certain elements that leave you blinded to other things. Congratulations to your whole team for putting a completed game out there! :) Kudos!

Pure hype.  Just an obnoxiously convoluted puzzle game.  And I love puzzle games, but come on.  This has a lot of those obnoxious point-and-click tropes, where they have "cleverly" (read "annoyingly" to anyone whose confidence in their own intelligence doesn't need to be reinforced by figuring out infuriatingly contrived puzzles) hidden things that seem like part of the backdrop, and make them necessary elements of gameplay.  There is also no instruction to guide you, and tell you things such as "the further you drop onto an enemy, the further you bounce back up", which is QUENTESSENTIAL KNOWLEDGE for completing THE FIRST DAMN WORLD.  And while I understand that at least SOME people enjoy the point and click elements, because it makes them feel smart when they find them, I don't think anyone enjoys sitting around for two hours, trying to desperately realize things such as the long drop onto an enemy = high bounce.  That should be part of the game's nonexistent tutorial.
Anyone who calls this "fun" probably just needs to see a shrink about their confidence in their own intelligence.  I can't possibly see why anyone would put up with the level of shenanigans this game brings, unless they DESPERATELY, PAINFULLY needed to feel better about how smart they were.
Meanwhile, me and my friends, most of whom consider themselves intellectuals, found this game to be very dull and trite.  For all the internet hype around this game, nobody I personally know enjoyed it.  Just goes to show you, you buy enough good reviews from the right people, or get the right person as your fanboy, and you can have just all kinds of undeserved money and praise.

So this game has totally taken me by surprise! I was expecting a short experience in playtime similar to shelter 1/2. I knew it was an MMO but expected pretty much just a sandbox of pointless frolicking. I have however never found a game that has engaged me like the way this game has. At first I played this totally wrong, there are many things to collect and I played it by running off on my own looking to find every item in every corner... THIS GAME DOES NOT WORK LIKE THAT! Every collectable, which consists of Flowers, Animal Unlocks, Skins, and Emotes (recently added Food) spawn randomly thoughout the whole overworld on a timer and eventually disappear. You never know where things will be and the point is to find random animals (players) and just, like ... hunt... for unlockables, and you do so as animals, using just simple emotes/body language. I can not believe how much depth I have discovered in a game where communication consists only of a small list of emotes. It's so simple, yet I have found packs of animals (from 2 - 20) who communicate and coordinate flawlessly on hunts! It's an amazing experience and different from anything else I've personally played. Now I can see this game eventually getting boring, it is after all very simple in nature, but that feeling of understanding one another on such primitive bounds is so fresh feeling that I can see myself playing this game for many more hours to come. I do want to unlock all Animals/Skins/Emotes. This game is still being updated with new content, like I said before with the addition of food so who knows what will show up next! This game is extremely relaxing and player interactive. Don't expect any hardcore action. You can not die here, you play how you want to play and if your like me who likes to collect all the things this game has more point to it then you would expect. It's an excellent game and very beautiful. I've have seen reviews complain about the world being to small... but I think its just perfect, any bigger and you just wouldn't run into other players like you do and form packs for hunts. Oh yes and forming packs is advisable because helps a lot with earning your unlocks because this game has big totem stones called obilisks which when found require 2 - 4 animals to open and sometimes require specific species. You can find every unlock randomly scattered around the world but it's slow and much easier to form packs to help each hunt for obilisks. Another complaint I have read, and I agree with this, is some of the animal unlocks require the other games of shelter to be owned to unlock. I already own them all so this is not a negitive to me, but if I didn't own the other games I would feel pressured to own them to get the full enjoyment and experience I can out of this game... so yeah if you dont own the other Shelter's just know you will be limited on species, and yeah that kinda sucks. Otherwise Incredible game! Come frolick with me! =3

I loved this VN. Absolutely loved it. Loved the warm, beautiful art style, the magic-filled, highly political world, the writing (pretty good dialogue), the enchanting music, the characters (everyone felt "real" to me, with their own motivations, secrets and unique relationships with each other) and the Clue-like concept of a murderer hiding amidst a small community trapped/surrounded by a frozen wasteland. I would recommend Solstice to anyone who loves a good mystery plot, with some magic thrown in.
One thing to note: if you like VNs mainly for romance, the romance here is only a small part of the game. Also you don't have any choice on who you can romance. It's pretty much 1 person for each protagonist (you switch between a female and male character, who are each fleshed out quite well).
I would have preferred more interactions and developments with whoever you're romancing, but since that's not the main focus of the game, I can understand that. Also, I remember one of the other commenters mentioning 'gratuitous sex and violence', and all I have to say is: Where??? There's kissing and blood, and that's it. Where's my gratuitous sex and violence? Got me all excited for nothing.
Anyway, my biggest gripe with Solstice is that it's woefully short. I finished it in less than 10 hours. At $20, you can decide for yourself whether it's worth it or not.
You can go back and try out other decisions to see how things would play out differently, but it's not as interesting when you already know who the killer is. It would have been great if there had been more branching possibilities, like revealing a different killer for example.
Nevertheless, if you don't mind these points, and you love a good (if short) compelling story revolving around a small group of rich characters, go ahead and pick Solstice up.

The most characteristic example of the horrible writing is perhaps the two optional "romances." I know people crap on BioWare romances, but maybe we should be kinder than them, because if Bioware is jejune, then this game is outright juvenile. Two characters have sex once or twice, and I'm to believe they're in transformative love now. All plot points and themes involved in this visual novel are about as substantitive as that--they rely on stereotypic scripts and cliché turns of phrase.
I can't bring myself to muster any reaction to this game other than apathy. It's good that I didn't pay $20 for it.

This game is absolutely amazing! And I say this with 100% certainty knowing all too well that I can't get my game to save.
