is a short and sweet puzzle/platformer with an quasi-innovative time-manipulation aspect.  The ability to rewind time not only allows for intriguing gameplay, but also provides a good way for there to be challenging puzzles without the game becoming unnecessarily frustrating. If you like puzzle/platformers, this should be high on your list of games to try.
The game mixes elements of puzzlers and platforming to form its identity. And there is a comfortable familiarity to the game which should feel inviting to most gamers. It starts off mostly focused on thinking-based puzzles and then a little while into the game there does start to be some platforming aspects sprinkled in, where your reaction time and precision abilities will be tested.  But for the most part it's pretty mild and not that hard.  Again, the time-manipulation also helps alleviate some of the difficulty of the platforming sections. It works out so a large majority of people should have an easy time enjoying
And as you progress through the game you will unlock different time-manipulation abilities which will need to be used properly to complete your quest. So the gameplay evolves throughout the campaign, keeping things fresh and keeping your mind active.
There isn't much of a story to be mentioned, but the game doesn't really need one. There is a strong influence of old school platformers (i.e.: the early
games). In that vein, there is a basic purpose to your actions, but no need for a sprawling narrative.  Your quest in
is to traverse hostile lands to rescue a kidnapped princess, what else do you really need to know. Also, there isn’t that much of an immersive atmosphere either. The ambiance feels very nondescript and purely functional. However, none of this is a bad thing;
is simply a game that is focused on gameplay, purposefully minimizing the other distractive aspects.
And so I definitely recommend you check out
if you’re a fan of the puzzle/platformer genre and are looking for a new game that focuses on gameplay. Also if you are someone who loves a real challenge, the speed-run achievement can give you a nice "run for your money.”

Despite the slight optimization problems, this game is truly amazing. The story, although it may seem poorly thought out and rather dumb, is actually quite good. It reminds me a little of Enders Game. The gamepay changes depending how you play, sure you can run in guns blazing chucking grenades every which way, but you can also lurk in the shadows, and play it a bit like Amnesia.
Along with great gameplay, and amazing story, this game is, well, atmospheric. Every character feels alive, every mutant embodies insanity, the Dark Ones visions make you feel something. In a way, you feel like you're actually part of the game.
On top of all that, I should probably mention the morality system. The game doesn't even really explain it, but its there, underlying all of your gameplay, but not necessarily getting in the way. Its not like Unturned where you're either Hero or Bandit, its the little things that build it, like talking to people or playing guitars.
The games horror aspect is also really good. It may not really be a horror game, but it has you on the edge of your seat. It never lets you feel safe for long enough for you to get bored, which keeps the game moving nicely. Its not jump-scare scary per-say, its more the music, the dark, gory visuals, and the overall graphics and feel of the game.
I guess I should also mention the graphics; they're intense. They don't make the game, but they surely don't break it. The outdoors is lovely, bright, but also grey and captures the post-apocalyptic feel. The stations, gloomy and war-torn, but also full of life with the npcs and fires, etc. The tunnels- gloomily lit, bodies strewn around, terrible sounds playing.
Overall the Metro Redux games are some of the best games I've played, and they may not be Half-Life, but they're sure as hell worth your money. 9.5/10

Very strategic with unique play style. The game is based entirely on cover system, so rushing isn't really a key factor in this game. You need positioning & the element of surprise pretty much. Grenades, mines, & traps can stop your opponent a ton but placing them in the right spots gives you the upper hand. The game is somewhat balanced but there's always going to be one unit you're going to absolutely despise beyond anything in any RTS title. The servers are pretty good too, I haven't lagged out of games or anything. Sometimes if an opponent or your teammate leaves there is a chance you can drop from the game but it can be entirely based on your pc or internet speed. My favorite faction is the Oberkommando West because they're very strong mid to late game if you play your cards right. They can rush early game but are a little slow compared to the other factions in the beginning. They definitely gain aggresion later on which is what I like. I like the fact of proxying bases on any part of your territories. It's pretty cool because you can use your bases as a distraction when the enemy is trying to take a point. It gives you a ton of vision but without those buildings the Oberkommando are nothing. It will always be my favorite faction, and the germans in general are just the right fit for me. I occasionaly play allies as the new British expansion came out but for now my main choice will be the germans. Definitely pick this game up if you love RTS games, I guarantee you wont be dissapointed. Realistic: 10/10 | Gameplay: 10/10 | Mechanics: 8/10 Definitely worth purchasing if you're into WW2.

-DISCLAIMER- This is a long review so don't bother reading unless you want a lot of information about this game.
Tired of dying and respawning and dying? Tired of those trolls online? Hackers? Come play Meadow, it's sure to calm you down.
Meadow is one of those games that you can play for hours without screaming at the screen.
From the creators of the Shelter franchise comes Meadow, a game that...isn't really a game.
As they put it, it is a forum in disguise and that's exactly what they've made it into. Just look at the pictures and video to get an understanding because they give you what they show you, unlike many things on the market.
As a side note that i'll explain later, extra animals can be unlocked via owning other games which I do own.
You start off being given a badger to play as, an adorable creature. You roam around a land trying to find flowers and food which you run over and will be given "essance". Collecting this essance works like experience, the more you collect the more you unlock. Over time as youre essence rises you'll be given puzzle pieces, which can also be found in the wild, which slowly unlocks emotes, skins and other animals. After you collect enough puzzle pieces you'll be able to play as a frog, and then a rabbit, and so on.
When I started I had no idea what I was doing, I was running around when I found a fox who spoke in emoji's that I somehow understood and followed him around leveling up together. This is how the game works. It seems confusing at first but suddenly you are able to understand this "language" and this "game" and it can be quite enjoyable. My 4 hours have been completed in 2 sessions because I am able to play for a couple of hours at a time without becomming bored. You can make massive groups in the 50 person servers, I made a 36 person group in one which we all roamed the world following an eagle. The world you are placed in is absoloutely beautiful. To the wet swamps, the massive crystal caves, to the hidden waterfalls, to the vast wastelands, the world is beautiful.
The music adds upon this to give such a calming time.
I have seen people in the "negative reviews" comment on the fact that you have to buy the other games to unlock animals. This is not the case at all. There are 4 animals that you can be if you own the seperate games. These are not a "YOU MUST BUY OUR GAMES" these are "Here are some rewards if you do own our games :)". Simply, there are 4 animals from games and 8 from not owning these games. These 4 do not add anything THAT special. There's an adult badger, a larger version of the first animal you play as and slightly faster. There is an adult lynx, quite fast but that's it, if i'm correct you can still unlock the baby lynx. There's a baby bear, honestly one of the cutest things i've seen but nothing that makes it a massive advantage. Finally, there is an eagle. This eagle is there to view the beautiful world. As the eagle you cannot pick up items so you cannot level up faster as the eagle, you can still unlock the white eagle by being in the top 100 of essance collectors but you dont need the eagle for the full experience. Actually, you don't need to own any of these 4 animals for the full experience because I've hardly played as the 3 of these that I do have because I enjoy the ones you're given for free much more.
Overall, if you're in a bad mood or just want to feel good, play Meadow. It's cheap, but offers so much for this price tag. A beautiful world, great music, amazing people and community, and such cute creatures. "When you remove the ability to hate, the world becomes a remarkably different place." -Bayrock and honestly that is so true. You cannot hate in this game, you cannot troll. This is a game that I suggest playing late at night, when the day is over.

Throughout this game I have made many friends and lost them already. It's surprising how many friends you can make without speaking a word.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The  concept is interesting, mixing casual match three gameplay with rpg elements adds a sense of progression and and depth to what is otherwise a very casual game and genre in general but I feel like it wears thin way fast and the game is about as long as most big rpgs out there. After a few hours when difficulty ramped up I started to realise that maybe mixing rpg fights with a genre that's pretty much entirely based on random chance is not the best idea. Because of this, skill plays very little part in the battles, you can one sidedly beat you opponent if luck is on your side or maybe you'll lose a significant part of your HP before even making a first turn. To turns tides in your favorite most you can do is grind for more numbers and grind gold to buy things that will give you even better numbers, not exactly exciting imo.
I feel like the game would be more fun if enemies didn't have spells to deal damage without the need to match tiles since that feel very uninteractive and the player should have viable healing options across all classes to offset the RNG. Right now if you're doing bad you might as well concede and try again cause enemy will probably have some guaranteed damage up their sleeve or they will get a lucky skull combo even if you try to control the board (I kinda think this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t cause there shouldn't be a scenario where 3 new tiles dropping in from the top are 3 skull tiles in a row), but if you had some healing you'd be able to focus on matching needed tiles so you can get back on your feet.
As is this is a very grindy game that's balanced against the player with increasingly difficult enemy encounters and heavy reliance on having good gear and stats, to a point where it feels more like a game about grinding than a casual match three title.  I don't think the combination works and if it doesn't why buy this instead of a proper RPG or a more fun match 3 game?

Meadow is a game that I personally enjoy (shown by my 50 hours in it) and so do many others, but not everyone is going to enjoy this game. If you like animal games, collecting stuff, and/or roleplaying, this is most likely the game for you. If it isn't, you still only payed a maximum of $3 for it, so it's easy to get enough hours/enjoyment from it to make that money worth it before it dies out. Do be warned, however: there are animals you can only get buy having Shelter games and there is no chat.
I'd personally call this game a walking simulator. You mainly run around the map all day. This game is as small and simple as it's price, so this can be expected, but it doesn't take away from the game much at all. The map may seem large at first, but you get used to it and learn it's more of a medium size. Not so big you get lost, and not so small you get tired of it quickly. There's quite a few obvious landmarks to help guide you through the map, such as mountains.
So clearly, you explore a lot, and of course, there is a reason for this: you can collect things. Similar to other Shelter games, there's plenty of things to collect and plenty of achievements around collecting. In this game, things do spawn in specific locations, but will respawn after a randomized amount of time. You can find food, flowers, obelisks, and magical floating crystal things. Each time you colllect one, you get some essence, which are your points. Collecting also lets you unlock animals, emotes, skins, voices, and actions.
This game is also good for roleplaying. With no chat, the game is slightly more realistic. Roleplaying is quite simple and can be fun as long as you don't lay around rather than do something such as hunt.
And as for the chat, no, it's not a problem at all. In fact, it's a big part of Meadow. One huge benefit of using emotes is you can communicate with anyone which allows a wider range of players to play the game with each other. The game basically has its own language that the players speak and is quite easy to learn, though it could still use a few more emotes.
Might and Delight's Shelter games all have unique, simplistic, artsy types of graphics that make the game easy to run and look pretty. They use patterns for their textures which is something I haven't seen in any games besides Shelter games. While the textures are nice, there isn't too much else, since the game is simplistic and easy to run. It doesn't have any advanced lighting and extreme graphics to make a realistic world, but it still looks nice and only fits with the game's style to not have such things. You can probably run this game on just about any computer just fine.
In this game, I can promise you lag, but only under one condition: very, very large groups. In this game, people will often group up, and sometimes, this can be a problem. In relatively average groups (maybe 5 or so people) you won't be affected. But sometimes, there will be way too many people, and this will cause your frame rate to drop to a range around 10 fps in extremely large groups. I've tried turning down my settings, but this lag seem to be unescapable. Groups this large tend to be uncommon and can be avoided if you wish.
Other than lag, really the only problems are bugs and glitches (and the fact that you can climb everything but the center tree since it has an invisible barrier). Bugs are common when it comes to you and other people, since sometimes, other players will be spinning around an axis, upsidedown, or moving while stuck in a position (laying, sitting, etc.). I have had times where I fell through rocks, but that's only twice and didn't do anything. Most bugs are just silly screenshots. As for glitches, you can do things such as go underneath the landscape.
And there you have it, what I have to say about Meadow. I'd recommend it to people who like Shelter games and/or animal games in general, since then you have access to more animals. It's quite fair and better than having to make those microtransactions just so you can look cool. Instead, you only have to buy another game for a cheap price. If I missed anything or anyone has a question, I may or may not be able to answer it.

I bought this game for a Nintendo DS back then; and I think it's still the game I played mostly on my 3DS, hence you won't find the hundreds of hours I spent within the game on my steam-record. That I played it for .... phew... 10x ? maybe more ... should tell how much I love this game. For me  - it's THE one and only Match3-Puzzle-game. It combines "Bejeweled" with an RPG. Of course I never expected anything like "Planescape:Torment" or "Morrowind" when I bought "Puzzle Quest" - the story is very linear, but it offers its surprises. You even gather a party - your members basically are some kind of "passive buff" against certain opponents -, but they have their own backstories and personalities. The artwork is - of course - JRPG, but I think it's nicely done. The Graphics look better on a bigger screen, which is why I alwas was seriously considering to  buyit for the PC, too; since one can only review games in the own library I decided I'd use the discount to be able to tell everybody who great this game is.
"PuzzleQuest" is ideal for idling away a lot of time. If you don't feel like questing you can dig for runes, forge new items, train your mounts, conquest some cities. Unless you activate it there is no "Time to make your move"-countdown (only when you train your mounts), which makes the game ideal when you have a day with slow reaction.
The sound is nicely done. Of course the music gets "boring" after a while, when you play the game excessively. But the "theme" is very catchy, and especially since I am used so much to the 3DS-sound... well... just imagine the Chipmunks singing Nightwish's "Ghost Love score" and then you hear that song for the first time as it was intendet. That's pretty much my experience with the game's sounds and music.
Of course, having played - and beaten - the game so many times I figured out that there are some combos in spells, mounts, items and skills that give you a huge advantage, even against the (cheating) A.I. I'd recommend for any non-druid to get a spider-mount, and for the druid I'd recommend a griffon. The web-spell is a great help. Still the game feels challenging enough that I started it once more.
P.S. I don't know how much I can say about this subject, but look for "Puzzle Quest - Revenge of the Plague Lord" and maybe "How to play "Revenge of the Plague Lord" with Steam Version" ... or something like that. You might find a nice little surprise ;)
P.P.S. : There is a F2P-game called "Gems of War". It feels pretty much like "Puzzle-Quest", but the reason why I always prefer Puzzle Quest (despite already knowing every aspect of the game) is that "Gems of War" hooks me into farming a lot. Which is why I prefer the "offline"-version.

Overall: Very hard to review as parts are excellent but other parts are very frustrating. Too much irritation in its current state to recommend, I simply don't want to play it that much. Please note every negative review has huge downvotes no matter how reasoned or fair it is, the community here has some pretty hostile elements (although plenty of good people as well).
So the GOOD:
Fun combat, good customisation, great look and feel, satisfying feeling to winning a battle. Nicely polished story and cutscenes, good acting, and a lot of care and attention has been put into it.
The BAD:
All of which is set against the mission design which is very disappointing by comparison. The moment that it isnt a fleet vs fleet battle the influence of random chance becomes much too high. Playing a planetary bombardment mission? The locations randomly spawn too far away with too little time to get there even though you positioned in the middle to give yourself the best chance, no chance of winning the mission. Assasination missions where your ships don't even fire a shot before the enemy has escaped and you fail the mission. Escort missions where one time the enemies are nowhere near you and its a walkover, and the next time they are all over you and there is no chance of victory. Data stealing missions which are really poor.
Judging this game as fleet vs fleet combat only then its a good recommendation, some balance issues but thats understandable.
Judging this game on the campaign where you lose missions without any chance of success and there are big penalties to progressing the campaign from that point on, its highly frustrating having so much be random with the player skill not being able to mitigate, I don't enjoy playing it at all. I like hard but fair games, difficult isn't the problem, its the lack of correlation between player effort/skill/strategy and the results you get.
So overall its a negative, too much of the game is not fun to play and has not been designed well enough, which is really unnecessary as the core mechanics of spaceships fighting each other is excellent.

Quake Live is my favorite game. Why? It's fast-paced, takes skill, has some great community members, and is pretty cussin' fun.
Quake is often described as a game that's easy to learn but impossible to master. You can get set up quickly and a sense of why the movement, gameplay, sounds, and visuals (as old as they are) are intoxicating. And, yet, some people have been playing for years, are scary good, and it takes some time to learn the game to compete with them.
It's had many iterations and, like chess, is really well balanced. As it was put in a post once, in Quake you don't wait to get better weapons or items to improve, when you get better, you realize it was your own hard work that got you there. And it’s totally gratifying when you can start to hang with folks who schooled you before.
I can see how some people are critical of some of the changes (and I myself miss the Quake 2 Capture the Flag days). But to be honest, the addition of new maps with the Steam conversion has breathed new life into the game.
A tip for the newcomers: learn to weather the curmudgeons. One of my favorite things about playing Quake Live is the community. If you play often you get to know people and joking around with them is half the fun. However, there are some sour grapes in the mix who will treat you poorly and might kick you off a server. So, a) you might need to learn to have a thick skin and b) consider starting with the Free For All games at first before joining some of the team games.
Bottom line: Quake rules. Join the party.

Update: Sept 29, 2017 - Not sure how it's possible, but the game crashes are even worse than a month ago.  Steer clear for another month. -sigh-
TL;DR - If there were an "in-the-middle" recommendation, I'd use it.  For now, I simply cannot recommend.  Too inconsistent with poor performance overall. My suggestion is that you review the discussion board for this game to see the patterns that are emerging both in the community and with the developers.  You'll get an idea very quickly as to what you can expect for the next 3-6 months for this game.
The longer version:
--------------------------
The game is basically Ark Survival but with fantasy creatures instead of dinosaurs.  It has a few neat features like capital cities for each race and vendors you can buy/sell with.  Fun to play.  Official servers infested with exploiters at the moment (certain mounts allow you to glitch inside a building to shut down its defenses).  Not region locked, so expect asian hordes to wreck your #!@& when you're offline.
Server stability is hit and miss (not ping related, but with 52ms ping to a server I can swing my axe to chop wood and not get a response back from the server for over 3 seconds), yet an enemy mob can hit me 10 times in the span of 1s and drain 75% of my health.
There are some unique features like being able to become King/Lord of a city (with a few unique bonuses that come along with that), being able to sell to/buy from vendors and donate money so they expand their inventory.  You can rent housing (until you're strong enough to survive in the wild and build your own base).  You can purchase a horse, or tame something to ride when the appropriate skills unlock.
The single player experience is lacking - there are features available in multiplayer that just don't work in single player.  They have not been worked on at all while multiplayer fixes come out frequently.  Overall, the single player experience will teach you all you need to know, but you'll miss out on about 30% of the available tames that are available in multiplayer.
I'll keep playing, but try to snag it on sale if you can.  It *could* be a good game if they can pull it together and focus on the imporant stuff.

When the great movie critic Roger Ebert said that videogames are not, and will never be art, half the Internet rushed to convince him otherwise. Braid was one of the games they showed him as examples of art in form of videogames. He dismissed it saying he's not "persuaded that I can learn about my own past by taking back my mistakes in a video game", and called the story "prose on the level of a wordy fortune cookie".
There was hardly a worse choice of game to show the movie critic -- not because it's a bad game, but because it relies heavily on hundreds of hours of other games' experience, playing with it, twisting the familiar mechanics, betraying the expectations and subverting the rules. Hours that Ebert obviously never experienced, so the words like "Your princess is in another castle" meant nothing for them, and the subversion that came with them (I'm not going to spoil that) never connected to anything.
I'm not sure what the game's true story is -- it might be about the atomic bomb, or about a creepy stalker with a crush, or about time travel. What I'm sure is, it's about these hours we've spent playing Mario that suddenly turn inside out, showing that what once used to be a simple kid's fun can work as a mature artistsic medium, telling stories and bringing up emotion without a single line of text.

The game mixes elements of puzzlers and platforming to form its identity. And there is a comfortable familiarity to the game which should feel inviting to most gamers. It starts off mostly focused on thinking-based puzzles and then a little while into the game there does start to be some platforming aspects sprinkled in, where your reaction time and precision abilities will be tested.  But for the most part it's pretty mild and not that hard.  Again, the time-manipulation also helps alleviate some of the difficulty of the platforming sections. It works out so a large majority of people should have an easy time enjoying
And as you progress through the game you will unlock different time-manipulation abilities which will need to be used properly to complete your quest. So the gameplay evolves throughout the campaign, keeping things fresh and keeping your mind active.
There isn't much of a story to be mentioned, but the game doesn't really need one. There is a strong influence of old school platformers (i.e.: the early
games). In that vein, there is a basic purpose to your actions, but no need for a sprawling narrative.  Your quest in
is to traverse hostile lands to rescue a kidnapped princess, what else do you really need to know. Also, there isn’t that much of an immersive atmosphere either. The ambiance feels very nondescript and purely functional. However, none of this is a bad thing;
is simply a game that is focused on gameplay, purposefully minimizing the other distractive aspects.
And so I definitely recommend you check out
if you’re a fan of the puzzle/platformer genre and are looking for a new game that focuses on gameplay. Also if you are someone who loves a real challenge, the speed-run achievement can give you a nice "run for your money.”

One of the best and innovative Indie games in history, Braid is a puzzle platformer that which is a very unique game.
Gameplay: Braid is a basic platformer but it gives you a very unique mechanic which is time travel. Anytime throughout the game you can rewind the game in case if you made a mistake or its required to solve the puzzle. Everything gets rewinded even certain enemies and collectibles. Collectibles are puzzle pieces which are spread throughout each world you will have to collect in order to unlock the next few worlds.
Story: I honestly didn't care for the story since the main aspect of this game is the gameplay itself. But from what I can tell is the story is told through books before the start of certain worlds and leaves the story to the player to figure out since it doesn't explain it directly. Therefore the story goes for immersive storytelling which IMO is the best way of storytelling in video games!
On your first playthrough you could beat the game in 3 to 5 hours but still leaves you to find all the collectibles you missed or you can do a dedicated speed run mode through certain levels or the entire game; try beating the game under 45 minutes, pretty tough...
Conclusion: Braid is a beautifully designed Indie game with a very unique platforming mechanics that if you are a fan of the genre you shouldn't miss out on this.

Despite the slight optimization problems, this game is truly amazing. The story, although it may seem poorly thought out and rather dumb, is actually quite good. It reminds me a little of Enders Game. The gamepay changes depending how you play, sure you can run in guns blazing chucking grenades every which way, but you can also lurk in the shadows, and play it a bit like Amnesia.
Along with great gameplay, and amazing story, this game is, well, atmospheric. Every character feels alive, every mutant embodies insanity, the Dark Ones visions make you feel something. In a way, you feel like you're actually part of the game.
On top of all that, I should probably mention the morality system. The game doesn't even really explain it, but its there, underlying all of your gameplay, but not necessarily getting in the way. Its not like Unturned where you're either Hero or Bandit, its the little things that build it, like talking to people or playing guitars.
The games horror aspect is also really good. It may not really be a horror game, but it has you on the edge of your seat. It never lets you feel safe for long enough for you to get bored, which keeps the game moving nicely. Its not jump-scare scary per-say, its more the music, the dark, gory visuals, and the overall graphics and feel of the game.
I guess I should also mention the graphics; they're intense. They don't make the game, but they surely don't break it. The outdoors is lovely, bright, but also grey and captures the post-apocalyptic feel. The stations, gloomy and war-torn, but also full of life with the npcs and fires, etc. The tunnels- gloomily lit, bodies strewn around, terrible sounds playing.
Overall the Metro Redux games are some of the best games I've played, and they may not be Half-Life, but they're sure as hell worth your money. 9.5/10

I got this game the day it came out knowing I couldn't play it cause my Surface Pro couldn't run it. I did get it fix but i honestly don't remember what i did to fix it. I now have a differnt more powerful laptop that has NVidia 940MX and 12 gigs of ram. And game runs great.

I bought this game 3 times. once for my self, once for a middle school buddy of mine, and once for my sister so that way we can still play together even though school has started up. My buddy and I tried playing online only to find out that you can't just play with your friend. you can only play regionally or world wide. A new update dropped yesterday so maybe they finally put it in along with the new player but My friend and I had to search for each other regionally to fight. Thankfully we had no issues finding each other but it is still a problem that should have been implemented when the multiplayer dropped.
Overall in terms of the gameplay it is a blast and it is just like the older DoA games just updated and more fancy looking. The Deed is a short adventure game in which you plot to murder your sister, and do your best to pin the blame on another member of the household. To do so, you must carefully consider which murder weapon to choose, what evidence to plant, and which aspersions to cast to create a cogent narrative of someone else’s guilt.
Despite the overall bad reputation of RPGmaker games (and I myself have played some pretty atrocious ones), The Deed is a rare example of a well-made one: interesting premise, nice-looking sprites, and (most importantly) well-written dialogue. The game is short (around 15 minutes per run), but figuring out how to frame each member of the family gives it a fair amount of replayability. Given the low price and the short time investment, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone with even a slight appreciation for murder mysteries.

7/10 - A cute, easy little murder-sim that's definitely worth the dollar it asks of you.
In Pilgrim Adventures'
, the player is in control of Arran Bruce, an elite family's estranged son given bloodlust over having been excluded from his father's last will and testament. On the night of his father's birthday party, Arran pays a visit to his parents' manor with the mission to kill his heiress sister and inherit the family fortune.
The player is given access to the entire mansion with the ability to interact with all NPCs and most objects, with the night progressing through four phases: one to find murder weapons/false evidence/NPCs, a second to eat a birthday dinner with your family, a third to plan and carry out the murder, and a last to answer a detective's questions about your actions and "what you saw". These gameplay elements come together to present a game bearing features of puzzle, social simulation, and exploratory gameplay, all fleshed out and elusive, encouraging the player to experiment with what they say, where they look, and so on. I will say, though, that I wish the game's achievements showed more ingenuity (and less interface spoilers).
also shows commendable ambition in its characters, fairly well-developed for a cheap quasi-whodunit cast. More unique than the standard flat caricatures common to the genre, these characters offer concise, vibrant backstories, as well as hidden vulnerabilities to exploit when attempting to relieve your character of culpability. As a character-focused narrative, the game's story benefits greatly from this depth.
is distinguished from other games of its ilk in this regard especially. Unfortunately, this ambition is not without its downfalls; the game's many attempts to be subversive can be hit or miss, and the ones that fall flat, fall flat
. One prominent example: literally every victorious ending.
. Topical? Deep? Maybe. Unsatisfying and pretentious? Definitely.
All in all,
pushed the limits of the murder mystery formula, and left a flawed but satisfying taste in my mouth post-completion. It's a pulpy, casual adventure rich with poisoned food and pointed fingers, with the quality and price of a candy bar. I say try it out!

Short Version: An solid RTS with a good campaign and enjoyable multiplayer. Excellent immersion into the Warhammer 40k universe with cutscenes that will have you roar 'For the emprorer!' as the goosebumps on your neck reach maximum goosebumpiness. The game has issues but will provide at least 20 hours of enjoyable entertainment and I reccommend it to all RTS or Warhammer 40k fans
Long Version:
The campaign is very, very good. It extended strategic thought from individual fights to the wider campaign maps, forcing you to accept losses and priotise various resources over others whilst trying to please numerous factions and make game changing decisions. There is a clear, narrative curve, the game introduces you into world, mechanics and characters as briefly as possible, then the game throws a seemingly irreversible situation in your face. Your losses mount beyond your control and you cannot reverse this, merley stem the tide. However, the game never seems unwinnable, you are never left questioning what the point of it all is, it gives you a sense of deteremination to push on, in the name of the imperium, and hold with your every growing battlefleet and I shall mention much else for fear of spoling the experience, but the campaign is definitley the best part of the game.
The ships themselves deserve their own section. I personally love the imperiums ships (which you use exclusivbley in the campaign), they pack the weight to ram the enemy but retain the manuverability neccessary to escape botched rams or ambushes. I love the light cruiser the most because of its versatility, but the battleship is a close second, an almighty floating cathedral to the Emprorer with the guns that make heretics the universe over wet their pants at the thought of their firing (as you can tell I am now really into the universe). You also have access to upgrades, allowing you to supellement their abilities and imrpove in areas you feel require it, allowing you to create a fleet that matches your playstyle and make you think (Thats not a fleet, thats MY fleet).
Level design is mediocre at best really. The various missions presented in both the multiplayer and singleplayer are fairly basic and can easily be beaten when you work out some sort of strategy. Equally, the AI is not challenging enough at normal difficulty, it fails to prioritise targets, focus fire or keep its ships together, i felt i lost more ships to my own mistakes than enemy skill. True, its only normal difficulty, but a small spike in AI difficulty would immensley aid the sense of fear at the beginning of the game. The maps are dotted with small enviromental features which sometimes come into play (but usually don't), however the skybox (spacebox?) are always gorgeous really make you take a second look and just mutter 'wow'.
The multiplayer sees you creating a character within 4 possible factions:
The imperium (jack of all trades, master of none)
The Orcs (Tanky brawlers)
Choas (long range, overwhelming firepower)
Eldar( fast moving, hardhitting)
but it is plagued by balance issues i personally feel. Certain ork setups (i.e two heavy cruisers with tractor beams) and Eldar fleets are incredibly powerful and typically ROFL stomp oppenants into submission, the choas are very difficult to play well are can often be crushed but even a comlete newbie, the Imperial Navy will generally hold its own. I should mention everything I just said in regards to multiplayer is opnion, every player will be find their most like faction, or the one they can 'work' the best, and will likley disagree with me in what I have just said. But, the multiplayer works and is fun, it in now degrades the overall package.
I have probably missed some stuff but I do reccommend this game ferverntly. As an RTS fan but also a grand strategy buff, this game managed to work the shaft AND cup the balls in a way few games can, the campaign is immersive and intresting, bringing me back time and time again to push on to victory, the multiplayer isn't my thing but it rarley is. Again, if you like a good campaign, a good RTS, a good Warhammer 40K game or anything else i have mentioned, stop reading and get the game, you probably won't regret it!

Summary: if the Complete Bundle goes on a good sale again, this is a no-brainer BUY.
Having played every generation of Civ, I think this is probably my favorite. There is a lot of content (I bought the bundle with all of the DLC when it was cheap, so I can't comment on the "vanilla" game), and most all of the changes from previous Civ games make for a better experience.
A few downsides: The AI seems a little loopy sometimes, including your own automated units. Trusting workers, scouts, etc. to do anything rational when set to "auto" is definitely a misplaced faith. Also, the game is EXTREMELY unstable for me in the Windows touchscreen configuration (I am using Windows 10), but runs fine in the DirectX9 setting. Online play has mostly been smooth, although we do still get the odd crash. Also, as with all Civs, the endgame drags on a bit in my opinion.
Positives: The religion, culture, and happiness systems on this game add a great deal of depth and character to play, allowing one to adopt very different approaches from match to match. The "one unit per hex" rules, which may seem a little foreign to players of earlier Civ generations, is worlds better than the old, mega-stack combat system. If you've played any Civs, this one tightens up all the parts and adds some peripherals without messing up the core mechanic.
Mixed: City-states and the new political system are both interesting and an improvement over previous Civ attempts at international affairs, although the World Congress/UN system still feels a little stiff, and with default settings the City-States can almost be too important to the game, although of course the number present can be modified in the settings. Graphics and voice acting are solid- nothing to blow you away, but serve their purpose (I miss Nimoy's Civ 4 narration!).
Upshot: If you've ever enjoyed a Civ game, and you can pick up this package at a good price, you'll be playing one of the strongest renditions of one of the best strategy games of all time.

Braid is one of the best arguments for video games as an artistic medium. This game is made up of much more than than its pleasantly detailed art style and its perfectly meditative background music with a few clever puzzles thrown in for interest. No, Braid is a game that focuses on exploring a concept, on teaching a truth, through challenges it presents to the player. Each of the game's six worlds begins with a few paragraphs of pure exposition, but the purpose this serves is more to provide context to the questions that follow than as storytelling. With the primer read, the world begins with its unique take on time manipulation - its own 'what if' in the form of puzzles. Solving these puzzles grants the player a piece of a larger picture and, more importantly, a better understanding of the complexities involved in playing a scenario out over and over again until the desired result is achieved. These 'lessons' are confined to their own particular world; the new mechanics don't build on each other, which is in itself another lesson.
As incredible as teaching through player experimentation is, what makes Braid truly great is all of that pretension can be skipped by if so desired. The player can run right past any annotations without pause; what remains are puzzles that are just as engaging, art that is just as charming, and music that is just as sublime.

Metro 2033. This was originally a book written by Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky about the aftermath of a nuclear war that resulted in Russia being struck with numerous nuclear weapons, obliterating the surface and all life on it, leaving only the people who had fleed to the Metro stations alive. It was a neat idea, and from what I hear since I haven't read it, an excellent book. So excellent in fact, Ukrainian based developers 4A Games asked and collaborated with Glukhovsky to make a video game about it, which was released in 2010 and spawned a sequel that was released in 2013 called Metro Last Light. Both games were recently released to port them to the XB1 and PS4, however they also released it to the PC because... why not? I'll review Last Light Redux when I get around to it, but I'll review this first. So what did I think? Let's take a look.
STORY: The story follows a man named Artyom, the usual silent protagonist, excluding the loading screens where he monologues about what goes on. After his home station Exhibition is attacked by a mysterious group of mutants known only as Dark Ones, a group of vaguely humanoid shadow creatures who manipulate peoples minds, Artyom is sent by the higher ups of Exhibition to Polis Station to get assistance against the Dark Ones. The game chronicles his adventure to Polis Station and the mission against the Dark Ones. What you do during that journey will affect the ending; there is a karma system that is not mentioned in the game that will decide what ending you'll get, so watch what you do, though Last Light goes with one of the endings and not the other as canon for the game, so make sure to remember that. It's an interesting journey, I didn't get bored during it at all, which is all I can ask really. One thing I wish this game went into would be the lore behind the WW3 in this universe, I hear they go into it a bit in the book, but for the gamer who is just getting into it from the game and want to know more about the universe like me, we want to know more about it. Otherwise, it's a good story.
GAMEPLAY: Shooting is nice, though if you want to get far, shooting might not be the best idea. I'd recommend stealth for the game, lethal or nonlethal doesn't particularly matter necessarily if you dont care about karma. The reason I recommend this is because ammo is pretty rare and it's best saved for when you go up against some of the mutant animals. There are also segments where you go up onto the surface, where you'll need a gas mask and air filters to be able to move around without suffocating. Air filters are a bit rare as well, in fact along with normal ammo, I ran out near the end and I had to sprint around like a madman in order to find another. High quality military rounds also double as money in this world, so if you use them you literally shoot money, but they're also more efficient in killing. Overall, it's pretty good.
GRAPHICS AND PERFORMANCE: The game looks a heck of a lot better than it did back in the original version. The surface world is breathtaking in how it looks. The metros look pretty nice as well, they got the feeling of a claustraphobic refugee camp-esque setup in some areas while others look properly abandoned and gloomy. The game plays at a decent  framerate for me, though if you have a better rig than me you will be fine.
CHARACTERS AND VOICE ACTING: Artyom is voiced well enough, though you only hear him in the loading screen, which makes things kind of awkward when they ask him anything in-game and he doesn't reply. The voice acting is good enough, they actually get Russian actors instead of awkwardly throwing in actors of any other nationality, which was necessary for this game.
OVERALL THOUGHTS: The best way I can sum up this game is this: Imagine Fallout if it was more of a traditional shooter. Yeah, that's a good way to sum it up. 9/10, it's a pretty good game and I say get it if you get the chance.

And now for a review about the actual gameplay.
You'd think they'd have fixed all of the usual problems with the level scripting by this point in the X Wing series. Well, they haven't. When I say scripting, I'm referring to all the stuff that happens as you progress through a mission. So many levels will have you lose because of buggy, confusing scripting, unclear goals, and the like. For this single reason, I cannot recommend the game - the single player story is a frustrating mess. They give you the ability to skip some levels and they give you the ability to turn on invincibility but at that point it feels like you're just forcing yourself to slog through a buggy game. A game realeased in this state this year would be unacceptable.
Even when the missions aren't buggy, they are just poorly paced - you'll find yourself sitting there waiting and doing nothing for several minutes, often. If you then fail at the end of the mission, guess what, you get to sit through that section again.  Yeah it's not like I wanted to play a game or something.
Now, if that doesn't bother you so much, this game is pretty awesome. There is lots of voice over, improved graphics, a more personal story, more complex missions spanning multiple sectors, and all sorts of improvements that make the simulation more immersive. It's just too bad they couldn't work the stupid bugs out of their cruddy level scripting and overall stupid mission design. This has always been a problem with the X wing series, and it's just sad that they never really fixed it for the final entry in the series. RIP LucasArts, at least Republic Commando was really good.

The originals off putting faces, character designs, glitches, bugs, awful FOV, buggy stealth general lack of polish and bad optimization were huge hurdles I had to leap over back in the day the day when playing the original Metro 2033 but it was a game with an interesting story, richly detailed indoor environments, great interactive scripted sequences, immersive atmosphere, amazing monster designs and unique challenging gunplay. Replaying the original now is even when wearing a rose tinted gasmask is hard to enjoy.
Metro 2033 Redux takes a good game and makes it into a excellent game. This is no Half-Life:Source which just dumps the old game into a new engine or takes a 32 bit application and makes it 64 bit. No. This is like Resident Evil's Remake. Unlike many a "remaster" The REDUX isn't a slight spit shine. It makes massive noticeable improvements and while also making the title more cohesive in regards to the Metro 2033/ Last Light canon as the improved, more detailed, memorable and recognizables designs of the factions and monsters Last Light incarnations have been brought to Metro 2033 redux. The bandits no longer wear stupid hockey masks and now look a lot more convincing too.
It's like what Black Mesa did in regards to Half-Life except unlike Black Mesa Metro 2033 takes the original maps into the newer engine and only overhauls the maps that looked like♥♥♥♥♥♥ While I could be a little nit picky about slight tonal changes made with the lighting in certain environments these are just differences not downgrades. The visuals and performance far exceed the original which to this day still will give bad performance in certain areas and crash constantly. The outdoor environments were pretty last gen looking even in the visually impressive original but they've had HUGE changes made to them thay bring them back to life. Instead of just using higher res textures or higher poly renders of models to replace older ones they decided to keep the same layout but completley rebuild them. Artyoms original phoned in performance has been re recorded by Artyom newer Last Light voice actor.
A few cutscenes that cut to third person have been rendered in engine in first person thus maintaining immersion AND keeping it true to the series style. The gameplay improvements from Last Light have also carried over. This is like if MGS 2 were re released with MGS 3's controls and movement as oppossed to doing something like Doom 3 BFG which just allowed the player to have a flash light on even when holding a weapon which was never possible in the original Doom 3. Stealth while a cool idea NEVER seemed to work properly in the orginal with an alert being sounded even after perfectly ghosting through an area. Stealth works properly now even if it is a little unconvincing that just being in the dark may keep you hidden. I prefer that to just having a guy see me through a wall and attempting to fire his way through it.
Last Light changes aside you will need to save your ammo and canisters even more than you did in the original and Last Light as they haven't skimped out on the difficulty or hardcore modes. The one change I don't like is the menu but there I go nitpicking again.

I'm going to start this review with one statement: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME UNLESS IT'S ON SALE
TL;DR: Dying Light is a fun game with tons of potential, made un-fun by too many stupid design choices and it being so obviously optimised for console play that it's frankly quite insulting to even offer it on PC. If you can get it from a Steam Sale or Humble Bundle, definitely do it, but this is not worth £40.
Pros:
- Parkour. Seriously, this is great and the main reason I'd recommend this game.
- You can dropkick zombies. Seriously, this is the greatest thing to ever happen to the zombie game genre.
Cons:
- Combat is stodgy, drawn out, lacks any elegance, and weapons are frankly useless. It takes half a dozen smacks directly to the head with a claw hammer to finish even the most basic infected. Humans can take upwards of 30 strikes, and are also cabable of reading your attacks and blocking them with some insultingly bad animations to justify their invulnerability. Swing a hammer at a dude's legs? Oh look he swayed his head, attack invalid. *facepalm*
- Level design. Oh boy is this my biggest gripe after combat. If you're going to have a parkour game, EITHER you need to go Mirror's Edge and railroad the level, or you need to go Assassin's Creed and spend a lot of time making sure all buildings have logical routes up and down. Dying Light decided to go with secret option three of "let's just slap everything together in a hastily assembled shoddy mess and watch players slide back down walls that look identical to the ones they were climbing earlier". Seriously, nothing is more frustrating than seeing that they've only bothered to make half the ledges climbable and you now have to walk 100 meters round a building to find the route they wanted you to take, rather than the actually sensible one you found.
- Durability is a joke, and not a funny one: if they're aiming for "hard hitting realism" then how about this? Drop-forged steel hammers don't break into a million pieces after two swings at a skull. The skull breaks. So good luck having to break flow every 10 minutes to pointless trash a piece of gear to get the weirdly specific components you need to repair the weapon you're using. And thank goodness that while you're doing all this you have to use a controller-friendly menu that refuses to give you even basic information and is about as mouse-friendly as a cattery
- The story so far (no spoilers but some critque) seems railroady, cliched, and dull. Pretty much everyone is a boring horror movie trope with appalling-decision-itis, you have no choice as to what you might want to do in cutscenes (even if that is 100% against how you've been acting the entire rest of the game), and frankly I don't care about anyone in the damn city. It's a real gripe for me when games say "free and open world" then force you to follow their stupid, predictable path in cutscenes.
- Night-time is scripted for certain missions, and scripted BADLY. Walk out to do a mission at dawn? OH NO, that short walk you've done a dozen times actually took 18 hours!
- Enemies aren't scary. The only difference between day and night is not "heart-pounding action" it's "how many bloody times am I going to have to repair this pipe before his head finally explodes?"
- Graphics are decidedly average. I'm running on highest settings across the board and I keep thinking I've fallen into an old Far Cry game. The "survivor sense" that lets you see enemies skeletons is a shoddy knock-off of Sniper Elite, and fails to show bones breaking thus rending it utterly pointless.
- AI so far is deeply underwhelming - stand on a roof with survivor sense on at night and you can literally watch it rain zombies onto the cold unforgiving concrete below as they're too stupid to navigate the terrible building design.
- Multiplayer is great with friends, but an absolute joke if you leave it on public play. Anti-cheating is OFF by default, and "Public Game" is the default online setting, and since there's no kind of level cap between people joining your world you're basically in for a crap shoot. I got lucky and got someone nice and friendly willing to go at my pace, but as he was a million times more powerful than me he could have just run off and complete the entire story, and I wouldn't even have been able to keep up with his running speed.
- Side quests are all the same thing: "X wants some Y, got to Z and find some Y for X". There are occasional gems but be prepared in the most part for flow-breaking slogging with crumby rewards.
- Levelling up isn't really a chance to feel powerful, as much as a chance to remove one of the many stupid limitations placed on your character.
A good level system should make each upgrade feel like a serious bonus to your character. Dying Light has one or two like this (See: Dropkicking zombies, above) but the majority are just things which should have been built into the game. Your character constantly feels like he's got those abilities and has just decided not to use them, it's like playing the first 10-15 hours with a person who has deliberately handcuffed themself to a fridge and won't explain why.
And finally, the "skill trees" aren't trees at all, they're lumps. You need very nearly everything in each lump so basically enjoy grinding the wretchedly bad combat to earn enough XP to make the combat less awful. The only choice you have is do you want to throw your weapon and walk over tediously to pick it up, or break it against the adamantium bones of the zombie wolverine horde?
I'm going to give this game more of a chance since so many people seem to have different feelings, but after 6 hours of solid game-play I feel less rather than more hooked. Maybe I'll edit my review somewhere down the line if the story manages to pull some kind of miraculous heel-turn and when I've earned enough lump-points to put down the Plotonium weights I'm forced to carry, but I sincerely doubt it...

I am not usually a fan of zombie games in any regard, I am however a sucker for pakour movemnet systems which prompted me to try this game. After beating the game twice here are my thoughts on dying light.
Story: The story here is just there to explain why you're killing zombies and running all over the place. That being said the story is not bad at all just average. The voice acting is good and believable but the main villan is not the best and the story overalll there are no major twists and no super interesting characters. You see some internal conflict in the main character kyle crane so that is a cool point. The game looks pretty good and now runs pretty good. I beat this game the first time on the xbox one and that almost ran native 1080p. On my gtx 1050ti with an I3 4170 and 8 GB of ram it does pretty well. Overall the story is passable and will get you from point A to B.
Gameplay: This is a first person melee/shooter open world game that uses a parkour system as the main mode of transportation (actually the only mode in the base game). The world is filled with zombies and the game has a day/night cycle that is a main focus of the game. Zombies are usually not hard to take down during the day but at night they are stronger and faster. There are also zombies that only come out at night that will wreck your popsicle sticks. There is progression in the game especially the parkour. At first you'll basically be weak and barely be able to do parkour or combat, but the more you do it the better you'll get at it. There is co-op in the game and honestly its the best way to play the game and the game becomes much easier in co-op as it is pretty hard in single player. There is also a pvp mode where you can play the zombie and invade people's games but I am not going to pretend I cared about that or actually liked it. Overall the gameplay is the reason to play this game both in single player and in co-op at least for me.
Bad stuff: I do not have much to complain about other than the uber difficulty in single player (its obvious it wasn't meant to play that way) and the average story.
Final Verdict: Honestly guys this is my most played game on steam so that should tell you something (and should also tell you how much I play on PC) I'd recommend this game nowadays at full price if you have friends to play with or if you really like parkour games. If not I would wait until a sale happens for it.

I was torn about whether or not I could recommend this game.
Maui is a fun small hero's quest about a hero trying to save his sister. It is charming game with enough character that while it takes inspiration from windwaker I wouldn't call it a rip off.  The music has 3 tunes from what I have caught and they are all pretty good. One song plays through most of the game and I didn't get annoyed by it after a long period of time. I really enjoyed the credits song, and the song played at the climax was effective for the moment. The graphics are inspired by windwaker, and the characters have char, This is a world I would explore. I also enjoyed reading all the Hawain cultural entries. Also this game was made by a small group of students, and is a free game. There is a lot of potential here for this to become a game series with more experience and resources. I really liked this game, and wanted to recommend it. I can't though due to poor/unresponsive gameplay, poorly implemented mechanics, poor system performance, and glitches.
The main character does not handle well. You can stand at awkward angles causing your hits to miss enemies while they hit you. You can end up sliding off of edges because you keep moving after you stop pressing the button. Combat feels terrible. TheThe final boss is a matter of running far enough away, using a special attack, running before he can hit you, and repeat until he dies.
The 4 ability mechanics don't feel like they make a difference outside of the one puzzle they are intended for.
(POTENTIAL SPOILERS WHILE EXPLAINING WHERE GLITCHES HAPPENED)
Glitches - My first playthrough I was able to speak to the first old man after eating the fruit and not planting a seed, causing me to miss the achievement. No eating or replanting the fruit would let me get the achievement after that and I had to start over to get it (not a big deal).
I must have missed something on my first playthrough as I went straight for the Ku Shrine. This caused me to die in 2 hits (acording to walkthroughs you are suppose to survive 3) making it impossible for me to beat him as the game doesn't let you move or dodge. I throught I was stuck as the checkpoint respawn keeps you there. When I reloaded the game you are out of the shrine and the game thinks you beat it and it gave me the achievement. (This works on all shrines)
Even using the speed up I couldn't get the yellow shell to the alter in time as (with a keyboard at least) I couldn't run directly diagnally to the alter. The super speed also causes you to move after you stop pressing the button, and its hard to handle with only 10 fps.
The third shrine I ran into the mud to have the boar run past me. The boar then sits there at the edge just running in place (I could still move around him though).
The game has a lot going for it, and I like it. In it's current state though I can't recommend it. I know it was made by students, but gameplay and glitches would need to be cleaned up in order for me to be able to recommend it. But it's free, it certainly has things to offer, and if I saw a remake/sequel made by the developers with more money and experience (while obviously expanding on the world as well as fixing the gameplay) I'd buy the game. If the positives I stated sound good enough to to check it out, then you have no reason not to. Just don't expect much out of game play.

Overall, I would highly recommend this game, especially if you like puzzle/platformers.  The levels are very well designed with almost every world centered on one particular obstacle or feature.  Generally, you start out with simpler stages that show you the feature in question before you take what you learned and apply it to larger, more complex levels, an excellent example of the "teach without teaching" principle.  The final world is a potpourri of everything that you have learned previously and is understandably harder, requiring a good amount of thought and planning to get through.  However, even after playing through every stage, I had yet to come across a single obtuse moment or rely on a solution that came completely out of left field.
My only gripe with this game is that some of the worlds are so dark that it can be very difficult to see where the walls, floors, and ceilings are, though the stages are still quite doable after some stumbling around.

I bought this game since I had many friends who told me about it.
Sorry, but I do not recommend this game. I felt like I was playing a game that was trying to combine things that simply did not seem to go together very well. There were good things, but there were bad things, too.
Combine elements from Mirror's Edge and Dead Island as well as a story that could have been in Far Cry, and you get this game. That might sound pretty good and all, but I felt like the game felt dragged on the more I played it. It seemed to me like most of the things that are supposed to make this game unique felt rather incomplete.
I felt like most weapons seemed underpowered besides guns, which you don't get until you are at least halfway through the game. I sometimes find myself hitting a zombie 5+ times with a cleaver on the easiest difficulty, and it still happens to be alive. A normal zombie should definitely be dead after 2 or 3 attacks in my opinion. Another problem was the durability of weapons. It felt like after ~10 attacks with one weapon that it would need to be repaired. I found myself always needing more repair tools. At least headshots with guns are an instant kill, even though it attracts virals.
The parkour is basically like Mirror's Edge. Good, but I was looking for more flashy stuff such as wall running.
I thought the RPG elements were very lacking. I did not find the skill trees to be very interesting but rather linear. The loot also was not very exciting. You will usually find crafting components, things you will sell for money, or green/blue rarity weapons. I don't remember myself finding many purple rarity weapons let alone orange for that matter. That made loot very underwhelming for me.
The graphics are above par. Expect a lot of gore (obviously). They aren't glitchy, and I'm at least grateful for that.
Most of the sidequests felt too generic and pretty repetitive. Many of them usually leave you with similar objectives each time. Most of the arena or parkour challenges in particular are the ones that are especially bland unless you are competing with friends. I found myself skipping many sidequests for the sake of playing through the story.
The story was good, but not "The Witcher" good. The story was lengthy, but felt dragged in some areas. Most characters had unique behavior, but I felt like some twists in the story were too underwhelming or predictable. I won't say too much about the story since I wanna hide spoilers.
In the end, I felt like the game was less about the zombies and more about taking out a terrorist group and their leader. I cannot recommend this game for $60. If you have played Dead Island, Mirror's Edge, Far Cry, or a combination of both, then you will probably find some enjoyment, especially if you are playing with friends and it's on sale. However, if you are looking for a zombie survival game with deep RPG elements, then I would save your money and buy Dead Island or maybe try DayZ.

Meadow is a beautiful, open world that will have you awed in only a few minutes of play. I bought this game during the steam summer sale and I already have 21.8 hours of play, I had no idea I'd become so addicted to such a simple, beautiful game. Meadow starts you off as a badger cub, letting you explore the open multiplayer world looking for puzzle pieces to unlock new skins, animals, and emotions. Sometimes you'll find puzzle pieces around the world as you explore, but most the time you need to open obelisks, which take more than one player to unlock. This game brings people together, and the best part is that you can't communicate with them through text or with a microphone! You have to use your emotes and commands to make groups, follow people to obelisks, guide people to obelisks, and sometimes you need more than one other player to unlock bigger obelisks as you go. I personally loved this feature the most, being able to communicate in only emotes made it so much easier to talk to people in-game who may not speak my language, giving me a new experience to explore with someone I may have never thought to explore a game with. As a player who generally enjoys playing solo on multiplayer games, I have to say this is one of the first games that truly made me want to make friends and be close to strangers in a game to complete a common goal we all have in it, to unlock new features and to enjoy the beauty of the world around us.

The best Warhammer 40,000 game in a long time, if not of all time.
The main gameplay loop of battles with small numbers of customisable ships with many abilities, and different mission objectives is just so much fun, so satisfying, and endlessly interesting to experiment with.
The level above that is the fleet management - the fact that ships can be disabled in battle, and you will lose them for the next few games, but that you can at any time voluntarily withdrawn any or all of your ships is just brilliant. It turns every game, which otherwise might be a self contained skirmish that doesnt mean anything, into part of a larger picture where you're not just thinking about this battle but the next two or three as well.
The visuals are beautiful. I found the voice acting and characters in the single player campaign to be the most engaging of any Game Workshop computer game I've played (and I've played most of them) - striking the best balance yet between rediculous melodrama, funny moments, and swashbuckling epicness!
Tthe single player campaign allows you to win or lose any individual battle, giving tangible benefits or penalties for doing so, but not *too* much so (it seemed to me) always possible to continue despite constantly feeling overwhelmed in the middle part when every faction is against you. I feel like this is a massive improvement over other games where you *must* win every battle, and I really enjoyed it - I'd encourage anyone about to start the campaign to play on Iron Man mode, so there's no temptation for save scumming, the result of every battle is permanent - it really adds extra tension to each battle.
The multiplayer experience so far has been equally positive, and carries over the persistent qualities and ship leveling from the single player, which is great. The one thing I would like to see improved is to give players a multiplayer game mode where they can completely choose both their fleet (without leveling) and the mission type. A practice mode essentially.
Further development of the game is also looking awesome with Space Marine, and Tau fleets confirmed to be on the way, and a Tyranid fleet is also a future possibility.
I have no hesitation in recommend people buy and play this game. Choose your faction and join the fight amoungst the stars. But remember, the Universe is a big place and, whatever happens, you will not be missed...

This is quite the interesting game. A mix of puzzle and RPG sounds really cool, and it is. To start off with, the "battle system" is the puzzle portion. You take one turn between you and your enemy matching jewels. Doing this gives benefits depending on what you match. Colored gems give mana for spells, stars give experince, gold gives money, and skulls damage your foe. Matching four or more gives you another turn, and five gives another turn and a wild card that can match with any colored gem and multiply the benifits. It's very complex for a puzzle game.You have to think carefully since your enemy can take advantage of the board just as much as you, and you could give your enemy a really good move if your not careful, you can also have moments where you might want to risk damage for more gold or experince.
The rpg portion is well done and adds more layers to the battle system. You have stats, classes, spells,and equipment, and all this has massive influence on the gameplay. You can also capture cities for more money, learn enemy spells, forge equipment, use mounts(and level them up too), and complete quests. All of these things give diffrent variations of the battle system as well to keep things fresh. And yes, this game gives you a lot to do.
The controls are fine as you are mostly clicking, and I love the sound effects as they give matching gems a very satisfying punch, and the sound track is very nice with a middle age fantasy feel.
The game also has a story and this is where it starts to show flaws. It's cool that they did this for the game, as it gives the game an epic feel, and I do like the story altering decisions. But this story is very generic at best (evil lord bad, you kill him) to strange plot points (how is there an expert undead killer, if the undead hasn't  been seen in centuries?). The A.I. is also really cheap. There is nothing wrong with a challenging game, but an enemy that seems to know what gems are coming down(and responds acordingly) is a bit much. This can make even random encounters tedious if your just trying to get somewhere. You can counter this
with a well built charater though, so it's not game breaking or anything.
Overall this is a very uniqe game with plenty to discover and enjoy. You may need patience at times but this is a worth while game that's diffrent from most and I think it's worth playing. 8/10

At the time of posting, I have 110 hours in this game.
+ Great graphics
The game is absolutely beautiful in its current state. The textures are high quality, and everything is perfectly detailed.
+ Great environments
Each biome and are of Dark and Light is beautiful and well-crafted. Whether you're farming in a forest, struggling to stay alive on a volcano, surviving on the snow-whipped mountains, or battling wraiths on a shipwreck-crowded island... The environments in Dark and Light are hand-crafted, non-generated beauties. Every area offers an interesting take on the world and gives true immersion in a truly believable world.
+ great clan-based home building
Although it can be a little buggy at times, base building is a lot of fun and makes sense. You'll need support beams to keep your building's structural integrity in tact as you build higher and wider. In addition, Dark and Light introduces house sigils. House Sigils protect your base from any player who's house has not declared war on yours. Once a player's house declares war on yours, you have 12 hours to prepare for war and make sure you don't get caught with your pants down. You can place automated magical turrets and monsters around and inside your base to protect it while you're offline, thwarting off any raiding players who aren't prepared. There are many different building types to build with, ranging from shabby structures that offer minimal protection, to wood, stone, iron, and manor. You can build large beast gates to safely store your tamed mounts and animals, as well as many different decorations and interesting items to place in your home to give it a more "homely" feel.

+ RPG levelling system for you and your tamed animals
Simple, yet fun level mechanics. As you level up, you gain skill points to level up your stats, simple as that. Where it gets interesting is the knowledge trees. Once you hit the level requirement, certain knowledge becomes accessible. For example, when you hit level 20, you can access to the woodwork knowledge tree. To level up this knowledge tree, you must perform actions associated with that knowledge, like gathering wood and crafting woodwork items. There are many knowledge trees for you to work on and it never limits you to a class.
+ Cities, lords, vendors, community.
When you spawn, you spawn in the city associated with your race. You get access to many NPC merchants to buy and sell with using gold. Using this gold, you can rent homes around the city, purchase a horse, or purchase many different items from other players or merchant NPC's. Donate to these vendors to increase the tier of items they sell to players. In addition, each race may elect a lord each week. A lord gains access to the castle in their respective city, can enforce actions in the faction, and gains access to special mounts. As of right now, Dark and Light offers a proactive community. After 110 hours, I have rarely come across negative, toxic, KOS-style players. When a group of griefers and exploiters joined the server, the entire server joined together to wipe them out, together as a community.
Now, the negatives.
- Buggy mess
I know, it's early alpha... So this is a given. You'll run into issues like severe lag, people glitching to get into your base, and unresponsive melee combat and farming. As of right now, these issues are very annoying but it's not a deal breaker to me.
- Long loading
Takes some people upwards of 10 minutes to load into the game.
In summary, I won't be very harsh on the game as it just came out under a month ago. It has amazing potential and already has plenty of content to keep you busy for many hours. I am over 100 hours in and I still have so much to get and learn. My review is already very long, so I've left a lot of things out, such as the awesome clan systems and great design work on weapons and armor, as well as the in-depth customization for character creation. The developers are pushing out updates constantly, adding new features, optimizations, and bug fixes every single week.
This game is worth it for the price being asked, hands down.
