Civilization V is a very addictively fun strategy game. The fun historical facts thrown in, along with the personalities that have related bonuses for having that said leader make this game more challenging and increases the replayability. Having it on random is not nearly as fun, as you do not get to line up the bonuses with the map that you will play, but it does add to the difficulty, if you, for instance, get Queen Elizabeth I on a map that isn't good for naval combat, which is her biggest bonuses.
The fun with Civilization V that keeps me coming back, is it is fun to build, fun to be diplomatic, though the computer controlled players are very unpredictable and will hate you no matter what in the end. For instance, I was in a position of being friends with a map of 15 other civilizations, when just after declaring our friendship, 3 declared war on me. I took their lands and that set me to dominating the map, so I cannot complain too much. I ended up winning through culture in that match, which brings up another thing that absolutely love about this game. Victory is not any one thing. You can win by being diplomatic and convincing other civilizations to vote you as world leader; you can win by decimating your foes and taking their starting capitals (or all cities if changed in the options); you can win what I find as the easiest way to win, via the culture victory; and you can win via science, and launching a space shuttle into space, leading to the next game which I will be playing soon.
The combat is also fun to watch, and after playing for quite some time, and when you are going for a faster match, you can turn off the combat animations and have it instantly display the health changed and results. While you have the animations on, however, you can see each troop do their own specific type of attack or defense. The naval combat is my favorite thing to focus on, as having a good naval fleet is very powerful in this game. There is nothing like having an aircraft carrier, a couple of missile cruisers and a couple of nuclear submarines loaded along the shore of your next target. It takes a little bit to get built up that powerful, so you have to be diplomatic to start, especially if you try to hold off making too many troops up to that point. If you do not like naval combat and prefer ground troups, you will love the giant death robots, which obliterate their enemies. Strategy of using them is important, as you can easily lose your strongest troops if you do not plan your attacks well. The maps you choose also make a huge impact on the flow of the game, and your play style within it.
Whether you are militaristic, diplomatic, scientific, or a builder of culture, religion and/or trade, this game has a path for you to take for victory. I definitely recommend Civilization V for strategy gamers, and all gamers who might be on the fence.
I personally am not impressed with Civilization VI, and will be enjoying this game a while longer, until Civilization VII finds its way about.

Awesome game. Easy to learn, hard to master. Replay value is as high as it gets due to 28 unlockable playable ships (10 ship frames with layout A, B, and C). Each ship and each layout feels quite unique, and ship-specific achievements add to the replay. I was a little disappointed when I found out you can't craft your own ship, but with all the different ships and layouts, I think it would cheapen the game if there was such a feature.
There's definitely a learning curve, so don't expect to win right away. There's a big random factor to each playthrough which may be annoying at times, but keeps it from getting boring or predictable.
As far as outfitting your ship, you start with a small crew, several systems, and a weapon or two. From there you cruise around the sectors and find shops that sell a randomly generated equipment and hire out crew. There are so many weapons, ship augments, and systems for sale, no two playthroughs will be the same.
Everyone I know who's played this says it's hard, but they keep playing and enjoying it. Addicting and marvelously unique playthroughs. 100% satisfied with this product.

As for the levels themselves, they're generally pretty fun, but there's an entire world (a quarter of the game) themed around filling parts of the map with (a limited supply of) water to swim higher. Eventually you'll come across a map where the level of micromanagement and precise timing turn fun into drudgery.
To be fair, though,  it is very well polished for an indie game.

Why this game has the name Rainbow Six in it I can only make guesses; because its the only way it would sell, because it continues from a Tom Clancy work, because it is close quarters counter terrorism? I don’t know, but the fact is this has little resemblance of the original trilogy and I assume is more like Lockdown plus with many of the trending mechanics at the time of its release.
So after having played through Story Mode I am going to go through everything that was obviously noticeable and significant in comparison of having played R6 3 Raven Shield and watching plays of 1, Rogue Spear and too little of Lockdown as well as the added or replacing things that made Rainbow Six Vegas feel like I was playing a totally different IP and a not-so-much-more impressive shooter compared to others of its time and following.
First group of things are operative related. None are present from the original R6 trilogy but a short mention Ding Chavez did occur, Instead of the originals you are a team of three and take full control of the leader. The other operatives supposedly have their specialties but it is not measured like in the other games and it is more related to plot objectives (explosives and electronics).
Gear selection has changed. Only you can customize and you can carry two primary weapons, two explosives, hand gun. You also have thermo-vision, NVGs, snake cam (replacement to the heartbeat sensor) and to some weapons suppressors which you also give the command to attach and remove at the same time as you. Guns do have different attachments, select fires, iron sights and stats (Damage which might actually be more important in this game than the original trilogy, Accuracy, Range, plus Magazine Size; Rate of Fire and Recoil not measured). Still it felt like there were more options in Raven Shield. Something they did better though was each character having their own voice actors however I should mention terrorist quotes are very annoying.
Then there is mechanics, the ones everyone should be familiar with now. There are three of them being:
regenerating health, having to revive downed partners before their time runs out and lean being replaced by locking to cover.
Tactics. No map blueprints, not much point since it became get from point A to point B. The real tactics here is planning how you enter an area usually with multiple entrances. What you do is point to your team what door to stick to and until you give them a command or they get shot at they stay there giving you the ability to approach from another side. There are also Rules of Engagement, Follow/Hold, Move and stated earlier use of suppressors for a stealthy approach (even though enemies in other nearby rooms wont hear non suppressed gun fire).
The other single player mode is Terrorist Hunt and again it is not similar. It is done Lone Wolf and there is no extraction point making it a must to neutralize all enemies.
So what else do I have to say? I think it is okay that Iron Wrath was the last supposed real Rainbow Six game. Surely 8 games, expansions included plus Takedown (South Korea only release) were enough. Its too bad though that instead of ending properly R6 continued on to become nothing outstanding.
With there having been planned Rainbow 6 Patriots we can assume that Lockdown was considered 4, Vegas 1 considered 5 and Vegas 2 considered a stand-alone expansion pack. If you are curious to try "Rainbow Six 5" you should really first start with Vegas 2 because of all the added features and think of Vegas 1 as extra missions.

If I had one word to describe this: Awful.
The art may be decent, but the story, which should be the main point of a visual novel, is really bad. In less than 10 minutes of playing I stumbled upon clichés after clichés.
The game is divided into three branches, each putting one of the character in the main spot, with the Innkeeper, being the link between them.
It starts out with The Prince having a wet dream about Elisa. Honestly, that was a bit too much, and that's right at the start. Right there, I knew I would dislike the game.
The personality of each character seems to be really fluid, not constant, and it just screams "bad writing!". They are also all jerks with almost no redeemable qualities, even if you choose the good option.
First, there's The Prince. Depending on your choices, he's either a cheapskate, a liar, a thief, someone's not respectful, someone who doesn't know what privacy means, or even a beggar. He also may force Elisa to do his binding, or even threatens the merchant for what he consider a small amount of money. No matter your choices, at least 2 of them will happen because he's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ human being.
Second, there's the merchant. He's one of the most decent character, but still, he's trash. Not as much as the Prince. The Merchant acts as the rival of the Prince. He can be a liar, a thief, or a scammer. He also force Elisa to accept his gifts (where we see that she is highly uncomfortable) and he manipulate people to make him look good. Ew.
Third, there's the Knight. The character with the least amount of interactions, and that's a good thing. He start off as saying women are worth nothing. Like, right at his introduction, we get to know how misogynist he is, sweet! He continue off, with the other characters saying he hasn't met the right one. That's some great heteronormative dialog here. He could be gay or even asexual, but the author doesn't want to. (I mean, I can let it slide a bit, depending on the time period this is set in, but... We don't even know if it's in the real world or a fictive world...)
Anyway, the knight is a jerk no matter what you do, he'll treat the staff like♥♥♥♥♥♥ Depending on your choice, he may also treat Elisa like♥♥♥♥♥♥ too! He even spout a line totally not made for him, to the prince: "Respect others if you want to be respected in turn." ... Yeah, the same guy who treated others like♥♥♥♥♥♥ Wow.
Lastly, there's Elisa. Not much is said about her, she seems to be doing drama for her amusement, and in one route we learn that she somewhat manipulate the men who love her for her pleasure.
In one route, we get to see a bit about her past (by the prince who decides to read her private journal, from when she was a kid.) It's pretty much 5 pages of "I'm sad my dad died." It just feel shoehorned here, and it ends up only being used so the Prince scores points in her heart by blatantly lying about his mother's death.
As for the engine itself... There's so much things wrong here. For no reason, I ended up on the title screen... With the game still playing. I could continue reading dialog while I was on the title screen. It happened 3 times, and I don't know how it happened. If you click-hold and move, it would be like you selected the background, which is so ♥♥♥♥in' weird.
The skip function is really slow. I haven't tried autoplay.
Honestly there's way better visual novel worth your time here, even for free. This one is just an uninteresting mess full of bad ideas, and it just makes me way less interested in the main game; which will be without me, for sure.

As a long time fan of the franchise, CoH2 stays true to the old "if it isnt broke, dont fix it" adage. ive heard many people complain that the game is basically the same as the old CoH, just in a different theater of war and with different units etc. people also complain that sega turned the game into a pay-to-win DLC money grab, even though it absolutely is not because many of the stock generals that come with the game are arguably bettter than the ones you can buy in the store.  While it is true that the same mechanics and gameplay are for the most part still present, there are many, many new things added to the game that will change the experience of the game yet will not annoy old CoH veterans such as myself. For one thing, units will no longer have to tediously move around cover such as short walls or sandbags. now, they can just vault over it if you so desire them to, allowing you to get to the fight quicker as well as set up an ambush point. visibility through the fog of war is made much more realistic now. In the old CoH, units had a fixed circle of view that allowed them to see units even if they were behind a building. now, your view is obstructed if your unit is up next to a building or the enemy is behind smoke. The addition of new armies, generals, and units adds brand new ways to play and new strategies to utilize rather than the same 3 stock strategies available in the old CoH. It also includes a whole new campaign story featuring the soviet armies that is very engaging and fun to play. when THQ went under, many of us CoH fans had very grim expectations for the future of CoH, as well as the promised sequel that was to come. I didnt know what to expect when i heard SEGA was to take the reins. but now, i am happy to say that SEGA did a brilliant job in carrying the torch and keeping the franchise alive and thriving. if you are a fan of the series, RTS' in general, or just a WW2 buff in general, this game is definitelly worth the buy.

At the time of posting, I have 110 hours in this game.
+ Great graphics
The game is absolutely beautiful in its current state. The textures are high quality, and everything is perfectly detailed.
+ Great environments
Each biome and are of Dark and Light is beautiful and well-crafted. Whether you're farming in a forest, struggling to stay alive on a volcano, surviving on the snow-whipped mountains, or battling wraiths on a shipwreck-crowded island... The environments in Dark and Light are hand-crafted, non-generated beauties. Every area offers an interesting take on the world and gives true immersion in a truly believable world.
+ great clan-based home building
Although it can be a little buggy at times, base building is a lot of fun and makes sense. You'll need support beams to keep your building's structural integrity in tact as you build higher and wider. In addition, Dark and Light introduces house sigils. House Sigils protect your base from any player who's house has not declared war on yours. Once a player's house declares war on yours, you have 12 hours to prepare for war and make sure you don't get caught with your pants down. You can place automated magical turrets and monsters around and inside your base to protect it while you're offline, thwarting off any raiding players who aren't prepared. There are many different building types to build with, ranging from shabby structures that offer minimal protection, to wood, stone, iron, and manor. You can build large beast gates to safely store your tamed mounts and animals, as well as many different decorations and interesting items to place in your home to give it a more "homely" feel.

+ RPG levelling system for you and your tamed animals
Simple, yet fun level mechanics. As you level up, you gain skill points to level up your stats, simple as that. Where it gets interesting is the knowledge trees. Once you hit the level requirement, certain knowledge becomes accessible. For example, when you hit level 20, you can access to the woodwork knowledge tree. To level up this knowledge tree, you must perform actions associated with that knowledge, like gathering wood and crafting woodwork items. There are many knowledge trees for you to work on and it never limits you to a class.
+ Cities, lords, vendors, community.
When you spawn, you spawn in the city associated with your race. You get access to many NPC merchants to buy and sell with using gold. Using this gold, you can rent homes around the city, purchase a horse, or purchase many different items from other players or merchant NPC's. Donate to these vendors to increase the tier of items they sell to players. In addition, each race may elect a lord each week. - Buggy mess
I know, it's early alpha... So this is a given. You'll run into issues like severe lag, people glitching to get into your base, and unresponsive melee combat and farming. As of right now, these issues are very annoying but it's not a deal breaker to me.
- Long loading
Takes some people upwards of 10 minutes to load into the game.
In summary, I won't be very harsh on the game as it just came out under a month ago. It has amazing potential and already has plenty of content to keep you busy for many hours. I am over 100 hours in and I still have so much to get and learn. My review is already very long, so I've left a lot of things out, such as the awesome clan systems and great design work on weapons and armor, as well as the in-depth customization for character creation. The developers are pushing out updates constantly, adding new features, optimizations, and bug fixes every single week.
This game is worth it for the price being asked, hands down.

I absolutely love this game and have plenty of fun with it, but there several problems that Firaxis needs to address. I had hoped that these problems would have been fixed in Civ 6 but it turns out that Civ 6 was just a money grab and not a suitable, well-designed game.
So I went back to Civ 5 after a long time of not playing it and realized how fun it was. But it's really problematic. I'll start with the bad things:
AI Have Split Personalities - Each AI has two parts to its brain, one that controls units and orders them to attack/move/improve tiles and one that orders cities on what buildings/units to produce/construct. This isn't a problem on its own but in Civ 5, both parts DON"T communicate and their logic is very silly. The part responsible for unit and building making will just produce workers or settlers because that's what's it's programmed to do no matter if there are no tiles to improve and no good city spots. But what's worse is that the part responsible for moving the units does not communicate to the other part and say stuff like: "Hey buddy, we need to work on food tiles since our city is starving instead of building   a settler!" and etc., unfortunately, they don't do this and because of that, the AI wastes time, production and resources.
AI Make Stupid Mistakes - This is something I have come across many times. I remember when I was attacking Poland and there was a fort near the capital guarded by Artillery and Tank. One of my badly injured units is returning home and THEN BAM! Both the artillery and tank just leave and began attacking my damaged unit, leaving the fort empty and vulnerable. I occupy and easily capture Warsaw, one of the most stupidest mistakes I've ever seen before. All the time, the AI will always order their military units to attack weak or injured units instead of attacking strong ones that are capable of doing lots of destruction.
AI Aren't Good at Science and Caring About their Cities - AI will have unfair advantages at the beginning of the game, starting off with already discovered techs, then in about 40 turns, I've already elapsed them in tech and they're struggling to push out of the Classical Era OR they are keeping up with me but the techs they research don't give them any benefits or anything new to help them out. They just simply choose a random one. And they definitely don't know how to take good care of their cities. They will build an endless number of trading outposts when they have plenty of fertile, flat land and make their city starve or they build too many farms and focus on growing food when they actually need money, they start losing money and can't support themselves anymore. OR they start building a crap ton of military units and find out they don't have the funds nor the resources to support their giant army OR they start attacking lots of civs when they minus happiness! If your empire was unhappy then you likely wouldn't attack anyone.
AI Are Sensitive - They're sensitive in the way where they will denounce you for little things and get upset over nothing. I remember once when I defended Russia from France and Mongolia, brought them back to life after I liberated their capital, and after 50 turns they were declaring me filfth because I was 'settling too close'. They declare war on me, I take their cities and then everyone calls me a warmonger. And don't get me started on Gandhi, ugh. He drops a nuke on a city, you declare war on him = everyone hates you.
In general, the AI are poorly programmed, illogical, silly and waste their own time and resources. They don't make good decisions and make smart little remarks that ends up with their entire empire getting blasted away by nukes and death robots. BUT, I am making this a good review, because even though they are pretty stupid they can make some pretty good armies and fight quite hard, it's quite thrilling. I also like the seriousness of the game and the graphics as well as the general way everything works. The game is very good, but the AI need a lot of tweaking. I would rate this game a 8.5/10 and recommend that you should buy it. :)

This is an intriguing little game and an excellent example of how a worthy idea and theme, kept simple at its core can be a great example of an Indie game and indeed a standout amongst many of the same, same, RPGMaker clones that are currently available on Steam.
The heart of this mystery themed game is very much in the Agatha Christie style of who-dunnit. The truly novel approach here is that you will play the perpetrator and with limited time and information at hand, go about committing "The Deed" of a perfect murder. Think of any classic dinner themed murder mysteries, where your actions and the careful selection of "planted evidence" and "murder weapon" is an endeavour to both commit a perfect crime and frame someone else with your actions. Where generally you would be investigating the crime in a game of this type, the handy switch here has made for a game that is a standout in an otherwise crowded market and some might say, tired genre.
In a sense this is little more than an advanced version of paper, scissors, rock, simple enough but with enough scope to have you thinking of all the possible combinations and how they might play out. At about 20 minutes in length for a play through it is more than likely you will be playing this one many times over to get the perfect or just most interesting result!
At this price or indeed the even further reduced sale price that I picked this up for, it is almost a no brainer purchase for anyone who enjoys a mystery themed adventure game, or indeed just anybody looking for a short but entertaining distraction.

TL;DR There wont ever be a Arena FPS on the same level as Quake, RIP Unreal Tournament & Arena Shooters in general.
Put simply, the Ultimate Game of Skill.
There's no easy way around it, no arguements to settle... simply no reason to disprove the statement above; because no other game offers the same mechanics like Quake does, arena shooter or otherwise. We can't even compare its age old rival Unreal Tournament, since that game has been chopped and changed throughout the years... its really just a cheap knockoff. (Not taking out UT99's Facing Worlds... excellent map) Quake's formula remains unchanged since its original incarnation and has stood the test of time.
And plus to compare any shooter to Quake is like comparing Apples to Oranges.
Quake is set apart from other FPS or Arena shooters by having a near perfect engine for precise control and movement, very efficient netcode carried over from the excellent netcode of Quake 3 means that the game feels like a LAN-Party even with 50-100 ping... however I don't recommend playing games over 100.
The gameplay also differs from the fact there's no random variables, no luck based elements involved. The entire game is set about by "chance"... the chance that a rocket might hit... but that is all controlled by you the player, since every weapon has 100% accuracy and movement is considerably faster than any other FPS. There are no "headshots" or easy kills, it simply doesn't exist and therefore does not hold your hand in the chance you 'may' get a random headshot as such. If someone kills you repeatedly its just a sign they're a far better player than you are.
This system allows people to play with consistency that isn't often seen in other games, you never really lose the skills you had in Quake... more likely people just get better than you are, the engine is timeless. There's also Map Control to consider, don't want to pick up items? Expect to respawn very quickly. You simply can't play the traditional gametypes successfully without trying to get the items on the map, you don't start with power weapons (loadouts are now an option thank god) and thus you're at a tremendous disadvantage the moment you spawn.
So with no easy entrance for beginners why do I recommend this game? Quake is the only game that offers a true 100% skill based Competitive Experience, the fact there's no random variables should be plainly obvious. Games like CSGO do have an excellent competitive community (though salty D:) , but there is always going to be a random element in the game. The Quake Community is truly amazing, do poorly in a game vs a better player... they'll critique you, give you tips etc... you get the odd elitist but the reception overall is awesome. :3
Also the new update is great imho... sure its Pay 2 Play... but so was Quake Live Premium and that was BS. If you had Quake Live on Steam beforehand you got it free... so why all the commotion?

I am guilty of spreading the video game plague among my friends, and have turned several of them onto Steam. In the event of a successful conversion, I am usually met with one question: "Well, now what?"
With thousands of titles available through Steam, it can no doubt be overwhelming to newer players as to what games they should invest in first. When giving loose advice to newcomers (as well as experienced gamers feeling "stagnant" or "stale"), "Braid" is one of the first games I suggest, and for many reasons.
"Braid" is a relatively no-frills puzzle/platformer with a whispful and captivating aesthetic. The story is so-so -- perhaps a bit of a bummer and maybe a little too personally indulgent (and, thankfully for some, nearly totally optional), but such a motif ties very well with the game's style. What is more impressive is how the game's core mechanic -- time manipulation -- plays with the theme of loss and regret, and blends it all -- the awareness of perception and the present, what is current, and what is being swept away by the current -- into a game.
"Braid" takes real and mature details of the tragedy of life and makes it not just digestable, but fun.
Of course, tight controls and interesting puzzles are what make "Braid" so enjoyable. The in-game problem solving is rewarding. Players feel smart when they cross a wide and deadly chasm or snag a particularly elusive puzzle-piece, which makes "Braid" hard to put down. Thanfully, considerate design allocates for moderate level and chapter lengths, promoting breaks in gameplay and giving players incentive not to swallow "Braid" in one gulp (though it is tempting).
To me, "Braid" exemplifies what (some) games should be -- simple, engaging, tight, rewarding, and fun. The game succeeds in exactly what it sets out to be, and such purity can truly leave an impression. "Braid" is on my shortlist when the topic of "Video Games as Art" comes up. Without hesitation, I encourage you to add "Braid" to your library, and to dive into it when you can give it the attention it deserves.
If you enjoy puzzle/platformers like "Braid", you may also want to check out "Limbo", "VVVVVV", "Closure", and "Fez". If you are looking for other games that touch on true, mature psycho-social details like loss, anger, confusion, and regret, I would recommend "Anodyne" and "Lisa". All of the aforementioned games can be found and purchased on Steam.

Braid, from the mind of Jonathan Blow, is considered by many to be a masterpiece.  A grand testament to what video games can be.  A deconstruction of expectations.  A philosophical treatise on the nature of relationships and perception.  It is all of these things, and more: it is also an excellent puzzle platformer.
At first glance this appears to be a (gorgeous) standard platformer in the vein of Super Mario Bros.  But things are deeper than they first appear.  Make a mistake, and you’ll be prompted to hit X (Shift).  No explanation is given, no tutorial is displayed.  Press the button, and you discover that you can rewind time.  This seems a small thing at first.  Great; now you do not have to restart a level from the beginning!  But this is so much more than that.  Obstacles that would be unfair or nigh-impossible in a standard platformer are simple puzzles here.  The way you play this game turns your expectations of platforming upside-down, inside-out, and yes, in reverse.
Tim is searching for the princess, who has been taken by a monster, and using his time-travel powers, he must collect puzzle pieces to find his way to her.  All of the deep exposition is given to you at the beginning of each world, leading you into the next time-bending puzzle.  And oh, how the puzzles twist your brain.  You become comfortable with rewinding time, then you are given objects that do not respond to your reversals.  There’s a world where you can create a shadow who replays your past actions.  There’s a world where time only moves forward if you do.  Each time-shifting mechanic the game introduces will totally subvert your expectations and change your strategies.  Each puzzle builds on the last, and presents new and unique challenges for you to overcome, making you think backwards and stretching out your perceptions.  Even the same puzzle, when presented with a slightly different flow of time, can have vastly different solutions.
The graphics have a lovely hand-drawn quality to them, and are simply beautiful in their simplicity.  From Tim’s house to the golden light wafting through the trees, the 2D world is just a treat to take in.  Where the developers could have gone with a retro 8- or 16-bit design, this high-definition hand-drawn aesthetic really makes this game stand out.  Every frame of this game could be a painting on your wall.
But the music, oh goodness, the music.  The folksy, dreamy, strings-and-piano style throughout most of the soundtrack will soothe you.  A puzzle that seems almost impossible, well that’s ok, because you get to listen to this wonderfully peaceful music while you think on how to manipulate time.  Rewinding time will cause the music to rewind itself, giving you a weird sensation of wrongness when you do it.  This kind of sound wasn’t meant to flow backwards.  You’re breaking the natural order of things when you do that, though there’s no repercussions except the musical unease.  It’s a perfect complement to the gameplay, and the larger themes at play here.
Braid is not a difficult game, not in the traditional twitchy-platformer sense.  The puzzles take deeply lateral (and inverse) thinking to solve, and there’s thankfully very few cases where you’ll have an exact understanding what to do but lack the necessary dexterity to pull it off.  Most every puzzle is easily skippable, and you can always return to earlier stages to retry them.  The game’s mechanics complement the story wonderfully, and you’ll end up asking yourself some very deep questions.  What would it mean for my relationships if I could reverse all of my mistakes?  How would I interact with people if I was the only one moving forward in time, and everyone else was moving backward?  What is the true cost of obsession?
Too much ink has been spilled arguing what Braid is about.  This game is one of the greatest of all time, a piece of art, a glimpse into the human condition.  And I guess that means we should argue what it is about.  The ending completely changes everything you thought you knew, and I won’t spoil it here for those who haven’t finished it.  There are plenty of other places on the internet for that.  The philosophical subtext, hinted at through the storybooks and even in the gameplay, will gnaw at your mind for a long while after finishing it.  Everyone should play this game.

X-Wing Alliance was the X-Wing I originally wanted, and I consider it to be the best game in the series. There's more craft here, you can see planets more closely than older games, and you can hyperspace to different sectors to perform different goals. Some flyable craft like the YT Corellian transports can dock with and carry cargo containers. Missions start you off in a hangar, where you can see activity going on around you, and you will sometimes have options for different fighters. There's more of a story this time, as you play as Ace Azameen, whose family-owned cargo business wants to stay out of the Galactic Civil War, but you are eventually dragged into the Alliance side after the Imperials seize your home. While X-Wing and TIE Fighter did give your character a name and backstory, they were limited to the manual, and you were otherwise a faceless pilot. Giving your pilot an identity here seems like a good idea because you have something personal to fight for, and makes you feel like you're stepping into a bigger galaxy.
This is all fine...until you have to do family missions. Every once in a while, in the middle of your Rebel Tours, you'll be called back to do some work for your brother and sister, trying to get your home back. Sometimes it even ties into the Rebel plot. But it feels like you're being torn away from your duty. "Do I still have to work for you people? I have better things to do." Which brings me to my next problem: difficulty spikes, which as I recall, tend to happen during family missions.
Another big feature is the final campaign: The Battle of Endor, where you get to fly the Millenium Falcon itself, including into the Death Star superstructure, which is probably the hardest mission in the game. Not only is it cramped, but the obstacles change every time you reset. On top of that, you're not playing as Ace anymore, you're playing as Lando, which means while Ace's story does get a happy ending, it also comes to an abrupt halt. I also didn't even want to fly the Millennium Falcon. I wanted to fly a B-Wing and take on Star Destroyers. Oh well...
There is a multplayer function, with a sort of mission editor, allowing you to put in any craft, up to and including Super Star Destroyers. This seems good, except you can't define where they are placed, or special conditions, making this inferior to the competitor Freespace 2, and the FRED program. However, the number of playable craft is greatly expanded, and you can even fly the Firespray-class ship (famously used as Slave I).
Flaws aside, this is certainly the best X-Wing game, and I do highly recommend it, just beware of the harder missions.

This is no doubt the best zombie game ever made, and one of the best games overall in recent years. I've been playing it since about 6 months after release. When I saw the trailers on tv at first I really didn't pay attention, as I thought i was just going to be another one of those contrived big name games. After I started researching it, it seemed interesting, and I have to say it was one of the best game sales I ever made. Techland of course has experience with zombie-type games from Dead Island, so when they had the idea to take it to the next level and make a more serious, realistic, and dark story around it, they came up with the concept for Dying Light. On top of that, they also were able to create arguably the best open world parkour ever made, with such fluency and variety of movements coupled with tools like a grappling hook. They have stayed engaged with the community throughout all of 2015 and 2016, slowing down in 2017 to work on other projects presumably. During that time they released much desired DLC from the community, including the all-parkour challenge The Bozak Horde, the huge expansion The Following, some smaller dlc items including missions and weapons, not to mention free updates adding updated content. The amount of variety of quests in the game is amazing as well, both throughout the main story and all side quests. Some of the side quests, especially, have a deep meaning when helping people in need in the qurantined city where the outbreak is centered. Dying Light also has a surprisingly vast variety of weaponry, from different sorts of guns, swords, knives, hammers, bats, etc. Each is customizable with  both upgrades and blueprints which can add elemntal effects to them. They of course have the ability to collect many, many more outfits for your character and many upgrades and skins for the buggies in The Following. There are many traders where you can barter goods and money you have found to get weapons and other materials needed to craft items. There must be hundreds of blueprints in Dying Light, I'm not even sure if I have them all. You can make anything from potions, to medical supplies, to shurikens, to shields, etc. The base game has 2 huge maps and one smaller one, of course the following adds an even larger one. There is 4 player cooperative multiplayer in which you can complete quests, just run around the maps, or compete against each other in freerunning or zombie killing challenges. To go even further, there is a Be The Zombie mode which is an assymetric game in which players run around the maps at night time attempting to destroy zombie hatching pods while a powerful zombie, controlled by another player attempts to stop them. There is also the ability to make your own games and maps in Dying Light with the developer tool, and the community has made a large variety of content to enjoy, some of which has been included in the base game. Dying Light is surely reccommended, an unforgettable experience it is.

I'm not a huge match 3 fan, but this is the best combination of match 3 and RPG/Fantasy play that I've seen.
When most people think of match 3, they think "Bejeweled."  There is really no comparison with Puzzle Quest, which is orders of magnitude more engaging.
The expansion on the map is compelling, and the variation in puzzle types and ability to learn enemy spells and conquer cities for income makes this possibly the only match 3 you will ever want to play.  If I could go back in time and "unbuy" all the other match 3 games I've purchased and only have this one, I'd be happy - even if I had paid full price for this.
The difficulty curve is what makes this - because you can be stuck in your tiny kingdom for quite a while before you "break through" with the right equipment (or maybe you got lucky with RNG -- that happens too).  There are some brutally difficult research puzzles too, and the crafting is very good.
The AI is quite forgiving too - it doesn't always go for damage even when there are obvious moves on the table.  After playing it for quite a while it becomes clear how you have to avoid the risk that a move you make might expose you to an attack.
I think the developers are quite aware what a great "gem" (haha) they have here, so they don't put this on sale often.
The game offers an enormous amount of content for a match 3.  I've played almost 18 hours, and I've gotten (from comparing my progress to a filled-out map someone had posted a screenshot of) about 15-20% complete.  That means I can expect around 100 hrs or so to finish the game.  Ridiculous.  This explains the price tag - there's so much content.
However I wouldn't be surprised if they were to reskin the whole game while keeping the play the way it is, just to milk the original player base.  That wouldn't hurt - but it's really all about the gameplay and this has it down as what I would call the quintessential match 3 game.

Munin is a combination of two games. Both of them are puzzle games, but will make you feel completely different.
The first one is a simple, casual, FEZ-like experience - there is no open world, nevertheless the game requires reshaping its levels and looking for new connections between seperate parts of the areas. It allows you to take your time, think your way through a level and enjoy the music as well as the dark, moody graphics. I really like this experience.
However: every time you die the game forces you to play the entire level from the beginning. During the first, casual parts of the game it's not a problem, since you are allowed to make mistakes while playing and to experiment with your surroundings without being constantly punished. This "first game" is hidden in various parts of Munin and is not just a first "part" of the game.
But that's where the "second game" comes in. Multiple "worlds" (sets of levels) have included mechanics which are lethal for the player's character - rivers of lava, rolling boulders, lasers and so on. In these worlds almost every mistake results in a respawn, and if you are not that good in puzzle games and/or you don't have a good reflex and precise controls, you will try-and-error each level multiple times, repeating the same actions over and over again. Just like in the games from the 80's and 90's which couldn't afford to be that long and instead required multiple attempts to beat their harder parts.
If it's not a problem for you, you may find Munin an amazing experience. However I kinda hate repeating the same thing four, eight or twelve times just because I fail in the later parts of the level. That's where I start to become less enchanted and more annoyed and start to hope to find more levels from the "first game" - less challenging, yes, but also less frustrating. Especially since I don't consider respawning the player and moving him back a challenge.
A bonus minor issue: jumping is sometimes pretty bad and counterintuitive.
From other positives: each world makes a good job teaching the player what its unique mechanics do and how to exploit them. The game tries to represent Nordic myths without using cliches and stupid popcultural nonsense as horned helmets, Thor's hammers, snakes and so on. Developers actually tried to represent their very own interpretation of Edda (or maybe Poetic Edda, I'm not sure) and focus on the mood of various realms. Sometimes it results in quite silly ideas (especially lasers), but there are pretty interesting visual designs and majority of the game provides maximum results from minimal resources.
My favourite part of the games is when an enormous giant (nomen omen) shows up in the background and just casually passes by. It could not even be there, but was a fascinating view supported by cool sound effects. Unfortunatelly there is not many addition like that, but they are surely very welcome.
Some of the levels have also their own sounds and music, what is also cool.
Not a perfect game, but it doesn't need to be (especially if you buy it for like one euro) and it doesn't try to please everyone. If you think it's screenshots and promotional video look attractive and you like puzzle games, you will probably not regreat giving it a shot.

The AI in this game doesn't cheat despite what so many negative reviews say, but what *is true* is that the strategic opportunities presented on the game board are typically so few that you are pigeon-holed into doing one thing or the next.
Most of the time it feels like you have very little choice on the outcome; just take the most obvious and beneficial match on the board which is never hard to figure out, then hope what cascades is more beneficial to you vs the AI.
I refunded.  Yes I did.

Braid is an interesting game, and a culturally important game. I'd hesitate saying it was a really "good" or "fun" game for me, at least if I want to be really honest.
I probably did come into it with heightened expectations. I did play it years after its prime, but I did not see it as the game-changing visionary experience it was hyped to be. Of its contemporaries, I'd say FEZ touched me much deeper emotionally, even though FEZ has zero explicit emotional narrative, and Braid was pretty much built around emotions. The theme was touching, but still I left the game with a slight feeling of disorientation, "what the hell just happened", and my thumb hurting from holding right down on the d-pad for roughly 75% of the time spent playing. :)
(Now I probably sound like I hated the game, when in fact I did not. I do feel like it was an "incomplete" experience, but a worthwhile one - I just wish pacing had been faster.)

The Deed is a short RPG Maker game with a funny name where your goal is to murder your sister. You spend the first part of the game wandering the house and talking with your family while searching for weapons to use for the murder or for evidence to plant, and then after taking two items you move into the murder phase, in which you use the items you picked up to try to set up a murder that pushes the blame away from you. It's a simple game, but the different items and locations do just enough to lend a bit of creativity to it. If you just go for a successful murder and leave it at that you'll probably finish the game fairly quickly, but the fun of it is doing various things just to see what happens. You can challenge yourself by trying to get away with killing your sister with your bare hands, or see what the inspector says when you show up to the interview with things like your sister's underwear. It's not the deepest or the longest game, but for $1 The Deed is a pretty neat little diversion.

*Long review warning* tl;dr - get the (vanilla) game when it's on sale.
DOA 5 LR is, at its core, one of the best fighting games that's ever been made. It's got a huge roster of characters, all of which are at least viable, and is extremely fast and fluid. If you're new to the series, the thing that sets DOA apart from other fighters is responsiveness. You can interrupt your own elaborate punch combos with a dropkick (assuming your character has one) without issue. This isn't a series about filling up meters or throwing the most/biggest/etc. fireballs. Nor are you limited to the combo(s) the developers came up with if you intend to combo in the first place. A punch is a punch, period. If you've ever watched a film like Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon or The Matrix and thought bitterly to yourself "Why the **** isn't there a fighting game like that?!", you'd do well to play DOA.
Starting from such a strong foundation, you might assume that it'd take a lot of effort to screw this game up. And you'd be right. The developers have managed to sabotage nearly everything good about this game. You can play against some of the best players online... if you're lucky. But it's just as likely you'll get paired up with someone who doesn't want a match with you, over and over, for tens of minutes. And you and the other person can cancel all you want, but the random match system will (literally) never take the hint. So why not just arrange matches through the lobby? Because there isn't one. In fact, it's impossible to choose who your opponents are in online mode. The lag is as bad as its reputation indicates. It's not always gamebreaking, but it's certainly gamebreaking some of the time. And there are several cheaters. The DLC is alarmingly expensive, but at least it's almost entirely removed from core gameplay. It's nearly all cosmetics. There's one pay-to-use character, but fortunately, not a very good one (so not pay-to-win yet). The keyboard controls aren't customizable at all, so you'll be wanting a third party controller to play the game. Ideally one with its own key remapping software. As for the reports that Team Ninja have put out a press release demanding that modders censor themselves while modding this game? That's sadly true. It's hard to adequately describe my contempt for such repressiveness.
So am I saying that DOA 5 Last Round has such outstanding core gameplay that even the efforts of its own developer can't completely derail the experience? Yes. Unfortunately. I've been playing fighting games for over 20 years and, upsettingly, this seems to be the topmost achievement in the genre. It's the most apt swan song its series could aspire to, and absolutely worth putting $10-$20 into when it's sold at a steep enough discount.

Please disregard Steam saying I have zero hours in this. The original boxed version of this game was purchased for me 17 years ago by my parents when I was much younger. I've played through the campaign many many times, and spent a lot of time experimenting with the combat simulator. I repurchased it on Steam so that I don't need to drag out the cd's anymore.
This is a great and very fun space flight sim. It's all fly-by-wire so don't expect the feel of Star Citizen or Elite Dangerous. It does give you some good control over your ships though. You can manage power between your lasers, shields, engines and beam weapons. Diverting energy from one to another. It is always soo much fun when you've completed your objectives just in time as reinforcement Star Destroyers start pouring in from Hyperspace, and you now need to divert all energy from all other systems to your engines so you can GTFO before Tie Fighters smother you. There's even one great mission where you need to fly THREW them to escape, passing right over Vader's massive Super Star Destroyer as it bares down on you.
As well you can set shields to focus on the front, back or equally both sides of your ship. Usefull when heading straight into the madness, or when a fighter is stuck on your tail. When flying ships with turrets (like the Millennium Falcon) you can even jump into the turret, and set the auto-pilot to chase your current target as you try to blast it. Just like the scene from A New Hope.
There's around 50 missions and they're all fairly unique, exciting, and lengthy. The story starts right after the battle of Hoth and ends at the destruction of the second Death Star. With you piloting the Millennium Falcon right into the mouth of the massive beast. You play as Ace Azzameen, a young freighter pilot for your families transport business. There are two types of missions,
Rebel Mission's: where you'll be piloting various Rebel fighters in skirmishes for the Rebel Alliance and
Family Mission's: where you'll be piloting a Corellian YT series small freighter (similar to the Millennium Falcon) doing jobs for your family to help build your families transport business.
The missions are more then just Go to point A, blow up Object B, and escort Ships C. There are capture, hunting, recon, infiltration and even base defense missions. It's pretty varied and I never found the game to go stale. Even playing it recently.
This is where I get a little sad. The game is split into chapters with many small story lines that all relate to the two major arc's The war between the Rebel and Imperial republic and the story of your family.  The family story arc unfortunately ends on a massive cliff hangar right before the battle of the Second Death Star. After that the game is over. It's clear the developers had planned for an expansion pack or sequel to continue the family story but due to the poor sales of the game that never happened. You spend a lot of time with the characters and I personally became very invested in the story. I was disappointed to see it never truly finished.
There's a combat sim that lets you put together custom (all be it simple) skirmishes. I spent a lot of time in this. It was fun putting together these massive battles with Star Destroyers and Calamari Cruisers clashing while the space in between and around is filled with fighters from both sides swarming like mosquito's.
I never played the multiplayer so I can't comment on that.
One negative I suppose is the graphics sure have not aged well. BUT for the past DECADE there has been a small loyal group of great guys who have slowly sloooowly been retexturing the whole game (They've pretty much done the 95% of the game by now), and have created some mods to allow it to run better on modern hardware. It's not Star Citizen but they've done a great job with it. The new textures they have created look great at 1080p. And I love what they did with the interiors of the ships. Their website is
They just recently made it compatible with the
version of the game, and appearntly that does not work with this version. So for now you may be better off to buy that version instead
(sorry Valve.) It's been about a year since I played the game. And I got the widescreen fix from another site but I think they have all the fixes needed on their site now.
The game runs great natively with an Xbox 360 or Xbox One controller. You can easily re-map the controls in the ESC menu. Although, you will need to use the keyboard a bit still as there is just too many different hot keys to all be mapped to those controllers. Don't worry though, in the thick of it the controller alone will be fine to adjust systems, swap weapons and do all the maneuvers needed to survive.
And that's it. As you've probably noticed I've a great deal of nostalgia for this game. But I've played it recently and I still love it just as much as I did as when I was a kid. It's not too complicated yet not too simple. The missions are lots of fun, and the story is engrossing. I personally highly recommend it.

Great game for those loving strategy, resource management, and tactics.
It is a slow, strategic unit-based game when on the battlefield, and you have infinite time to come up with your optimal strategy to destroy your enemies. You are never stressed because of lack of time to think.
When on the world map, you get to decide which trainings to assign to your soldiers, scientists, and technicians and where to allocate them to be most effective. You perform research, make weapons, etc. There is not a whole lot of buildings to be made, unlike alot of strategy games, and they only perform specific functions.
The game is slow at the start, but it picks up the pace after the Inter-galactic gate opens (don't quit playing until this point, because that is when it gets good).
The map variety is somewhat lacking on the generic maps, but there is more variety once you get into the different races and their specific maps and structures.
Same thing with units. You will only see 2 different types of enemies until the galactic gate opens, at which point 3 or 4 more types will be available.
There is also a cool RPG element to it, in that each of your soldiers/scientists/technicains levels up every once in a while, and you get to distribute Attribute points to help them perform better. Sadly, you cannot create your own character, although that would be cool to see in a DLC or future expansion.
Weapons come in good variety. There are melee weapons, old firearms from Old Earth, new firearms that can be researched, scientific lasers used by scientists, and then alien weapons of many different kinds.
Although gameplay is somewhat linear near the beginning, as you go on your research and production decisions will have more impact on how you are able to deal with certain challenges and such.
Generally a good and challenging game. Very rewarding feeling when you complete each mission. (especially if you've lost a soldier before :P)
Also, bit of advice: Your UFO can carry 7 people maximum. CRAM AS MANY PEOPLE IN THERE AS YOU CAN. If you don't, then it can be easy to be overwhelmed by enemies, and then everything gets messy.

If you're looking for a decent Xcom-esque game, then Afterlight certainly fits the bill. Although the innovations are outweighed by a number of annoyances this just means that it's not as good as one of the most beloved strategy series, no real shame in that. It is the third in the UFO series after Aftershock and Aftermath and focuses on a human colony on Mars attempting to fend off alien encroachments. So lets see how it stacks up in various categories important to squad based tactics.
. While it lacks the customization of Xcom (if you loved this, change the rating to a D), I found the hardcoded team had enough personality to carry me through. Uta (aka BattleGranny) was a highlight but the others were distinct enough without being (for the most part) grating. This is furthered by some people having dual roles, so your scientist/soldier could be medic and your engineer/soldier could be driver/bomb disposal. Nowhere near Jagged Alliance goodness of course and unfortunately voice acting in the base was at times painful and repetitive. Sadly, the aliens you can get onto your team have limited usefulness due to their slow speed so a bit of potential variety is lost there.
The lack of squad AI (other than average pathfinding) really hurts here. The game is crying out for opportunity fire, without it you need to pause every few seconds to change targets. This becomes less of an issue as the game goes on, but other problems emerge. Due to factors I'll get into later, combat is quite repetitive and there are annoying quirks with having multiple stances (eg. kneeling/ standing) in the one selection. There are fun moments and the first few times of charging in is great but it all becomes one toned once you reach the mid game, other than hazardous expeditions where you need robots. Even though my squad in Apocolypse and Terror From the Deep all ended up with the same weapons, at least you had useful psych attacks and plenty of variety before the endgame.
Similar sort of fare to any other game of this ilk, you bring in your war trophies and the eggheads find exciting new ways to splat the enemy. There's a bit of text detailing your results (as long as you go to look) which is well written and interesting and there are a good variety of research paths, it's only towards the end that you'll run out of techs. It is baffling however that there are no pictures. It sounds shallow as I type this, but I loved seeing the aliens/ weapons up close on the research screen. If you don't care about that, by all means bump the score up to a B but for me that was the biggest letdown of the game. I mean the previous UFO's did a great job on this, would've it been so hard here?
I was going to rate this as a D, but that would be ignoring the fact that your soldiers (and basebodies) go from wimps to superheroes stat-wise during the game and there is an marked difference in performance. The perk system is well implemented and the lack of any cap means your people improve right to the end. My disappointment stems from the trouble that, after midgame, your weaponry can stay the same, with the exception of the heavy stuff. The katana is ridiculously good and dual wielding pistols or a shotgun also rip through enemies and other than some addons these are not upgraded at all. So rather than stuffing around with snipers or midrange weapons (the latter of which do improve but not enough) you're best off charging in and killing them before they can fire. As I said, great fun the first few times but gets old. On the less visceral side of things, terraformation is very cool and has a noticable impact.
The idea of having four different races split into various teams all competing with you and each other for Mars is great and the diplomacy, while shallow, is at least a distinctive feature from the X games (kind of, Apocolypse did something similar but differently). The reason for the average rating is the variety within those races. For some reason, the Robots- resident pushovers of the Red Planet- seem to have a lot whereas the more interesting ones have only 1 type, oh, and a harmless pet. At least the red faction (who I spent 80% of the time fighting) had a decent number of different units but after mid game you've seen them all and only two require slightly different strategies. Compared to the number of units in the first game of the series, Afterlight is a letdown in this regard.
: Honestly, I find the tech progression more interesting than whatever kooky stuff is presented in these alien encounter games. There are a few twists and it's pretty well told (though you may want to familiarise yourself with the preceding games in the series). Although you can choose who to ally with, this doesn't impact the story. So, solid if unspectacular.
: This is what saves Afterlight from the ignomy of being worse than its prequels. While Aftershock has better enemies and both have pretty pictures with the techs and better progression, Afterlight boasts a vastly improved interface. I think I only had to look on the forums twice, most things are intuitive and aside from some nitpicking, hassles are few. Also the later release year really shows in the graphics. Again, modern games largely outdo it but it's not a huge jump.
So this gets a recommendation from me, with the following proviso. Play the Xcom series (as far back as your primitive UI/graphics tolerance allows), Jagged Alliance 2 (hey, there's aliens on one map) and the underated Spellcross first. After that you may want to play the older UFO's for the plot (I didn't and it was fine though) and if you're still finding that you have an alien zapping itch, particularly if you like your combat up close, I can happily recommend this to you.
Tips- You can bind 3 groups of soldiers to a key. Don't attack yellow until you have a hazardous area team in place. Don't get too attached to your aliens soldiers, they can't compare with humans in the long run.

All match 3 games rely on some level of RNG. Despite all the skills/spells/leveling options that offer the illusion of control, this game is far more RNG-reliant than any other match 3 game I can recall.
There are really three dynamics that cause this:
1) You alternate turns with an NPC
2) Match 4/Match 5 give whoever took the turn another free turn
3) a slim chance for other actions to create free turns
You can strategize all you want, but as long as you aren't making clear mistakes, at least half the time you will win or lose on whichever player gets cascading matches/chained free turns.
And while the story is pretty standard undead invasion stuff, there's barely even any attempt to flush anything out.

After spending quite a lot of time in this game I can say that I did enjoy it a lot.
Suggestion for those who are looking to try this game out
-By any cost avoid official servers. If you plan on playing alone play singleplayer and if you plan playing with friends do it on private servers with at least 2x exp rate.
Reasoning to avoid private server is
They are very laggy . Desync is so bad that even basic stuff like gathering resources can take you a lot longer. There are no rules on official servers , there are no admins and there's no ping lock. There are people abusing glitches and cheats all over the place. You will have players just flying picking you up and the next thing you will see that you're swimming in ocean so far that there's no way you will survive.
As for the game I really enjoyed the spell aspect of it. Turning into wyvern your self , zapping people with lightning bolt even making walls. While it has a lot of potential for pvp there has to be a lot of balancing done. The map felt fairly big and there was a lot of places to explore. Also in comparison to ark I liked that you can't just get a high level very basic dino and just destroy everything around. While taming a high level creature will definitely bring some higher stats it won't be to the point where basic flyer oneshots wild "flying tank".
Something that I really hated about this game is magic shard gathering. It's needed for everything. From low level spells up to basic base defense. And there's only one efficient way to do it - draining spell which has a chance to give you from 1-5 magic shards or just a rock or wood. I felt like I'm doing daily chore for 1 hour every day to just keep 2 shields up.
Leveling o god... it takes way too much exp to reach max level. I stopped playing as lvl 54 on official server after 184hours of playtime. Yes I could've reached lvl 60 by abusing some grinding methods but that's just stupid.
In general I felt like I could've better experience by playing on private servers and I do really feel like EA release was a bit rushed. Something like basic resource gathering should been adressed in alpha or something...
I complained about lot of stuff but I did truly enjoy this game even with all the random bugs and glitches and suggest to try it out avoiding official servers.
As for now I'm done with this game and hoping to see it in a lot more polished state after 6~months.

I picked this game up as a fan of Daedalic's point'n'click adventure games, and because I was intrigued by the inspiration the game took from Norse mythology. I was underwhelmed on both points... and yet I have a hard time giving the game a thumbs-down.
On the mythology side,
features some really beautiful artwork in its title screens for each world in the game, complete with strong original poems inspired by Old Norse poetry. These manage to create a strong atmosphere for the game, and a sense of being part of a mystical world... which does not translate at all to the gameplay.
essentially takes the standard "X has lost his Y, and must regain it by collecting lots of Z" storyline, fills in X, Y, and Z with Norse inspiration, and then slaps it onto a puzzle game. In short, the setting and story are far less relevant to your motivation to proceed than your standard "must solve puzzles and collect lots of Z" gamer mindset.
The gameplay itself, I found to be a bit of a mixed bag. The visual aesthetics of the game play were initially disappointing (though suddenly, unexpectedly impressive in a couple of rare moments), but eventually began to grow on me. The basic gameplay mechanic gives you the ability to manipulate the surrounding environment by rotating sections of the screen to alter connections and pathways in the landscape. With either 3 or 6 panels per level, finding the solution is occasionally simply a matter of combinatorics—simply keep eliminating possibilities until you find the only one that works. But with other mechanics that are introduced as the game progresses, such as switches that activate/deactivate depending on the rotation of a particular panel or runes that need to be aligned at the edges of two panels before a particular Z becomes collectable, the puzzle-solving can become enjoyably complex.
Personally, I ran into a level early in the game (in the 2nd world out of 9) that completely stumped me, and quickly lost interest in playing (see motivation, above). I came back to it several months later, more interested in collecting some more of the game's 18 achievements than in collecting Z, and found a rather straightforward solution for the puzzle that had blocked me. From there, I completed the game over the next three days. And this is why, even though I initially intended to, I can't give the game a negative review... because in those three days, I actually found myself enjoying playing and making progress.
It's not an enthusiastic recommendation, but if you happen to find this title on sale and like solving puzzles/collecting things, the artwork and (eventually) the gameplay may make the purchase worthwhile.

Civilization V is a very addictively fun strategy game. The fun historical facts thrown in, along with the personalities that have related bonuses for having that said leader make this game more challenging and increases the replayability. Having it on random is not nearly as fun, as you do not get to line up the bonuses with the map that you will play, but it does add to the difficulty, if you, for instance, get Queen Elizabeth I on a map that isn't good for naval combat, which is her biggest bonuses.
The fun with Civilization V that keeps me coming back, is it is fun to build, fun to be diplomatic, though the computer controlled players are very unpredictable and will hate you no matter what in the end. For instance, I was in a position of being friends with a map of 15 other civilizations, when just after declaring our friendship, 3 declared war on me. I took their lands and that set me to dominating the map, so I cannot complain too much. I ended up winning through culture in that match, which brings up another thing that absolutely love about this game. Victory is not any one thing. You can win by being diplomatic and convincing other civilizations to vote you as world leader; you can win by decimating your foes and taking their starting capitals (or all cities if changed in the options); you can win what I find as the easiest way to win, via the culture victory; and you can win via science, and launching a space shuttle into space, leading to the next game which I will be playing soon.
The combat is also fun to watch, and after playing for quite some time, and when you are going for a faster match, you can turn off the combat animations and have it instantly display the health changed and results. While you have the animations on, however, you can see each troop do their own specific type of attack or defense. The naval combat is my favorite thing to focus on, as having a good naval fleet is very powerful in this game. There is nothing like having an aircraft carrier, a couple of missile cruisers and a couple of nuclear submarines loaded along the shore of your next target. It takes a little bit to get built up that powerful, so you have to be diplomatic to start, especially if you try to hold off making too many troops up to that point. If you do not like naval combat and prefer ground troups, you will love the giant death robots, which obliterate their enemies. Strategy of using them is important, as you can easily lose your strongest troops if you do not plan your attacks well. The maps you choose also make a huge impact on the flow of the game, and your play style within it.
Whether you are militaristic, diplomatic, scientific, or a builder of culture, religion and/or trade, this game has a path for you to take for victory. I definitely recommend Civilization V for strategy gamers, and all gamers who might be on the fence.
I personally am not impressed with Civilization VI, and will be enjoying this game a while longer, until Civilization VII finds its way about.

There are some things to be commended about this game-- the graphics and game mechanics in many ways do the original BFG tabletop game justice, and fans of the old Games Workshop Specialist Games may enjoy it simply from a fluff standpoint. It's a joy to see Imperial ships animated in a video game at last.
The fleets each have their own flavor, though I can't really vouch for the balance of the game. Certainly using the environment to your advantage is a major tactical priority, as is customizing your ship's abilities and micromanaging at LoL levels.
Unfortunately, however, the game seems to stop short of anything approaching its real potential. it sometimes presents mission types which are as often frustrating as fun. The gameplay tends to be repetitive. Many of the most fun scenarios from the tabletop game-- planetary bombardments, Exterminatus-- are missing. There's no campaign option for a group of players the way a true BFG grognard would want-- the only campaign map used is for the single player Imperial campaign. Levelling up your Admiral grants new abilities and roster slots, but in the end it doesn't realy feel like progress; the ships look the same and the benefits are small.
It also honestly feels like GW/Tindalos cut a lot of corners: the ship's captain portraits are just different heads pasted on the same body, the 2D art cutscenes tend to cut and paste sprites, the voice acting's passable but the dialog and world-building-- the latter being the soul of 40K-- is lackluster or absent. There's no variance in the ship models, two ships of the same class are just exact copies, and no option to paint or customize the ships (truly a sin from a 40K perspective). There's even typos.
And while it has many things to commend it, at the end the game just feels... shallow. Unfinished. It has the feel of a mobile game, not a PC title. If Games Workshop wants to bring 40K into the video game world, and it should, it needs to stop doing so in half-measures.

Ok... I played it almost 70 hours. And i still have a pending refund request.
So where do i begin?
First of all, it's actually a very promising game. It does catch the spirit of 40k, spaceship battles, competetive multiplayer, and all. Problem is, all is beneath is a thick mud of technical issues. Half of my games, i encounter with the issues about;
a) Randomly ships stop responding to any given command. Then it crashes.
b) You lose all of conrols. Including the ability to chat. Then it crashes.
c) It goes alright. No apparent issues. Then it crashes.
d) Skills stop working unless you set them on auto mode. Then, it also crashes.
And real problem is, all those issues did persist after 2 patches. It had an extensive period of early access, a seemingly good period of time to solve those. But it was not. Even after release, even after it was patched some good amount of times, it's still a broken mess.
Ok, it's about the technical problems, now let's move to others.
I'm not actually a competative multiplayer person. But this game actually offers much about it, which i would not deny. And still it fails to deliver, that i would explain.
First, it does not offer any kind of ballance based on personal skill (elo). You can easily face a brand new fleet with your maxed out death squad. Or vice versa. So, while it is one of the games that have most the competative potential, it fails right ahead. Your victories or defeats, do not carry further than some bonus renown or... anything, after some point.
Second, the ballance between races are terrible. I was an Eldar player, and people literally begged me to not to bring a battleship in some games. Rightfully. While there were ways to deal with it, it required lots of specific loadouts, and if the opponent were orks, Only way that could work were was bringing minimal amount of line ships and fill the rest with escorts.  On the other hand, Nova cannon spams truly gave me a pause. A pause.
The third problem is, the playerbase. I don't play FPS games, like CS:GO or battlefield. But compared to my previous experiences, i have never seen such immature and intolerable people in one place. It feels like all the 12 years olds suddenly took an interest in sci-fi, and decided that this game is place to settle. Brace for the impact...
If you are thinking about to buy this game, consult your psychologist first. It does have a kick aimed to your nerves.

Do you like strategy games? Do you like giving orders to gigantic golden floating snowploughs with guns strapped to the back? Do you just really like beating yourself over the head with a Games Workshop hammer every three years, and haven't had a Dawn of War game in so long that you're beginning to get withdrawal symptoms?
Don't worry, Tindalos Interactive has you covered.
For those of you who may have tried Battlefleet Gothic: Armada during its beta test - don't worry, it's a lot better now. This game is actually surprisingly well polished (barring the occasional egregious typo), and while I can't claim to have played any multiplayer yet, I can promise you, the campaign is tippity-top quality. Golden and bedazzled with two-headed eagles, from start to finish. In fact, I'd argue it's better than the Dawn of War campaigns ever were - it completely negates the old irritation that DoW campaigns fell prey to - that of allowing the story's interesting material to congeal at the beginning and end. This is one well-paced story mode.
The only real criticism I can make, beside the occasional crash at the start of a battle, is that the game's friendly advice and some of its tooltips (particularly where regards convoy missions) are utter tosh. Don't split up your transports - keep them together. I've never lost a ship that way. Not much of a criticism, huh? I guess the game could use more fleets and factions to play with - but then, Tindalos has that in the works. Check back in six months.
I'm writing this review in the full and complete knowledge that you have probably already long since made up your mind about whether this is the kind of game you'd enjoy. If you like playing ship-versus-ship line battles (in space) (with snowploughs) this is the game for you. If you don't, go read another positive review. There's no shortage.
It's pretty enough, but the puzzles IMXP are very much "read my mind" puzzles, and the story is obtuse and incomprehensible. Style over substance here.

If you're a fan of the Rainbow Six series (Rainbow Six, Rainbow Six Lockdown etc) then you're in for a real treat. This is a 3D first person shooter with great graphics and low computer overhead meaning it will run on lower spec machines. The light mapped graphics stand up to the best graphics of today's games despite being many years old. Don't get me wrong, it isn't an older title in the sense that it looks aged because this game rocks in graphics and playability.
The single player game is an incredible story driven adventure that finds a squad leader unravelling a mystery that progresses through a series of very large and complex levels tackling concrete goals given to you by your commanding officer.
In this incarnation as the squad leader you direct the actions of your three man team through orders given through your controller (mouse, keyboard, joystick etc). The command system is very simple yet complex enough for you to apply real tactics to just about any situation.
Your team mates act intelligently and tactically as well providing dialogue during and between battles. Working with the smaller team makes for a much more action packed and tense game, where often you will find yourself in fire fights far outnumbered. In such cases you must rely on stealth and superior tactics to overcome the enemy.
The game also includes breach and clear mechanics when your storms an entrance, you can use flashbangs, fragmentation grenades, smoke grenades (great combined with the squad's IR vision mode) and white phosphorous grenades (combined thermal fragmentation and gas grenade).
The game also includes a great multiplayer option with team and non-team deathmatch game variations. Often it comes down to search and destroy vs ambush tactics and leads to some hairy and memorable moments in battle.
+ Top notch graphics
+ Great controls
+ Good sound
+ Excellent Multiplayer (though the mp community seems non-existent as of this writing)
10/10 and well worth the price.
