I can safely say that this is the best 40K game I have ever played, and I have played many of them. I am not familiar with the tabletop game itself, but this rendition catches the overall feel and aesthetic of the 40K universe almost perfectly.
Let's break it down, here are the ups and downs:
Neutral:
* The difficulty, assuming you play on Hard or Heroic.
Make no mistake about it, Armada is a very difficult game. Here, "Hard" means exactly that - the game is going to grab you by the throat and force you to GIT GUD or ragequit.
This is good in the sense that it not only gives you a true challenge, but it forces you to think outside the box and device strategies for winning battles. This is not an RTS where you can just select all units and roflstomp everything in sight - try that and you will die very quickly.
At the same time...well...there are several points, especially in the mid-late part of the campaign, where the battles simply feel plain unfair to the point of being broken. Enemies will start to outnumber, outgun and (importantly!) outrange you to the point where you wonder if you are even supposed to be ABLE to win battles anymore.
Pros:
* Great attention to detail. Ships and skyboxes are meticulously crafted.
* The AI is actually pretty good and offers challenging battles.
* Good variety in available scenarios
* Great customization - highly diverse fleets, ships, skills and upgrades make for an enormous variety in gameplay and strategy.
* Great voice acting.
Cons:
* Writing this, the game is in need of some balancing. This is likely to be fleshed out in coming updates however.
* Campaign gets pretty repetitive over time, as you have long stretches where you are limited to running the same kinds of missions.
All in all, great game. Don't miss it.

Forget the 40k license and don't let that buy forgiveness here.  The campaign is not so much difficult as it is mean.  If you lose two battles, then you get punished by only being able to declare one battle per turn - which means the enemies gain ground twice as fast.  It's an instant death spiral, and there is no "retry" button when you lose.
Hey, but you're here for the multiplayer right?  That's the real reason someone wants this game - to play with their friends, or maybe competitively against random strangers, or even dream of league play.  Well, none of that is going to happen at all.   I'll list this out very specifically:
1. You cannot invite a friend to a 1 vs 1 game.  Period.
2. You can only play 2v2 against 2 random opponents if you invite a friend.
3. You cannot ever choose who your opponents are.  So you'll never fight anybody you know.
4. There is no comp-stomp cooperative PVE.
5. You cannot choose what points limit of battle you're going to play - you always play maximum size for your level (which there are 8 ranks).  So, 250, 300, 450, 700, etc...  You'll always play top tier, and have no choice in it.
6. Balance - don't even consider that the four factions will be in any semblance of "balance".  Even in the tabletop that doesn't happen.  However, GW compensates for this by letting you have 1000 points to spend and you buy units and abilities from that pool.  Overpowered things cost more, so it sorta balances out.  Here, my cruiser costs 100 points, and so does everybody else.  And it doesn't matter if I have rank 1 or rank 8 upgrades on it, still 100 points.  So, good luck with that.
7. Multiplayer connection problems are fierce and constant.  2v2 games rarely complete without one of the four players getting dropped.  There's a particularly nasty bug where even in 1v1 you can have the camera snap to the corner of the map and none of your key or mouse inputs work - yet you're still in the game.  There's also no protection against alt-F4 logging out if you're losing either, so I never know if someone quit because I was winning or they got bugged up.
8. If Tindalos doesn't get their act together QUICKLY then this game will be a ghost town in 2 months or less.  Look at steamcharts for the population of their previous title Stellar Impact:
Month 	        Avg. Players
Last 30 Days 	        1.8
April 2016 	        1.9
March 2016 	        1.8
February 2016 	1.9
January 2016 	        2.6
There is some hope here, if they fix this thing.   The player base has been 100% the nicest folks.  Everybody says "gg" after a match.  Nobody has been a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about losing or gloated about winning.  Mainly we discuss bugs, or compliment each other on a tactic that worked.  There hasn't been a lot of "cheese" since the big nerfing that went on in the first patch.
Look, I don't expect that my Orks are ever going to be competitive against Eldar because they're super fast long range and I'm super slow short range, so they can just kite me all day from beyond taunt radius.  I'm fine with that, because it can be fixed in due time.  The inability to play with your friends and inability to play a match to completion due to disconnects is going to break this game's back before it has lived long enough to get fixed.
Tindalos still has Stellar Impact priced at $10, while it has ZERO player population.  It's not a horrible game, but even the best game is worthless if nobody is playing it.  Why aren't they wise enough to drop it to $2 or even go freemium with it and pump the population back up, and then make money on DLC?  If they're not saavy enough to see that writing on the wall, then I have zero faith they're going to do right by this title either.
The 40k license buys a lot of forgiveness about balance, because 40k never had any balance in any incarnation.  But it makes us double sensitive about quality - and you gentlemen are squandering that carelessly.  This game needed 6 more months of closed beta patching before you let it hit the street.  Now it might be too late.

Rainbow Six Vegas is yet another part of Rainbow Six series, tactical-themed FPS. This time around there are no more planning and you control only two other squad member. Yet it's all good fun. It came out in 2006 and was made by Ubisoft. Also, it was made for X360 first, so it came into PC territory like a proud direct port, lacking slightly in options and not optimized very goodly. At least it got patched up since then.
It also came out for X360, PS3 and PSP. The first two should be similar, but PSP is different game. You play solo in that one. It doesn't interest me not even slightly, I am here to see squad members work along with me. You are supposedly saving those two squad members, being lone wolf.
Technically, well, yea. Port from Xbox 360. Used to be unoptimized, but I am sure that computers nowdays can easily just power through it. It still however rarely freezes for half-minute. Steam Overlay doesn't work either, have fun alt-tabbing.
Even worse, PC version did not support widescreen monitors at release! And while they patched widescreen in later, it still doesn't every wide resolution and even worse, the HUD is still designed for 4:3 monitor. So do some full-screen graphics. Like "to be continued" screen. Oh, yea, cliffhanger alert.
But I am pretty sure that there are fan patches to fix those.
Multiplayer servers were supposedly shutted down, but it actually still works, just requires UPlay account, at least now. Yep, new players will have to fancy around with email adress as nickname, from what I understood. Well, at least it works.
Community seems to be kinda there. One times I tried there were no servers, other times there were 5 of them, with players. Seems like people only play Cooperative modes only nowadays, you will not find any Competetive players vs players. Sadly, they all seems to be quite protective, as all the servers I encountered were password protected, so I didn't get to check out multiplayer in these few days.
And well, what can I say. It sure was made as a show off for Xbox 360, showing off itself with Unreal Engine 3, while trying to be accessiable to new players. Though, to be honest, I really dislike graphics in this part. That's because while they are cool on technical side, the art style is just awful. Or, rather, it feels like developers applied a really bad brown hue blur effect all over the screen. Music also isn't hot, being urgent but not very awesome. Shame that Rainbow Six main theme is gone.
Oh well, at least Vegas setting is kinda cool.
Also, yep, this Rainbow Six is now all about telling a good story and having fun. Not more planning before mission, head into action, main hero. Take on them with your regenerative health, until you get instakilled by sniper shot and realize that you can't just charge on even on Normal. Nope, it's still tactical, somewhat, sorry Doomguys.
It also got cover system implented, where you hold a button and go into third person mode, as Logan hides behind a wall. You are supposed to spend most of your time in this mode, but personally, I kept forgetting that I can do it and instead kept crouching behind corners, aiming and shooting from the first person mode. Rainbow Six Vegas was an effective and divisive reboot of the Rainbow Six series. It took the previously slow and tactical shooter series into a much more modern cover shooter direction. I say divisive because Rainbow Six Vegas caused a split in the fanbase between people who wanted a faster cover shooter and people who wanted a slower game where you plan your movements before executing.
Rainbow Six Vegas largely takes place in the titular city of Las Vegas. You play as "Logan" an operative for the titular "Rainbow" special forces team who enters the city to combat a terrorist threat. The storytelling is a bit muddled and you generally don't pay attention to it that much. It mostly serves to get you from point A to Point B and shoot some baddies.
What Rainbow Six Vegas is most well known for it's cover shooter gameplay. While it is faster than all of the previous Rainbow Six games it's noticeably slower than say, Call of Duty or Gears of War. The game is built around using your squadmates to move to different positions so you can flank or take enemies out from a distance. It's much more forgiving as well since it has regenerating health and the enemy AI is fairly dumb. Since you die very quickly the game doesn't devolve into run and gun but it still feels much slower than it should.
Besides the campaign, Rainbow Six Vegas also has multiplayer and Terrorist Hunt. The latter is where the game excels in my opinion. In Terrorist Hunt, you and a few friends can team up to take out AI enemies in a series of multiplayer maps. It's very enjoyable and replayable and is where the bulk of the time you spend playing the game will end up. Deathmatch is also available but good luck finding a game for it.
It's hard to really describe the original Rainbow Six Vegas without describing how much better it's sequel was. While I do recommend the game if you're a fan of modern shooters and desire something that requires slightly more thought behind it, the sequel comes generally more recommended.

As much as you want to encourage independent development in gaming, there are truly some creations that should never see the light of day. Take
. It's far from the worst horror title on here but it shares a lot of their traits: it's dull, sparsely plotted, ugly, buggy and cobbled together with pre-purchased assets to the point where there are copies of 'The Daily News' lying around proclaiming that 'UNITY MAGIC IS HERE TO STAY!!!'. Come on. Really? You want that in your horror game?
The stand-out mechanic here is that sprinting will eventually kill you. A red haze closes in around your field of vision as your heart begins to give out, doing more and more damage as you go. There's three enemies in the game: a bird, some sort of brain damaged starved gorilla that honks like a goose and the invisible water monster from
and all of them will kill you in a single hit if you've been abusing the run key... which you will have been on account of it taking too bloody long to walk between locations.
It's the random cobbled together nature of
, the sheer laziness of its design that kills it. First you're in a public park trying to grab a key from a crazed magpie, then you're running around a sewer flipping off power boxes, now you're in a refinery running around a lava pit...? What is this, Quantum Leap? You wander from a submerged flood tunnel to a warehouse in the space of one door. Good lord. Hope they're storing bath toys in there.
Like I said, I don't want to crap all over what is obviously somebody's very early design effort but just because you make something like this doesn't mean you should sell it. This is the kind of project you make and revel in the experience of simply having made it, take what you've learned and move on; not charge £6.99 for it on Steam.

Summary:
The Deed is a short but unique experiance worth playing, especially with such a small asking price.
Detailed:
I've always had a fantasy for a game where you play as a murderer in the murderer mystery. A combination of the freedom of assassination methods given in Hitman, with game mechanics allowing you to frame other suspects and create false alibis.
The Deed may not match this lofty fantasy game in my head, but it delivers a satisfying but short experiance.
You play as the murderer and must murder your sister, whilst framing the other people in the house or making it look like suicide. To do this you have to to interact with the characters to learn new opportunities and plant 'evidence' around the house and choose an appropriate murder weapon.
You'll be suprised on the details the game picks up on during your first few playthroughs. For example I used a knife in the kitchen as the murder weapon, but I talked to the maid in the kitchen, so the police investigator picked up on that deducing I could've potentially taken the knife. After doing the same and not talking to the maid, the police investigator was oblivious to it, only suspecting the maid.
Once you've played through it a few times and learnt how to manipulate the events of the game, framing your target and minimising suspicion is simple and satisfying.
Some flaws include repeated dialogue getting tedious during your multiple playthroughs.

Puzzle Quest is a fantastic little ''gem'' of a casual match-3 puzzle game with some RPG elements thrown in. The story is the typical fantasy fair with orcs, ogres and the like, the characters are usually stereotypes, but can be interesting at times. The game really shines in its blending of match-3 puzzle mechanics with RPG spells and stats. There's also a few different modes that come from different actions you can take, such as interesting puzzles you have to solve in order to capture creatures to learn their spells, or a modified version of a standard battle where you have to match anvil shaped gems to craft items  It really helps break up the monotony of random battles. The game can get really intense and there will be times when it feels like there's a ton of things going right for the computer, but make sure to always think ahead when mathing certain gems and it will make things much better.  The one gripe I have with the game is the constant random battles you can't avoid unless you train your mount to the appropriate level, which takes a lot of grinding in and of itself, so it can drag on, but when that happens you can always just quit and come back later.
The music is also something I wanted to touch on. It's surprisingly good. Some of the tracks are a bit "eh" in terms of sound quality, but what some lack in sound quality others make up in composition quality. Many of the songs are exceedingly catchy and really help to convey the mood of a certain location or bolster the feeling of winning/losing in a battle. The boss battle theme and the Dwarven theme are probably my favorites.
If you enjoy match-3 games with a surprising bit of depth, RPGs with a twist, or both, then you'll probably be able to sink many, many hours into this addictively fun game. It's a great time waster, especially since it can run on most any rig, I personally play it on my laptop in class sometimes. It's a game that's been on everything from the DS, PSP, Xbox 360 and even old, mobile phones, I've owned it on my old circa 2006 Nokia and fat DS, even, and definitely do not regret picking it up a third time.

*NON SPOILER REVIEW*
The Deed is a great example of a simple but fun game, no deep epic storyline with twisting conflicting backstory or characters you're forced to give a damn about. The game sets itself up with the bare essentials and it is up to you, the player, to explore further into the game's story. Now what makes this game stand out is how this is optional and how it feels much like a board game such as Cluedo, or even a choose-your-own-adventure book. You have the characters, the premise, the 'clues' and methods. There's multiple ways to approach each event that takes place throughout the day.
With this, The Deed indeed gives off a natural fruition of replayability and it's unlikely you will succeed in committing the crime the first couple of tries. You should note who you talk to, when you do and for what reason - but be careful - revealing the truth of why you did to any NPCs can alter your chances of being caught or not as they may seem suspicious of your behaviour. Given the natural conflict you have with your father, even being kind can give your purpose away. It truly, truly feels like your choices have actual, permanent changes to both the NPCs and environment.
It's amazing how a game less than $1 can offer so much fun, replayability and investment from an immersive and interesting point of view and do so much right more than AAA modurn gaemz (especially from the overrated joke that is Telltale Games and more recently Life is Strange). This game proves you do not need top-tier voice acting, explosions, quest markers and a mini-map to spoon-feed the player into being artificially interested in the game's world.
As I said, this brings me back to the days of board games and choose-your-own-adventure, not many video games can do that for me nowadays so it's refreshing to see one that does it - and does it right - for a criminally underpriced price. I strongly recommend this game to players who love choice and freedom, board games, RPGs and detective stories. I understand the simplicity in nature, the questionable 2D art style and lack of dudebro shooting will put alot of people off, but I feel given the price of the game it doesn't matter if you don't even like the game as you'll probably just refund it anyway.
A couple of things I want improved however, is perhaps a real-time on-screen inventory system as opposed to the default JRPG-esque inventory menu, more original sound effects to boot and an in-game clock that you can view anytime. Perhaps with the grandfather clock. Aside from that, I would like to see more games of this nature by this developer - more scenarios in different environments?

Ok, first, my background:
I'm a PC player, I don't own one of the latest consoles. I used to have an X-Box, and I had DoA3 and DoA2 Ultimate back then. Haven't had the occasion to play any other of the DoA games since then, so there won't be any comparison between this version and another one.
First of all, pay attention to what controlers you have plugged to your PC, I had my old Sidewinder on, it prevented me from getting past the autosave notice screen.
My PC isn't state of the art, and I'm playing with old Logitech Dual Action gamepads, on Windows 10.
It looks just dandy on my PC, it runs perfectly, I can put AA alright. It plays just how I remember it from the old Xbox games (excepted I've clearly lost my touch, man, I can hardly counter anything for now).
I play with japanese voices and french subtitles, because usually dubbings are garbage (DoA5 defaulted on English voices for me and, apparently, the comment on dubbs is true whatever the language :p). Apparently, a part of the cast comes from Virtua Fighter 5. Some of those seem to retain an English voice, and the sound quality is different (lower). It's a detail, a bit annoying, but nothing major.
There's a few players online. Latency is equal to your and your opponent's connection, nothing more, nothing less. I've have an opponent where it was like playing  on the same computer and he was sitting next to me (zero lag or anything), and one where it played like in slow-motion, rather than usual cut-and-go lag thing. I don't know if it's a feature or not, it's not great, but at least it's playable, unlike how it usually goes.
I heard you can't choose who you fight againstn which sounds like a bummer for those who have friends with the game too, who want to play online.
Pros:
- it runs great on my computer, I've had no glitch so far either.
- it looks pretty good still, of course you won't get all amazeballs on it, but the DOA series has its visual style that's unlikely to evolve much no matter what tech evolutions we're going to get through (excepted the monkey, what a lazy modeling job, seriously :p). More polys, better flowing hair, stuff like that, yeah. More realistic faces or whatnot? You're never going to get that with DOA.
- It's on PC, I mean, we don't have much choices when it comes to Beat them up on PC, unless you want to sell a kidney to get the latest Street Fighter.
- it's a DoA game - if you've ever played a DoA game and enjoyed the experience, you won't feel lost, it's more of the same, everything is the same, just updated, with a bit more of everything (34 characters or something? it seems they've added characters from other games, like some kind of cross-over game).
For the cons:
- there's the english voices forced on the VF5 characters whatever language you pick
- the DLC, seriously, the price? Good thing, there's only one I'd consider buying, a new character (a Samurai Warrior one, apparently). The rest is just clothes, so they're of no importance.
- online play has no dedicated server, so connection is only as good as the worst of either players' connection.
- apparently can't pick who you fight against online.
- the story is pants... naaaah, seriously, who cares? :p
- It's a DoA game - if you didn't like the previous ones for any reason, you won't like this one either.
Conclusion:
So, if you ignore all the weird people who will buy this version just to compare it to their superduper console version which was bound to be superior anyway (we're not talking about an upgrade frrom an old console game like Valkyria Chronicles, we're talking about a port from a very recent game on last generation consoles. What do you expect, seriously?), if you have no access to a console, if you played a DoA game before and enjoyed it, you're going to like it. If you're curious, give it a go, it's a pretty damn good Beat them up. It's pretty, it runs great, and it's fun.

Like many others, I found this game interesting, as well as unique. The prospect of the game is how and who do you have your sister killed and framed for, as titled,–"The Deed"–it's quite dark, bringing in the question to not only the main character, but you. Why? Was it worth it at the end?
There are multiple ways in killing your sister, and a couple of people you can frame. The way you plant false evidence, the weapons you choose, and where you were. Honestly however, the game is quite short, with it only lasting around 10-15 minutes. But with the variety of ways to kill your sister and who to frame, I would say you would be able to squeeze out at most 2 hours. There is minimal dialogue because of this, so you don't really know much about the character and his "life away from his family" other than that they are dysfunctional and your sister is "mentally insane" (but for it's length it's a lot) which makes it straightfoward; find someone to frame, find an evidence to plant, find a weapon to use to murder, and run to a place.
However! The dialogue is actually quite an interesting feature in the game. What I mean is, depending on how you plan to interact with your family, the butler, and the maid, may or may not bite your butt back during the inspection, which can consequently make you suspicious. Most games, tend to overlook this, which would of made the game more unique to you.
Pros:
Interesting genre of a game
Atmosphere is fitting and nice
Many ways of doing "The Deed" resulting in multiple runs
Dialogue affects outcome
It reflects on you at the end, was it worth the inheritance?
Cons:
I have not much to say, other than it being short and maybe a lack of voice acting.
All in all, the game is an interesting experience, and for a buck for 2 hours is highly worth it.

Cute graphics - I've seen one comparison to Wind Waker, but to me it was a little of that and a little of Okami.
Story - Also reminded me strongly of Okami, which is never a bad thing. It had just the right balance of exposition and info to gameplay, also.
Music - Excellent. Fit the game, without being intrusive, which is what all video game music should strive for.
Combat - I came to this directly after fumbling around in Dark Souls, and I feel like the combat in this is just as harsh and unforgiving. I wasn't expecting to have to kite in this, and exploit the fact that enemy health doesn't regenerate while you run and eat healing items. Basically every enemy killed me in one or two hits, and in the case of some of the enemies, that would mean having to run across the entire island again to get back to them.
Quests and map - The quests were a little unclear, and the map was no help at all. Granted, the island is small, and there are only so many places to check for things, but with no indication of even a general area to look in, it had me running around aimlessly until I stumbled upon the thing I was looking for. Also, that the text doesn't change after you get the item is a bit confusing. I'm super ADD and fight with brain fog every day, and by the time I got my coconut I'd already forgotten what I was supposed to do with it. The shrines aren't even on the map, and there's nowhere to get more detailed quest info, like "once you get the coconut, take it to the shrine to _____, which is on the western side of the island". Or something like that.
Overall, for a first game, it's pretty good. The concept, art, and audio are really solid, and while I did have a couple of brief instances where my framerate tanked for no clear reason, it ran well on my system. The combat, as I said, can be challenging, mostly due to controls, which could use some tightening and the option to change mouse sensitivity within the game. I'd also love to see an in-game cursor, I feel like it would help a number of things. The developers seem to be really active, as the game only came out a couple of weeks ago and they've already released a patch to fix some bugs and clarify some things in both the game and the game's menu. I think this is a really promising start for these developers, and I hope Maui turns into a bigger game at some point, because it's really quite lovely!

Mix together a bizarre regenerating health system that seems to randomly choose whether you die in one hit or not, which defeats the purpose of regenerating health, and cover-based shooting in flashy, claustrophobic Casino environments and you have Rainbow Six Vegas.
I beat this on the 360 when it originally came out and had a fun time with it, though I don't remember it being anywhere near this frustratingly bull♥♥♥♥♥♥  Enemies will no-scope you from cover from 200 feet away with a shotgun and insta-kill you *SOMETIMES* or maybe do barely any damage to you.  This inconsistency makes the game feel like bipolar mess which can either make you feel like breezing through it, or smashing your keyboard in rage because of being one-shotted by some♥♥♥♥♥hat hiding behind something you should clearly be able to shoot through, only to reload the checkpoints.  And yet, I still found myself wanting to push onward and beat the annoying♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
It combines a beyond simplified interface compared to previous Rainbow Six games with no pre-planning, but offers reasonable weapon customization.  You can freely add a silencer to almost any assault rifle or pistol, and it gives you the option of using the shield which I found worked and sometimes it didn't.  The AI is reasonably smart, and will try and flash bang you, use lethal grenades when you're using the shield a lot, and I found that they can lose track of you during a fire-fight.  Silencers appear useless at first because of the linearity of the game, but I found it helps keep the AI guessing where you are, so that they won't always be able to find where the fire is coming from during combat, or right before, so it's less about finishing objectives undetected and more about utilizing stealth as a way to ambush.
The objectives are quite visually appealing with lots of interesting design choices in the environment, and enemies don't just instantly ragdoll when you kill them, as you'll see a mix of ragdoll with the physics of where you shot them plus an animation based on where you shot them, which makes kills very satisfying.  Overall, Rainbow Six is no longer the tactical shooter it was.  It is now a Cover-shooter, with tactical elements.  I suppose the change was evident from Raven Shield to Lockdown, but it seems they've done what Lockdown couldn't, which was making the game interesting for the player.
P.S. For some reason, Vegas 1 looks better than Vegas 2, and plays better than Vegas 2 as well.

Saints Row 3 was my first entry into the series. I had a blast with the intentionally ridiculous gameplay, including GTA-ing cars by jumping through the windshield, killing enemies via "Testicular manslaughter", streaking around without a stitch of clothing on, flying VTOLs to cause mayhem, cruising around with homies, the list goes on. The plot was also hilariously memorable, particularly the good ending where the Boss pursues Killbane to Mars... and it turns out to be a make-believe film set.
Everything's back in Saints Row 4, but in a very recycled way that reeks of COD. I get the feeling that the devs got lazy and wanted to reuse as many SR3 assets as they could, and structured the plot to fit this. You play as the President of the United States, who gets abducted (along with other Saints) during an alien invasion and has his/her mind stuck into a Matrix-esque simulation of Steelport, the city that SR3 was set in. The President breaks free with the help of a few key Saints like Kinzie Kensington, but it's too late - Earth is destroyed. The President and the remaining Saints end up living on an alien ship. For some reason, the Saints decide it's easier to fight the aliens by remote-tapping into their Matrix, rather than assaulting their mothership. The President re-enters the Matrix and frees even more abducted Saints, and causes mayhem in the Matrix which somehow weakens the aliens. I haven't gotten that far into the game yet so I don't know what'll happen next.
The gameplay takes place almost entirely inside the Matrix. Outside the Matrix you just run around the ship talking to your Saints nothing more. There are a few super-lame romance scenes that you can do over and over again with most of your Saints. If you want combat, you're going into the Matrix, which recycled just about everything from SR3, from the building geometry to the car models to the HUD elements! I almost thought I'd launched SR3 by mistake. Sure, the police cars show alien symbols, there are alien billboards everywhere, and the water is intentionally displayed as a graphical "glitch", but otherwise the city of Steelport is copy-and-paste. There was no need to introduce the player character as the US President - that really made no difference to the plot and seemed like a marketing ploy more than anything else.
Yeah... it sounds like the perfect excuse to recycle assets instead of putting the effort into creating a new world. SR4 tries to distinguish itself from its predecessor by giving you God-like abilities within the Matrix. You can jump as high as a plane, run at super speed, throw fire and ice from your hands, levitate objects like Magneto, and so on. Unfortunately, all these powers, even at basic levels, feels very cheap and give you little incentive to get into vehicles, which were a big part of the SR3 experience. It's almost like having cheat codes turned on by default. It's also very easy to grind for the resources and cash (or "cache" as the game calls it) to upgrade your abilities to the max, thanks to Clusters (essentially upgrade points for powers) being located literally everywhere, and also a wealth of very easy side missions like store hacking and tower liberating.
It's fun for a bit, but it gets old quickly. I don't see myself finishing the game anytime soon. Maybe in a few months when I'm super bored...
On the technical side, the game seems to use an unchanged SR3 engine, which means the graphics look very dated, but the game will run very well even on lower end PCs. It's fairly well optimized with responsive PC controls, good graphical setting options, and overall excellent performance. The controls sometimes show some console-itis, especially when changing weapons, but otherwise are perfectly serviceable.
For those new to the Saints Row series, I recommend buying SR3 and sticking with it. SR4 may spoil your impressions.

When I played Braid in 2008, I didn't pay attention to one puzzle and finished the game using a walkthrough. Since then, I have matured as a gamer and I decided to revisit Braid. To my surprise, I began to complete puzzles without looking at walkthrough and by the end I completed the game completely without looking at a guide, except for one puzzle.
Everyone knows what Braid is; it is famous for being pretentious, but thoughtful, confusing and difficult, enigmatic, but engaging. All of these adjectives could be valid, and I agree with some of them, but not all of them. Then, really it is up to you to make out what this game really is to you.
At its core, it's a puzzle game. What I enjoy about the puzzles is that they don't require precision or finding specific objects to open other objects so that you can move forward, but instead require you to logically understand the mechanics in front of you. Each world has a few levels and each level have a few puzzles in them. There is a symbiosis between each puzzle in each level, meaning that if you understand what happens on the first puzzle then the next puzzle just adds to the second puzzle. Gosh, this makes the game feel gratifying since again, the mechanics are mostly due to you understanding the logic of the game.
Now there are problems with a few puzzles. There are a 2 puzzles that require you to do a "jumping trick", which I won't ruin for you, but I felt that these 2 puzzles really detracted from the overall clean puzzle design. That is my only problem with the games puzzles, but I also might not like these puzzles because one of the puzzles took me a few days to solve and the other one is the one puzzle I had to look online for the solution.
Overall, you could play this game, but you don't have to. I enjoyed it, you might not. It's critically acclaimed, but so are a lot of games. Besides all of that, it's what you want from your game. I never liked puzzle games, but now that I have played this game, it's the only genre I want to play. Thank you, braid.

Flying around, destination to destination and rappelling down from a helicopter to engage a great threat, be it terrorists in Mexico, Vegas or the Hoover dam, this is one of the best (if not the best) co-op tactical shooter experiences you will get.
Seriously one of the best R6 games out there. The graphics are great (once you adjust brightness to around 4-5, which makes the contrast much nicer and the game look less bland) and it seriously beats out its sequel, Vegas 2. Interesting level designs, believable and awesome attention to detail- from the wrecked slums of a Mexican ghetto, to the wealth driven Vegas strip with poker chips flying out of slot machines, it's truly a wonderful achievement for a 2006 game. The shooting is wonderful, with a great cover system that, while not entirely realistic, is great for a tactical title. The AI shout commands at eachother, exclaim words of disbelief as their comrades perish, and your allies are not brick stupid like in Vegas 2. It is not without flaws, though. The AI will ocassionally spazz out, this is easily fixed by ordering them to move somewhere, and the game has not been updated since 07, its highest resolution setting makes the Xbox One giggle- this is easily fixed with an auto-patcher
and brings the game up to date. The game lacks a lot of graphics options, which were supposedly included via a launcher the CD version came with.
The story is wonderful, very compelling and intriguing- very Tom Clancy-ish. You can tell they actually cared when making this game, as opposed to its rushed out, still-the-same-graphics and models, sequel.
If you want my honest truth, this game is everything Vegas 2 should have been. The customization is the same, the music is better, the audio is better, the settings are much better and the characters are not utterly stupid. The ending to this game is far more rewarding than the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t they threw in with the sequel, not to mention the plot twists actually make sense and will make you go "oh" as opposed to make you giggle like a rampant meth addict like it will in the sequel.
If you want a serious, interesting co-op experience...buy this. If you want a game with same-same guns and a decent unlock system, with the same graphics as its predecessor (06 vs 08, same ♥♥♥♥ing graphics and models, gg) you'll want to buy that POS named Vegas 2.

For example, not quite a spoiler but if you want a hint:

The Deed is a simple RPGMaker game where you control a man trying to get away with the murder of his sister so that you'll be the sole heir to the family fortune: you'll be able to explore the house, steer conversations in a certain way and gather one weapon and one evidence piece to try and pin said murder on someone else, or make it look like a suicide.
While sporting simple mechanics and low production values The Deed's concept and its trial and error gameplay are good enough to make it a worthwhile purchase.
-novel concept
-decent amount of different weapons and evidence pieces to find and plant
-each dialogue has three different answers and they can raise suspicions on certain people, or yourself
-there's enough different ways to get away with the murder to provide a fair amount of replay value
-very simple graphics
-basic sounds
-skipping the intro and all the dialogue you've already seen can get annoying in the long run when replaying the game
I've made about five different attempts at murdering the sister in my hour with The Deed and got away with it four times, but only once I was completely successful in pinning it on someone else: it was pretty fun and once you play once or twice and see how everything works it becomes a sort of puzzle where you try to find out who is related to each object/evidence piece/dialogue choice.
Sure you can't expect high production values, deep characters or an amazing story but the game works well and the concept alone is novel enough to warrant at least a few playthroughs until you can get away with murder. Adding to this the fact that the game is less than a dollar I'd say it's worth a shot to experience it for yourself.

I will keep this review short. I am sorry to say that I give this game a thumbs down.
Now sit down you little pervert, I am going to tell you a great, well maybe not great..more like sad..story..
Way back before Dead or Alive 5 released on PC I remembered how much fun I had had playing it on the 360, so I checked the forums and read the store page description - online added in 3 months, looked like decent support from KT and Team Ninja would follow release, and they replied on the forums that they would not be bowing to the SJW crowd with their character models, which earned my respect and a pre-order. Then, it all went down hill faster than you could say, "but bouncy boobs!"
It all started with the initial slap in the face - PC gamers did not get all the stages that the consoles received, nor even all of the stage SFX(we still have the stage-outs, though..oh joy!), and then the backhand- the game's graphics are serviceable, but nothing like they could be, or should have been. This is a port of the arcade version, not the newer, shinier, better looking, with better graphics and features the consoles received(one could argue no jaggies here, but still..). This will never receive an update to put it on par with the superior console version because it's not running on the same engine - which includes damaged outfits, better skin shading etc., Fine, I could live with it. I had bouncy boobs and slick moves to keep me entertained.
Then comes the 3 month mark, and lo! the online was not released. Instead, it came to us in the form of a beta. It was functional, but barely - plagued by crashes, a lack of options for region selection(players could select a region, but only on a very broad, very basic level - thus players would be paired up with people from EU despite picking NA etc.,) no cross-platform and no lobby system. They kept pushing its official non-beta release back, and kept pushing it back until it was finally released a significant period of time AFTER the date stated on the store page - and it is basically the same as beta with slightly better matchmaking and fewer crashes, but still none of the other noted options. It looks like we will never get those options, either. Moreover, there are not many people playing online anyway. While we're mentioning updates - Did I mention the significant lack of any substantial updates in any way, shape, or form? Yeah, that's right. None.
Just to beat us over the head even further, they release loads of costume DLC at a cost, on average, on par with the price of the game or double it. Ok, they're just cosmetic and some of them include a hefty amount of costumes but again - those costumes do not feature any of the destructibility or additional SFX given to those who buy them on console. Not only that, but they keep vomiting out these DLC costume packs without actually updating the core game. We have barely received any of the balance updates et al., that the consoles have received. Not only that, but they're also releasing a DLC character for the PC and consoles and, you guessed it! PC doesn't get the stage she comes with, but consoles do. We also don't get any of the destructibility of her outfit.
Then, to pour salt into the gaping wound and kick us while we're down, the rest of the game is ACTUALLY FUN. It runs smoothly for me fully maxed out- on both a gtx780 and the replacement gtx980ti. The animation is fluid, looks nice, and attacks look like they genuinely flow into one another so it's fun to pull off a fancy combo. It sounds nice, the character voices are also decent, and the roster is quite large with each character feeling satisfyingly unique in fighting style and animation. In addition, there are neat water effects (wet clothing after a fight from sweat, or when a character falls in water) and it's nice to see dirt on a character's skin with a bead of sweat trickling down his/her head after a fight.
Even better, no matter how experienced someone is in the fighting game genre - anyone can pick it up and play it - I recommend a controller or a fight stick. I did not try it with keyboard. A new player can still witness the flashy moves resulting from his/her inputs and cool combos just as much as an experienced player - granted the experienced player can pull off more combos etc., because the skill ceiling, I believe, is fairly high and the combat system is decently complex.
There's also a single player story mode that's, well, there...The story isn't really much to pay attention to and the only purpose it serves is to get players used to some of the characters' combos and such.
Oh and did I mention they even added the ability to choose how bouncy the boobs are?
( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) HOW. BOUNCY. THEY. ARE! ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°) Bless our adolescent perverted little hearts.
So to conclude, if you're someone who is really desperate for a fighting game to play offline with friends and for an excuse to slobber all over your keyboard as you watch the heaving of your favorite DOA5 waifu's breasts - then I guess you could spend the $40. For anyone who wants a fun, competitive, well-supported fighting game with responsive developers who actually care about their PC community -- I beg you, please look elsewhere.

If you focus on the AI's moves as you play you will start to notice that it's playing several moves ahead and knows the gems that are going to drop. The AI also knows when the combos are running out and it will strategize to have the board reset be on its turn - which often nets it two or three combos and skulls galore.
Perhaps you think I've just had a bad experience (especially given all the positive reviews) but honestly if you pay attention you'll see these issues too. Sure, I could grind to overcome the skewed RNG and the psychic AI but I don't find the grind enjoyable while I'm being cheated so this game is going on the shelf.
PS If you are going to buy/play anyway, I recommend turning off the hint arrow immediately. While the arrow will show you where you can get a gem combo, it does not take anything else into account. Many times (before I shut if off) I found myself setting up the AI for a skull or 4-combo by taking the move advised by the hint arrow.

As a person who enjoys JVN and welcomes any others that would fall into the genre, i'll have to say that this has great potential to become a remarkable game. As of the current build it's only about 20% of the full release so things are bond to change, added, and improved on so i'll just list some pros and cons like a normal review but add some notes on how I alone would like to see happen so I won't speak for everyone that played this.
*Pros~
Soundtrack-
I do like the music they play into the backround since it sets up a mood like what a good soundtrack sould do for a game. I guess all I have to say is to maybe add more and different kinds of songs to play for certain parts of the story in of just "if it's deep meaningfull moment, play this one, if it's calming, play this other one." Clearly i'm not gonna ask for a different song for every other scene, but something new would help make a important part of the story stick with you.
Art-
I don't want to say too much on the art style since they said they would like to have it animated later on so right now I enjoy the characters and the backround. Love the style they're working in so hope it countinues on but just as wishful thinking i hope for animated backrounds like leaves falling or moving water, but that's just me wanting to get a little bit spoiled.
*Cons~ (not really bad things, just things I would like to see changes a bit before the final game)
Choices-
The choices in here are nice and adds different paths for everybody to explore and experinces as a first time or to branch out from their original path, but I personally I found going through the story a bit confusing. Example, Myself rooting for the prince I ended up finding Elisa working hard in the rain with laundry and helps her out. I patted myself on the back for earning some love points form Elisa but ended up making her cry and watching my arch-enemy the merchent get a kiss for being her "white knight." In a sense it could be a good or a bad thing that the choices are vauge so it isn't as easy as most games would do "spend time with girl A or B"(or C or D or F and so on if what you're playing is a harem type JVN) but even when I find it difficult to go down a path I want since i'm a "go perfect first time or go home" type of player I do on the other hand like the item system since it does make you think ahead on what you may need it for and if it's a good idea to use it in the current fork in the story, though will make it a bit tricky to full clear the game when it comes out but that's a problem for "100% clearers" like myself ;)
Character Depth-
Like most JVNs the girls (or guys if you like the otome types) have what I like to call the "Tag" being what you would label a character for example the shy and quite girl or the tsudere or the mature girl and so on. Right now as I see it the Prince is Status since that's pretty much what he's using to win over Elisa, Merchent being Money and Monotery things ( I do hope they add more depth to him or else he'll become something on the line of the rich antagonist in a Disney movie ) and the Knight is Honor and Respect but the game only touched on him briefly so there could be more to him like why he dislikes women and you have to go and open him up ( like a egg or a pudding cup, maybe a jar of jelly would suit him better ) and then there's the two girls you meet at the start though one does show up later if you pick the right choices for some nice eye-candy. More importantly for me as least is Elisa, I really have high hopes for her since I would like to see her more as a girl with a personality and flaws instead of a goal for one of the guys the win over. I'm not trying to sound like a feminist or anything about Elisa being a end-game goal but when the days over that's she is BUT I would like to see a deeper story for her like when we saw a bit in to the past when
peeping through her diary so I can really build a connection with her and actully really want to win her over as a girl then a way to beat the game. Overall a deeper story for each of them so they could be a lot more then their "tags"
As a close up it is a good game for a teaser for the full game and honestly if it improves from this build then it's a game i'll get for myself and heck if you don't want to listen to me and if the full game is free like the prequel, no reason not to give it a shot for yourself instead of reading a review from a weeb and then after playing it ask yourself was it worth the several mega-bytes of data. For anyone considering buying this game, either full price or on a deal, I certainly think it's worth it. With over 1100 hours logged (yes, a month and a half of my life spent playing one game) I don't think I've ever regretted one of them.
For beginners the game is generally nice and easy to pick up, requiring fairly little micromanagement to compete or even win in the lower half of the difficulty scale.
At higher levels the game does require a touch more control from the player and a fairly reasonable level of knowledge of the game to get the best out of each civilization. You might not win every match, but that's part of the fun of this game.
Trial and error, trying out new approaches, different nations and shooting for different win-types give a lot of replay value to even the base game. Expansions Gods & Kings along with Brave New World really help to flesh out the whole experience, bringing the flavour of religions, espionage, trade & ideologies into the game and allowing you to shape your empire more to your desire.
There are plentiful mods available from the workshop too with some really talented contributors that have been directly responsible for many a night spent going into the wee hours, lovingly appreciating the golden glow of the 'Next Turn' button.
There are other games out there which provide more depth of strategy -
But that's not to say that Civilization V suffers from a lack of it, instead I feel that this game is more rewarding to the player when you do something noteworthy in the game, like building a wonder, being the first to open up an ideology or freeing a previously vanquished Civ.
This game just scratches
a little better.
Anyway, if you do purchase this game, I truly hope you enjoy it.

It's a game that makes you hate it but as you play more and more you learn how to get better.
It's a game about raw skill, and there is definitely a fine curve in playtime to skill.
First you learn what each weapon does, and then you figure out how everyone is using them to learn how to use them yourself.
You pick up tricks from watching other people play, such as rocket jump spots.
It's a game about knowing your opponent, and not letting them know you. To win is not just to outshoot, but to outthink and to outtime and outmaneuver your opponent takes years of practice.
Don't think you care enough to practice hard for 10 years? You don't really have to, but if you play to be the best that's what it takes.
Movement is a big part of the game as well. Simple things like walking can get really deep: wallstrafing, circlejumping, rocket and plasma jumps are all very commonly heard phrases and very useful tricks.
Its a game about "anything for an advantage." Previously mentioned movement techniques finely tuned on specific portions of maps can provide just the slightest fraction of a second cut off to get to the red armor before your opponent (which provides 100 armor points and is a very good advantage)
Its a game about knowing what fights to take. You may have all the rockets, plasma, and rails you can carry, but you wont make it far with just 25 hp and 30 armor. (this is where knowing not only where weapons spawn, but health spawns and what kind of health can provide a great edge in the game)
It's a great casual game as well, I find, but a bit daunting to get into. When you lose to someone significantly better than you, look at your failure objectively. "Did i miss my shot, and by how much?" "What kind of weapons and armor did he have, should i have even taken that fight?" This will ease getting better tremendously rather than just going with the flow because it will save you huge amounts of frustration and confusion.

If you are uncertain, it's 2 dollars, get your friend in and just have a blast.

Probably the best entry in the Puzzle Quest series. This one also happens to be the first.  I will also note, that at the time of this review I only have 5 hours of gameplay, however have played the first Puzzle Quest on numerous platforms.
I has been ported many times, and has not suffered at all from it.
The game blends classic RPG elements like leveling, stat building, parties, main and side quests, shops with items and more with a simple match-3 puzzle game concept. It executes it very well.
The colored gems represent mana, aside from the purple stars and stack of coins which yield experience and gold upon matching. There are also skulls to match that damage your enemy. In puzzle quest your objective is to damage your enemie's health down to zero by either matching skulls or using the mana gained through gems with offensive spells. There are also other types of spells, meant for healing or a form of crowd control so the pace and complexity rises there and can add some fun gameplay and combinations to your moves. There are also the mechanic where if you match more than 3 of anything in one move, you gain an extra turn. The combination of all these makes for exciting, strategic gameplay.
The cons are that the story is rather stale, but this is firstly a puzzle game before anything else and can easily become overlooked. That is the only negative thing I can really come up with. Clever game; good fun. Highly recommended.

For a Strategy Game and for having an RPG elemet to the ships, I find Battlefleet Gothic Armada Fulfilling in those aspects. Campaign Gameplay will be the deciding factor to your success. If you go in guns ablazing you most likely will miss out on your objectives. Most of the time you'll find yourself hitting the space bar to make last second changes to turns or attacks almost every moment. The best opponents are Traitor ships which are the Mirror forces, followed by Chaos ships and Orks. But the hardest race is the Eldar.
I think for such a flimsey ship design they are quite fast as the tend to boost away from you in every engaugement utilizing hit and run tactics as well as the Hammer and Anvil strategy. But for better part of the campaign there is only Cruiser Clash where you have a head on fight with them in most cases you will win. But any other mission they will out right Run you down, or escape. So My suggestion, if there are any Eldar battles you want to take on, go only after Planetary assault and Cruiser Clash. Nothing else is worth the Rage Quitting headache you get when you keep trying to go after their transports or Admiral's Ship.
As for the Orcs be prepared fo constant rammings as their ships will boost into your ships like Kamikaze pilots. Getting in close is a big risk if you want more effective hits. But it's a gratifying feel to see a Killkroozer explode when you hit it with everything you got. Tough as they are they still die just the same.
The Chaos ships are a good challenge as they will use ambush tactics before their Capital ships come into play. Be ready to focus fire your ships on the capitals as they are their real strength.
Trator ships are fun for a starter opponent letting you mach the enemy using the same ships till the campaign progresses and the three other races are introduced.
I will recomend this game to any one looking for some fun thinking. But remember this, The game will make you feel your defeat and will be unforgiving if you don't watch your mini map for any ships trying to out flank you.

First impression after a handful of missions played:
It's great, it's awesome, I love it! Maybe I'm biased in that I play the tabletop game and I love the setting (40k), but hey, it's a great game even if you don't know about it yet.
They nailed the look and feel. Seeing the model ships come to "life" is probably every tabletop nerd's dream (mine at least) and I love it. The details are great, they're true to the original models pretty much down to the last tiny detail. Thank you graphics designers, lots of <3 your way!
The game plays somewhat fast paced but at least in single player you can slow it down. You level up your ships in the campaign and they gain different abilities that you can use active in battle. Besides focusing on having your ships facing the right way, attacking the right enemy, preferably at the best facing, dodging torpedoes, bombs and whatnot, the actives help differentiate your ships into specific roles.
The campaign seems neat so far, nothing spectacular but gives a good introduction to the setting and the enemy races. They're exactly as stereotyped as you hoped they'd be, which is a good thing. On the positive there's a lot of different mission types and they all play differently which makes for good variation. It seems like story missions win or lose give different outcomes that might affect the campaign later on. I look forward to see what happens.
My biggest issue right now, and it's really minor, is that if you restart a mission the enemy composition of ships is randomized. I guess this is both good and bad, but it does make a given mission a bit random in difficulty. The same mission might be easier or harder depending on the ships you face.
Oh, and somewhere I read that some were concerned about the lack of 3D movement. It's really not an issue and I think it would just overcomplicate things. KISS works here as well.
TL;DR: I love it, get it if you love BFG, 40k or just sci-fi ship combat.

The game is based on hunting terrorists in Las Vegas and true to other Rainbow games, a single head shot can kill you or your enemies. There is no tactical planning or waypoint setting, but a map can be overlaid in real time to show enemy/friendly positions and objectives.
During the game different approaches to reach objectives can be made which may involve fast roping, abseiling or ladder use to traverse drops and climbs. Your team of two non-player characters can be sent to any location within view (but not separately) and are reasonably reactive to incoming fire taking cover and returning fire when required. The range of weapons and customisation is vast and picking the correct weapons for the scenario is vital for success. My favourite action is being able to sneak view under doors and tag enemies for the NPC's to attack before door entry is made. Onto the health system, there is no health bar in this game. Instead when you are shot your vision becomes blurry. This means you have to take cover and rest until the blurriness has gone. It may not be a realistic health system but it adds to the intenseness of firefights and works very well.
There are a ton of weapons to play around with. Sub machine guns, light machine guns, sniper rifles, shotguns, pistols, shield. All of these are tweak able with different scopes, magazines, laser sights etc.

Still one of the greatest indies ever made.

EDIT: For those asking, QA = Quality Assurance, which is the official title of most Game Testers and other people who find and track bugs in games. They're paid professionsals--game developers--who help to ensure that released (live) games are as free of major issues as possible,
help ensure betas/alphas are at least resonably playable so that players can provide useful feedback.
DISCLAIMER:
If you don't understand the situation between Snail and Wildcard regarding DnL and ARK, go educate yourself. There's good reason this is an "ARK clone" and it has nothing to do with Snail stealing anything. I mention ARK in my review but Snail's relationship with Wildcard played no part in my decision to not recommend Dark and Light. Below I judge DnL/Snail on their own merits with references to ARK for context only.
REVIEW:
The status of "Early Access" does not absolve developers from all responsibility for game-breaking bugs. Early Access does not give developers license to treat their players like QA.
Snail is currently sitting on the wrong side of the above two statements.
This game is in early alpha and is not nearly up to the quality one
expect of an early access game. Do not buy this game unless you want all the pain points of being QA with
of the tools and advantages available to actual, professional QA.
This game is gorgeous. This game is huge. Exploring the map is breathtaking... and infuriating. The current state of the engine means it cannot load the game assets fast enough, and the game will stutter to the point you'll be unable to play for anywhere from several seconds to many
while it catches up. In the meantime, you can only hope a creature does not come by and pick a fight while you're essentially helpless. And when you die, you lose everything including (probably) your mount, just like in ARK. Expect to start over from next to nothing repeatedly, possibly daily. It doesn't matter if you're an experienced player, the bugs
kill you.
Like ARK, creature models' collision is not a box or cylinder, but the actual model itself (or a low-poly version). Swishing tails and flapping wings will cause your character to rubber band, get stuck, and otherwise provide constant obstruction that would be comical if it weren't so damn infuriating. Same goes for dead creatures, which have both ragdoll physics and collision, leading to runaway physics simulations that can bring entire servers to their knees when a corpse goes ballistic and "explodes" into a mess of flashing triangles. Even if that doesn't happen, you'll often be prevented from getting close enough to harvest a corpse by all manner of spines, horns, and hilariously contorted limbs.
In short, this is a big beautiful game with so much potential. I actually like it better than ARK. Or, more precisely, I like what it could be. And if Dark and Light's only major issue was lack of content I could get behind it. Unfortunately, the developers want to treat their players like QA, instead of like players. Bugs which are causing players to quit are not handled with the urgency that they would be in a live, released game. Live game or not, they still have real-live (and paying) players who aren't going to wait around a couple of weeks for critical issues to get fixed.

I used to play a lot of Warcraft 3 and Age Of Empires 3 when growing up, and have recently gotten back into competitive RTS games with COH2 being the first I've spent more then 100 hours on. I intend to keep playing right now, as I think this game has a whole lot of potential and continues to go on great sales (50%-75% off is totally worth it for the base game + Western Front Armies).
Like Relic's other games, in COH2 you build squads of soldiers and single vehicle units from  your base, and  fight against the opposing player on a rich, destructable map. Skirmish games are Victory-Point based, meaning you try to hold certain points to reduce your opponent's score over time; as long as you are holding 2 out of the 3 victory points, you will be causing their score to go down. When it reaches 0, you lose.
You don't gather resources, instead resources trickle in based on your current army size / population, and the sectors on the map you have captured. The main resource is manpower, which is used for purchasing every unit and upgrade, and you receive more for, the smaller your army is. The second most important resource is fuel, which allows you to build vehicles and research upgrades, and finally there is munitions, which allows your units to use their abilities, such as throwing grenades, placing mines, and getting better guns. Fuel and Munitions are received based on capturing and holding more points on the map.
PROS
- Very fun multiplayer battles. COH2 is much like a game of chess, where there are hard counters, soft counters, and many elements to the battlefield. Although base-building is not a major aspect of the game by any means (and that is something I usually love in my RTS's), there is enough going on to keep a player thinking the whole time.
- Blowing up buildings! Placing Mines! Artillery Barrages! Tank battles! Machine Guns and Mortar Support Teams! FLAMETHROWERS! Units are fun to use. Nearly every unit has at least one upgrade or ability, so even though you may have less than 20 units on the map, there is a lot to do with them - set up the MG in the right place, sprint your sniper to better cover, have your mortar throw down smoke bombs for a flanking assault by your shock troops, or perform a risky ramming maneuver with your T34 tank.
- Randomness (known as RNG) gives an exciting element to the battle. COH2 is still figuring out the right amount of it, but it makes responding to what happens in a battle as important as making good plans. Sometimes, your AT gun misses three shots in a row, allowing your opponent's tank to blitz through your lines. Other times, you hit those three times, penetrate one, and knock the tank's engine out, leaving it dead in the water. Will he risk his engineers trying to repair it, or will you manage to clear the crew, leaving the tank abandoned, and take it for yourself? #adapt
CONS
- Three main multiplayer systems could be better, in my opinion: Commander, warspoils, & ELO ranking.
:::::Commander system is regarded by the community to be inferior to COH1's, where you would pick a commander and then be able to spend your command points on . In COH2, you are allowed to take 3 Commanders into the game, and pick one during the game, which will give you a single "Roster" of 5 Units and Abilities. Different Commanders for each faction are mostly different mixes of the same pool of about 12 units and abilities, some combinations of which are regarded as clearly stronger than others right now. (12/27/2014)
:::::Warspoils is the reward for playing multiplayer. 1 Commander, "Intel Bulletin" (in-game stat upgrade, i.e. +3% Rate of Fire to your machine Guns) or Vehicle skin is randomly rewarded for about every 3 hours of playing the game in multiplayer. You have no control over what you will get, duplicates are common, and there is no way to trade/craft these. It seems the developers are actively looking for feedback to improve this system, and I hope to see it changed in the future.
:::::ELO Ranking for automatch is not transparent. Without third party tools, you are unaware of your rank, and you are unaware of your opponent's relative skill level. I feel this should be made more transparent.
- Singleplayer story is a little lackluster, being what got this game in trouble in Europe upon launch. Much of the story focuses on war crimes committed by the Russian Red Army. If this does not bother you, the missions are varied and interesting.
- Community needs to improve. Ranked Automatch with random players is a staple in modern RTS games. The intense tactical nature of this game means that you will lose some engagements in a skirmish; this is OK. Unit preservation and coordinating with your allies is very much a key element to winning, but often it is hard to work with strangers over the internet.

Double Action Boogaloo. Where to begin with this game. I will say one thing, it's fast paced. REALLY fast paced. It's one of those shooters that extremely fast paced and yet, it's so easy to jump into and learn the controls. In a nutshell, take the kind of slow mo insane stunts pulled off in The Matrix and make them into a game. Anyone can be good but only few will be masters. There's a whole variety of movesets to learn, from combat rolling to backflips to slides. And though there are only a few classes and a short list of weapons to choose from, none of those aspects, from what I found, really seem to affect gameplay in any way. Just experiment, find the weapon set of your choice or go on a brawling fest, and just get invested into it. What makes the game stand out from the other Source Engine shooters is it's sense of originality when it comes to gameplay and mechanics and the comical situations and kills you'll find yourself getting. If you ever wanted to be like those pro Call of Duty players that 360 no-scope players from across the map or pull off other insane stunts to get kills, then this is the game of your dreams. But don't expect sniper rifles. At it's current state, weapons seem to be balanced pretty nicely and I personally think sniper rifles would ruin the fun. However, I recommend the Persuader for those of you who want to get one-shot kills. My only con is the player base, which dwindles at points. But personally, with unique map design, a host of weapons and abilities to choose from, and a variety of movesets that make it stand out from it's rocket booster predecessors, this parody of insane slow-mo stunted killfests should definitely have a place in your steam library.
I give Double Action: Boogaloo a 8.5/10

As of the current build it's only about 20% of the full release so things are bond to change, added, and improved on so i'll just list some pros and cons like a normal review but add some notes on how I alone would like to see happen so I won't speak for everyone that played this.
*Pros~
Soundtrack-
I do like the music they play into the backround since it sets up a mood like what a good soundtrack sould do for a game. I guess all I have to say is to maybe add more and different kinds of songs to play for certain parts of the story in of just "if it's deep meaningfull moment, play this one, if it's calming, play this other one." Clearly i'm not gonna ask for a different song for every other scene, but something new would help make a important part of the story stick with you.
Art-
I don't want to say too much on the art style since they said they would like to have it animated later on so right now I enjoy the characters and the backround. Love the style they're working in so hope it countinues on but just as wishful thinking i hope for animated backrounds like leaves falling or moving water, but that's just me wanting to get a little bit spoiled.
*Cons~ (not really bad things, just things I would like to see changes a bit before the final game)
Choices-
The choices in here are nice and adds different paths for everybody to explore and experinces as a first time or to branch out from their original path, but I personally I found going through the story a bit confusing. Example, Myself rooting for the prince I ended up finding Elisa working hard in the rain with laundry and helps her out. I patted myself on the back for earning some love points form Elisa but ended up making her cry and watching my arch-enemy the merchent get a kiss for being her "white knight." In a sense it could be a good or a bad thing that the choices are vauge so it isn't as easy as most games would do "spend time with girl A or B"(or C or D or F and so on if what you're playing is a harem type JVN) but even when I find it difficult to go down a path I want since i'm a "go perfect first time or go home" type of player I do on the other hand like the item system since it does make you think ahead on what you may need it for and if it's a good idea to use it in the current fork in the story, though will make it a bit tricky to full clear the game when it comes out but that's a problem for "100% clearers" like myself ;)
Character Depth-
Like most JVNs the girls (or guys if you like the otome types) have what I like to call the "Tag" being what you would label a character for example the shy and quite girl or the tsudere or the mature girl and so on. Right now as I see it the Prince is Status since that's pretty much what he's using to win over Elisa, Merchent being Money and Monotery things ( I do hope they add more depth to him or else he'll become something on the line of the rich antagonist in a Disney movie ) and the Knight is Honor and Respect but the game only touched on him briefly so there could be more to him like why he dislikes women and you have to go and open him up ( like a egg or a pudding cup, maybe a jar of jelly would suit him better ) and then there's the two girls you meet at the start though one does show up later if you pick the right choices for some nice eye-candy. More importantly for me as least is Elisa, I really have high hopes for her since I would like to see her more as a girl with a personality and flaws instead of a goal for one of the guys the win over. I'm not trying to sound like a feminist or anything about Elisa being a end-game goal but when the days over that's she is BUT I would like to see a deeper story for her like when we saw a bit in to the past when
peeping through her diary so I can really build a connection with her and actully really want to win her over as a girl then a way to beat the game. Overall a deeper story for each of them so they could be a lot more then their "tags"

Dead or Alive 5 Last Round is a superb game just like the variants before it, but putting aside the nickel and diming there's too much wrong with the PC version(performance not being an issue, game runs nicely).  The PC version lacks stages from the console versions and the graphics aren't as good as the PS4 and XBone versions.  Also, no Steam cloud.
My major gripe with with this version though is the button bindings.  Sure you can bind fighting controls to whatever but non fighting controls are messed.  I have a custom arcade stick that's dual modded with a Mad Catz 360 controller and a ChImp SMD.  I can use my stick in either ChImp or 360 mode.  If I use it in ChImp mode, I have to use the first button on the top(or 1P) as the confirm button, the first button on the bottom(or 1K) becomes cancel.  With every other fighter, 1K and 2K are confirm and cancel.
It gets worse with an Xinput controller.  The pause button isn't start, it's bound to the right stick(which you have to press down).  That may not be too bad if you're using an Xinput pad but if you're using an Xinput arcade stick you don't have a pause button.
This could easily be fixed if Team Ninja were to make a patch that allows you to bind everything like Ultra Street Fighter IV on PC allows, but they won't do that.  And because of that I don't recommend this game.
