Metro 2033 Redux review
Game description
Metro 2033 is set in post apocalyptic Moscow predominately inside the metro system. The year is 2033 many years after world war 3 which sparked the beginning of the end. The story follows the protagonist Artyom as he must travel across the metro to seek help from an organisation known as polis in hopes that they will help him save his home station from a new and seemingly unstoppable enemy that in dangers all the people of the metro.
Positives
Metro 2033 is an amazing looking game that provides an atmosphere that I have experienced nowhere else. Every NPC ,whether important to the story or not, will have their own (often depressing)  back story and you can listen in to random conversations and hear each NPC's  story reminding you that the protagonist Artyoms story is just one of countless stories taking place it the metro adding to the immersion and gritty realism of the already immersive and realistic game. At the parts of the game when you are travelling alone or have been separated from whoever you where with you will often feel a sense of being alone and not knowing where to go or what to do in some areas. The game is extremely detailed to the point where you can get things like dirt, flies and blood from people or the monsters you killed on to your gas mask making it harder to see and shoot. If you get hit on the head by a nosalis you will begin see cracks on the sides of you gasmask they will get bigger the more damage it gets hit. eventually it will brake completely causing you to suffocate if you don't find a replacement soon enough which I think is pretty cool.
When in the metro you get a constant sense of being trapped and a feeling  that a group of nosalis will be around the corner or will jump down from the ceiling and catch you of guard. However the game is not solely set inside the metro occasionally missions bring you above ground. When on the surface not only do you have to worry about the odd nosalis but you have to worry about the watchmen which are like wolves on steroids and on top of this you  will  you have to worry about a demons which are large flying predators that will picking you up and can drop you in the middle of a pack of watchmen ,which happened to me several time and was surprisingly terrifying, and if that was not bad enough this often causes you to lose your bearings so you have to figure out where exactly you are which makes the game more challenging and intense.
The fire fights feel really intense and realistic. when an enemy is shot he will react but falling back a bit losing his aim and him and his friends will threaten to kill you for being a communist Nazi or capitalist(just like real people). You feel like the people you are killing are people and not sacks of meat there only to be shot by you to move the story along but at the same time it is pretty satisfying to shoot your enemies in the face with a pipe shot gun. The game is not just about running and gunning as in some places it is smarter to try and stealth like if you have little to no ammo. sneak past you enemies or  kill them silently when they are alone but you must be careful because they will notices if one of the others has not returned to his post. it helps to put a suppressor on one of your guns to kill more than one enemy quickly and quietly however just because I have added a suppressor to my weapons does not mean that I can just casually stealth through the rest of the game as enemies can  still hear when you shot and when a body falls if they are close enough but they won't recognise it as gun fire but will often come and investigate making things a bit harder.
The guns themselves are incredibly detailed (like the rest of the game) to the point that where you can tell if you're low on ammo by looking at the magazine if the bullets are visible because you can see each bullet depending on the weapon. The number of gun you have available is not that small but I would have liked it if there was  more to play with. However the gun customisation in Metro is very extensive and depending on how you customise your gun it can change the way you play the game entirely . You can put extended barrels suppressors extended magazines and more on to your guns I even managed to turn my revolver in to a makeshift sniper rifle.
Negatives
However this game is not  perfect and is not without its problems. The first problem/bug I had was in the tutorial stage. Every time I would bring up my lighter and compass  the game would freeze and I would have to minimise it to fix it luckily this seemed to stop before I got in to any fire fights. later in the game for no reason I would put my military grade ammo in to my gun without realising and shoot it all despite the fact that I had plenty of regular ammo. I personally don't like that Artyom is mute every time someone talks to him the conversation comes across as very one sided and we know he can talk because he does when you are loading a new chapter and no one else is around (but that could just be a social anxiety thing). lastly it would be nice if the game was not so linear and it gave you the freedom to look around and discover things on your own.
I dream of the day when there will be an open world metro game.
Conclusion
In conclusion Metro 2033 is one of the best game I have ever played and is extremely under rated. It does have its problems but they are far outweighed by the many positives it has to offer. It is an amazing game that will always be one of my favourite games and I would 100% recommend this game to anyone who likes very atmospheric  post apocalyptic first person shooters.

I love this game. Let me start of by saying, it's definitely not everyone's cup of tea; if you're looking for a game with strategy or fighting or a clear end goal with a huge community online daily, this is not for you.
Meadow is a game where you play as a variety of different animals, which are unlocked as you play or by owning previous Shelter titles, which the game is based on, with different minor skillsets - frog swims faster than others, pheasant has a short range fly, eagle can fly properly etc.
You explore the map, discovering caves and little known groves while searching for collectables called essence. Essence comes in two main forms:
- flowers of varying rarity for which there are achievements for collecting.
- puzzle pieces that allow you to unlock new skins and emotes for your current animal, but also unlock new animals to play as.
Group play is rewarded by randomly spawning obelisks in the world that require a minimum of two animals to unlock and some larger require a group of six including specific animals. The community is small but very friendly. Communication is through the use of emotes showing things in the world such as essence, flowers, obelisks, a "this way" arrow, "we need to climb/swim" etc, and emotional expressions for your animal - happy, sad, waving etc. Despite minimum levels of communication, bonds form quickly after running with the same animals for a while, people often come back and help if you're stuck climbing somewhere or have fallen behind and people are usually sad to see you go after being part of their mixed up herd for a few hours.
As the game goes, there's no end goal, it's exploring and collecting. The game looks beautiful and the map is large with multiple terrain types. There are a variety of animals and skins to collect and a leaderboard for essence collected.
As someone who suffers from depression and anxiety, I've found this game has a calming effect and helps me unwind for a few hours and I've seen this stated in more than one review before my own.
Highly recommend this game if it sounds like your cup of tea and can't wait for new animals to be released!

I've played the game for a long time in the metro on my PSP during my apprenticeship. It's the perfect time waste for a 30-60 minute game session.
The game features a big world with many quests and characters. You travel to different points on the map and battle classic creatures of the fantasy genre like rats, spiders, skeletons, ogres and shiny paladins.
There are different classes available for your hero. Warrior, Paladin, Druid and Mage. They have different skills and needs. The warrior for example is focused on red stones. Meanwhile the druid need many yellow and blue stones.
You can gather equipment for extra spells or boost your stats like earning more power points of a colour, when you make a chain with them.
The basic gameplay concept is to puzzle. You try to switch the stones to make chains of 3 or more. You also have direct attack stones (skulls) or for experience and gold. The game is challenging and you will have a lot of fun.
On the long run you do every time the same. Puzzle. So it can be boring on long gaming sessions. But for a quick game you will have a cool game.
The resolution is max 900p but still manage to fill your 16:9 monitor. Depending on your monitor upscale possibilities you will have different visual results. But overall it looks nice.

Honestly, Blender is THE best software for animation and modeling.  and the amazing part? ITS F R E E
Coming from somebody whose studying Animation, I prefer this over to Maya for animation. I just like how organized the dope sheet is, so I can keep track of every rig part that has been moved. Thats what I really disliked about a lot of other animaton and modeling programs.. Yes you can put a animation key on the rigs, But if your like me, you end up forgeting what body part you put keys on. But with Blender, It lists all the parts you've moved in the dope sheet, so it's easy to keep track of all of it. It also makes refining an animation a breeze.
The only thing that sorta stinks for animators is that Blender has a lack of Rigs to use, especially if you can't make one yourself. But, This has encouraged me to actually look up the rigging process of characters, and see how it's done. Now I know how to make Characters rigs!
As for modeling in blender, It's Really Good.  It will take a few hours to get the basics of blender down, but trust me, its worth it. The interface really confused me at first, but once I messed with it for a bit, and started learning shortcuts, and figured out what most things did, It was very easy to navigate, and make models.
I wish blender was more industry standard. Because this, is just incredible.

I've spent hours playing Rampart with friends and consider myself a veteran of the original.  My comments here are based upon both the original Rampart game and Castle Chaos as it's own unique game.
The Good:
+ Very similar to the original Rampart
+ Fun to play by self or elbow to elbow with comrad
+ 4 players, not 3 like Rampart
+ The gnomes add a fun and irritating element to the game
+ No huge investment of time needed to learn and master
+ Most of the gameplay elements are easily adjustable from main menu
+ Statistics feature
+ Catchy theme music is a perfect compliment to the original
The Not so Good:
- The odd psedo pixilization of the wall shapes makes it difficult to visually manipulate each piece when repairing or building walls.  Ie: the pieces blend together and appear as one while moving them next to one another.  The original Rampart the pieces were simple solid colors.   An option to use solid color shapes with outlines would be my preference.   This issue alone is nearly a deal breaker for me.
- No online mulitplayer capability (yet)
- Only ONE map?  really?  The original had at least 2 or 3 as I recall.
- The clouds don't appear to have any purpose other than asthetics.  I could be wrong here.
- No mouse support.  I understand the unbalanced advantage a person would have if playing a local battle with friends with only 1 person using a mouse.  At least in single player battles the mouse should be an option.
Suggestions:
* A detailed recap of how the score is tallied up after each round.  This would be helpful so players know where their points are derived and what they might focus on with the next round.
* Rework the graphics overall.  Either make them 8-bit, 16-bit or semi modern.  The current look is a mish mash that isn't pleasing to the eye, IMHO.
* The game just ends after the last round isn't much of a spectacle.  Maybe there could be some sort of a bonus round or double points thing, or maybe a target round shooting at moving targets.  Just ranting on how to kick it up a notch here.

Braid plays in a similar vein to late-game Toki Tori levels; your character has some control over time as its primary action, but I would say Braid takes the time manipulation to a stronger level.
The main theme outside of time manipulation is the puzzles; each room of the house contains space for a puzzle whose pieces you are collecting as you play. After each 'world' is completed, you put together the simple puzzle, and move on to the next world. As you progress, books on podiums prior to entering the world tell parts of your story.
Time manipulation plays a large role in the game, and becomes crucial as you get closer and closer to the end. It was a new playstyle for me, but definitely fun to work with to solve some of the puzzles. I think the puzzles, in addition to the story, were well-crafted. I initially ignored parts of the story, but it does end up being pretty good.
If you like puzzle/platformers, you'll like Braid.

If Saints Row 4 had recieved more fine tuning I might've liked it. Unfortunitely, there are simply too many annoyances that are all the harder to ignore because of SR3. SR4 is basicly SR3 with more insanity, more references/cliches and lazy writing,  and more annoying minigames.
SR4 sets you up as the Neo of a Matrix-like world, and that's part of the problem. The main SR4 environment still feels like it was made for SR3 levels of player ability. This translates into controls that feel horribly clunky at times, most often when pushed into a corner. The difficulty increase required to keep up with a more powerful player results in mobs, bullet-spongy enemies, and insta-kill attacks. Paired with the still-intact rag-doll and stun-lock system of SR3, the adjustments made for SR4 can leave you with alot of frustration and cheap deaths. There are simply too many missions where I died without a clear understanding of why or due to fighting the controls and stun-lock versus actually fighting the enemy.
Much like SR3, there are many side-missions to embark on. However, alot of them just weren't that fun for me. The worst turned out to be the store-hacking minigame, which helped me discover another aspect of the game I've come to hate. Essentially, to "buy" a store like you could in SR3, you have to hack it through a pipe-based puzzle. If you fail to complete the puzzle in a set time limit, the authorities will automatically be notified. Once the authorities are notified, there seems to be no way to lose them. You are forced to reduce your wanted level by chasing a stupid gold orb that can end up taking you miles from the store you were trying to hack. If you fail a second time, the process starts all over agian. I want to own the stores like I did in SR3, but I'm not willing to suffer the puzzles (which I have failed more than a few times).
I can't enjoy SR4; I can only do my best to finish it (because I bought this before Steam refunds were a thing). There are soem amusing activities and one-shot missions thorughout the game (piloting a mech is always cool), but the sum total isn't actually "fun." SR3 is fun. Play that and consider SR4 only afterwards.

It might say I have next to no time in this game, but that's not true. I've played about 10 hours of it in offline mode; I wound up getting about 2/3 of the way through the game.
This game is probably one of the most overhyped ever. It has some unique selling points, though. The art style is good, the story is really cool, and the central power is really awesome. Time control is a really unique power that many games haven't managed to implement well. For a while, braid implements it well--sometimes. Most of the puzzles don't really revolve around you using time reversal as a way to solve puzzles, but just trigger certain things once per level in very specifc circumstances. You're mostly walking around for the whole game.
However, every new stage in braid is based around a new "version" of this time control mechanic. This means that the original mechanic doesn't get to grow and be explored in new ways. Let's compare Braid with Portal: in portal, you start off simple, just moving yourself and objects around. Then it gets complicated; you add in turrets, lasers, light bridges, and then movement gels. Every time a mechanic is introduced it _builds_ on the previous ones you've learned and takes the central power in a new direction.
In braid, the first power you have is the power to reverse time. This is explored for a bit, then you move on to other worlds. Here's some sample powers: one world has you move around, then "send" a shadow copy of yourself that follows the steps you just took that you have to interact with to solve puzzles. Another has the world run like a music box, where time moves forward as you move right and backward as you walk left. Do these sound related to the first mechanic you learned? Because they're not at all. What's the point of learning the core puzzle mechanic if you're going to drop it in the next world? The game could basically be described as a collection of 6 time-based different puzzle minigames, but not as a puzzle game that follows a good, challenging progression.

(Which is actually a pretty good idea, Mr. Jones. You ought to do that. Price it where there is some discount per tutorial, like 0% to 50% off, depending on how long the tutorial has been on Steam. A few deeply discounted vids would make the bundle worth it, even if some have already bought some of the tutorials. With the new Steam bundling, it no longer penalizes you for having already bought part of the bundle. No double charges.)
There are three videos total. The first one talks about:
* What is speedpainting?
* How do you get better at it?
* Knowledge (anatomy, mechanical design, the world of information relevant to design, etc.) is critical and there is no shortcut to that.
* Tool (brush preset) familiarity is also critical.
* Time limit yourself, with an agenda (an actual specific goal for the subject).
The second one shows this in action with short challenges.
The third shows a 15 min speed paint that illustrates what can be done in that time frame and one way of iterating through the painting to add refinement in the given timeframe.
Is it worth it? It's not a silver bullet, since that doesn't exist. It is some discussion by a professional, and some examples of the work flow. Something like this *might* be found on YouTube, but good luck finding it. Everyone and their dog has made a video and called it a "speed paint" because some illiterate chowderhead heard the term "speed paint" somewhere and used that term for his sped-up video instead of the age-old, correct term of "time-lapse." Consequently, there are probably, no exageration, 4.7 MILLION 'speedpaint' videos to go through to find the "Concept Design Speed paintings," of which there are precious few. It took me going through 700 MLP, SU, and every sort of anime fan art 'time-lapse' videos mislabled as "Speedpaint" before I found a video from Cubebrush, an actual Concept Design artist.
In short, real concept design videos are hard to find. It may be worth paying for if you really want to learn the techniques.
(BTW, I suggest Concept Design artists start calling "speed painting" something else, such as "concepting," or at least religiously use "Concept Design" and other related keywords on their web sites and videos, since "speedpainting" has been utterly polluted now. I suggest a unique word like concepting so that searches are more accurate, since "Concept Design" is a very broadly used term as well, and certainly isn't restricted to "speed painting" techniques. Rant over.)

I haven't really dipped into Multi-player at all so this is a review exclusively of the single player campaign.
Summary:
Blowing up spaceships feels weighty and is addictive and fun. I've probably not been this hooked on an RTS since Command and Conquer, I love the fact that a campaign fits into bite sized scenarios of 5 minutes a piece. This fits much better with my schedule these days, yet you can still binge on a bunch of missions in quick succession.
I've made it to chapter two so far, in about 30 hours of play time. I suspect I've still got quite a lot more to see but even if what I've discovered is the entire depth of the game I feel like it was value for money.
Overview
The structure of the single player campaign is pretty simple, you get a map showing several different systems. You start off with a couple but quickly ramp up to 5 or 6 in chapter 2.
Each system has a number of planets you must defend and these planets are attacked at random by the various forces arrayed against you; Eldar, Orks, and Chaos.
You have to take randomly generated missions to reduce the threat, with most mission types being playable from the point of view of the attacker and defender.  A few examples of such missions are: a straight forwards fight to the death, stealing info by boarding a capital ship, assassinating an admiral,  running a blockade, and laying siege to a planet.
Failing a mission generally increases the difficulty and whilst you have the short term effect of the loss of the world you were defending it also increases the likelihood of that particular foe stepping up their attacks.
Also n any given turn you also might have a story mission. Failing these have long-term effects beyond just making the game harder, so far artefacts I've rescued have proven valuable, although how valuable would be a spoiler :-)
What I didn't like:
I'd have liked the option to play as different races in the campaign, even if it was just a generic campaign without the story missions.
What I think needs improvement:
It would be nice within the vanilla mission types if you could get a twist occasionally that changed the objectives. It'd keep this from getting too same-y.
Explosions sometimes look a bit disappointing.
Short range warp jumps can't position the ships on exit and seem pretty short distance.

The best Warhammer40k game in a loooong time. The campaign and skirmish AI can be tough for players that are not used to naval tactics, fast decisions and quick changes, as the ponderous speed of some vessels can change all of the sudden, if boosters are fired or a teleport exposes your back. If you get used to it, it is beatable but still fun.
Multiplayer and skirmish are missing some standard featues of modern RTS games, but these will be patched in the next weeks, according to the devs. Same goes for multiplayer balancing and general stability, MP is fun but needs some work. As the devs patched the beta every week and did so with the release version, too, I'm confident to get a nearly perfect game in the next few weeks. Until then it's still a good game every 40k fan will enjoy, and every RTS fan should at least take a look at!

Compared to more hardcore Tom Clancy games like Ghost Recon Advanced Warfighter, RB6V can feel like a simplified generic shooter. That may indeed be the case, but it's fun and quite replayable, especially in co-op mode.
The gameplay is reminiscent of Gears of War, except you're in first-person mode when not in cover, and you can issue basic tactical orders to your teammates. You'll probably never actually do any fighting from first-person mode, however, because your ability to take damage is very limited even on Normal difficulty, making it almost impossible to win a gunfight without using cover (which puts you into third person view, and lets you blind-fire if you want which is pretty cool).
A few of the basic tactical options like the ability to change the weapon rate-of-fire and attach suppressors are present, which is much welcome. You usually have a choice between going all Rambo into the next area, or playing it safe by going in stealthily and taking everyone by surprise with a few well-placed stun grenades. You also get to feel like a badass in some sequences, rappelling down the side of a building then crashing through the window and saving the hostages.
The game can be hard at times, but in a way that feels justified and encourages you to rethink your strategy instead of yelling at the screen. It can get frustrating when you fail a mission because an AI teammate went down, but that's not too common because the AI is quite smart and is often capable of clearing a room without your help.
Co-op is where this game really shines. It's essential to coordinate the attack plan before opening the next door, and that makes for particularly satisfying breach moments, as you mercilessly pick off those terrorist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and then yell "Clear!".
As is typical with Ubisoft, the game wasn't well optimized and had many performance issues at launch. In 2015, that's no longer a problem with any modern PC able to nail this 2006 game, but there are still a few annoyances that show how little the devs cared about the PC. You can't use the steam overlay. You can't bind controls to mouse thumb buttons. Your choice of screen resolutions is limited unless you edit the ini file. The graphics options are quite limited.
If you want a fun co-op shooter that does a decent job simulating tactical special ops behaviour without being too hardcore, get this game (and an extra copy or two for your friends).

Pretty good, but not without flaws.
I played on Classic with Enemy Within.
I'm not going to elaborate on the pros, but here are some annoyances I noticed.
- Sometimes shots are exchanged through walls even though the enemies shouldn't be able to see each other. Since it works both ways, it's not that bad, but still annoying.
- Moving with the flying armor was awful and in the end I didn't use it anymore. Sometimes, the soldier moves to strange places or can't land e.g. on trucks when in other levels he can land on them. But even without flying, sometimes a click sends a soldier to a different level than you expected.
- I really disliked that most enemies don't seem to move over the map before they are discovered. And if the player finds them, they get a free turn to move around. So, no suprises for the soldiers.
- Terror missions are often a PITA, but only because the levels are rather small. This way sometimes all enemies are triggered in the first few rounds and your team is overwhelmed.
- You can sell alien artifacts but not XCOM items. So unlike original XCOM you can't earn money through manufacturing. You also can't sell items you don't need anymore. This is made worse by the awful lists in the game. If you scroll with the mouse wheel through them, they jump over some of the items.
- Speaking of money, you always have to little money. It seems to forcefully limit your progress by design. I'd rather prefer a possibilty to get ahead like in the old games.
- In general the game is really bad at teaching the player what aspects are important and which aren't. The tutorial leaves a lot to be desired and overall the game lacks direction. If you look back at the old XCOM games like XCOM Apocalypse, it had a novel sized manual, while this game merely a 5 page installation leaflet.
Add to this that you e.g. can't get countries back, once they leave the council. The importance of satellites escaped me at the first game and I almost lost the game. The downside is that this favors a very specific strategy at the beginning.
- The squad size is too small. You start with 4, which is ridicously small. In the beginning your team is weak anyway, but if you lose a soldier you just lost 1/4 of your attack strength. At the end you have 6, which is ok for most levels. Still on bigger levels you need to stick together otherwise a group of enemies will kill off your soldiers easily.
Yet, it's a good game amd I might play it again in the future. The levels are nicely randomized and it rarely feels like you play the same map over and over. The fights are fun, although sometimes a bit random. Thankfully you can save scum. Otherwise the game would have driven me mad.

Many negative reviews of Dark and Light talk about its problems such as server desyncs, lag, and frame rate drops. I will say, that while I understand many players suffer from these problems, I have had very few issues playing on a PvE unofficial server. The game is early access, so expect problems, but I recommend trying the 2 hours allowed before refunding on steam and seeing how it runs for you.
As far as gameplay, I never played Ark or Conan Exiles, but I understand it plays similarly to them - the fantasy setting is what captured me to begin with. The basics of the game are solid and surprisingly deep, giving you a lot to play with - even on a PvE server or singleplayer lacking the dynamics of player versus player.
The game has many kinks to iron out, some particularly urgent (such as glitching through shields in PvP) and other less so (balancing, such as most armor sets being useless, likely because they lack passive buffs they are supposed to have), but the positives are numerous as well. Overall, I encourage those who are on the fence to try it out like I did. Personally, I expect to get many more hours out of what the game has available now and look forward to the likely massive amount of content that will be added over the next year.

If Saints Row 4 had recieved more fine tuning I might've liked it. Unfortunitely, there are simply too many annoyances that are all the harder to ignore because of SR3. SR4 is basicly SR3 with more insanity, more references/cliches and lazy writing,  and more annoying minigames.
SR4 sets you up as the Neo of a Matrix-like world, and that's part of the problem. The main SR4 environment still feels like it was made for SR3 levels of player ability. This translates into controls that feel horribly clunky at times, most often when pushed into a corner. The difficulty increase required to keep up with a more powerful player results in mobs, bullet-spongy enemies, and insta-kill attacks. Paired with the still-intact rag-doll and stun-lock system of SR3, the adjustments made for SR4 can leave you with alot of frustration and cheap deaths. There are simply too many missions where I died without a clear understanding of why or due to fighting the controls and stun-lock versus actually fighting the enemy.
Much like SR3, there are many side-missions to embark on. However, alot of them just weren't that fun for me. The worst turned out to be the store-hacking minigame, which helped me discover another aspect of the game I've come to hate. Essentially, to "buy" a store like you could in SR3, you have to hack it through a pipe-based puzzle. If you fail to complete the puzzle in a set time limit, the authorities will automatically be notified. Once the authorities are notified, there seems to be no way to lose them. You are forced to reduce your wanted level by chasing a stupid gold orb that can end up taking you miles from the store you were trying to hack. If you fail a second time, the process starts all over agian. I want to own the stores like I did in SR3, but I'm not willing to suffer the puzzles (which I have failed more than a few times).
I can't enjoy SR4; I can only do my best to finish it (because I bought this before Steam refunds were a thing). There are soem amusing activities and one-shot missions thorughout the game (piloting a mech is always cool), but the sum total isn't actually "fun." SR3 is fun. Play that and consider SR4 only afterwards.

Snowball is a charming little game. A bunch of pixel kids get together and made a pixel pinball snowscape with assorted contraptions. So while wintery jazz music plays, your snowball careens around an obstacle course of snowbanks, abandoned railroad cars, fir trees, igloos, giant flippers, snowmen, targets and ice crystals. (There are even telsa coils, of all things. I don't know why. Clever children, I guess.) A large bonfire waits at the bottom to reduce your snowballs into so many tears, so better try bouncing it back to the top. That's really the only thing I dislike: unlike a lot of pinballs games, once your ball gets to the lowest area you have a devil of a time getting it toward the upper part of the gamefield again. It's possible, but most of the time your ball will bounce around an area almost devoid of any of the fun bits, and even clearing the main play area still gets it to a section where it's all too easy to get it to slide back down again without really accomplishing much of anything. No, the physics of the moving pieces don't make much sense, and nothing else does either, really, if you think about it too much. Just accept that the premise is a wild mash up of a pinball machine with a Rube Goldberg device with a healthy dash of A Charlie Brown Christmas thrown in and you'll know where this is coming from. It's like a wildly nostalgic reimagination of the whole neighborhood of kids taking their toboggans and sheets of colorful plastic off to the hills between the primary school and the nearby farmer's field. If you lived in a warmer climate or an urban area, imagine instead that it's like a day at the water park, but frozen over and without the silly arm bands and having to get your parents to fork over a wad of cash. And because it's just a game your nose hairs won't freeze off. If you lived it, you know what I mean. All the game needs is Steam trading cards and a few tweaks to getting the ball around the playfield and it would be nearly perfect. Additional playing areas and even a construction ability would have been icing on the cake. But it's still a cheap little diversion for a bit: that's a frosty mittens-covered thumbs up from me.

I was planning to do stuff this weekend, but apparently I played 22 hours of Puzzle Quest in two days.
...okay okay fine, I'll write about the actual game.
There are 4 classes, each have their different set of default spells, and you learn spells as you level up. This is an RPG after all, albeit a linear one - with quite a lot of sidequests and the main quest is lengthy, my game play time at the moment is pretty much an indicator of a single playthrough, which was ~36 hours.
So what's the quirk of this game? The battle system. The battle system is based on Bejeweled, and as you match pieces, you get mana, gold, exp or deal direct damage. With mana, you can cast spells. And if you put 4 in a row or stun the enemy or the like, you can get extra turns and it can get quite crazy if you have a Frozen Rod, have 1% chance of stun for each of your blue mana (so with 41 blue mana you have 41% chance of stun on every instance of dealing damage), and some other stuff. As you can tell, there are items that manipulate the gameplay on both your side and the enemy's.
You can also capture monsters and use them as a mount (and gain an extra stat based on their level and get an extra skill to use in combat), or you can research their spells. You can also craft your own items with runes you can collect. Each of these uses a system that is a variation on the base battle system.
VERDICT: If you like strategic gameplay and you're oddly addicted to Match-3 puzzle games, and enjoy a decent (even if not the most unique nor the most complicated) story, and decent music, then this is definitely a good game. It really depends on whether you enjoy the combat or not: because you'll do a LOT of it in this game. But hey, I enjoyed it.

This game is a wonderful piece of art, and it's clear that a lot of love went into it. The soundtrack is amazing, incredibly relaxing and does an excellent job at stoking the fire of curiosity in you. The graphics are wonderful even on low settings (which it automatically switches to if you have a not-so-strong computer like I do), it feels like it's right out of a storybook. The gameplay is minimalistic, yes, but that doesn't mean there's nothing to do!
At its core it is a social game. You're meant to explore and meet people along the way. You can only communicate through symbols that pop up above your head, either one or two at a time, and it works brilliantly! You never really feel like you can't get your point across because you never feel like you have to communicate anything complex.
Example. You come across some players. Use the hello emote! Jump up and down! Use the group symbol and question mark! They said group and check mark? FRIENDS. Oh, one of them said group and arrow? Follow them! Off you go, a nice group of new friends, exploring the world!
That's all there is to it, and yet it feels so fulfilling. I just got this game tonight, expecting to play it for a few minutes and then get bored but boy howdy I played and played... Received the achievement for playing 2 hours as my first animal... and I kept going.
Along the way while exploring you'll find these big stone things called obelisks. Most only take two players to open, some take more, some require specific species to open. Opening these obelisks rewards you with puzzle pieces which will help you get more animals to play as, and more skins & emotes for the animal you are currently playing. You can see the benefit of grouping up, but you may feel rushed by your group. You can and should choose your own pace, take the time to smell (and collect) the flowers. There'll always be someone who wants to take it slow!
This game is a relaxing ride, meant to be enjoyed at your own leisure. Don't let yourself be caught up following others and not having a good time because you're trying so hard to keep up. Let the music and scenary take you away and meet some new people while you're at it.
To take this review for a turn, I'll have to mention the controls. A lot of people are really hard on the controls... They aren't as bad as they sound. They take some getting used to, and you'll want to stop by the options menu to remap some keys to your liking. Maybe the turning could use some tweaking by the devs, but otherwise they flow really well for this type of game! Give yourself some time to really try and adjust to them before turning up your nose and calling the controls awful.
Anyway, hope this review was coherent enough? It's my first review for anything not on a smart phone! The game was just that impressive to me! I would recommend this game to anyone, but in particular I think casual gamers and collect-a-thon lovers would enjoy this game most. Also if you enjoy this game please think about getting the soundtrack too! It's wonderful, relaxing and the money will support the devs for their hard work!

I began playing Civilisation during Civ IV, and spent many hours on that and it's expacs before I repurchased the game for Steam. No steam Overlay unless you add it as a non-Steam game (lol) and no support for wide screen resolutions... Great game, but this stuff pisses me off.
I'm not saying the game is bad. It can be real fun but these things just won't let me enjoy the game at its full. I need the overlay because that's a useful way to communicate with my friends in-game. I've already asked for Ubisoft support. What happens is this: Usually the exes of Steam games are modified so that they HAVE to detect Steam and the license prior to run. Here, Ubisoft went lazy and made a runme.exe (search your binary folder) that reads a runme.data Inside runme.data is specified the name of the exe (in this case R6Vegas_Launcher.exe) that will en up being executed. The runme.exe is the one that holds the Steam license validation... Yes, Ubisoft didn't modify the actual game exe to be compatible with steam, it created another one with the validations that calls the retail one. So if you run the game from Binaries folder Steam won't track your game time. Is it really THAT hard to modify the game exe so it can be fully compatible with steam?
Okay the game is old, forget the resolution, (there is patch that changes the congif file online that does the job) give me the overlay with tracking and I'll be able to recommend it.

The AI is definitly the strong point of Vegas, being in the Story mode or Terrorist Hunt, they actually present a challenge since they never do the same thing twice, they flank you, flush you out of cover or retreat if outnumbered, wich give some replayability valor to the game.
The Story is interesting with some turn overs, but isnt complete in this game (end with Vegas 2) and can be played with friend in coop mode, that is blast, about Multiplayer cant really say nothing since tough the game have interesting mechanics that can work out in multiplayer very well, i play R6 for its single and now coop feature and didnt bothered with multiplayer.
Its definitly a must have shooter, not only for fans of R6 (since they have very little in common), but for players that like FPS very action oriented and with some tactic mixed up, and now you can get it for reasonable price wich make your purchase worth while.

Being part of the Steam community for maybe 2 months has taught me that some people dont research games before buying them on Steam. DOA5LR is no exception. When Team Ninja announced a PC version of DOA5LR is coming to steam it was out of no where because people wanted it and people like me were saying things like "It's not gonna happen, give up." and well we were proven wrong because it did. It was announced that it was going to be based on last gen's version (PS3 and XBOX 360). This was 1 out of the 2 things this version people had problems with.
The other thing was online being delayed. This was fixed later on but exclusive to ranked matches and no way to make your own lobby like you can in the console versions. Looking at the game's achievements list I noticed something here, the Lobby rlated achievements from the console versions are no where to be seen coming to the conclusion that this version was never ment to have them. So based by these facts, the game is fine for what it is. At least unlike last gen's console versions DLC is still being supported so PC users still have the upper hand over last gen because as of 10/13/2015 Team Ninja dropped DLC support for PS3 and XBOX 360 users and the Halloween 2015 Costume Set being the last DLC set for last gen.
Another thing people have an issue with is DLC being expensive. DLC is an optional thing but I would have to agree that buying the whole pack is upsetting if you are like me and only use a handful of characters and not all of them that the pack comes with. How DLC is being handeled here on Steam is very weird. You are forced to buy the whole pack and not have an option of buying 1 DLC for a specific character you stick to like you can on consoles.
Pros
-Fun fighting game experience
-Over 30+ characters to choose from
-Story Mode
-Training Mode
-Arcade, Time Attack, and Survival Mode
-English and Japanese Voice Over options
-Online
-4K resolution support if your PC supports it
-Controller support
Cons
-DLC is in bulk (you are forced to buy the whole pack unlike the console versions but optional)
-The lack of playing with friends online via invite as an alternative of no Lobby matches is odd.
Final Rating: 8/10

Let me tell you the story, a story of a very unique game called Meadow. I bought Meadow on an old computer, tried to run it and it failed miserably..Last christmas however, I got a shiny new computer! And the first thought in my head was 'Could this run that game Meadow?' hint..It could! I loaded up the game in the morning, wandering around as a small badger cub. I ran into a fox, which led me to a goat. Suddenly, this fox and goat started talking gibberish to eachother, strange symbols flashed on my screen, they seemed to have a mutual agreement and started walking away. I was completly baffled by this..'How did they know what the other was saying?' I asked, confused. After collecting a few crystals, I accidentally hit the P button, which revealed a screen to me..Later I realized the images on it were growing as I got more crystals! I was starting to understand! I think about what game I thought Meadow was then, and what game I know it is now. One of my favorite things about this is..You figure it out on your own! Which just adds a kind of magic and mysterious feature to it. The not understanding of it made me want to play more, to figure it out, to understand! And when I did, it was like a whole new world had been opened up to me. Meadow is a game about calmness, finding and letting go of so many amazing friends, and realizing what it truly means to be alone sometimes. I opened up steam for the first time in years. Had 6 bucks on my wallet. I browsed around games, found one that caught my eye..and I spent the last of my money on it. I was disoriented and confused, but knew that I loved it. And I really do love meadow, I have made a bunch of amazing friends on there that I meet up with and play with..But if Im being honest, I much prefer the times when I gather up a small group and play for hours and hours..And find what wholesome people are with me, people join the group and make it larger, we split away from the large group..We wander, laugh, say goodbye one by one, say hello one by one, show eachother secret areas, go across to the edge of the world and back. These are the things that make Meadow such a special game to me. It taught me that..Its okay to let go, because everytime you do..You meet someone else, someone who might show you an amazing area you've never seen. You find something else, something that awestrucks you and you HAVE to show the next group this! With everything that you let go, something new is found. And with everything new that is found, something else is let go. The friendships that are made, and then demolished, are the best ones. Those are the ones that you remember. Thanks for reading.

Puzzle Quest: Challenge Of The Warlords is an addicting puzzle game with an added roleplaying element. The title was developed by Infinite Interactive and published by Namco Networks America. Anyone who has played Tetris, Bejewelled or any similiar game will be quite familiar with the puzzle portion of this fantastic title but for me, as a heavy R.P.G. fan, it was this part of the game that really makes it stand apart from the others in the genre.
As in the start of a typical roleplaying game you select your character and class before the terrific story sends you traveling across a vast fantasy world in search of quests, battles and loot. I found the story to be extremely compelling and at times humorous. It definitely keeps your attention and makes you want to wander about and converse with any person or beast that would cross your path. The combat, of course, takes place in puzzle format and tasks you with matching pairs of colored gems, skulls and other items while casting spells as well as a variety of other attacks and moves against your opponent. As you battle you earn experience points which you can spend upgrading your skills as well as accquiring gold and loot with which you can better outfit your character. You also have the option to capture opponents and hold them in your dungeon. You can then learn new spells and combat tactics from your prisoners as well as use the captured beasts as mounts as you traverse the world.
The game is presented very well with a combination of fantastic hand drawn manga-like art for the cut scenes as well as an old school top down "Legend Of Zelda" like world map. Shockingly one of the best parts of the game in my opinion is the music. I can't stress how great the soundtrack is in this title as it expertly captures the fantasy theme of the game. I fell in love with it after just a few days of playing the title. The sound effects during the puzzle battles are terrific as well. You never get tired of hearing the explosions, coin drops and other tell-tale effects when you successfully connect a line of gems and cause a cascade that devastates your opponent bringing them to their knees in defeat...absolutely priceless. I never thought I would be a fan of puzzle games but the Puzzle Quest series has, no pun intended, cast a spell on me. Highly recommended! I think I like this one better than Puzzle Quest 2 which I adore.

I don't write reviews on games I buy normally, nor do I play these sorts of games normally. If you would go through my library at the time of this writing, you would say "Damn this guy likes a lot of RPG's and FPS's!"
But this time I decided to give something new a shot.
Meadow. What can I say about it that other people haven't.
Well, for starters, if I had to compare it to another popular game that you might recognize, Journey.
This game is the PC, Animal version of the Playstation game Journey.
Now you can take that however you want, but what I mean by that is this game invokes the feelings for another that Journey did when I first played it on my PS4. (Yes, I know it originally came out on PS3, but I never played that version :P )
Travelling around this beautiful land, finding your way around aimlessly is the most fun I've had in a game like this since, well, Journey!
I ran into another Badger cub in the beginning, we unlocked a few shrines together, then I lost him. The feeling of losing someone you didn't know personally may of been miniscule, but it happened nevertheless.
I didn't know this person, nor could I hear their voice, but that didn't matter. Because we were accomplishing a similar goal with a very primitive way of communicatiing with eachother. Emotes and Symbols.
The Graphics are are pretty well done on the skins of the animals themselves. They're a cross between sudo-realism and a crazy cloth patterned art style. The world that you roam is covered in this cloth patterned art style as well. All I have to say is it's beautiful to look at, and easy on the eyes. I was so relaxed and at peace while playing it.
This is most definitely going to be a game I come home from work and hop on when I'm stressed.
(No frog pun intended, Yes you can play as a frog!)
My only advice for NEW players is two things. When you start off, zoom your camera WAAAAAAY out, as far as it will allow. Trust me, it helps.
Secondly, USE THE MAP. I spent the first 30 minutes of the game wandering around looking for other animals to help me solve shrines that I couldn't open alone. The map solves this problem by literally showing you where all the other animals are congregated in your map/server.
My one suggestion for the devs is to allow ALL animals to "Sprint" in the water, not just the amphibians. I mean, make them FASTER than the other animals, but please make everyone else a little faster. It's sometimes unbearable swimming across a LARGE lake that takes 5-10 mintues of real time.
All in all, I want everyone to play this game. Give the devs the money they deserve for making such an experience akin to one of my favorite games of a generation, Journey.
Thanks devs, and keep up the good work!

Leaving a full review for blender would rquire spending more time than for an essay. There is so much to say about this software, because in its own respect it is completely and uttterly unique. So lets get started by talking about what blender is.
Blender is probably the most extensive and modern application that you will find for free. Considering how many thousands of dollars you pay not only once, but yearly for softwares such as Autodesk Maya, or Cinema4D, Blender is your enlightenment. Because, guess what, it is completely free. Free, doesn't mean that this software was last updated in the year 1995, and features nice grey to black gradients in a truly ancient application. In this case free means a regularly updated piece of software that contuinuously brings new features to the table such as the new eevee realtime rendering engine in the so far developer build, blender 2.8. Blender serves not only as a complex 3D modeling software, animator, and even a video editor, but also as a great tool to do simple simulations and particle effects. The person who said ¨you get what you pay for¨ has never used blender before.
Don't let my large number of hours fool you, the majority of those hours was my computer rendering a large animation, because rendering takes ages. This is whether you are using the blender internal rendering engine, or cycles rendering engine. Both rendering engines have their perks and I feel slightly inclined to use blender internal (call me a newbie if you will). If you are starting with blender, start with blender render, is far easier, but less versatile. I just usee it, because my current project is very important and I want to use what I know rather than diving into something completely different. However, if there is one thing that I would say blender does poorly, is optimize your hardware. Blender internal cannot use the GPU to render (sorry Titan XP users), so I'm stuck rendering with my CPU, so a  clip that is around 600 frames (or 10 seconds) can take upwards of 2 hours to render. Not quite sure about render times on other 3D programs, but I know for sure that after effects can beat that number by a factor of 100.
Oh, by the way, cycles render engine allows you to use the GPU to render *cheering Titan XP users*, but it isn't much faster either *awkward silence*.
Blender is daunting. Some people open up the interface for the first time and immediately start working like a pro, those people are also from the 5th dimension which exceeds all space and time. Noone opens Blender without any experience and says  ¨I can figure this out easy as pie¨. But that is why we have the internet my friends. Google tutorials, you will need them to start in Blender. l still don't know all the features of the program. Ask me about textures and materials and I can help you. Ask me about particles and simulations and I'll google it for you. Blender looks daunting at first, but don't let that scare you. Once you learn the basics, you will realize the wide range of possiblities. You will start working on small projects and once you are more comfortable, you will move onto bigger ones. You aren't going to make an epic dragon in Blender and animate it so that it eats fedoras on your first attempt. You'll probably just make a box and move that around, fedora eating can wait.
You know when you're grinding on runescape, or trying to make it out of silver. You keep on practicing until you get it just right and then you'll feel so happy and accomplished. Now that you have blender you can practice and practice and make an amazing video and put on youtube and earn money with it. Plus you gain loads of experience in 3D modeling, animation, etc. that might help you find a cool job. Blender may not be a game, and you may not find it as fun, but it is *rewarding* and with rewarding I mean, *WOAH THIS IS AWESOME MOM GET THE CAMERA OH WAIT ITS ALREADY A VIDEO FILE IM RAMBLING SO EXCITED OMG* When you finish your first render and you look at that video file and you realize you created something, it is one fo the most satisfying feelings in the world. This is quite a difficult game to truly love, but it was certainly more than enough to hold my interest. It can only be described as an RPG crossed with Bejewelled. So I guess in effect it is Bejewelled with a purpose, utilising a system of coloured gems to fill mana reserves to use special abilities and attacks, skulls to deal direct damage with your weapon or gold & xp gems to boost your cash and level respectively.
Much like an RPG it involves a class system which doesn't limit what equipment you can wield, but affects what abilities you can use. The class also determines the nature of your powers - Warriors will generally gain abilities to increase attack or deal direct damage while mages can change gems on the board or remove them entirely.
You'd be forgiven for thinking that this is a dream union of two very different genres, but it's in the storytelling which lets this game down. The story is the same old recycled "Dark Lord guy comes back from the dead.. again.. and wants to kill everyone" RPG cliche. This in itself isn't a crime, but the fetch/kill side-quests don't really do much to appeal to your adventurous side with often difficult fights combined with relatively poor rewards, coupled with the "random encounters" which are merely the same monster appearing and disappearing on the same route. Free roaming is not on the cards, but rather a system of clicking on destinations on a 2-D overworld map linked by lines to represent travellable routes. The Tavern system isn't that cracking either with the "rumours" not being worth the coin you pay, mostly as they are things you'll figure out yourself by PLAYING THE GAME or have absolutely no useful information whatsoever.
Now, if there is a dealbreaker in choosing this game it is without a doubt the AI. It is painfully obvious when the computer "player" makes a mistake (eg. forfeiting a turn bonus by missing an oppertunity for 4 or 5-in-a-row, a row of skulls etc.) that is very very obvious. Also, when they make said mistakes they seem to have some kind of uncanny luck, as these mistakes seem to trigger big combos dropping down from the top, almost as if they know the order of the gems above the top row in play. You will often find you fumble and struggle for similar combinations, or any good combinations at all.
All in all, the game isn't bad. If you can overlook the dialogue, the rigid "exploration" and the AI, which if it were a person would have won the lottery a dozen times over, you will find a largely enjoyable experience with some nice artwork and visuals. If it's going cheap, get it!

This game is really, really quite good.  I mean, really good. It is a 4x game released under Sid Meier's name, and as the title may suggest to the more astute observationalists, it's about civilisations. (For the fifth time, even.) More precisely, Civilisation 5 is a game that puts the role of civilisation builder in the hands of the player, handing them the tools to select what path they want to take their society down. You can focus sheerly on religion, and through a network of missionaries spread your religion across the four corners of the map, and this feature is greatly expanded in the Gods and Kings. (we will get to the DLC in a bustle.) Or you can focus on military and use your powerful military units to conquer the map, uniting all nations under your strict rule. It's really all up to you, and that kind of choice lends greatly to the replayability. So what's the game feel like? How does it work? Civ 5 is a hex based, turned based 4x strategy game, and so the gameplay on land plays about like you'd expect: click where you want to move your units, use their actions for that turn, manage your resources and cities, maybe expand territory, so on so forth. Outside of that is where most of the systems truly lay. Perhaps largest are the Social Policies function and the Diplomacy function. With social policies, you engineer your societies priorities, and by progressing in the social policies tree you are able to select perks and rewards accordingly. For example, if you wanna focus on sheer income and capital (first of all, you monster) then you could select the commerce tree, and progressing down it unlocks new things to help you produce that sweet sweet $$. This applies to the other distinct social policies, and that diversity lets you mix and match priorities as you are not locked in a tree once you unlock it. Diplomacy, inversely, concerns other nations (and your own's relation to them) In many ways this function can be seen as just a quicker way to access world leaders (You can also click on a territory they hold to talk to them, essentially allowing the same function) As a whole, this mechanic is what allows you to trade, form alliances, form protective agreements, allow travel thru land, declare war, and so on. This allows for some really interesting♥♥♥♥♥♥ For example, my first playthrough involved me as the Shoshone Tribe of Native Americans, a really fun faction that comes with really neat bonuses. All faff aside, Rome started to encroach on my cherished borders before too long and tensions rose sharply. I tried to forge a friendship with Caesar to discourage his imperialism, but it seemed as though it was to no avail. Trade routes we had were our only solid bond, and before long I denounced him for the whole world to see. Even further, I mustered a tiny force to attack his bordering cities. Needless to say, I lost, and the following alliance lasted mere turns before he backstabbed me and stormed my civ. Eventually it took a coalition of world leaders I worked tirelessly to form to bring Rome down, and give my civ breathing room at last.♥♥♥♥♥♥like that is what sucks me in to a game: getting immersed in the stories it lets me make. This game is not perfect: it essentially requires its DLC to be as good as it can be (BNW and GaK are the two musts but the rest also serve to enhance it) and it does awkwardly romanticise many of the past's errs, but god damn if this is not one of the finest games ever made. It gives the player a world and it leaves the player to make with that world what they will. The sheer scope of its mechanics is what breaths so much life into what would otherwise be a generic hex based "end turn sim", and it really is something of an acheivment that I must reccomend.  If this were a numeric based system, it'd get like a 9.5 out of 10. Honestly. It's brilliant.

Throwing "Tom Clancy's" on a title usually means that the game is going to have some meat, or say solid content to it. The only downside is that this means Ubisoft is the sole publisher/developer of the title; boy do they love console ports.
Rainbow Six is an anti-terrorism organization who tries to stop threats before they become the front page news. With this, you lead a team with 2 other squad mates to tackle challenges that take place in close quarter building environments and city streets.
By commanding your squad mates, you progress through the challenges in the cohesive story. The single player story is about 10 hours’ worth of content, which allows you to get to know characters and game mechanics well. As with many other Tom Clancy games, there is always a sci-fi twist that doesn't seem "out of this world".
With your squad mates, you can clear rooms, rappel down the sides of buildings, and coordinate to take enemies out. If one of the squad mates manages to go down, the other can be ordered to revive them. In the more likely event that both squad mates go down, you revive them with a "hypo". While there is an "infinite" health system in place, you will still find yourself dying quite a bit.
Biggest issues out of the game? Let's start with checkpoints, checkpoints, checkpoints... The worst thing known to humanity continues and was a "feature" back in the day. Rainbow Six doesn't escape this, and it will make you rage. People still arguge about checkpoints somehow defeating "save cheating" (the "art" or plain intelegence to save before big battles). This is simply untrue due to the fact that consoles simply couldn't save that much data back then. It was a technical reason (and poor one) that has infected modern games.
The "blur" or what seems to be some horrible pain effect isn't good at all. Because it's a console port, the memory and cpu usage had to be kept down and this horrible awful effect does its job. It is also strangely not optimized that well, so systems on the edge of requirements will suffer frame issues when effect kicks in.
Multiplayer, while it does exist, requires an Uplay account, and then a small chance of someone playing multiplayer as well. There are no dedicated servers it seems, so a peer-2-peer system is in place. Only good thing that seems to come from multiplayer is the very precise customization options, it even surprised me in fact.
Using an older version of the Unreal engine, AI has issues following and getting into positions sometimes. Once you play enough, you will get used to it. I came in knowing that, and automatically accounted for it. Your experiences will vary in this regard with high certainty.
Keys are places in odd spots on your keyboard, and there's quite a few to remember. Left alt for instance changes squad engagement rules and then pressing and holding r shows the gun equipment radial menu. V, B, and N are for room entering commands which change based on engagement rule set.
Beyond these aspects, I had fun playing the title. It was unique, yet required some chasing to get it to work on Windows 7.

This is a positive recommendation review on DnL with a feature comparison to its related parent game, ARK:Survival Evolved at its own release (closest comparison) .Discussing bugs is out of scope since I began writing this, another update was released fixing some of them, so the review would not age well if I did.
1)
From an early-game ‘workflow’ perspective, I found this to be an improvement on Ark, which suffers from ‘player displacement’ when you die and respawn prior to beds etc. You are familiar with your start zone in DnL, you know where to run, which you will be doing a lot, and it is a safe harbour, which removes unfairness and RNG from the process. It’s great for orientating you at the early hours of gameplay (pre-level 20). Side note – Sprint lasts a good (enough) time, which similar to an MMORPG ‘corpserun’. This gets you over that initial “hump” before you craft better ways to reduce downtime from death penalty. I find the consistent starting place is anchoring, less time wasteful and suffers less disappointing RNG. Your own opinion on whether this is better will vary.
2)
As well as giving you a consistent and safe start, you have NPC’s, and more importantly, guards protecting you from everything except flying beasts (right now) which gives the early leveller a well-established tactic of “Run Like Feck” to kite mobs to the city guards. This is a massive comfort, since creature’s aggro onto you with line of sight and can be quite pedantic with their threat tables. Once you make it on there, it’s a grudge for life. NPC’s (which now respawn) are useful to trade with but cannot be abused (time locks on selling). This makes for an alternate playstyle catering to those with lower risk-reward thresholds than others. It also means access to a useful mount, early on. Take it or leave it, it’s a sliding level of difficulty you can use, or not. To summarise, the City and NPC’s are a great addition that bring some extra life and utility but aren’t breaking the core gameplay, just augmenting it.
3)
Hunger and thirst are NOT annoying at default levels and don’t cripple you. Same as Focus (wakefulness), Stamina and Mana. You must gather a wider range of objects than Ark, you don’t need to eat to live. In fact, food is a by-product of what you do already, and fits into the play workflow excellently. This is super important! This stuff cannot be annoying or else the game gets tedious. The limits set by these resources are important but not detracting. They make it so you are not invincible, but you need to tend to yourself every so often. Your own opinion may vary, as would the server settings and further development impacts.
4)
I find this way better than Ark. Whilst you have character levels which increase your statistics in both games, in DnL, to access recipe’s, you are not gated directly by level, instead you gain recipes by doing the related gathering or crafting. You get better at stuff by doing the same stuff, which allows you to focus on what you do and give you your own goals rather than just levelling as a grind. Or simply put, if you want to level your house building, build house parts. Want to level magic? Build staves and magic items. This means that your friends levelling at the same time actually have different recipes available to them (since we all do things differently). With three people, we found one concentrated on home comforts, one on taming and one on combat. But no one ever planned it that way.
There is a (currently broken) tutorial system guiding you on what to do, which would, when fixed, give players a great introduction to the game and sets goals to guide you. It would also be completely ignorable but for the interface element being stuck there. The UI is overly invasive for it and it’s inflexible, but the concept is useful. The crafting progression is great and less strictly gated, although, in real terms, yes, you cannot get high end things immediately, but you can lean certain ways. It’s more about Player choice.
5)
From my memories of early Ark, I don’t recall the targeting and movement being as good. However, I’m open to folks saying the two are in parity now. I certainly thought that DnL was better at its EA release than Ark’s and didn’t recall being ever able to run forwards and look backwards, which is definitely a great part of kiting.
6)
Ark WAS horrible at this point in development, and I despise being constrained in character creation personally. The DnL characters, both male and female look fantastic in DnL. But you can also get funky and make something resembling a troll or goblin using the sliders and the odd skin colours like black, blue and green. From playing games with my wife the last 11 years, I can tell you that females NEED character customisation. She also says, “The hair is ♥♥♥♥ and I want more hairstyles”. Valid, we need the fairer sex in gaming. But overall, this is one of the better character creations I have seen anywhere and better than Ark in terms of variation. Except hair. Again.
7)
It’s interactive, fun and better in every way … except in the one same way Ark is bad. That there is no feedback during the stunning/fatigue phase. I believe taming would be less frustrating/confusing if this was changed. Slowing the creature progressively, or a bar over its head would work. Tying a creature down with magic rope looks and feels great. Clearly subject to change, but it’s already more fun and cool than Ark, for me. There are other methods later in game also using magic. Similar in that taming is there with the same end result, different process to get there. How much you see it as different really depends on your point of view. I like the concept of rope myself.
8)
It’s a personal differentiator, but we don’t really have this genre well covered in FPS. I can’t say how the high end PvP works with this, but for low end PvE, I prefer the concept to Ark’s guns and higher end weaponry. Enough to say, if you like magic and dragons, you will like this. It persuaded some of my non ‘Dino-phile’ friends into DnL on this very basis. It’s still a personal thing though. I hear observations like, “This is an Ark reskin”. Apart from the key differentiators I’m listing here, it’s also fair to say some people don’t get turned on by Dinosaurs, and mythical beasts are more their thing. You cannot knock those subjective opinions, it’s the key differentiator, but not the only differentiator.
9)
A cheeky mob that knocks you out and robs your things and makes off. Worth a mention just because it’s so cool. You can have epic gameplay hunting down the thieving b&^%&*s trying to get your stuff back. It’s great dynamic content that we should see more of. It’s become personal with the AI! After speaking to a 1K hour Ark player, this made its way into Ark in slightly differing ways. Knockout has always been there in Ark, stealing your stuff came later, the two, however are nicely combined in the Goblin, with a more immersive package.
I hope the game continues to develop in the same way as I am enjoying it very much!

Elisa: The Innkeeper - Prequel is a visual novel with an emphasis on choices. The prequel is basically a short demo for a longer game. The game is slightly unusual in not having a protagonist, per se. Your perspective changes from one character to another as the game progresses. I don't particularly like that during scenes with multiple characters present, the perspective changes between characters. I find it gives the narrative an inconsistent tone, and can be confusing. This is in line with the game's description though ("His/Her judgements affect every character and their actions, like a god that watches everything from above.")
The artwork is very nicely done, as is the music. The dialogue can be a bit spotty, and the engine the game is built in has some issues with resolutions and scaling properly. My biggest complaint is that I don't really like the character of Elisa, which makes the premise that everyone who meets her falls in love with her somewhat difficult to swallow.
The developers clearly put a lot of work into this game, and it's actually not bad. The game also seems to receive regular updates, and as of the time of writing, the game is free to play. There's no reason not to try it out while the game is free. I may update this review once a price has been set.

It's nice to see a visual novel not set in high school in Japan.
is set in what appears to be an Italian fairy-tale village, and follows a handful of relatively unscrupulous characters as they attempt to manipulate each other. To what end? That's determined to a surprising extent by the player's choices; very few visual novels I've played change so completely depending on what the player decides.
This is a small preview of the game (which has met its funding goal on Kickstarter), and so doesn't reach any actual resolution. Still and all, there's enough here to get a feel for the characters and the world, and to make several interesting choices and pursue different threads. The art style is cheerful and pleasant, the music is excellent, and the dialogue, while a bit rough around the edges in places, is often well-written and funny.
The developers of
are accessible and open to player feedback, which is nice, and they've actually released an update to this demo version, adding several new features (and Steam achievements) -- that kind of dedication is nice to see, given the number of games that end up perpetually stuck in "early access." The Kickstarter has met its initial funding target, but is still running as of this writing -- there are plenty of stretch goals still to meet!

The Atmosphere in this game is god tier in eye candy quality and its performence IMO is one of the best optimized games for FPS but sadly its not perfect.
The story is kinda meh in the grand scheme of things but the world,creatures and weapons make up for this more or less
The creatures even tho few in varity are very well animated + design for what they are and combat against them is more or less what you expect
The weapons in this game all look like workshop made contraptions more or less which adds to the feel for the game. Although the weapon shops are pointless since after a few begining areas you will find weapons with upgrades on the corpses of those who you kill/ found dead.
Also if your a fan of shabby russian humor this game will serve you well.
Now for the bad parts
The AI is derpy as hell, I expected so much from the monsters of the metro but the human AI to lack a great quantity of IQ points. They won't spot you when they should be able to see you and their headlamp is directly pointed towards you and they won't be concern about piles of dead bodies stacking up but are alerted when they find a dead comrad.
Lastly the AI will very easily lose track of you when you break "Line of Sight" and resume hunt mode till everyone in the room is dead.
Another moderatly bad part is that the game doesn't tell you how things work most of the time. For example at the shooting range there is no direct notfication that you have infinite ammo at the range and your ammo pool will not be used or that your mask can break durring combat and only can be repair by switching it out with one thats in a better condition than your own (This means you cannot go to the shop to get a new one/repair it). Some of the mechanics are moderatly easy to figure out but sometimes it can cost you if your not carefull.
Last thing that effected my gameplay is that durring the middle stages my nightvision was toggled on before every cutscene/event moment and did not let me switch it off. This lead to a couple parts of the game where I was stuck in Nightvsion when i wasn't suppose to have it on in the 1st place.
To conclude everything. Does this game has its problems? Yes. Should that keep you from buying+playing it? No. I whould say the "feel" of the world in this game is a good enough reason to pick it up when its on sale.

I tend to have high standards. But I also have low expectations, so I can be pleasantly surprised occasionally.
I didn't expect much of Snowball! from looking at the store page. It looked like a simplistic little flash game (yes, it is flash), but, hey, it's pinball, so I bought it anyway.
Turns out, it's actually excellent!
There's only one "table", but it's quite expansive (camera scrolls up and down), and the mechanics are surprisingly deep.
Basically, you collect jewels, which disappear as you roll over them with a snowball. There are also targets that disappear when you hit them. There are teleporter holes, gates (one that you can control), multiple launchers, multiple flippers, multiple multiball sources (one based on locks, and a quick one for hitting snowmen). Many trees that serve as bumpers. There's a little breakout game in one of the mini-playfields. There are tesla coil magnets you can control to make the ball orbit around them. There's an igloo and a castle. There are big fans you can control. There's a little triangular bumper you can raise. There are acceleration lanes. There are score multipliers and streaks. Some targets and jewels appear when you do certain things. Mini-jewels respawn (as a different color) when you collect enough of them (it takes more each time). Megajewels respawn too if you manage to collect them all (not easy!) You can nudge (but it costs points). And probably something I'm forgetting.
Wait, did I say "basically"? Oops.
Anyway, yeah, it's pretty good. Very fun. Will keep you occupied for hours. Oh, and the art and music is great too.
I hesitate to mention this, since they deserve your money, but this game is also a free flash game you can find on the net (e.g. on miniclip). But by buying it here, you get achievements (took me about 2 hours to 100%, but I'm an expert), leaderboards, the warm feeling that you're supporting good indie devs, and possibly also exclusive features not in the free version (I'm not sure about that, but it sounds like they'll at least be adding new stuff). The game has only been on steam for a day, but I'm still sad to see that only about 100 people have played it.
Because someone is bound to ask, the physics are pretty basic... obviously. This is ok.
Now, there are a few wrinkles:
I experienced two technical glitches - one time the game froze (game breaking), and one time the camera glitched slightly. Dev said he's looking into both.
Update: I originally wrote about keyboard only controls, but controller support was added a few days after release (though, as of now, needs a deadzone update).
Still, these hitches don't make me remotely question my purchase.
Highly recommended for both pinball experts and dabblers.
