[ Before I begin let me underline that I like blender a lot, but it was a rocky road to get there in the beginning.]
Though Blender offers a lot of powerful tools and allows you to generate  really professional and nice results, it is far from being an intuitive or straight forward software.
Having worked with tools like Maya or 3ds max or even simple tools like Sketchup I must say blender is unfortunately sometimes very ♥♥♥♥♥y in its behaviour. Especially working with hierarchy is not intuitive at all.
Would you like to group, join or parent objects ?
Well anyway just because you grouped it or parented an object, doesn't mean you can easily duplicate or even move the whole... no, you still need to use some keyboard shortcuts to select everything.
Being used to precise positioning, like all other software easily allow you to, you will get frustrated quickly here, because it is a lot slower and less simple to work with exact measures.
Context sensitive keyboard shortcuts can also really suck.... just because your cursor is not above the 3d view a common shortcut is either not working or gives you a completely different result than you've expected.
Blender is quite easy to learn and once you get around the "how to"  it can actually be a lot of fun, just be aware, the frustration factor of this tool is 20 times higher than in other tools.
And don't get me started about the undo stack.
All you people switching from Sketchup be warned, it'll be 1-2 weeks of pure hatred towards blender before you start liking it. However once you got used to this awkward tool you never want to switch again. Also the results really make up for the extra frustration in the beginning. Not to forget that it is a free tool.
The community is also huge and there is always an answer in any forum to your question.
Numerous tutorials also help to find your way into it easily.
If you have the patience give it a go!

I've been a fan of the Rainbow Six series since the beginning but after Raven Shield the series headed in a console centric direction. While Vegas has the console feel but still it a great game on the PC.
The play commands Logan Keller the new team leader of Rainbow, a international anti-terrorist organization, sent to a Mexican border town to capture Irena Morales who is a terrorist ringleader. Failing to capture Irena, Keller is ordered to head to Las Vegas to handle a new crisis there. The story is on par with any Tom Clancy book or game so it filled with action and a couple plot twists but overall its not memorable.
Gameplay takes on new features from previous installments. One is the cover system much like Kill.switch and Gears Of War players can take cover against almost anything and either blind fire to give covering fire or pop up and shoot. Another add in is a regenerative health system that is much like any other game that has one. In previous Rainbow Six games before each mission but with the going more console centric that went away and was replaced a simple order giving control scheme which in Vegas was refined and is pretty simple to give your team members orders to breach, grenade, flash, clear, etc.
Sound FX do sound great in the case of the weapon fire and other general FX's and the voice work is good and fit the game well and while the soundtrack is good and fits the game its just the same orchestral work like most games.
Overall the game is a great game to experience for fans of the Rainbow Six series.

This is the best zombie survival game I ever played. Here are the reasons why:
0. Athmosphere. The game has tons of this. Everything you do and everywhere you go, the makers of Dying Light ensure you feel you are in Haran where everything has gone to hell. It never get's easy and it never get's pretty.
1. The open world is big. It's not huge, but big enough to run around, climb, dive, roll and whatnot, to your heart's delight. The open world is also very beautifully detailed and believable. I have played this game A LOT and I am sure here a enough locations I have never seen. Zipping around with the grappling hook never gets boring. The climbing and parkouring is very cool. So cool actually, that I can't help but notice how fit this main character is. He really is a tough Crane... But still.... Don't go out into the night unprepared!!!!.
2. The story is nice and has cool twists. It is not a well written novell, but has enough depth, plot-twists, character building to be enjoyable. There is also some semi-filosophical badass talk by the main bad guy: Rais. Which makes him extra cool actually. The story also helps you discover the game and it's possibilities. The story helps you become a better player. This helps achieving the higher skills needed to play on nightmare.
3. The difficulty levels are well balanced, so you can learn the game, master it and Still have a challenge on the nightmare mode. This will always be a challenge. Character advancement is also well worked out, so you get to learn new skills, before you learn new ones. The skills you learn really make a difference too. If you think you are the boss, than try and play the 'be the zombie' mode as human vs a human zombie. It will be...... refreshing. ;-)
4. Side plot to the main story make for nice distractions from the main story if your into it. These side stories actually change the world sometimes. That is nice. They also add the most 'fluff' to the world. All the people you encounter are nuts and pretty funny, even if they seem sane at the start.
It is a shame though that you can't reset the side stories, after you finished them all. That would give you a way to keep earning xp after ending the main story.
5. DLC is very nice as well. "The following" adds a huge open world and buggies!!!!! Now you can just drive over piles of zombies. The night is still dangerous though. Bozak horde is a cool challenge to your skills and for a while I enjoyed to shave seconds, sometimes minutes, off my time in this challenge. Especially when you team up with a friend.
All in all. A very, very cool game.

It really is a fun game. Just a shame I did not notice it earlier and that it did not grow into something more.

I found this game by lazily scrolling through Steam's under $10 list, and it caught my eye. Absolutely fantastic game, so relaxing and beautiful to play and the abstract world is breathtaking. Playing as cute little animals, paired with their funny emotes and noises is an instant pick-me-up when you're feeling down. I loved the level of team-work and socialisation in the game and found it really heartwarming when my group would find another player and bombard them with emotes and noises in greeting. The first time i played it I spent about 5 hours in one sitting just roaming around and collecting things, I was having such a blast I didn't realise how late it had become.
I even found myself progressing through the game in the sense that as I started out as a little badger cub, I followed around a lynx and a fox while they led me to the collectibles and helped me out, and as time went on I found myself switching my animal to a fox or a goat, and helping out the little newcomer badgers in turn. It was a funny little cycle of newbie > amateur > pro where you were passing along the help you had recieved in the beginning. Definitely reccomend this game to anyone looking for a cute, lighthearted experience which helps you relax and smile. My only warning is to be careful as it's easy to get so lost in the game you lose track of time. ;)

I really
wanted to like this game as a huge fan of the table top, but I'm massively disappointed.
Thematically it’s perfect, and if you are fan of the 40k universe it’s a real treat, and will definitely increase your enjoyment of the game. Graphics and sound are really good also, the combat feels visceral and the general look and feel of the game is great. At times it can be really fun to play, especially 2v2 with a friend.
Most matches will about 5 minutes. You level up admirals to build the fleet, you dont have free control to pick whatever you like whenever you like (as in the table top). Campaign is okay (I've not played a lot yet) but it seems to mostly be a string of skirmish missions in essence. When playing online you don't have control over what map or game mode you play, or points size, its all random.
It’s not release ready, buggy with frequently crashes. It’s missing major features at release; team chat, AI battles with friends, fully open skirmish modes, fully fledged match making and ranked matches. There is a
to deliver some of these features but they may not be arriving for months. It also looks like the Space Marine DLC will be late.
If you are expecting massive fleet engagements as shown in the trailers, or even something more modest like 10 ships a side – don’t, you will be disappointed. In a 2v2 game unless you want to spam escorts, you will have about 3 ships per player. The points limit is crushingly low, and
it’s not going to change anytime soon.
The game is so simple, the gameplay is so
shallow. The table top was a naval engagement game, which allowed detailed control of weapons, movement and abilities. This plays more like a battle arena game. There is no real negative aspect or risk to using abilities, and there is no resource cost, so you just spam them as fast as possible. There is limited control over weapons, they just constantly fire. This means for instance you can’t time your weapons for increased effectiveness.
You control ships with point and click movement, but ships take wide turns to get to places so you never really know where your ships are going. Units don’t maintain formation (a la Total War games), and there is no control over speed. This means it’s almost impossible to move your fleet in a concerted manner, i.e. escorts will always arrive in battle before your cruisers.
This game was released a month late, and it feels like it still needs a few more months. If you like 40k then you may like this, otherwise I would pass.

Just completed the Campaign and have spent 60 hours in the beta doing Skirmish and Muti so i thought it be a good time to give a review.
Firstly the graphics look fantastic and the game runs very well on my rather average PC. All the ships look just how they do in table top. The imperial ships look so beautiful with all the tall spires and cathedrals. The map designs look gorgeous with planets, suns, asteroid fields, ice crystals and my fav being the blackhole map that reminds me so much of the movie intersellar. I've experienced 2 crashes in my 85 hours of playthrough and both instances happened during the beta so im happy that they have dealt with the little problem.
Secondly the campaign is brilliant. I think the voice actors done a very good job and speak in the way you expect people in the 40k universe to speak. The campaign was long and took me just over 40 turns to do but every turn had some form of speech by someone of some incident happening or some big bad coming into the system. The cinematics are truely awesome and really keep close to the lore. i really love the art design and music with chapter 2 "entering the warp" scene where the crew are praying being a masterpiece.
I did the campaign on normal and i can say its just about the right difficulty (For someone like me that likes hard games) any higher and i could see myself throwing the mouse or keyboard at the wall mainly due to how random the campaign can be. The problem being is that every time you replay and load the same mission your enemy will have a completely different set up and be in completely different location on a completely different map (asteroids, mines and gas being in different locations). This can pretty much make you win or lose automaticly depending on the mission and it can be incredibly annoying when everything is stacked against you because of the RNG. All you can do is restart and load the mission up. This really is the only bad thing i can say about the game. Hell, i even lost the first mission because the first shot the defence platform did after the shields went down critical hitted me and took my generator offline and then took double the time to warp out as abaddons 100 ships slapped me down hard.
Thirdly the balance of skirmish and multi is completely fine. For those of you who were not in the beta you have no idea how bad it was back then. You had Eldar Holofields that worked even better then they do now.  You had insanely OP Assault boats that at the time made Chaos the go to race. You had insanely OP Taunt that was auto win when playing Orks. You had Nova Cannon that didn't even show up on the map and fired alot faster. There was alot of things that have been sorted out and balanced and right now things are pretty much good. Some work probably has to be done on Eldar but for everyone else it is near enough perfect. Literally all it comes down to is "Git Gud" for the most part.
The Micro in the game is perfect balance of not requiring to be a korean SC2 God and good enough that the game isn't a "a" and left click game. You can choose all the options that you want the computer to do for you by right clicking on all the skills you don't want to personally control yourself. Boarding and lightning strikes is usually a good one to do for new players. Ships are very slow even as Eldar so i can say that game is rather slow paced and not that many ships you have plenty of time to do all your skills and planning. If the game is still to micro intense for you? Just press space bar and it slows the game right down for everyone. There is literally no way i can see people complain about micro in this game. The only theory i have is that they are LOL kiddies that are so use to playing just 1 character with 4 abilities that when they come to a game where you have control 3-4 "characters" they instantly get anal prolapse.
8.5/10 - Campaign battle balance rather off as its pure RNG. Alliance battles and data collecting are awful. If you get Both in the same battle.. Pray to the Emperor. Tiny bit of race balancing needs work. Other then that a brilliant game. A must buy if you love the 40k universe. You won't be dissapointed. Can't wait for the space marine DLC.

This game is really, really quite good.  I mean, really good. It is a 4x game released under Sid Meier's name, and as the title may suggest to the more astute observationalists, it's about civilisations. (For the fifth time, even.) More precisely, Civilisation 5 is a game that puts the role of civilisation builder in the hands of the player, handing them the tools to select what path they want to take their society down. You can focus sheerly on religion, and through a network of missionaries spread your religion across the four corners of the map, and this feature is greatly expanded in the Gods and Kings. (we will get to the DLC in a bustle.) Or you can focus on military and use your powerful military units to conquer the map, uniting all nations under your strict rule. It's really all up to you, and that kind of choice lends greatly to the replayability. So what's the game feel like? How does it work? Civ 5 is a hex based, turned based 4x strategy game, and so the gameplay on land plays about like you'd expect: click where you want to move your units, use their actions for that turn, manage your resources and cities, maybe expand territory, so on so forth. Outside of that is where most of the systems truly lay. Perhaps largest are the Social Policies function and the Diplomacy function. With social policies, you engineer your societies priorities, and by progressing in the social policies tree you are able to select perks and rewards accordingly. For example, if you wanna focus on sheer income and capital (first of all, you monster) then you could select the commerce tree, and progressing down it unlocks new things to help you produce that sweet sweet $$. This applies to the other distinct social policies, and that diversity lets you mix and match priorities as you are not locked in a tree once you unlock it. Diplomacy, inversely, concerns other nations (and your own's relation to them) In many ways this function can be seen as just a quicker way to access world leaders (You can also click on a territory they hold to talk to them, essentially allowing the same function) As a whole, this mechanic is what allows you to trade, form alliances, form protective agreements, allow travel thru land, declare war, and so on. This allows for some really interesting♥♥♥♥♥♥ For example, my first playthrough involved me as the Shoshone Tribe of Native Americans, a really fun faction that comes with really neat bonuses. All faff aside, Rome started to encroach on my cherished borders before too long and tensions rose sharply. I tried to forge a friendship with Caesar to discourage his imperialism, but it seemed as though it was to no avail. Trade routes we had were our only solid bond, and before long I denounced him for the whole world to see. Even further, I mustered a tiny force to attack his bordering cities. Needless to say, I lost, and the following alliance lasted mere turns before he backstabbed me and stormed my civ. Eventually it took a coalition of world leaders I worked tirelessly to form to bring Rome down, and give my civ breathing room at last.♥♥♥♥♥♥like that is what sucks me in to a game: getting immersed in the stories it lets me make. This game is not perfect: it essentially requires its DLC to be as good as it can be (BNW and GaK are the two musts but the rest also serve to enhance it) and it does awkwardly romanticise many of the past's errs, but god damn if this is not one of the finest games ever made. It gives the player a world and it leaves the player to make with that world what they will. The sheer scope of its mechanics is what breaths so much life into what would otherwise be a generic hex based "end turn sim", and it really is something of an acheivment that I must reccomend.  If this were a numeric based system, it'd get like a 9.5 out of 10. Honestly. It's brilliant.

As a game PuzzleQuest: Challenge of the Warlords falls into the category of 'fun enough' gameplay. There's enough pleasant reward based feedback loops to keep a dude interested. But the story, the dialogue and the art direction are all so bland, so generic, so throw away that I can't /look/ or /read/ anything without wanting to smash my head into the wall. There is not /one/ thing here that hasn't been stolen, cribbed, cannibalized and copy/pasted with no real original input from the developers. I felt like I was playing a simulation of like... a world created by taking ever description of a fantasy realm by Salvatore, Brooks, and Anthony and blended together into the most homogenized word soup before being doled out to the artists and writers with a stern 'Do this' issued with each spoonful. Puzzle games are ubiquitous enough that you can find one just as fun as this deal without having to read the worst that nerds have to offer.

For a Tom Clancy game it still does have that tactical shootery thing going for it, but they've butchered the ordering system. Instead of being able to give orders to individual members or different squads you just have the one squad. You can control your character independently of the other two guys under your lead, which you cannot give independent orders to. It feels a little awkward being that this whole ordering system was executed pretty well in previous games.
The checkpoint system is in full swing and it is annoying. This isn't one of those games that rewards tactics so much as being very twitchy and knowing where the enemy will come from before hand. Vertical coverage is not an advantage. The only tactic I found that worked with the mechanics implemented in the game is continuously pulling feints and flanks on the AI which seems to be continually distracted. The AI also doesn't implement some tools really well. They'll sometimes just throw a smoke grenade your way and all you can say is "Thanks for that," but that doesn't help you when the AI can somehow see through the smoke in many places in the game.
Is it fun? Somewhat? I played it to the end and it's not something I'd subject myself to again unless I had a few friends along for the ride. It just doesn't appeal to me on the basis that I like to plan things out and it's hard to do that in one go, with the obvious advantages of cover and gaining height on targets, when the enemy can spawn in behind you and your men are plain disobeying orders left and right.

IMMERSION: X-com employs severl methods to attemp to immerse the player. It has player agency in abundance. Characters can have personalised names, outfits, skills, and weapon loadouts. Players can also customise base, adding a sim city like element to the game. Players are given almost total freedom to control those characters in combat. There's very little frankly that is outside of player control. 15/15
DIFFICULTY:The game does have options for difficulty, but they are not clear what they do entirely. The game is not easy on any difficulty, but the options are there. It seems that the difficulty is somewhat flexible, as players learn more and become more familiar with small unit tactics, the difficulty increases. On the other hand, the interface does not contribute to the difficulty. 7/15 mostly for the ambiguity.
LASTING APPEAL: Varies, the game may really engage players, or it might not. With so much player agency available, the game may cause players to lose interest in the game when events conspire against them. 8/15
Conclusion: (Subjective) the game is good, i suggest at least trying it, pick it up during a sale if you must. 10/15, good but not perfect, it has some rough edges.

After sinking seven and a half hours into this game, I've come to the firm decision that it is completely unworth the price being asked. To go into specifics; the game is a carbon copy of ARK, roughly during the first release of the game. Having run over the two hour refund point, I decided to pry deeper to determine the game's worth and found it severely lacking.
It's as if the developers were handed an early build of ARK and were told to iterate upon it; everything from the ground up is so akin to ARK that it's beyond uncanny. The art assets, animations, models, gameplay and systems almost entirely stem from ARK: Survival Evolved. That being said, it's not just a fantasy/magical reskin of ARK, it's a poorly done one at that. The game itself has not benefitted from the countless patches that it's progenitor has, representing several steps back in game development. The only differences I can see between this game and ARK are the following;
The levelling system has been changed slightly, where ARK rewards levelups with statistic increases and experience points to spend on Engrams (Schematics), this game offers statistic increases and a passive levelling system to unlock crafting recipes; examples being that to unlock Fire magic the game recommends you harvest magic stones from the environment, harvest/kill Fire Elementals and similar creatures and other tasks. Some of these specific progression trees have bizarre suggestions; the Air Magic tree progresses every time you harvest Fur from an animal, for example.
The game features slightly tweaked models of standard creatures; additional features modelled onto the existing animals are the norm, such as Panthers having strange facial spikes and other adornments, with little other changes. I will note that there are a very few limited models such as the Spectral Reapers and Skeletons that to my knowledge don't exist in ARK, being one of the few examples of original content in this game outside of the admittedly well made architecture features in the NPC townships.
While ARK has an appreciable grasp on the English language, Dark and Light has a strangely inconsistent one; certain animal profiles or in-game tasks feature well written and knowledgable usage of English, while other lesser noticed aspects such as load screen tips or obscure dialogue features very broken language that doesn't seem to understand the basic structure of English sentences; likely a result of a foreign development team having a professional translator provide their services infrequently. While I'm not against localization/translation, in this case they've left a large amount of dialogue seen through the game in it's unaltered and barely translatable state.
Finally, Dark and Light's sole redeeming feature that ARK does not have (at least, not when I played it last, over a month previous) is a directional dodging mechanic which makes the combat feel slightly more engaging and active, though ultimately coming quite short. Certain enemies become trivial to defeat at the lowest levels by simply dodging backwards when they start their windup attacks, while others such as Panthers are simply too quick for the dodge to do anything. However, the difficulty in these fights is simply running away and leading them to the radically overlevelled guards nearby which will gladly kill anything too troublesome for a player, allowing them to loot the corpse with impunity.
TL;DR - ARK: Survival Evolved clone with very little original content, back from a month after ARK was released and in a similarly poor state of bugs and content. The only way I could possibly recommend this game is if someone has never, ever touched ARK and wanted to try it, which would negate the rapid onset of "boring, done it already" mindset that comes with this game. Even then, I'd simply recommend one of it's competitors, such as Citadel: Forged With Fire. Save your money, just buy ARK or something else. Even if this game manages to ever leave the shadow of it's source, it feels too derivative to be worth playing.

To play this game you have to have unlimited ammo cheat or you will not have money to buy upgrades for your weapons nor will you ever have ammo. The game is like playing any other game on nightmare mode. You get to point in the game where all you do is die.

Dying light instilled a very good sense of fear and caution early on, and while the story is solid no surprises or wow moments were had( but that's just me). The character movement and combat has weight and feels smooth. Gameplay in general is very good. Though some of the in game scavenging and other things can feel repetitive in nature. The rewards rarely really rewarding till very later in the game or on the hardest difficulty. Regarding the nightmare mode, the game can become extremely fun with some experience in the game and decent gear, but for new players nightmare can be very punishing, leading me to believe that the game deserves at least two play throughs to experience nightmare mode. Co-op and multiplayer in my opinion were easily the most fun and best part of the game. Zombie invasions are extremely exciting and have a nice progression as you unlock more skills and abilities as the zombie and survivor. Playing with at least one other friend is highly recommended in my opinion. DLC is a very big change from the base game spreading things out and introducing the buggies, but this introduces a bit of a problem. Without the cars movement to and from objectives can feel almost impossible as the distance is massive and you will at times find you buggy to be very far away after death. In conclusion dying light is a very fun game with some imperfections, but if you like experiencing a scary zombie open world adventure with friendly and enemy players then it's worth the money.

“5:12 PM - [T-A!] Whoota: bad voice acting,♥♥♥♥♥♥script and bad netcode.
5:12 PM - [T-A!] Whoota: I didn't come for any of that.
5:12 PM - [T-A!] Whoota: I came for brightly coloured♥♥♥♥♥♥”
That is a genuine quote, from me, justifying my purchase of
It is without a doubt, the most fan service oriented fighting game out there, but it sacrifices so much in exchange, that you must be one hell of a fan to forgive all of its shortcomings.
As it happens, I am not a
fan. I do like fighting games, and I like to own a lot of them, so that when friends come over I can pop one on the TV and we play a quick bit of loser passes the controller. Dead or Alive is excellent for this because it’s system and execution are extremely welcoming to anyone. You have a button for punching, and one for kicking. One other button to grab, and one button dedicated to no-selling your opponent’s punches and kicks by catching them with the right timing and then rubbing it in their faces. It is simple, easy to learn, hard to master. Beginners will be delighted to see all the cool stuff their guy or gal can do with just a few button presses. While dedicated players can read into the complex stun and juggle systems to really lay the smack down on your opponent.
The game comes with a tonne of modes, and a tonne of content. This DoA once again comes with a big, fleshed out story mode. Over 50 chapters, each bookended with cut scenes and voiced dialogue. It is not particularly well written and performed. In fact it is downright embarrassing at times. The majority of the plot was completely lost on me. An evil corporation is has been taken over by the ceo’s daughter and she is trying to start the company off with a clean slate. Best course of action? Well let’s do everything the old company did again, exactly the same, and pretend we didn’t know. Once again a Dead or Alive fighting tournament is held to invite the world’s greatest martial artists to determine who is the best. How this serves anyone is completely beyond me, but I guess any excuse to have girls fight each other in impractical clothing is as good as any.
Rounding out the modes are your traditional one-on-one versus modes. Arcade, survival, team battles, you name it. There’s even a photo studio to snap pics of your favourite characters in your favourite costumes. Let me tell you, there are costumes. Even without the outrageously priced DLC, the game contains a lot of costumes to unlock. From army fatigues and suits of armour, all the way to sling bikinis and skin-tight leather cat suits that leave very little to the imagination.
All these modes and costumes are nice and all. And even when you’re playing the game, you notice the graphical fidelity as the characters each drip with sweat and get visibly dirty. Insane effects such as exploding helicopters, collapsing skyscrapers and giant Buddha statues all pass the venue at a smooth 60 frames per second.
Pretty good.
Except that it isn’t.
While all your modes are present in this game, one is seriously broken. The online mode is a train wreck. Devoid of practically any modes besides ranked match, the online component is an afterthought. Furthermore, the connection and net code are generally abysmal. Frame and input lag are commonplace. You can’t play with your friends, you can’t play for fun. You must play for real all the time and you have to do with a colossal handicap. That is, if you can even get a match going in the first place. Unsurprisingly, with such awful online battles, no one is going to want to play it to begin with.
And even then, when you dismiss the online, you’re still left with a sub-par port. This PC version is based on the PS3 version. Which is a direct affront to anyone with a decent rig. The PS4 version is out there, laughing at anyone who spends money on this husk. Sure it looks nice, but it could have looked so much better. No, instead Koei would have you pay premium for the privilege to play this on a PC, in a washed out form. Additionally, the game is unstable; shutting the game down crashes it. Framerates jump and dive between cut scenes and gameplay. Not a big deal, but it shouldn’t be happening. Furthermore, the default button layout leaves much to be desired. For instance, pressing the tumbstick pauses the game. Certain combination buttons are found under the start button instead. And if that weren’t enough there is the DLC.
Humour me for a moment. Go to the steam store and look up this game. Yes? I’ll wait. Don’t worry. Look at the DLC. See that? That is more than the game costs or is worth. Sure, it’s a truckload of costumes, but why so expensive? Not even Capcom is this exorbitant in its pricing. This wouldn’t be so bad it is was entirely optional, but the game has the nerve to dangle it before your eyes like you could possibly unlock it by playing the game. No. Not even close.
Evidently, despite all of its exquisite costume crafting and scintillating jiggle physics, the game has all the makings of a quick money grabbing scheme. Busted online and poorly optimised performance make the game a complete joke in respect to its basic price point. I can buy the PS4 version for less. You can buy the PS4 version for less. If you want to play DoA5 Last round, buy the PS4 version. However, you can’t or you must have some way of posting prettily rendered T&A on steam, then you could, possibly, maybe, consider getting this on a sale.

Dead or Alive 5: Last Round is a very simple fighting game, using a total of 4 buttons for each type of attack. One button for Punch, One button for Kick, One button for Block and One button for Throwing. These 4 buttons make for a very simple gameplay mechanic. There's also various holds that can be used as counter attacks, and certain attacks that stun the enemy for more combos.
Oh, and Boobs.
Online could be quite a lot better, though.
TL;DR:
Pros:
- Simple fighting mechanics that are enjoyable(Unless you try combos, good luck with that)
- Graphics look sweet
- Lag is minimal, only in the Overlay
- Stages have their own things that can be used to beat up someone
- 1v1 matches and 2v2 matches are available
- Did I mention Boobs?
Cons:
- Some options HAVE to be configured by selecting "Config" instead of "Play"
- Some characters that were muscular look as if they slacked off for 15 years
- There's boob jiggle physics options, but no breast size options? Pfff.(This is only adjustable with Cheat Engine, by the way.)
- I heard Online wasn't as smooth as it was intended to be, and it misses a Lobby option.
- Overpriced DLC. However, last time I counted, you got around 80 costumes in 1 pack, and they're very detailed. So I am sort of in a mixup between if this is a Con or a Pro.
All in all, I do believe that this is a very solid game, especially for something Free-to-play.

You know, I love this series, I really do, but DOA5LR is, at this point, one of the rare Triple Dips in gaming today. DOA5, DOA5: Ultimate, and now DOA5: Last Round, because clearly someone did not bother looking up the definition for the word "ultimate." To put it another way, this is their "Dead or Alive 5: Game of The Year of The Year Edition" (making yet another term meaningless).
But I bought them. I bought them all. I trusted the team and preordered each release, only to be let down by their aggressively "free to play" style DLC add-ons which amount to nothing more that digital dress-up, and I bought all that too, because I've (less and less emphatically) been calling myself a fan all this time, and then they bundled it in with the subsequent release and offered even more DLC.
But the game is good. The gameplay is fun, the story mode is ridiculous nonsense that only has the new Mortal Kombat reboot series as a rival.
I can't recommend this though. Why? Because I feel there's a 75% chance they're going to put out DOA5: Final Lap or something and do it all again. When is the safe time to buy a DOA game under Koei? On Day One if you don't care about everything you're NOT getting, or more likely, the day they release the next numbered DOA game.
That's not even mentioning how substandard this PC edition is, shipping without online play and based on the PS3 release's physics and lighting, and not using all the bells and whistles of new costumes. The DLC costumes don't tear, even though the price of said DLC is still in denial. The place to get this series is on console, if you get it at all. Who cares about online play and graphics when you've got hundreds of dollars of DLC just waiting for you? That's what matters, right? The funny thing is DOA5 really is sort of Free To Play on console, with rotating fighters available.
It's sad because you see this nightmare skin shop that  DOA has become, and you see how far former creative director/team lead Tomonobu Itagaki has fallen with Devil's Third on Wii U, and you wonder about what an alternate DOA5 might have been like. It really was one of those "sum is greater" pairings.
This is the last DOA game I'm buying. I've been beaten, I feel like I've lost. Not really sure how much of a win that is for the publisher though. Kind of weird behavior if your goal is to make money and all.

tl,dr: Break_In is a game where you steal other players' money while protecting yours and that, with it's new and most recent updates, offers deep base customization for a multitude of different possible defense strategies and, due to that, is a much more varied and engaging experience than it was before. It's well worth the money!
Break_In is a game where you're tasked with stealing money from other players. These players, just like you, have their own base (from a choice of 3 bases with different sizes, sets of placeable units, and increasing costs of purchase), with their own chosen layout for said units. Your job is to adapt your attack strategy to their defenses and make it into their computer room, where you'll hack their account and transfer their money into yours. If you get caught while doing so (because sometimes luck just isn't going your way), you have a certain amount of time to get out, or their personal armies will rain down on you and cause a world of hurt... It's your choice!
While the game is in Early Access, the recent tonal shift of the way the game is played made it a much better experience than it was before. Break_In used to be a game of memorization, while now being a game of adaptation. Recent updates added a grid-like system that lets you place certain units in many spots of the map, allowing for base customizations and configurations that were not possible before, making the game fresh for attackers and defenders.
While the range of weapons is still small and maps are still being added, many new features are planned. The seasonal competition system also keeps the game interesting for even late arrivers to the game.
If you're interested in a first person base raiding game that now offers a good layer of attack/defense strategy on top of it , give Break_In a go. It's worth it!

Ill make this short and sweet: I love this game and it can be pretty addicting. But to help with figuring out if you'd buy it or not, ill just do a giant pro/con/neutral point list and a quick conclusion.
Pros:
-Unreal 4 engine
-Warhammer 40k setting
-Decent balancing between the races
-Highly customizable fleets (esspecially with orks.)
-Beautiful epic chior music
-Very satisfying battle sounds and fantastic voice acting
-Good option menus
-hotkeys for abilities
-Clear objectives on each gamemode
-AI is compitent enough to enjoy the game (can cheat in certain gamemodes, see cons)
-Can create your own games that will not punish your fleet in order to test strategies with randomly generated fleets or your fleets from skirmish or multiplayer mode.
-Campagin is very well constructed and present a lot of choices
-Option for "Ironman mode" for campagin which prevents saving for hardcore crowd
-Easy to find a game in multiplayer
-2v2 co-op in multiplayer
-Tactical cogitators that put the game in slow motion and allow planning and strategy in order to keep up with the action
-Dev team plans to add more content and new races (Edit 6/25/16: Space Marines have been added, Tau will be next race)
Cons:
-Certain races need particular ship upgrades and weapons to defeat other races (Ex: Chaos will kite your ships with long range weapons while they move at fast speeds which make them difficult to catch if you do not have nova cannons, upgrades to increase the range of your weapons, ordinance bay, or long range lances.)
-Races will have natural disadvantages that can ruin a playstyle for certain players (Ex: Eldar will be extremely fast and manuverable, but will usually be blown up if looked at the wrong way due to their fragility.)
-Insubordination is a thing, and your ships will try to disengage a fight. You can execute them, but it causes stacks of mutany which make them ineffective the more you execute people on that ship.
-In Campaign, Skirmish, and Multiplayer, it is possible to be locked out of your fleet if you lose all your ships and are unable to repair them with renown. Leading to having to delete your admiral and create a new one. (granted, this is rather difficult to do as ships repair themselves after 1-2 games depending on how damaged they are, and making new admirals is not as punishing as it seems unless you are doing the campagin.)
-Certain gamemodes are annoying to a majority of the players since they revolve around running away from your enemy and warping out of the battle, which slower races are at extreme disadvantages vs faster more manuerverable races.
-AI cheats often in gamemodes which involve evading opponents (Ex: In assasination, you could destroy the enemy ship right before it warps out and watch it explode, but it will still count it as a defeat, this may be more of a glitch though)
-Multiplayer matchmaking is imbalanced and will usually pit a fresh new admiral vs high level admirals with various upgrades.
-Tatical Cogitators can be activated in multiplayer, which can be fairly annoying if your game goes into slow motion randomly.
-Tutorial is shown in the campaign prologue, so in order to start learning how to play, you must start the campagin, less you blindly walk into a match.
Neutral (pros and cons depends on the person):
-Stays true to the tabletop, meaning that boarding, lightning strikes, critical damage, ect are based off % rolls and can be entirely random. However, it can be influnced to decrease negative outcomes (Ex: increasing your crew of troops will increase your troop value, which reduces the chance of the enemy successfully boarding you. 70 troop value means 70% chance the enemy will fail.)
-Campagin is high stress, as it will force you to play imperial navy and defend several solar systems in multiple sections of the gothic sector, which can be overwhelmed very quickly with orks, eldar, and chaos attacking all the time. Worse: planets can be destroyed if you do not respond to them in time
. It is basically the "Everything is falling apart around me" simulator (which is extremely accurate to the imperium of man's lore.)
Overall, a very good experience for me, but it can be addicting and difficult to put down. The game is relatively forgiving to admirals who take care of their ships even in games they lose, but can be very harsh if you have your ships gain heavy damage or flat out destroyed. The main con of the game to a majority of the community is that some of the gamemodes are extremely frustrating to play. The game has a bright future though, and it is easy to get into as hardcore and casual players (avoid multiplayer if you plan to play this casually, as you will not survive.)
And remember: hit the red button.

Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Vegas is if anything a mediocre FPS that while entertaining at times, doesn't bring anything new to the table. Really, the game is just simply put, average.
The plot is a straight out of a generic action-thriller movie that involves a WMD in the middle of the Vegas Strip, and only you and your squad can save Sin City and all its morally-questionable fun. This plain jane story is presented through some of the cheesiest voice-acting I've ever heard; foul-mouthed terrorists and an overly 'Murican protagonist are the first things your auditory senses will register. Your squadmates are no better either, although Jun has to be the less obnoxious of the two since he has the decency to not spout off 80's era catchphrases and one-liners every 15 seconds.
Gameplay is as I've mentioned before, mediocre and not notable in a market that's got more shooters than rounds fired in the average round of Battlefield. The only real variety that Vegas has to seperate itself is a cover mechanic and a few contextual commands for your squad (such as breaching a door). While this may be a step above something like Call of Duty, compared to older Rainbow six games, such as the legendary Rainbow six 3, the oversimplified mechanic is a major letdown. Regardless, the cover mechanic is helpful in combating the hordes of profanity spewing bad guys who seems to have more ammunition than braincells. Once again, your squadmates aren't all that smarter, but they do make a handy distraction when the brown hits the fan and can do a decent amount of damage if you set them up in a good spot where they can rain down lead.
While we're discussing "raining down lead", Vegas 1 does offer a reasonable selection of weapons, but sabotoges itself with some odd, clunky, and pointless mechanics. Firstly, you are given infinite ammunition for your pistol which detracts from the realism and practically turns your other two weapons into dead weight. If you pair this up with the Shield, you get invincibilty against all frontal attacks, an endless supply of rounds, and a defenstration of any and all realism; the same realism that Tom Clancy games often attempt to emulate. As for your two-handed firearms, you are offered Assault rifles, Submachine guns, shotguns, light machine guns, and sniper rifles. You will find the most use out of Assault Rifles and SMGs since every other weapon is overly crippled in some way shape or form.
Shotguns will knock down a goon in one satisfying shot, but have limited range, low rate-of-fire, and slow-reload (we'll discuss this later)
Light Machine guns may offer you a chance to live your fantasy of being rambo, but that gets cut short when the fact that it can't hit the broadside of a barn leaves your staring at the sky with your blood-splattered eyes.
Sniper Rifles, like shotguns, can take out enemy mooks with a single bullet (headshot not required) but since most of this game takes place indoors...I'll let you figure that one out.
As promised, now we discuss the worst part of this game and the source of it's fake difficulty: reloading. Once you press the "R" key, your character will, beyond all odds, defying all sense of self-preservation, adamantly reload his weapon or die trying. The saving grace is that reloading is manual-only, but when your primary is a shotgun or light machine gun and a hostile decides to come over and see why you aren't lighting him up, you're a goner as there is no way to stop the animation. You can't switch weapons, can't throw grenades, can't order your squad around, all you can do is watch your character get helplessly riddled with bullets because of an idiotic design flaw.
In Terrorist Hunt, which is this game's version of Gears of War Horde Mode, all you do is clear out 15~60 terrorists from the multiplayer maps all on your own. Easier said than done as the game enjoys spawning badguys behind you and into rooms you've just cleared making for some cheap deaths and even more fake difficulty. I know flanking around or behind your target is a tactic used in reality, but Counter-Terrorist teams also don't send you into firefights alone in reality either. As annoying as Jun and Micheal can be in the campaign, you'll start to wish they were there to watch your back.
To conclude, if you are a hardcore first-person shooter warrior then you may find Rainbow six Vegas to be enjoyable, but if not, don't waste your cash on this game. It's not good enough to be fun and competitive; it's not bad enough to laugh at. It's plain average.

Metro 2033 is an excellent, immersive, hugely atmospheric, and suspenseful single player experience.  While fairly linear in how you progress through the game, there is still a lot of exploration you are able to do, and scavenging for items to help you survive.  The only non-linear element is the games subtle moral points system, which will determine the ending of the game based on the actions you take during the game, though you are never prompted about this and you will have to be paying very close attention to figure it out.  The survival apsect is excellent.  If you explore your surroundings and are good at conserving your ammo and gas mask filters, you will be alright, but running out of any of these could put you in real danger, potentially having to go back a level to do it better, which only happenned to me once early on and I learned my lesson after that.  I love the little details like your watch (which tells real-world time as well as monitors how much time you have left before you need to replace your gas mask's filter), being able to wipe rain, mud, and blood off of your gas mask's visor, and having to recharge the batteries on your electrical equipment (flash light & night vision goggles) .
The stealth mechanics are great, though there were a few difficult areas with little cover that took many tries to figure out a method of getting around enemies.  The story itself is excellent, the protagonist is silent and it rarely ever brings you out of first person, making it a lot like Half-Life 2.  All the characters in the world interact with you in unique ways, with a lot of diversity among the "background" npcs, who also interact with you (for example, if you walk up to someone and stare at them they'll tell you to bug off).  The mysterious nomad, Khan, is probably one of my favorite video game characters.  Tons and tons of details to the world and environment around you.  A lot of games from this era were all about the nitty gritty grey realistic vibe, but some how this game, with all that, still manages to create a beautiful game environment that often feels more like an alien planet than it does the Earth, filled with mutants and demons.
The redux version improves just about everything in terms of graphics making it look like any other modern fps game, aside from some slightly dated character and facial animations which sometimes make the enemies and characters look like they are out of a Serious Sam game.  The game is a solid 10-12 hours long depending on how much you explore (keep an eye on your watch timer when on the surface!).  There is plenty of replayability, despite being linear, since there are four different mode settings which change how enemies behave, how much health you have, and how scarce or plentiful items are, which changes up how the game plays.
This (and Last Light) is one of the best games set in a post-apocalyptic environment that I've ever played, and one of the best singleplayer experiences I've had period, perhaps a close second to getting to play Half-Life 2 for the first time.  Hell yes I recommend this game, and I only wish a playthrough of it lasted more than 12 hours.   If you don't want to pay the full $25 for 2033, the 2033/Last Light Redux bundle often goes on sale.  I got both games for a grand total of $10.  Best $10 I ever spent.

Meadow is a relaxing game,which may be a relief to some, considering the contrast to the previous might and delight games .(namely, shelter 1, shelter 2 and paws, all of which I would recommend) In this game you run around as a variety of animals including: badger cub, frog, rabbit, goat (easily mistaken for a deer), fox and  pheasant, with more to come; there are also other animls that are unlocked by owning previous shelter games including: lynx (if you own shelter 2), badger (if you own shelter 1), lynx cub (if you own paws), bear cub (if you own all of the aforementioned games) and the eagle (if you own all of the games, all of the soundtracks AND all of the e-books). The goal of this game is really to just enjoy socialising with other players, and thanks to the fact that this game doesn't use a chatbox, there is no room for toxicity and/or swearing. The way you communicate may seem complicated at first, but eventually you learn how to patch emoji-like pictures together to hopefully make a sentence that your herd can understand, speking of herds, you can also find these unnamed stones scattered across the land, breaking these stones (which take a certain amount of animals, sometimes specific animals) will unlocked gems of various colours each unlocking eaither a new animal, a new emote or a new skin; the best thing about this system is that it actively encourages you to join a herd, however, due to the large map, most of the time the nearest hered is far away from you, leading to ages of running into nothingness, ALONE, which i'm sure that the developers didn't intend to happen, however, once you join a large herd the feeling of community is unbelievable, it really does feel like a family, it's finally a multiplayer game about living as a group and not ruthlessly murdering each other with guns and grenades. So in conclusion medow is a short, yet artistic game that is truly unforgettable, the sense of being welcomed is probably the strongest I have ever felt in a game before, and considering that it comes at a bargain price of £1.99 ($2.55) I would highly recommend this fresh and innovative game.

TLDR: This game is rough and unpolished, but I like what I see. It is clearly a labour of love by the developers and has a lot of potential. I encourage anyone who likes visual novels to try it out.
Pros
-----
-Mechanics/transitions are smooth.
-Art is good and manages to convey the characters' emotions.
-Music is great. It would be criminal not to release an OST.
Cons
------
-The story unfortunately doesn't make sense. For example, the prince was worried that he might have signed a contract while he was drunk. He finds out he didn't (phew). But he signs it later anyway
. Edit: According to the story, he signed it because he needed the money. There's 2 problems with that; 1. If the prince was desperate for money, he certainly didn't act like it. 2. The prince seems bipolar; one minute he's worried sick and the next, he's just... unconcerned about the contract.
-The background is not well fleshed out; we are not given an idea of how powerful the prince is so have no sense of how weighty his pledge to protect Elisa, or how rich the merchant is compared to other merchants, etc.
- It may be an artistic choice not to have a main protagonist, but it makes it harder for the audience to sympathize with the characters.
- The characters are quite one dimensional. The prince is arrogant, the merchant is snobby and the warrior is a mysoginist. Not very appealing.
There is still work to be done, but the seeds for a potentially good game are there. I will follow this game with interest, and wish the developers the best.

Take a classic puzzle game (think Bejeweled), add RPG elements and a plot progression where all battles are carried out through  that puzzle sequence where both players alternate while sharing the board, and you've got the general idea of what Puzzle Quest is.
Puzzle Quest is a silly wrapper around the puzzle game which ends up strangely compelling - you get special abilities your character can use which use "mana" depending on which colored jewels you combine. You collect experience and money by matching those, and deal damage to your opponent via lining up skulls. Victory is defeating your enemy before your own health runs out. It manages to take an already addictive formula and make it even more addictive.
I was first exposed to this game via the Nintendo DS game, and honestly think that the game is more suited to a mobile platform than to the PC, but the game is still a lot of fun here. Check it out if you haven't.

Blender is an incredibly powerful piece of software that you have full access to for the generous piece of: nothing.
As I'm generally a bit short on money I've never bought softwares considered to be the industry standards, netiher have I used any studentlicenses for said softwares. I don't really need to either, as the options available in Blender are plentiful and you have everything you need at your hands to create some truly incredible pieces of work. The sculpting tools are a favourite of mine, as I'd argue that they put up a fair fight towards softwares like mudbox.
One thing I'd like to get out of the way is that compared to a lot of other modelling softwares, the workflow in this can take quite a bit of getting used to, but once you've figured out where everything is and customised the layout to your preference, then everything flows together quite well and everything feels natural.
Unlike a lot of other free softwares, this one doesn't feel cheap. It isn't. It is a free but powerful piece of engineering that has continuously been worked on for many years and shouldn't be scoffed at due to it's pricetag. It has recently garnrered more respect and has started to become accepted in bigger companies and with it being on steam, accessing and making sure your Blender is up to date has never been easier.
This review might sound a bit like some form of infomercial but I promise that you won't be disapointed if you try it out. Just try and stick through the somewhat steep learning curve and clunky UI and you'll find an incredible 3D-modelling software.

I was surprised when blender was added to steam's software list, but not surprised when autodesk released a cut down version of maya to compete alongside it here. Please, expect this from autodesk and proprietary vendor lock ins...once you stop paying them, they will go out of their way to throw you under the bus.  I have student files from when I was using softimage 3D 3.8 back in the year 2000 that I can't open.  Fine, go learn autodesk software so you can join the game industry that loves having access to support and a comprehensive development community, but keep in mind they work on two year cycles and abandon anything old, even if it's still useful, because they're addicted to vendor lock ins and, here's the biggest problem, IT managers need to protect their jobs.  The old saying was 'you never get fired for buying IBM', and today's principle is, in a production with 69 million dollars for a budget, you can't rely on open source software because if something goes wrong, it's on you. Bottom line, are you an IT manager using someone else's money and have no stake in the assets you create beyond two years?  Then maybe blender isn't for you.  Here's how advanced Blender is...after a week when open toonz was released in march, 2016, they had already incorporated some of the open source code into a beta of blender.  They are fast, competent and most importantly, a passionate development community.  Blender has a future, and what you make with blender will be able to be added in anything you do in the future. Mama's Spaghetti Recipe
Ingredients
2 tablespoons olive oil
2 tablespoons olive oil
1 anchovy fillet
2 tablespoons capers
3 cloves minced garlic
1/2 cup dry white wine
1/4 teaspoon dried oregano
1 pinch red pepper flakes, or to taste
3 cups crushed Italian (plum) tomatoes (such as San Marzano)
salt and ground black pepper to taste
1 pinch cayenne pepper, or to taste
1 (7 ounce) can oil-packed tuna, drained
1/4 cup chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 (12 ounce) package spaghetti
1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil, or to taste
1/4 cup freshly grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese, or to taste
1 tablespoon chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley, or to taste
Directions:
Heat olive oil in a large saucepan over medium heat.
Cook and stir anchovy and capers in hot oil until anchovy crumbles, about 2 minutes.
Add garlic; cook and stir until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Pour white wine, oregano, and red pepper flakes into the skillet and increase heat to high; cook until mixture reduces and about 3 tablespoons of liquid remain, 2 to 4 minutes.
Stir tomatoes into the skillet and bring to a simmer. Season tomato mixture with salt, black pepper, and cayenne pepper. Reduce heat to medium and simmer until slightly reduced, about 10 minutes.
Stir tuna and 1/4 cup parsley into tomato sauce, breaking up tuna with a wooden spoon while stirring. Reduce heat to medium-low and simmer for about 10 minutes.
Bring a large pot of lightly salted water to a boil. Cook spaghetti in the boiling water, stirring occasionally until almost cooked through and still slightly firm to the bite, 9 to 11 minutes. Drain and transfer spaghetti back to the pot.
Pour tomato sauce over spaghetti into the pot; stir to combine, cover the pot with a lid, and let sit until spaghetti is cooked through, about 3 minutes. Ladle spaghetti into bowls, drizzle with extra-virgin olive oil, and sprinkle Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese and parsley over the top.

This redux edition of the quintessential original game that got me into my favourite genre of post-apocalyptic, survival horror and adventure combination with FPS elements is an absolute masterpiece. Metro 2033 redux follows the story of humanity's survival, in 2033 through the eyes of an overnight turned hero, but brilliant individual Artyom. After his home station is attacked by "dark ones", mutants unknown and misunderstood by the remnants of humanity, he sets out on a quest to save his station from the coming doom, initially told to do so after an elite Spetsnaz remnant named "The Rangers", one of whom, the best of the order Hunter sets out to fight this threat does not return, Artyom is abruptly spruced into action. An overwhelmingly graphic, tinge and cringe worthy and at times I, a man of the military discipline cried. It touched my very soul and what it means to be human, why we exist the way we do, and why we are our own worst enemy, not the mutants, not the world, not our weapons, but OURSELVES, we destroyed everything we built, in the name of greed, righteousness and the victor. Amazingly done levels, with action sequences, spooky lone adventures and the ultimate feeling of success, however not in the light you always see it so.
9.5/10

Usually, I find no reason to review a game this early on. However after a single day with the game, I need to write the review I wish I could have read BEFORE deciding to purchase.
1. You do not decide what upgrade goes where.
Why does this matter? When attacking a structure that has upgraded, I already know where the cameras are. I know where the guards are. I know how the landmines are places. Upgrades slow me down, but I can rob every target I hit 100% of the time after only a few trial and error runs. There is no cheeky battle of the wits between intruder and owner. This is without a doubt 'the' game killer right here, as it's the biggest feature that appeals to people (and myself).
2. High value targets pay the most, and can be robbed over and over.
Why does this matter? Well you'll find where the vault is, spam it until their bank is dry. You then become a high value target for someone else to do the exact same thing to. It is inherently broken and I do not see a way it can be fixed. There is no exception here.
These two problems alone loop endlessly back on eachother, as you will discover for yourself if you choose to play. I see this going one of two ways. Either enough people purchase to allow for a nearly full rebuild...or the game becomes an ironic vessel for heist-ing 10 dollars from my safe that I'll never see again (which I'm cool with, I love irony).

It's basically Bejeweled with RPG elements thrown in.  Every colored set of gems is for a different element, and you have to spend these element points to cast spells to damage the enemy.  Otherwise you can match 3 skulls and damage the enemy directly.
Winning a combat round gives you experience towards your next level which in turn grants you access to new spells, and gives you some skill points to distribute towards making certain elements more powerful, or to give you an overall boost in the game.  You also have equipment that adds certain effects such as reducing the amount of damage you take, increasing the damage you can do, or even reducing a certain element from your enemy when you fulfill certain conditions.
In a way the game reminds me a lot of "Gyromancer" except you do the matches directly instead of doing the "bejeweled twist" style matches.  The only thing not "bejeweled" about this game is that there are no special exploding gems created for doing complex matches.   You do get a free turn if you match 4 in a row, and if you match 5 in a row you get a free turn + a wildcard piece added to the board.
There's also some gold pieces to match for more money, and "purple stars" for experience. In addition, certain stats increase the likelihood of these non-element matches giving you a free turn, so sometimes it's worth giving it a shot even if you'd rather be collecting the elemental pieces (red, green, blue, and yellow).
The music is decent, the graphics are kinda flat but it does the job, and the story is.... there.  I mean, so far it hasn't added that much extra to the game but it's not cheezy either. If you're a fan of Bejeweled and puzzle games it's worth checking out.  If you're dying for some real action or deep strategy, you should probably look elsewhere though.
Besides it has a lot of bugs that irritates, mainly with the cam, it is very fun like the previous one. Good puzzles. Unfortunately I played only with 3 players and not 4. 7/10

If you love strategy games and are interested in WWII this is the game you are looking for. As a player you will be able to choose your favorite faction to play with, favorite infantry and even vehicles; with this you will develop your own strategy to win battles. If you don't know which Company of Heroes 2 game you should buy first (since there are three stand-alone games now), it is definitely this one. The campaign is fun to play, and certainly a good way to learn the basics of the game. Then there is the online modus, which for me is the most interesting part of the game. Here you will fight epic battles against other players. It probably will be hard if you aren't familiar with other online rts games and because playing online is faster paced than the campaign is. As a beginning player you have a high chance to get beaten often, but if you continue playing you will get better and will play better and way more fun games. So beginning players don't give up!! When you are finished with the standard game you are able to make the game more interesting with the expansion packs. If you like the online gameplay I would recommend buying the Western Front Armies and if you like the campaign I would recommend Ardennes Assault (although I haven't played it yet). I hope this review helped you and I hope to see you in the game!

At first glance, Rainbow Six Vegas appears to be a very clunky and out of touch shooter, but taking your time to get familiar with the controls and commands reveals quite possibly one of the greatest tactical shooters ever made. This game was released in 2006, so at this point the visuals are a little dated, but still attractive, and easy to appreciate for their time. The mechanics are excellent, with cover based combat and the team command system, this game is about as intuitive as it gets. You will not find a dislike to have about it.
It's a good game if you have friends to play with.

I don't exactly feel great not recommending this game. Being a fan of the series, it really is a shame that it's turned to what is it today. I'll try to be as honest as I can about it. Right off the back the game visually is a pretty game. As time passes, it holds up well. When the game came out there were delays, and promises that weren't kept. Disappointing, yes, but I felt like this was an oppurtunity for the modding community to really shine. The first thing that came to mind was texture updates, making the game look more "next-gen". There were some, but it was then later buried under the massive amount of "fanservice-like" mods, which was also expected. The DLC for the game is outrageously overpriced and when compared to the versions of the DLC that were released for the consoles, some of them are missing some pretty cool and different features. Such as Console only costumes and certain costumes that can change form in mid game. I couldn't get myself to learn how to play with the keyboard, so I plugged in my Gamepad (Xbox One controller), it was immediately recognized and I went on to fight. Everything at the time felt smooth and just as I can remember any DOA game, with the exception of a few changes, like a few different moves and button combos. With every update it seemed the game just got better and better, mainly performance wise. Things ran smoother, until an update some time ago, it created a problem with  the gamepads buttons not registering. A highly popular example, both L and R Triggers, the kick button, in this case "B". and it just made the game unplayable. There was from the Devs of a patch that would fix this, but that day seem to have never come. I haven't tried online due to the gampad issue, but from what I hear, it isn't too great. It's sad to say that I'll probably be refunding this game sometime soon, spend my money on something that isn't broken.
58 hours of my life I aint getting back. Was it worth it? Probably not, but I had fun. Buy this game if you want to waste your time, cause it's real good at doing that.

To anyone who has not really played turn-based strategy before and is thinking of starting here, let me tell you that XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a great choice. My only prior experience with strategy games was Civ 2 back in high school, so I was very hesitant about getting into XCOM, but on my brother's advice I tried a game just to see if I liked it.
I did not like it.
I freaking *LOVED* it.
While this game is fiendishly difficult on the harder levels, the easier levels are not too much for someone who is new to turn-based strategy and the mechanics of the game are easy to pick up. (Harder to master, but that's another story.) In the first few months of ownership I played through several times, finally graduating from casual to normal mode, and then just when I thought I had a decent handle on it, the Enemy Within expansion came out. And I fell in love with the game all over again.
There is such a simple joy in seeing your satellite board lit up a reassuring blue, in watching a party of SHIVs kill everything that moves, in beating back the aliens and finally kicking them off your planet. If you're on the fence about this game, don't be afraid to try it out. (I highly recommend the Enemy Within expansion as well.) It's an awesome game and it's more friendly to newcomers than you might think!

I can't recommend this game enough. Rainbow Six is my favorite book, and this certainly does it justice. Sure it's a first person shooter, a genre that is almost sucked dry by the industry, but this is a fresh take on the "absorb bullets and mow down anything that moves". You go out of cover, you're dead in three shots, maybe less, since enemies can and will headshot you. This may seem like a turn off, but honestly, it feels so good in firefights because the guy that you're shooting at isn't just a faceless enemy in a room full of bad guys, he's the one who could potentially kill you. The checkpoints could be better, but I guess it's saying "Stop being a ♥♥♥♥ing idiot. You can't stand out in the open in this game." Also, your teammates...they're another layer of strategy. You have to constantly manage your team, citing whether they should shoot first or return fire, put suppressors on, follow you, or breach doors. They're definitely not invicible, and sending them across the room to mow down the enemies while you take cover could bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥later when they're both down and pretty far away, and you have to revive them whilst getting shot at. This game is super extreme fun. 5/5.

This redux edition of the quintessential original game that got me into my favourite genre of post-apocalyptic, survival horror and adventure combination with FPS elements is an absolute masterpiece. Metro 2033 redux follows the story of humanity's survival, in 2033 through the eyes of an overnight turned hero, but brilliant individual Artyom. After his home station is attacked by "dark ones", mutants unknown and misunderstood by the remnants of humanity, he sets out on a quest to save his station from the coming doom, initially told to do so after an elite Spetsnaz remnant named "The Rangers", one of whom, the best of the order Hunter sets out to fight this threat does not return, Artyom is abruptly spruced into action. An overwhelmingly graphic, tinge and cringe worthy and at times I, a man of the military discipline cried. It touched my very soul and what it means to be human, why we exist the way we do, and why we are our own worst enemy, not the mutants, not the world, not our weapons, but OURSELVES, we destroyed everything we built, in the name of greed, righteousness and the victor. Back when I was a teenager, the XCOM series of games kept me amused for a long time. Back then games were much more basic and you didn't mind the repetitive nature of the games as they made up for it with a bit of imagination.
Over the years I had occasionally wondered what happened to the XCOM universe and craved something similar as the strategy games I'd seen didn't offer the same level of depth.
It wasn't until I was in my 30's that the XCOM series was revived and I was pretty excited. The trailers showed all my favourite parts of gameplay from the original series and the graphics looked quite shiny.
Well all i can say is that this is one game that did not meet my expectations. Well actually it did, but it did nothing new. The gameplay is fun for the first few missions, but then it gets repetitive... really repetitive. The modular way in which maps and buildings are randomly generated is clever, but it doesnt change the gameplay at all, it is still the same turn based combat over and over again.
The real issue i think is that the difficulty relies too heavily on RNG. I've had playthroughs that have barely made it past 2 weeks of game time because i was unable to keep up with the number of invasions with the resources I had, and on the flip side, ive had playthroughs where i have only had one invasion in the first two weeks of game time.
The research and progresssion system is ok but is nowhere near the level that you would expect. Exxentially it is a time gate to keep you playing through the repetitive nature of the main game, which is a problem because the items that you research and craft do not change the game enough to make it worth the wait in some cases.
Essentially Enemy Unknonwn is not a bad game, it is fairly robust and as long as you dont mind grinding through hours of the same thing it will suit you just fine. If you are expecting a big in depth game with a huge story, This probably isn't the title for you.

So, my buddy and I played Ark before it was cool.  And now we are playing this.
Is this Ark with magic.  Well...yes and no.  The game is very clearly using Ark as it's foundation, and many of the interfaces, commands and sound effects are straight up from Ark.  But it really has it's own flavor.  They NPC cities are fantastic looking, the monsters are fun and different and the goblins make you want to bash small green men everywhere.  Especially when 2 of them manage to stun you and steal all your stuff.
I like the leveling/crafting system.  Though it can be a bit grindy, I like that you have to use a skill to get the skill. instead of the engram system that has you selecting stuff your not even sure if you can use.
Flying mounts are nice and fast without being OP and the magic spells are very nice.
Pros:
* Ark like world building
* Beautiful map with what looks like room for MAJOR expansion.
* Polymorph.  Brings back old Hexxen flashbacks when I polymorph an enemy into a sheep. (If only it could be a chicken)
Cons:
* Bit on the grindy side.
* Locked in 3rd person which makes targeting things a pain. (Supposed to get fixed in a later patch)
* Whitelist only server doesn't work quite right.  I had total strangers in my server.  Had to change it to a password server.
Overall:  7/10   This will change if the devs keep moving this forward and don't get all nerf happy like the Ark devs did.

Battlefleet Gothic is a game i have been waiting for ever since the release of the tabletop version. All in all this game is fun to play and doesnt look too bad either.
So far my main experience has been with the campaign. Here you are put in command of a small fleet that grows and gathers experience over the course of several battles. The battles themselves are very fast and usually over in 5-10 min. Unforunately several problems dull the experience...
Pro:
+ Battlefleet Gothic is awesome base material
+ Graphics aren't too bad
+ Campaign is fun to play
+ Cinematics are only slightly animated but still pretty cool
+ Experience and skill system of the ships
Con:
- Stability is pretty bad at the moment. Currently I have crashes around once every 1-2 hours of game time
- Fleet size in battles is way too small to convey the epic nature of the battles. I know the fluff material and even there the battles (at least some) are a lot larger. Anyone arguing that this is not the case is requested to look at the cinematics... These in one case show 3 emperer class battleships. So why not allow those during a battle?
- Much too small total fleet size: you are given a roster of ships (1 Battleship, 2 Battlecruiser, 3 Cruiser, 4 Light Cruiser, Escorts) that you can fill with the ships of your choice. These slots are not even sufficient to have one of every ship...
- AI in joined battles: In some campaign battles you share your fleet with the AI while the enemy has one large fleet. These are unbalanced as the AI is random in both its choice of ships and in actually fulfilling the mission objective leaving you at a great disadvantage.
- general bugs: there are too many to count and a lot of them are glaringly obvious. This should not be the case with a game of such limited scope and with a fairly long postponment and beta time.
- skirmish mode: you have the same limitations to fleet size and fleet roster as is present in the campaign. This is both annoying and frustrating. In addition you have to grind your way through several dozen battles to unlock ships. That is simply needless.
- multiplayer: lacks several basic functions from team chat to a simple lobby system or even match making. Also you can not play games against a friend.
- company communication: as mentioned there are a multitude of bugs and problems. If you check the technical discussion forums you will discover that most of the threads there are not answered by the developers and several topics go completely unanswered.
TLDR:
The base material provides a great background and the battles are fun to play and quite pretty. At the same time the limited scope of the game and the large amount of bugs make it completely unworthy of its current price.
