Dead or Alive 5 Last Round is a Fighting Game (if you can't already tell).  Although, personally I think it has as much as if not more to offer than other fighting games on Steam.
Firstly, let's start off with what modes are available:
In Dead or Alive there are plenty of modes that you can play, So I'm sure you'll find one that tickles your pickle or floats your boat..
This is quite obvious, this is a story mode that's split up in to 72 chapters, and then each chapters are split up into characters. So you get to grips with most of the characters in the game. The story continues from Dead or Alive 4, but if you are a newcomer it's not too confusing. For me personally I enjoyed the story mode even though it was short, about 4 hours. But the story isn't where the most fun is..
Where the most fun is in the game is, shock horror! The fighting section. Surprising, I know...

Here we have the "Fight" section of the game:
There are many options to choose from and each has their own flair.
Here it's the player vs CPU or another player offline. You can use controller or keyboard for each player. If playing against the CPU you also have the option of changing the settings.
Options include:
In this mode you can also do tag team mode, against the CPU or a friend offline(but we all know you don't have any xP).
Arcade is split into Solo and Tag matches, the idea here is you pick a character (or 2 for tag) and battle your way through a random set of opponents. In these matches you get points depending on how well you play and at the end a score is amassed and put on the leaderboard (which is local to your PC).
In arcade arcade mode there are 8 difficulty levels they span from Rookie to Legend
Time attack is similar to arcade mode, you pick solo or tag match, pick your character and difficulty level and battle through a set of opponents. Only, this time it's not score that's your main concern. It's time. You have to try and beat all your opponents in the shortest time possible and then your score is put on the (again offline) leaderboard.
Again like Time attack and Arcade before it, Survival has similar properties (Solo/Tag team, difficulties). But here you have to try and last as long as possible and amass points. The fights are endless until you lose.
Finally we come to Team Fight, here you pick a team up to 7 characters and fight your opponent be it CPU or a friend offline.
You have the same settings options as Versus (Com Level, Max Health,Time Limit).
In this section of the game, it's here to help you hone your skills so you can truly say "I'm a fighter".
It's split into:
In this mode you as usual can pick tag or solo mode. Then you are put into whatever stage you want and have a CPU (or a second controller) which you can use to train against. There are many options like you can set the CPU to do A high/mid/low strike, Set their CPU Level [1-8], even make them walk round you in endless circles so you can dance together :D
Here you can learn all the basic moves for each Character and can track your progress via a percentage displayed when choosing a character. It's pretty self explanatory really.
The tutorial is a tutorial. But, seriously in the tutorial there are 42 sections which teach you all the basic game mechanics you'll ever need to know. There are 42 parts which include mini tests for you to show off your skill (or lack thereof).
This is where you really get to grips with characters. Here there are many combos for you to learn for each character and they're set out in a similar fashion to the tutorial. A handy feature here is that you can choose to repeat the combo until you get it perfect.
Ah, finally the review is
There's more?!
Here, unfortunately, is where the game starts to go sour. In the online mode there's not a lot of content. You have ranked match, ranked match and everyone's favourite; ranked match. There's also a leaderboard so you can gloat to your friends about how you're great at using a bot online to beat unsuspecting players...
The ranked matches are simple.  You can search for a solo or a tag match. You can specify region; Any/Same/Nearby
Then you can specify opponent's strength min/max which ranges from LR all the way up to Diamond. and finally there's an option "Previous Opponent OK", which tells the game whether you're ok fighting the previous opponent or not.
In the ranked mode you get points for defeating your opponents in a match and lose points for losing a match. What dictates how much you win is; your rank, your opponent's rank, whether either player has a win streak and the loss streak wither player has. In the ranked matches the stages are randomly picked and the matches are first to 3. That's sort of a setback as you can't customise your match like offline. There also aren't any lobbies, so if you want to play this game with friends that might be a challenge.
In spectator mode you get to creep on your opponents in matches you've saved or better yet pit 2 AI against each other and creep on them :D. You can enter photo mode and pause/play the footage, zoom in, change the focus and switch which character the game focuses on. Photos you take are saved as screenshots on Steam and can be uploaded to the Steam Cloud.
Here you can watch all the story mode videos, character win/lose poses and private paradise videos (if you have that DLC) you've unlocked.
Here you can look at all the titles you've unlocked and set them as your title card which is displayed online in Ranked matches. There are a total of 999 titles so there's plenty to do there.

This prequel shows quite a bit of potential for what might come at some point in the future and although I doubt that it'll be one of the most memorable VN's in history, chances are, that it is still gonna end up being quite enjoyable if the developers decide to really put work into it.
From what I was able to gather from that small peek into the game (one 'playthrough' of this Prequel only took 30 minutes), we are following a somewhat poor prince, who, dispite his lack of wealth, is very arrogant and constantly goes on and on about pride and honor. At the moment, he's selling off his castle to a merchant and after the deal is done, he ends up in Elisa's inn, together with the merchant. In said inn, both he and the merchant announce to each other that they are in love with Elisa, the Innkeeper (I'm sure you were unable to guess that one...). Both show this in a different fashion: The merchant via expensive gifts and the prince by talking about the aforementioned pride and honor. Elisa's interested in neither though and is instead shooting for the third character, a knight, which showed no interest whatsoever in her and left during the other two's argument.
First off: I love the setting of it being in a medieval city (Florence, to be exact). As someone who loved Akagami no Shirayuki-hime. a setting like this is right up my alley.
The OST is equally enjoyable. So far, every single track was really relaxing and nice to listen to, which is a big plus.
The third thing I liked was the usage of SD-art for the choices (oh yeah, you can make choices in the story). The small pictures help deduce what exactly the choice means and also - on a side note, lol - are really adorable =w=.
Now, in it's current state, the game is far from perfect though. And by this I don't mean 'the characters are bland', 'the story is incomprehensible' or 'my chickens were set on fire by this game's developers', but what I mean is that there are several things concerning the funtionality of the game that could and should be improved on. In the following lines, I'll list the things I figured could use some improvement. I hope that at least most of them will be considered for the final version, as I really want to see this one be good :D
Ok, let's get going:
First: The options menu. Please let us see immediately what impact a change in font, opacity etc. will have. As it stands, you have to leave the options and look at the actual VN-part for every slight adjustment you want to make. Give us examples right next to the individual options to make things just that much faster.
Second: The start menu. There are two VERY crucial tabs missing in the start menu. A tab that leads you straight into the options (you first have to go into another screen by pressing on a button in the bottom right corner and only then you can open the options...) and also a way to close the damn game, lol. I had to Alt+F4 because there is no way to exit the game normally at the moment.
Third: The text. There are two things for this again. Firstly, give us entirely different colors from the rest of the game for the box. As it stands, there are multiple choices, but all of them are colors that will also appear in that area during the game, so reading can turn out to be a bit tough at times. One way of fixing it would be to use two colors for the text (one as kind of a border, one as the 'inner' part of the letter) like in the Sunrider games. Secondly, make the difference between thoughts and speech slightly more visible, please. There were multiple instances where it took me a second to realize that the character was currently thinking and not speaking. To fix this, you could either just make the ' - ' signs bigger or use brackets instead, which (at the very least to my stupid self) are more noticible.
Lastly, two minor things which really didn't bother me too much but I feel are worth mentioning anyways: Firstly, if there's a way to make the background music fade out rather than just stop abruptly, that'd be a thing worth implementing, because the sudden change in music might be a bit odd at times. Also, there are some (very few) spelling mistakes here and there ('rememmber') which are obviously not dealbreaking by any means, but it'd probably still be a good idea to take a few minutes and fix them :D
All in all, I really think that this has quite a bit of potential, all they have to do is make the story as enjoyable as they can and iron out the present technical flaws. I for one am definitely looking forward to hearing from this again in the future :3

Well, this game is certainly.... ambitious.
I don't mean to say that the game is bad, but it may be biting off a bit more than it can chew in terms of promises and expectations. It's promising to be available in 6 or so different languages, to make the player the equivalent of a god by giving several actually important choices to make, and saying there are RPG elements. I played the game in english and saw various typo's ranging from excusable to terrible, the choices that I could make mattered but not much more than in most VN games, and the RPG elements aren't actually there.
So it is bad? No, for an indie visual novel and especially for one that still seems to be in alpha or early beta, this is good but it might be overselling itself a bit. It's trying to advertise itself the way the top-tier console games you see in tv commercials advertise itself, and it simply cannot live up to such hypes. (Neither can those console games usually.) I took a look at the kickstarter page for this game, and the way the writer expressed his passion about this game is the kind of description I would like to see here. The way he describes how dedicated he is to completing this to the point of funding it out of his own pocket would be better than the promise of god-like choice that simply cannot be delivered by any game. Because even within this prologue I could feel the limits of the choices every time the story returned to kinetic when the knight introduced himself.
So is this good? I'm going to say yes, yet this game seems to be a rare niche even within the indie VN niche. (Heads up, if you don't know much about the western VN niche, you're better skipping this paragraph.) In fact, if the game can't set itself apart from the otaku/otome labeling, the marketing pool will be incredibly small. To explain what I mean: I like to play otome VN's even though I'm a guy, while most otaku VN-fans wouldn't be caught dead playing one. Is this an otome game? No, because the protagonist is a man. Yet it is, because three men are all pursuing the same woman and it sounds like she'll be the one to decide who she'll pick. And that sounds like the way I tend to play otome games: putting myself in the shoes of the male route and romance the protagonist girl rather than the other way around. So if this is indeed the plan of the finished game: you playing three men trying to seduce the protaggirl, I'm going to love it. However, most people will not, otaku and otomo alike. And I know people like me are of a rare breed even within the already small western VN-niche.
Disregarding the otome/otaku conundrum, is it a fun game? Yes, I think it can set itself apart from the rest through it's characters. The self-proclaimed protagonist Prince is definately not your cardboard cut-out protagonist with no actual character, he's an self-entitled ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and has many flaws which is actually refreshing for once. And the other two male characters are no different. Even the real protagonist Elisa is not some simple girl to be seduced like a trope girl, but already promises to have many facets and strenghts to her character. And the art with which the VN is visualised, from the amount of CG to the way they can blend the backgrounds with the people walking in it (which is more difficult than you think), is quite excellent. And with a teaspoon of Ziegler genius added, all the elements are there for a good game.
If there is one thing that I'm hoping they'll change though, it's the engine they were using. No offense to the coder, this in hands down the best homecooked engine I've seen thus far, but it's just sad to see a game already limited by funding spend time and resources on an engine whose performance is barely comparing to the basic features of Ren'py. As a result, there are 14-year olds who wrote a fanfic story and put it in VN-format who're already this game's equals in terms of coding and configurations.

I had this game for PS3 and loved it, so I wanted to get a copy on my PC as well and bought it here.  I don't know why, but it's only showing that I have 6.8 hours played... I have that each time I've played it at a minimum.  I'm guessing that's my time played while online, I usually go offline and play mostly offline.
This game is great, I really can't describe it any other way.  I do like RTS games and action games mostly, but it is just so interesting.  There are various classes, weapons, armor, and other equipment, and then you choose skills for your characters when you level them.  You build your base with each room having a different function, some have bonuses when built next to another room of the same type.
There's really so much to discover in this game, and you can play it at your pace.  I put off attacking the alien base for so long, that I ended up having near end-game enemies by the time I did it.  I probably screwed myself a bit in that way, but I was able to do it.
Beyond the base building and resource management are the missions, which are the highlight of the game.  You get a squad of up to six soldiers that will either explore a downed or landed UFO, explore an abduction site, defend a city, or find a person and escort them to safety.  There are also the story missions, which tend to be different than the standard missions (like attacking the alien base).  For all the hours I've sunk into this game on both PC and PS3, I've never actually finished it.  There are so many ways to go about it, I've restarted so many times to set myself up better to not lose any nations from the program.
The game really consists of your base and the missions.  At your base you will manage your soldiers, the rooms of the base, research, buying and making equipment, managing satellites, and looking for missions.  You look for missions by scanning the globe looking for UFOs or abductions taking place.  When you're scanning, it accellerates time, which is required for various research and building.  The missions are turn-based.  You explore a map, having your soldiers move and/or use an action each turn.  They can only move a certain amount of spaces and do a certain number of actions per turn.  I think every mission I ever encountered required me to clear the map of aliens, even the escort missions.  So for example, I have to find a dignitary and escort them to safety.  I can quickly find him and escort him, but then I have to clear the map before it's done.  The bonus to saving the guy quickly is that he will live, and less aliens will be on the map.
To summarize, it's really a great game no matter what type of game you like.  Almost anyone can find something they like in Xcom, especially if you love sci fi and aliens.

For a free program, this is great. But, if you don't know what you're doing, then you're going to want to either check the internet for vague text based tutorials, low quality video tutorials that actually know what they're doing but you can't make out what's going on so it was basically pointless, or phone a friend that may know something about it... Luckily for myself, I do know someone with an idea on what to do, but again, I generally search for tutorials that are horribly done. But, with that out of the way, let's get into the Pros and Cons of Blender...
Pros:
-Free. Nothing needs to be said further.
-Optimized. Again, not much needs to be said after that...
-Many tools. The tools can be confusing, and not even useful at times (like the Grease Pen or whatever it's called), but there are many of them so I guess that makes it better...
-UV Mapping. If you don't know what that means, don't worry. Basically, it just means that you can apply a texture to it. It's difficult, and most of the time you'll scream in anger and throw your computer out the window due to how unforgiving it is, but it is there for you to use...
Cons:
-Clicking anywhere can mess up the spawn point for a new object. Yeah... And the location isn't exactly easy to reset back to 0...
-Some things can completely mess your model up and make you restart. No need to go further.
-Frustrating. This isn't the easiest program to use...
To be honest, it's not a horrible program, but it is, however, unforgiving if you don't know what you're doing... If you're making something in say, Unity, this is good? Again, if you know what you're doing (and I don't), but if you don't... Well, good luck with finding what you're looking for. And if you want to learn how to use it, you're going to be sitting for quite a while learning how to use it through trial and error... At least try it, it's not bad, and it's free, but it's not for everyone to use it.

Blender is a great free alternative to other software, but coming from using AutoDesk Maya or other AutoDesk software, you will notice that you get much less in Blender. Simple tasks like bisecting a vertex or face requires more steps, and the UV unwrapping and texture baking in Blender is an aboslute nightmare. I've gotten used to modeling in Blender over the years, but while Maya or other software makes a painful task like UV unwrapping and mapping and texture baking a relatively straightforward process, doing the same will make all but the most veteraned Blender users rage quit. To this day, I often give up on projects or spend hours trying to figure out what I did wrong in the texturing process when trying to export into a game engine like Unity. If you're patient and cheap, you may reluctantly choose to stick to Blender. If you do not shy away from expensive purchases or have little patience at all, I recommend you buy a copy of AutoDesk Maya or a similar software. It will save you a lot of time and horrifying frustration.

has a simple,
game concept.  Find items on the screen that fit the list of objectives.  Simple.  And while such a simple concept might not be particularly exciting, the nice thing about such simplicity is that you
the developer's couldn't possibly screw up something so simple.
Except that this is from Ensenasoft.
Despite the ridiculous simplicity of the concept,
still manages to deliver game-breaking bugs that could not possibly have been missed if there had been any kind of playtesting whatsoever.  The game is clever enough to recognize that an item might fall into more than one category, for instance, but this can work to your detriment: if the game wants you to find "2 fruits" and "2 apples" and it knows that there are two apples in the playfield (which count as fruits) then it deems the level correct.  But when you click one of those apples, it deducts one point from only the first target list it encounters (fruits, here), and removes the apple from the field.  After one more click, the game is satisified that you found all the "fruits" but still expects you to find 2 apples, but now all the apples are gone.
To compound the injury of occasional unwinnable levels like that, the game plays a truly harsh and objectionable alarm sound as time runs out.
Too simplistic a concept to amuse anyone over eight years of age.  Younger children will be distressed by that awful alarm sound.  And
will be annoyed by the brokenness of the game.

PROS
1. Realistic Combat
I was very awed by the way the monsters moved in combat. The movements looked fluid as opposed to combat in Half Life, where the fight between characters are very "blockish" or "robotic". E.g. The watchers attacking Bourbon and Artyom while moving to Riga Station.
2. Interactive Background
It is amazing to see the demons fly around in the background and see them swoop into the active zone. Compared to other games, where the background is just an unending cinematic loop, this provides a sense of realism. E.g. The demons flying around Moscow.
3. Moral Points
It is interesting to note that there are points that will affect your morals in this game. While it is not explicitly shown, it is a good guide to note.
4. Traps
Holes in the ground, tripwires, hidden cans. All these traps make the game so much more exciting.
5. Sneaking
There are some occasions where you can sneak by and avoid combat totally. This really gives the game variety. If you don't want to, you can fight.
6. Story
Some Cthulu-like parts included. Very interesting. The dream modes don't really make a lot of sense but it is an interesting aspect.
CONS
1. Movement
Following characters around is not smooth. E.g. Bourbon leaving Exhibition to use the tunnels. He will walk to a point and rotate about that point before continuing his walk.

Very crappy. For a country that makes tons of weapons, it is strange that their post-apocalyptic nightmare will have such rudimentary weapons like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You would think that their technology would at least be in the 21st century, not Cold-War era.

The adults look the same. In 2 different zones, the children scribble on the floor wearing the same clothes. Very boring.

Tutorials not teach you how to use the sticky grenade or the knife throw.

The scenario in the hidden subway with the child ghost was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Every other spider web in the game can be pushed through, yet this scenario requires you to turn on your lighter to burn the web. There are no hints to use fire and people are known to get stuck at this particular scenario.

How does it change the game? The only difference is an annoying "Press T to change the filter" and minor cracks in your mask to simulate damage taken.

Braid is a puzzle-platformer with character. The base of the game is simple. Take mario-like platform mechanics and add time manipulation mechanics to the mix. But the game uses these mechanics to make innovative, fair, and interesting puzzles which require an understanding of different consequences of these mechanics.
Many may think that Braid may seem unorginial with its obvious influence from Super Mario Bros. Many also point out that time-manipulation is not orginal either as it has already been done in other games like Prince of Persia Sands of Time and a few other titles. The difference is that Braid fully explores the time-manipulation mechanics and tries to teach the player the consequences of all of its rules through its puzzles. The puzzles and gameplay mechanics make Braid engaging and interesting.
The game tries to respect the player as much as it can. It avoids planned rewards and other forms of serious manipulation so that the gamer is playing the game solely by his/her own choice. This is completely unlike the way most games today are structured. Most wave rewards in the gamer's face in order to keep him/her playing. The goal of these types of games are to get lots of people playing for long periods of time so that the developers can make maximum profit. Unlike these games, Braid's goal is to provide an interesting and unique journey to the player that respects his/her time.
Not only is the gameplay interesting, but the story is as well. The game has books of text presented before every single world. Many may see these books of text as a waste of time, and as a result, most people skip them. The goal of these groups of text are to explain the metaphorical relevance of the gameplay to the story. By skipping these, you are missing an important part of the game. They serve as a way for understanding the meaning behind Braid's mechanics. The game wants to prove a point to people rather than just be entertaining. The game wants to develop whoever plays it as a person.
The ending to Braid is extraordinary. Like any great book, Braid has many interpretations on what the game is supposed to mean. The game takes a lot of effort to fully understand as the story and gameplay have a considerable amount of metaphorical relevance to the game's true meaning. The journey of determining what it all means is a great experience in itself.
Braid is a video game unlike any other.

This game has great potential but is completely let down by several extremely rage-inducing factors.
1. MATCHMAKING
The matchmaking system for multiplayer matches in this game is beyond ludicrous and extremely aggravating and frustrating. Only a masochist would enjoy it, and you will most likely get very angry because of the game's ridiculous mechanics.
First of all, you are forced to level your admiral up from level 1 to level 8 to even be able to field the ships you want, being forced to use small, weak vessels for a very long time before you can actually use battleships or even battlecruisers, also being forced to level your captains up in an insane grind to get new skills and abilities. There is also a "Renown" system which awards you with points after each game, won or lost, but not if you capitulate (concede). This currency is used to buy upgrades and new vessels, or to repair damaged ones.
Now this would be tolerable if you actually got put up against players at the same level as you, but the reality of it is that you are consistently put up against players with level 10 Battleships or Battlecruisers against which you have absolutely zero chance. The game "tries" to balance this out by giving you more points to get a larger fleet, but it is completely irrelevent if you only have 2-3 proper line ships and then have to take a boatload of crappy little escort ships.
The matchmaking system is COMPLETELY RANDOM and you have absolutely no choice in who you face, and the only way to choose your fights is to waste time starting one, seeing the points difference, entering the game, then capitulating, giving the opponent free renown while you get nothing (but make sure to upgrade your Navigator, derp).
To add to the frustration of this, if you lose a ship in battle you have to wait TWO GAMES or spend 50 - 100 renown to repair them before you can use the ship again, so if you have no renown then you are forced to capitulate or take crappy escort ships for two games, giving other players free points for "winning" and giving you absolutely jack all. Furthermore, if you flee the battle with a ship by using a Warp Jump or by capitulating, your ships have a 45% chance to get LOST IN THE WARP, making them unavailable for 1 match, and you can't spend renown to make it available.
You can however mitigate this by upgrading your Navigator, but this requires grinding and time, and also makes your ships weaker in battle because you can't spend points on things you really need (like better guns or morale). This forces you to just sit there half the time and watch your much weaker fleet get torn apart again and again by vastly superior fleets, because even if you flee you can lose your ships. Ridiculous.
2: CAMPAIGN
The Campaign mode is enjoyable because of the excellent voice acting and a cool-looking star map between missions, but it's just sugar-coating - the campaign is literally just a series of copy-paste missions that are literally the same as the multiplayer with very little variation.
3: BUGS
The game is buggy as hell. Remember those frustrating matchmaking mechanics? Well they are compounded by the fact that half the time your screen will freeze, your camera will lock, your interface will become inaccessible and the game will also just crash to desktop a lot of the time as well giving you a "Fatal Error". The servers are also dodgy because you will also get disconnected more often than you should, preventing you from even joining games and kicking you out of a game.
Imagine that happening just as you're about to pull off an amazing victory against all odds.
Also the game is full of stupid typos and grammatical errors in the UI.

Meadow: A interactive MMORPG that you don't communicate in
I decided  to write my review for this game based on my perceptions and interpretations i have had in the game. This game does both have pros and cons, so i will list the pro's first, as always:
PROS:
-No language, only emots in the game makes for a clean game, so even young children can play this game.
-A relaxing atmosphere.
-Different animals with different speeds and sizes.
-Most people will be nice to you in the game (not all, but most, please see cons for more info on this).
-Nice graphics, for the type they are.
-Disabled gamer friendly game. Be aware that hand issues may slow down your game.
-Developer cares about their game, and is making changes to the game based on feedback.
-Low price of game on steam compared to other priced games.
-New updates every month!
CONS:
-MMORPG (the reason i have this in con if you have a social disorder like me, some things in the game are hard to understand).
-People who ignore you when asking to join their group, or when you play slow and small animal, do not wait up for your slow animal to collect skins or emotes for a slower animal.
-No map that is helpful for newer players, or players just awful with directions in this game (like me!...but i made a suggetion for it!)
-Skin and emote collecting feels like a choire, especially when you have the above issue with no one to slow down so you can get the essences for them. Also, unlocking new animals can be tedious this way too.
-Repetition. Look for people to help you hunt obelisks, get rejected by faster animals, look for another groupd to open obelisks, join them, open obelisks, someone on it leaves..rinse, repeat.
The good and the bad  of the game, from my point of view, are above. I feel the game is a positive, but as stated, there are some negatives i have found. The developer may fix these issues, or someone may suggest a fix for some of these issues in the forum. I recommend this because i find it fun for what it is, even though im not a fan of MMORPGS. The community is mostly nice, and it sounds like the game may get some updates soon, so a positive for that too.
ONE other thing of note to know before purchasing this game. There are only animals for loyalty customers for the series to open if you own more of the developer's game for this series. If you do not own the other parts of the series, you do get 4 animals to unlock (cub badger, frog, goat, fox). There are many other animals you can unlock, but be aware you have to buy the rest of the series.
-CONTRIBUTIONS-

Objectively speaking, this game is inferior to its predecessor, Civilization IV. The main reason I say that is that the AI seems completely incapable of understanding the one-unit-per-tile mechanic that was introduced in this game; it's far easier to make an enormous "stack of doom" and use it to wipe out your enemies, which was a totally viable strategy in IV. The AI in V is also much worse at diplomacy and almost guaranteed to hate your guts for being a warmonger, which might be realistic but not very fun. For these reasons, if you play mostly in single-player, as I do, IV is arguably the more enjoyable game.
V is still the game I keep coming back to play, though. The number one reason for that is that it looks fantastic. Call me shallow if you want, but when you spend hundreds of hours with any game, I think it's pretty damn important for it to look good. The UI is pleasing on the eye, and the terrain and (most) leaders look so good that I still get excited to explore the world every time I start a new game. The switch to hexagonal tiles was a massive improvement and one that I'd struggle to give up if I went back to playing IV.
As a strategy game, it ticks all the right boxes, including the most important one: it makes you think. You might do well on the lower difficulty levels by learning a good starting strategy and sticking to it, but to get better at the game you really have to be able to adapt to whatever combination of leader, land and neighbours the game throws at you. That's where the fun lies; that's what has kept me hooked for all this time - just starting new randomised games. Every one of them is different. Highly recommended.

A bunch of artistically stylised (albeit visually muted) objects are strewn around the screen at different scales and angles and you are tasked with finding and clicking on the right ones from a list within a certain time limit. Click the right one and your time is extended, click an incorrect one and time is deducted. The number of targets is increased with each stage, but then resets every twenty stages, and, likewise, the time limit or reward/penalty is also adjusted and reset with progression in a similar way. And that's the name of the game for the whole of the one hundred stages in Adventure or endlessly in Free Mode.
Nothing else about the game is changed in any way from the first level to the last. There aren't really any new objects introduced after a certain point, or any new mechanics to play around with to switch things up. Actually, wait, I lie... They do change something; the definition of an object. On one level you might have to find three "sharp things" and click on a sword and a knife and mark them off the list, then click on a saw and incur a penalty. But in a later level, when given the same objective, clicking on a sword or a knife will count as a miss while the saw is now a hit. You'll find plenty of inconsistencies like that with other objects throughout and it sometimes can end up a coin toss as to what the game is looking for.
This isn't a bad game, exactly - it's all fairly well presented and competently enough put together - but it just isn't very interesting either. It's frustrating to think what it could have been, how there could have been themed stages with objects to find based around foods or sports or transport, sci-fi, pirates, animals, tie-ins where you have to find characters from your favourite games... the possibilities are damn near endless. Or they could have played around with colours and had some items in black and while in another stage they could all be multi-coloured, then in the next one given realistic colouring. Or even have them rotating at different speeds and directions. Anything to spice it up a little. Instead, everything is the same ho-hum style and presentation and there's nothing left to get excited about or surprise you.
I wouldn't call the game lazy as such, it's just... lacking. It's the bare minimum that it needs to be and nothing else. Maybe it's OK to keep young, easy entertained kids amused in certain doses over time, but for everyone else there simply isn't enough to really get your teeth into. The thing you'll really have the hardest time finding here is the fun, and whether you find it or not, you're still gonna be losing time. Find something better to do instead.

Braid is possibly the hardest 2d platformer I've ever played—it also might just be my favorite. Most difficult 2d platform games are "difficult" because you have to have perfect timing with your jumps or race against a side scrolling window of doom. Braid is not like that. Braid is difficult because you have to insanely clever in order to solve the puzzles in each level. I readily admit that I was not clever enough for about a dozen of the levels and resorted to looking up the solution online. I'm glad I did though because most of the time after seeing the solution I knew I never would have figured it out.
Braid reminds me of the game Portal because of the puzzles solving aspect. However what I didn't like about Portal is how, particularly in Portal 2, the game reuses the same puzzle over and over again with a slight variation in order to increase the length of the game. To my surprise, the solution to each puzzle in Braid felt unique. This also made nearly ever single puzzle a challenge because I would not see the solution right away.
I like how Braid did not force you to solve each puzzle in order to move on in the game. Instead you can run right past them and instantly come back and do them when you felt like trying again. This was a good compromise for the gameplay that allowed the puzzles to be as hard as they were.
Perhaps my only gripe against the game is how solving some of the puzzles required doing things that I didn't even realize were possible at the time. At one point glowing platforms are introduced where when you stand on them you can move time backwards but your character does not move. These magic platforms were not explained by the game at all that I can recall and the player is on their own to figure out what it is they do.
Finally, kudos to the developer for making the game efficient. Braid runs excellent on my Macbook Pro with intel graphics. The game launches instantly and I can be in-game like 10 seconds which makes is very easy to launch the game for a quick level and then quit out.

The story, which I had thought was a highlight going into the game, is literally just poorly written flavor text that flashes on the screen before you enter a world, that you couldn't care less about if you tried. The watercolor art and the classical music playing during the levels really showcase the pretentiousness of the devs. Finally, in my opinion, while some of the mechanics were entertaining at first, many of the puzzles are poorly designed and frustrating, even with the somewhat unique time reversal mechanic. Something is wrong in any puzzle game when I am unable to beat a level simply because a mechanic wasn't introduced properly. Yes, of course I believe puzzles should be challenging, but in a much more genuine way. I never had to use the internet for Portal or Portal 2 even for the challenge maps, and yet I always eventually found the solutions out after taking plenty of time scanning my surroundings. With Braid, I had to use the internet on more than three of the puzzles and each time I felt completely ripped off.
The bottom line is that Braid just isn't very much fun. If I play it for a while, it sort of grows on me, but once I quit, I can't force myself to go back and play it. It also makes me angry that Jonathan Blow has the audacity to go on record and criticize other, far greater video games than his own, the least of which being Bioshock Infinite. For as many problems as Bioshock Infinite had, it's still a far more entertaining game than Braid.

After playing the game a bit more, I decided to go through and re-write my review towards this game.
I still recommend this game, but after logging almost 60 hours into the game as of now, I definitely would recommend it more than I originally thought with the first review. Meadow is a really pretty and fun to play little game where you can get in and have fun with friends as the viariety of animals it gives you to play as. Not much to do besides have a nice time enjoying the music, sights, collecting, and interaction without chat. Even though that, this is probably one of my favourite games ever as of now.
Depending on if you've bought the other Shelter products, you may start out with just a small badger cubm with no clue what to do or where to go. When I first played, I was a tiny lynx kitten, and I sorta just roamed around in the darkness until I met a friendly rabbit who led me to a bunch of flowers, crystals, and obesliks. They taught me what to do in the game, simply by using emoticons with different pictures on each. That run with the rabbit really sold it for me with this game, because the fact a rabbit managed to teach me how to play the game, from somewhere else in the world from me, with only pictures and emotions, was really impressive. I started to love how everything just fell into place, without the need of words at all.
Now, here I am, with almost all achievments, playing everyday, and almost 60 whole hours put into playing Meadow. Trust me, this game is an amazing experiance. You go around collecting flowers, crystals, breaking mysterious stones, explore the huge open world, and make mulitple friend along the way. There's dozens of skins and emoticons to unlock, and a big map to go explore and have fun in, as well as tons of groups and animals to go join and befriend. The music is wonderful and I love to listen to it, the sightings and scenery are beautiful to simply stand and look around in, (seriously, how awesome is it to be a fox sitting under the northen lights on top of a snowy mountains?) and the sound effects really put it all together wonderfully!
If you love slow-paced, beautiful sight-seeing, "walking simulator" type games, then Meadow would be perfect for you. Regardless, it's only $3, and it has a lot to see and do for such a small price. I would recommend Meadow to anyone who would seem to like it, and I definitely think that if you're thinking about buying it that you should. It's a briliant experiance to have! :)

I have spent a good amount of time on this game and I think I can give it a fair and realistic review.
In Meadow you play from a variety of different animals and explore the world in search of Obelisks and Puzzle Pieces. These are required to unlock new emotes, skins and different animals. This can become tedious over time which is why I wouldn't recommend playing this game for a long period of time.
Meadow is a quiet little game that is enjoyable to play every now and then as it relieves me of stress and relaxes me. This game is a little gem in my eyes. The community seems rather friendly and I've yet to see anything negative regarding this. This game emits a positive and creative vibe.
However Meadow is not the same as Shelter 1 and 2. There is no hunting and there is no survival involved. The game is peaceful and there is no killing or threats involved. If you want a game filled with action or are looking for a game similar to Shelter then this is NOT the game for you. This game has a more relaxed sense of gameplay and is suitable for an audience looking for a peaceful experience. You will not be on the edge of your seat whilst playing.
I will mention that to unlock every bit of content in this game you will need to buy all of the Shelter games, soundtracks and books (all of the DLC). By doing this you simply unlock the eagle character and a few unique emote actions and sounds. I personally wouldn't bother buying everything unless you absolutely want to.
Overall, I enjoy this game. It's stress free and I've had many funny moments with my friend on here, we even made an inside joke from our experience. It's not the most action packed of all the games out there, but this game is unique and is good for its price. I would recommend this game.

It is not action packed, it isn't entirely clear with what everything is, and you sort of have to know what you're getting into before you actually get into it. What you're getting into is a slow [or fast, I'll explain in a minute] paced game that literally just involves you wandering around finding flowers, ore, and big stones that may require multiple others to break open to get more ore. The ores are used to unlock different animals, skins for the animal you are using, and emotes for chat. Some animals are only avaliable through owning other Shelter series games, but honestly I don't see this as a huge problem because the games are reasonably priced and you'll end up using your favorite animal the majority of the time anyways.
The community is very kind, although there is no way they could be otherwise [unless of course they leave you in the dust when going to break open a stone], and from the time I've been personally playing, if you happen upon a group they'll almost always slow down or help others figure out where to go through the various symbols you are given to communicate with others. It's a very good game if you're just looking for something to distract yourself from life. More often than not if you happen upon a HUGE group it always splinters into seperate groups eventually, so I do tend to try to head towards the smaller 4-7 groups of others rather than the 10+ groups.
Flowers are not difficult to spot at first, but the more rare ones can be in harder to reach places. They don't really serve any purpose other than to improve your score [which if you get on the leaderboards you're able to use a white eagle, and after you reach certain milestones in your point score you unlock more emotes, but that's all I've figured out that it is useful for] so mainly you're really only wanting to go after the ore, and pick up flowers as you will.
I can see some people easily getting bored with it, considering you aren't given any goals and you basically just make them up for yourself.
TLDR; It's very simple and pleasant gameplay, has a visually appealing art style that reminds me of scrapbook paper, and would be nice to play during a quiet rainy day.

First of all, allow me to say that I am a massive Warhammer 40k fan, so the things you'll read below will come with a certain bias, though I will try and thread the middle of the line.
So what is Battlefleet Gothic: Armada? Its a Warhammer 40k themed RTS that pits four distinct factions against one another, each one with ridiculously large weaponry mounted atop of even larger ships, as well as abilities and playstyles that represent the original lore surprisingly well. In the case of Orks this means yelling, shooting, and literally stuffing crewmen into torpedoes in order to get them to the action as quickly as possible, sanity or safety be damned!
But even if you ignore all of the Warhammer 40k elements I would still say that Battlfleet Gothic is one of the most interesting RTS games I've played in recent years, though its not without its faults, most notably the rather shaky multiplayer balance.
But first, allow me to briefly go over a couple of elements that make Battlefleet Gothic an enjoyable experience for me:
* The main reason I find the battles so compelling is the customization system which allows you to specialize your ships in a variety of ways, all of which play similarly enough to not be confusing, but also distinctly enough to offer a unique way of handling any situation. For example, if you ever get bored of playing with the standard Imperial loadout that focuses on heavy frontal armor and powerful broadside attacks, you can invest some resources into swapping around weaponry to create a fleet of fast-moving carrier ships that prefer to attack indirectly through the use of bombers and boarding parties.
* The second reason is quite simple, the battles are a bundle of quick, chaotic fun. Since most of them last 10 minutes or less its hard to get angry if you're losing, and any victory you secure won't get dragged out for so long that it stops being exciting. All of this combined means that for me personally Battlefleet Gothic has that magical ability to vacuum free time, the same way games such as Civilization IV capture their victims. The temptation to start up another match right after winning the previous one is deceptively attractive, and most of the time results in me having a completely messed up sleep schedule.
And speaking of messed up, here are the two main issues I have with Battlefleet Gothic:
* If you're not a fan of Warhammer 40k, or if you simply don't care about the lore, you're most likely going to be extremely disappointed with the campaign's story as its comically cheesy, melodramatic, and often downright ridiculous. I had a good bit of fun with it, mostly because the voice acting and overall themes are spot on, but its well worth mentioning that those of you that aren't Warhammer 40k fans might have a less than stellar experience. The campaign gameplay, however, I have very little complaints about, so if you don't give a rat's tail about the story, you'll be perfectly fine.
* The bigger issue is the problem of balance. There doesn't seem to be any matchmaking available to separate new and experienced players, which as you might imagine results in a complete and utter stomp. The secondary problem is that some matchups are inherently imbalanced, especially the early game Eldar vs Orks one. The issue stems from the fact that Orks are slow and inaccurate while the Eldar are nimble and mostly long ranged, so almost every single match ends up the same way - the Eldar run away, and the Orks pointlessly chase after them until they inevitably get whittled down. There are ways to counteract this, but in the early game where Orks only have one type of ship available they are completely out of luck.
Battlefleet Gothic: Armada is a great RTS, but more importantly, it is a great Warhammer 40k game. It has managed to not just capture the look and feel of the universe, but also use its key elements and lore to further enhance the gameplay, and make the whole thing an immensely enjoyable experience.
It is currently in need of some balance-fixing in order to reach its true potential, but outside of that I have very little issue with saying that Battlefleet Gothic is well worth your time, especially if you're a Warhammer 40k fan. If not, I would suggest doing a bit more reaserch, or simply waiting on a sale as I can't really guarantee that the campaign will be up to snuff if you aren't a lover of Warhammer 40k branded cheesiness.

I've heard that Steam had a new review mechanic introduced, so I came here to recommend my favorite Lara Croft/ Tomb Raider games in recent years.
First, let me tell you something. Several months ago, my college roommate and I spent whole night playing this game without even raiding any single tombs, but we still had a lot of fun together. We were just using mines and rocket launchers to destroy those ancient ruins and each other, but it's so entertaining and relaxing than we expected.
Lara Croft and Temple of the Osiris is the only game in this franchise that stays true to its roots after they reboot the series. You can hear one of the best soundtrack and head back to the most familiar location, Egypt, just like those good ol' days. The visual is stunning and the puzzles are very well-made, providing with enough challenges but not driving you mad. And if you have some friends to play with, this game definitely worth every penny. You can either play it alone and enjoy the exploration all by yourself, or have fun killing your teammates to beat their high scores, which provides some replay value as the puzzles will change dynamically according to how many players are in your current game.
This game was not very well received and had some serious bugs and performance issues at launch, I cannot even play with my friend back then. But after some patches I had already killed Isis countless times, in one of my friend's 4 players co-op game. So I really can't find anything that prevent me from recommending this little gem now.
Want a genuine Lara Croft Tomb Raiding experience? Looking forward to some online or couch co-op with some of your buddies? You won't regret grabbing this one, I enjoyed almost every seconds in this amazing adventure. As for any long-time TR fans, this game will be like a time travel ticket, you can find all your lost good memories you used to have with this iconic heroine in this fantastic journey.
10/10 would kill Egyptian Gods again.

This was the hardest thumbs down I've ever given a game. I want to enthusiastically give it TWO THUMBS UP!! But I can't. This game was clearly well designed in ship mechanics, art, platform, layout, and detail given to each class of ship. This game however, fails spectacularly in tactics. In that it has and requires none. I'll try to explain.
Here's the dilema almost any naval game faces whether it's on sea or in space. Realistically, naval combat can last for hours, and hours chasing someone and nit-picking them, OR two sides duke it out and very quickly blast one another. So a game dev can't make a never ending map for those games where one guy just wants to run fast. SO, they have to make a grid to form the "arena". This is where Armada fails big. The majority of the missions they developed favor the "chase me" game style. Missions like, assassination, data recovery, break through, convoy. If your fleet is faster you will likely win those missions easily because you only have to escape this grid arena. When in all actuality space doesn't end simply where the grid ends....it goes on, and on, and on, much like this review I'm giving. So if speed equals wins by default, you practically remove tactics from the game. For me that's a HUGE no-no. Armada badly needs more missions that force two opponents to clash with one another. Devs, in short, since a naval game needs borders/grid/arena you have to create more than one mission (cruiser clash) where the overwhelming majority of the ships you designed can be fielded properly. If not, what is the point in having anyone but the Eldar in this game?

What kind of problems the game has:
-Pathing used by vehicles can cause them to be stuck: rotating to do a 10cm acceleration backwards, rotate again to adjust another 20 cm, rotate again and go normal speed => Vehicle is lost 90% of the time this happens.
-Throwing abilities something doesn't work: i.e. you launch a grenade and the soldier just do nothing, not even autoattacks.
-Many other bugs of troops pathing, getting stuck in front of death units etc... you'll notice them when playing some games
-Lack of a user-friendly Editor
-Lack of the possibility to watch a replay at a certain point. If you skipped past 10 minutes from the replay, you can't go back, you have to watch it till the end OR reload the replay from the begin and wait for it to reach 10 minutes.
-When a player leave in a multiplayer match an AI takes his place. Unfortunately AI is bad scripted for this kind of game: IT CAN'T HOLD A POSITION. This game is all about holding positions, especially if the situation is in a stall. The AI just go everywhere with one squad, one light vehicle, one tank and harass the positions. Totally trash I'd say. Sorry developers.
Advice: when a player drop either Remake or just leave if its in your team, the match at the begin will seem doable, but later the AI will screw it up surely.
-the RNG (Random Number Generation) System tries to simulate reality, sometimes this give space to raging results as the simulation can't take account of all real life variables, it just goes with an arbitrarial miss % at 3 different pre-set range: Near-medium-far. This means if you attack an enemy squad(4) with 10 soldiers and you go just about 1 meter out of their nose, you'll see how much resilient troops are in this game. Possible solution: make a function that calculates miss% based on the actual distance, i.e. at less than 1 meter it should be like 5-10% miss, then scaling higher.

Very good game, very good value.
Although old, Race 07 is still a very good game with a good amount of content. I got the base game + all DLC on sale, but even at its regular price Race 07 is a game worth buying imo. There's a good number of car classes & track locations, enough to keep me busy for a long time, and on top of that the game supports mods. Race 07 doesn't have as many mods as rFactor1, but there's still enough to provide a lot of variety to the game.
Race 07 has a number of options for practicing & setting up custom races against AI, as well as custom championships. One can do a championship with full race weekends and realistic rules or simply setup a quick race with whatever car/track they want.
I'm playing the game with a Xbox 360 controller, controller support is pretty good, default controller settings work well, game lets me customize button setup, driving cars without driving aids require precision but controls feel intuitive.
Graphics are slightly better than rFactor1, graphics are dated by today's standards but look pretty good for a game released almost 10 years ago.
Sounds are good as well, engine sounds, gear changes, collisions, etc.
Overall I'm very glad I bought this game and would recommend it to anyone looking for a good racing sim, especially if they're on a budget or if they want a game that can be played on older pcs.

Hypnosis is the B Movie Cult Classic of point and click games that you never knew you wanted, until it fell into your lap for $5 and you were just
It is simple, satisfying and gloriously strange.
The graphics are surprisingly good, while the constant shift in level theme/art style provides much entertainment. The story starts with simple mystery, and then cannonballs into an intergalactic psych romp full of cartoonish twists and turns. I am still trying to figure out whether the game is intentionally funny, or unintentionally so, but either way, just like Ed Wood's B-Movie Classic, Plan-9 From Outer Space, this game features all your favourite celebrities (without their permission) and allows you to DIVE INTO THEIR DREAMS through the POWER OF HYPNOSISSSSSS. [note: therefore it is nothing really much like that movie I mentioned at all]
Seriously, Grace Jones, Einstein, Richard Branson, That Dude From The Big Bang Theory...the gang's all here and they're just begging for your cleavage-aided psychiatric assistance.
SOME may say that the puzzles are too simple and easily solved, but to them I say NAY. My main grievance with Point & Click games is that they always feature that one frustrating puzzle, which you can never solve so you cannot continue playing. And that makes me feel kind of stupid. Hypnosis features puzzles which are as easily solved as an 8 year old's homework, so they're great for your self esteem. And, just like your favourite elementary school teacher, the game gives you GOLD STARS for completing puzzle battles (also good for the self esteem). But the real prize is watching this weird, weird story unfold.
After completing the game and witnessing that truly epic ending, I can only recommend it as the best, terrible game I've ever played and would highly recommend it for anyone with a good sense of humour and a spare 5 bucks.
Now for my few critiques:
1. Unsure of why the main character needs to be randomly sexy and have a standby boob-adjusting animation. I would like to point out, that as a psychiatric professional, I would consider her low-cut outfit inappropriate for the workplace. Don't even get me started on those ones from the store O_O
2. Continuing the above theme - Do Maya and Dr Blanche understand the concept of patient-doctor boundaries? *spoiler alert* Hiring your patients, hypnotising them against their will, getting all up in their brain and then telling them how to live their lives - pretty sure that's a breach of like all of the psychiatric rules.

When looking for an easy but enjoyable game, Hypnosis is a good one to play for an afternoon.
The story is pretty basic, you are a hypnotherapist who gets called by the police to come to a secluded little place in the middle of nowhere which serves as a clinic, all of this because your exboyfriend (who works there) has vanished.
Meet some of the characters: (who are THE MOST stereotype characters in the world) a punk teenage girl who thinks her parents don't love her, an autistic indian who loves writing code, a confused mathematician who lookes like einstein etc.
As a hypnotherapist  you ''dive'' into their subconsciousness, where you have to find out what the problem is and how you can fix it. I found this to be the most fun part of the game, as every consciousness is unique and can be fun to explore. And despite the fact that the characters are rather bland, it is fun to get to know their inner thoughts better.
You battle so called ''phobias'' in an easy battlesystem, don't go looking for a challenge here.
The main storyline is actually less interesting than the characters.. I found it to be rather dissapointing.
However the game is enjoyable and very easy to play through, it only took me about 5 hours (and this is even when you use all of your ''talking'' options and exploring options). So i wouldn't buy it for more than 5.
And, as an official psychologist, i have to say that every psychological aspect of this game is complete nonsense... really, what a load of crap..
But in all, an enjoyable game to play if you don't want to think too hard and just have fun for a few hours!

Ok let's start off with this. FTL is a space strategy roguelite rpg thingy that's incredibly hard. If anything I said made you wince in pain you are an ape with no taste in videogames, go play Call of Duty or something. Anyway for those of you still interested FTL is a game where your thrown into a world with nothing but the ship you chose to start with, your crew, and your wits. Your goal is to go through a bunch of different sectors and kill the boss, getting stronger and more decked out as you go. I've done about ten to twelve playthroughs give or take and only have three ships and have only won once. This game is hard and is mostly luck. The main thing that let me win was I got a second burst laser for my ship. This let me send six projectiles at any point in the ship. This is enough to get through the max amount of shields and hit the ship for two hull damage. As I said this game is luck. Throughout your travels you'll come across random events. When you find one you get several options. Some make you pirate god of the cosmos others make you a research subject. Then there are blue special options that let you resolve the conflict without any problems. One last thing. Screw that stupid giant spider event that always kills one of my crew members.

Very easy to use, load times are great, hotkeys helps speed up the modeling process and animation is very simple. In my opinion, it's easier to use than 3DS Max. You can also find all the help you need online with thousands of tutorials on Youtube. And of course, one of the biggest advantages is that it's free.

From the same people behind Dead Island, Dying Light is a significant improvement over the gameplay style that game founded.
However it throws parkour into the mix, making traversing the city of Harran a breeze once you've masterered it, add a grappling hook and you feel like a superhero at times with how fast you can move.
The zombies in this are pushovers during the day but during the night? If you don't have the right equipment then you will die.... a lot. They become more aggressive and harder to kill plus variants that only come out at night will chase you relentlessly unless you use flares or a safe house to evade them. Skill points are doubled during the night though so the risk can be worth the reward. Also, the virals can burn in hell, I don't care if they're recently turned people which means they're faster and stronger, that doesn't bloody mean that they learn parkour and are suddenly pros at it. One of my biggest gripes with this game was constantly being attacked by these♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥even when I was being silent.
There's a story but its so bland and uninspired I don't really remember much of it. You're sent in by the GRE to retrieve a document about a cure for the zombie virus from some warlord, who then kills the doctor who had the cure and for some reason doesn't have you killed despite the fact he has numerous chances to. Oh and you cut off his hand and he still doesn't have you shot on sight even though he has countless armed minions!
Somehow the story went from being average to just a downright slog in the last act. The dream sequence nearly put me to the sleep, it was unneeded and felt incredibly out of place. And the boss fight.... oh my god, the boss fight. It strips you of all your items bar a machete, so there's no healing, even worse is that the boss does a chunk of damage which also knocks you down, and (god I hate when boss fights do this) he has minions. Yeah, you can kill them and they won't respawn if you die but why do so many boss fights in games have to freaking use minions? Its so cheap.
Its sad that the final fight with the big bad turns into boring qte fest but there ya go, that happened. I was glad to beat the game not because I enjoyed the story but because I wanted it to be over, so I could go back to exploring and actually having fun.
Bar the main story, there was a healthy helping of side quests, and by side quests I mean fetch quests. There was way too many instances where the game would make you go get an item and come back to the quest giver only to be told you needed another item. Why they can't just tell you every bloody thing they need in one go, I'll never kn.... oh right, padding! There are also challenges in which you have to kill a certain number of zombies with a weapon or use parkour to get to a destination in a fixed amount of time.
Outside of the story I really enjoyed the game, but whenever I did have to do the story I just wanted it over with.
The sidequests were mostly fetch quests and the npcs I occasionally encountered were dull as all hell.
Combat was a blast and combined with the exploration, the best part of the game is merely just exploring.

The clash between the attempt at a serious story while also trying to make it funny with the "save the princess" cliche shouldn't really belong in a game.  The game tries to be serious, but the developers load it with comical features (ravenous pink bunnies, goombas being shot out of a cannon, chandeliers falling on bosses to kill them, etc.)
The core gameplay I thought was excellent, but everything wrapped around it kind of sucked.  Don't get me wrong, this is a great puzzler.  It's not one of those things that you solve in one go.  You will think about every level and will not know how to solve all of the puzzles automatically and will resort to the Internet for guides.  It's actually a really hard game.
There are also speedruns at the end for replayability.  The speedruns are of five levels you have played before, and then a speedrun of the entire game again.
Are the puzzles logical?  Well, they should be.  Often times I found myself just screwing around, reversing time back and forth trying to get something to happen.  But sometimes I knew exactly what I needed to do, and I executed everything perfectly.
Would I recommend this game?  Not for a $9.99 price tag.  If it goes below 5 dollars, I'd say it's a good buy for puzzle lovers.  If you are one of those people who don't appreciate a good puzzle, I really would pass, since this isn't the game for you.
I want to stress how good the level design is in this game.  The developers really make great levels.  The only problems are the distracting antitheses.  Like I said before, I wouldn't bother looking at this game unless it's 5 dollars or lower, and if you are on the verge of buying it, only buy it if you really appreciate a good puzzle.

Meadow is a simplistic feel good game focusing on a medium sized open world and its player animal inhabitants. There are no clear objectives, no quests to manage and no survival characteristics. Exploring the world and collecting plants and stones are the main gameplay features.
Communication is so intuitive and basic that every player is able to jump straight in and interact with other players. Emotes, signs and gestures substitute an ingame chat, thus there is no language barrier. Sooner or later you'll find yourself in a gleeful pack of forest animals à la Disney.
It's important to note that there are a total of 10 playable animals, of which only 5, in a few cases 6, are playable for players who don't own any other Might and Delight products on Steam. So if you're looking to play a specific animal, I'd advise to read up on these animals before buying Meadow.
The beautiful abstract art style and interaction with other players are the two main points that make this game so enjoyable for me. Players looking for a story or survival gameplay similar to the previous Shelter games will probably miss the challenge. I'd still recommend this to anyone looking for a relaxing multiplayer experience.

This game is thought provoking. Its puzzles are mentally delicious. Its story is kinda loose, but also super intriguing. Its ending left me mindblown at 1am and needing to tell everyone I knew to play this super awesome game. Its graphics are art. Its soundtrack is beautiful and peaceful, which is necessary to counteract the frustrations of puzzles. If the soundtrack was not so calming, things might have been at risk of being broken in frustration.
There is a satisfaction that comes with making it through the entire first run-through without looking any puzzles up and being able to say, “I figured it all out. All of it.” Another cool thing is that everything in the game is put there for a purpose. It’s kinda like how in a good piece of literature, every word should fight to be on the page, or else the author is wasting the reader’s time. In this game, nothing is wasted or thoughtlessly placed.
Overall, 9.15/10, would recommend to anyone who wants something different and challenging that works the brain muscle more than average. I subtract most of a point because I am still left with too many questions, almost like the game is too metaphoric to get its message across. Also I’m point stingy. It still is satisfying enough and thought provoking not to lose a whole point. Perhaps I just need more time to reflect and replay. I am highly satisfied overall.

To give an example
Assassination missions:  target the enemy Admiral, but when playing the AI who will run to the far corner of the map no matter which race it quickly becomes an excersise in frustration and against Elder who out pace everyone else by a considerable margin it becomes almost undoable
Planetry Assualt: as an attacker it purly depends on luck, a random spot appears anywhere on the map and you have a minute and a half to get your slow moving ships to it, there is no strategy invovled only the luck of happening to be on the sport or near it.
And then we come to the special encounter missions, I am writing this after a mission against a Ork Space Hulk and its supporting fleet where I was allowed the grand total of 600 pts (for those familiar with the board game a Hulk was 800 on its own) in game this got the me  a mighty fleet of 1 battleship and 2 battlecrusiers  now with the 0rk support fleet I estimate that there was an enemy force of arounf 12-16,00 pts and that is just insane, my 1 AI controlled support ship deployed at the wrong end of the map and did NOTHING. This I will admit has left me frustrated. Not only as I got poned as badly as you would expect but because I have had no opportunity to deploy my fleet on mass which at lvl 8 consists of a Battleship 2 Battlecrusiers 3 Curisers and 4 light Crusiers.
These special encounter missions are a prime opportunity to deploy a MASSIVE fleet and watch it everything explode but no instead I find myself facing ships unique and hard to kill ships with the same small skirmish force I have had in every other mission and it is driving me nuts.
There is nothing wrong with the core mechanics, the ships function as they did in the board game more or less, its incredibly pretty and they AI is adequate if not ground breaking but getting beyond that into the core single player game and you find thats all there is, the core mechanics surrounding a glorified skirmish mode disquised by the actors of the British Theatre guide hamming it up with the best of them, there is no sense of grandure or acheivement, just another slumming it thespian either patting me on the head or chewing me out
if all you want is to replay the table top game on your PC then get the game its core mechanics are fine (bar a little AI damage stacking in its favour) but if you were looking for a game which give the true feeling of the Gothic War keep on walking, the game will frustrate you to the core as you slog through ultra hard mission hunting giant enemy craft with just a few ships while a huge task force just sits at Port Maw doing nothing
If you like half hour loading screens every time you want to play this game is for you.

Essentially RPG title with lots of things going on, there's even ability to craft gear or you can besiege cities to get tithes from them. Enemies can be captured for mounts or to learn new abilities/spells from them that are not available to your selected class (a mount comes with an ability of its own, too). And of course besides the main quest to get rid of Big Evil you get plenty of side quests, helpful companions, and there's even some gossip in taverns to enrich the lore.
Except the core game mechanic of resolving any kind of challenge that pops up is... a puzzle game of the type "match 3+ pieces in a line", possibly best known from Bejewelled.
During standard combat you go in turns with your enemy, gathering different pieces for mana and executing special moves if you have enough, or there's a type of piece to deal direct damage (skulls). Some challenges slightly differ, like training mounts has time limit for turns, capturing enemies is a static puzzle to clear up the whole board, and learning spells is about matching enough different pieces (sadly for the latter it's a failure when you're out of moves, so the hard spells are pretty much impossible to learn from captives or at least not really worth it).
This mashup works pretty well and is quite addictive, you always want to have just one more battle to advance the story and maybe okay just one more... and the time flies.
Game has some balancing issues though, designers maybe get a bit carried away and some choices of gear/mounts/spells are clearly superior than others, whereas some even work against you if you use them. But of course you don't have to play with a min-maxer attitude for one, and secondly it doesn't really impact the game just makes it bit less complex than you'd think if you decide to ignore most of the choices. But you still have to get to proper levels to use some, and figuring out the real deal is part of fun too :]

Ah yes, the classic match 3 puzzle game. There's a lot i liked about this, but... holy hell, I didn't expect such a massive amount of grinding in a puzzle game!
Just about anything you want to do involves the puzzle grid. Want to make an item? Battle. Want to research a spell? Battle. Wander around the world map? Battle. Talk to a person who only says "who are you?" Battle.
My first game completion showed 300 games won. Considering some matches can last 10 minutes, this gets old painfully quickly. Whereas Might and Magic Clash of Heroes felt short on battles, this game is the exact opposite. It really is obnoxous, especially when some quests will perpetually throw battles at you until you decide a different option. It almost sickens me to think that there's a bunch of other character classes I have yet to complete.
As the game goes on, you'll swear that the computer cheats. It almost always does an optimal move, and it finds ways to crank up its mana in few turns. Fortunately you can also become pretty godly, but it takes a long while to reach that point.
Annoyingly, most of the enemies scale to your own level. This basically means you aren't getting stronger, if your enemies are keeping up with you.
Note that there is an expansion available on the Steam forums for the game. Since the original company basically no longer supports the game, you can grab it for free.
Overall, fun at times, frustrating in many others. I'll give it a 8/10. It certainly kept me busy, and one day if I'm bored I'll probably revisit it for the hell of it.

There are many different race formats you can choose from such as; mandatory pit stop, timed event (endurance) or a 2 race format including a grid reverse. Gameplay Video:
Playing as Maya Anderson, you travel to a mental institution in some attempt to help patients who have all recently gone 'insane'. That's where the fun begins. Stepping inside each patients subconscious by using your hypnosis powers will take you to a crazy world filled with objects related to thoughts of that person.
One of the first things you will notice inside these worlds are 'phobias'. Running into these enemies loads a battle scene where you must work cells along pathways to take majority control of the 'nodes', interesting blend and adds almost rpg-like elements. Further along you uncover missing pieces of the memory that will present you with 'puzzles', much more adventure-like in nature, generally involving simple combinations of items. Completing these tasks is the primary form of game progression.
The lovely artstyle and themes of each world alone make Hypnosis standout, while making you want to continue playing. Couple that with a well read fully voiced story and decent price, we have a winner. Cheers. :)
