Play Length: Less than an hour.  This is just my impression of the game, so you should take it with a bunch of salt.
Positives: I generally like the graphics.  The painterly style is kind of nice to look at.  The concept of the puzzle design being about turning back time seems intriguing.
Negatives: As far as the gameplay goes, I just couldn't wrap my head around many of the puzzles.  Many of them seemed like I needed to come back later, because I was missing some ability, but I wasn't quite sure.  Unfortunately, I can't comment on the puzzle design with much authority because I just didn't want to play the game very long.
What I can say for sure is that this game was off putting for me.  I'll try to put my finger on that... mainly, it's the soundtrack.  I hated it.  Soundtrack is very important to me, especially for a platformer of this style.  But this game's soundtrack is all wrong.  As music, it is nice enough, but as a soundtrack it just doesn't fit what is happening on screen.  It's non congruent.  It's also not particularly good soundtrack music as none of it is very memorable.  It basically sounds like someone just grabbed some random music off their ipod and just through it in background while I played.  I think this non congruency might be why some people accuse this game of pretentious-ness.  To be "pretentious" literally means to put on a pretense of something you're not, and the soundtrack alone sounds like it's screaming at the player "this game is very serious and important!" while not at all trying to fit what was happening on screen.  The very definition of pretentiousness.
From what I've heard, this pretentiousness also extends to the story, but unfortunately I can't comment on that.  What I can say is, besides the soundtrack, there was just something about this game that really put me off.  Maybe it was the overall feeling of the game, that feeling that all of the components aren't meshing well together.
Overall: I'll be the first to admit that this not a great review.  What a review is supposed to do is inform about a game, and I don't know enough about it to provide much useful information.  If I worked for a gaming publication, I wouldn't publish this.  But you know, I'm just a guy who tried the game, and this is my personal impression of that game.  For me personally, the first hour of playing this game was enough to put me off from wanting to play any more.  Feel free to take that for what you think it's worth.
About my rating system: I have two things I rate on.  Overall score, and soundtrack.  Personally, I feel like game soundtracks are tremendously undervalued; to me, it's a vital factor in getting me into the game.  For the score, I grade on a scale of 1-10, and I try to grade in such a way that each number has a meaning and equal importance.  The meaning of each number are as follows:
0: Garbage, 1: Awful, 2: Poor, 3: Underwhelming, 4: Mediocre, 5: Decent, 6: Good, 7: Great, 8: Excellent, 9: Phenomenal, 10: Masterpiece

Game Rating: 4 (Mediocre)
Soundtrack Rating: 1 (Awful)

This was a difficult one to review.  I tried playing it once a few months ago and found it difficult to get into for some reason - it just irritated me and I found the controls clunky.
I tried again more recently and it was more enjoyable, once I'd played with the key bindings and been a bit more patient with the game.
The graphics are certainly very good.  The audio is a mixed bag - this is one of the few times that I've had to turn subtitles on in a game, because the dialogue is often impossible to hear clearly; even when standing a short distance from other characters.  The music is forgettable and certainly doesn't really add to the atmosphere very much.  The setting itself though is intriguing and well-realised and it's refreshing to see a game set in an unusual (i.e. non-American) locale.  I don't understand why Artyom is a silent protagonist in-game though when he narrates the loading screens - there aren't that many instances where it's really noticeable, but it seems like an odd decision.
The combat mechanics are pretty decent though I found my gun auto-aiming for me at times (certainly not reliably, so I didn't find very useful - if they're going to insist on auto-aim, then at least make it work properly) and I couldn't find a setting to turn that off, which was frustrating. The level design varies considerably from "extremely good" to "frustratingly obtuse".  Considering that it's a fairly linear game, it was disappointing to have to resort to online walkthroughs on more than one occasion because it was entirely unclear where to go next.
The most frustrating aspect of the game however is just how buggy it is.  I'm running a reasonably high-end gaming rig and experienced crashes.  Crashes to desktop.  Crashes to black.  Crashes when exiting a level.  Crashes when loading.  Crashes at the opening menu.  Total system lock-ups on more than one occasion, necessitating a hard reset.  The game randomly unbound every single keyboard command once for fun, requiring me to edit a configuration file manually to be able to use the ESC key to pause the game.  The mouse sometimes doesn't seem to stay bound to my main monitor when in game either, so sometimes firing a weapon would instead cause the game to minimise to the desktop, believing that I suddenly wanted to read an e-mail in Outlook on my other screen (I did not).
All-in-all, I can't recommend the game in its current state.  I certainly don't think it deserves the level of praise that it receives.  It is decent, sometimes even very good, but it is not an instant classic by any means and the repeated issues with the game's stability come close to ruining the experience.

When the game works, I enjoy most aspects about it. The ship combat is fun, and maneuvering around to avoid rams and firing arcs mid fight is a pleasure. I can't really comment about balance, but to find something that works requires experimentation and maybe the patience to read through the game's wikia after playing for 10-15 hours.
As for the bugs, it's a little obscene. I've been playing 2v2 with my friend and that seems to be where the most bugs are.
One game right from the start, I couldn't see what faction one of the enemies was and it was displaying the other enemies faction as something he wasn't. When we get into the game, it still displays incorrect factions when placing our ships. We get into the game, and the fight starts off well despite me choosing poor ships for the fight. Then after the first ram or two (I play orks), my camera jumps to the far side of the battlefield and refuses to move. The game auto-capitulates for me. During all of this, my friend sees the correct factions, doesn't have the buggy camera, and sees the enemy as capitulating. I got a defeat while my friend got a victory.
Other than that awkward game, I've run into two instances of fatal errors, two matches where I can't use thrust, three or four games where my friend can't use any abilities whatsoever, and two or three games where the improper factions are displayed... in 32 hours of play time.
I want to like this game because I've had a lot of fun in it despite some game mechanics I've found annoying. Frequently, ships try to leave battle early and if they're destroyed, you have to play a couple games without them while they get fixed. Often, you get matched against players with higher level admirals than you, and those are usually losses. The game puts you into random game modes where the only one I've enjoyed is cruiser clash. And because of the way the factions are set up, some games and some game modes are automatic losses or wins depending on your faction. Luckily, the games are usually under ten minutes.
If the bugs were fixed, I think I could recommend this game, but it's important to know what kind of game mechanics you'll be playing with.

I'm really in the middle with this game so far.  The premise is promising, the gameplay is unique to me and quite a lot of fun.  I so far haven't experienced any real bugs like some others are saying.  My main gripe really is with the game modes.
Some of them are a blast and just let you experience the tactical nature of the game, but others feel cheap or remove all tactics and force you down a singular route.  I can understand the numerous game modes to try and keep it fresh and offer variety.  But when there are modes where you have to either destroy a single ship or steal data from a ship and escape they aren't so much unique as simply dull.  The defender basically just tries to run away as much as they can for the duration while the attacker ignores all other ships and just rushes the target.
There is little room for tactical or strategic thinking, there is only one clear path to success given the highly limited time to accomplish the goal.  And it is this mode plus Planetary Assault where you have randomly appearing points you have to get a ship to in an arbitrary time limit or else you don't bomb some target in time that you really feel the lack of speed with the Imperials and Orks.
It sounds so far like I'm whaling on the game, but thats simply because I'm frustrated.  It is a game that has such potential, amazing visuals, unique and interesting gameplay that is held up by ill thought out game modes that sap the fun.
I really hope they make changes to game modes, tweaking the boring ones to allow for multiple strategies or at least making them more optional in the campaign/skirmish to which modes you take on.  Overall I'd recommend this game if you can be patient, learn it and are able to get through some potentially irrating modes for the more fun moments.  For me I can't see myself getting too invested in it as it currently is due to the frustration factor, but it certainly will be a game I'll play from time to time to experience its unique and fun gameplay (When the random mode I get will allow me to)

XCOM. The franchise that launched a thousand memes and probably ten times as many blood pressure problems. The game that it's said your soldiers are just as likely to shoot their own cover as they are the enemy you told them to hit. Well, let me tell you right now that's not true.
They're much more likely to do that.
So here's the deal. XCOM is (and always has been) a turn-based, squad-level, brutally tough tactical sim. If you're all about commanding massive armies in the defense of Earth, move on. We're going to ask you to protect the planet and we're going to give you four people to do it. Six if you pay us enough.
When you get right down to it, XCOM is the antithesis of the tank philosophy. It demands surgical application of force, and done so that your limited forces are able to work together. Once you hit mid-game, that's the only way to survive. Players who bring a sledgehammer to this game are going to end up beaten senseless in short order. You need a scalpel. And lots of luck.
On the positives side, it's a beautiful game. Everything from maps to UI is detailed and well-rendered. Everything you see makes sense (well, most of it, anyway), and it was put together with care. The tactical simulation is top notch and is essentially a game of chess where the pieces don't move one at a time. The level of forethought, planning, and tactical finesse the game requires of the player is a refreshing change from the "shoot at everything, bulldoze the level" approach many games take. And if you take the time to develop your tactical skills and fight smart, you'll be rewarded. Not richly, maybe, but rewarded.
On the flip side, XCOM continues to be notoriously skewed against the player. The RNG hates you, and there are all kinds of invisible fetters that are tinkering with your die rolls, meaning that 80% chance to hit probably isn't. That whole "90% chance to hit - miss three times in a row" meme isn't joking; it'll happen. But that's part of the process; if your tactical plan is resilient enough to accomodate that kind of bad luck, then you'll come through. If not, well...time to recruit some new troops.
As a particular bonus, customization is a big deal in XCOM. Building your base is entirely up to you, as is the equipment loadout carried by every one of your troopers. No automatic decision system is going to trip you up. You can even rename your soldiers and give them nicknames. And after your sniper misses his FIFTH 90+% shot, you'll get a certain amount of satisfaction in nicknaming him "Elmer Fudd."
This is a game for the chess players of the world, not the CSGO crowd. If your idea of tactics is to Leeroy Jenkins it, the aliens are going to have you for lunch (possibly literally). But if you like thinking about your combat and applying complex tactics...welcome to the fight.

From the same people behind Dead Island, Dying Light is a significant improvement over the gameplay style that game founded.
However it throws parkour into the mix, making traversing the city of Harran a breeze once you've masterered it, add a grappling hook and you feel like a superhero at times with how fast you can move.
The zombies in this are pushovers during the day but during the night? If you don't have the right equipment then you will die.... a lot. They become more aggressive and harder to kill plus variants that only come out at night will chase you relentlessly unless you use flares or a safe house to evade them. Skill points are doubled during the night though so the risk can be worth the reward. Also, the virals can burn in hell, I don't care if they're recently turned people which means they're faster and stronger, that doesn't bloody mean that they learn parkour and are suddenly pros at it. One of my biggest gripes with this game was constantly being attacked by these♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥even when I was being silent.
There's a story but its so bland and uninspired I don't really remember much of it. You're sent in by the GRE to retrieve a document about a cure for the zombie virus from some warlord, who then kills the doctor who had the cure and for some reason doesn't have you killed despite the fact he has numerous chances to. Oh and you cut off his hand and he still doesn't have you shot on sight even though he has countless armed minions!
Somehow the story went from being average to just a downright slog in the last act. The dream sequence nearly put me to the sleep, it was unneeded and felt incredibly out of place. And the boss fight.... oh my god, the boss fight. It strips you of all your items bar a machete, so there's no healing, even worse is that the boss does a chunk of damage which also knocks you down, and (god I hate when boss fights do this) he has minions. Yeah, you can kill them and they won't respawn if you die but why do so many boss fights in games have to freaking use minions? Its so cheap.
Its sad that the final fight with the big bad turns into boring qte fest but there ya go, that happened. I was glad to beat the game not because I enjoyed the story but because I wanted it to be over, so I could go back to exploring and actually having fun.
Bar the main story, there was a healthy helping of side quests, and by side quests I mean fetch quests. There was way too many instances where the game would make you go get an item and come back to the quest giver only to be told you needed another item. Why they can't just tell you every bloody thing they need in one go, I'll never kn.... oh right, padding! There are also challenges in which you have to kill a certain number of zombies with a weapon or use parkour to get to a destination in a fixed amount of time.
Outside of the story I really enjoyed the game, but whenever I did have to do the story I just wanted it over with.
The sidequests were mostly fetch quests and the npcs I occasionally encountered were dull as all hell.
Combat was a blast and combined with the exploration, the best part of the game is merely just exploring.

This Beta is taking place in order to test the new CFN system. The reason why offline modes are unavailable is because they want us to test out the new online system. It's not a Beta for the game, it's a Beta for the new system. Us being able to use Ed early is a little bonus.
As someone who's been playing SFV since day 1, I can definitely notice a few new things.
Pros (new CFN)
-The aesthetic of the new interface is very nice. Character select screen and backgrounds/look sharper and are much nicer on the eyes
-When browsing for a Battle Lounge, you can now actually see people's flags because they now load in time, which makes finding battle lounges much simpler.
-The new CFN seems to be faster when looking at things such as rankings, replays, and people.
- They added the ability to actually register friends
- There's a nice friend activity bar on the right in the new CFN interface. You can see what your friends are doing, and it will tell you what time it happened too (if they opened a battle lounge, lost, or won against someone).
- I definitely got matched up with a lot more people similar of rank and country
Cons (new CFN)
-After winning 1 match (out of 2) in online battles (I was only doing casual) it would show the characters nice little song and dance, and then we'd both say yes to keep the battle going, but then the game would just kinda stop and I'd lose connection. This has happened more than 3 times.
-Loading times in Battle Lounges seem much longer
Now for Ed
Pros (Ed)
- Looks hella dank, it's a very nice model
- His personality is actually portrayed through his moves, idle animation, and taunt (example: his head swivel after whiffing his C.HP)
- Very fun to play
Cons (Ed)
- Not fun to figure out
- He seems easy at first, but once you get down to brass tacks there's tons of little nit-picky things with this character that you need to get good at in order to do certain things
- an (almost) full screen charge punch that's safe on block, and if it hits you can follow up with S.MP, C.HP into PP for around 300, add a critical art for maximum spaghetti
- Attempting to do his combos that you saw in the reveal trailer is a lot harder than you think, and attempting these in random matches online is impossible for most of us right now, so all you can really do to practice this character is cheese it up with a friend in a battle lounge
- After an Anti-Air CC with his C.HP, if you dash (as Ed) forward and do a move, it'll register that you're crossing the other person up, and make you face the opposite direction (wich you aren't) and make your move totally miss. I think this is a bug, but then again, the same type of stuff happens with Ken and his V-Trigger.
It was risky of them to allow us to use a new character with the training mode enabled, but that's the chaotic good of Capcom. Giving us something so fresh and new and cool that we just gotta use it, but the only way we can is to go online. I think the new CFN is amazing, and all I can ask for is that they fix the issue where connection gets lost after the 1st match while both people are waiting while "ready'd-up".
TL;DR : It's good. I think the new CFN will do just fine and that Ed will make for an odd new character. Just fix a few little things, and we're good to go.

This Game Is Awesome. Why? Because: Great Atmosphere,Gameplay And Story!

The Good:
- The puzzles in this game are remarkably innovative. It is clear that a tremendous amount of condensation was put into designing each puzzle so that nothing felt superfluous or too convoluted.
- The art design can simply be described as beautiful. Beyond the sheer elegance of the art style, the aesthetic managed to brilliantly communicate the emotional subtext of the written narrative.
- The music in Braid was absolutely superb.
The Bad:
- (No spoilers) my biggest gripe with Braid was the way in which the final arch of the story was told. Instead of proving context to clarify and give unambiguous meaning to the events of Tim’s journey, the story’s conclusion was muddied by more abstraction. Additionally, if popular interpretations are correct, then the intended story could have been more effectively fleshed out from the onset.
Final Verdict:
To me, I relished the journey of Braid, not only due to the art design and puzzles on screen but also in my attempts to decipher the story before its conclusion. Whereas I assumed the curtain would eventually be pulled back, I was disappointed by the unnecessary ambiguity in the final act. Nonetheless, the game is still worth playing, albeit at a discounted price.

To me, the most interesting parts about Braid are the art style and the core gameplay mechanic. While I can't do anything but praise the style of the game as well I will do so. Be praised Art Style! Your rock!
The core mechanic, however, is a double edged sword. It basically is all about turning back and replaying time. You can do so manually at all times or sometimes you'll have a special time mechanic on your hands:
In example, when your movement is queued to the entire game world. Walking forward will move you and the time, standing still will freeze it and walking backwards will rewind it.
There are quite a few different time mechanics within Braid, but since I'm not all that evil I won't do spoilers here.
Oh yeah you can walk and jump here. That's like the platforming part. It's solid but nothing special without the time travel thingy.
While this makes for an amazingly fresh gameplay experience, some of the puzzles tied to it are ridiculous. You'll spend hours upon hours to solve a single game screen just to get frustrated as hell, turning to a youtube guide if your computer can still play videos after you've tossed it through your entire apartement, out the window and ran it over with a truck. Twice.
Some of the puzzles later on even require the usage of tricks never hinted at, let alone explained wich just seems cheep.
There may be the 1% of players who will dedicate their live to solving those puzzles without a guide but there's a 1% of people who try to invent time travel itself in the real world as well without much success. So yeah.
Another interesting thing are the collectables. You can run through almost the entire game, skipping all puzzles. Now it won't do you and good and you'll be done with the Braid within 15 minutes. So don't do it. Embrace the rage! By collecting certain things you'll uncover other certain things wich will uncover 6 very certain things and the games ending. Wich in itself is a thing. So ya. Getting those collectables is the goal of the game.
There are a few more things I wanna praise here to look in the mirror tomorrow morning, hating myself for being mainstream or something.
Yet another great apsect this game does have for it is the music. it's great. I do have the feeling that it is intendet to calm you while the hate about not solving puzzles inside you does grow to an infinite amount of pure rage. Just like the visual part of the game it feels "real". As in, all hand made. A warm piano accompanied by a soothing Cello charm your ears while you are afraid of blowing up the house on the other side of the street if your speakers fail to work all of a sudden. Or if you use the time mechanic (wich you have to) for it will rewind the soundtrack as well wich sounds god awful. So basically, the music makes you afraid of solving the game... Soundtrack, you've nailed it! Except for the fact that you make me staring at the screen not doing much at all cause I am afraid of rewinding you.
The story is surprisingly deep for a puzzle platformer. Not deep in the sense of an epic story that will unfold before you but deep as in you'll find yourself thinking about it... in fact, Braid is kinda vague on the story thing with a bunch of diaries as your only lore. But those diaries are, in fact, very well written and thought worthy... You'll (or can... there are those people) squeeze your thoughts in a philosophical attempt, triggered by those diaries in the game... with about 30% of your brain cells while the other 70% will be occupied crafting a pipe bomb you'll stick into your computer, watching it blow up in satisfaction about the running gamescreen fading to black while you'll get caught into the explosion. Story, you are awesome! Kind of.... Kant would like it I suppose.... or Tolstoi. Maybe...
(Dat ending though.... 12/10)
There are more likable aspects about this game (like dropping huge objects on people and jumping on heads) wich do result in the same awesome but not awesome part of the game. In the end, it is indeed a great game wich you should buy but it also sucks♥♥♥♥♥for it will ruin your day whenever you start it. Wich probably means you shouldn't buy it.
So buy it! Or not! I dunno.
You'll have to answer yourself a simple question: Is the massive frustration worth the whole lot of joy you'll get from this game? I do not regret buying it at all but damn! This new computer was expensive!
Yet again... dat ending though! 13/10!

Braid is an excellently crafted puzzle platformer, with fantastic gameplay mechanics in an absolutely beautiful hand-painted world. Within this setting, a love story emerges slowly, and then completely turned on its head.
The gameplay of Braid is centered around reversing time to return objects or yourself to a previous position. This mechanic is expanded upon in multiple changing iterations between the worlds. This mechanic is also utilized to partial tell the game's story, which is mostly told though cryptic stories and allegories within books before starting worlds.
Story is very cryptic throughout most of the game, slowly being revealed through reading the books, telling a tale of unrequited love. Story should be experienced first hand, so I won't go into it any further here. If you like introspective analysis of self, that is very metaphorical and philosophical, I would highly recommend it.
Braid - 9 out of 10
A fantastic puzzle platformer with a story that might not be for everyone, but is set in a handpainted world that is utterly beautific and euphoric.

This isnt going to be a bash thread, just personal opinion and observation. I am aware, this is Early Acess and we're here to test and the game is only 30% complete, just find my bug mega thread if you don't think i was commited =p. But with that said as a company you still have to find a way to hold the interest of your "testers" especially when they're paying you to test instead of the other way around...
In the beginning the grind was almost nice, you were getting player levelings, you were leveling multiple skills at once and unlocking things left and right.
Then you start to hit around level 40 and things to start to slow down but hell you're 60% into your levels thats supposed to happen. You still have some cool things to look forward to, Iron greatsword, Mithril robes/armor... Ton's of "end game neato's" to unlock.
Then.... you hit level 50.... you unlock the Iron tier... you finally start to feel safe because ghost scythes and hammers arent doing 200+ damage to your 6k health doors. But then you realize... This
tier takes BRONZE.... you know that magical stuff thats need to craft those pesky spell towers and ammo that you need hundreds of....
At this point you're left with a decision. What do I do? Do i stop crafting turrets and ammo or do I leave my base stone and skip iron to work towards manor tier? *takes a peak at manor tier* ....... the mats required are ASTRONOMICAL! Its insane.... the amount of mats to craft a single piece of that tier is upwards of 1k iron, 500 bronze thousands of stone and twine... its crazy....
Currently I have a house of about 9 people, I'm "The Buildier" with about 15 forges it would take a full day of smelting just to iron out your whole base with those forges running around the clock to completley "iron up" a full base under a seal or longer... and thats without turrets.
A full day might not sound like a lot. But to your average players, your casuals, your solo's. Thats just a ladder you aren't going to want to climb.
While i'm on the topic of seals, The bubbles are just way to small... If you want to protect all that you own from the roaming wraiths, players, sabers and everything else on the map that wants to kill you... you must put it inside of a House Seal Bubble. These bubbles are are just far to small. You can fit about a 8x7x9 base inside of a seal.
Now that might sound substantial, but when you take into account, Boxes, work benches, altars, seals, reviving altars, spell towers, endless boxes, summong pools, crops, beds, PLAYERS, TAMES, etc that space fills up faster than you would think. So basically you have to have multiple seals going. But again those pesky little suckers run on Magical Essence.
Now you might ask, " Why is this a big deal essences are cheap? " Well they are, they are very easy to make aswell... but the big issue is thhe glass bottles, you need HUNDREDS of these suckers and its crafted with Charcoal, Which is very heavy, sulfur power, and Quartz powder which is also very heavy... You also have to craft these little suckers in your inventory...and guess what they're used in EVERYTHING not just house seals. you need THOUSANDS of these little guys. but the biggest issue is everytime you want to craft bottles, atleast on a large scale you basically have to set aside atleast 30 minutes of your "play time" or MORE just to craft the bottles, then another 10 minuts to fill the suckers.
Anyways as it stands now between the essence grind and just the god awful smelting time it takes to make bronze/iron things its just way to much of a grind. I appreciate the mat grind, I'll farm it all day long, where it stands now minus the manor tier it feels very balanced. But the "craft time" is just god awful way to long in my personal opinion.
For the first time since release a few house mates and I decided to go out and do some raiding. The first house we through a flag at it turns out the players there were offline and we were stuck waiting TWELVE hours to wipe these dudes. They had it long coming and it was very disappointing we couldnt hit these folks. Absolutley nothing we could do... we decided to wait 12 hours and come back.
So we come back 12 hours later the war preperation is no longer showing up in our house management we swing by with a ghost scythe and go to wap wap wap and nothing... absolutley nothing... couldnt do a darn thing...
Whatever we move on... We find this very pretty stone base, that someone has obviously put days of work into, easlily 20+ man hours. Walled off with a gigantic wall all the way around, atleast 15 foundations long, 5 wide, and about 8 walls high. The wall itself was easily 20 foundations all the way around and 2-4 walls high. The poor soul forgot to re-activate his house seal... (probably shut it off due to my Magic essence rant above). We stroll in with a few lightning wall's we had looted because we live on the floating island and its constantly bombarded with meteorites and wraits and elementals just drop stupid good loot at way to high  of a chance of dropping. Anywho we rolled in with 5 lightning walls, prolly take you about an hour to farm the mats for those things...  first lightning wall goes up, his first set of walls go down... we hop in crack open all his boxes, make 5 or 6 of our own to store on shipping trips back to base. This takes all of about 5 minutes.
We land we break wall, we loot... 5 minutes... ALL OF FIVE WHOLE MINUTES to completley neutralize his HOURS of time making this stuff.... But we don't stop there... These guys are of a different faction, they've raided friends... we wanted them to pay. hell we've still got mad lightning wall casts. so we spam them all over his base. 5 fully broken lightning walls later he has 3 foundations left... Just 3... we even took down his giant wall.
Thats right with about an hour's worth of farming we literally deleted... and I mean deleted. hours upon hours of this guys work in a total of about 15 minutes. thats just insance in my opinion.

- Completley recheck and rebalance the cost of manor tier
- Remove Bronze cost from iron tier, Hell even bump the iron cost a bit
- Spells and Magic should not affect buildings, minus telekenesis
- Make glass bottles craftable inside of a Magic Altar
- Reduce the consumption of Magic Essence in the house Seal OR make it so the house seal is no longer a bubble, but more or less protects everything its attached to.
- Remove or severly reduce ORP protection from the House Seal.
- Make it so when players are offline ORP doesn't make their base invulnerable, instead significantly reduce the amount of damage a player can do to the structure while players are offline. ( we have PVE servers if you don't want to be raided offline. , and if you take a look at other games they seperate ORP servers... this is all done for a reason)
- Remove wild life damage to structures
- Reduce the levels required for building tiers ( it shouldnt take you 5 days to achieve even minor safety in stone)
- Reduce smelt times for all metals or make a "magical forge of fast smeltyness of magical awesomeness"
TLDR: Thanks for taking the time to read my thread. I will definatley be returning back to this game, but as a level 55 with nothing much left for me to do because i refuse to even look at manor tier and raiding either being just a stupid cake walk or completley impossible... there just is nothing left for me here for the time being! This game has serious potential It also has a lot of really cool things that were a lot of fun. I did enjoy every bit of my 160 hours. But now the grind is just to exhaustive and aside from that there is nothing left for me! See you folks around

Meadow: A Game Review
So to start off with I'll tell you about the game play, then I'll tell you the story, and then I'll tell you my opinions and pros/cons.
The game play consists of walking around collecting, "Flowers" and,"Essence". Flowers serve no purpose besides giving you points and earning achievements You know, normal collectibles. You find flowers by just walking around.
Now Essence allows you to unlock emotes, new animals, and skins, to show how cool and pro you are. You get essence by either finding it in the world, or breaking open, "Obelisks". A Obelisk is a rock in the shape of a kiddie house, a square with a point on the top. You break an obelisk depending on what it needs. A obelisk with two dots requires two animals, no matter which animal they are. But a taller obelisk might have pictures of a rabbit, and a badger cub on it, with two of each needed. You will have to have two of each to break it open, and collect the essence inside.
You will find plenty of animals in the world you are in, a server, or a meadow as they are called in game, can hold up to fifty people at a time as of February 2017. This may change, but right now it's 2017. There are three servers for each area of the world, Europe, Eastern US, and Western US. Essence are also  points as well, and being in the top 10 in points allows you to play as an eagle, or if you own all of the games, books, and soundtracks you will also get the eagle. Sucks to be you if you don't have that kind of money.
The choices of animals you have are plenty. For a new player to Meadow, you have the Badger Cub. Badger Cubs are slow, beginner animals. The next animal is a frog, and then you have a rabbit/hare. I will list all of the animals now, in order. Badger Cub, Frog, Rabbit, Goat, Fox, Badger, Lynx, Lynx Cub, Bear and Eagle. After the Fox the rest of the animals are locked. You must have Shelter 1 for the Badger, Shelter 2 for the Lynx, Paws for the Lynx Cub, and all three games for the Bear Cub, from paws.
My problems with the game play is that beginner animals are really slow, and can often fall behind if you have made a herd of animals to break open Obelisks. They, as the first animal you get, are very common as well. My other gripe with this is that the controls are a bit hard to grasp at first.
The story is, nothing. There is no story! Just wander around and be an animal. You are just plopped into the world, free to wander and shout at random animals passing by.
My opinion on this game is pretty simple. I like it. It's a nice time waster which, if you have a day off work or school, you can play for many hours, unlocking all of the emotes on animals, unlocking skins on animals, and gather all of that, sweet, sweet essence.
Pros:
+Game is very pretty
+Animals unlocked via the game are balanced well
+You can do almost whatever you want.
+Can name your animal after memes
+Easy game to play
+Nice time waster
+Great fun if you are drunk
+No bullies or unwanted people here.
+ Nice music.
Cons:
-Pop ins are very common
-Lags on older computers
-Game feels like a test instead of a game.
-Almost all assets are reused from other Might and Delight games.
???:
=No voice chat or text chat
=Some animals unlocked from other shelter games are not very well balanced/same uses as other animals
=Controls
=World is huge

It's hard to ignore the fact that the PC version of DOA5LR is a second-rate version of the game.
Tecmo Koei has opted to port the PS3 / Arcade version of the game instead of the more up-to-date PS4 version.
This means that new stages are missing from the PC port, and new graphical features (such as the 'Soft Engine') are missing from the PC version.
It's taken many months for online functionality to come to the PC version (promised to come soon after launch), without any lobby support! Only ranked matchmaking is supported.
The (optional) cosmetic DLC is only available in expensive packs, and you can't pick costumes for just your favourite characters. Additionally, the clothing damage feature on some of the costumes is not available on PC (as it's based off the PS3 version, not the PS4 version).
I would greatly hesitate to support another Tecmo Koei game on PC until they show they can treat PC players with respect.

I've long since considered these isometric Tomb Raiders' the more 'pure' form of raiding tombs.
Lara Croft and The Temple of Osiris is the successor to Guardian of Light with the same prefix. This is an action puzzle platformer/twin stick shooter from an isometric view.
I say these are the more pure form of tomb raiding compared to the 3rd person action games because they seem to focus more on puzzle solving, of course there is still action and boss battles but these isometric physics based puzzles take you back to a time when puzzle solving was the main draw. But on top of that the action feels really good, really smooth.
Now before anyone goes crazy the reason this game is getting mixed reviews is because its very poorly optimized, it hitches all over the place. Frame drops every ten steps. If you have the ability to play this in a non ported version, I'd do that. But if like me you do not have another device to play this on. The technical issues can be overlooked. The game still feels really good. The hitching is not desirable, it is definitely an issue. I by no means encourage this behavior and do not advocate this level of tolerance from developers or publishers but it the game remains quite playable indeed.
There is a main map that has entrances to multiple tombs in your quest to reassemble Osiris. Filled with extra challenges throughout. Weapon upgrades, rings and amulet slots to alter the properties your your abilities and items. You can also play up to 4 player co-op. I did not attempt to use this feature as I prefer to play alone. Though I would guess from how I solved some of the puzzles the co-op seems a little unnecessary and perhaps a bit chaotic. At least compared to Guardian of Light. I, myself would advocate playing single player.

Temple of Osiris seemed like an easy followup to a budget hit, and then it took a dump all over the floor.
Lemme back up. On the face of it, this looks like Guardian of Light but with a higher playercount and a more involved "hub world" between stages, and if it was nothing but that, it'd be pretty good! But then you dig in a little more. One of the first things you might notice if you play co-op and solo is the game doesn't (seem to?) have alternate layouts for SP vs. MP. This was a huge thing in the last title because you needed to be able to solve some puzzles or collect all items - unless I've missed something, though, there are some items which seem 100% uncollectable without death in Temple of Osiris without a second player to toss a grapple or lift you or hold buttons.
Okay, but maybe you don't need all the health-ups or ammo+ powerups. You just want to complete the challenges in each level and earn those rewards. Those still exist on every level, and they're varied and the score targets are still around, so yeah, one little issue's fine if it plays the same overall, right?
Then you come upon a chest.
See, a lot of your unlock rewards are going to be very... spartan. This is because all those gems you're picking up for score are being counted, and you have to spend them on chests of varying degrees which are an item lottery. Boy, you better believe the chests contain better gear than the challenge rewards, by a huge margin. At one point I gambled and got an "Epic Amulet" - health and ammo regen, higher treasure/refill drop rate, faster bomb speed. The best amulet I'd found from challenges, which I was going out of my way for, near endgame? Treasure drop+ and bomb power+ and it made me weak to cold. (Weapon variants are also locked in the chests, which was a fun surprise but explained why my armory was a bit slim.)
Alright, so some simple bad ideas, but you can just cheat up some cash and turbogrind the chests if you need. Well, that's not gonna fix the bugs. This game is crash-prone and abandoned by its devs, with real common bugs still being inside. Collision issues, some enemies not taking damage reliably*, and once I had a camera hang on I'm not entirely sure what, but it wasn't Lara, making that stage a real pain until I reset (killing my score challenge...)
It's not good, fellas. The best positive I can bring up about it is "the DLC is implemented pretty smoothly and when I went to look for the extra tombs at endgame, I realized I had already found and done them in the campaign without knowing". Second place is "it has post-game content and challenges", except the very first one of those I did was a combat challenge, and an enemy fell outside of the world, but it had an AOE attack. Cue dying to invisible screams and uninstalling as I write this review. Avoid, please.
* Maybe this one was just me! But oh my word the "bomb them when they're down" lizards refused to respond to damage 99% of the time for me, even if I teabagged them with a friggin' explosive. They'd take 4-5 to kill, and keep in mind this still involved knocking them down first...

I wanted to play this game. I wanted to like it as I liked LC:GoL, but it's too messed up and buggy, at least the PC version is.
The graphics are seemingly "better" but the perspective is worse and it's actually even harder to control Lara. Sometimes she wouldn't move at all and seem like she was stuck at a corner because the game expects her to move away from it in another direction first before she can move around the corner, sometimes she would actually BE stuck after she'd just climbed up a ledge or jumped onto some object (and the only way to continue was to commit suicide), sometimes she would run crazy fast and right down into the next chasm or whatever.
Also, controls are generally chunky and not immersive at all, and her movements are odd. Contrary to the controls in GoL, there's a constant impression that she glides and slips more than she actually moves, and it's hard to get her to move from the spot she stands in and exactly in one specific direction (of the 8 she can move in), so she sometimes moves too far away into the wrong direction first, or she jumps into the wrong direction.
The game also crashes every few minutes, though luckily it autosaves pretty often, so I didn't lose a lot of progress but I lost much of my interest in playing it.
The "puzzles" aren't hard to understand at all, but the exploding balls in particular and in combination with those weird controls, pretty much made it impossible to finish some of them. I simply grew tired of repeating the same 2 minutes over and over and dying to some weird unforseeable or buggy crap. At one point, I died about 50 times, often just short of the fraction of a second (and yes, I did it the way it was supposed to be done), then I gave up. I couldn't solve it and I couldn't go back or leave the tomb or anything, so I simply quit.
Guardian of Light was way easier and way more fun to play, and its "puzzles" were a lot less aggravating.
Temple of Osiris music was good (as was GoL's) and graphics seemed moderately appealing too, though its engine obviously wasn't made for the PC keyboard+mouse controls. GoL's controls were off-key too, but at least not nearly as much as ToO's.

Strengths:  Let me first say that my two boys and I had a great time playing this game.  In 3 player local mode, the boys were using Logitech gamepads while I used the good ol' keyboard/mouse.   I found character movement with keyboard a bit difficult especially when needing to tightrope or hanging from cliffs and ledges.  However character movements with the gamepads were a breeze.
I've noticed that other reviewers experienced bugs and game freezing.  My experience has been rather different.  In 13 hours of gameplay we have had no problems whatsoever.  All boss encounters, trash mobs, and puzzle solutions seemed to work as the developers intended.
I will note that I'm running Windows 10 along with AMD cpu and gpu.
The actual gameplay was quite fluid and well paced.  There could have been more interesting loot to be had, however the weapon upgrades were great.  I found the flamethrower endlessly satisfying :)
Weakness:  Don't expect to be hugely challenged.   An 8 and 9 year old were fully engaged, however an adult probably won't break a sweat at any point.
Never got the "Find Match" feature to actually find someone.  I suspect that's due to a rather small community.
This is my biggest complaint about the game - you can only maintain 1 saved game at a time.  I thought when the kids went to bed I'd start my own 1 player game on the side, but no.  I couldn't do that without blowing away the 3 player game we had going.
In the end would I recommend this games?  For sure.  It's a pretty good time and for 5 bucks you really can't go wrong...at least while the sale lasts.

Objectively speaking, this game is inferior to its predecessor, Civilization IV. The main reason I say that is that the AI seems completely incapable of understanding the one-unit-per-tile mechanic that was introduced in this game; it's far easier to make an enormous "stack of doom" and use it to wipe out your enemies, which was a totally viable strategy in IV. The AI in V is also much worse at diplomacy and almost guaranteed to hate your guts for being a warmonger, which might be realistic but not very fun. For these reasons, if you play mostly in single-player, as I do, IV is arguably the more enjoyable game.
V is still the game I keep coming back to play, though. The number one reason for that is that it looks fantastic. Call me shallow if you want, but when you spend hundreds of hours with any game, I think it's pretty damn important for it to look good. The UI is pleasing on the eye, and the terrain and (most) leaders look so good that I still get excited to explore the world every time I start a new game. The switch to hexagonal tiles was a massive improvement and one that I'd struggle to give up if I went back to playing IV.
As a strategy game, it ticks all the right boxes, including the most important one: it makes you think. You might do well on the lower difficulty levels by learning a good starting strategy and sticking to it, but to get better at the game you really have to be able to adapt to whatever combination of leader, land and neighbours the game throws at you. That's where the fun lies; that's what has kept me hooked for all this time - just starting new randomised games. Every one of them is different. Highly recommended.

I will start right now with the main problem of this game: it’s too short! About 5 hours are required to finish the game, according to your ease with the riddles.
Braid is a platform game, so the scenario is not apparently very developed: we control a guy, and we have to save a girl, who is, of course, in a very far place.
Nevertheless, if we wantit, we can read at the beginning of every world the story and the psychology of the characters, who are very interesting.
There are 6 worlds to be crossed. The first world serves as tutorial, and afterward each world has its specificity which is presented in their respective first level. The difficulty is increasing in every world.
The main characteristic of Braid is that the character never dies; if he "dies", we use its power of rewinding to return more or less quickly (we choose ourselves the speed) to the wanted place (for example, just before this jump which we have pitifully missed, or at the very beginning of the level).
As a consequence, this feature of "rewinding" is going to be differently used at every level which will have an appropriate specificity: in the 2nd world, we shall sometimes have to deal with objects or monsters which are insensible in the rewinding; in the 6th, there will be a possibility of having a shadow clone which reproduce the action made just before. So the riddles have variable difficulties and forms.
There is a double objective in each world. The first one is obviously to arrive at the end of every level, what is very easily made. The second is to collect all the puzzle pieces in each level, what is less easily made. By completing the puzzle of every world, we free the access to the very last world to reach the 100% of the game.
Otherwise, it is beautiful to see. It is homogeneous, the worlds are well thought, colors and shadows are attractive. It’s like paintings.
Finally, it is beautiful to hear. Musics, essentially classic and lyric, allow a fast dumping in the game.
Conclusion: Braid is a very good game experience, with beautiful sounds, interesting gameplay, and especially mewing rabbits with a flower on the head. Yes, you read well.

I bought this game because I liked the fusion of a cooking sim with a shoot em'up, which is a bizarre yet quite fitting combo in this game.  You drive around the US in your truck making more and more complicated tacos, fighting against more and more dangerous enemies and mutants. It's satisfying and addictive, in the sense that I can mute the game and chill while playing with a podcast or tv or radio in the backgrond. In a way it's like other driving sims, but involved enough that you can't zone out but also easy enough that you won't be terrified of what the game asks you to learn and do. I like being able to upgrade your taco truck in a variety of ways, with different weapons, decals, armor, and tools that make the game new. Multiple playthroughs allow you to take different routes and change how you play to make it last longer.
That said I wouldn't say this game is an absolute must have. The repetition of the game sets in early, so if this doesn't click for you in the first two hours I would return it. If you enjoy the relaxed nature this game works in, even when you are blasting zombies to pieces, then its definitely worth playing.
The big problem really comes in the fact that buying ingredients for your taco truck can be a bit of a pain because only 1 of the 2 types of pit-stops sells ingredients, so if you get unlucky and run a route that has the wrong stop 2 or 3 times in a row, you have to leave without selling tacos to the hungry survivors. If you don't feed them they die and, in my playthroughs, don't come back until I start a new game, meaning you can really screw yourself over without planning even on the easy difficulty.
This means you need to grind in the early game to get enough money to buy enough ingredients to go on longer trips, which becomes more and more needed as you get closer and closer to the end location, especially because you will get the wrong kind of stops that force you to go without buying the ingredients you need for 2 or so stops.
As for the map this game dissapointed me because if you want to go East and then North, good luck, because finding the on way that heads to the East Coast was annoying and caused me to lose a few games until I found which way took me there.
Lastly, as of this review, the achievements do not unlock at all, and some people have trouble playing the game. The devs haven't said anything about this, so be wary of not being able to play. I suppose I got lucky but I have yet to figure out what the problem is due to a lack of discussion about this game. I hope that in wirting this review more people will play this game and get some ideas going.
I would reccommend this game mainly because of its scope: its made by a small studio and shows it by having a great little charm and some shining aspects that really hint at what a bright future is ahead of the devs. I think that if this game is used as a test of sorts, then "Gunman Taco Truck 2" could be an absolute blast. The ideas in this game are wonderful, and if are polished and perfected, will make a successor a truly unique and fun game. Play this if you want to have good few hours, and want to see a project HOPEFULLY evolve in time.

First of all I'd like to mention the good stuff. The game is a great package for the money. I haven't heard of another realistic racing sim you could pick up for that little cash. It takes itself very seriously and is very driver focused. It looks like the real deal most of the time (the rules, the damage, the race weekend etc). You can also make comprehensive adjustments to your car and there's a good selection of different tracks.
However the game looks like something that would come with a box of cereal, meaning extremely cheap (check the price once again). The car selection is woefully small (half of them comprising of caterhams and radicals with different power outputs). There are a lot of customizing options as mentioned, but they didn't bother to explain what kind of effect these changes would have on the cars performance or at least mentioning the basics of car setup. The AI are like oiled up bricks and don't make a satisfying opponent. If by any chance you find yourself off the tarmac, then you're essentially on rails, because you can't steer or break or accelerate. The cars themselves (mainly with stability control off) are far too nervous and unbalanced meaning they will frequently spin (especially high hp cars). This results in extreme effort put into driving clean, fast laps, but the rewards are not in any way satisying. Not once was I smiling whilst playing this game. I could kind of tolerate much of it, but the idiotic driving characteristics was the last straw - the gear you're in, affects the understeer going into a corner and also the braking distance. Also cars with maximum amount of downforce, happily skidded about. And once you start putting on a few dlc-s (to get more cars and tracks), the price climbs quickly (20eur+) and it just can't compete with the alternative titles.
Overall a good racing sim if you're in need of a racing game for less than 5 eur or if you're into a challenging realistic (as good as they came in 2007) racing experience then give it a go. But there  are so many far better alternatives to this game that I don't see the need for a regular car guy to own this.

Developed and published by Casualogic, StarFringe: Adversus is a strategy game with clear 4X (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, and eXterminate) influences. It is the dev team’s first project on Steam and while it’s still in Early Access, it does provide players with complex skirmishes against the AI.

StarFringe is in dire need of a singleplayer campaign and some form of multiplayer. The AI in the custom battle mode, does hold its own but I doubt it will be enough for the game’s current asking price. The developer does stray from the traditional real time strategy formula that more often than not, involves constant base management and resource gathering. You need to protect your mothership, for instance. Losing it means game over and the entire gameplay encourages an almost locust-like approach in which the few resources available are finite and you have to expand over other systems at an accelerated pace if you wish to survive. The AI factions certainly won’t give you much room to breathe since they are quite greedy themselves. Thus the skirmish mode rapidly transforms into a classic “survival of the fittest” scenario.

No doubt StarFringe: Adversus, looks beautiful. The attention to detail, the diversity of the units and the weapon effects, show clear signs of quality and the efforts that went into this game so far. As always, there is room for improvement, but I can’t complain that this strategy title might be lacking in the looks department.

The soundtrack is regular Sci-Fi fare with just the right amount of diversity, to never seem too repetitive. I do hope that once we get a nice story to this game, we can also expect some voice acting. No strategy title should do without it. Players deserve to have the units confirm the currently issued orders. It’s tradition. You can’t break that many norms, Casualogic.

+ Beautiful graphics
+ Steam Achievements

- No Trading Cards
- Requires a story mode
- No Multiplayer options yet

I have to say that I found the game’s difficulty quite pleasing. It will be a very good RTS alternative to triple A titles, if it can pull off a singleplayer story and offer at least some co-op skirmishes. The presence of Achievements gives me hope that the developer wishes to introduce Trading Cards too, at some point. A badge for this game would be most welcome and from what I’ve seen of the Early Access so far, StarFringe has a lot of potential.

Battlefleet Gothic: Armada is an RTS about space battles between huge amazingly designed spaceships.
There's no base building or resource management, only spaceship battles.
I haven't played much multiplayer (mostly because I got destroyed there), so I'll focus on my singleplayer and skirmish experiences.
The game puts you in the command of a space fleet.
You start with a couple of light cruisers - they are relatively fast, but have light weaponry and are quite squishy.
You'll gain XP, level up both your ships individually and yourself.
Leveling up ships will allow you to upgrade their skills, level up crew (that'll boost ship stats), and install new ship skills.
You won't be able to get all upgrades, so essentially you are forced to specialize your ships for variety of roles - from long-ranged snipers to close-quater assult ships.
Leveling up yourself will get you more slots for more ships (thus allowing you to have a wider roaster with more specializations) as well as to get higher class ships - cruiser, battlecruisers, etc.
Campaign is built in a very XCOM-y manner - you can win or lose missions, but the campaign will continue.
And the result will depend on winning or losing key (story) missions.
In addition to story missions, you'll get invaders who try to capture your worlds.
Losing worlds would mean losing bonuses or getting debuffs.
And, of course, there's no way to reclaim all of the worlds - so you'll have to pick carefully.
The combat mechanics are somewhat unique as well. You'll have to angle the ships to get the best shot.
You'll have to speed up or slow down your engines to evade enemy fire or align properly for that best shot.
You'll have to use your skills and maybe even run away to keep your ships safe.
Combat is pretty fast paced - it usually takes about 5-10 minutes of real time per battle.
But if that's too fast for you - there's always a way to slow down time to carefully think your next move through.
In general, it's a pretty enjoyable experience for a casual RTS player like me.
Talking about the downsides - so far I'd only had a few crashes after alt+tabbing too many times. And that's about it really. Game runs at solid 60fps, no bugs were encountered.

Playing this game brings me pure joy and happiness. The music, graphics, and gameplay all meld together to a pretty cool experience.
I'd explain the game mechanics like a mixture of The Oregon Trail with a tiny bit of the Binding of Issac. Of course, this game has nothing to do with fighting poo monsters as a nude child. Each playthrough is random. No two games will be alike. If you die on your journey. It is game over, and you will have to restart.
The goal of the game is to reach Winnipeg, Canada. Where there are no taco trucks. Your mission is to bring tacos to Canada so your business will thrive forever. The game starts in San Diego, California. You will get to choose your route of choice (Not all routes will be available on each run, it is randomized). On the way to each city, you will take control of your taco truck on a 2D track. Your truck has a mounted gun and you have to kill anything in your path. Each animal you kill becomes a meat ingredient for your tacos. So it's important to kill anything that moves so you have plenty of meat stocked up.
Every town will either have a grocery store, or a garage. Grocery stores will sell you core ingredients like cheese, salsa, or onions. They are super important. If you don't keep a steady stock of ingredients, you will lose the game. You can fill up your fuel tanks at every stop. The price of fuel raises the further into the map you travel. You can see the fuel requirements to each town on the travel map.
Garages sell you truck upgrades where you can spend scrap that you find. You can buy repair kits, armor plating, HP upgrades, or even a whole new truck!
You can also accept random delivery jobs that may pop up. It's either a package delivery, or giving customers rides to the town they request. They will either pay you with cash or scrap. These are totally optional (but worth it, if you can pull it off).
My one major criticism is the towns you stop in. Each stop more or less looks the same. The backgrounds and enemies do change the further you go, but you will always see the same grocery stores or the same repair garages. All of the customers are the same in each town. Each person you see will always look the same. They will always wear the same clothes. One game I think of is "Organ Trail: Director's Cut". Each town had a unique screenshot to show you what city you are in. I think if Gunman Taco Truck had a unique backdrop for each city, it would really add to the game.
(Oh, and steam achievements are currently busted for some people)
Don't let that put you off from playing the game. It is very fun. It's worth the money (especially on sale)

While the Warhammer liscense has been thrown around to some bad devs before, this is not one of those times. The Gameplay is fantastic, variety and customization is nicely done aswell.
Singleplayer
-A lot of RTS games usually have campaigns, but they're usually boring or just too slopily thrown together to enjoy. This game's campaign is nothing like that. It has great cutscenes, ones that warhammer fans absolutely love with that imperial touch. The game makes you feel like you're really part of the story. On the first playthrough you can't wait for your next turn to see what cutscene and priority mission comes next. Failure in these missions is not like most games. If you lose you don't just restart, you lose those ships and have to wait for a turn if damaged or two if destroyed. If you fail a priority that just means Abbadon will have more at his disposal to use against Humanity. After completion of the first playthrough you may end up playing again trying to pull victorys on missions you had previously suffered defeats.
Multiplayer
-The Multiplayer is a lot of fun and can keep you entertained for hours. The randomly generated maps make things a lot more interesting because it allows you (And a teammate if you do 2v2) to strategize and prepare for engagements around various gas clouds (which give you camoflauge.) and asteroid fields. (which damage you if the proper upgrade is not installed.) I found that even if I was losing, I could still grin as I would have caused so much destruction that I would feel the victory was well earned by the other player.
All factions play quite differently and allow for plenty of variety in playstyle.
-Imperial Navy ships are heavily armored and are generally covered in macro cannons for devastating broadsides yet lack the speed some may wish to have.
-Chaos ships are quite fast and have weaker armor but still enough to survive some of the broadsides that the imp navy can throw at you. Their extra launchbays and long range assaults make hit and run assaults somewhat viable.
-Ork ships are massive and are extremely resilent to damage. While Imp navy is tough, they can't say they're Ork tough. Ork ships have massive healthpools and strong armor aswell has having lots of ramming damage. While their accuracy is not the greatest, their weapons hit the hardest in the game aside from Eldar pulsars. An Ork battleship is one of the hardest things to kill in this game.
-Eldar has quite the weird playstyle and can have a large learning curve. While Orks have their best weapons on their prows, Eldar have ONLY prow weapons meaning you must always face what you want to shoot. Eldar also lack shields and instead have holofields and allow you to dodge and absorb incoming fire as long as you move. Eldar ships are also very fast and can turn extremely fast. This combined with only forward firing weapons mean you only have so much time to fire else you ram what you're shooting at, something that is lethal for the fragile eldar ships. Things like Vauls maneuvre (allows you to instantly do a 180) make this much easier to perform however.
I have to say things were shaky during the Beta but things are quite balanced and tweaked now. All in all, this game is a great experiance and a must get for fans of the Warhammer series. I can only hope there is only more to come with space marines on their way and a mystery fleet already announced. So what are you doing? Buy this game! For the Emperor!

This is one of those games I've dreamed about existing for awhile - an adaptation of a tabletop strategy game that supports customisation, persistent unit development and that plays well.  Battlefleet Gothic:Armada may not be for everyone, but it's definitely for me!
Minor technical niggles and a couple of odd design decisions aside, and given I can't speak to the multiplayer as its of no real interest to me: between the campaign and solo skirmish with 4 drastically different fleets to master, there's a lot of game here - and it's quality!
Gameplay wise, you might be mistaken for thinking its a micro-heavy rts, but in reality, due to the active pause system and the generally small number of units involved, even at high point values, it plays more like a fast paced turn based strategy or "tactics" title.  It's quite unique and there's a level of depth to learning the game and how to best command and combat each race that's rather satisfying.  Two thumbs up here!  Keep up the good work Dev's!

I can understand that most people would never give this game a chance because of it's name, but honestly this game is pretty much amazing.
The combat is a mixture of the match-3-jewel gameplay of Bejewled and typical RPG gameplay. The twist is the jewels you match translate into the mana you use for skills, and many skills inflect statuses on the field itself. It comes down to a surprising mix of casual and strategy, as you wonder if you should clear all the blue tiles to make other mana easier to collect, or if you should remove all red to keep your opponent from unleashing his best attacks? Where's the best place to remove a 3x3 area? If I remove this one, will it start a 4x chain? Will doing this avalanch?
The battle system is better refined in the sequel, Puzzle Quest 2, but future itterations of Puzzle Quest (of which there are a surprising amount) all fail in one major thing Puzzle Quest nailed: The sheer variety of things to do. Puzzle Quest has mechanics for taking over cities, capturing monsters, learning their spells, acquiring allies, and several other features that future games simply don't have. It is for these varities that make Puzzle Quest: Challenge of the Warlords the best in the series.
The last point to mention is that Puzzle Quest works with mods. It is extremely important to mention, however, that Steam's support for these mods is limited. While mods for the game work fine (and are easy enough for me to make, say, a new class in a day or two) and are generally pretty neat (the new items mod adds several items, each of which can completely change the strategy you use throughout the game), Steam Cloud undoes most of this effort as any backed up modded files will be automatically downloaded sans mods to any future computer- causing frequent crashes and problems for future itterations.

It's certainly addicting and fun, at least while you're doing well. Not to mention that using built-in exploits and leadership skills (read: tag-teaming boarders and fires, or luring said boarders into the med bay and fighting them with heals) can be pretty gratifying. However, I find a large margin of error to be the fact that it's just as fortuitous as, well, real space travel and war... in our present with our technology. Seriously, what kind of faster-than-light spaceship crew doesn't have anything better than a fire extinguisher? Why can't we isolate the cabins to vent oxygen only from the ones that are on fire? What material did they build it from that is so mysteriously flammable? And once you think you've got the timing of the weapons right and everything, and you've fully upgraded your shields and you've got decent weapons and a dependable dodge rating, the flagship puts up a kind of underwhelming fight... at least until suddenly your entire med bay is on fire and your crew drops dead because the system is too damaged for heals while you're still getting battered by the flagship but since all hands are on deck (and dying) to put out the stupid fire then your shields reload as slow as molasses in a vaccum and then you just die. Like you never even spent any time working your butt off to get your ship the best it can be, all those thrilling escapes and chases by the rebel fleet and the times you went six jumps with three hull points left and got to a repair station by the skin of your teeth, like those never even happened. And why? So you can do it all again. Nothing compared to the rush I get when I start off a fresh adventure, but it's agonizing to have to start from the bottom every time, considering this is the only permadeath-upgrade-your-way-unscripted-rpg game that I own or have ever played. No idea why I keep coming back to it, but I do and I can say I'll keep playing until it manages to really♥♥♥♥♥♥me off, and considering the way I died against the flagship on easy and I've still got the stomach to hit restart, I can't see myself rage-deleting the local content anytime soon.

There are lots of reviews on this game so I'll just list the pros and cons vs the old XCom: UFO Defense
*Pros:*
- Great voice acting
- Immersive tutorial for new players
- This time the cover actually means something and you can flank/get flanked
- Lots of mods (you have got to play long war)
- Laser weaponry is actually pretty good in this one
- Terror missions are focused on saving civilians and not leveling the whole block like the good ol' days
- Escort missions
- Capturing live aliens requires more strategy
*Cons:*
- You get to find the alines in small groups that you have to spot, they never come looking for you
- You don't get to engage in full force; 6 soldiers max
- Maps are not randomly generated
- You can't throw equipped items or pick them up from the floor
- Line of sight and illumination have little to no effect
- Only one XCom base mission and one Alien base mission
Great game overall, worth every cent.

Leviathan warships is an excellent game for its price. The base ship variety is somewhat limmited, but there are three dlc packs available which all contain three new ships, raising the total amount of ship types available to 14. And even if you don't want to buy any dlc, you can customize the loadout of the ships yourself, providing an endless variety of tactics. I feel the game can be somewhat unbalanced at times, but there are still plenty of viable tactics available and some strategies that may seem overpowered at first can usually easily be countered.  The biggest problem with this game is the playerbase, or rather, lack there of. There are very few people playing this game at the time of me writing this review. It can sometimes take a very long time to get into a game. That is also the main reason i'm writing this review; to get more people to play. Let's taco bout this game.
While the story is not focused on as much, it does give a short background. Showing that some scientist happened to press a button, launching nukes all over the United States. Destroying the land and mutating most of the creatures. You come in as a humble taco truck driver on the path to Canada. Why? Canada needs taco trucks and it is the perfect place to let your family business thrive. Luckily, you are equipped with a gun on your taco truck and mechanics willing to upgrade it.
Luckily, you can turn off the prologue. As hard as Gunman Taco Truck is you may not be able to see the ending anytime soon.
While the gameplay seems simple with only needing the mouse and arrow keys, it hides a complex system under the layer. Containing two parts: the highway and the town.
The three laned highway is where you can kill the mutants threatening your truck. As the truck will auto-drive, all you need to do is worry about is shooting those mutants and side animals with the gun mounted on your gun that can be either be automatic or manual. Don't forget to pick up the meat and shoot up the signs to get scrap, those will be needed in town. However, it can get too hectic to pick them up as you do need to tap again. After you progress through a certain checkpoint, bosses will appear to make you play differently. These get harder and harder as you go and will generally cause you to die when first encountering them. While the tutorial can make it hectic with the help boxes popping in and out as you try not to get the truck destroyed, it is not as bad once you get used to it. Once reaching your destination, be ready to go into strategy mode.
In town, there will either be a store or a garage along with a gas pump and a slot machine. You do know in advance on the map you view so you can strategically progress. The stores contains the toppings but will miss a key component, such as cheese or salsa, that you will be boned if you have none. There will be a rare time where this mystically golden fan, costing around $399, or it being robbed by a mutant. Hope that it wasn’t robbed, it will likely spell disaster unless you planned ahead for it. Garages put those scrap you collect for use. You can upgrade your truck here by getting a whole new truck with a new gun, add-ons that gives you armor, and permanent add-ons meant to help you just as sucking up the meat and scrap for you. A tip, if you need to repair your truck, upgrade it if you can. It will automatically repair your truck if you upgrade to a new one.  The gas depends on where you are, ranging from $30-$110, that fills up your tank fully while the slot machines either give you scrap or money (I never really used it much unless I was 1 scrap away from a truck upgrade). I do wish there was a way to get toppings another way or get a bigger gas tank.
These two parts don't really seem to go together but Gunman Taco Truck makes it work as you need both parts. You need to do good in the highway for the town to go smoothly and vice versa.
While the gun sounds can be a little loud without changing the volume, everything is very nice and well done. Everything is covered from each mutant type having a different sound to the customer’s voices. The squishing of the mutant bodies going under the truck, the thuds against the truck when hit, the skidding noises, even the cheers and voice lines of the customers are great. I looked forward to hearing around the same four lines from the customers, especially one being so funny to me. The satisfaction and dissatisfaction well voiced and bringing in a proud or shame feeling. Paired with the great soundtrack makes it even better.
The 2D pixelated graphics brings more charm to the game. Gunman Taco Truck is very detailed, allowing a background to show you what mutants you will be dealing with effectively and everything is very distinct with the colorful palette. While some do blend in well due to how small they are, you can not mistake them for something else. As you shoot them, the blood spurts out and you can run over their remains to get more. Don’t want any gore? Turn on Piñata mode where colorful stuffed animals filled with candy pops out instead. You can tell what the taco has and what ingredient it may be easily without having to hover over it. Even the customers become super detailed.
There are small details as well, your truck leaves tire marks each time you switch lanes and when you go to a town two fire tracks are left (no doubt a reference to Back to the Future). If you’re truck is damaged, holes and fire will start appearing, even your gun will stop working if your health is too low. As you progress you can also get decals to put on your truck which is a nice addition, though I do wish we can move them ourselves. I couldn’t help but crave a truck plastered with decals.
Gunman Taco Truck runs well with a few hiccups here and there during the highway section. Some people have experienced trouble with the game crashing however. There have been some bugs I have experienced which you can read in the discussion board for more details. In short, including not being able to travel due to moving the map, accidently double charging for gas,  and buttons not coming off of the screen (but only happens with a certain action, don’t worry).
While some events are set in stone, the roads, orders, and threats you face do change. You may of been salsa rich the last game but this game you happened to be cheese rich. Or having to cancel some of the customer’s orders when you didn’t have to before. I’m not sure how randomized the stores are, as I noticed the same missing ingredient was true for the next playthrough, the robbing is random. The garage also randomize their upgrades excluding the whole truck replacement. I came across the upgrade that sucks up meat and scrap early on one playthrough  but now I can’t find it in the beginning. Your strategy can also change between playthroughs, slightly changing up how it ends.
Depending on whether or not you want to see the ending, Gunman Taco Truck can last a long time.
+ Artwork
+ Variety and quality of sound
+ Complexity under simplicity
+ Gotta have one more game before I leave
+ Mashup of two different parts that go well together
+/- Some bugs can cause you to be in a horrible situation if accidently stumbled upon
