This is one of those games I've dreamed about existing for awhile - an adaptation of a tabletop strategy game that supports customisation, persistent unit development and that plays well.  Battlefleet Gothic:Armada may not be for everyone, but it's definitely for me!
Minor technical niggles and a couple of odd design decisions aside, and given I can't speak to the multiplayer as its of no real interest to me: between the campaign and solo skirmish with 4 drastically different fleets to master, there's a lot of game here - and it's quality!
Gameplay wise, you might be mistaken for thinking its a micro-heavy rts, but in reality, due to the active pause system and the generally small number of units involved, even at high point values, it plays more like a fast paced turn based strategy or "tactics" title.  It's quite unique and there's a level of depth to learning the game and how to best command and combat each race that's rather satisfying.  Two thumbs up here!  Keep up the good work Dev's!

This is a great Tactical RTS, of that there can be no doubt.
The tactical cogitators ( Slow mo mechanic) works great to help you strategise in make tactical decisions all across you fleet. You might not use it in the begining when you only field 2 or 3 ships with few to no abilities, however in the end you are likely to use it in every battle.
Another great thing is the ability to customise you ships allowing you a variety of different options that can fill in niche positions across you fleet.
You can combine these options to create long ranged carriers, knife fighting / ramming monsters or a big and bulky tank you can teleport infront of your fleet to create a giant wall of steel .
Things such as the "Favours" system also brings something extra to the game.
The fact that you do not spamm out units and instead level the ships is in my honest opinion a great way to "bond" with them.
One should never be afraid to lose, the consequences can be dire but it is not a true issue.
The story is great, if you like the WH40K universe.
The cinematics/storytelling is spot on, I must admit that I broke out in goosebumps during the last cinematic. It felt truly epic, the music is also quite good.
The fact that you are given some choices on how to deal with the Eldar is also nice.
I have not played the multiplayer since it has gone live but the sense I got in the Beta was that it was fun enough aslong as you like the style of the game.
Some match types are more enjoyable than others.
I had 2 FATAL ERRORS during my playthrough of the campaign, which where annoying but nothing too big.
I noticed that the FPS fluctuates a tad here and there but nothing major like say XCOM 2.
Should you buy this thing?
If you like WH40K, RTS's, Bombastic choirs in the background while you fire missiles away, then yes without a doubt.

Star Explorers is a vastly ambitious followup to Anomalies that applies Michael Schmidt's trademark procedurally-generated alien weirdness to an entire galaxy. During my explorations, I've come across alien temples lurking on foggy green worlds inhabited by hostile entities made of steam. I've stumbled through barren, pitted deserts marked with the occasional lake of frozen sulphuric acid. I've seen lush jungles where bipedal, flat-headed aliens bathe in pools of mercury.
I've also died a lot.
See, the galaxy Schmidt has created here isn't cruel. "Cruel" implies that it cares. And this galaxy is terribly, terribly uncaring. Finding a planet with usable resources requires you to sift through a tremendous amount of data. When you find a planet worth exploring, it's likely this world is inimical to life -- too hot, too cold, seething with radiation -- and, as you try to find a cave that may contain the fuel crystals you need to sustain your interstellar voyage, your explorer's suit condition and air tank tick down with terrifying speed.
Right now, as I'm typing this, I have Star Explorers open. I'm orbiting a red giant. I risked it all to come here, hoping against hope that one of its nine planets would contain fuel crystals. I found a planet with the right composition to grow these crystals. When I touched down and found a cave, I discovered that it was full of crystals -- but not the right sort. Just worthless emeralds. I don't have enough fuel to return to the mothership or travel to another star system. I'm trapped.
Wait, though. There's another planet orbiting this star I haven't seen yet -- it must've been on the opposite side of the red giant. It's the right variety, too. I hop out of my landing craft and, after a few minutes of searching, find a cave. THIS one has fuel crystals! What's more, at the end of a corridor, I find a chest with an improved space suit, allowing me to survive even more dangerous worlds.
I'll put off dying for the moment. I've got some more stars to explore.

I am one of the few people who quite enjoy No Man's Sky. Because NMS is lacking in gameplay and variety, I thought I try Star Explorers, as it seemed to be a similar concept (exploring procedurally generated planets, collecting resources etc.) and often Indie developers have very nice and novel ideas that make their games interesting.
But whoa, this game is nothing that should be let loose on paying customers yet. In the first 3 minutes I got *three* crashes, just by setting my screen resolution to something near to my native resolution (because the exact resolution of 1920x1200 was not available).
I can see that the developer seems to be loving his work, but honestly, the graphics are really simple like in the 90's and I did not feel that I want to spend much time with this game unless it gives me interesting things to do.
Warped to the first station, then off to my first (and last) planet, found that inside my ship there is not much I can interact with, left my ship and walked around. The planet had a hot environment, with some liquid that looked like lava around small islands, I heard several different sound cues for my health dropping (So hot. This planet is really hot. Oh, argh. Or similar, probably all recoreded by the developer himself, which is fine for an Indie title,) then I ran through what seems to be lava to another island where I saw something like another spaceship, entered that spaceship, found it to be empty, sat at that ship's console, and then I decided that I rather want to play some more polished games. And I actually play a lot of simple games on my notebook, including 8bit games...
Will refund and might try again in another half year.
As far as casual games are concerned, you could do much, much worse than this game.

Its a shame really as DOA LR is actually a great fighter, sadly the developers just don't seem to care about its PC fanbase.
At its core its a good game, the fights are fast and fluid and the characters are interesting and varied, its pretty satisfying countering your opponent and sending them flying off the edge of a cliff. The game has no problems running at a constant 60fps and from what I've read it works well on lower end rigs too. The problem is that the developers decided to charge PC users for a next-gen version of the game and then give them the PS3 equivilent instead.  As it stands it uses the PS3 versions effects and is missing the improved 'soft engine' that the PS4 version uses to improve the skin quality of the characters. On top of this there are 2 complete arena's missing that the PS4 got also, the developers have stated that these missing features will never be added to the PC version of the game.
Next problem we have is the promised online mode, this was supposed to have been implemented within 3 months of the games initial release but as of writing this its still nowhere to be found. There is a beta version of the online component you can use to tide you over but its completely bare bones and seldom works anyway, fights either lose their connection mid-way or suffers from lag so extreme that its completely unplayable.
Last but not least is the extremely overpriced DLC, there's several packs of costumes (which provide nothing other than asthetics) which cost more than the actual game itself, it costs literally hundreds to buy them all and to add insult to injury the breakable clothes component from the PS4 version is missing as well.
If you're a fan of the series and you can grab it on sale and you're not bothered about the missing graphics, features or online mode then there's plenty of single player modes to play and costumes to unlock to keep you occupied, for me though it simply isn't good enough to be expected to pay for a next-gen game and instead be presented with a half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥port from a years old gaming system and still have no online mode to boot. I'm a big fan of the series and think it has a lot of potential but to be honest I'm just glad I got it on sale as I'd be pretty miffed if I'd paid full price for what in reality is the PS3 version of the game.

I'm surprised that so many people gave this game thumb downs. For me it's quite enjoyable. I haven't experienced any major bugs or performance issues. Puzzles are nice, though they are not very sophisticated. With the help of friends you can beat them easily, but on solo you need to work a bit more.

The game gives a casual feel and has no difficulty setting (unless you want to complete the challenges, in that case it can be nearly impossible especially the no-damage challenges.) There are vastly different types of arsenals and items you can collect and buy with your gems, making replaying the game not entirely pointless.
Graphically it looks nice and uses the same engine as Tomb Raider 2013. Story and casting are mediocre, but for a casual game you might as well forget about them. However the game satisfies me greatly that it uses 'matured' Lara instead of young Lara like in modern TR games. It reminds me how awesome she is as a tomb raider.
My verdict: 7/10. Get in on sale if you still have doubt. But as a TR fan, you shouldn't miss it.

text:
Lara Croft and the Temple of Osiris was a charming and enjoyable experience. The gameplay is simple and easy to pick and play with multiple people. The graphics are atmospheric and lighting especially creates a warm, immersive environment. The soundtrack is fantastic and is true to the adventerous spirit.
The game itself is a platforming, puzzle, action, party game that's fun with friends or solo. It has native controller support and the controls are intuitive. The puzzles are fun without being overly intense and the pacing of the game keeps you in the action until the very end. There are plenty of things to collect but the game doesn't smother you with collectables. The combat is fun and the boss encounters are unique. The platforming elements are fun and reminiscent of the classic Tomb Raiders.
The only qualm I have is that the game seems to crash a lot. In the 8 hours of the main story the game crashed around 20 times. Thankfully, the autosaving and checkpoint system is very generous. Some areas, like the challenge tombs, seemed to elicit crashes more than others.

An ABSOLUTE masterpiece. This is a puzzle platformer with incredible artwork, a delightful soundtrack, and an amazing storyline. The puzzles are perfectly put together and are VERY well done and creative, I can't even begin to imagine how someone would come up with most of these puzzles. Throughout the game you're given different powers, whether they can slow down time in a specific region, or rewind the world, they are given to you at perfect points throughout your adventure to keep you interested, and are incorporated into each puzzle professionally. Braid was an absolute delight to play through, and there's no reason why it should ever not be recommended: I honestly cannot find any flaws in it's design. People that rate Braid bad probably aren't that good at puzzle games or got fed up with it. I know there were a few points where I felt like giving up because some puzzles aren't obvious in the slightest, but when comparing Braid to other games of the puzzle platformer genre, it is clearly the king. The storyline is told by text for the most part, and a few cinematic-like scenes. The ending is breathtaking, and I HIGHLY recommend Braid above even most triple-A production quality games. The sincerity and heart put into Braid is incredible, and you can feel it radiating with every step you take. I can't recommend Braid highly enough, I think it's an experience any gamer should partake in. The asking price of $9.99 is very fair, as Braid is lovingly crafted and has a very good playtime given it's genre.
I don't give out many near-10's. Only about five so far and I've played hundreds of games. Braid deserves this score, as it's flawless and is up there in my top 10 games of all time, as well as being near the pinnacle of my favorite gaming experiences.

So. Long story short. It's really, really badly optimised. The same major issue that Ark has had since it came onto Steam. After spending an hour toying with settings to try and get a playable, stable framerate. I gave up and decided a refund is way better a use of my time.
The recommended specs are just unreal. I'm in the middle ground somewhere. So to get an idea of what sort of weirdness i came across:
1920x1080 - all settings set to low, everything turned off, all sliders bottomed out. 28 - 32fps
1280x720 - same settings. 28 - 32fps
800x600 - same settings. 28 - 32fps
Now, at 1080, with everything maxed out. 10fps.
Now as i said before, my rig is mid to high range in terms of specs. So i should be able to get a reasonable fps. What i find really peculiar though. Is that you get 20 frames even with everything turned off and at the lowest resolution.
Overall, i love the concept of the game, i love the look and feel of it. The world is large with a massive amount of potential, but unless they take the time to seriously optimise it? the player base will be small unless someone decides to give everyone a 6 core I7 and a GTX 1060.
Sad times. Honestly, this shouldnt be on early access at the moment. It's far too early in production and the performance issues matching Ark:SA just make it more apparent that this is an attempt at a cash grab.
Maybe in a year or two when it's had time to mature but right now i honestly say. Don't waste you're money until it's much further in development.

Bug still breaks the game when I get to the alien base invasion mission.  This alone gives it a thumbs down.
As for actual gameplay:
1. They removed the ability to shoot wherever you want.  You used to be able to blow out walls and doors with regular weapons, not just rocket launchers.  You could shoot out a wall and allow another soldier to then shoot an enemy, or remove that enemy's cover.  Now you can't unless you want to level an entire house with a grenade or rocket.
2. After getting to the broken alien base invasion that crashes to desktop, I still have no idea how cover works.  You get the little icons showing half and full cover, but half the time the aliens are shooting my people in the face through walls while I miss 95% to hit shots.
3.  The aliens get to literally drop into maps where ever they want.  You could be going through a map perfectly fine and dandy, and then the game will drop random thin men and other aliens directly onto your positions, even sharing the same exact squares your players are on.  This has nothing to do with tactics, it's cheap RNG designed to punch your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in.
4.  You never get the drop on aliens.  They get a free turn when your soldiers "discover" them.  So, halfway through a movement your soldier will spot an alien, and then your soldier pauses while the aliens get to scramble out of the way and take cover.  It's a free move they get each and every time, so instead of rewarding you for close quarters tactics like the old games, it's like you're discovering and pulling aggro on random enemies that always see you first.
I understand that moving soldier A who spots two aliens frozen in place (because it's not their turn yet) can set up soldier B (who hasn't taken a turn yet) to blow them up with a grenade or rocket (without the ability to see the aliens directly) could be seen as "cheap" but this used to be accounted to soldier A informing soldier B where the aliens are upon discovery.  Now it's just another facet of RNG that leaves you at a disadvantage to make the game more difficult than it needs to be.
5.  The little "Blizzard" style World of Warcraft animations get annoying after awhile.  Every soldier and alien and robot is always dancing around doing some huge grandiose awkward animation that's so over the top it ends up silly and falling flat on the humor scale.  It pulls the wind out of any horror and despair the old games had.  Honestly these cornball dancing animations and the UI that looks like it was designed for an iPad seem to be something people either love or hate.  Well, I kinda hate it.  It's Diablo 3 vs Diablo 1.  It's PG vs Rated R.
I could go on and on but I'd rather track down a god damned solution to this idiotic video memory crash bug.  I can't stand devs that abandon stuff when it's still broken and they ♥♥♥♥ing know it's broken.

Edit: My husband wrote the original review. This is my review. I've actually played the game.
THIS GAME IS AMAZING!
First off, the MUSIC! The music just gets you right into that "match things" mood. If you are kicking behind, it ramps up with your adrenaline and you push yourself to an epic win. If you are losing... well, let's just say you'll know that tune and when the announcer chimes in that your hero is near defeat it's totally okay to start sweating.
Next, the actual game play is so smooth! Some matching games can be kind of jerky or have a slower response time. Puzzle Quest does not! It is smooth and seemless. The battle load screens don't last too long and walking about in the RP world isn't cumbersome or annoying. You can even rapidly click through dialoge if you don't care and just want to fight!
Did I mention the music? Because this is seriously some of the best music.
Also worth a paragraph is the strategy aspect. If you play correctly and put some thought into it, this game can be as intense and engaging as a game of chess. I have logged my 600+ hours on almost exclusively my druid, who should be one of the wimpiest in the game. However, using tactics and planning, she can whoop any enemy. Pick your skills, items, spells, and mounts carefully. Know your enemy's weaknesses. Know the board mechanics. Manipulate everything to your will and you will surely master Puzzle Quest.
Of course, after 600+ hours you would think I would be bored with the game, right?
NOT AT ALL! I return to PQ faithfully on a regular basis when I want a respite from the world of MMOs, MOBAs, and RTSs.
So go on, what are you waiting for?

Wow, what to say about this game? Truely it is an experience worth having.
This is a game which is purely an experience, and it really is a unique one at that. I'm having trouble finding the words, because even thought it isn't a game I'd see myself play 6 hours or more a day, it's a game that lets you experience the positive side of interacting with people.
The game offers you a few emotes to start off with, as well as some symbols so that you can communicate certain needs to other players. The game is simple, what makes it unique is the interaction between other players. The game is essencially about unlocking puzzles that give you various unique emotes and skins, as well as new animals that you can play. However, it is the most fun when you find people. Because with more people, you can unlock more of these "stones" that open and give you puzzle pieces. Usually they require about two people, but the larger ones require even more, or various types of animals to open. This is where the fun part is.
Because you rely on other players, people want to interact with you and engage with you. They want to find other players, they want you to just run about and have fun. And because the interacting is so limited, there's no room for negativity, trolling, or etc. Even thought I'll admit I highly doubt anyone would purchase this game just to troll. This is a kind of game people who want a unique gaming experience would purchase. This is a brilliant game for kids IMO.
I don't have anything negative to say about this game. I had a lot of fun, and I don't regret ever buying it, because just the interacting alone is absolutely adorable and fun. The most people I met at once was I think about 7 of us, we were running about finding these unique stones and puzzle pieces. And we just had a load of fun. We waited for each other, signaled(barking or etc) to each other where we were, and if we needed to wait for one another. We'd tell each other if we found any flowers or puzzles laying about, and, another player that I met(playing a bobcat, I was a badger) showed me some really unique views. So if you're reading this, super cute and kind lynx, please feel free to send me a message I'd love to connect with you!

Excellent turn-based strategy game - one of the best.
In this sci-fi themed alternate reality, you play as the defacto leader of XCOM - an anti-alien resistance. You get to command and conquer from your own base, where you'll get the opportunity to research, build facilities, hire soldiers and advance your military in an RPG-esque way. I've began playing QL in early 2009 when the web platform went open beta and Q3A since day 1 in 1999 that Quake 3 went on sale at the stores.  Yeah I'm old. The 1-2 hours has been me "trying" to motivate myself to rejoin the game.  Still cannot get past, the past...
This game has always been an excellent game, and I'm sure it still is.  Very fast paced, heart pounding, adrenaline pumping action that requires fast thinking and quick reflexes.
But, the past... "much" of what the game is today is a product of the efforts of talented fans and enthusiasts that were motivated to become mod developers back in the day.  id took 10 yrs of that, packaged the more popular maps and mods all up and in 2010 released Quake Live.  Not that bad of a move considering that Q3A was getting less populated. But pretty bad, IMO, when they took much of what was community contributed and required a subscription now to access the content.
A few years ago they decided that it was okay to stop supporting the Linux/Mac support and leave many of those in their subscription plan high and dry.
Now, this last month they've done away with the F2P and slapped a $10 price tag.  May be worth it, it is still a good game.
I don't personally trust this title anymore.  Wouldn't surprise me if they want more money in the future after having paid the $10 for another "change" in their business model.  And man do I hate not being able to give this game a positive recommendation specially after all the time I've invested.
I wouldn't buy it for $10 myself and instead would suggest to check out an early access on Steam called "Reflex".

In a space capsule (sci-fi analogy for "nut shell"), FTL is a roguelike space crew simulator.  If that sentence appealed to you at all, go ahead and buy the game with zero regrets.
A typical gameplay session consists of picking a jump point to go to and getting into a battle scenario and/or dangerous space phenomenon/multiple choice scenario.  Battles focus on using your ships strengths most effectively to destroy or disable the enemy ship.  You assign power to your various systems (Shields, Drones, Weapons, Engines, Cloak, etc) and during a very difficult battle it becomes a very tense balacning act.  Luckily you can pause the game at any time to weigh your options.  You also run into phenomenon such as solar flares and meteor storms that pose a threat to your ship.  To make matters worse, these encounters typically coincide with an enemy attack.  You also run into decision-making scenarios that can either help or harm your ship and crew.  Should you send crew to that planet surface to fend off an attack of alien spiders?  There will be a reward if you succeed, but you might lose a crew member in the process.  During these scenarios, if you possess a specific type of crew or system it can give you an additional choice amongst the options that greatly tilt the outcome in your favor.
Prepare yourself for frustration though.  Having a good run typically means that you were able to stockpile large amounts of scrap and run into the right merchants at the right time selling exactly the right things.  Some ship types are particularly hindered if you aren't able to expand their capabilities in specific ways to offset their inherent weaknesses.
FTL is a very inventive game that simultanesouly scratches the roguelike and hard sci-fi itch.  It is also at times a very difficult or even unfair game, but if you like your roguelikes then this won't dissuade you.  As a bonus, the game also has a great musical score that fits the theme perfectly.
This is a must buy for me.  I would also love to see a sequel that expands the core formula by placing it into a open-universe setting rather than a linear branching path progression.

Short version:
Gunman Taco Truck has easy accessible gameplay, but difficulty in resource management, enemy types, and your ability to click fast enough to shoot enemies. The game is full of character with loads of easter eggs and hidden elements that result in it feeling very rich. The developers are also releasing updates and new content on an almost daily basis with talk of new bosses, features, leaderboard, trading cards, achievements, and a host of other things meaning that this game is only going to get better.
Long version
After 24 hours of playing I can safely say that it's worth its price. The basic premise is that you're a taco truck business owner and you want to escape the post-nuclear wasteland that is the USA and move to Canada where it's safer, and they don't have taco trucks (so it's a good business opportunity). There are 2 main features to the game, shooting monsters on highway levels and collecting their meat, and making and selling tacos with the meat of the monsters you killed.
The game's mechanics are quite simply, just click on things you want to shoot during the road scenes, and drag ingredients onto the tortilla to prepare tacos. The difficulty in the game comes down to resource management, and different zone on the map having harder and harder enemies. You need to buy ingredients for your tacos (cheese, salsa, etc.) with money you earn from selling tacos (you start out with 6 of each of the main ingredient). None of the stores have all the ingredients, so you can't just continuously sell tacos in one place. Also, gas/petrol costs money (with it becoming more expensive in the higher difficulty zones) so you need to manage your fuel, money, and ingredients.
You can also get metal scrap from the highway scenes which is used to purchase upgrades like armour and weaponry for your truck, and you can also spend scrap to buy a new truck, and repair your current one to full health. Upgrading your truck gets you more health and better weapons, which you'll need for advancing through tougher areas.
Elements of the game like the content in each of the stores is randomised, so it's a different game every time. The available paths you can travel are also randomised, so sometimes you need to take a different route to get to a city. So it has a lot of FTL-like elements to it.
The developers have also been updating the game almost on a daily basis (this review was written shortly after launch) and they'll be adding more content and features including Steam trading cards, leaderboards, more achievements and new bosses. So they're dedicated to making this game better so it will only improve over time. They've also included loads of content with the things that the characters you interact with say and do, often being quirky, funny, or just purely bizzare.

This is a nice combination of a couple of different games, and plays like a collection of mini-games strung together, but well done.  The graphics are your standard retro-style graphics, but well done, with them not taking the excuse to do sub-standard models, as some developers using this style are wont to do.  The controls are very standard, and the entire game plays with a mouse.  When firing weapons, you have the choice of clicking manually or using an automatic version of the weapon, although with a caveat (more in gameplay).  Overall, a great first impression.
As I said earlier, it's like a string of small mini-games, but they are setup well, and integrated well.  You travel from city to city, picking up ingredients for tacos, unlocking new recipes for tacos, and selling tacos.  You can also repair and upgrade your taco truck and weapons.  The basic game play goes: (a) leave city for another city, travel on the highway, shooting up mutants, animals, and obstacles for meat ingredients, (b) arrive at city with the option of fueling up, serving tacos for money, upgrading your taco truck, and buying topping ingredients from the local store.  Rinse and repeat.  You may serve tacos as many times as you like in each location..
The highway is a simple 3 lane highway your truck auto-drives down while you use your roof-mounted weapon to take out on-coming mutants (humans and mutated animals, the latter of which drops meat for your tacos) and other obstaces, and fire at items on the side of the road like metal signs (for scrap) and animals (like cows, for carne asade). When an entity that drops something dies, you still must click the item to pick it up, even if you're on automatic weapon fire. This can make auto weapon fire a pain to use.  It would be nice to see them switch to an auto pickup in this mode also.
This is like many standard food serving games ... customers arrive with an order for a taco, and you must build the taco by using the ingredients in the right layer order, and within a reasonable amount of time. Quick service gets you a better rating and tips.  After serving, you either keep satisfied customers or lose unsatisfied ones.  If a customer orders something you don't have the ingredients for (you've run out, etc), you must cancel the order, and they are unsatisfied.
You purchase toppings for your tacos here (cheese, onions, salsa, mold, etc). Outside the store is also a gas pump to fill up.  It's a one-shot fee that simply fills your tank up, so strategic refilling is necessary. You can increase your tank range as you upgrade your truck.
Here you can upgrade your truck in a number of different ways, and also use scrap (from shooting signs on the highway) to upgrade various items.
Also, while parked, you have the chance to have a band of mutants come roaming into town that you have to shoot up to protect your customers.  This might give you some sorely needed meat for your tacos and allow you to make some money if you were about to move on.
Since the game gives you the option of going to the city of your choice (here are both green cities (easy) and red cities (hard) that you can choose to go to), and also lets you serve tacos until you run out of ingredients, the progression is very much up to you, which I like.  If I need more money, I can just serve people until I run out.  In addition, considering that not all cities have all ingredients, there is some strategy in keeping ingredients in stock, and you *can* back yourself into a corner and not be able to serve without having to cancel your orders and even lose the game if bad choices are made.
The base gameplay doesn't change, but your orders, the threats on the road you face, and so on, do change some. I don't think it would be a game I would replay, but I could see someone playing this again as something fun to pass the time.
The retro theme works really well for this game, and the performance is what you would expect out of a non-demanding game. Even folks with integrated graphics should be able to run this. The title has native 4K resolution support.  My system tore through this like molten steel through room temp butter; I'd like to see an option to limit your frame rate in-game so that you're not wasting GPU cycles when you're getting 1,000 FPS.
A solid concept with a few items here and there I'd like to see changed. The game suffers a bit on the replayability side, but the rest of the game makes up for it.  A great first entry from this programming family, and a worthy addition to my library.

Battlefleet Gothic: Armada is a sublime recreation of Battlefleet Gothic, a now sadly defunct Games-Workshop board game set in the grim-dark universe of Warhammer 40,000. You take command of a fleet of ships and traverse a 2D board with your vessels having to take careful notice of their manuevering and alignment with enemy vessels and all while avoiding (or using to your advantage) various environmental hazards (such as debris fields). The game takes careful notice of finer details such as momentum and these details can even influence your tactics during battle. A great (and dramatic) example being the ability to sail a ship into an enemy vessel; ramming them with your own spaceship. Aim well and use the correct ships for this tactic and it can be very useful for dispatching tougher foes.
Every servant has his place, no matter how lowly or modest. To know it is his greatest comfort, to excel within it is his greatest solace, and his master's contentment is his greatest reward.
As the commander of your fleet you get a choice of many different ships, this selection expanding as you fight in more battles and yourself gain experience, that can grow with the gaining of experience during battle. This then allows you to fit them with skills, upgrades and customise their crew priorities. These features might seem slightly overwhelming at first but with a careful understanding of the game mechanics they can allow for quite a lot of tactical customisation in a fleet.
Contact with alien races always renews one's faith in humanity. It is my belief that foreign travel narrows the mind wonderfully.
In both Singleplayer Skirmish and Multiplayer you may command one of four discrete races: The Imperial Navy, Chaos, Ork Pirates and Eldar Corsairs. Each race is very distinct in the ways that they play and the tactics they favour. They are far from simply different skins on the same ships. Both Orks and Eldar can prove quite challenging to play, with the game recommending the Imperial Navy and Chaos for beginners. I second this notion!
The universe has many horrors yet to throw at us. This is not the end of our struggle. This is just the beginning of our crusade to save Humanity. Be faithful! Be strong! Be vigilant!
The Space Marines and another, yet unannounced fleet, are yet to be added and buying the game early means you can get these DLC for free on release bringing the total number of playable factions to 6. I'm personally interested to see how the Space Marine fleets and the Imperial Navy differ tactically.

If you're looking for a fun stratagy game set in Warhammer 40,000's deep universe then this is a great choice full of flavour, solid gameplay and a long single-player campaign with promise of an OK multiplayer experience.

This is what happens when you make a video game and heavily base it off of a board game. A board game with an incredible concept. If you ever played Battle Fleet Gothic table top, then you would have already bought this game. If I wrote about all things that are great with this game, you would be reading this for hours, so I will break it down into the overall concept.
There are no bases, but in between multiplayer matches, you will manage your fleet, you earn points and levels, which allow you to get more cruisers of different classes. Personally, I don't really like this system, and would prefer if you didn't have to grind to get more ships. You select which ships you bring into combat, and the mission is randomized. You have your main cruisers which are your main focus generally, and you bring along smaller frigates. These frigates lack fire power but have speed and meneuverability, they are great for scouting, getting behind the enemy cruiser where it can shoot without fear of retaliation, but another interesting purpose is intercepting ordinance. For example, an enemy cruiser just launched a bunch of assault boats to board one of your cruisers, your cruiser alone won't be able to destroy them all, and as such will take critical damage, but if you keep a frigate close, you can send it over to intercept the bombers, the turrets on the frigate will shoot them when it's close enough. The same can be done against torpedos.
Your cruisers are slower, but durable, and it is so interesting the things you can do with them. In a convoy escort mission, you can use your cruisers to sit between your frigates and an enemy ship. the enemy projectiles will physically hit your durable cruiser instead of the fragile escort behind. You can use your ships to ram others, the bigger the ship relative to the ship it hit, the more damage it will deal. Imagine using a light cruiser to pit meneuver another cruiser that is chasing one of your ships. All these things are possible.
They also added an upgrade system in the game, which has some nice upgrades, and some stupid ones. Like taunt, which is just silly. there are things that help you detect and identify enemy vessels, and certain offensive weapons like bombs, and statis bombs. The latter freezes time for all the ships caught in it for 15 seconds, leaving them vulnerable to lance fire. it may seem like a long time, but you must understand, in this game, it takes several minutes to kill a cruiser, unless you absolutely muder it, catch it in a bad position and focus fire on it, then it can die in 30 seconds. Except for the Eldar which will die in 10-15.
The balance between the ships so far seem fair, with the exception of the Eldar, as of now they are too weak, because of their stupid shield design, as long as they move they take less damage, but the problem is, it doesn't prevent lighting strikes. As in a cruiser teleports a boarding party onto the enemy ship. You can't prevent that unless you get lucky, you get  in range to shoot and they will lighting strike you, no matter what you do. If you lose a sail, you lose a portion of your speed, which means your ship is screwed, it can't escape so it will die. They really need regular shields like all the other fleets

I am rambling a bit, but there is just so much to this game I can't fit it all in this review, bascially, the mechanics in this game are very unique, the game is fun, and the strategies numerous. Which people seem to have problems with. So I will name a few to help you out.
_____________
When fighting the Imperials Always assume they have a nova cannon in their fleet, spread your ships out as you approach. make sure they can't identify your frigates, those are easy kills for a Nova Cannon.
When playing as Orks, make sure you have a few Launch bays, you can send boarding parties far away, weakening the enemy ships to finish off later. When fighting orks that do this, make sure you keep your frigates near your cruisers, your frigates have to intercept them.
When playing as Eldar, the running silent order only really works with them, because they are so fast, you can have one of your ships distract an enemy, while the others stealthily move behind for a surprise attack. Also as Eldar, never cluster your ships, already spead them out, your enemies will never be able to catch them and allows you to attack at any angle if they turn their back on one of your ships.
When defending a convey, always make sure your cruisers stay near the Transports, don't leave them with out a guard, if you do, your enemy will ram the ships which will kill them in seconds. If you keep your cruisers in the way they can't hit your transports. When doing convoy escort as Eldar, you can't keep your ships near your transports, because you can't soak fire. spread your tranports out, and have your warships hound your enemy as they persue the transports. Get behind them and shoot, they can either turn around to engage you, but then your transport gets away, or they can accept it and chase the transport as they get gunned down. It's pretty bad no matter what they do.
Torpedos aren't just for damaging your opponent, they are great to deny area(cutting off escape routes, etc.). You launch many torpedo salvos in an area, your enemies can't go there now. Torpedos are really only effective if deployed in mass.

A very solid and faithful adaptation of the classic boardgame. They have massively improved on balancing from the actual boardgame. Four different fleets currently, all of which play slightly differently, Imperials are slow, tanky ships that fight similar to a style from the 19th century. The Eldar are hit and run experts with deadly pulsars, torpedoes and mobility. Chaos is a little in between, with a mix of mobility, firepower and armour that does not really match either. Orks are slow, short ranged, heavy hitters with customizable ships. There are a number of game modes that keep it from being the same skirmish match again and again, data collection for instance is basically tag with battleships and boarding parties. The promise of future fleets also looks interesting, Space Marines are announced but potentially we could also expect more ships for Chaos and Imperials, a fleet for Dark Eldar, Tyranids, and Tau (two actually, the latter is by far the better one though).

A beautiful little gem of a game, I can't say there are many others like this one.
Meadow isn't a game where you have to survive against the elements and hunt other players, nor is it a game where you log on to chat to your friends. Instead, you'll find yourself exploring the world with other players and communicating using little pictograms. It doesn't sound too great on paper, but it's amazing in practice.
You could be anyone, and the animals you've just met could be anyone. But that doesn't matter, because now they're your friends and you're playing together. No swearing, no griefing, no trolling, no problem - just a bunch of strangers playing the same game together.
You'll never make more friends than you will playing this game, and for the price it's a steal.

Giving a 7/10 for originality (for a match-3 game I mean), 5/10 for presentation, and 4/10 for effort.
I liked the steampunk setting but it's seldom used. I appreciate the thoughts put into the match-3 system, it manages to be fresh.
I disliked a lot of things, though...
- Looks like it's all randomized. I started a hard game and found it a bit hard. After a couple of zones, I started an easy game and it was even harder. Wut?! So much for the difficulty curve.
- It's not that it's particularly hard, but it's tedious. You have to constantly keep an eye on your stats and just make sure they're better than the enemy's. Who's usually very dumb (they don't match obvious matches), their AI never changes, only the techniques they use. A single fight can last for 3 minutes, or 10 to 20 minutes if you're unlucky (no good matches to make, enemy constantly getting repair tools). Things get a bit faster when you get most of the 'good' skills (Firestorm and Timebomb, for instance).
- The UI is acceptable, but matching animations are very stiff and slow. It's lacking in life. It feels very amateurish. What was acceptable 10 years ago for an indie is no longer the norm. I would recommend using CheatEngine and their SpeedHack to set the speed to 2.0, it makes the animations much less annoying.
- Also, the matchable items, while they're relatively different from one another (which is important in that kind of game), are still hard to spot because so little thought was put into the gameplay. Just having background colors for items would have made it much better than what we got (full transparency). Just look at the screenshots... Reminds me of Candy Crush Saga. Which isn't exactly a 'great' match-3 game.
- Something I've seen in many indie games: there's only one battle song, and it's a freaking short song on a loop. It's a nice song (from a royalty-free library I believe, so it wasn't made for the game), but you'll end up turning off the music after a while.
- Again a staple for indie games: the ending only lasts for a few seconds and is very underwhelming. But I guess it's okay, since there wasn't much story to begin with. Also, final boss? What a poser. He was one of my shortest fights... Maybe I was lucky, I don't know.
- There are many things that don't serve any purpose. Building towers? Seriously, I never saw any difference with enemies. After the first few zones, I just skipped the towers.
- You can't go back to a previous area for grinding. You're stuck with the one shop in your current area, and too bad if you missed a good skill in a previous shop because you didn't have the gold for it.
- The save system is just as bad. Once you win the game, you can't replay the final levels. You have to start again. I'd recommend backing up your save file, if you find it.
- Many little bugs, especially on the map: navigation spots sometimes have their hit area off by several pixels, requiring some pixel hunting; jumping on a spot with a tower AND an enemy will make you fight the enemy, but you'll have to move back and again if you want to go to the tower; moving to another spot during the enemy animation will not allow you to avoid an enemy, but it will deactivate whatever element you move to (shop, tower).
- Have only played the single-player campaign. Not interested in multiplayer as of now.
Overall, even though I have more complaints than congratulations to give, I didn't hate the game as much as I thought I would, and that's why I finished it. It takes about 3 hours to see its 'end'. Gets my recommendation solely on the condition that you love match-3 games and don't mind getting into the occasionally excessively long single battle. (You can always hit Esc to quit the game and restart that fight later, perhaps with better luck.)

I've been playing Quake 3 (and now Quake Live) since 1999, and had been a part of the TDM, Defrag, and later the RA3 communities. By far the single best FPS arena game I've ever played. Maybe my opinion is rooted in bias and nostalgia, but I sincerely believe that no other arena FPS game has come close since. Most FPS games these days have gone the way of military weapons and "realistic" gameplay and you rarely see a game that brings that campy fast paced action that id Software introduced to the genre ages ago.  Mods that were introduced to Quake 3 have been adopted into Quake Live and while the game doesn't have nearly the same size userbase as it used to you can still take your pick of gametype and still find a game.
I think that the people leaving negative reviews complaining about the $10 price tag have unrealistic expectations. This game is OLD, and keeping this game alive requires money. Most of us who were playing before the switch ended up getting the game free anyways. Here's to hoping that this game stays alive for more years to come.

Okay, first off I'm not a huge DOA fan, I've always "liked" the game but I never considered it a serious brawler and so never spent much time with it,

Part three long enough to realize that it was broken (my opin) and then dropped it in favor of games like SF and played through the story of part 4 long enough to get one character ending.
I'm saying all of this so you understand that I'm not a hard core DOA player.
Anyway, when I read that DOA5 was PC bound I was super excited as I'd read some good things about the games engine etc and right away preordered the thing!
Right off please note that I do not have a ps3/4 so I have nothing to compare this game with and no gripes about the missng stages or soft engine blah blah.. I'm using SweetFX with my game also so I'm quite happy with how it looks, is animated and how it plays.
My Gripes amount to being slightly annoyed that no matter what I unlock or how long I play I can't seem to unlock any achievements probably beacuse of the fact that there is STILL no online play, something I really want, however, this was actually a good ting for me.
Typically I don't explore a fighter very much beyond vs and story mode and if there is online then my efforts will be concentrated on that. I might get into the tutorial to help but mostly I won't bother with the other options..
I went through some of the achievement list and some of them don't even requre online play but I can't seem to have them unlock even though as far as i can tell, I've dont them.
In this case you could say I was forced to explore this game more.
What I've found...
I played the story mode which takes you through just about every character (just about but not all) and found that I really liked how this one was done. It's long, longer than most fighters really but not impossible and I'd say enjoyable.
It's different from the traditional story mode in which you pick one character and  play though that characters life story.. In this game you're playing through the DOA story and will end up playing as a number of characters going through the main DOA core story and every character which is directly involved with DOA (sort of)
Offcourse if you're expectnig an epic story line here then dream on it, sucks!
(like just about every other fighter out there's story mode)
So nothing surpising here and I didn't care. It was long I saw most every ones story in one swoop and didnt need to play it over and over multiple times to know what happened to every one.
In a nut shell I liked it, nuff said.
After that I played a bit of arcade to unlock content. I've got 23hrs or game time so far.

(yes unlocking costumes takes a while even when you go tag battle on rookie where you have to finish in 5 matches and unlock two constumes each time)
After unlocking most characters costumes, I went on to the tutorial where I learned more about the basic aspects of the game.
To my surprisze I'd been playing the game wrong!
I played it like I did every other DOA, completely loosing sight of the counter system.
By now I've realized that the game is way deeper than I gave it credit for and now believe that it could very well be considered a serious fighter.
(I doubt it every will but if people spent more time with it then yes they would enjoy it and prob take it serious)
There's an other mode which I tried (forgot the name) where you pick about 5 characters and go head to head for a 5 character 5 round match up. I actually found that very fun weirdly enough.
okay so not much of a review and loads of talking but what do I think about the game?
Fun fun fun!!!
I had a good stress free time playing this title and was pleasantly surprised at just how deep the game can be.
Just how much fun it was and just how much I enjoyed playing it..
I'm very happy it came to PC and I do for sure recommend it inspite of it's very few glitches and lack of online  play which I'm not holding my breath on even though It's been "coming" for quite some time now.
The characters are beautifully modeled the costumes are quite good the engine is stable and to me much less broken compared to other editions of the game I've played in the past.
So if you're a doa fan or curious enough to pony up that kind of cash for it, don't have a ps3 or 4 and you can keep an open mind then I'd say you're safe getting this one. Otherwise wait for online and a discounted price then go for it.
If you have a ps4 then as others have said there would be no point in getting this for PC as what I've heard is that the ps4 version of this title is the best version.
So Recomended?

The Metro series are two of the best shooters I've had the luxury of playing. This one happens to be my favorite game of all time, so this review may be a bit biased.
The gameplay is fantastic, there is a mix of stealth and shooting sections and one never overpowers the other. Stealth is vastly improved over Metro 2033, using the PathEngine and adding stealth kills/knockouts with an animation. The graphics are gorgeous. The Dead City's derelict beauty, the underground Metros feel more cozy and humanic, monsters more terrifying. The swap from 2033's 4A engine to Last Light's modded 4A engine was nothing but beneficial and the game looks superb. This game is optimized so damn well. It ran on my horrid laptop at 45 fps 75% of the time except when I was on the surface. The game looks great and performs even better. The sound design is pristine, HUGE immersion factor. The story is the best in a FPS I've ever played; to sum it up for you:
"You are Artyom, a man who lives in Exhibition, but when Dark Ones threaten your home, you must go on a perilous journey to the heart of the Metro to warn the rest of the Metro of the apparent danger."
But like every good game, there are some flaws here they are:
- Artyom's sleeves will randomly change during cutscenes, I never realized this until my 4th playthrough so it's not very distracting and it never randomly happens.
- The game sells itself as a horror game but I've never really felt scared.
- The moral point system doesn't really matter since Last Light begins off the bad ending.
- The stealth system works for the most part but the way it is built will allow you to crouch right next to an enemy undetected as long as you're in a shadow. (Your watch's light sensor)
This game is one of the greatest I've ever played or will play, I have no doubts it will ever leave my top 10, and with this my final verdict is a:
9/10: Fantastic mechanics but little nitpicks like sleeve changing can really bring you out of the immersion sometimes.

Don't be deceived by the age or the price of this game. It's very good.
The amount and variety of content puts many later titles to shame, and so does the AI.
For the first time in a long time, I can race the AI without simply strolling through the pack or watching a single file of cars disappear over the horizon leaving me to hot lap alone. In addition, I have yet to be rear ended or shoved off the track by the AI, no matter where I am on track or how slow I am going. If you have track position, the AI will respect that as best it can, however if you try things like cheap late dives up the inside, they will hold their line and you will get clumped. This enables you to battle with the AI for fun under proper 'Queensbury Rules', which is how it should be.
The only other game I can think of at the moment that has AI close to this is Stock Car Extreme.
In addition, the AI cars also have their own little battles between themselves from time to time which helps greatly with the immersion and I have yet to see any AI cars get bunched up and stuck anywhere. (Quick Tip: Don't max out the number of AI cars when you race. Keep the AI numbers on the low side and this will further help to avoid congestion.)
Graphics are fine, and with a little graphics card tweaking (anti-aliasing in particular) it can be made to look very nice - not photo realistic, no - but still nice looking. Smooth and and clean.
Force feedback is also good if you take the time to tweak the settings to your liking. One advantage of being an older game is that there's plenty of information on the internet to help set up most wheels properly.
Kudos also for the clean and clear user interface. Everything is laid out logically, and setting up races and competitions (you can also create your own custom competitions by the way) follows a nice logical flow through track and car selection to get you to race day.
So, if you're at all frustrated whilst waiting for a fix or patch on your latest photo-realistic uber-racing sim, do yourself a favour - spend £2.50 on this and have some serious fun in the mean time.
Highly recommended.
P.S. I've spent quite a bit more time playing this game than the numbers above would indicate, before writing this review. :)

It’s hard to find good Lovecraftian games, despite the popularity of cosmic horror. All too often a title will seize on the monsters or the twists of eldritch horror without capturing the despair and madness of the unknowable. But then there are magical exceptions like Deathstate, games that purposefully eschew the despair and madness and use the monsters and twists to make a completely awesome shoot-em-up. The cosmic horror elements really just serve as a jumping-off point for an entire universe of planar strongholds, enchanted blades, powerful tomes, and thousands of soul-sucking monsters to blast.
Good Professor Elinberg claimed to be on the verge of a monumental discovery in astral projection, but no one took him seriously until he up and vanished. A motley crew of scholars, drifters, and stranger beings have taken up residence in his previous residence to follow his trail into the unknown. By entering the Deathstate (roll credits), these explorers can enter realms of madness, populated by impossible beings guarding secrets of cosmic portend. Armed with enchanted weapons and artifacts, you will guide them to the final destination of the Professor and the terrible discoveries he has made.
In other words, you need to magic your way through fifteen levels of dimensional hellscapes to reach the thing the Prof sought. Each level is a vast maze of walls, channels, pits, and statuary separating you from the exit portal. Also standing in your way are several hundred enemies, everything from skeletons to star children to succubi to sarcophagi. You’ll need sustained fire from your magical arsenal to bring them down but can augment your spellcasting with weapons, grimoires, artifacts, potions, and organs dug from the entrails of the cosmic horrors themselves. Most of those can be found in chests or bought from strange mummified merchants to be swapped around but the organs do indeed come from dead enemies and are permanent additions (and stat boosts) to your increasingly confounding biology.
The actual combat is one of the most unique aspects of Deathstate. It purports to be a single-stick shooter, which means all you need to worry about is moving. Your magic auto-targets nearby enemies using its own priority system that is somehow plenty smart enough to never get you killed. I’m not sure why exactly it works so well because I think it’s just targeting whatever’s closest, but in dozens of runs I’ve never once felt like I was cheated out of life. It helps that your upgrades can turn your pew-pew magic into death beams, gouts of flame, homing missiles, or flying psychic battleaxes as well, and while there may be moments where you feel you’re not killing fast enough they pass very, very quickly.
Deathstate smartly gives you literal hordes of monsters to melt with your fantastic cosmic powers, and your high rate of fire means you’ll chew through most of them like candy. That’s not to say they’re not a threat, of course. There are more than enough vicious creatures to make your life hell even as you mow them down. Your foes generally fire off tons of slow-moving shots, making this one very much a bullet hell game where you can fortunately focus more on dodging than aiming. You have a dash move that makes you very briefly immune to attack that you’ll need to cut through denser patterns, and you might also find some trinkets or other items that can negate attacks from time to time.
Levels are assembled in sets of four under a specific map type, and maps are paired so every time you run through the game you’ve got a 50/50 chance of doing the last one over again or traveling to the alternate one. This helps keep runs fresh, as enemies are unique to their map and the two maps in a pairing often play completely differently. Once you beat the game you’ll find shrines to desecrate that raise the overall difficulty of the game, generally making more enemy shots appear and fewer pickups drop. While the base game isn’t too challenging the different desecration levels ramp up quickly, leaving you plenty of room to improve your dodging and magicking.
The real draw here though are the dozen playable characters and hundreds of unlockable items and enemies to find in your journeys. For a game with straight-forward levels and challenges Deathstate hides a surprising number of secrets, some I’m still struggling to uncover nearly a dozen hours in. The clean pixel art is perfectly fitting and the chiptune soundtrack is superb, drawing on inspiration like old DOOM midi classics to provide an ominous, understated backdrop to the chaos. If anything the simple mechanics can start to lull you into too great a comfort, only for the roguelike difficulty to come slap you back down. It’s ultimately a chill game and a terribly fun one at that, especially since you can play it exactly how you want. Even those unsure of the roguelike genre would be well-served by giving this one a try.

This is one of my favorite games of all time.
Positives:
-The Atmosphere and background is fantastic. It makes you feel like there is a huge story, waiting to be uncovered.
-Item descriptions are cryptic (In a good way), and allude to a larger world.
-Items and organs are unique, with their own flavor and uses.
-Utterly unforgiving. Despite the auto aim feature, the game is a wonderful bullet hell and roguelike.
-Enemies are flavorful, and each one is different.
-Secrets. I have beaten this game, and I still have not seen every item, or fought every enemy. Another feature is the complex and strange ways to unlock certain things to access areas. You may stumble upon them by accident, or you may search for them, it doesn't matter.
-Awesome soundtrack. Seriously.
Negatives:
-Needs more levels. With 7 levels that can be unlocked normally (with one that can only be accessed in very certain circumstances, I want to explore more.
-The automatic firing actually adds a little bit of frustrating difficulty. The autoaim makes focusing on deadlier enemies very hard.
Final notes: This game is great, and I wish there were novels describing some of the worlds and creatures.

I've been using Blender for over a decade now; before making the switch I used Maya for several years. At first I was mainly looking to avoid the exorbitant license fees that Autodesk charges, but once I made a serious effort to learn Blender's workflow I fell in love with it and have never looked back. It was way more light weight on resource usage, opens almost instantly, rarely crashes, and is so much faster to model with once you learn the important hotkeys. I also felt it had Maya beat hands down for rigging and animation as well. Over the years I found myself turning to it for digital sculpting and video editing as well and Cycles is finally nearly where I'd like it to be for me to make the switch from the Blender Internal renderer, at least until 2.8 comes out and we get the viewport overhaul that will bring with it the modern real time PBR workflow that I've been looking forward to for years now.

This is a unique take on Match-Three Competitive games. It adds an area limitation - you can only make matches on your side, but matching 4 or more moves the divider over a column for the rest of your turn.  This adds an additional level of complexity (on top of the traditional match-3 combat options like collecting resources and using abilities) which works surprisingly well. The story is laughably unimportant and the graphics are workable but not impressive. But honestly, none of that matters - the gameplay is sound and a lot of fun. If you're a fan of Puzzle Quest or Gems of War, this is a good, distinctive take on the style.  It's relatively short, but there are lots of replay opportunities.

Please pardon my lack of Steam time.  After winning a giveaway for a Desura key, I played and ended up buying it myself because I wanted it on Steam too.  I've completed the campaign and fought in quite a few of the smaller battle modes.  What follows is my Desura review:
The line which divides player access makes Bret Airborne shine. Anything along the outer edge is relatively safe while items neighboring the line are in danger of being stolen. The grace period allows players to shift items around instead of being forced into specific swaps. There is a tug of war as large matches move the line towards the opponent and swapping items with no match moves the line towards oneself. Being aware of items to steal and large matches to perform is encouraged further as skills may count those events as bonus resources.
The campaign is short, upgrades are offered in small quantities and player's can't grind endlessly for funds. The result is analysis paralysis is reduced and players are encouraged to try again with different options. There are also other modes for session-based play.
The story is just an excuse for puzzle battles, but that's fine. [When I played on Desura,] I would have appreciated the ability to play in a window, grouped skill messages to avoid (rare) spam from opponents and the ability to immediately jump around a map when enemies are gone. These were all minor annoyances though.  [Since then at least some of these, like playing in a window, have been fixed.] =)

I played CoH a bit and I actually liked it. I can't recommend CoH 2 though for so many reasons I actually don't know if this game could be considered "finished".
One of the least important things are the visuals for me when it comes to RTS games. CoH2 looks like a slightly updated version of the first installment, but there's one huge difference between the two: Performance. Having a still quite powerful system, CoH 2 struggles excessively to maintain a framerate above 20 fps on my Core i7 at 3.6GHz. Make sure you have at least 8GB of RAM or else the game will stall for multiple seconds every now and then during gameplay.
Then there is the pathfinding of the units. This is actually the biggest, buggiest negative point I have with this game. Ordering your units is an absolute pain. Vehicles are the worst of 'em all. You can let motorized units (trucks, halftrakcs, tanks, pretty much everything that is a vehicle) retreat while driving backwards. It sounds like a good feature, not exposing the weaker armored rear part of a vehicle and not having to turn around first saves time and hitpoints, right? The point is, whenever I do that, the vehicles go insane. I just had a match where I lost tons of vehicles because they turned their back towards the enemy and drove TOWARDS THEM after using that feature. Standing in the middle of multiple enemies, they didn't last long.
The pathfinding itself is horrible as well. Units can get stuck in each other so often, it's laughable. Don't ever order a vehicle to drive past some infantry units. The latter will go insane, run back and forth around the vehicle, and the vehicle gets stuck. For a couple dozen seconds, if you're unlucky.
Pressing T' for infantry units is bugged in my case almost every time. Units simply won't retreat, no matter what. I click on the button, I hammer the T key on my keyboard, nothing... My units just enjoy getting slaughtered.
Unit selection is awkward as well. You should not try to click on your units, click on their respective icons instead. Otherwise you will select other units very often and wonder where the hell your build options are because you accidentally selected your grenadiers or something else even though they were not even close to your mouse pointer.
Then there are the microtransactions. Of course you can say you don't need these, but come on. You can get specific units and actions only with some commanders you don't have from the start. You can play a couple of hundred matches and hope that you'll get a (totally random) drop with what you need, but instead you are more or less expected to buy the stuff you need from the store, just like other 'factions', missions, maps etc. If you want the complete game, you better invest a couple dozen bucks after you bought the game if you want to play it competetively.
Oh, and did I already mention that it runs very bad?
Get CoH 1 instead. There, you get a complete game with much better performance and less bugs like in CoH 2.
Not recommended.

In a space capsule (sci-fi analogy for "nut shell"), FTL is a roguelike space crew simulator.  If that sentence appealed to you at all, go ahead and buy the game with zero regrets.
A typical gameplay session consists of picking a jump point to go to and getting into a battle scenario and/or dangerous space phenomenon/multiple choice scenario.  Battles focus on using your ships strengths most effectively to destroy or disable the enemy ship.  You assign power to your various systems (Shields, Drones, Weapons, Engines, Cloak, etc) and during a very difficult battle it becomes a very tense balacning act.  Luckily you can pause the game at any time to weigh your options.  You also run into phenomenon such as solar flares and meteor storms that pose a threat to your ship.  To make matters worse, these encounters typically coincide with an enemy attack.  You also run into decision-making scenarios that can either help or harm your ship and crew.  Should you send crew to that planet surface to fend off an attack of alien spiders?  There will be a reward if you succeed, but you might lose a crew member in the process.  During these scenarios, if you possess a specific type of crew or system it can give you an additional choice amongst the options that greatly tilt the outcome in your favor.
Prepare yourself for frustration though.  Having a good run typically means that you were able to stockpile large amounts of scrap and run into the right merchants at the right time selling exactly the right things.  Some ship types are particularly hindered if you aren't able to expand their capabilities in specific ways to offset their inherent weaknesses.
FTL is a very inventive game that simultanesouly scratches the roguelike and hard sci-fi itch.  It is also at times a very difficult or even unfair game, but if you like your roguelikes then this won't dissuade you.  As a bonus, the game also has a great musical score that fits the theme perfectly.
This is a must buy for me.  I would also love to see a sequel that expands the core formula by placing it into a open-universe setting rather than a linear branching path progression.

The game is actually a lot more difficult than I expected. The driving sequences test your reflexes from all that♥♥♥♥♥♥coming towards you while the taco-making sequences are like one of those memory games. There's also resource management involved too, with the food ingredients, scrap parts and money. If you suck at both of those, you'd wind up dead on the highway, beaten to death by a gang of chainsaw-wielding marauders (just like real life!).
The artwork's great; it's in those sprite-based style reminiscent of those old Flash games on Newgrounds or Kongregrate like Infectonator. Music's good too; its Tex-Mex style fits the game but isn't particularly memorable.
It's a pretty solid game, but there's a few minor flaws too. Some of the text in the game uses a generic font that just seems out of place (such as the numbers when you hit an enemy) and could've used a sprite-like font to fit in with the rest of the game's texts. There's also a slot machine minigame in some shops that you can win money with, but there's nothing in the game the scoring system (if there's any, because there's no controlling each slots so it could be completely random). Also, it's probably a bug, but I see a few posters in the mechanic shops have their text unaligned (running out into the walls and floors).
Ultimately, I'd give a 5/7, because it's one of those games that's only great for short-bursts of time. A mobile version that you can play on-the-go while waiting for public transport though, now this would be the perfect game for that platform.

I was very pleasantly surprised by this game.  I heard of it years ago, when it first came out, and dismissed it as not worth bothering with.  When I heard that you auto-fire at the nearest enemy with no option to aim manually, I couldn't imagine it being any good.

To start: I used to add a much longer header to these reviews, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: For the most part this review is going to be something of a retrospective,  as most anyone reading this will already know what Braid's gameplay entails. If you don't, however, here's a brief explanation: this game is a puzzle-platformer in which you can reverse time, and use various gimmicks in tandem with the time control in order to solve puzzles. Your controls are (on the 360 controller) analog stick/D-Pad to move, A to Jump, X to reverse time, and that's pretty much it until World 6 in which they add another gimmick.
Now for the retrospective: this is one of the many games that I never actually got around to playing when it was new, so I'm able to go into the game without any presumptions of the quality of the game. Basically, this review is for those who are wondering how well the game holds up to this day. I can confidently say that, given the deluge of puzzle platformers spurred on by games like this, that this game holds up quite well. There weren't really any dumb puzzles that required an obscene amount of platforming precision, the difficulty curve of the puzzles was good enough to make the solution not always obvious, but never so obscure that it gets frustrating, and the puzzle pieces within the stages were all pretty fun to get. One thing that may be a bit bothersome is that the game does expect you to find out the mechanics of the gimmicks for yourself, which I know is annoying for some people playing the game (for example, you can boost enemies upwards by jumping into them from beneath, but the game never tells you about this and it is required for 100%), but I never had too much of an issue with it.
To be honest, the most disappointing thing about this game is its length: the game only took me three and a half hours to beat, and that was all in one sitting. I would have liked to have seen a level editor for this game, as I think there is quite a lot of room for elements of the various gimmicks to be explored. However, at the very least the game doesn't overstay its welcome, and after beating it I do feel somewhat satisfied with my time. For me, this wasn't exactly a puzzle game that blew my socks off, but it is a fun, simple, relaxing puzzle platformer, and for some that's all you really want. 8/10.
Story: It's difficult to talk about this game's story, because there both is and isn't a story. There is a story in that there is a semi-coherent chain of events that you as  the protagonist go through, but at the same time there isn't, as there really is no conclusive ending. I will say that the last level of the game does serve as a surprisingly effective setpiece with which the game ends on, albeit not necessarily an ending. Still though, given the vague allusions throughout the game, the final level does come as something of a twist, and a fairly good one at that. There are various interpretations on the Internet for the actual circumstances of the plot, but going off of just what's in here, I'll give the game a 8/10 for a good, although short story.
Graphics: I'll just get the technical stuff out of the way: if your computer doesn't run this game, I feel bad for you because you may actually be using my old garbage Dell Dimension E310 that could hardly run XP with an anti-virus installed. I'd recommend that when the game launches you change the screen size to your resolution, as leaving it on Auto puts it to 1280x720. Anyways, all that aside, the game is simply gorgeous. The environments never stop being beautiful, the sprites are very well animated, and there's just a lot of detail here. Excellent quality through and through on the graphics front. 5/5.
Sound: The OST is very much inspired by classical music of the 16th/17th century, so if you're really into that sorta thing then you'll have a great time with the soundtrack. For me, the soundtrack provided a nice backdrop to the game itself, but I do find myself having a bit of a tough time remembering any of the songs from the game, even after having just played it. This may just be a thing with me, but nothing on the OST really stood out to me. Apart from that, there really isn't much else to talk about here. 3/5.
Overall scores are: 8/8/5/3; cumulative score of 8.0/10. I'd say that this game still holds up quite well to this day; however, I don't necessarily think it's as amazing as some people are making it out to be. Then again, I may be an uncultured pleb or something i dunno

Alright. This game deserves a much better review than the one I did last time when I only had like... 20 hours or something.
...Anyways.
After investing 875+ hours (and more to come!), I believe it's safe to say I very much enjoy this game. However, I wouldn't dare call this a mere game... no. This Meadow deserves to be called something more profound, more passionate.

Everybody's journeys are different, some more profound than others, and some more disconcerting. Some are the kind you would often reminisce, extol its pleasantries. Some, however, are the kind you would want to stampede over with a goatherd. A bouquet of pheasants, perhaps? The choice is yours. Although, a journey is not meant to and should not end. You will always bump into new findings along the way, new people to interact with whether to befriend or to antagonize. Again, the choice is yours. In Meadow, you will find that overtime, it is up to you on how you want to experience every moment. Every moment is bound to stir some different reactions in you, and it is bound that not every, single one will be pleasant or bad. Journeys have its ups and downs, and that's okay! I've certainly had a fair share of them. Despite this, it isn't all so bad. When you take a step back and simply take a gander about your surroundings, take in the delicateness of Meadow's ambience, you realize how truly beautiful everything is and allow it all to engulf you in a warm, serene embrace. That is the one thing that a bad moment in a journey can never take away from you, but, after all...
...everybody's journeys are different.
Throughout my 875+ hours, I've met a lot of fantastic people, all of whom are in a special place in my heart today (y'all know who you are~) Of course, I cannot deny that I've bumped into people that have certainly made my skin crawl and mouth... banter, but this ain't a perfect world. Meadow is certainly something that can touch your heart in a comforting manner. Your first playthrough and future playthroughs should be done as you see fit and allow it to build from there.
Explore. Relax. Loot. Destroy.
Collect pink, blue, and/or yellow crystals to garnish your flower/fable salad.
Cackle like the evil baby badger you are while you chase other animals down with mud.
Burn shrubs. Burn animals, maybe. Burn the entire sky! (Gotta buy something first before you do this though!)
Devour gigantic fruits that may be bigger than your entire body (unless you are a goat, eheh.)
Form a debatable topic about whether acorns are fruit or nuts (trust me, it happens.)
SKREEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE- into the void!
Fall into the void, even!
...
As you can see, Meadow is quite freeform, especially when you realize it's worth maybe like... a dozen of eggs or something. That's quite a deal, I would say. But, hey, like I said, it's up to you on how you start your journey, right?
If that's true...
...what are you waiting for? Go ahead and start it!
