A quest to make a good review. Let us....oh wait we have one. I will go over the game in a pro/ con style for Dream Tale and finish things off with my conclusion.
Pro:
Simple makes for fun. The gameplay style is a simple platformer focused around the use of these power orbs that grant the player the ability to glide, rocket up, or slowly ascend up. Its basic at its core but that is what makes it fun. Nothing too complicated just good old platforming.
Great story. The story is nothing too note worthy but i enjoyed the story that was there. The amazing part is to actually complete the story you must collect the keys to open the last level and finishing the last level grants the resolution of the story. Mind you these TVs found throughout the levels do spit out some hints to the story it is very welcomed.

Whats that glorious sound i hear in the game...music? Yes the music like the story isnt overly amazing but I did enjoy the music that was presented in each level. I want to say the game had enough music to count on one had but it is fine. The music help produce mood in the game, a sad or lost feeling can be infered though the music which ties in with the girl's journey to find her dog that went missing. It also doesn't help that you see messages like BFF on one of the TV with this music.
Collectables to collect. The game has a few simple collectables to find. Theres the puzzle and the keys. Keys are used to open the final level while the puzzle.... i am not sure what it is there for but it forms a nice picture. These items are in some well hidden areas so exploration is your friend. Also do not die when you find a collectable since if you die, the item will be removed from your inventory and you will need to back track to pick it up again.
Short game for cheap price. The game is short and can be fully completed in maybe 2hrs. Why is this a positive? It is because the game is cheap and it only gets cheaper on sale. Its only $5 so i say that is a good enough price for what you get.
Challenge but not super meat boy levels. The game isnt so simple to the point that it give you the win so easily. Later levels provide a nice challenge so enjoy the simple jumping over enemies and little bottomless pits while you can. You will soon need to dodge enemies while flying through the air with limited special power.
Con:
Really can not think of a negative for the game.
Conclusion:
This game was really cheap when i got it and i certainly got my money's worth. The story, music, gameplay, all of it was a nice experience. Sure it is not sonic or mario levels of good but it doesnt need to be. All you need is a good idea and provoke a mood by the player then boom you have an interesting experience. The game went for the sad mood and it did it well with subtle story points combined with music. I really wanted to see another version of this game. Maybe include achievements with another version. Finishing the game left me wanting more but not in a bad way like some people think it means the experience wasnt good enought. What i want is more because it was so good, i had my full enjoyment with the game and I would love to see more of it. Besides if I didnt like the game then why would i recommend it?

I've played every Civ game that has ever been released and I have to say that this one is my absolute favorite. Although the vanilla game lacked quite a bit of complexity, with the DLC's the game feels like the perfect balance of complex strategy and simple gameplay. Unlike other titles in the series, building wide / tall feel pretty balanced, with tall builds paying off in the early to mid-game with huge productive cities while being fairly weak militarily, and wide builds paying off mid to late-game with a booming economy and strong military capabilities but suffering culturally or technologically because of the slow start. Overall, in my opinion, the best Civ game released to date.
Pros:
-Relatively balanced wide vs. tall
-Culture is relevant even if you aren't going for a culture victory
-Culture, tourism, faith, empire happiness, & city state diplomacy are nice additions for complexity
-Victory types are relatively balanced on standard and quick settings
-Penalized for city spamming but rewarded for good city placement
-Late game ideologies allow you to easily fufill late game fantasies of conquest, expansion, booming
-Varied Civs which are all -at least- viable (bad civ with a good start better than a good civ with a bad start)
-Strategic planning is easier with simply accessed tile/multiplier/building data
-Fun multiplayer!!
Cons:
-Map sometimes feels a bit cluttered
-AI gives varying degrees of difficulty (Sometimes very easy, sometimes moderately competitive)
-Warmonger penalties last basically all game
-Faith ceases to have substance late game (basically just a source to buy great people)
10/10 would one more turn again.

I got Civilization V back when it was freshly released, and like many players I was extremly unhappy with the way Civ V was a massive step back from Civ IV. A lot of people say that the DLC makes Civ 5 fun again, but you can't simply release a broken game and then sell DLC to make it what it should have been from the start. That kind of practice just leaves a sour taste in your fans' mouths.
I bought Civilization I on release, and every other version since. Civ V is the first one that I can't even begin to enjoy. It's a massive step backwards. It's basically no longer Civilization, but some weird war game without any of the depth that made all the previous versions fun to play and saw the series progress with each iteration. If anything, Civ V is kinda like Civ I in that it essentially removes all the additions to the series in between.
The big difference is that Civ I was actually fun to play and gave you the feeling of building a "Civilization to stand the test of time". This is a monstrosity not worthy of the name. I definitely won't be purchasing Civ VI in blind faith - and I never thought that I'd say that about a Civ game!
Now a lot of people are saying the same thing about Civ VI - severely lacking in many respects and not a patch on Civ V; buy Civ V instead. I would urge you to not buy Civ V either. It's quite clear that this is Firaxis' preferred approach to releasing games, and you should not be supporting a company like that.

This game deserves credit, for the following reasons:
*It is scary. But not Outlast scary, it´s sort of less horror than jump-scares and simply the sounds and visuals. Especially the sounds. They´re mostly the same all the time, but sh*t they are scary, every time.
*It has (fairly) good shooter mechanics. The weapons shoot realistically and the damage models are solid. What makes it interesting is that there are no specific damage points. You don´t know how much damage a weapon does, you just have to try it out. Makes the weapons choice just that much harder, and trust me weapons choice does matter in this game, depending on if you want to have a fun and entirely possible expirience or a difficult and far-less fun experience.
*It has puzzles. Well, not many and they aren´t really that difficult, but it make the game more challenging and makes this not just an ego-shooter, but also sort of a thinking game.
*The story is amazing. It is filled with plot-twists, creative levels and, most importantly, russian.
There are of course a fair share of bugs, or things the game does not tell you which makes it a lot harder. I experienced this myself. the game does not tell you that if you press (M) to hide your weapon Librarians (Monsters later in the game) will not attack you. This doesn´t spoil much as you can of course try to kill them, but it´s extremely difficult and takes up too much ammo. I wasted hours on that level and had to rely on outside help, even with normal mode on. I also had some other places where I required outside help, where the game was not explicit enough, but the main thing is that you acctually have to listen to dialogue, otherwise you are clueless.
Overall, I´d say that Metro 2033 is definitely a good buy, especially if it´s on sale as it is now, and it appeals to many genres. If you like FPS, puzzle and horror games, this is definitely the game for you. And let me also add that the fact that I even bothered to write this review, and make it so positive, just goes to show that this game is definitey worth a buy, just like its sequel, Metro: Last Light, which I am yet to play but will soon review too, if it impresses me as much as this game does.

I honestly don't think i HAVE to review FTL. To me and my friends it's kinda a stable to Steam. If you have a Steam account, you should try FTL. I know people who HATE losing, and this is a game where you usually lose... they like FTL. I've had days of just sitting around with friends, playing FTL, losing, passing the controller and just having pure phone.
Pros
1: It isn't a game about becoming the BEST in every way. It's a game about figuring out what works for you and developing on it. Makes it much more interesting and increases the replay value. You're not going for 100% upgrades or the best weapons, you're trying to find what you can, what's good for you, and sometimes ANYTHING at all.
2: The choices aren't static. You don't memorize what is the right or wrong thing to do. Sometimes you have to just prepare for the worst and even then you'll have to make tough calls. I tend to pick the moral options, and it bites back at me sometimes. My friend chooses the safest options, never gets bitten but never reaps the greater rewards.
3: No multiplayer, still a great multiplayer game.
4: Story is passive and isn't in your face. Perfect for this type of game.
5: Death is CRUSHING... in a good way somehow...
6: Lets you do a lot of different things you should be able to do.
Cons
1: FTL's challenges are random. In itself this is a neutral aspect. HOWEVER. because of this there are some rounds of FTL that feel like the game HATES you which isn't always the best feeling. Sometimes on Easy you'll get nothing but pirates after pirates and then you hit a dead end you didn't see coming and the rebels catch up. Game over... bit disapoint.
2: Everytime you have to make a choice there isn't much of an indication which option is right... because there isn't any right answer. The correct answer is randomized. If you hit a situation and have the right upgrade, crewman, or weapon then the game gives you another option that is almost ALWAYS a great one. However you'll run into more choices which could be anything. It can make some of the choices feel worthless. If it had subtle clues to which one you should pick, it wouldn't be a problem at all, random correct answers is a great idea... but there isn't any clues really.
3: The ending is entirely luck based at times. You get one shot and even if your ship is top notch you can get unlucky. Once I had a perfect ship, exactly crafted to defeat the final foe... i met a pirate on my way to the final foe and the pirate had missles... LOTS of missles. My ship beat the pirate easily. However i took a good deal of damage. I go to jump to the next system... and system around me is going to be taken over by the rebels... So i have to launch direction into the enemy. I win again but have lost a bit more hull. So, when i go to jump, i remember a repair station near by, check the map, it will be taken by rebels so i can't go there. I have to go into the final battle directly from 2 other battles. I manage to fight off the first form of the boss but now i'm in the red. I go into the next stage and i get down to one hull point and i beat the second form. Third form comes around and i wipe out the crew in the ship, which causes the enemy ship's auto-repair AI to kick in and it reactivates it's rockets just long enough to blow the last point of hull damage off my ship. So after all my hard work, my striving to survive and defeat the enemy, i'm beaten by a rogue missle shot from a magic AI that appeared because i wiped out too many enemies too quickly. So, once again, the ending weighs a lot more on luck then it should, which tests my patience a bit at times.
There are features i wish made it into the game or the later update... however these features i want are extras, nothing needed for this game to be great. The 3 cons i found are nothing more then minor annoyances when they hit their worst... so most of the time the cons aren't even there. Overall?
5/5.

Incredibly unbalanced factions (not supposed to be balanced I guess), meta that plays like a facebook game, and studder that wont go away regardless of settings.  No matchmaking based on level, so you'll likely get rolled 500 times by people with ships several levels higher than you before you can even compete.  Once your ships are destroyed you have to wait a couple rounds to use them again, so half of your games will be played with suboptimal ships or useless escort ships that literally get plowed through by anything bigger than an asteroid.  The progression is such that at the beginning of your MP career you will have one ship.  By the end, you will have a dozen.  But because of unit cap limits, you will never get to use all of them at once, so forget about huge fleet battles, that ain't happening here.  And for a game that focuses on small ship engagements, would some kind of formation button have been too much to ask?
Yeah, it's pretty, but the gameplay, meta, and MP are downright awful.  Hope you like both players pausing every few seconds to use all their ships' hotkeys, because that's the gameplay in a nutshell.  This is not a competetive multiplayer title, and I don't believe it ever will be.  If you get it, don't get it for the MP because you'll be really, really disappointed with how it turned out.  If you do, prepare to spend a couple hours in the forums looking up the best faction and best cookie cutter builds and copy them exactly, because that's the only way to consistently perform well.  One faction literally and figuratively runs laps around all the others laughing.  Such is the balance.  Don't want to play as that faction?  Then you might as well play singleplayer, because the other 3 factions do not compete in MP.
One of the few games in my library I've considered refunding, as the MP is simply not what was advertised.

TL:DR this is how zombie games should be done. Gives you plenty of weapons to kill zombies and plenty of zombies to kill. If you just want some fun mindless violence this game is for you
Dying Light has become my favourite zombie game. You play as Kyle Crane, an agent who gets parachuted into a city called Harran that is having a pretty large zombie infestation. You can pick up loads of different melee weapons, upgrade them with the blueprints you collect and use them to kill lots of zombies. The combat in this game is great and is lots of fun. As you level you gain new types of attacks that give you more options for your zombie killing and even though you do a lot of zombie killing it never got repetitive or felt like a chore.
Parkour is also a big feature of this game and you can quickly scale buildings and run from roof to roof helping you avoid the large crowds of zombies and get around the city quickly.
The Enhanced addition also features the Following DLC which features a whole new map set in the countryside and it also gives you an upgradeable buggy to drive around and mow zombies down with.
Dying Light is tons of fun whether you play alone or with friends. I cant recommend it highly enough.
Good points:
- combat is really enjoyable with loads of upgradeable weapons and the game gives you plenty of zombies to use them on.
- the parkour works really well in this game and makes getting around easier and more enjoyable
-the day and night cycle is a handled brilliantly. During the day zombies are more docile and easier to kill. At night there are more dangerous  zombies that will chase and batter you. It honestly makes being out at nighttime terrifying.
- The Following is an excellent DLC and while seperate from the main game you can transfer your main game character and items to the DLC and vice versa
- with a group of friends or a good group of randomers the co-op is brilliant
Bad points:
- Not so much a criticism of the game but the community. The online options allow you to set your game to offline or private and despite this there are an annoying amount of people who leave theirs set to public, and will immediately drop out or kick you if you join.  Just set your game to private if you want to play alone.

The opening cutscene had me so psyched; for being an older racing sim, it looked fantastic. NEO's the real deal. It's not formulaic enough to be called a true roguelike, but not divergent enough to deserve the broader designation of a "roguelite." It's a post-apocalyptic RPG with a heavy emphasis on wilderness survival and simulation. As such, stats are stripped down to basics like weight, condition, and value, and precise character proficiencies are replaced by broader traits and flaws. Very few tropes you'd expect from the genre are played straight. You haven't got hammerspace, levelling, or precise stats. It feels very organic and makes every encounter feel extremely tense. If you're fragile or unskilled in combat, it might take just one good hit with a wrench to do you in. Conversely, avoiding combat is quite viable and can be a rewarding experience. The setting, again, is rarely played straight. Sci-fi, occult mythology and real world influences create a world probably unlike what you'd expect. It's brutal, unapologetic and overall pretty believable.
The game takes killing very seriously. Unlike games it may seem superficially reminiscent of, it never makes the assumption that the player character is inherently stronger than NPCs, or even able to make a kill. And in a post-apocalypse, killing people should be a very serious, major event. In NEO, it is. I love that. The interactions in encounters can get downright disturbing. You might wallop someone real good only to have them kill you when you decide to show mercy, or you might crawl away from a fight battered and limping only to die slowly from blood loss and exposure. If you want to live, you have to do cruel things. You've gotta be willing to smash a beaten dog's head in, or stomp a fellow human to death, up close and personal, brutally. The fact the game doesn't shy away from stuff like this drives home a real sense of rawness and tension. While fights might be sparse depending on your playstyle, you've gotta be constantly prepared for the very worst. It's the feeling games like Fallout have never really been able to drive home, and the fact that it's conveyed so vividly in a game with such sparse graphics really drives home that this is special.

Deathstate has to be one of my favorite rogue-like shooters on the market.
Enter the Gungeon and Nuclear Throne are great, but Deathstate simplifies controls enough to make the game that much more challenging, throwing wave upon wave of enemies at you like you were playing a good remake of Gauntlet.
The auto-shoot feature might seem like a cop out or downgrading what the game can be, but it actually morphs the game quite a bit into its own thing.  Instead of being just another bullet hell dungeon crawler, it starts to inherit more of the traits of a Geometry Wars or the mobile games Spirit or Tilt to Live where you are constantly moving to avoid enemies and enemy fire to stay alive while mowing down the now Coachella-level of demons around you.
Upgrading is also visually interesting as you literally take organs from dead demon bosses and... eat them?  Consume them in some way?  Either way: you become them and they become you.
The only criticism I could possibly level at the game is its Synthwave color scheme not really being justified by the game itself, but that is a tiny complaint in an ocean of now dead skeletons I shot with my Scientist who is addicted to bottles of mystery chemicals.

So, after nearly 5 hours in this game I'm finally gonna give it a review. I do like this game, and have been a huge Roguelite/Roguelike fan since Isaac got popular. I've played a bunch of them, good and bad, and most don't engage me as much as Deathstate does. It's a fun game, and challenging to boot. However, I feel like it's challenging for some of the wrong reasons. I'm gonna go over why.
The first thing I'm going to talk about are the things I really like in the game. I like the update to the visuals. I played this game before that, and hated it simply because looking at that grainy screen and terrible animations was painful, and in any game if you can't even look at it, it's not gonna be a good game. All of that was fixed in the visual update, and the game looks great now. It maintained the aesthetic it was shooting for, but managed to be brighter and more pleasing to the eye. The references in the game are cool (particularly all the Cthulu mythos references) and sometimes made me chuckle a bit. Some of the items are super fun, and getting cool synergies is a blast (talking about you Laser Sword and Shoot more bullets rank 3 >:D) and it's honestly why I play these games. Enemies and levels tend to be very diverse and interesting, and the game always feels like it's changing.
Onto some of the bad things, and while the good things slightly outweigh the bad, the bad are REALLY bad. One thing that I hate is the combination of the time limit, and no mapping. I understand it adds a challenge, but god is it annoying. If it was only one or the other, I wouldn't care that much. But both is simply infuriating. You have to entirely rely on RNG to be powerful enough to kill enemies fast enough to progress through the level. And it's not just finding the exit to the next level, it's finding the miniboss, checking for a shop, finding any chests, altars, giant chests, book stands, forges, etc. And if you're really powerful and wrecking things early, you might be able to secure some of this stuff. But sometimes you end up running out of time scrambling to get SOMETHING so you can have a bit of power to actually kill things. If I don't find a book or sword by the third level, I forfeit. Because I know without at least one of them (and it has to be a good one too) I won't last a chance making it through the second level in time. Also backtracking is nearly impossible because of the lack of a map and the time limit combined. Wanna try to get 30 more gold to get that book from the shop? Oh wait, you can't find the shop again... too late shadows consume you. They seem to have toned the timer down a bit, but it still punishes you for not getting good items, which is based entirely on RNG. This is the only game where I've seen it punish you more for bad RNG rather than no skill. Games like Binding of Isaac and Enter the Gungeon both reward you even when you're behind. Is the game harder because you got♥♥♥♥♥♥items? Yes. But with enough skill, you have a chance to make it through. I've seen people do the first 4 or so floors with only the starter pistol in Gungeon. I've seen people do entire Isaac runs with absolutely♥♥♥♥♥♥damage. Sure, it took them like an hour, but they still did it. Deathstate you don't have that option. If you have♥♥♥♥♥♥items, you aren't going to make it. And that is that. The only way to get good items is to explore, and the only way you can explore, is if you're strong enough to kill the enemies fast enough.
Another HUGE problem is the games horrible lack of any invurnerable frames. You have your dodge, which gives you maybe one frame of dodge on the basic characters. And you have maybe half a frame of invulnerablity after you get hit. But that's it. If you get caught in a corner, or can't get down a corridor before a hail of bullets comes flying down it, you can very easily get your entire health bar melted nearly instantly. It is next to impossible to react as fast as this game wants you sometimes. And this is a bullet hell game. And it means hell. See, comparing again to Gungeon, you get invulnerable frames long enough to take a breath and see what you did wrong in Gungeon. In Deathstate, you don't have time to think about what you did wrong. You just have to keep dodging as you get hit. Because if you're still being shot at, you could take 2 or 3 before you even figure out how you got hit. So instead of the thought process being "I got hit, how, oh that's how, ok I'll dodge that next time." it's "I got hit, oh♥♥♥♥♥♥more bullets, dodge dodge dodge". It feels horribly unfair sometimes, because you don't get any chance out. The only thing you get is your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dodge which only feels like it works half the time.
My last big complaint about this game is the true randomness of this game. Now, most games such as this, you are guaranteed some kind of upgrade each level. Isaac has item rooms, boss items, and shops. Gungeon has two item rooms, a boss item, and a shop. Deathstate has a miniboss. And he drops one passive item. That's all you're actually guaranteed. Things like books, swords, relics, extra items, potions, etc are all complete RNG. I've had levels where I got a book, a sword, two giant chests, an altar, two minibosses that dropped organs, and a shop. I've also had runs where I got nothing but minibosses for 3 floors and got absolutely destroyed on level 2 because I had no real upgrades. Tying in to my earlier complaint, it feels ENTIRELY up to the game whether you succeed or not. And if the RNG of getting items isn't enough, it seems what enemies you'll encounter on each floor (and how difficult they are) is also RNG. You can get really hard bullet helly enemies on the first floor, or nothing but skeletons. I've had times where the first 4 floors where harder than the second levels 4 floors. I've had times where the 2nd level's 4 floors are literally harder than the last level. The enemies, despite having the same visuals, tend to randomize their attacks. There's no "this enemy attacks in this way" with all of them. Some enemies completely changed mechanics in different playthroughs. It's frustrating, because after playing for nearly 5 hours, I thought I had most of these enemies (at least on the first couple of floors) patterns down to where I could reliably dodge them. But instead they completely changed attacks, and now I had to relearn a new enemy. Bosses also have no pattern. They just shoot at you, increasing in bullets after they get to half health. While some have some kind of normal firing pattern, they will throw in other random bullets or things like dropping skulls or lasers just to throw you off of dodging said pattern. So everytime you fight a boss, it's going to be different. After roughly 20 playthroughs, I don't think I've had one run where the enemies on the first floor are all the same as a previous run, and to me that feels unfair. It's hard to get good at a game that isn't even remotely the same any time you play it through.
So, all in all, or TL;DR this isn't a bad game per-say, it has it's fun times, and is a good challenge. More hardcore people could even play something like Endless or the god-forsaken unholy unfair gauntlet that is Insanity mode (aka ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t fiesta). I probably wouldn't pay full price for this again, but it's not bad if you wanna get a new roguelike to ♥♥♥♥ around in and it's on sale.

Deathstate's a great little game, it's not the best but I really don't have anything to complain about.
For those who might not understand the way the game works from the store description: Deathstate is like a twin-stick shooter that aims for you. There's no button to fire and you don't have to aim. You automatically lock on to the closest target and fire at it. You'll probably hit it.
So with that out of the way, Deathstate is a game where the combat is less about how you fight and more about how you move and in this aspect it really shines. Movement is fluid, you always move how you would expect to move based on your input and you have a neat little dodge which allows you to quickly move in a direction, destroying enemy bullets along the way. It's very short and you definitely can't plow through fields of fire with it but it can help you out in a pinch and learning to use it properly is very important. The thing is, I tend to forget about it but surprisingly it hasn't hindered me greatly, though I imagine that if I used the dodge more frequently I would be much better at the game.
There's plenty to unlock and new runs never feel samey, there's plenty of characters with different stats, abilities and passive effects to toy with and the visuals and soundtrack are pretty nice. Not the best, but still pretty damn good.
"Not the best, but still pretty damn good." sums up the game pretty nicely actually.

Not even 10 hours I have on this game and I can already say a lot of things about it.
1. Beautiful graphics
- This game has similar graphics to Shelter and Shelter 2. Textures are really different from what you see nowadays in other games (in a good way) and everey single piece of the map is pleasing to look at.
2. Game mechanics
- Mechanics in this game are quite simple. WASD - move SPACEBAR - jump and some other added features. and TAB is used to show all your emoticons and actions you can do on your animal.
3. Community
- The devs made this game literally a wild experience. There is no chat and no way to speak on the microphone. The only way to communicate with other people is with emoticons (like emojis) which you use when you want to express yourself. (It appears above your character). There are also emoticons to tell someone where to go (uphill, downhill, across the river etc.)
4. Character customization
Meadow offers a lot of character customization. For each character the emoticons are different, you have to collect these things called essence to unlock them. Red essence unlocks a new piece of your map for emoticons, Blue essence unlocks a new piece for skins. (Yes you can get new skins for each animal) and the Orange essence unlocks a new piece of your map for a new animal. You can even get new voices! (They are used to attract attention or maybe tell where you are.)
Basically... get this game!! It is so relaxing and fun!

Lara Croft and The Temple of Osiris is a sequel of the previously published game, The Guardian of Light. This game was released in December of 2014 on PC and both PS4 and Xbox One.
Like the first game, The Temple of Osiris is an adventure game with a isometric view of Lara. This game also includes co-op like the original, but this time offers the choice of more than two characters.  Lara returns with her classic dual pistol setup whilst her other friends have their own unique set of abilities and weapons. The game focuses heavily on puzzle solving, like the Tomb Raider series; but also with a little bit of platforming and gun-play thrown in too. All of the puzzles are easily solvable if you have any sort of experience in puzzle games however.  All of the gameplay elements which were in the first game are in The Temple of Osiris such as grappling hooks and bombs, and nothing really new is added in this respect. It's just more of the same.
Graphically, The Temple of Osiris looks really nice; it's not top of the range graphics as you can see from the screenshots, but it does have a very nice art style, and it fits the genre and setting of game very well.  It looks very much like a Diablo style game. You get to see a variety of different environments and all of them can have different weather effects in them too.  Some of the latter levels really look special, they give you the feel of something epic is about to happen as you are exploring all of these deep and gorgeous looking tombs.
The story is very linear, you can't really effect the outcome of the plot in anyway; you have to collect "keys" in a specific order. It would of been nice if you could of changed the order in which you have to gather them, just to give the game a little bit of an open world feel to it; however I can see why they stuck to a linear style so that you are fighting against the right difficulty of enemy according to your equipment. I really did enjoy the story line though; the ending is amazing and something which I will remember for a while since the last boss fight is so epic!
The Temple of Osiris is fully voice acted; and done very well, Keeley Hawes voices Lara Croft - as she did in the previous game, and a number of other Tomb Raider games since 2006 (apart from the reboot in 2013). The game also includes very classic Tomb Raider sound tracks, both increasing the urgency in certain events, or creating a creepy and spooky atmosphere.
I found The Temple of Osiris to be a little easier when compared to the first game, whether this was because I was used to the type of puzzles I was encountering, or just because it is plainly easier, I'm not sure. But none of the puzzles are mega hard and even I didn't have to resort to looking up the resolutions online. Boss fights can easily be conquered once you work out what is needed  to be done, granted this can take a while but the execution is easy. I personally found the platforming aspect to be the hardest aspect of the game.
Beside the abundance of puzzles in each level, you can collect gems which in turn can be used to open treasure chests at the end of a level. These chests hold loot, such as rings and pendants. I really liked this aspect; as it allowed you to customize Lara to play however you wanted her to play. I personally opted for a more speedy build, so had run speed increases and weapon firing rate - so spent a lot of time farming gems in order to find the right equipment in the chests to that end.  Each level also comes with a few option challenges that you can complete, these can vary from completing the level in a certain amount of time, or simply not dying - these too reward you with gems allowing you to open more chests at the end. There are plenty of other items and pickups to find along the way on each level, such as permanent stat boosts to health and ammo pools.
A full playthrough of The Temple of Osiris took me just under eight hours to complete. This game is a bit shorter than the original, however I see there to be more potential for replay-ability in this game. I would be more inclined to boot this game up once I have finished it since I can carry on using my same save file to complete challenges and try to find more loot and collectibles. With the addition of the co-op mode too, which result in you having a different playing experience since a number of the puzzles and events change depending on how many people are playing - The Temple of Osiris is a game which I think you can get at least eighteen hours out of if you really push it.
The only technical problems I had with this game was that sadly I wasn't able to play it on 4k resolution without frame drops; and even on 1080 I still got the frame drops but not as server, it was only really noticeable when I was in a water heavy environment. Given that I can play more recent graphically intensive games on 4k and full graphical settings, I don't think The Temple of Osiris has been optimized as well as it could. This game is also heavily reliable on you having a controller to play with. It is horrible configured for using a keyboard and mouse and is just downright uncomfortable to play if you do use them. Stick with your controller to get the best out of this game.
To sum up, I really enjoyed Lara Croft and The Temple of Osiris - whilst all of the gameplay elements are the same as the original; the game's world, story and replay-ability really make this a better title for me. Tomb Raider fans really should experience this game, and anyone wanting an introductory game to a puzzle and action genre style game will get a welcoming experience here too. The price tag of £14,99 may be a little steep if you are just planning the one playthrough; but if you are wanting to have a game which you can get almost twenty hours of gameplay out of when played with friends and aiming to complete plenty of challenges, you should not hesitate to pick this up. Everyone else just looking for a one hit pony, will probably want to wait till it goes a 50% sale.

Dream Tale is a simple, bare-bones platformer in which you are a young girl navigating a trippy, space-y dream-world in search of her dog.     I was hoping for an exploration experience along the lines of Knytt, but that's not really what this game is.  It's broken up into a series of mini-levels that each take about 90 seconds or so to finish, provided you don't die.  Controls are limited to walking and jumping, and the only goal is to reach the portal and collect as many pellets as you can along the way to increase your score.  Touching an enemy or falling into a pit is instadeath, and results in you restarting from the beginning.  There is a checkpoint system implemented, but not very well - if you die, you begin from the checkpoint, but your level progress is reset in terms of points and the things you've collected.  You may also find the titular keys scattered about, and they are collectable, but I can't figure out what they do, if anything.
While Dream Tale plays just fine, there's a few areas that could use some work.  The store page boasts four worlds, but they all look extremely samey - I'd love some visual variety.  I'd also like some enemy variety, too - there's two basic enemies - the blobs that crawl back and forth on horizontal platforms, and the blobs that fly in one of three preset patterns.  I'd love to see more incentive to complete the game with perhaps an achievment system of some sort or more of the occasional mid-level messages to add to the story.  If this stuff was developed, this title could certainly be better.
However, despite its drawbacks, Dream Tale manages to score a positive review from me on the strength of its level design, and on the placement and implementation of the handful of powerups that aid your journey.  In this area, there was a little variety and challenge, and a few hard-to-reach areas or semi-hidden routes.  Do you go for the extra points, even if you're risking death?
Bottom line: I had an evening of fun with this title.  I'm not a high-score seeker, so I don't have much incentive to go back and play this again anytime soon.  If you're considering this title on its own merits, you could honestly find other titles that have more to offer.  However, if you're looking at this as a part of a bundle of some sort, well, then you might get a pleasant little suprise, as long as you aren't expecting more than 90 minutes of play at most.

Battlefleet Gothic: Armada is set in the Warhammer 40k universe - the famous franchise from Games Workshop. This title is based off of the table top game of the same name and, overall, does a great job of capturing the spirit of the original. In this game, fleets of ships which are miles long duke it out in spectacular ways. Micro-management skills are key here, and though it may seem daunting at first, it becomes second nature in no time, and you always have "Tactical Cogitators" at hand to slow things down when needed. As you position your fleets in various ways in order to adapt with the changing battlefield, it becomes extremely satisfying when your plans work and enemy ships flee the theatre or erupt, leaving a shattered wreck in their place. There are a plethora of tactics for every race against every other race, and figuring those tactics out will be essential to victory. Do you ram that ship who is trying to warp out of combat or would that hurt you more than your target? Do you take large capital ships into battle or stick with smaller, more nimle escort ships? Do you board your enemy? Sacrifice a ship in order to spring a trap? Use environmental hazzards to your advantage? Your options are numerous.
There are differences in this game to other adapted Games Workshop titles: Blood Bowl and Space Hulk stuck to dice rolls, whereas BFGA does for the Battlefleet Gothic table top what Dawn of War did for the Warhammer 40,000 table top - that is to take the concept, do away with the dice rolls and turn based gameplay and then reinvent it as a modern, RTS game. As an old Battlefleet player I can tell you that BFGA is a fine recreation of a classic (albeit overshadowed) tabletop game and doing away with the dice rolls and turns was the best decision to make for the video game.
Currently, there are 4 races in the game: The Imperial Fleet, Chaos Fleet, Ork Raiders or Eldar Corsairs. There are 2 more races to be included in the game, one of which will be the Space Marines and another race which, as of yet, has not been revealed.
The game modes included so far are a campaign, which is very linear and brutally punishing but has a wonderful atmosphere which beautifully draws you in to the Warhammer universe.
Multiplayer, is currently matchmade only. While there is a 2v2 game mode where you can invite a friend as an ally, you cannot manually set up opposing teams which, quite frankly, is a very bizarre oversight. There are plans to add more customisation to this in the near future.
Solo skirmish is where I spend the bulk of my game time. Here you can pick a fleet (you can use multiple fleets, having a few fleets for every race if you wish) and commit to a game against the AI with random game rules and "renown" limits which assigns point values to certain ships in order to keep the match balanced. In this mode you level your ships, assign upgrades and crew bonus' as well unlock higher tier ships. You can also enter your fleet into a "Custom game" Where you won't level anything (but won't have to worry about damaged ships, either) but have more freedom to choose game modes, renown limits and which race(s) you will face. I feel that this game mode is where the much requested "Co op vs ai" feature will come in to play, but as of right now, you are stuck playing alongside and against AI fleets and it's pretty pointless.
This game has the potential to be great; it may be the next Dawn of War in longevity and scope, so here is hoping. There are at least two more races to come. In time, I hope that more will be added. As it stands right now, it desperately needs the ability to invite your friends into custom games as not everyone wants to play against strangers and the AI can only last for so long. Fleets are also smaller than in the table top, from what I remember, so hopefully renown values will be extended. I have faith, however, and fully recommend this great adaptation - in my opinion, the best Games Workshop video game to be made in years.

Yes. But with caveats. Disclaimer: I've not played the game all the way through the campaign, but I have put about 30 hours into to so far with about 10 of those being on the release.
It all seems to be a very thorough adaptation of the original game. The graphics are incredibly detailed and everything is accurately reproduced from GW's original art and descriptions. I can't say that I find fault in any of the features, ships, or races. I want to like this game.
But there are problems as I see them, the game as a whole very much needs help with in-combat micro-management.
1: There is no ability to set formations. If I setup a group of ships in a line formation - - - -  then they will eventually all shift to abreast as they move | | | | . If I set them up in a line formation they damn well better stay in formation or I'm shooting a captain that breaks rank. It doesn't matter if I set 6 ships 2 abreast in a line or what. They should maintain it unless I say otherwise.
2: There is no ability to set 'wingmen'. I should be able to link two or more ships together that have standing orders to not drift more than, say 3000 units from one another. This is important because ships left to their own devices tend to wander off on their own, and it requires constant attention from the player to monitor and give new orders. I should be able to say to one ship, 'this ship in your lead....follow him and attack his targets always.
3: Both A and B are important because while you can set priority targets the option for doing that is extremely cumbersome, and the player only has the ability to prioritize 4 targets at any given time, and you can only do it by clicking on each target one at a time. There is no 'panel' window that allows you to set them all on one pane. You can also only prioritize targets you've identified. This is kind of STUPID because if you have missions where you have to assassinate a flag ship or transports, or capture data, then the flag ship and/or the transports/data should >always< automatically be #1 and they aren't. This leads me to complain about the fact that all transports should be considered equal priority, and that would be #1 starting with the closest.
4: Ships, by default, probably should never full stop on their own. This isn't to much of an issue if you're telling a ship to use it's port/starboard weapons primarily, because they will always just circle each other then, but if you tell a ship to focus on prow weapons they just come to a dead stop once they get in range. This, particularly, is a problem when playing Eldar, whose only defence is speed. Once an Eldar ship gets within range, and it's set to focus on it's prow weapons, it will just become a sitting duck and die. Bad Eldar.
5: I should be able to chain movement orders. This isn't an issue (much) in combat, but if I want to pilot a transport around a minefield or asteroids, I shouldn't constantly have to go back every so often and issue new orders.

A lovingly recreated tabletop game turned into an RTS. Game is all about micromanaging a fleet of giant spaceships but remember that the game is based more on ship of the line combat than space combat and as such there is no 3D plane. Players coming from the tabletop will notice that the game has added skills, these range from bombs and sensor disruptors to probes and boost refuels. There's a total of 4 factions as of release:

Imperial Navy, the jack of all trades featuring highly armored prows and mighty nova cannons.
Chaos, a long range fleet that focuses on kiting the enemy and features lots of carriers.
Orks, slow moving ships that loadouts are highly customisable, also expert rammers thanks to the "Big Red Button" which gives them a massive speed boost but pretty much locks them to go forward until the boost runs out.
Eldar, the difficult to play glass cannon faction, has the fastest ships but they have no shields and instead use hollowfields which decreases their chance to get hit, also has pulsars, highly damaging lasers which can shred through enemy ships should all three beams land.
All in all a very good game for Warhammer fans or perhaps even fans of ship of the line type combat

A follow-up to the fantastic Lara Croft and the Guardian of the Light, Temple of Osiris promises more of the same in an Egyptian setting. However, this time around the adventure feels less polished, the puzzles far more straight forward, and the co-op interaction stunted.
I played through the game entirely in two player co-op, which was one of the highlights of the first game for me. There are few games that fulfill both action and puzzle-solving in a co-op environment. I was disappointed to find that the puzzle design here is much more simplistic than the intriguing puzzles that made the original such a gem. Even by the end of game we barely broke our stride. Puzzles were mostly straight-forward, often requiring very little actual timing or cooperation.
There are boss fights with interesting and unique tactics this time around, which felt genuinely fun to experience. It's just a shame this inventiveness never fully carries over into the rest of the puzzles and level design. Diablo-esque random loot systems have been introduced to spice up the game, but instead feels like a hollow grinding chore rather than an exciting "what will I get this time..." thrill. Changing a character's equipment will affect their playstyle (much like the first game), but this time feels more prone to chance with the random loot system than an honest progression.
The design choice of Egypt is pretty much a go-to when you consider forgotten tombs, gods and lost treasures, and whilst this may be lazy, it is well represented in the game. The story is terrible pulp schlock, whilst the first game was guilty of this too, at least it made it seem fun and like a guilty pleasure, here it feels lazy and tired.
If you're absolutely desperate for more isometric tomb raiding, this will certainly hit the spot, but it won't satisfy for long. It's a shame this game feels like a miss-step from Guardian of the Light, rather than the sequel it deserved.

If you’re familiar with Far Cry then it pretty much is that. Dying Light is an open world FPS heavily driven by parkour and adventure but with zombies.
Typical story here, Zombie Outbreak, Quarantined town and the best way to find a cure is to send someone in from the outside to find out what they know. However things are never as simple as get in, get out and there’s a bunch of stumbles along the way.
Like any open world game you can just do the story quests and get through the game pretty quickly or you can do all the side quests and grind for all the skill unlocks if you want to get the maximum amount of the lore and content out of the game. Personally when I play a game like this I go for all content so I got a total of 88 hours content from the game.
The base game itself has a lot of content split between 2 different maps as well as random events, challenges & loot areas. The story is pretty good and there’s lots of side content to explore like Quarantine Zones, Parkour Challenges & side quests that offer good rewards. There is a deep crafting system for weapons that allows you to modify and upgrade weapons to add extra effects like fire, bleed and toxic or add mods for damage, durability and handling depending on the rarity of the item will determine how many you can add. Later on there are guns and plenty of them so you can go full swordsman silent archer or soldier if you want.
The DLC "The Following" while not a very interesting story wise allows you to drive, upgrade a buggy and run over zombies in the country side. That alone is worth giving it a go. Though if your deal is story itself I don't think The Following offers anything over the original game to add to the story and can easily be skipped with no loss.
The Bozak Horde is a time based challenge mini DLC that acts kind of like SAW where you have to do what "Bozak" says in order to survive and you will earn rewards through each successful round. It only takes about 30 minutes to beat but in co-op it took us a total of 2 hours before we beat it. It's by far the hardest thing in Dying Light because of the variety of challenges you have to complete in a very small time frame not knowing half of what you are really doing sometimes.
You are rewarded with a special bow at the end but it’s pretty meh considered by the end of playing through the Following I already have golden shotguns, crossbows and assault rifles but it’s an extra to replace the existing bow so why not.

You know what this is? It's a game. I mention that only because the creators seem to think they have actually built a magical device that is a REAL racing experience. But it's not. It is a program on a computer, and frankly not a very good one either. The problem with so many of these "racing sims" is that the people playing them and the people making them will not acknowledge the fact that these are games, built for entertainment value. The view of the world from inside a car is a whole hell of a lot different from one sitting in front of a computer screen. The same rules don't apply. For instance, no matter how good a setup you may have you will never actually be able to feel the car tires start to lose grip. This is a very, very important part of driving that you cannot replicate. But let's be honest here; 99.9% of the people who play games don't have a wheel and pedals and a racing chair - it's just too expensive. Most people will be playing these games with controlers, and will only have a few hours at a time to dedicate to playing. It takes years to learn how to be a real race car driver, and frankly if the people playing these games could be racing car drivers they wouldn't be playing a frankly appaling port of their job. This is a game, but because the makers of this game refuse to admit that it is a game, it's not very good. Unless you are a harcore racing game fanatic, you will hate this game. if you are a hardcore racing game fanatic you will be playing something much better, like Project Cars. This is a game with no real dempographic, and it really shows. Lot's of technical detail, very little enjoyment. I paid $2 for a bundle of seven racing games and I guess this is a classic example of caveat emptor. I got what I paid for.

Even for early access this game is very rough. Runs like crap, unless you have really good hardware. Even going lower settings doesn't help with some hardware. I guess this would be an awesome game if you like to farm, farm, and oh yeah, farm some more. Killing things is a chore with melee. Good luck getting the public servers to recognize that you even hit anything. Ranged weapons are much more consistant, but it feels like mobs are a bit high in health. Even lower level mobs can have hundreds of health depending on what creature they are.
While offline my animal died, as something tore through my house, but somehow didn't kill my character. Not a huge fan of things being destroyed while offline. I have better things to do than babysit my stuff all day every day to make sure this doesn't happen. I think all of these survival games need to tone down on that. Sure, I get eaten while playing, fair enough, while offline is just lame.
The way you learn things in this game is utter crap. Farm certain materials to level the ability up, then you can start to learn them, but only after you also hit the level requirement. Starting out you can't build many things, so you have an overabundance of materials that you can't do much with. You can sell some to vendors (if they are alive) and if they are accepting orders. Apparently someone thought it would be cool to have a cap on just how much the NPC's would buy. Makes no sense when you could have up to 70 players trying to sell mats they don't need!
This game world isn't built for this kind of 'Ark' game style. It was an MMO world before hand, and is now being used wrong. Turning a once MMO into survival/rgp/mmo isn't really working at the moment for this game.
Until they fix the linear path of how to level characters and make it feel like you have more options other than killing or farming, and the ability to sell other things then what the NPC's want to buy, this game has lost my interest entirely.
EDIT: While I still have the same misgivings about this game, It's gotten funner. Although the issues above still persist. It seems the latest patches have made things even more laggy when moving across the map. Even a high-end i7 6700K / GTX 1080 Ti PC gets crushed by FPS drops while flying or moving around on land into new areas of the map. Even coming back through the same areas this happens. My Ryzen 1600, and friends i7 4770K PCs fair no better in these areas. Doesn't matter if you are using an SSD, or even have 32GB of system memory. Optimizations are in massive need to fix this almost game-breaking issue.
I would recommend waiting at this point. I can't tell if the game is ever going to get better. Or pick it up if it goes on sell for 10 bucks if you are that curious. Just be prepared for the FPS drops, they are quite significant and horrible.

This game, I really wanted to enjoy this game considering I always enjoyed ARK: Survival Evolved but preferred the fantasy genre, however, there are simply too many issues for me to continue playing at this point in time
I have to say, if you're a fan of melee combat this game is not going to be for you YET, the hitboxes on both creatures and especially gathering nodes such as Trees are abominable, good luck hitting that tree you're after. The best advice I can give you is just to take a run at the tree and wildly flail your axe around, that's probably the most efficient way of gathering in this game.
I understand that this game is in early access so I was prepared for the crashes and buggy gameplay, however, when setting up a server becomes a mini game of not letting the game randomly minimise and never reopen my enthusiasm starts to wane.
Considering this game is strongly based on ARK you'd think the devs (same company I believe) would have anticipated some of the many exploits that are rampant in this game so far. Congratulations on building a large iron base that is secure with locked doors, unfortunately, someone just stuck their dragons head through the solid wall and breathed fire on all of your hard work, which leads on to my other problem
Remember the big problem with ARK's official servers? you bet they flooded over the Dark & Light! enjoy spawning into an official server to be spawn killed repeatedly by 10+ Chinese players on dragons using macros and all the other cheats that are better explained on Reddit and the steam forums, oh, and if you really do manage to get past the spawn killing, have fun in the ghost towns of the island considering Official server's NPCs do not respawn, Yeah, the devs forgot to add in respawn timers for the vendors/guards/NPCs so have fun doing very little in town.
This one isn't a very strong point due to the game being so early however there has been a trend of the devs locking complaint threads with copy paste answers such as "It will be looked into" and then going on to provide in depth support to any of the Chinese threads which set a worrying precedent.
Assuming you can run the game on good settings, this game is very pleasing to the eye some of the spells look great and villages (at least from the outside) look nicer than ARK's box forts.
The magic system is arguably the reason I purchased this game, it looked fun in the trailers and it very enjoyable in this game when everything comes together and works the way it is supposed to.
Overall, I'd say that while this game looks nice and certainly could turn out like another ARK: Survival Evolved, depending on the Developer's response to critical issues and dedication this game could quite easily become another Reign of Kings, being left by the roadside. I do hope the game evolves into a more polished experience though and will be following its progress.

Graphics- 8.5/10

Managing everything can become a hassle at time, as I said you have limited scrap and supplies so you need to use them sparringly and prcisely on what you feel is best and when is best. This game isn't one you can really ♥♥♥♥ around in unless you're doing really well and can afford to. Other than that it's a very fun and challenging game and I feel that it's one that deserves a sequel if one hasn't been made yet.

The follow up to Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light, Temple of Osiris puts it back in control of our favourite archeologist, this time in Egypt.
The story centres around the Egyptian gods Osiris and his evil brother Set.  Set is attempting to take over (as per usual) and it's up to Lara and her helpers to collect the required items to build Osiris' powers and put a stop to Set.  Like Guardian of Light (GoL), Temple of Osiris (ToO) is co-op multiplayer, but this time you can play with up to 4 people instead of just 2.  The puzzles are there, the monsters are there (this time all from Egyptian mythology) and it plays just as you'd expect it to play.
If you enjoyed GoL then you'll enjoy ToO as well.  There are some great little cut scenes and once you've finished the main storyline you can continue playing in order to complete all the challenge tombs and pickup all the collectables you may have missed.
A great little game to play solo, but like GoL, it's much more fun to play multiplayer.

You control a character invading a dream loaded with mobs; what you need to do, kill mobs, is pretty straightforward. The game autofires and aims your main attack, which was a bit shocking to see at first, as I thought that would suck the fun out of the game. But, I feel this puts the shift mostly on tactical positioning and dodging. I wouldn't let that mechanic be a deciding factor in getting/not getting the game. You still do control two attacks; one character based and one that you can potentially find in the maps.
Speaking of maps, the game cycles you through various maps as you progress that have different enemies. The variety of enemies keeps you on your toes, but most are predictable and controllable in a small group. Maps will throw in obstacles to make fighting more difficult, too.
Special items can be difficult to find in the map itself, so the first floor may feel a little slow. Once you find a few items, though, the gameplay picks up and I personally become more bold in my attacks. But, unlike some similar games, I don't think this game relies too much on finding the right item combo. Sure, some items are good and stack together, but it's not a luck of the item draw on whether you make it to the end.

The night was dark.
It was not the normal darkness that resulted from the lack of light to illuminate the shadows,  it was the dark that suggested that the very concept for light had never existed before it. The kind of darkness that hid all manner of terrible creatures that the mind could only imagine, and even some beyond that. It was the darkness of the void that came before the light and the firmament.
Damascus wore it as a cloak around him.
Where other creatures hardly strayed far from the the light, his kind lived and even thrived without its warm touch. The light was as much of a stranger to him as the Yuctou Sea was to the lesser beasts of the Endless Desert. But he did not need the light to ‘see’. He observed all around him as he made his way through the forest by sound alone. He could hear ever chirp, every chitter, every rustle as the breeze blew through the trees. He could hear all manners of nocturnal creatures hunting their prey, just as he was.
He moved his feet deftly as he made his way through the forest, his feet avoiding any branch to break and leaves to rustle as he silently made his way closer towards the road that cut through the woods, and towards his quarry.
Odd, Damascus thought to himself as he caught sight of his prey.
The carriage had stopped in the road, surrounded by men with torches. From here he could hear their voices, geering and snickering.
“It’s a simple matter, gentlemen.” said one of men, “Pay the toll, and we let you walk away with all your innards staying where they belong, otherwise...” He was talking to the driver of the carriage who sat atop it, holding the reins of his horses , doing his best to keep them from panicking. The driver simply looked at the man, saying nothing. Brigands most likely Damascus thought.
“Maybe your ears don’t work,” he growled and began to speak louder, “I sai-” he was cut off as an arrow hit him in his chest. He sputtered and groaned as he fell to the ground. The other brigands around him didn’t have time to panic before they too were taken out by more arrows flying through the air. Not one missed their mark. Not one arrow didn’t result in a dead man.
Several men dressed all in black, wearing bows and quivers on their backs, approached the carriage and knocked on the side. Damascus was surprised he hadn’t noticed them before, but he knew his quarry wasn’t going to travel alone. He was content as they hadn’t noticed him either.
He was going to have to do this next part carefully, he thought to himself. He readied a stone into his sling, and starting to swing it, slowing picking up speed to make sure the sound didn’t travel far.
A portly man dressed in opulent clothes opened the door of the carriage and leaned out the side. “Is that all of them?” he asked one of the men in black. He nodded. “Good work. I’ll make sure your men receive a bonus once we reach Middlerei-” He stopped for a moment when he noticed one of the men in black turn towards the woods.
“Is something the matter?” he asked. One of the men had noticed Damascus, staring right at him in the darkness as he swung the sling. There was an attempt to scramble for a bow, but it was too late. He sent the rock flying at tremendous speed, hitting the portly man between the eyes. He slumped forward and hit the ground with a loud thud.
Damascus didn’t have time to celebrate his kill, though, as the men in black started to fire arrows at him. They were well trained, and perhaps could see well in the dark, but the forest was too dark to keep track of his moving form for long as he weaved through trees and brambles with deftness no human could manage. Many arrows came close though, some too close. He had to dodge one at the last second after hearing it whistling through the air towards him.
He had ran a mile through the trees before he could no longer hear the men chasing after him, safe once again in the comforting darkness, for now...

10/10 going to play again the moment I finish this review. The story was interesting, and the characters made satisfying choices. The gameplay was fun and even the travel became more fun as I progressed. Combat rewards a higher level of technical skill, while allowing those less skilled to merely scrape by. Immersive controls allowed me to lose myself in the story more easily than in other games. Be warned, starting off is a bit slow, but the game gains momentum as you progress.
Additionally and importantly the fact that guns are not necessary to complete the single player campaign was a huge green light for me. I went in expecting it to be way too shooter-ey, but was pleasantly surprised that the best way to hunt is to blend in and be quiet. The melee skills all have their place, and when they are used with camoflauge, sneak attack, and/or cloak potions your character becomes a whole new level of awesome. For those who want to shoot, enjoy. If you stay mobile the run and gun strategy works quite well, and you can come back later to pick up the loot if you so desire. If you prefer to hold your ground, be wary. Flares act as weak safe zones, and it is easy to be overrun if you do not take out enemies quickly enough. And ammo can easily run out before the night is through. If you prefer something a little more technical, bows are absolutely fabulous. Take into account wind and gravity while shooting your arrows and get headshots to maximize efficiency. For me, the hack and slash style is my main staple, with a little sneaky business mixed in.
The three basic skill trees grant enough points to gain every skill they offer, so prioritize your stats by what you want to try out first instead of worrying about what you will need end-game. The Legend skill tree is where a build is more important, as leveling up your legend rank takes infinitely longer than the basic trees. If you are playing the expansion, your driving rank is just like the three basic skill trees. I recommend leveling up the mechanic skills first so you have a better time keeping your buggy running, but in the end it comes down to whatever you want to try first as all skills will be attainable once you finish leveling the skill tree. I found the skill trees easy to understand and the skills themselves all added great aspects to the gameplay.
Now let's talk physics. The phsysics of the game are actually quite good. Apart from a few NPC glitches where they fall through floors on rare occasions, the game is smooth and sound. The gravity makes sense, as does the flow of motion and momentum. My criticism of the physics is that there is not a good deal of surface tension on the water, so jumping into water from heights has never hurt my character. But water is done well in the depth you sink after a fall. If you jump from a certain height, you sink proportionately deep upon impact. The grappling hook is a bit silly, as it's usually a straight pull instead of factoring in the player's current trajectory heavily. This means close calls can be even closer without dying, andswinging around things doesn't always work like it should.
Graphics wise the terrain is stunning. The weather is great. The sunsets are beautiful. The zeds are gruesome. And the NPCs are horrible potatoes that talk. It's easy to run on max settings, but if you have an older PC medium settings actually deliver an astonishing framerate. While low settings still look good enough, and run on just about any PC that isn't a calculator powered by a potato. To put a frame of reference on the game's taxation, my PC has an FX 8350, CM Hyper 212 EVO, PNY SATA SSD, 16GB of DDR3 1600 RAM, a Sapphire Nitro R9 390, and a Rosewill Photon 750W PSU. I hook it up to a 2560 X 1080p freesync ultrawide. The game runs smoothly at max settings with max view distance, but has the occcasional stutter once every few weeks if I leave too many background programs running. If I use medium settings with max view distance, my monitor never ever misses a beat for any reason.(even if I'm running videos in the background) I haven't tried streaming yet, because my PC is definitely not built for that. But your basic streaming PC should be able to handle it with ease. If you use a Ryzen 7, Ryzen 5, or an i7 CPU and an adequate GPU you shouldn't have a problem with recording or streaming while gaming on max settings.

Dying Light has become my favourite zombie game. You play as Kyle Crane, an agent who gets parachuted into a city called Harran that is having a pretty large zombie infestation. Company of Heroes 2 is, despite its many flaws, a very fun RTS and I love the game's core setting of the Easter Front of World War II (my personal favorite historical period to read and talk about as a history buff). There are significant mechanical improvements from the first game, the grpahics are better, the online (at least in my experience) is pretty stable, there is good unit variety, and more. However, there are some significant negatives. First off, the campaign is crap. The story is dumb and spends most of the time hammering in a message that the Soviets were evil. I mean, really? The Red Army were the heroes of the entire European theater of the war and are the primary reason for the defeat of Nazi Germany (similar to how the US was the primary reason/nation behind the defeat of Imperial Japan in the Pacific theater). Not once can I recall in the campaign story not trying to portray the Soviets as the bad guys; they never go into the attrocities the Nazis comitted. Instead they actually make up attrocities for the Soviets to comitt just to again make them seem evil. If the game is called Company of HEROES, WHY ARE YOU MAKING THE MAIN CHARACTERS LOOK LIKE THEY ARE EVIL? This is especially confusing given how in the previous game and expansion packs they made it quite clear that the majority of the Germans weren't evil; war is hell, there are no real good guys or bad guys. The main character is uniteresting and the ending is also really dumb. The Theater of War mode is fun and a good concept for a mode but to truly experience it all you are forced to buy DLC for it. Why, for a triple A game with a price to match should we have to pay more money to experience a complete package? That leads to another major fault which is all the major and micro dlcs present which they expect you to buy. It is wrong and it is absurd. Its hard to say wheter or not to reccomend this game as such. The setting is great and the gameplay is fun, but the story is trash and misuses its setting as well as being bogged down by the absurd amount of dlc one is expected to buy. Unless you are a fan of the setting and well tuned RTSs than I'd say skip it. If you were looking for a WWII game to delve into the Eastern Front of the war seriously then I'd recommend you to skip it.

Being a game released just after THQ filed for bankruptcy, it was initially released in the state you might expect. There are also many fair criticisms against the game, such as the one-sided narrative in single player, but looking at this game in 2014 combined with the current state of CoH1 (pretty much dead), I have to say this is probably not only one of the best ww2 games I've played so far, it's one of the best RTS games available today. It's not as polished and supported as other giant RTS alternatives like Starcraft 2, but when it comes to game mechanics, it's without a doubt one of the best.
There are a couple of main components that sets this game (and other THQ games like Dawn of War) apart from the others, you may have heard of them but I'll list them briefly:
1. Point-based resource "gathering". You don't have to gather any resources, period. The points you capture on the map gives you a certain income over time. Map control is therefore crucial, losing 75 % of the map at the beginning of a match gives you a significant disadvantage in unit construction.
2. Cover system. Putting your infantry in "yellow" or "green" cover will significantly increase their resistance to incoming fire. This forces player to play a "cover-to-cover" kind of game, which increases complexity. Cover can be natural (trees) or it can be constructed (sandbags). Cover can be run over and destroyed by tanks or artillery.
3. Scavenging. If your opponent has upgraded a squad with an extra weapon (anti-tank, MG), there is a chance that the squad drops the weapon in question. If you shoot out a tank, it's a chance you can re-crew and repair it. The joy of playing Soviet infantry, which by design is very cheap to build, and winning a match by capturing blown-out tanks, anti-tank weapons and machine guns is just indescribable.
TL;DR This is a must-buy if you like RTS games, and it's not your average RTS.
