I absolutely love this game. Actually, ever since the first Shelter game, I have been in love with the series. This isn't my first time playing such a game (there were one or two other mmos with similar things) but I believe Might and Delight pulled it off in a way that the others didn't. I am not usually one for MMOs but this is definitely the exception. Though no words can be spoken, I have met many new friends on this game. Now, as many other reviews say: don't come here looking for a survival game. This is not that. It is exactly what the studio says, a forum in game's clothing.
I’ve always loved the patchwork quilt style of textures and the more geometric, stylized animals. It was a breath of fresh air for me. And I can also say for certain, these games always strike an emotional cord for me in their simplicity and ability to make me care about the characters: be they the kits or pups, or other players on the MMO.
I only really have a couple of complaints myself. I recently bought the rest of the DLC I didn’t own in order to get the eagle. I love flying around but I really, really, really dislike that there are no other skins unless you reach the top 10. I don’t expect anything fancy but a few would be nice (especially considering I spent more just to have the eagle to fly). Even more than that though is that there is only one emote. I cannot communicate effectively with other players with that even when considering body language. The eagle lacks in almost all areas that the other animals don’t. I really do hope that they update that. I would at least love to have basic emojis and directional ones. Still, flying around is fun.
I would definitely recommend this game to others. It's fun getting in a large group to explore- especially when no one is left behind.

I'm going to start this off by noting that several other reviews seem to feel an early access game should be complete. They shouldn't, and this game is not. This review is of the game in its current state and takes into account that this game is currently being built. Simply giving a game a negative review because it isn't as playable as you want does not help people who want to know more about a game. So on to the review and off my soapbox.
DnL is a rework of a vaporware MMO and is being built on top of a familiar ARK groundwork. This is because DnL is owned by the ARK developers parent company. There are pros and cons to this. DnL is much further along than ARK was when it was released, but, there are some confusing settings (i.e. mention of dinos and tribes). The pros outweigh the cons in this situation since the developer can work on expanding the world and less time on recreating the wheel.
It should be noted that within 20 minutes of buying the game I did refund it. Why? Well I wasn't too crazy about the graphics at first and wasn't immediately willing to give it a try. Well, I am glad I didn't let my impulses get the best of me. I watched a few videos and ended up buying a copy for myself and my survival game bro. We now have our own server and have nearly 200 hrs combined in the game (he plays much more than I can).
In the games current state it does have some issues. There are tweaks that need to be made and there are flat out bugs that break some of the games features. However, no issue or bug makes the game unplayable to me. Some of these issues actually make the gameplay hilarious (with a few drinks) and help aide in our adventures. For example, the other day we decided to move our base and found a nice plot of land. We began work on our spikey walls and needed a massive amount of wood. Running through the forests chopping down every tree I could I came upon a goblin. Now, prior to the latest patch I could breath on these things and they would turn to mush. Apparently I missed the goblin buff and this guy knocked me the hell out, killed me, and took all my stuff. In what was meant to be a quick late night temporary fortress it turned into a chase across a river and into a gang of goblin buddies. My bro tried to come to my rescue, but, we were quickly overwhelmed. The tides have turned and goblins are running things now. 1-2 hits from their club lead to your doom. After changing our tactics (range spells) we were able to kill them off, but, not without losing our pride. Apparently pride isn't an item you can get back from a goblin treasure chest. This is just one story of the games current imbalances, but, if you keep your cool you can make the best of it. Oh, watch out for the reapers, skeles, griphons, and more than roam the noob area. Actually, theres not much of a noob area so grow some cojones before you play this game.
Now, beyond the bugs there is an absolutely gorgeous game with a variety of environments and gorgeous cities. The world itself is not even finished but what is available today is huge. There are plenty of details in the map and I can't wait for the caves and dungeons they are adding. I am a huge fan of the skill system because it actually makes sense. Gaining knowledge of particular abilities or recipes comes by actually doing related tasks. If you want to make a wooden house you gather wood. Why would killing creatures and gaining levels give you the knowledge to build a house? It wouldn't and this game implements a system that makes sense.
Over time I will add to this review but for now I am going to lay out the pros and cons of the game in its current state. Again, keep in mind the game just hit early access.
Pros:
- Beautiful environment
- Fairly developed game code (Based off Ark)
- Great skill system
- Awesome combat attacks/animations unique to each weapon
- Huge world (with more to come)
Cons:
- Bugs leaving some features (Crops for example) unusable
- Issues with server code causing rubberbanding and unhittable creatures/resources
- Wild/Tamed creature imbalances
- Weak melee combat damage
- Lack of "noob" areas
So, if you don't mind some feature breaking bugs, but, an otherwise fun and playable then DnL is for you. If you wanted a survival game with magic, dragons, factions, and more then DnL is for you. If you didn't, then just don't buy it.

"Please select the region where you reside."
(I forgot the exact wording, so I'm paraphrasing slightly) "Your selection will be tied to your steam ID and it will be permanent, you will not be able to change it."
So let me get this straight Capcom. Before I can play your game with other people from
, I have to be
in
location? "Come play with people you've never met before, so long as you're not going to go out there and meet them." What even? Well who cares? Many people spend their entire lives in the same country they were born in, so whatever, right? It's not like people, in the age of digitally interacting with people ACROSS THE GLOBE actually ever TRAVEL, do they? Well I'm sorry Capcom, but I am apparently one of that rare breed of people who do.
"Well so what's the issue? Just choose where you reside." The fact that they deliberately phrased it that way, rather than the common and ambiguous "Choose Your Region" is the problem. Here's a scenario:
-10 months out of the year you live and work in a foreign country (so if you're being physically present there that long, you are more than likely there on a
Permit).
-2 months out of the year you return home to the country of your citizenship, in which you have the status of a
(by whatever criteria that country determines residency).
-You haven't settled down, so you might actually move (perhaps home, perhaps to another country) once you are tired of working in the foreign country you've been working in for the past however long you've been there.
So where do you propose I choose as unchangeable place in which I am residing, Capcom? I mean really, the very Steam ID you link it to can be set to different regions, and yet I can never change my region for your game? Granted, this scenario likely does represent a minuscule portion of the players of this game, but it is, one: the case for every expat I've met here (anecdotal, I know, but still) and two: (in the general sense of people travelling the world but wanting to play their Steam games while abroad) a growing trend.
Now is this all semantic waffle? Possibly. But the complete inability I suffered to join any matches, whether my VPN was on, set to different regions, or off, testify to the validity of my frustrations. Though it could all just be that the Capcom Network itself is terrible at setting up matches, which would be another big issue in and of itself.
tl;dr "Play with people ALL OVER THE WORLD, but only if you STAY PUT, DAMN IT" - Capcom

Don't get me wrong, this is a very well-made game with excellent music, visuals, and strategic choice. Every game you play will be different...in a way. The ways to customize your set up for each game is varied with different map sizes and shapes and different civilizations to compete against.
When you take your first few turns you get a burst of excitement as you found your first city and begin to explore a brave new world wondering what might lie over the horizon. You obsessively click Next Turn as you plan out what victory you aspire for, where your next cities will go, and how you handle your neighbors who look at your lands with envious eyes. Perhaps you decide its WAR, the epic war music fills your speakers, and you pit your might against your opponent. You win your first big war and your civilization turns into an empire! This is perhaps the most fun bit of the game.
If the game could end at that point somehow I think you'd be missing little else because from there on the mid game turns into clicking things to turn numbers into bigger numbers. You click things and you make the numbers bigger and you rejoice! However after a million turns of this you begin to feel the tedium of micromanagement and the lack of meaningful reward. By the time you get to the end game you're just hurrying to wrap the campaign up already and by the time you do win you just get a little picture that says "Oh, you've won. Good job, I guess." Not to mention that if you play on Prince the AI is absolutely brain dead and if you play higher than Prince then the AI blatantly cheats to stay competitive.
It's for this reason that I can't really recommend this game. It's very addictive, yes, but for the majority of the game you're not enjoying yourself nearly as much as you did in the beginning. I think the addictive aspect is actually a detriment to the game because despite your inability to stop, it's not fulfilling anymore. Very well-made game just too time consuming for the limited satisfaction.

Pros:
-The game itself is good. It’s one of the major fighting franchises for a reason.
-It runs well. It’s a PS3/X360 game after all, and it had been optimized for a low-profile PC-based arcade board as well, so it runs perfectly with shadows on at 60fps at 720p and FXAA on machines below minimal requirements. Don't be fooled by the i7 requirement; if you can run other last-gen games fine then you can run this.
Cons:
-It’s a PS3/X360 game missing features from the PS4/XBone version, even stages. The only next-gen “features” are high resolution and true antialiasing, as if you couldn’t do that with any other game.
-No key rebinding.
-Actually, scratch that: when you plug a controller in and customize it, it DOES MESS with the key bindings as well. You got used to the default keys? Congratulations, now the keys have swapped just because you configured the buttons of a controller.
-DLC comes in big bundles only.
All in all, I’m enjoying the game and I don’t regret buying it, but this is a case where I honestly have to give a negative review because of the amount of disdain this port was done with.

So far I only played the single player campaign. The game is good for the most part: good tutorial, easy to understand, epic voice acting and atmosphere. The thing that ruined it for me though is the timed mission objectives.
Let me explain: the game is basically slow-paced with meticulous movement control of the ships. I mean just turning ships around takes like forever. The thing about timed objectives (like planetary bombardment, data recovery, or assasination) is that they need you to move too fast. For assasination or similar missions, at least you kind of know when the timer for the warp will start (when you damage the target ship heavily or steal the data or whatever), so you can kind of plan for it. But even if you do, there is no guarantee your abilities to stop the warp would work, and if it fails you kind of need to have a second ship in range with it's ability cooldown ready, and even then there is no guarantee. As for objectives like bombardment, you kind of need to know where the objective will appear before it does, else you probably won't be there in time.
Also unskippable in-game cutscenes are a problem, especially when you fail a mission..which is most of the time for me. For a game of such a slow pace and limited tools, the mission objectives feel like they're from another game..they're really not compatible.
TLDR: cool game but missions objectives often contradict game philosiphy and design.

Well mixed feelings about this game... about 7 hours into the campaign and the only way to survive is to save prior to each mission and replay if you lose... the allied AI is moronic... if you're not capable of micromanaging all of your ships at once you end up losing.. extreemly unforgiving gameplay on NORMAL mode.. here are some examples of the missions you get:
Assasination missions... you get only 2 minutes to kill a specific enemy capitol ship... it hides in the far corner and takes almost 2 minutes to reach while fighting through it's allies.. forget it..
Data recover mission: board an enemy ship to steal data and warp out... what they don't tell you.. boarding puts your warp out on cooldown... but not the enemies... you bord them, take the data.. moments later they board you and warp out before your ability to board them is off cooldown... lame.. and don't think about trying to board with another ship... we'll get to that..
Cruiser clash:  this one is fun... straight out slugfest.. likely cause there are no special rules for the AI's to mess up..
Convoy escort:  way to easy on the attacking side... almost impossible to defend... no fun here..
And now the worst part... the AI... these ships have no idea how to manuver or fight on their own.... example... my battlecruiser is sitting beside an enemy ship at point blank range... I order it to attack.. what does it do, turn tail and run... why?  cause it's inside it's 'engagement range'  and wants to be further out... and since none of the ships have guns in their rear arc... you have to constantly micromanage everything... commanding one or two of the larger ships would be massive fun... but constantly having to worry about a whole fleet who can't make the simplest helm ajustments to avoid mines, torpedos, asteroids, or even seem to manage to keep their guns on the enemy... just drives me mad...
Now you're probably wondering how this is a 'mixed' review when it sounds so bad..  Well I'm a major 40k fan and this game hits the atmosphere right... and in missions where you have a small number of ships and few or no goofy special conditions... the game can be quite fun.. Here's hoping they spend some time on fixing this game up..

Braid is a physics based puzzle platformer created by undeniable genius indie developer Jonathan Blow. In different levels, particular laws of physics are exhibited, making the player rethink reality
Is this game worth my time and money?
Braid is the best 2D puzzle game I have ever played. That includes everything that could reasonably fall under the category "puzzle." I'm not just talking about video games, I mean everything in existence. This journey will push your brain past were it has been evolutionarily programmed to go. When you first pick it up, you will be surprised at how easy it is to learn.
However, beginning to understand the more complex inner-workings of gameplay will abruptly force you to rethink this initial evaluation. This game is extraordinarily hard, but every drop of time invested will repay you in the form of intellectual conquest. Combine that with the fact that Braid is on Steam for a measly $9.99, including a free demo, and I would have to give this one a solid 10/10 for overall value. This score does not come easy, but I would recommend Braid to everyone I ever met ever.
Genre
Braid is a puzzle platformer, but it goes way beyond the call of duty. Jonathan Blow's intimate understanding of physics makes itself abundantly apparent within the first couple stages. At first glance, it looks like any other platforming game. Once you start to play it though, you will soon realize that it takes this genre to a previously unfathomable level.
Gameplay aspects like time-dilation, parallel time dimensions, and other physics manipulations make it almost a crime to lump this game in with a previously mundane genre. Many puzzle games have strived to achieve this level of excellence since Braid launched. We should thank Blow for pushing the boundaries of this variety of game.
Controls
On the surface, this game plays just like any other 2D platformer. You push right to walk/run, you hit a button to jump. It takes a literally negligible amount of time to learn how to control your new protagonist, Tim. The controls are exceptionally smooth. I experienced no issues with glitching or otherwise controlling the character.
Anyway, that's how the basic controls go, but that's where the similarities end. Soon after beginning the game, you are given a new action button, this one is capable of reversing time, and it is a chief aspect of gameplay, but more on that in the appropriate section.
Gameplay
You are kind of just thrown into gameplay. There's no tutorial or anything like that, but you don't really need it. Jon Blow gives you everything you need to know to beat the game through intuitive exploration. What very shortly becomes clear is that you are supposed to be collecting those tantalizing puzzle piece looking things. These pieces are only accessible by completing different perplexing aspects of the level.
There are going to be moving platforms and enemies that stand in your way, but the real hurdle is your own cognitive process. Once you collect a bunch of these puzzle pieces, you realize that you can put them together. The collectibles gained while completing puzzles are yet another puzzle, and a literal one. Its goddamn genius.
If you die, you can just rewind time. This becomes a much more important mechanic when the game introduces new physical properties and manipulations. These changes to your physical realm become increasingly difficult to rationalize. In one level, time is directly dependent your character's position on the x-axis. This effects everything in the game. If you stand still, so does time. If you walk backwards, time moves backwards. It is awesomely disorienting.
At a certain point, you are introduced to what I can only interpret as a visible parallel time dimension. Any platforms, enemies, or puzzle pieces that exist within this dimension are not subject to any of the temporal manipulations that are occurring in the dimension you are in. These objects exist within the same spatial dimensions as you, evidenced by the fact that you can physically interact with them. Further in the game, you are allowed to record multiple versions of your character in order to work collaboratively with yourself. It is a fantastically psychoactive experience.
Story
To disclose too much about the storyline of Braid would be a gigantic spoiler, and I'm not going to do that. I will say this, when you finish the game, everything you thought you knew about the story is shattered. Hopefully this isn't too much of a divulgence. During the first playthrough, all you really know is that you are in this castle looking thing, and there are doors that lead to fantastic worlds that challenge the ability to augment your thinking. There are references to a princess, you are apparently trying to reach her. She is, predictably, typically in another castle.
There's no real incentive to complete these puzzles other than your own intellectual drive, and some ambiguous text on these stone tablets about the princess and some haunting subjectively idealistic philosophy. Everyone seems to interpret these passages differently, which might be Blow's goal. It might be that there is a definitive interpretation and he just wanted to be playfully esoteric. Making things weirder, there is this underlying format of unwavering rationalism and calculation in the actual mechanics of the game. Perhaps he is juxtaposing these two realms, the true answer is beyond me, and he's not saying.
Replayability
As I previously alluded, when you replay the game, and I suggest you do at least once, you will understand a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ more about what is actually happening. You don't have to clear your save file and reset everything, all of the levels are repayable at any time. Just run through them again from beginning to end. The only bummer is that, in all likelihood, you will remember how to solve a good portion of the puzzles. The upside is that you can skip most of the regions that you already solved, since the puzzle piece will be in your inventory and not on the level.
You'll still have plenty of challenging puzzling to do since you probably missed a decent portion of them in the first playthrough. You will probably be able to find previously unfathomable solutions because of things you learned later in the game. This will give you something meaningful to strive for when you play through the levels again. There are many other hidden aspects of the game that you only realize after dedicating a considerable amount of time to the game, but I'm not going to spoil it for you. This makes the game engaging for many hours to come. Seriously, 10/10.

Go around to every "safe house", make it safe, and then complete a handful of "fetch quests" (that have zero purpose or impact on the game or world) surrouding that safe house while following a painfully bad written story (plot hole after major plot hole and + "it's a trap!... it's... ANOTHER TRAP!... ANOTHER TRAP!") and to top that off a half implemented parkour system (can only climb up, can't even climb down).
Take the combat, loot, and coop from Dead Island where you have a complex system of "force" (breaks bones) vs "cut" (severes limbs) with a multitude of fun ways to kill zombies, a bunch of unique zombies with their own strengths and weaknesses, massive loot grind on par with Borderlands/Diablo, and four player solid coop and shoot that with you "dum dum zombie gun" and you have Dying Light. No more "force vs cut" with a slew of different ways to kill enemies you are left using only a couple items (crossbow/bow, sword [or same class] and flares) as everything else is too weak or draws too much attention (noise makes "infected" spawn endlessly now... no seriously, ENDLESSLY- even in fields) so they NEVER get used. Unique zombies now "do it all", yes they climb, charge, spit/throw, ect! No more Left 4 Dead, Dead Island ect where you have unique zombies where if you know their weakness you can exploit that weakness (like dodging and slicing the "Ram" in the back for example) and have fun doing it- nope, just pull out your crossbow and shot them in the head before they insta kill you. Unique loot grind killing bosses or groups of enemies for drops? Nope! Get your DLC and insta get the best gear in the game and never change load out AGAIN! Fluid coop? NOPE! Every, single, cutscene forces players into a single area before you can continue with ANY quest (even those pointless fill in the blank side quests) and forcing them to watch painfully long cutscenes in which there is only a "main character" (no unique four players).
BOTTOM LINE TLCR
Is Dying Light a bad game? Hell no... Does it deserve a 90%+? OMG no... If you want a coop loot grind with zombies (Borderlands with zombies) you should pick up Dead Island and Dead Island Riptide as they are hands down, without a doubt better games... You want a parkour open world rich storyline and lore experience? Pick up the Assassin Creeds as they are without a doubt, hands down better games... You have already played Dead Island and Assassins Creed and hate them both? Run away from this game screaming... You love both Assassins Creed and Dead Island? You'll enjoy this game and find it worthwhile but in the end end up wishing that it could have done one thing great vs a lot of things mediocre.

This game was fun while learning it, but it has proven to be a massive undertaking of micromanagement.
1.  Your units have absolutely no sense at all.  Any tactics you try to employ have to be micromanaged at levels of minutia that are unreal.  Especially vehicles.  I don't expect the game to play itself, but when I have a tank providing overwatch and another tank or unit closes in on it, I would expect my tank commander to turn the tank and put the frontal armor plus coax downrange against the enemy.  Doesn't happen.  Infantry aren't much better.  Then try to use effective pursuit and exploitation or retrograde and delay tactics against the enemy and it gets really painful.
2.  While there are a variety of units overall in the game, the units are somewhat limited for each faction individually.
There aren't a lot of other singular faults in the game, but I will say the first one I listed makes for very frustrated play.  This is not a strategy game, this is a pure and simple tactics game.  It was fun while I was learning it, but once I got the hang of everything I realized that my tactics could easily be outdone by the stupidity of individual units.

This game might be good if you stick with it, but the combination of a very steep learning curve, low accessibility, and scarcity of useful items made me pass on this game. It's a punishing game, make no mistake. You will die, and often. You'll die because you got wounded during the initial encounter (no spoilers) and couldn't find any bandages, you'll die because RNGesus didn't favor you and you haven't been able to find any decent loot and now you're dying of hypothermia quite a lot because you start with only a hospital gown... and you can't take one from someone because they'll most likely have better stats and a cleaver when you only have a piece of broken glass and a handful of dirty rags.
The lack of a tutorial or even any tips on how to navigate the convoluted UI had me spending most of the time I have on record figuring out how to even play the game- I believe I spent about ten minutes looking for an 'attack' button during my first fight before I realized the game didn't tell me or make any indication that I was apparently too far away from my target. It's not a very intuitive system and you might have to turn to user guides to figure out how to even cook meat, because nothing is obvious and this game holds its mechanics like Gollum would the One Ring... the only difference being that this game isn't the one to rule them all.
I don't mean to rag on the game. I'm impressed that there are people that can not only survive, but thrive- and enjoy themselves while they do so. Finding loot and actually surviving for a bit is a very nice experience, but these moments are too spread out over a whole lot of dying. In my personal opinion, NEO Scavenger is just too difficult, too tedious, and too unfair to be enjoyable.

Probably the best turn-based strategy game I've played. I bought XCOM during the autumn sale, thinking I might find some enjoyment in playing it, but now that I've invested almost 30 hours into it, I wouldn't have regretted buying it for the full $39.99 price.
Personally, I think it's amazing. It's so in-depth - everything is thought through. For a turn-based strategy, a format that you wouldn't expect to have any depth, this game has a developing storyline that keeps you wondering, scientific research descriptions and interesting character interactions in cut-scenes, and I've personally found that I get so emotionally attached to the characters in the game. The soldiers in my squad aren't just units on the screen, they're people, with their own personalities and special abilities. They each contribute to the team in their special way, and even though the game doesn't GIVE them personalities, they are somehow still formed just by playing the game and using your imagination.
The graphics are very nice, the interface is complex, but easy to learn and adapt to, and the turn-based battle field is multi-tiered and very fun to play in.
I would STRONGLY RECOMMEND this game. 10/10.

That being said the game certainly feels ARK inspired, but adds a whole other new level of mysticism and uniqueness which is what I've been looking for. I hope that the game continues development and surprises me just as ARK did.
I'll be watching this and a few other titles closesly. It's up to those of us that purchase these types of games to give honest reviews and to tell the future consumers of the health and overall condition of the game, I will certainly be checking the pulse on the game and I hope everyone else does the same.
So, let us dive into the game itself.
Dark and Light is a very easy game to jump into. If you know survival games you should have no problem when exploring and getting a feel for the world. What this game does right is create atmosphere and I found myself saying "Wow" a lot more times than I have in the past with these types of games and even with ARK overlays and feelings the title still feels like it's one of it's own. Certainly it could be a runner up next to ARK with more updates to the game itself. The spells, creatures and schematic system is also unique as is a lot of other aspects to the game. Take for example skills as a whole, in other survival games you spend points or find schematics and have to sacrifice the access of one item for another most of the time, however in Dark and Light you do not have to choose to be limited to that. Everything is on a leveling basis, if you want to have a schematic in a certain area all you have to do is level that area up and you automatically acquire the building right. This means that you could go out, explore and get resources and level up things without you even noticing. And it's not at all slow, the EXP to level ratio is quite balanced which surprised me for an early access game. It feels more fluid and more fun this way, to turn off your head and see wherever or whatever you can find before starting up your little home.
All in all, Dark and Light feels like home. It feels right and it's refreshing to see that the survival genre isn't locked in cash-grabbing purgatory.
I hope to see this game thrive and do well. I have a feeling that if more work is done, more spells are added and more areas and maps to explore were to appear that this game could be the next big thing.

I often read reviews by people who say a game is "broken" and suspect they were just unlucky. Well, if this is the case, then I and my friend were both spectacularly unlucky! This really does seem to be broken.
We bought the game to play cooperatively, online, on two machines with different specs. Both were well above minimum spec, and yet the issues we found were:
* Game displays black screen instead of menus etc. (one machine; found a work-around on the forums - this seems to be a common problem)
* Painfully slow frame rate (both machines, frequently)
* Cut scene dialogue gets out of sync (one machine)
* Cut scene dialogue refers to plural people when addressing single person (both machines, single player)
* Game inserts second character into game for no apparent reason (seen once, one machine)
* Game ceases to recognise XBox360 controller (one machine, once)
* Control of characters sluggish (both machines, always)
Those were all encountered in "2 hours" of "play". When I say "2 hours" of "play" I actually logged 29 minutes playing, and spent the rest of the two hours online looking for solutions to these problems (only one viable work around to one issue found in that time - not a good use of an evening.)
This game is *great* as an explanation of why a lot of people pirate games before purchasing them - publishers do themselves no favours releasing games this "temperamental" (tactful description) and Steam does itself no favours selling it.
Whether it's great (or even good) in any other sense, we couldn't say, as it was basically unplayable on both machines.

I've played a few rogue-like games (Rogue Legacy, Dwarf Fortress, Don't Starve) and have embraced the notion that "losing is fun."  This takes a bit of getting used to, when so many push you through a story and drag the game along as a mechanic of "do this part, and now you can go forward."  Now, that can be fun, don't get me wrong.  Games can be a form of storytelling, and indeed there is a sense of accomplishment when you actually complete something.  But if you're playing FTL to win, you're probably doing it wrong.
FTL is somewhere in the middle of the absurd pointlessness of games like Dwarf Fortress (you can never win, but you do a little bit better each time) and games like Rogue Legacy (Cool, you got 10,000 gold this run... you're going to be so much stronger for your next run).  You can actually win FTL.  That last sentence hits home the real point of a game like this: it's not about winning, it's about doing well.  This can be difficult to see when there is a forward direction to reach, a ship to upgrade, and an actual final boss encounter.
Several of my friends who also play some Rogue-likes note that they are frustrated by investing a great deal of time into something where the random number generator just deems your game impossible to win.  I agree, that sucks.  FTL suffers from this problem: sometimes there's just not enough scrap to make it work, sometimes they throw a crazy hard oponent at you right at the start, and if you're interested in winning you're better off restarting if you can't make certain milestones by, say, the third sector.  FTL does, however, require a great deal of strategy to make work, and part of that strategy is being very adaptive.  This is why, say, Don't Starve gets boring quickly because you end up trying to invent ways to make the game interesting after easily mastering survival.

I am not a shoot 'em up fan. I know that's not the best way to start a review, but hear me out. The genre leads to more frustration than any other for me, so I was hesitant to pick this game up. As far as downsides, there are occasional asteroids that are rather unpredictable and very hard to maneuver through. Shooting helps, of course, but they can divide and ricochet wildly. This did add to the tension though, so it most certainly was not an unwelcomed challenge. I really enjoyed the power-ups and that they come organically through gameplay, which I feel allows the player to focus on staying alive, not worrying about controls. The power-ups can actually have perfect timing, aiding in tight spots as enemies become stronger, more agile, and more erratic. I would most certainly recommend GalaxIverse to anyone, even players like myself that avoid or ignore the genre. A really nice thrill of a game.

Saints row 4 is a crowning achievement (Better then the third, that's for sure!)
PROS-
*The super powers really help set this game apart (plus, who doesn't like juming five buildings?)
*The writing for the story and characters are out standing, getting (mostly) rid of the stupid dirty joke garbage the third saints row had. The villiam has great writing, I can't press this enough, it's just so good!
*THe humor is pretty good, whether you're climbing a nuke, or you're in a 60's sitcom, you'll get a laugh out of this game.
*The graphics (on max settings) weren't improved by much, but they still look pretty good.
*A bunch of the side mission/activities are extremely fun to play (fraud being my favourite)
*optimisation is extremely good in the single player
*There's a bunch of gun custimisation, you can make your pistols into robo cops gun!
CONS-
*Gunplay seems to be just an after thaught in this title, the game kind of expects you to just use your super powers, which is nice and all, but I like scoring 5 headshots in a row with robo cops gun.
*While there is alot of gun custimisation, it all seems reduntant once you get super powers, which is a shame because there are some really cool skins for your guns (the pulse rifle, for example)
*Just like guns, cars become obselete once you get your super powers, this is made worse by the fact that the new/improved car custimisation system is awesome! Unfortunately, the game basically punishes you for using cars.
*Like many people, I believe the game gives you super powers far too early. If they had given them to you perhaps half way through the game, this would help with the redundancy of the cars/guns.
*co-op is LAGGY!!!! It's seriously un playable at times, if you want this game for co-op, you have been warned.
MIDDLE-
*They basically re used the same map from saints 3, and added a few things here and there. I don't really hate that, I mainly just thought "after you guys decided this would be a full game, couldn't you at least give us a new map to run around in??"
VERDICT--
Saints row 4 is a worthy addition to the saints row franchise, it has great humor, addicting gameplay amongst all the other great things about this game. There are a few problems, but they don't really take away from the experience or the fun to be had here. Unfortunately, this is basically the last game in the franchise, I suppose it's good it ended on a good note then!
I would definately reccomend this (I don't use a number system because it's flawed)

is an intense game, almost nerve-wracking at times, but generally rewarding as you plan and fight your way through droves of alien invaders with a variety of classes, equipment and abilities. You might find yourself save-scumming (reloading saves for better results), but that happens to the best of us. The game will push you to take risks and deal with consequences, both in long-term strategy with base, crew and international management, and in short-term with tactical combat. While lacking in a few aspects such as a deeper plot, and leaves some optimization work to be desired,
will get your tactical thinking at full throttle for a steady incursion of (sometimes brutal) enemy forces.
Notice this review covers the base game content plus DLC and the
expansion pack as one product.
Developed by Firaxis and 2K Games,
is the first in a series of reimaginings of the classic strategy game
(also known as
in some regions). Directed by Julian Gollop, the award-winning game gives the player the control of a secret elite military organization called XCOM: the E
traterrestrial
bat Unit. After the confirmation by XCOM that a series of freak incidents spread worldwide were the first few units from an alien invasion, the unit deploys with full force to learn, adapt, and fight against the alien menace. As the Commander of XCOM, the player must train their soldiers, expand their base, respond to alien activity, adapt and make the alien technology our own, and drive away the enemy invaders.
In 2015, after the occurrence of several mysterious incidents of alien nature, the XCOM Project is activated by an international Council of Nations. Its objective: to study, reverse-engineer and neutralize any alien threats to humanity, led by a single officer only referred to as "The Commander", introduced into the operations center "Geoscape" by Central Officer John Bradford, the main co-coordinator of XCOM alongside The Commander. In XCOM HQ, The Commander meets Dr. Moira Vahlen; the science team lead of XCOM, and Dr. Raymond Shen; the Chief Engineer of the unit.
The invasion starts out rather subtly, with minor localized incidents of alien activity mainly perpetrated by the archetypical alien "grays", dubbed Sectoids in the game. Over time, the continued resistance of human forces causes the aliens to take steps by deploying units containing several alien species and mechanized units with more aggressive, war-like behavior and role.
If XCOM's prove successful, the integrants from the Council of Nations remain with their continued support to the project, with additional crew and funding as rewards. Should XCOM fail to provide the Council nations with proper defense against the alien threat, the panic among the populace rises beyond repair, all ties and support towards XCOM being cut by the nations leaving the project.
Through the course of XCOM's operations, an alien-sympathizing shadow group referring to itself as EXALT emerges, publicly encouraging the nations to surrender to the aliens and hand over control to them in exchange for their technology and guidance. However, EXALT is in fact a militant armed group, actively disrupting XCOM operations throughout the globe. With the EXALT threat causing unease in the worldwide populace, XCOM is tasked with taking down its leaders.
As the invasion progresses, XCOM discovers the leaders behind the attacks against Earth -- a mysterious alien species only known as "The Ethereal Ones". Being the heads of the invasion, it is first imagined they came with the intent of wiping out humanity or conquering Earth. However, their purposes towards humanity are revealed to be something else...
The combat aspects of the game are played in a tactical turn-based-strategy format over four difficulties and the option for an 'Ironman' mode (disables reloading past saves of a game; decisions are permanent), with players controlling their squads throughout the maps and positioning them in 'tiles', coordinating their instructions and attacks. Cover is paramount in the game, as exposed soldiers are guaranteed to take additional damage. Should a soldier's health ever fall to zero, the soldier can either be knocked unconscious into a 'bleedout' timer (to be possibly stabilized or revived during the mission, or evacuated with the surviving squad members if the mission is completed before the soldier bleeds out). If the soldier does not enter bleedout on health depletion or has the bleedout timer exhausted, they are permanently killed and removed from the roster.
Attacks in XCOM: EU are made using percentage-based chance rolls based on the attacker's "Aim" stat, with an additional roll for critical hits with additional damage. The chance for a target to be hit is increased or lowered depending on conditions such as the presence of cover, the distance between the attacker and the target, the target's base defense value, their specific traits, relative height of position in comparison to the attacker, etc. Targets can receive increased damage depending on whether or not they are in cover, being flanked, or through special attacks and traits from soldiers and aliens alike.
In some cases, missions are preceded by "Interception" segments. In this mode, XCOM launches their interceptor aircraft in order to shoot down enemy UFOs that are detected through satellite networks. If the interception is successful, this will prompt a mission for clearing the UFO crash site and potentially acquire new technology from the downed UFOs.
At the Geoscape, the players can manage the base by constructing additional facilities for XCOM HQ, selling unnecessary supplies at the "Gray Market" for extra funds, managing XCOM's Interceptors, creating and equipping new weapons and equipment for their soldiers, customizing their squad members, scanning for alien activity and deploying missions.

Don't get me wrong, this is a very well-made game with excellent music, visuals, and strategic choice. Every game you play will be different...in a way. The ways to customize your set up for each game is varied with different map sizes and shapes and different civilizations to compete against.
When you take your first few turns you get a burst of excitement as you found your first city and begin to explore a brave new world wondering what might lie over the horizon. You obsessively click Next Turn as you plan out what victory you aspire for, where your next cities will go, and how you handle your neighbors who look at your lands with envious eyes. Perhaps you decide its WAR, the epic war music fills your speakers, and you pit your might against your opponent. You win your first big war and your civilization turns into an empire! This is perhaps the most fun bit of the game.
If the game could end at that point somehow I think you'd be missing little else because from there on the mid game turns into clicking things to turn numbers into bigger numbers. You click things and you make the numbers bigger and you rejoice! However after a million turns of this you begin to feel the tedium of micromanagement and the lack of meaningful reward. By the time you get to the end game you're just hurrying to wrap the campaign up already and by the time you do win you just get a little picture that says "Oh, you've won. Good job, I guess." Not to mention that if you play on Prince the AI is absolutely brain dead and if you play higher than Prince then the AI blatantly cheats to stay competitive.
It's for this reason that I can't really recommend this game. It's very addictive, yes, but for the majority of the game you're not enjoying yourself nearly as much as you did in the beginning. I think the addictive aspect is actually a detriment to the game because despite your inability to stop, it's not fulfilling anymore. Very well-made game just too time consuming for the limited satisfaction.

I really REALLY want to enjoy this but in it's current state it sort of stresses me out. I'll admit some of the problems are probably my fault and some are just my personal tastes getting in the way.
Pros:
-Can be peaceful and relaxing and a nice time killer.
-Nice Music and in some places nice atmosphere
Cons:
-No instructions at all. Personally I've never been a fan of games just dropping you in pants or not, while you stumble around desperately trying to figure out what the game expects from you. After I while I began to understand what the game wanted from me but hell-- SOMETHING would have been nice upon opening the game; a simple "Go find the sparkles! Use WSAD to move!" would have been nice. I'm also not a fan of games that seem to favor using as little words as possible; as far as I could tell there was no chatbox and you could only communicate to others thru emoticons and symbols and even the map and inventory was barren of words.
-Not a fan of tank controls. Probably an unpopular opinion and one that I know is again a personal preference, I would have liked an option to change it, personally.
-The style was one of my biggest gripes to me personally. Everything has this weird rug pattern on it that I feel makes everything hard to make out-- I found myself squinting constantly in an attempt to figure out where a mountain, rock or animal start and stopped. Everything just kind of muddled together and was kind of unappealing to me. Maybe a highlighted outline around animals and trees would help? I don't know. It's not something I expect them to change since it's obviously a stylistic choice, but I think it's worth noting.
-The game crashed on me about 4 times within an hour. I have no clue why.
-There was also a few times I seemed to keep getting stuck on nothing? Tho I admit this might just be me getting stuck on something that I can't really make out because of the style choice or the fact that I'm not good with tank/wsad controls, so take this con with a grain of salt.
If you've played Endless Forest or Journey and liked both of them you'd probably like this one. However I personally had the same problem with this game as those two games. Lack of objective or any proper explanation in games tend to frustrate me and it tends to go downhill from there for me personally. So if you didn't like Journey or Endless Forest you also might not enjoy this game.
PS - I plan to pick up this game again at some point in the future and give it another go, hopefully the crashing has been fixed and looking on it with fresh eyes might make me enjoy it more. I can't be too upset with this gamer tho because of it's price. This is a gentle 'not recommended' that I know is partially based on taste.

1) Technical
2) Matchmaking
3) Network
4) TimeZone
Technical
There seems to be a small delay and small issues at launching the game. But once that gets out of the way I am greeted with a new problem. The game shuts down at around a quarter of an hour in? Maybe more? Not sure as I had enough time to forget about it before the program stopped again.
At 61 minutes which was my first session the game closed probably 3 times I think, maybe 4. So that is indeed around 15 to 20 minute log-ins.
Disconnects and the game crashing never took place at irrelevant moments or during fighting. It happened mostly after a fight and once before 1 fight (so that would have been 1 more fight I could enjoy). So I am assuming something with the loading and syncing between sections in the game.
It also has no re-connect? On the match I lost connection (before it got me in, when it says a New Challenger thingy thingy) I rebooted the game in less than a minute and noticed there was no re-connect option which given the time delay the game load up has would be an option that could be there if you reconnect straight away. On the other hand it could create more problems in waiting as the opponent had to wait for the match and then has to wait for a reconnect too? Perhaps a choice would be nice there, the likes of "wait for opponent to reconnect". Which would still be faster than waiting for a new match.
Matchmaking
In that time I was able to play against 5 people (3 ranked 2 casual, or I think 2 ranked 3 casual?). And from that 1hr I was fiddling about with settings often, checking out the profile and other profiles, as well and taking little breaks between each "search match" was on the way. So I would say I was around 30 minutes idle (not searching for match, casual or ranked).
This brings us to 5 matches in about 30 mins that being an average of 1 match every 6 mins. The wait times at this point I would estimate at around 3 mins? Which would be ok I guess though the wait does feel a little large since the matches might not last too long. Compared to other games the matchmaking time is ok. And it does seem to match you with same ranked people so you can't take to account all the people that are online.
With a little AFK and alt-tab I actually did not mind that much those wait moments passed rather fast.
Network
My location is Greece, which does not have the best pings out there or fast internet compared to the rest of Europe. The matches however were responsive enough with 4 out of 5 being good to exceptional.
Especially for my connection which is thanks to the neighborhood quite slow (4mb/s max and a crappy upload). I also play from time to time SF3 with GGPO and I have to say that SF5 felt MORE consistent and stable than that for my connection. 1 or 2 matches actually felt the best I have experienced online.
The locations it pitched me with were Spain, Austria and 2 from Germany and 1 more I think I can't remember. The only connection that had stutter and sync issues was 1 match from Germany.
So I was pleased on that end, can't expect too much with my location and I was in fact surprised with the performance. I don't think SF4 was as good for me. Sure many of you say SF4 reaches better network quality, and that is probably the case for better connections. SF5 seems to be doing something that also helps lower end connections though, and that is good as it means more people to play with.
Timezone
This annoyed me a lot. The game opens up at 11:00pm here and closes at 10:00am? Seriously? And UK that is 9 to 8 in the morning? What kind of testing is that? The EU region is pretty much overnight. I know its hard with 1 time gap to cover all regions but it seems we got the worst end of it all. Someone will miss out on the better time sure, but it just feels unbalanced. Give or take some hours here or there would really fix this by shifting it 2 hours in the one or other way.
I mean US west is 1 afternoon to 12 at night, US east is 4 afternoon to 3 at night (best time table all around thanks for screwing the EU region once more like that) and even Australia is running at 7am to 6pm. Japan at 2am to 4pm is also a lot better taking the morning to afternoon.
This time should be rotated so the peak hours are all around, not in ONE region only. That is silly.
So far this BETA seems to be doing things good. I like it.
And yeah I know, matchmaking is still long. It always will be people. Have some bloody patience and understand how matchmaking works. There is the same amount of matchmaking wait time in most games out there and more. It needs a much larger audience to have faster matchmaking times so don't complain about the system at that point. The problem is the player capacity, not the system. At which point, simply be patient and enjoy the game with the community that is. The rest of such complaints sound spoiled and selfish. Not to mention regional time differences. You wont ALL be online at the same time so chillax.
As for all those whining about no single player and training and offline mode... And not recommending this beta for that reason. You people are all kinds of special aren't you? Bottom dwellers I assume that simply wanted to play the game for free. No-one that purchased the game would be complaining about such nonsense since they have all offline content.
And no sane and self respecting person would complain about sh!t not relevant to what the test is. That being, THE NEW NETWORK. Long story short, get a life the lot of you or shoot yourself in the face. Pick one.
Verdict
Thats pretty much the gist of it all. The stability of the game itself is not what it should be, but I assume this will be fixed as the normal version to the game does not experience such problems. The network performance during matches seems to be there. I need more time to test it ofcourse, but 4 out 5 matches at good performance from a crap connection stands at a good 80% stability which is more than I can say for both SF4 and SF3GGPO from my location and PC.
Matchmaking is timely, sure, and it should be as it does not slap you against experienced players. Casual or ranked, I noticed it pup you up against same rank players. I think casual could get away with mixing ranks a little more. I mean its casual. It could be a great tool to learn the game and have some unexpected matches against all ranked players. This could decrease matchmaking times.
The regional time the game is available for Europe is abysmal and pathetic really. Again 2hrs + or - would fix this and balance it out (adding to a mid day time or earlier night time availability) so all regions are half and half, not 1 region gets the best of it and the rest need to work around the clock. That is bs and for a test that is based on playing against others, really, how many people you think are online 12:30 at midnight on a working day???
I did not notice also a fix (I could be wrong) to onw of the complaints I see out there all the time. That you can't select matchmaking by flag or region. And thank god you can't. This is a competitive title. Ranking up by playing in your country alone cannot relate to the overall ranking of Europe or world or whatever. People that complain about this really I have no idea why they are complaining. Set the match quality to high (4-5 I think is it?) and you are good to go. Want to play with people from your country alone? Create a damn lobby. Simple.

Meadow is a cute, lovely game that makes you feel all around happy about the world. While it does not have a lot of "gameplay features", it is lovely to run around your fellow anonymous animal companions that you know for a short amount of time. It is refreshing to play a game based around communication - but yet has little means to do so. - as you play as an animal that can only show it's emotions and thoughts through basic emotes and signs. Yet, I have never felt more accepted in a 'game' as in meadow. No matter what you are - you can always join a running pack and more likely than not you will be needed when it comes to obelisks. It most certainly is a nice game to escape the general mainstream games and stop worrying about a general objective - or about being better than the others. Meadow is all about letting go of this idea and relaxing in a world with beautiful artwork and a friendly group of animals who - just like you - don't have any idea of who anyone is, where they're from or what they're like. (While their is a "peek" function to check people's steam names - this is easily turned off/avoided if you prefer this).
In my first adventure, I got stuck at the bottom of a cliff. I thought my group was long gone, but when I got up - they were all still waiting for me. The friendship in this game can move mountains - or at least give each other the patience to wait till you all get on top of it.
I would 100% recommend this game however, to anyone who likes these types of games. This is my first shelter game and I'm definitely happy I gave it a shot.

I love this game. Every attempt is a different adventure. It's fun even if you lose, since you get to learn that giant alien spiders are not truly a joke or that you should've fortified your doors when treading on mantis territory. This is a game where you have no idea on what you were doing in your first run, then get better, and better, and better as you play again. Don't be put off with losing - at least you know that you should've put out the fires sooner. As the game itself says, losing is part of the fun!
It can even be played on short bursts, or with one hand (which you use the other for eating snacks; it's a great setup). But despite its simplistic artstyle, you can get immersed in your adventure pretty quickly, and then you'd spend more time than you expected.
It's easily accessible, it's aesthetically pleasing, it's immersive, it's got a lot of content for its value, it's got a head-bobbing soundtrack, it's pretty difficult on the first run, and it's great. Don't be shy to play this on easy - I myself haven't beaten this on normal, either. I may try again once I reach 100 hours or so.

This is a bullet hell roguelike game with occult and satanic themes.
Pros:
-Decent variety all around--player characters, items, regular enemies, bosses, etc.
-Cool item design (except potions)
-Appealing art style, looks great
-Great thematic music and sound effects
-Interesting use of colors/visual effects as a difficulty mechanic (possibly also a con?)
Cons:
-Sometimes overwhelming amounts of layers of simultaneous visual effects, such as color inversion, fog, screen shake, blurring, heightened light bloom, screen rotation, and weird symbolic overlays. When a lot of these are happening in the game at once, and when you include constant bullets flying at the character from all directions, it can be difficult to see what's going on much less keep track of your pink hitbox (especially on the arcane level, where the entire background is a shifting purple light pattern)
-A few minor intentional design annoyances--for example, for a game that encourages speed (which is the case because of level timers and other mechanics), Deathstate employs way too many enemies that drop or shoot lingering fires, forcing the player to wait
-Gold/merchant system is boring and useless most of the time
-Potion system is also boring and doesn't seem to pay off too much unless you're a Scientist
-Difficulty is pretty solid, but I feel like the level timer hinders player exploration too much in later levels
Overall I feel this is a well-crafted game that is fun to play, and I can definitely recommend this to anyone who likes bullet-type games and roguelikes such as Binding of Isaac and Nuclear Throne.

Story is deep. I was surprised that a puzzle game could have such a good story. You play as Tim, an individual who is looking for a princess who has unfortunately been captured by a monster. It's not a plot which openly tells you what is going on per se, rather there is quite a bit of ambiguity (especially the ending which is good), which leaves the player to reflect on what is actually going on. Many themes play out in the story including desire, regret and making up for mistakes.
Gameplay is great, burrowing elements from Mario. Each stage pits you on one end of the map, trying to reach the end on the other side. Stages are unique, with different puzzles and goals to reach in order to pass, such simply reaching the end, eliminate all foes, using keys to open doors etc. Similar to stars in Mario, each level has a selected amount of puzzle pieces to collect. Each, piece collected helps to complete a picture which provides some incites to the story. There are platforms you can reach by jumping on them. You can also defeat foes by jumping on them and avoid traps by jumping over them. The only enemies are giant head things which walk around and may jump to different platforms (which reminds me of Gumpas). There are also traps such as pitfalls, spikes and canons.  You only have 1 life, so a single collision between a 'Gumpa' or trap will kill you instantly.  Fortunately, death doesn't end the game, instead this is the part where you make the most of your 'Time control' power. Reminiscent of 'POP Sands of time', you have the ability to reverse the flow of time, sending Tim back before his current predicament. Besides using it to save your life you can also use it to solve puzzles, by stopping time to allow  you to think of a plan or moving back objects to obtain items. Some puzzles may leave some guessing and frustrated, however with some patience they can be solved easily (or just use a guide).
Soundtrack is amazing. The music is very calm, with sorta 'Irish tune to it', and something you can listen to calm yourself (which especially helps with some of the puzzles). Sound effects are also good. there is no voice acting in the game, with the story told through text.
Graphics are excellent. The 2D-art style is vibrant and detailed. It is quite attractive and fits perfectly for the game.
Besides the main campaign, there is also 'speed-run' mode which is unlocked  after beating the game. The mode tests how fast you can get through certain stages in the game.
If your looking for a good story and don't mind some platforming and puzzles, Braid will show you how brilliance can be formed in a simple indie game.

I won this game at PAX East, when I drew a game key card out of a box. I had played it a little bit, and discussed it with the developer, and was pretty happy to grab a copy to play some more later. I'm glad I did, but I probably would have bought it regardless. Being a fan of Binding of Isaac, and other dual-stick shooters, I was interested in the prospect of a single-stick shooter, allowing you to concentrate more on the bullet-hell aspects of the game, and worry less about the accuracy of your shots. I also loved the core art design. Anyway,
PROS:
-Soundtrack is really good background music. Haunting and atmospheric, very appropriate for the setting.
-Creature design. A lot of games like this tend to stray when it comes to mob types, and the game feels less procedural. In this case, every new game feels like a new game.
-Rouge like/lite. I guess this is only a pro if you're into that.
-Control scheme. Feels very natural on a gamepad.
-Environments always feel mazelike, but you never feel lost. The timed mechanic makes great use of this.
-Lore is enriching and intriguing to get into.
-Unlockables!
CONS:
-When health is low, there's a harsh graphic overlay, so if you're doing poorly, it's only going to make it worse. I suppose it does, however, encourage you to play better.
-Impassable objects difficult to see. There are many corners and walls in the maps that are sometimes not clear. While I've appreciated the challenge this brings, it's sometimes rage inducing.
-HIt box unclear. Dodging the green bullets seems like a no-brainer, but the hit box seems to be centered around your characters midsection, able to pass through the head without harm.
Overall, this is a great game that could have handled some of the finer points better, but I still highly recommend it for any dual-stick shooter fan who also loves a good rogue like/lite.

Company of Heroes 2. The strategy game with intense WW2 action, a good physic engine and cool gameplay mechanics.
COH2 features a new weather system. Your infantry can turn into ice bricks in a few minutes, if you don't manage to put them into a building or vehicle. The other option is to make a fire. So infantry is bad on snow maps? No! Tanks can sink into rivers or seas, if you break the ice. This possibilities open new tactics. Your positioning is the key to win the battle.
The game is a good sequel of the first COH. It features a Russian campaign and now a US campaign as DLC. They will add more armies and story DLC in the future.
You still need to take care of sectors to earn resources and push the enemy back at home. A combination of infantry, tanks and artillery will do the job. But beware of the terrain and keep moving. Burrowing into the snow to make some defence lines will only delay the assault. Attacking is your best choice. You can't build defence anymore like in COH1. So the game gets more action. For some people this is good, for me it's bad. I enjoy long and heavy front battles. But this isn't possible in COH2. Sadly.
The infantry is searching for cover and can jump over fences now. Due the vision system of the game, it can happen, that behind the fence is an enemy. So look first, jump after that. Tanks have different hit zones and need to be managed. The AI isn't so good on path finding, so beware of your expensive toys.
The graphics aren't a real improvement over the first title if you look close. But overall they added new effects. You will have a real war feeling.

I've played the game to level 27 thus far on official servers (no exp bonuses or easy settings, et cetera).
I joined an official US server, US Knight 2. I was surprised to see many Chinese playing on the server (maybe half of the people online).
The newbie area has no NPCs, because the Chinese guild, BDLX (search for them on the discussion forums - apparantly they are on many of the US servers), wipes out all NPCs. They do not respawn. I've only seen one NPC in the game, at some kind of travel tower that doesnt work.
The mobs have no rhyme or reason to where they are found in the game. This means mobs spawn in the newbie dwarf city and high level creatures roam right near where you first spawn into the game. There are no NPCs for you to train the mobs to, since they are destroyed by players (in our server's case, the Chinese guild). You will notice some bunny looking mobs with levels ranging from 1 to 120 randomly in all areas, along with sheep frolicking with dragons, unicorns and ice wolves, anything you can think of just randomly thrown around on the map. You cannot tell what level a creature is until you are already right up on it (probably agro) and the fight with the mob is very different if it is lower level than if it's higher level... extremely different - even for the same creature. There is no "higher level" area where you know to find higher level mobs - again, they can spawn right in front of your very first login point.
The terrain is prone to bad geometry that you can get stuck in. There is no way to get unstuck except to kill yourself. This is worse for any creature you have tamed (which takes 20m to an hour from my experience). If a creature you have tamed gets stuck, it has to be left. If you are high level, you can create an item that will allow you to summon it (but this take a lot of materials that aren't just easy to obtain). In the time I played, 3 creature tames were lost this way.
The collision between you, one of your tames, and an agressive mob can leave all parties involved STUCK inside of each other. This happens very frequently. If you are stuck in a mob, you cannot move and will likely die. The same for your tames.
The melee within the game is wonky. If you use a sword, you have two attacks - one with left click and one with right click. The left click is a weak single swipe, while the right click is a dragon ball Z roundhouse swipe (I guess). When you press right click, your toon actually starts the animation about 5 feet behind your starting position. It is almost impossible to do any type of melee efficiently this way. It also will aim you in any direction but the one you want to swipe at. Many times, once you have pressed right click, when you go back to left clicking, the right click action will continue to be used. This must be a bug, but it isnt fixed. The other weapons in the game involved in melee are similar. The bow is the only weapon that did not have issues.
Magic in this game is crafted, meaning you craft what they call a schema. WIth a staff equipped, you equip a schema, such as fireball. As you use your staff to cast your fireball, the schema loses charges. It will break in the middle of a fight, and you will have to craft another one if you want to cast fireball again. These break very fast, so don't think you will be just using a lot of magic. Also, you have a magic bar that goes down when casting magic. However, this almost never runs out because your schema will break beforehand, or you will die. I havent been in any long fights where mana was an issue, even though I crafted potions with a 3 hour rot time in case I did run out of magic. Using magic also makes your focus go down, meaning you need to eat flowers <boggle>. So, when you use magic - your schema loses charges, your magic goes down and your focus goes down. Magic does do good damage to other players, in general though. Many of those Chinese greifers would one shot me at low level with a lightning bolt. Oh, and there are only a few spells.. maybe less than 10, and many of those are upgrades of lower level spells (fireball 1, 2.. etc).
Back to the BDLX guild, I'm not sure if they are from other games, but they have made a few servers that I know of unplayable. There is no region lock, so the US servers appear to be preferred to asian players. There is significant langauge barrier, and so far, I just see that they are hostile.
Video lag is something that is horrible. I have over the minimum requirements to run the game, and even on medium settings you will have screen freezes for more than 10 seconds when travelling into new areas. Sometimes swinging around too fast to fight a mob will cause you to freeze mid battle. When you are unfrozen, the mob has already had a few swings - which makes fair PVE difficult. On medium settings, the textures look bad (you can see some of my screenshots - I tried taking most at high levels, but many are medium settings).
Verdict: I could not recommend this game in its current form, and I am not sure about the company and how willing they are to fix some of the things that make the game unenjoyable and unplayable.

Great platforming puzzler.
Braid is one of a few games that rose during the 'indie craze' next to games like Super meat boy, Bastion and Binding of Issac.
Story is deep. I was surprised that a puzzle game could have such a good story. You play as Tim, an individual who is looking for a princess who has unfortunately been captured by a monster. It's not a plot which openly tells you what is going on per se, rather there is quite a bit of ambiguity (especially the ending which is good), which leaves the player to reflect on what is actually going on. Many themes play out in the story including desire, regret and making up for mistakes.
Gameplay is great, burrowing elements from Mario. Each stage pits you on one end of the map, trying to reach the end on the other side. Stages are unique, with different puzzles and goals to reach in order to pass, such simply reaching the end, eliminate all foes, using keys to open doors etc. Similar to stars in Mario, each level has a selected amount of puzzle pieces to collect. Each, piece collected helps to complete a picture which provides some incites to the story. There are platforms you can reach by jumping on them. You can also defeat foes by jumping on them and avoid traps by jumping over them. The only enemies are giant head things which walk around and may jump to different platforms (which reminds me of Gumpas). There are also traps such as pitfalls, spikes and canons.  You only have 1 life, so a single collision between a 'Gumpa' or trap will kill you instantly.  Fortunately, death doesn't end the game, instead this is the part where you make the most of your 'Time control' power. Reminiscent of 'POP Sands of time', you have the ability to reverse the flow of time, sending Tim back before his current predicament. Besides using it to save your life you can also use it to solve puzzles, by stopping time to allow  you to think of a plan or moving back objects to obtain items. Some puzzles may leave some guessing and frustrated, however with some patience they can be solved easily (or just use a guide).
Soundtrack is amazing. The music is very calm, with sorta 'Irish tune to it', and something you can listen to calm yourself (which especially helps with some of the puzzles). Sound effects are also good. there is no voice acting in the game, with the story told through text.
Graphics are excellent. The 2D-art style is vibrant and detailed. It is quite attractive and fits perfectly for the game.
Besides the main campaign, there is also 'speed-run' mode which is unlocked  after beating the game. The mode tests how fast you can get through certain stages in the game.
If your looking for a good story and don't mind some platforming and puzzles, Braid will show you how brilliance can be formed in a simple indie game.

I used 3ds Max and AutoCAD for some time back in the day. You could say that I could do stuff with them without too much hassle. On the other hand Blender is just terribly inconvenient. Its interface is too overly convoluted. It cannot be used without all those shortcuts. Even a simple function needs multiple key-presses without almost any kind of feedback during the entire action. Popup windows for functions like starting a new file or deleting an object are not real forms. They disappear once you move away your mouse so it is quite confusing for those who wait for a small window in the center to click on.
I am creating models right now which is fine although UV mapping is something that I had to wrap my head around. Moving vertexes and using background images can be done easily once you get used to the basics. One of the first things I did was to switch to left-click-select. Other functions on the other hand like the use of materials and textures are once again messy as hell.
My biggest problem however is that I cannot create old-school levels properly. I have a tool installed called Level Buddy which is useful for making "sectors" fast then build the entire map into one object. I can even split the faces with a few extra keystrokes that I had to hunt down. The problem is that I cannot apply textures to simple flat faces outside of the tool. Something that was so easy in Radiant is pretty much impossible here. I have to use UV maps which can be generated through Level Buddy's texture assistant. My only problem with this is that it is not flexible enough. I am still not sure whether I should use Blender or go with an in-Unity brush-based level designer. I wanted to it with the former so I would have a regular version of the geometry. I am just disappointed that I did not find anything as straightforward as Radiant was back in the day. Only if I could import those maps with ease.
Overall, I am extremely frustrated by Blender. It is like it was made by aliens or just simply made too different just for the sake of it. Like what I heard that it did not have an undo function for some time and veterans protested against it, kinda when it got implemented. That just feels weird. Getting into this program just needs too much time for anyone comfortable with usual softwares because it does so much stuff so differently. I constantly switch between Blender and Unity for example and while the latter works like anything else out there when I go back into Blender after a few hours I am using all the wrong buttons for simple navigation. Of course after I finish my modeling I am starting to Ctrl+F and do other stuff in Unity. While the two softwares work great on a theoretical level using them both back-to-back is just confusing.

So people who don't know what the Metro series is all about and are want to know. Let me just quickly summarise it for you.
Both Metro 2033 and Metro last light are built on the books by Dmitri Gloukhovski, were Metro last light doesn't follow it all the way through like Metro 2033 does.
The game is set in a post-apocalypse world where the third world war has taken place. The surface is now uninhabitable by humans, and is now infested with strange creatures called the black ones (No racism).  The games genre is quite mixed, it's a story driven "horror" fps with some survival elements. The "horror" in the franchise is based on the fact that you are screwed if you
1. Don't have any ammo
2. You let an enemy sneak up on you.
So on to the actual game than?
Story: 7/10
The story is not the best element in the game, it's quite boring most of the time, it's like this. Go to point A than point B and so on, there is some explorations involved but that's quite limited. The settings where the game is represented in are really cool, I will never forget my feelings of going out to the dead city for the first time.
Gameplay: 8/10
The gameplay is good, it feels nice most of the time. I find it quite hard to move around at sometimes, like when you are attacked by a group of  monsters, they will rush you most of the time even do you have a person with you (Which is not often). It feels really good to shot a enemy and actually killing them.
Graphic: 10/10
Simply said this game is beautiful, the amount of detail in this game is amazing. The surface is a really cool place to visit with all the mist that they have added to the game. Guns look really cool and corpses as well. The blood effect can be quite of sometimes, like F.E.A.R off.
Score:
8/10
Play if if you want a good time in a post-apocalyptic world, where you are the prey.
