I had already given up hope on Games Workshop licensed video games when Battlefleet Gothic: Armada dropped on my proverbial lap. It may be due to my low experience in tabletop Gothic or my sufficiently low expectations, but I actually found myself surprisingly enough enjoying the game.
It should be stated that the game is real time, which does mean it works very differently from the turn based tabletop version. However, unlike many other Games Workshop licensed video games Battlefleet Gothic: Armada manages to capture the spirit of the original -while- also providing mechanically solid game.
Matches are fast paced and typically last about 5 - 15 minutes depending on fleet size. Customizeable battle fleets and some half a dozen scenarios with different winning conditions mean that no match plays out quite like the last, though it has to be said that at the moment certain scenarios feel a bit lopsided, and the matches may get repetitive as nearly all of them seem to involve both players boosting to the middle and grinding it out. The winner is often determined by which one has the better fleet composition, faster reaction speed and greater control over their fleet.
Despite the repetitiveness and certain level of lopsidedness Battlefleet Gothic: Armada does have good frame on which to add features that increase the strategic depth, and even if those features were not added the game is still an enjoyable tactical space brawl game, although admittedly on the lighter side of the spectrum.
Is it Battlefleet Gothic the board game in video game format? No, it is not.
Is it an entertaining little space brawl game faithful to the spirit of the original? Yes!
Can you shout "WAAAGH!", fire all the boosters, and crash through your own vessels in order to ram your Ork space bukkit on the enemy flagship? Zog yes!

I’m a huge Warhammer 40K fluff fan (I read many of the books, and play the more widely appealing video games like the Dawn of War series and Space Marine/Eternal Crusade).
I love RTS games, too. I’d describe Battlefleet more like a Real-time Tactics game. The singleplayer campaign has been absolutely destroying me. Haven’t even had time to touch the multiplayer. I am on Turn 6 of the campaign, which is about 10-12 missions played.
You maneuver these giant space ships on a flat plane in space. The ships are super huge, so you need to account for some kind of space physics when executing the different thrusters, whether you are dodging some area-of-effect ability thrown by the enemy ships, or trying to line up torpedoes, or even committing to a last second ram.
In the singleplayer, you can slow down time to a crawl, but it’s a binary switch, either real-time or bullet-time. I feel like it doesn’t help tremendously during certain situations unless you’re having a lot of trouble managing all the thrusters of every ship in your fleet.
Launching torpedoes feels great. Ramming stuff feels super awesome. Teleporting a strike team onto an enemy ship as its shields are down and on fire in order to prevent it from warping out is awesome.
But man, the computer opponent, even on normal difficulty, is extremely brutal. If you like challenge in your real-time tactical stuff, if you crave micromanaging of a slightly different variety than StarCraft, this is it. The computer plays to the objective ruthlessly. I had to replay a mission five times before I got it.
In one mission, I needed to teleport a strike team onto an enemy cruiser to get data, but if they took out my shields and teleported their own dudes onto my ship then they’d steal that data back. So I needed to execute a bunch of stuff flawlessly and choose my fastest and most damaging ships, or the enemy would either be able to escape, or steal back the data and then escape.
In another, I had to protect an allied, giant capital ship from getting destroyed while it was not able to move at all. I finally figured out that it could deal with most threats from its front and that I should let it do its thing while I protected its rear, sometimes throwing my own cruisers in between it and enemy torpedoes just to keep the immobile capital ship alive longer.
Failing a mission also does not end the campaign. It makes the rest of the campaign harder, and probably even changes the story around. Being a tryhard like me, you can make a lot of save files to retry, but this process is not super quick, and there is no “restart mission” option in the pause menu. I feel like this kind of sucks. I know the devs sort of want you to live with your failures, but being a completely new player to this type of RTS, the friction in learning and the difficulty curve is massive enough. People will respond differently to this kind of thing.
The game’s interface is rough, and actually hard to read in some ways (text is tiny, sometimes in that really obnoxious “gothic style” font, and in some cases awkwardly cut off). I find myself using the bullet-time mode just to read various stats in the interface. There are hotkeys but you cannot rebind them.
It totally gets the WH40K stuff done very right. If you’re in for that atmosphere, look no further. All the voice-acting is over-the-top as it should be (a line from a commissar: “YOU HAVE BEEN PROMOTED TO FLEET ADMIRAL—THAT MEANS YOU’RE IN CHARGE OF THE ENTIRE FLEET!!!”), the cutscenes are almost all beautifully grim concept art pieces that are subtly animated, and the ships are intricately detailed in Unreal Engine 4.
As for performance, I was surprised to find that my Radeon HD 7870 runs the game very fine on Epic (the highest graphics setting) with the latest AMD drivers, even though my card is almost 4 years old. I was sure that it was just past the “minimum” requirements. However, before I updated my drivers, the game did crash twice on me, but not during critical moments.
Real-time tactical space naval battles are great but very hard to master even if you are coming from games like StarCraft, the Warhammer 40K setting is perfectly done, game looks gorgeous and performance is better than expected with my four years old graphics card.

Deathstate is not only visceral fun in its own right; it also makes for fantastic training for danmaku shooting games, and a great distraction from them if you want something a little different.  It scratches the itch of shooting and dodging in a very satisfying way, and out-Isaacs the Binding of Isaac while it's at it.
The game is a "single stick shooter", by which they mean you only control movement and the usage of your activated items.  The movement feels fluid and natural, and it's worth noting that the developers absolutely nailed the feeling of a true danmaku shoot-em-up, even down to things as subtle as the speed of enemy bullets, or the size of the hitbox proportional to your character sprite (not too tiny, not too fat).  Your character automatically targets the closest enemy, and fires without stopping.  This frees up more brainspace for you to focus on positioning and managing the enemy horde, within which always lurks a few stronger and more threatening enemies that need to be eliminated quickly despite the popcorn piling up in front of them.
There is technically a 2nd stick at work, here: using the right analog stick on a gamepad will activate a dash dodge ability that you can use to get yourself out of bad spots.  I don't know if this figures in more at higher level play than my own, but I find relying on it tends to actually end up killing me faster than if I simply played more cautiously in the first place.  YMMV of course, but there are ways to herd bullets into lines and create gaps through them without relying on a dodge, and these are still just as effective as they would be in any other shooter.
The game features a (unlockable, but easily so) dynamic difficulty system called Desecration.  You can find altars and desecrate them to raise the difficulty level of the game for the rest of that run, giving enemies more health, denser bullet patterns, and in some cases "suicide bullets" fired when they die (think Ketsui on the Ura loop, or 2nd-loop Dodonpachi).  There's also an Insanity Portal option, turned on before the run begins, that cranks up the difficulty right from the get-go.  It presents a significant challenge, even for someone with 1CCs of other games under their belt.
There is a pretty sizeable pool of items you can find, mostly in the form of ingestable organs, with a smattering of swords and books and other relics sprinkled in.  These unlock as you play, and I appreciate that a lot of attention has been paid to making sure that (for the most part) there aren't any that are useless or actively bad, with the possible current exception of items that change your firing to a burst or flurry, which removes your ability to handle the game's popcorn hordes with any sense of grace.
Grace is the key word with Deathstate.  It's fluid and fun in an immediately gratifying way, and is the kind of game where you'll "Just One More Run" yourself into the ground, only noticing too late that it's 1 in the morning and where did your whole day go?

I've played the game to level 27 thus far on official servers (no exp bonuses or easy settings, et cetera).
I joined an official US server, US Knight 2. I was surprised to see many Chinese playing on the server (maybe half of the people online).
The newbie area has no NPCs, because the Chinese guild, BDLX (search for them on the discussion forums - apparantly they are on many of the US servers), wipes out all NPCs. They do not respawn. I've only seen one NPC in the game, at some kind of travel tower that doesnt work.
The mobs have no rhyme or reason to where they are found in the game. This means mobs spawn in the newbie dwarf city and high level creatures roam right near where you first spawn into the game. There are no NPCs for you to train the mobs to, since they are destroyed by players (in our server's case, the Chinese guild). You will notice some bunny looking mobs with levels ranging from 1 to 120 randomly in all areas, along with sheep frolicking with dragons, unicorns and ice wolves, anything you can think of just randomly thrown around on the map. You cannot tell what level a creature is until you are already right up on it (probably agro) and the fight with the mob is very different if it is lower level than if it's higher level... extremely different - even for the same creature. There is no "higher level" area where you know to find higher level mobs - again, they can spawn right in front of your very first login point.
The terrain is prone to bad geometry that you can get stuck in. There is no way to get unstuck except to kill yourself. This is worse for any creature you have tamed (which takes 20m to an hour from my experience). If a creature you have tamed gets stuck, it has to be left. If you are high level, you can create an item that will allow you to summon it (but this take a lot of materials that aren't just easy to obtain). In the time I played, 3 creature tames were lost this way.
The collision between you, one of your tames, and an agressive mob can leave all parties involved STUCK inside of each other. This happens very frequently. If you are stuck in a mob, you cannot move and will likely die. The same for your tames.
The melee within the game is wonky. If you use a sword, you have two attacks - one with left click and one with right click. The left click is a weak single swipe, while the right click is a dragon ball Z roundhouse swipe (I guess). When you press right click, your toon actually starts the animation about 5 feet behind your starting position. It is almost impossible to do any type of melee efficiently this way. It also will aim you in any direction but the one you want to swipe at. Many times, once you have pressed right click, when you go back to left clicking, the right click action will continue to be used. This must be a bug, but it isnt fixed. The other weapons in the game involved in melee are similar. The bow is the only weapon that did not have issues.
Magic in this game is crafted, meaning you craft what they call a schema. WIth a staff equipped, you equip a schema, such as fireball. As you use your staff to cast your fireball, the schema loses charges. It will break in the middle of a fight, and you will have to craft another one if you want to cast fireball again. These break very fast, so don't think you will be just using a lot of magic. Also, you have a magic bar that goes down when casting magic. However, this almost never runs out because your schema will break beforehand, or you will die. I havent been in any long fights where mana was an issue, even though I crafted potions with a 3 hour rot time in case I did run out of magic. Using magic also makes your focus go down, meaning you need to eat flowers <boggle>. So, when you use magic - your schema loses charges, your magic goes down and your focus goes down. Magic does do good damage to other players, in general though. Many of those Chinese greifers would one shot me at low level with a lightning bolt. Oh, and there are only a few spells.. maybe less than 10, and many of those are upgrades of lower level spells (fireball 1, 2.. etc).
Back to the BDLX guild, I'm not sure if they are from other games, but they have made a few servers that I know of unplayable. There is no region lock, so the US servers appear to be preferred to asian players. There is significant langauge barrier, and so far, I just see that they are hostile.
Video lag is something that is horrible. I have over the minimum requirements to run the game, and even on medium settings you will have screen freezes for more than 10 seconds when travelling into new areas. Sometimes swinging around too fast to fight a mob will cause you to freeze mid battle. When you are unfrozen, the mob has already had a few swings - which makes fair PVE difficult. On medium settings, the textures look bad (you can see some of my screenshots - I tried taking most at high levels, but many are medium settings).
Verdict: I could not recommend this game in its current form, and I am not sure about the company and how willing they are to fix some of the things that make the game unenjoyable and unplayable.

With its very engaging and interesting tactical-strategy gameplay, XCOM can easily suck several hours out of any TBS fan. Especially if you're into sci-fi or challenging games.
Although some older fans might argue that it is not on par with its predecessors, the overwhelming majority agrees that it is a very enjoyable reboot of the series nonetheless.
That is not to say that the game is without its share of flaws, some examples are the relatively heavy reliance on random seed number generator (%) that can easily make some players flip tables and laptops alike as well as a few bugs here and there which you may or may not encounter along the way. But here, what suffers the most is the story. Don't go into it expecting an amazing plot, it is nothing out of the ordinary in that regard.
However what this game lacks in plot, it makes up for in gameplay... a LOT. Not only is it addictive and very replayable, the level of satisfaction upon taking on harder challenges and succeeding is outstanding. XCOM's very appealing design, fresh graphics and immersive atmosphere supported by a fitting soundtrack are all positive points that add up into how easy it is to devote a lot of time into it.
The macro-heavy part that is base management is very entertaining in its own right and the micro-heavy squad tactical action missions never get old. There's a good variety when it comes to the battle system, enough to keep things interesting and at the same time not so much that would make you feel overwhelmed, along with being fairly simple and intuitive.
Sending a squad of badasses into a dark battlefield, heavily outnumbered and making them prevail through sheer decision-making and a bit of gambling has never been more fun.

l::j ; HP
`;::k ; LP+MP+HP
u::b ; LK

f:: ; Throw
SendInput {g down}{b down}
KeyWait, f
SendInput {g up}{b up}
Return

KeyWait, c
SendInput {h up}{n up}
Return
space:: ; V-Trigger

KeyWait, space
SendInput {j up}{m up}
Return
Return
Return

I like RTS games.  I also like WW2 themed games.  So believe me when I say that I want to like this game.  It does a few things well.  The overall level of detail in the maps, units is good.  There are plenty of upgrade, customization options out there to help players develop their own strategies, tactics.  It has all of the basic elements of a winner.    However...  The A.I and unit path finding in this game are both awful.  Infuriatingly...unforgivably awful.  I appreciate the fact that the unit I.A can't be TOO effective, otherwise the game is just too easy.  But your units in this game totally inept.
- Infantry units will just stand around and get shelled to death unless you micromanage them.  They won't attempt to avoid explosions, fire...or make use of available cover.  They'll just die.
- Vehicles?  Utterly useless.   Don't even think of moving more than two of them at a time.  They'll run amok, cutting each other off, and colliding randomly all the way to their destination.  They'll struggle around every single terrain obstacle, taking the worst conceivable path unless you painstakingly direct them around every rock and tree.  This takes pretty much as much time as it would if you had just let them just traverse the entire map.  Some times they'll just do what they want despite all of your furious clicking and keyboard mashing.  They'll roll right over friendly defensive structures, destroying them and scattering your (previously well protected) infantry onto open ground.  They'll also drive straight onto your own tank traps if you let them.
I've seriously watched tanks and artillery rotate 300 degrees in the wrong direction to face a target, then fail to engage.  they'll just sit there.  Your infantry units will cohabitate with opposing units, often moving into point blank range before engaging.  The proximity/collision detection in this game is totally broken.
I've played the campaigns in this game, as well as Ardennes Assault (in the hope that they had addresses these issues)
My verdict:  There's no way in hell that I'll ever pay another dime to this franchise until they start fixing this garbage.  Playing this game starts to feel like a chore after a while because you'll spend half of your time making sure that your units aren't spinning around in a corner somewhere.
After 3 stand alone releases, and a mountain of DLC, there's just no excuse for such shoddy gameplay.  FAIL

various modes? Check.

Gameplay:
The gameplay divided into two pieces. One is offensive and other is defensive. The offensive part is where you combine moves such as Punch, Kick and throws to create combos and juggle your opponent. The fast & easily perfomed combos are really good and if you use tag mode, it even gets better. There is a lot of ways you can overcome your opponent thanks to the 3D gameplay. You can do side steps, You can trick your opponent with some characters The defensive part. This part contains moves called Counters (Hold) and is like "Parrying" in Street Fighter III & It really is one of the best part of the game.The best part is, it does damage! Yes. this part is really good and you can defeat your opponent without EVEN doing combos and other things. btw the gameplay is strong and it really is fun.
===
Character Roster:
The Roster is big enough to satisfy people. There's a variety of character each with their own fighting style. Some and fast & offensive, One is Tricky, Some are grapple and they are like King in Tekken.
Some are defensive and you must be careful when you approach them because they are make traps and when you fall in them, you're done. Each caracter has a big set of costumes to choose from.

Graphics:

Stages are really beautiful and the variety is nice. Maybe there's lack of some features like particles but It doesn't bad at all. Maybe you don't even notice this.

Damn. I really wanted to enjoy this. I needed a group grid dungeon crawler game after Legend of Grimrock II. What I didn't expect was a knock off clone that pales in comparison to the LoG games.
Even if it wasn't a clone it still doesn't really hold up well enough. The game itself was created by mainly one person and it shows. It lacks polish, isn't the least bit different from other dungeon crawlers and plays with repetition from start to finish.
But that being said it's not bad. It's a mixed bag. More of the same so-to-speak. It's not the gameplay that really fails. It is somewhat challenging but the weapons (both physical and magical) are so basic and the upgrading is too simple. It shows no real difference when improving attributes in the poor upgrading system. The ill-conceived inventory is confusing and lackluster. Nothing is quick access. Since there are no instructions most players unfamiliar with these types of games will get frustrated trying to figure out what does what in that respect.
The enemies are generic and move around very clunky and predictablly. The fighting system is a big flaw when it comes to dealing with them. Unlike LoG you can attack and move. This isn't the case here. The movement isn't allowed unless all four of the characters' attacks cool down. Very frustrating. It balances out though doing something that LoG didn't have: shortcut binding for attacks. This helps a lot. You can't bind both attacks for each characters but that's not that big of a deal. Speaking of cool downs: they are the same for every character regardless of class or level or weapon. This makes no sense and burdens battles.
Everything else is basic: secret switches (although there are more types here than in LoG), puzzles (fairly easy) and story. The latter is the most articulate and entertaining. There's a narrator but no voice over for the characters. The dialogue is funny and written well for the plot. Sound effects are bland and the visuals - namely the lighting - are quite nice.
I had issues with some glitches. The game crashed a few times and the further I played it the more problems I had with load time. It took almost full minute to interact with the stairs/ladders and then load to the next floor. Very odd considering I have a more than capable rig to play this.
The music is intenionally old school and quite annoying.
The game was fairly short and felt rushed with an open-ending.
It's a shame really. Maybe with some more work and innovation the next game in the series could improve. If not I don't see how buying it would be a good waste of your money and time. Unless you have a few bucks to spend and the time of course.

Deathstate is a "pick-up and play" style bullet-hell dodge-shooter.  Playthroughs are typically 15 to 30 minutes long and beyond WASD for movement the other main keys are "F" to examine and the arrow keys to dodge (all keys can be re-bound to whatever you like).  The keys needed to use potions and other items are helpfully overlaid on the on-screen display you see while you play.
Should you buy Deathstate?  Well, if you are a casual gamer like myself who likes to occasionally unwind playing simple yet fun RPG-styled games then the answer is "yes!"  Deathstate features a mix of science-fiction / horror-style chiptune music mixed with some very fun heavy metal for one of the mini-boss fights you can choose on every playthrough.  The metal track (called "Desecrate") on the Original Sound Track (OST) is thrilling.  I would compare it to the game version of an all-out table-and-chair throwing bare-knuckle brawl with Satan himself, set against the background of the cosmos.  Good stuff.
While I don't see myself putting hundreds of hours into Deathstate the game is, for what it is, fantastic.  It is a pick-up and play sci-fi horror-style RPG game with very simple game mechanics and challenging enemies and bosses.  I have heard some people find the on-screen overlay disorienting during long play throughs.  I haven't and I am prone to motion sickness.  I recommend picking up this game on sale if you enjoy this style of game.

Not bad. Not great either. Better than Dead Island though, clearly a sequel. The free running works well, though don't think it's on the same level as Mirrors Edge, it's not. The combat is decent and weapon crafting isn't bad, however weapons degrade with use and have a limited number of repair counter before they're trash. This sucks bad. Like many games that make you struggle for resources throughout, you'll find a good item every so often but hesitate to ever use it 'just in case'. My real issue is the great chasm between qualities you'll run into, you'll find a super power base weapon VERY rarely and everything else you find will typically be less than HALF as powerful. It is certainly more of a survival game, especially since the most useful resources are of course, the rarest. The other drawback is guns. They aren't useless, but as expected gun fire draws the undead. Ammo isn't that hard to comeby, in the wild sure, but every merchant in the game carries an unlimited amount from what I can tell. Originally the game didn't have a Bow/Arrow but it does now, it's excellent, especially if you can get the upgrades to increase it's damage out put. The biggest screw up in the game is the core mechanics and their consistency. More often than not I end up dying due to an explosive that I've thrown, this is because the blast radius and damage of explosives is highly inconsistent. This is compounded by the awful 'downed' mechanic which can leave you stunned on the ground being murdered for what feels like an eternity. It leads to a ton of rage quitting because your character simply wont get the f**k up, and you just sit there for what feels like minutes watching your health bar tick down, because you got knocked down by an explosive you've through a thousand times but this time for NO special reason the blast radius was double its normal. It isn't a game breaking problem, not in the slightest, but it is ultra frustrating and leads to more deaths than any other danger in the game.

I like RTS games.  I also like WW2 themed games.  So believe me when I say that I want to like this game.  It does a few things well.  The overall level of detail in the maps, units is good.  There are plenty of upgrade, customization options out there to help players develop their own strategies, tactics.  It has all of the basic elements of a winner.    However...  The A.I and unit path finding in this game are both awful.  Infuriatingly...unforgivably awful.  I appreciate the fact that the unit I.A can't be TOO effective, otherwise the game is just too easy.  But your units in this game totally inept.
- Infantry units will just stand around and get shelled to death unless you micromanage them.  They won't attempt to avoid explosions, fire...or make use of available cover.  They'll just die.
- Vehicles?  Utterly useless.   Don't even think of moving more than two of them at a time.  They'll run amok, cutting each other off, and colliding randomly all the way to their destination.  They'll struggle around every single terrain obstacle, taking the worst conceivable path unless you painstakingly direct them around every rock and tree.  This takes pretty much as much time as it would if you had just let them just traverse the entire map.  Some times they'll just do what they want despite all of your furious clicking and keyboard mashing.  They'll roll right over friendly defensive structures, destroying them and scattering your (previously well protected) infantry onto open ground.  They'll also drive straight onto your own tank traps if you let them.
I've seriously watched tanks and artillery rotate 300 degrees in the wrong direction to face a target, then fail to engage.  they'll just sit there.  Your infantry units will cohabitate with opposing units, often moving into point blank range before engaging.  The proximity/collision detection in this game is totally broken.
I've played the campaigns in this game, as well as Ardennes Assault (in the hope that they had addresses these issues)
My verdict:  There's no way in hell that I'll ever pay another dime to this franchise until they start fixing this garbage.  Playing this game starts to feel like a chore after a while because you'll spend half of your time making sure that your units aren't spinning around in a corner somewhere.
After 3 stand alone releases, and a mountain of DLC, there's just no excuse for such shoddy gameplay.  FAIL

I wanted to hold off on doing a review until I had clocked at least 20+ hours... unlike the vast majority of these negative reviews with many of them having under 1 hour... seriously? How can you even make a judgement on a game in that short of a time frame... especially a game with a massive world like this that honestly doesn't start to pick up until you get close to level 10... Lol. Most of these negative reviews were obviously done in a short burst of anger, or frustration because it wasn't running perfectly... *shrugs* Anyways, on to my review.
Let me preface this by saying the following: this is definitely an EARLY ACCESS GAME! Let's not forget what that means... this is not a finished product, and as such will have many bugs and performance issues. Any review should NOT be done primarily based on these factors at this point in the development process... but rather on what IS there, and the potential that the game has moving forward. But... then again that's my own personal opinion I guess.
I have found this game to be very immersive, and quite honestly... addicting. It has been the first game in awhile to give me that feeling where I was thinking about playing even when I wasn't on. I think this says a lot about it because it's still VERY rough as far as performance and optimization go... so you have definitely been warned... don't expect this to run smooth.
However, despite what some people have claimed... I don't think it takes NEAR the rig to run it okay. My PC is honestly getting pretty old... quad core AMD Phenom II processor and a GTX 760... definitely not a high end rig by todays standard... but yet, I can still play on epic/high settings after turning down a couple sliders... granted I only get around 20+ FPS... but whatever... that doesn't bother me terribly, especially since I'm only playing on a PvE server at the moment. My GF can even play this on our gaming laptop that has an even weaker graphics card... soooo... yeah... not sure what these other people are doing incorrectly that claim they have beast rigs. I think as long as your expectations are realistic, you should have a fun time if this is your kind of game.
The other thing that I wanted to mention is how annoying it is to see all these reviewers referring to it as an "Ark Clone". This game is supposedly owned by a company that bought Wildcard, and as a result, they were able to use their engine, and also some of the UI/Survival elements if I'm correct (not a 100% sure on this one). That is honestly where the similarities stop.
This game is a high fantasy, open world sandbox that focuses on magic, crafting, taming, building, and a lot of the stuff you would find in other sandbox/survival style games with a mix of RPG elements. Ark on the other hand is a game that has dinosaurs on some island with technology... TOTALLY different setting. If people can't see these differences then you should just stop playing games for a bit, and re-evaluate your entire perspective on life. Instead of focusing on what is the same (negative), try looking at it from the perspective of whether or not there's anything there that can be enjoyed (positive). Games almost always are going to be similar to something that preceded them... since it's incredibly difficult to have an original idea that is 100% unique... that goes for anything creative for that matter. The human brain always tries to compare things to something already learned/experienced, which often times gets in the way of finding enjoyment. If you're constantly searching for this elusive game that is completely new and original you will be disapointed time and time again.
Bottom line... if you like survival style and/or fantasy sandbox RPG games, and are willing to overlook a lot of the performance issues this game currently has (along with only 30% of the planned content in game), then I think there's a lot here that you could enjoy. You might have to tweak some settings, and try a couple different servers... maybe even one that isn't PvP if getting ganked isn't your thing (although goblins can still gank your♥♥♥♥♥ lol). It also seems to be way more fun when played with friends.
Anyways, I pretty much already feel like I received my money's worth out of it since I still plan on playing for quite a bit longer. I also look forward to them adding even more content moving forward... this game could be really amazing if they don't screw it up. I have mixed feelings about this game, but I am still willing to give it 7/10 (Just saying it right now, you do NOT want this game if you are going for realism. This is a GAMEPLAY and COMPETITION oriented game, meaning there are plenty of liberties made to forgive mistakes that a real war would never offer).
First off, you play this game for the single-battles, whether it be comp-stomp, fun pvp, or competative pvp (which I will get to). The campaign is not good. The story is cliche, and if you have not already heard of the controversy around the depiction of Russians in the single player campaign, it may rock your boat the wrong way. Story aside, the gameplay teaches bad habits, such as clustering troops and not managing your economy wisely.
Multiplayer is where I think the game shines, but comp stomp is not bad because the UI for setting up a comp stomp is very simple. You can easily get your friend into battle using the Steamworks, and practice against AI. It teaches bad habits like in the campaign, but it does get you into the competative mood, especially since the campaign is completely single player. The Theatre of War may be fun, but I personally have not played it much because the missions come in seperate dlcs. Luckily, they are not a key part of the game.
Pvp, especially automatch competative PvP is really fun. I don't participate in major league games, and not in official competative PvP matches. I am no gaming olympian. However I do play pvp a lot, and it is really fun. The game is over a year old right now and the balancing is manageable. Still some work, but overall the sides seem pretty balanced. Units are cool and diverse, especially now that you can win some content like skins and commanders as if they were TF2 weapons, making it less frustrating than before. You do not need Western Front armies, as the game still lets you view Americans and Oberkommando West troops owned by other players in the match.
If historical and gameplay realism is what you want, do NOT want this game. Company of Heroes 2 is to Team Fortress 2 as Men of War is to Red Orchestra 2. CoH2 is not a serious outlook on war. All soldiers speak your native language (in my case, English), will crack jokes, throw one-liners, and complain. It's funny, and adds to the game more than taking away from it, making each unit its own character (it's very easy to know who is in trouble when you hear the small and light cry of a Conscript squad leader as opposed to the deep rustled voice of a weapons crew officer, or the confident voice of a tank destroyer).
To add to the lack of realism, soldiers can run in front of machien gun without realistic harm (machine guns are nevertheless dangerous, but they are meant to be supressors, not killers), SMGs at close range just get a video-gamey damage bonus rather than mowing down enemies 5 metres away, and a soldier can stand undetered in fire if he has the health points for it. Only a few tanks can switch between ammo, and tank destroyers are balanced to be terrible with infantry DESPITE having defensive machine guns in order to be good at killing tanks. You also have special abilities like "For the Fatherland" or "Urrah!" which gives a squad some damage or speed or defense bonus.
It is very much a video-gamey video game. However, these all contribute to a fun competative environment, as real war relies on a lot of luck as it does tactivs. There is an RNG in CoH2, but otherwise, things are predictable. There is a rock-paper-scissors format more tailored to dealing with "spams"  rather than individual units. Dealing with an infantry spam armed with Panzerschreks that keep killing your tanks with impunity? Two Maxims can stop any infantry spam, with one Maxim covering the other Maxism, and visa-versa with MG42s against Conscript spams. Mortars kill weapons crews like MGs and AT guns if your tanks and infantry cannot do the job. Tanks provide extra firepower and protection to support the infantry, and tank destroyers provide an armored carrier for an anti-tank gun. Maintaining the survival of your units is also key (I personally do not believe in cannon fodder) because the more your unit fights, the more exp it gets, and the more exp it gets, the higher its veterancy. High-veterancy squads and vehicles get buffs in their defense, offense, reload, and speed, and sometimes extra abilities, such as the ability for an M5 AA Half Track "Kraut Mower" to "swooce" right into the battlefield behind that pesky machine gunner with it's "overdrive" ability.
All of these gamey elements coupled with I think an impressive matchmaking system make for a great competative game. The Match Maker is kind of an enigma, as it does not match based on levels (you can AFK your way up the ranks, that is why), but rarely do you feel like you are against smurfs, considering there is bound to be a competent player on your team as well, unless you ARE that competent player. I never play 1v1 or 2v2 because 3v3 and 4v3 really reward teamwork. Even if your ally never appreciates it, you sending your conscript squad to support an American rifle team (that's another thing, Americans and Russians fight side by side, because competition vs realism) just to see yourself racking up the exp from flanking shots as an MG 42 pins the Americans is really satisfying.
3/10 if you want realism or a good story. The campaign is bad, and it is far from a realistic game
8/10 if you are a company of heroes fan. It is a great successor to the previous game
7/10 for me on average
7/10 if you want a competative multipler strategy game. This is one of the few strategy games that actually is good at competative public multiplayer.

I've only played Meadow for an hour since I made this review, nevertheless, it is a game that I would highly recommend if you want to play a chill game whose only objective is to explore.
Meadow is completely open world, with a central hub where you can spawn or meet other new or experienced players. It's a strange experience playing a completely online game with none of the standard online commodities that have become standard. You can neither talk, nor injure other players. As far as I know you can't kill anything either. What is available instead is a giant rack of symbols you can use to communicate basic ideas and commands. They are confusing at first, but playing just for an hour I figured out what everything meant. As you play, you unlock new emotes, creatures, etc. What really was most enjoyable about this basic setup is that everyone usually has the same objective, find relics and flowers to upgrade and unlock new animals and emotes.
What I really enjoy about this game from my short time with it is being able to just group up with an enormous amount of people and just explore, within 20 minutes I had found a giant group of twenty other people and we ended up finding this cave system, which opened up into this awesome underground waterfall. And that is when the unique styling of the game really comes to light. When you find large expanses of land on a big hilltop with your big group of strangers,
There are few games that can pull of this kind of simplicity while remaining interesting and engaging. While I certainly can't suggest this to people who want a busier, action oriented game. If you have a few bucks to spend on atmospheric, chilled out game, this may be it.

Best $2.99 I've spent on gaming. This is such a refreshing online experience in the sea of toxicity that currently exists in competitive games. You log in, run around with other animals, and explore. Communication is done entirely with emotes and the experience you have unfolds completely naturally. It's almost impossible to explain the Meadow experience, so instead I'll tell a story of my first session.
I spawned as a badger cub. The interface was relatively intuitive, and I found my emotes easily. The controls were explained in the options menu which I took a minute to peruse. The first thing I noticed was the world. It's beautiful and whimsical; it looks as if it's made entiely out of a quilt. Shortly after spawning I found several other badgers and a handful of other critters all grouped up. I nosed my way in, tossed up a few friendly smiles, and I was accepted into the fold.
I gravitated to my follow badger cubs, and I noticed a larger gray colored badger which I assumed was a female. I decided to follow her around as her cub, and the other baby badgers followed suit. Soon, she was leading us on a grand adventure through vast forests, through a mountain, and we even found a desert! There are many different environments to explore, and the world seems to be a good size. Along the way we discovered many collectables which unlocked more animals, skins, and emotes for me to use. Everyone can collect them, so there is no "rush" or "me first" mentality. Everyone has access to each collectable before it disappears.
The part that stood out in this experience, and why I rate it so highly, is when I became separated from the pack. I was hopelessly lost after straying just a moment for a flower I wanted to collect. I turned back to find the mama badger with my brothers and sisters gone. It sounds silly, I know, but in that moment I was honestly sad. The pack I had been adventuring with for a good hour or so were no where to be seen. I felt so very alone. I crept slowly under a rock and cowered sending my crying emote and little squeaks of sadness. A minute or so later the mama came rushing back to me and nuzzled me out of my hiding place back with my brothers and sisters. It was probably the cutest thing I've experienced in a video game.
You'll either love this game or absolutely hate it. The experience here is one of a kind, and something that I encourage anyone even remotely interested to give a go since the price of entry is so low. I'm VERY glad I decided to give the game a shot, and it's found a permanent place in my heart <3

In the darkness I can hear the roar of dragons and howl of wolves. I've equipped myself with some leather armor and some makeshift weapons, thinking the darkness could'nt be too bad. Minutes after leaving my makeshift campsite, a pack of wolves attack. Taking a vantage point from a rock, I slaughter them. Next thing I know, a few meters from the slaughtered wolves I run into a panther. He is a tough foe, but I slaughter him as well.
Having killed a few wild beasts, my confidence in the wilderness grows. Out of the darkness an Ice dragon attacks. I'm no match for this and must run. I run until it hurts and am forced to take a break. I notice my stomach is growling and grab some berries from a nearby bush. Its not much, but it helps. As I stand there, regaining my stamina to contiune on, I feel something hit my ankle. Suddenly its multiple hits too my ankle. I'm knocked out. The darkness consumes me. What has done this?
I wake up and find that everything I had on me is gone. I look around and me and see nothing. What kind of foul beast could do this? A moment later its happening again. Darkness consumes me. As I wake, I realize hunger has taken the better of me and that I will be returning to the great beyond soon. My stomach lurches.
Meters in front of me, I see it. The foul creature born to torment new comers. A tiny loot goblin, whose ankle punches are more deadly than dragons. As I feel my heart beat grow louder, a fierce anger consumes me. It was never the giant wild beasts that I needed to fear. It was these tiny little creatures, born to troll. The Darkness consumes me.

First of, before starting anything, many players who thought that it will be a mmo of Shelter series, like lynx players would eat the herbivore animal players, they got wrong on there. You see, Meadow is more part of the Shelter Books that Might and Delight created: The animals from a specific, sacred Den, shares their tales and stories to the others. As in Meadow, you can guess at the start of the game, we do start in this Den! So basicly, we are in that friendly animal world from the books and the surrounding Grove where peace between animals should be.
Unlike the other Shelter games, we are in a wilderness as playing either a mother badger or a mother lynx (depending if you play the Shelter 1 or 2) and you have the role to make sure your cubs will survive until adulthood,etc, like a real life animal in a semi fantasy world, made for those animals.
Meadow is, as counterpart, the harmony between all animals, carnivore or herbivore, they are all friendly all together. So we are in that kind of universe.
Now that it is said, let's start up!
When I started playing the game, I wasn't expect to start as a badger (cub) seriously. I was thinking that we could have some choices but nope, we needed to unlock the others, first. So I did tried to do it alone on my side, it was a pain during my first night playing the game. I mean, I had no tips or something similar while playing this game, like a tutorial, but I did wandered around and collecting flowers, which they are used to increase points for the leaderboard only and steam achievements. Nothing too fancy here. So that was my first night and first time playing the game.
-On the next day, during the morning-
It was the bright, sunnay day of the morning. I can see something now! But this time, I tried to meet some people, which the first encounter was with a goat player. Kinda I followed him. He showed me a big , dark rock with symbols on them, the Obelisks and the goat emoted me to shout to it. We both did and we got loot from it, a golden fossil. It was then I started to realize that the better loots are inside those obelisks and also the bigger they are, the more you need the players around and some obelisks need some specific animal to work with. So you need varieties of animals while grouping.
As for the communications with the emotes, they are really to tell which one is after a few mere hours. But after unlocking all the animals you can, I can tell you that you do want all the furr patterns for each animals. GOSH there are so many for some, especially for that lil' badger!
As I mentionned in my Pro, each animal has their Pros and Cons around for the natural abilities. By giving some examples for what I mean there, the frog is an excellent jumper and the best swimmer in this game, but it lacks some speed while walking and running if you compar to the other animals. As for the rabbit, it is the fastest to run on lands (I did the test! It goes slightly faster than the eagle and the goat!). I do consider both the rabbit and the frog as a natural scout ally to explore around. As for the goat, tall in nature, I really think that animal can be a good idea for making them the leaders of the groups because they are quite easy to be spotted, their shouts and emotes are more larger than anyone else and easy to identify from afar. The starter badger is also a small one, not as good for jumping, which I consider it the worst in the list, really. but the average running speed, swimming speed are quite balanced. But their shouts are really those we can hear from afar compared to the Goat and easy to identify the location from where the badger is.
I will not put much comments about the Lynxes, cub bear, the adult badger (slightly better than the cub badger) because their are quite similar with the others and you need to buy the other shelter stuff and games to get them. Maybe except the lynxes because they run a bit faster than the badgers and swim faster too. For the Eagles, they just fly around with all average to fast speed, nothing much. They are also one of the best scouts if you bought everythings, including the books and soundtracks (which I didn't bought the books but I saw some bird players in the game).
In the overall....
Meadow is a relaxing MMO with a small community on it. It really makes a change compared to many mmo like World of Warcraft, Guild Wars 1 or 2 and other games with some actions in a vast landscape, openworld type. So, in the end, I recommend to those who are quite curious about what is a relaxing,chilling mmo, where there is no hp, no falling damage, no bad animals, only good and respectable players are in those small servers from the Shelter Community.
As for me, I hop on my rabbit as I go help those who are in the Grove!

Maybe temple of Osiris is an OK game as a 4-player co-op game. But it's mostly a bad sequel. Guardian of light surprised everyone with clever level design, a fun campaign, challenging secrets and most important for me, the amazing work that went into making it a great single player game, despite being designed as a co-op game.
Temple of Osiris feels like the opposite game: the levels are built as arenas with the occasional lever or ball to push. Most puzzles are straightforward, because they don't (or didn't bother to) use the potential of co-op solving. As a result, the single player campaign is the same as the co-op one, only harder. Also, My biggest pet peeve in recent games is putting everything behind a (virtual) paywall, with upgrades bought with collected gems, instead of rewarding exploration. Finally, the game is poorly optimized and can't run without hiccups on a decent system.
So, Temple of Osiris lost most that made Guardian of light so special, and is almost indistinguishable from other light-hearted co-op shooters. Not what I wanted, and certainly not what I expected when buying the game.

If you like Paws, Shelter or Shelter 2, you'll probably like this one too.
There's a variety of animals to play as (after you've run around as a badger cub and collected enough sparkly stuff to unlock new animals or have one of the devs' previous games), though I'd love to see more, like a fox or an adult bear from Shelter 2. And I never say no to more skin options, but the game does already have at least 6 different skins for each animal.
The map is quite big and has lots of different areas to explore, from snowy forests to huge caverns.
Communication with other people happens via over a dozen different emotes and icons. And screaming and jumping, of course. The emotes are adorable, and it always makes me smile when one person makes the winky face and suddenly everyone is winking at everyone. It's great.
One thing I think is an issue is that when there's a huge group of people running around in search of the runes/obelisks, the slower animals like badgers have to struggle to keep up with the rest of the group unless the faster ones stop every once in a while and let them catch up. Which doesn't always happen. And then by the time the tail of the group reaches the rune/obelisk, it's already broken and they don't get anything from it. Which sucks.
Also it'd be helpful if you could see the icons/emotes from people behind you/around you, even if you don't see the player. Occasionally someone spots something from the middle of the moving group, but have no way of getting the group's leads' attention until they stop. If they stop.
So all in all, Meadow is a very enjoyable game if you like running around as a cute animal with other people. The visual style is as pretty as in Shelters/Paws and there's a lot of places to explore. What I'd like the game to have is a bit more variety with the animals and maybe some way to keep a group together/communicate better within a group.

My favorite PC racing game/sim. The collection of tracks is fantastic and the racing action is some of the best out there. Level of control is great, adjusting control sensitivity is easy and you can get it exactly where you want it. Difficulty levels are fantastic as the % slider makes it so you can fight on exactly your level. So many racing games have easy, medium hard. In RACE07 if the AI is just slightly too challenging/easy you can make it anywhere from 1% to 100% easier or harder so you can find the precise difficulty you are looking for.
The game does has a few downsides but these do not stop it from being an excellent racer. The graphics are a bit dated (but certainly not bad) by modern standards, the car selection is a bit limited and for some reason spa francorchamps isnt in the game. The car selection is something that can be fixed by acquiring one of several DLC packs.
A must have product for any serious racing fan

Pros:
Looks Nice.  The environment is dungeon like, while the walls are fairly nondescript and repetative they still crafted well enough to keep the atmosphere intact.  The same can be said for the tiles, chains, torches and other asthetic adornments.  The monsters are smooth, well articulated and rounded with an ounce of cuteness that gives a warm feel to the game, even when being gouged to death.
Simple.  I don't mean that in terms of depth but in ease of use, as in a few clicks and you are away.  The character generation is neither bogged down in comnplex choices nor overly cumbersome.  While I do enjoy character creation that is complex and deep, I don't feel it is necessary to the enjoyment of a game every time.  Games like Wizardry 8 for example, while in this genre, would terrify someone not familiar with such games, whereas this one would not.  Sometimes all that is needed to build a bond between you and your party are names that mean something or are fun.  I went with 'Bob, Robert, Bobby Sue and Bobette.'
Nostalgia.  It's clear that the creator loves the genre and has had some experience of the classics.  There are touches of many other games in here for both the more recent convert to the old school.  As mentioned in another review the sound of the Amiga hard drive will make some chuckle and others scratch their heads.
Cons:
While there are many small things most of them nuances that vary from game to game and just take getting used to.  The only real issue I had, and unfortunately it is a really big one, is the lag.  There is a distinct lag in combat that means that you are unable to be as nimble as you can in other games.  In fact even the original Dungeon Master, made three decades ago, allowed more freedom of movement.  I found myself repeatedly hitting a direction key, while being attacked, but the party seemed unable to move.  Had my computer been old or obselete I may have been able to pin it on that. but it is not.  Also the fact that outside of combat I did not have the issue means that it is an integral problem.
*UPDATE*
Since writing this the Developer commented that the combat issue is by design.  Once you have commited to cmbat you are bound for a certain time.  While annoying it does get around the 'tricks,' in other games where you could simple walk around a monster and hit it repeatedly.  All you needed was four squares.
Because of this revelation I am going to change my review from not recommended to recommedned.  Knowing that this is deleiberate, and more realistic, makes the game more enjoyable.  Now I know that if I am not ready to fight, I need to run until I am.
So there you have it.  Pretty, nostalgic but very hard early on.  This is definately for those that like a challenge.

I suppose you could say that if you like games like Dark Souls, where the goal is to become absolutely livid but not enough to punch your monitor, then this game is definitely for you.

It would be nice to have more than just open space, near the sun, and near asteroids. How about near blackholes, where you either jump or kill your opponents after a certain amount of time before you and your opponent gets sucked into the blackhole. How about getting supporting fire from nearby allies in ally space if you meet certain requirements? Say you have an Engi, you are fighting rebels, and you are in Engi space, you would get fire support to help you kill rebel ships.
Also, more customization options when you pick your ship from the Hangar would be nice too. They should give players scrap to buy their own weapons, drones, crew, systems, and augments.
It would also be nice to get scrap every time you move to a different beacon. Think of it as experience points as you explore the sector and reward you for not dying.
If I were to score it, I'd give it a 7/10. That's pretty generous, considering that I'm not really into all this dying ad-nauseum rogues and rogue-likes/rogue-lites. Bones, zombies, bones and more bones. Enough bones to give you a necrophilia boner, but that’s enough talk about The Walking Dead, lets cast a (dead) eye over BoneBone:- Rise of the Dead Lord.
Story
You wake up to the sound of blissful silence, then you realise your rooster is dead and so is the rest of your chooks, OMG! no more gluten free, free range, R.S.P.C.A. approved, fresh eggs!!! Then you get attacked by your first wave of Bone-ified skeletons.  And that’s about it. Yep, the plot and story has about as much depth, as an eight year olds back story for his WarHammer Necromage Hero.
Game Play
Enemy attack from left of screen in groups, starting with one or two on first level and gradually get bigger, stronger and more frequent as your progress levels (also know as nights). They shamble and amble towards your tower on the right, and you must mow them down with your bow and arrow before they can destroy your tower. Be warned, lead your shots or your just wasting arrows. You start with being only able to shoot one arrow before each reload, you can upgrade the amount of arrows shot to a point, that you can make Legolas look like a junior boy scout.
Each wave or night of rattly foes is 60 seconds, after each night you can upgrade arrows, towers, fences and hire extra men to help (a jolly bunch who keep singing “Men In Tights”), up to ten men is the limit though.
If you survive your first five nights, a Merchant will arrive and will offer better Bows, Crossbows and Muskets. And he will return regularly after each five nights you manage to continue to survive.
The variety of the boney Beaus I have faced up to 8 levels have been the standard grunt, Viking, Giant Viking, Berserker and Bomber. Screen shoots indicate Zombies and Balloon Boners. There may even be more as you progress further.
Everything Else
Opening options is sparse with graphic adjustments of resolution, windowed or full and key bindings options. No sound or music adjustment, so just hit mute on the sound card and crank up the “Monster Mash”. You have a choice between Story and Endless mode, there is little difference between the two other than a story.
Game graphics is simple and elegant “Southpark style” on both the foes and background, which work very well. Your target crosshair is a simple but effective white dot, that is easy to see and hard to lose.
Sound effects are simple but are drowned out by extremely loud crappy music, so hit the mute. Controls are crisp and clean, so if you cant hit the skull of a Mammoth on a barn door at ten paces, no excuses, stop playing with your femur and go get your eyes tested princess.
BoneBone:- Rise of the Deathlord by Vladis Fire is a good casual action time waster that you will enjoy coming back to, and cheaper than a pack of wood nails too.

A fascinating Cthulhoid action roguelike. Deathstate can most easily be compared to Binding of Isaac, only with Mythos monsters instead of weird body horror.
Gameplay: They call it a "single-stick shooter", as opposed to a "twin-stick shooter". What this means is that you move your character, and your character automatically fires at the closest target. At this point, some of you are probably saying "Whaaaat?"—let me assure you, though, that this is both fun and challenging. The way I play, I have my left hand on WASD and my right on the arrow keys; the arrow keys activate a "dash" that lets you "phase through" bullets. Even though I'm not actively controlling where I shoot, I'm still making decisions every moment—What target should I move close to now? How close do I have to get so it's in range? Can I figure out its pattern and predict where I have to be next? Would it help if I dashed through this bullet, or would that put me in the path of something else? Can I run over there to the health item without running into bullets? Should I activate my character skill or my item skill, or should I save the MP/cooldown for when I really need it? Where should I go next in this level so as to find the exit before time runs out?
Once you get to the higher levels, it starts feeling more like Touhou than anything else, as you carefully maneuver through bullet patterns. (After all, in most Touhou games, don't you just hold down the fire button all the time?) You also accumulate various items (this is where the "roguelike" aspect comes in). The items modify your damage, rate of fire, bullet type and so on, and some give you skills that can be activated. You can only carry one grimoire, one weapon and one "orbiting relic", and they float around you; when you find a new grimoire, for example, you have to consider which is best for your current build. There are other weird and interestingly gruesome items like eyes and spleens, but you can collect as many of those as you like. Incidentally, the levels are organized into worlds, but randomly generated; each type feels different from the others, and within a world each level is slightly different, with a different combination of monsters for example—different monsters require very different tactics to take on.
While I, personally, was never that good at Binding of Isaac, I found myself able to get to the end of Deathstate with only a week or so of play. Of course, that's hardly the "end" of the game; I can play with more unlocked characters, I can use the "desecration portals" to increase the difficulty level...I have no doubt I could play this game for months, if not years. Speaking of unlocks, there are lots of them, which is a good thing; even if you die, very often you unlock something new to appear during play, which is gratifying.
Graphics: Pixel-y, but very good. There are all sorts of crazy monsters. Some are admittedly "generic", like skeletons or liches. Some of them are obviously based on things from Cthulhu Mythos stories, like the Starspawn, Gugs and Elder Things. Some are actually versions of the weirder Dungeons & Dragons monsters, like Modrons, Beholders or Grells (here "Hawkminds"). And some of the monsters are original, like the Molten Faces. As long as you don't hate pixel artwork—and you aren't grossed out by disembodied organs, or by flesh melting off monsters when they die—I think you'll be impressed with the graphics.
Speaking of graphics, I should mention the "scanline" effect. It's very well done; when you switch levels, it almost feels like your monitor is turning on and off (it's just a graphical effect though). There's also a "brightness" effect; when you get a health item, the screen glows with saturated colors for an instant. And when you get down to very low health, everything looks gray and washed-out. Also, when time runs out in a level, the colors start reversing, or sometimes phantoms appear all over the screen. And certain monsters can actually increase the scanlines or brightness, making it seem like when you get close to them, the entire game is being affected. These graphical touches act as cues for events in the game...and they also just appear bizarre and fascinating. (By the way, I think the scanline effects can be turned off in the options.)
Music and Sound: Excellent. Well, it's sort of a vaguely chiptune-esque feel; I understand the composers (well, everyone involved) were inspired by Genesis games; imagine Ecco the Dolphin meeting Cthulhu. Also, Carcassus will make you think of DOOM (in many ways). Honestly, I liked the music so much I bought the soundtrack DLC, and I NEVER do that. As for sound, there are lots of nice cues; you can tell when a health item drops somewhere in view, and you can tell that it's different from a gold drop. Acquiring health produces a nice "gulp". When you meet an elite monster, it announces itself with diabolical laughter—to say nothing of the demonic cackle that heralds a boss.
Story: The story is, admittedly, vague: You have followed a Professor into a dimension filled with monsters, and now you have to defeat him and/or escape. The, writing, however, is quite good; what I'm referring to, mostly, is the descriptions of monsters and items, tiny bits of Lovecraftian prose you can read once you've encountered/unlocked the thing in question. Also, between levels, various characters will pop up and say random things. This ranges from the Professor threatening you, to skeletons making references to old games, to the undead merchant saying truly bizarre things ("A brain is a terrible thing to only have one of"). The point I'm trying to make is that the story and writing don't have a big role—nor do they need to—but they're good for what they are.
IN SUMMARY: I'm coming back to it and playing it again and again. Highly recommended.

Very good tool, especially for just 5€. This tool is exactly what I have been looking for.
You can create versatile color palettes and save them in a project file (.json format) to further extend on those palettes gradually using this tool. You can work with multiple sets of colors at once, group and entitle them.
You could then easily take out color values (rgb/cmyk/hex) directly (to use them in a web project for example) or export them as either .aco (Adobe Color file), .png or .gpl file. So you can easily import and use your palette(s) in programs like Photoshop or Illustrator. I think the .gpl files are for GIMP. But otherwise you could also just import the .png file in any program and use their color picker tool to get the color values, that's just a tad less convenient.
There is also a built in color picker, where you can load a picture file, zoom in and pick colors quick and precisely.
The developer also takes feedback and ideas from the tools' steam community in consideration. So there seem to be more neat features in the works, which is great.
The only thing I don't like about the tool is the look of the round buttons. I would prefer are more Material Design-like approach but well, it's just aesthetics and up to your personal taste.
Feature-wise I'd just wish that when you are using color chords, that it would also show their position in the color wheel, e.g. displaying two other circles when using triadic colors that are linked to the selectable color circle. But that's also a rather minor thing.
All in all, I am loving it so far. Heavily recommended.

This game at the moment gets an 8/10 when it was released. This game is literially a rip right from the table top version of battlefleet gothic but this is a real time strategy game. No dice. Not a turn based game.
It is a fantastic game which was a surprise to me as it is better than what I thought this game would be. The story is split into 5 chapters and a prologue. The prologue consists of you learning the game along with following the story. Over the course of the 5 chapters, several events in the story line and lore of W40k occurs. Each chapter consists of events that occur during the years that each chapter covers before and during the 12th Black Crusade.
Story/Campaign:
You play as Admiral Spire of the Imperial Navy Battlefleet Gothic. It is your job to defend the systems and it's planets of the Gothic Sector from Traitor forces, Chaos forces, Eldar and Ork pirates during the events that take place during the 12th Black Crusade as Abbadon the Despoiler decides to attack the Gothic Sector.
I loved the campaign but there are very repetative missions (at least they are quick. But seriously playing Data Retrieval over and over and over again is repetative). The cutscenes are amazing! The music, voice acting and sound is amazing. The choices and mission results in some cases have an impact to the game!
This game consists on a space battles on a 2-D space using several ship types - escorts, light cruisers, cruisers, battlecruisers and battleships. You as an admiral of one of four factions get to select these ships and upgrade them.
More Information:
Micro Management Hell People are Talking About:
This so called "micromanagement hell" people complain about seriously makes me question if they have ever played the original Dawn of War series or Star Craft 1. Micro management in this game isn't entirely perfect, more on that later when I've finished this game's campaign, but it works! You are only controlling at best 12 ships maximum and can work with them.  This game is a really good strategy game that literially rips the board game the difference really is at least on the table top version you can think about what to do each turn. This game "solves" this the special feature that makes all of the statics and strategy in this game possible... It's called Press the Space Bar to slow down time... A lot of these people complaining about the "micro management hell" really don't seem to understand this concept. In all honesty, this game has much less micro management than Star Craft 2 and I prefer this for casual play and enjoyment.
2-D Space:
Umm... for people complaining.. It's a rip from the table top... Stop complaining. If you don't like it don't play it. Simple as that. This game is designed to be like this not because the game developers can't comprehend 3-D space or space comabt in games, yes someone complained about this -.-, but because it was from the board game that uses a 2-D space grid.

I bought this due to the all the positive reviews, and the low sale price. I had watched friends play it when it came it, and hadn't seen it since, so I was curious.
Note: Steam says I only played 0.1 hours because I played the Half Life 2: Update modded version of the game.
i7-6700K
GTX 1070
Windows 10
Pros:
Graphics are great for the age of the game.
Runs great on modern gaming hardware, no compatiblity issues.
Cons:
It's very subjective, but the mouse movement (at 60 FPS) doesn't feel like 60 FPS. There is some sort of faint lag (mouse acceleration is off) that is just enough to make the game a bit wonky as a shooter. Haven't seen it in any of my other games,
Some games have overly heavy tutorial modes, this game is the opposite. You are thrown right into the action with no explanation of what the environment can do. Some items are destructable, but its not obvious because you break them with a crowbar and they don't always look like something that a crowbar has any chance of breaking. Also, there is no explanation of what interactible objects can do. I kept walking by healing stations because they looked like decor, and didn't do anything when I activated them. Turns out you have to hold down a key, but the game will never tell you. I could understand if it was a puzzle game, where you figure out your environment, but you have other NPC's "aiding" you in this game that should be able to give  explanation.
Movement - as far as I can tell, you can only sprint....or super sprint... no walk. The default movement is sprint, and it seems to have a "skid" effect. Now, if this was not the default movement, but the "sprint feature", I could understand the realism of your momentum making it hard to stop moving while sprinting. But, there seems to be no walk or just "slow down", so I am constantly hitting objects, unable to turn into corridors while being shot, zoming past ladders I need to climb, etc. Kinda hurts the shooter aspect of the game.
Story - Didn't get very far into this, so I completely understand if others, who have played further into, love it. However, I was immediately thrown off by the fact that the first people you run into suggest that you are "famous and important", you showed up out of nowwhere, and yet they show no surprise at all, give you no explanations of what is going on, and send you away with no guidance and a deus ex machina suit they had laying around just for you, so you can start running and gunning. I had not played Half Life 1, so I litearlly read the game wiki for background before starting this, Unfortunately, the couple hours of the game do not link it to the last game and set up a new story at all.

Guns kinda feel weak but you can increase their damage with legendary skills. I prefer using bows so I'm putting all my points into bow damage. If you think bows are weak (I thought so when I first used it) don't ignore it just yet. With only 5 points in bow legendary skill, it added 160% additional damage for bows and I can kill zombies with one arrow to the head! Anyway, I like collecting crafting materials and crafting things to survive. It makes the game relaxing in this way. I turned off the music so I could hear zombies easier... But when it was on, the score was pretty decent. You might like it.
Lots of areas to explore and things to do, I hope you enjoy it as much as I have so far.

This is great software but it NEED's a better file format for save & load to make it more useful to digital artists.

Uses the simple complementary color methods.
Can adjust Saturation & black levels separate from picked color values to create highlight and shadow swatches.
Four common color formats are displayed as sliders and input box's.
Ability to generate named groups for color swatch.
Able to use the software without internet.
Negatives:
Currently has only one import/export format *.json
Conclusion:
I like the software it's easy to use and handy but it needs common file formats for it to be more effective. However it is a great option for mobile artists as current free alternatives Like paletton or adobe require an internet connection and though they have their own issues making them less usfull (adobe lacks Split complementery & paletton needs numeric input values) than this program and also lacking in an import options they do let you export to known formats that are widely supported by art packages.

Forget Enemy Within and nevermind the DLC.  Plain old XCOM: Enemy Unknown is simply the best.
The satisfaction XCOM brings comes from meticulously planning every move and pulling it off flawlessly.  Every defeat, every soldier's death matters to you personally (above the grunts, anyway) and it's seldom unfair.  Mostly it's because you were impatient or slipped up somewhere.  Sometimes it is because you stumbled into a situation you were woefully unprepared for, but even then it's because
didn't evacuate when you should have.
After a while the maps do become familiar, but enemy placement is always random.  Base building could've been a bit more fleshed out and interceptions are boring with you just giving one of three basic orders to your pilots.  But that's it for the negatives.
Enemy Within introduced timed elements to every mission.  I get what they were going for, but it forces you into a certain way of playing the game.  That takes away from the satisfaction of carefully planning a strategy and pulling it off perfectly.  And things don't go according to plan most of the time anyway, which forces you to adjust on the fly.
Extremely deep and satisfying, XCOM comes highly recommended.
Edit: At time of writing I had not played XCOM 2, so any comparisons made between the two were useless.

Do you want a game with minimal content, unique graphics and ridiculously peaceful animals?
It's not the type of game with a ton to do, but it is the type of game that makes everything you do count. Very fun, relaxing and surprisingly addicting, it may remind some players of "The Endless Forest", except done much, much, much, much, better. Much better.
Not for players who are looking for "Shelter 3." Although Meadow takes place in the Shelter world, it's vastly different. No screaming kittens to take care of, baby badgers to save from ThatOneThingAtNightWhoStoleLittleJimmy — actually no survival aspects at all. This means that all players' animals (there are no NPCs) will get along as well — from badgers to bear cubs — rabbits may befriend lynx, frogs could safely follow eagles, and so on.
On the not so good side, those who don't own previous Shelter series games, DLC, soundtracks etc won't be able to unlock everything. If one doesn't own any Shelter series products, they start as a badger cub, and then may unlock the frog, rabbit, goat, fox, pheasant and hedgehog (in that order) in-game. However, Might and Delight promised more animals (any new animals will be able to be unlocked in-game no matter what previous Shelter games the player has/doesn't have), which should hopefully give these players more options.
Also, the game has no text or voice chat. The only way of communicating is through a lot of emotes, and sounds. Players may choose to work as a team (which is needed to unlock obelisks, which have the puzzle pieces/crystals needed for new skins and animals), or travel alone, probably searching for puzzle pieces along the way.
Overall, Meadow is a great game, with much more to come. It's only a few dollars, and I believe it's well worth it.
