First of all, if anyone here is looking for something like Shelter 1 or 2, they are most likely going to be disappointed with Meadow. It doesn't have any survival or fight mechanics. There also is no real story or missions that you have to complete.
You might ask yourself now "What the hell is that game supposed to be then?" Well, you start with one of your available animals and run around in the world of Meadow on the search for other players, flowers, crystals and similiar stuff, which you need in order to unlock new animals, skins and emotes. You can use these to communicate with other players. There is no chat or voicechat in the game, so all you can do to "interact" with people is making noises and using your unlocked emotes.
I really fell in love with this game the first time I met a small badger family on the other side of the lake, welcoming me to their small crew and going on a hunt for crystals together.
Meadow is basically a very relaxing Walking-Simulator game, that is all about meeting others and going on a journey to experience the world together. :)
I'd give Meadow a solid 9/10 points for what it is!

I am surprised at how many negative reviews are for this game.    But alas here's my review for it.
First off, I would like to point out.  The game is a lot cheaper then it is on Console.  A total of 35 bucks to be exact.  Definitely better then a lot of games where u need to pay over 50 dollars for a game.
The gameplay itself is very smooth and i rarely had any framerate drops if any at all.  It is very enjoyable to play as the characters with the smooth mechanics, not to hard to master anyone if you know what your doing.    I saw very little issues in the gameplay itself.   and i rather enjoyed the game, as i didn't have to worry about petty achievements that Playstation Network and Xbox Live have forced upon us in this day and age.   and personally i find a game more enjoyable and fun, without achievements.  and when the gameplay is rather smooth.
and like any DOA game.  the designs,  animations, graphics are really beautiful for this era.  and i really like the designs of the characters.  the story too is really good even if a bit corny at times.
Rant:
As some may or may not realize, it had to go through the greenlight system to get Approved which is not cheap, thus why the DLC bundles are so expensive and cost more then the game itself. and Unlike PSN,  Steam has never once sold Individual DLC for specific characters, thus why they're all in bundles.  So its understandable why Tecmo Koei put them at the prices they are, so they don't go bankrupt.  This way they have more chances to make more games in the future.
While i am disappointed they removed the 2 extra stages and the soft-engine that the PS4 and I think Xbox One use for the game,  i believe they removed them for stability reasons.  So gamers would have less issues playing the game.  as this would  cause issues with the Vram, and Hardrive space.  causing more bugs then what little bugs are already in the game.  This would especially be evident on low-end PCS, and not everyone has a High End PC that is meant for gaming.  so this was probably done for that.
Regarding the lack of why we did not get online mode or the achievements immediately which by the looks of things we will be getting fairly soon.   importing a game into a PC is not as easy as it looks. as certain things would cause stability issues as I mentioned before.  so they had to mess with things so they can put these features into the game later on down the road,  of course they will not be there immediately.  as this is new to Tecmo Koei.  their mainly known for console games,  this is  one of their 4 games they have put on Steam and are still learning.  So given that i say online and achievements are secondary when it comes to gameplay,  enjoying the game, and the story mode.
Finally.  The game does not suffer any crashes as far as i have experienced so this is another Plus for the game.  As Koei did not half♥♥♥♥♥it like Bethesda did for Skyrim.  thus less crashes for the game.
Rant Over.
Now the only NEGATIVES i really have with the game is the occasional glitch or 2.  but that is minor compared to everything else in the game.   Sure u can't customized your keyboard gameplay settings or your gamepad if you use one.  and for some people who use Low-end Laptops or PCS in general.   they may suffer Lip-synching problems but if you keep your PC well maintained this will fix this somewhat.
I personally use Ccleaner and Smart Defrag.
Overall the Game gets an 8 out of 10 in my book.  Would i recommend this?  Yes.  to any Fan of the Dead or Alive Series, this game is honestly a fun and enjoyable game.  and i would recommend it to fans of the series.

I've played for years and it is absolutely the best racing simulation out there.
Well optimized, I've never suffered any stutter or lag whatsoever.
Graphics may not be absolutely cutting edge by todays standards, but there is certainly not anything lacking in the visual department. ( The actual game looks much better than the promo videos, believe me ) I do find that user made skins available at mod sites generally look superior to the stock car skins.
Cars have excellent physics and feel, controller set-up is easily customized to suit your style of controller and play, car setups can be finely tuned with many many variables which accurately mirror real-world tuneability. Alternately, pre-configured set-ups are available online.
There are a huge number of different cars and tracks to suit any skill level or particular interest, Everything from high-downforce open-wheel racing, to touring cars, minis, etc etc. I prefer the vintage sports cars myself, the Retro pack with GT Legends mod brings me back to the golden years of vintage sports car racing.
The modding community is still very active, there are too many user made cars, tracks, skins, and effects mods to list, which add a lot to the game, and are not very difficult to install and run.
In summary, if you are a racing enthusiast and you don't have this game, you are really missing the boat. Don't expect any "yo dude, that was so gnarly" as in, say, DIRT2. What you are getting here is pure racing, and nothing but. At this price, you're stealing it. So get it, and drive it like you stole it.
Is it easy? No. Are you going to jump right into the most powerful car and dominate the competition? No. This is not an arcade game, it's a simulation. There is a learning curve. You may learn that you actually suck, at first anyways. Ever watch racing on television and think; "hey I could do that no problem"? Here's your chance.

I come to Steam everyday with the hope that a decent dungeon crawl will be waiting for me... today I see "The Deep Paths" and knew it was going to be a good evening of exploration and battle, I was not wrong.
Fan of Grimrock, Ruzar and of course Dungeon Master will find some entertainment here, it's well done, it has all the elements we know and love, and the price is right.
** Update: I finished the game and here are some thoughts... There are no multiple mobs, meaning you never encounter more than one face-to-face, keeping that in mind, I have 4 well geared party members, one rat should be no match, nor one mole, it seems unbalanced in that respect. Floor holes are harmless, you can't step in to one and fall, you can fall if a trap door opens under you. No food, no water, no skills, no death unless your whole party is disabled. Secret buttons are everywhere as bricks, never saw a ring or chain with a ring that was activated. In comparison to other dungeon crawls the final boss somewhat weak, I found the game as a whole was neither too tough or too easy. The save positions are wonky, if you get too many the autosave can lockup the game and even go in a save 'loop', try to keep the number of saves to four or less.

Final Thought: Worth a play, maybe worth two play throughs if you want all the idols and orbs, even then you might come up short. I had fun playing and look forward to the sequel.

Deathstate is a fun game. There's not much doubting that. It's also very frustrating. Also no doubting that.
The mechanics are easy to master, and with the variety of mostly useless equipment that you can pick up, most runs will be quite different than each other, and this is a good thing. The graphical style is pleasing, and the colors are quite nice, even though sometimes enemy bullets seem to blend in with everything else. The music is very good, and is probably the first soundtrack I've heard in a while that had a true retro feel to it.
Bullet Hell, Rougelike. Painful heaven.
However, I think that there are two poor decisions made with it.
If you want to make a difficult skill based game, that's fine. Dark Souls is fairly difficult with mechanics that can be mastered, Touhou is a series another good example of that. However, I feel that even will skill, the reason this game will still be difficult is not because it requires luck, but rather because of the visual filter that frequently brightens and can sometimes pulsate, making bullets impossible to see. Or, at least, very difficult to see. I can't judge if this was an intentional decision to increase difficulty, or if it was simply a stylistic choice. It /feels/ like a cheap way to increase difficulty, and I don't like that one bit.
The second, and probably more minor and definitely weighing on my lack of knowledge, is that most of the organs in the game seem to provide minimal benefit if any at all. This could change later in the game, perhaps the slight pushes in either direction will affect the outcome of a run, and I can't currently say if that's true or not.
If I were to give this game an honest rating, I'd give it 6.5/10. It's decent and fun, and I will definitely be playing every other day, but I will always hold a small resentment for it in my heart for the cheap deaths it often presents me with.

Deathstate is a game that I wanted to like. The idea of simplifying 2D shooters to a movement only based scheme is novel. It allows the player to focus on dodging and placement. This would be great if everything built around it wasn't so faulty.
The music in the game ranges anywhere from tolerable to aural punishment. The Maze of Ix has undoubtledy the worst track I've heard in a game in years. The art style is quite nice, even though various enemies are recycled through areas. Half of the enemies are barely animated, though. Visual design choices also get in the way of the gameplay. One of the zones cycles through colors, and some of those are almost the same hue as the bullets. Using or picking up healing items accompanies with a blinding flash that blocks out vision of projectiles. The clutter and aesthetic bits strewn about the levels make it hard to tell what can be walked over and what can't. Factor in that characters get stuck on corners like they're coated with rubber cement, and you have chunks of life lost to bad movement.
Aside from characters getting stuck, the core mechanics of the game don't work as well as they should. Runs are almost entirely determined by the quality of items picked up. Some items are good, most are relatively unimpactful, and some are outright bad. Why have an item that increases damage but slows rate of fire to once a second when the player is going to be surrounded by enemies? The later levels are swarmed by high health enemies that fill the screen with bullets. That could be forgiven if the player wasn't also on a timer to get through each stage. If they items picked up during the run were below par, then winning is almost surely out of the question. Money even feels like a wasted resource because shops are rare and usually are either a straight up gamble or just have consumables, which may or may not be bad.
I don't recommend the game in its current state, and I don't expect it will improve drastically enough for me to change my mind. If you are considering this game, I strongly urge you to look at Nuclear Throne instead. Although much harder, Nuclear Throne is well worth your time and money.
(Sidenote: At the time of writing, many items in the game outright do not work if you use an XBox One controller. Expect to use your keyboard or another controller until this is patched.)
If you like what you see then you won't be disappointed.

This game at the moment gets an 8/10 when it was released. This game is literially a rip right from the table top version of battlefleet gothic but this is a real time strategy game. No dice. Not a turn based game.
It is a fantastic game which was a surprise to me as it is better than what I thought this game would be. The story is split into 5 chapters and a prologue. The prologue consists of you learning the game along with following the story. Over the course of the 5 chapters, several events in the story line and lore of W40k occurs. Each chapter consists of events that occur during the years that each chapter covers before and during the 12th Black Crusade.
Story/Campaign:
You play as Admiral Spire of the Imperial Navy Battlefleet Gothic. It is your job to defend the systems and it's planets of the Gothic Sector from Traitor forces, Chaos forces, Eldar and Ork pirates during the events that take place during the 12th Black Crusade as Abbadon the Despoiler decides to attack the Gothic Sector.
I loved the campaign but there are very repetative missions (at least they are quick. But seriously playing Data Retrieval over and over and over again is repetative). The cutscenes are amazing! The music, voice acting and sound is amazing. The choices and mission results in some cases have an impact to the game!
This game consists on a space battles on a 2-D space using several ship types - escorts, light cruisers, cruisers, battlecruisers and battleships. You as an admiral of one of four factions get to select these ships and upgrade them.
More Information:
Micro Management Hell People are Talking About:
This so called "micromanagement hell" people complain about seriously makes me question if they have ever played the original Dawn of War series or Star Craft 1. Micro management in this game isn't entirely perfect, more on that later when I've finished this game's campaign, but it works! You are only controlling at best 12 ships maximum and can work with them.  This game is a really good strategy game that literially rips the board game the difference really is at least on the table top version you can think about what to do each turn. This game "solves" this the special feature that makes all of the statics and strategy in this game possible... It's called Press the Space Bar to slow down time... A lot of these people complaining about the "micro management hell" really don't seem to understand this concept. In all honesty, this game has much less micro management than Star Craft 2 and I prefer this for casual play and enjoyment.
2-D Space:
Umm... for people complaining.. It's a rip from the table top... Stop complaining. If you don't like it don't play it. Simple as that. This game is designed to be like this not because the game developers can't comprehend 3-D space or space comabt in games, yes someone complained about this -.-, but because it was from the board game that uses a 2-D space grid.

I think this is a great game with even greater potential for future development.
The developers seem to pay attention to what players are saying and act up it, and they're activly encourageing discussions and suggestions. The gameplay itself is very fun, having played the old Tabel Top game I feel happy saying that they've done a good job of transfering this into a computer game format, as well as the strengths, weaknesses and abilties of the factions and ships. That said there is a lot of micro managing needed for each cruiser size ship, i'd say you can get away with grouping light cruisers and definatly group escorts, but the larger cruisers and battleships need to be managed individually whilst also working together. To help with this there is the "Tactical Cogitator" ability, which slows down the game time significantly, makes all the micro managing much easier to handle and gives you a chance for quick changes in course or activating several abilities at once.
So far I'm enjoying the campaign, its a nice touch that there are multiple outcomes based on your success or failure in story missions and the side missions. It takes a little while to get to a point where you have complete free reign over what areas you can opporate in as a new sub-sector activates for each of the first few turns. There is also a limit to how many times you can deploy per turn, so don't feel bad if you seem to be loosing worlds, its going to happen, but you can claw them back from time to time, I think its less of a difficulty mechanic and more to do with the overall story.
Downsides, the Eldar. They're just so damm fast and the Pulsar is very powerful, fourtunatly the Developers listened to the feed back and have re-balanced them. Micro manegment can get a little bit overwhelming in the larger battles, but i suppose the leveling up system is mean to help introduce you in stages so you can get better as you have to take on more.
Overall I fully recomend this game and hope to see it continue in the future.

Options include separate sliders for Music, Ambient sounds, Effects, and Voice, plus full-screen, aspect correction, and custom cursor. If you're new to hidden object games, click on the ? at the top right of the options menu, which will give you the basics.  There are four modes to choose from: Casual Reader, Bookworm, Scholar, and Choose Your Own (NICE!) and you can change the difficulty at any time.
Using a HINT during the adventure portion of the game will give you a directional arrow without discharging your hint.
The task bar is retractable, and can be locked in a open position, if you wish.  Items in the task bar with circle underneath them need some kind of interaction.  Click on the items to zoom in and see what needs to be done.  You may have to open a box to see what's inside, or combine with something else in your inventory.
The journal is a cell phone.  It's located on the bottom right side of the screen, and there are multiple tabs to click on:
, which has no spoilers, and records the all-important things you MUST know to solve puzzles, and it also shows you how long you've been playing;
, which is interactive if you've chosen it to be (in the custom settings) and DOES have a jump-to option (you can also access the map without going through the cell phone -- just look slightly to the left of the cell phone button);
, which I never used; and
, which has 3 tiers and a total of 24 possible.
The characters are colorful, and nicely-voiced.  I was surprised to see two cutscenes with singing (à la Disney,) but I can forgive those short lapses since the game is so good otherwise. ;D  Our helper Gears the Owl come in very handy when there are things that we wouldn't otherwise be able to reach... Nice not to have to find a ladder every time!
There are a multitude of ways that we interact with the game.  With books there are two ways:  The first is where we have the narrator read a line of two, then we find a couple of items hidden on the page to progress the story.  In the end we get a new item.  An excellent way to keep the players interested in the story!  The second kind is where we open a book, and there's a hollow space inside.  We then need to find fragmented objects across the scene (don't close the book!) and when you find the final piece, you have an item to help you on your way.
There are a couple of different kinds of actual hidden object scenes.  There are your "typical" interactive HOS -- Items listed in white can be found right away, yellow items are under/behind something, green items need interaction.  There's a HOS type where every time you find something, you see sparkles, which indicate that there's something hidden behind the piece.  The last kind of HOS has four locked tabs at the bottom.  We have to unlock each box with whatever shape you see (ie. keys, spades, etc.) to see the lists.  Once you find all four items on a box, you'll find an item hidden behind it, which you will have to place in the scene.  Place all four items to finish the scene.
Mini-game instructions can be found in the bottom right corner of the screen.
:
- Bonus Chapter
- Integrated Strategy Guide
- 45 roses
- 28 Morphing items, found in the hidden object puzzles
- 24 Achievements
- 8 Downloadable Music Tracks
- 6 Concept Art, showing before and after (for a total of 12 pics)
- 10 Wallpapers (NOT just glorified screens from the game!)
- 28 replayable HO Puzzles (tracks time and accuracy!)
- Sugar Rush
The bonus is told from another character's point of view, and takes place after the main game ends.  Be sure to keep an eye out for roses, there are still 11 to find!  You get to the chapter by hitting the 'Play' button once you've finished the main game.
Instead of having a helper, you will see that there's something else in that space.  Keep an eye on it, you'll need to click it, then click the screen to accomplish some actions!
This is one of the best bonus chapters I've ever played, with the content just as interesting and fun to play as the main game.
There is a point where we have a choice to make, and it WILL affect the ending of the story.
Just a note that there is one mini in the bonus chapter that requires dexterity (and/or great patience,) and that the final puzzle was timed, in a manner of speaking.  You have to accomplish something whilst being attacked, and these attacks undo a bit of your progress, so faster is better.
The hidden chapters are unlocked when you find all 45 roses -- 37 in main game and 11 in the bonus chapter.  The game brilliantly tracks your rose findings, and you'll see them in the bottom left corner of the screen (underneath Gears the Owl.)  If the rose there is gray, you still need to find the rose on your current location.  If you click on the rose at any time during gameplay, it will pop up showing ALL of the roses to be found.  Found roses are red, unfound are gray, and empty spots show locations you haven't been to yet.  If you hover the cursor over any rose (of whatever color,) it will tell you the location of the rose you've missed so that you can go back and find it - Even after you've finished the game!
If you go to the Extras section, there are three things there:  Gallery, Achievements, and Rose Hunt.  Click on Rose Hunt, then click on any gray rose to travel to that location and find your missing rose(s)! Once you've found ALL of the roses, click on each of them to create a puzzle piece.  Once all 45 pieces are placed, the hidden chapters will be unlocked.
There are three hidden chapters, each with a different theme.  In the first chapter, watch for clovers -- there are four hidden here!  You finish the chapter, add the token to the middle book... and now you're stuck!
Back to the Extras section, and there's a Collectibles section that I didn't even see! (Top left)  You have to complete this section before you can go on to the second and third hidden chapters!  In this section are NINE sub-sections.  Click on any area to go back into the game and grab the collectibles that, if you're like me, you didn't even know to watch for... Or perhaps they aren't unlocked until you finish the game, I don't know *shrugs*  There's one at each location, for a total of 45 collectibles, and the hint button WILL help you find them.  The area where our helpful owl was will show you which item you're looking for - very helpful!
NOW you can complete the last two chapters, #3, then #2.  Finishing the last chapter will unlock:
Sugar Rush unlocks a HOS with 100 items to find!  Just one more little bonus to this CE that has SO many extras, already!
The main game ended well, but the bonus chapter gives us some great closure. The graphics are very nice, the music never invasive, the gameplay and story also very good!
My only gripe is that, even though there are in-game achievements, we didn't get Steam achievements. :\
All told - even though I played this game four years ago - this game took me over 8 hours to complete, and is still one of the best Hidden Object CE's that I've played!  Absolutely recommended!

Are you looking for a realistic depiction of space combat?
Then what the hell are you doing looking at Warhammer 40,000 game?!?
This is a naval sim with a sci-fi coat of paint. AND IT IS GLORIOUS!
This is probably the best 40k game since Dawn of War. The models are beautifully detailed. The action is fast paced with an emphasis on micromanaging

The campaign is good. It’s the story of Abbaddon’s 12th Black Crusade, same backdrop as the tabletop game. The overworld gameplay melds the best aspects of a slightly branching story combined with the world map skirmish style of the original Dawn of War expansions. Almost every turn Abbadon or some Xenos does something to mess with you and you have to broadside their faces until they stop. It gives you a mission with added voice overs and story, most either introduce a new game mode or a variant of an existing one. For example there’s one game mode where you have to steal something and warp out, well the story mode variant is that you have to plant something and force the opponent to warp out. There are also unique opponents to fight, like a space hulk the size of a small moon that you need to torpedo to death. Otherwise the remaining 2/3s of the game is a skirmish game where you fight to maintain control of planets that let you upgrade your ships. That being said it’s seems to have caught the worst of both worlds by deviating from the Battlefleet Gothic campaign setting and introducing new characters, while still forcing you to fight Abbadon and having him escape in the end so he can star in the chronologically later Vlack Crusades. The ending also had someone who was either a completely unmentioned character or a character so minor that I forgot about him pull an Independence Day style kamikaze and win the day for everyone.
The cutscene animation can if charitable, be compared to a nice looking paintings with some moving bits added. Mostly the character stay still with some details in motions. If you aren’t being charitable then you can compare it to the webseries “If The Emperor had Text to Speech”. That’s when they aren’t using a slightly souped up version of the ingame engine to do stuff.
The voice acting is that mix of hammy and ridiculous that we’ve come to know and love from 40k games. Just goes to show, if you can’t afford good voice actors cast them to be horrible in the right way. Actor can’t emote to save his life? Cast him as an emotionless Techpriest! Actor so hammy Jews and Muslims should feel guilty listening to him? There’s an Ork Kaptin that needs to be played!
There is only an Imperial campaign. Apparently the desire to play as Chaos or a Xenos was heresy and the Inquisition burned it.
The gameplay is focused on maintaining the range and firing arcs of your ships, with significant amounts of ability micromanagement. This is aided by your ability to slow down time so you can coordinate all your ships. The races feel varied, with the Orks favouring close range and ramming, Chaos emphasises range, mobility and sustained fire, the Eldar have mobility and burst attacks, while the Imperium has armor and crushing mid/short range broadsides. The balance however is rather wonky, the Imperium are slightly overpowered in the release version. The Eldar were ridiculously overpowered in the beta, then they took a nerf bat critical hit to most of their survivability, while maintaining the need for even more micro than the other races.
The gameplay is has a number of game modes of various degrees of balance and fun. All of them can be won by shooting all your opponents until they are dead, but some have alternate means of winning. I have a particular hatred for the Data Retreival missions, you have to board the enemy and warp out with some mcguffin, but the enemy can steal it back. This rapidly degrades into a game of hot potatoe with whoever has the last boarding ability not on cooldown winning. Convoy missions are completely unfair to the defender at the start, and gain balance only in the later game, maybe even tilting slightly towards defender as you upgrade your transports. Planetary Assault on the other hand is a complete mess that is actually fun, you have to get to some point on the map with any capital ship and unleash the emperor's fury on some land target, it's a mad scramble under fire.

On normal difficulty however the AI is often a joke, I’ve seen them unload all their abilities on my scout destroyer. They seem to have been programmed to spread out their fleets, enabling me to wipe them out piecemeal. I rarely suffer significant damage. The Eldar AI in particular is laughable, they seem to be a rush to die within the first 2 minutes of the battle, they rarely survive. Infact the few times I’ve been defeated was because I had to share my points with an AI controlled partner, who promptly blundered his way into kill zone and died.
Overall I recommend this game to people who have little experience with the Warhammer 40,000 universe, but love naval combat. If you do have experience with the WH 40K universe, then you have already pre-ordered this game. Failure to pre-order it is heresy. It’s awesome, you should be glad you bought it. The Emperor protects!

Not bad. Not great either. Better than Dead Island though, clearly a sequel. The free running works well, though don't think it's on the same level as Mirrors Edge, it's not. The combat is decent and weapon crafting isn't bad, however weapons degrade with use and have a limited number of repair counter before they're trash. This sucks bad. Like many games that make you struggle for resources throughout, you'll find a good item every so often but hesitate to ever use it 'just in case'. My real issue is the great chasm between qualities you'll run into, you'll find a super power base weapon VERY rarely and everything else you find will typically be less than HALF as powerful. It is certainly more of a survival game, especially since the most useful resources are of course, the rarest. The other drawback is guns. They aren't useless, but as expected gun fire draws the undead. Ammo isn't that hard to comeby, in the wild sure, but every merchant in the game carries an unlimited amount from what I can tell. Originally the game didn't have a Bow/Arrow but it does now, it's excellent, especially if you can get the upgrades to increase it's damage out put. The biggest screw up in the game is the core mechanics and their consistency. More often than not I end up dying due to an explosive that I've thrown, this is because the blast radius and damage of explosives is highly inconsistent. This is compounded by the awful 'downed' mechanic which can leave you stunned on the ground being murdered for what feels like an eternity. It leads to a ton of rage quitting because your character simply wont get the f**k up, and you just sit there for what feels like minutes watching your health bar tick down, because you got knocked down by an explosive you've through a thousand times but this time for NO special reason the blast radius was double its normal. It isn't a game breaking problem, not in the slightest, but it is ultra frustrating and leads to more deaths than any other danger in the game.

- Multiple languages, but they are all bad translations, most of the times it doesn't even come close to what they are trying to say, this is very clear in the Menu where you can guess what everything stands for but the headers for each are wrong.
- The weapon shop is very unclear, you see stuff with a price (like another bow) but even when you have the money you cant buy it. It would have been beter too have some kind of "lock" symbol over the weapon icon to make clear it is progress locked instead of money wise.
Further more it is very unclear what an upgrade does, besides the wall (extra life) and the arrow upgrade (more arrows). All other upgrades have no explanation or non at all what the result will be of buying said upgrade.
For example there is a tower upgrade, it costs 5k coins, which is quite a lot ingame (you can buy one of the best bows with it), but it seemed to do nothing at all, maybe extra lives but it is no where possible to check said assumption.
- Another point on the purchase front is that you only at the end of a level can use your money, there is no other moment. So it is very anoying that when you save money for a better weapon, you cant revise that decision because of your choice to save the money, that you cant spend it anyway to beat the next level.
- The previous point wouldn't have been that big a flaw if you where able to replay chapters and earn extra money to improve for the level you are stuck in. Which is not the case.
This makes the game more a trail and error kind of game then anything else. Because if you get stuck, you have to restart the entire campaign to revise your choices. Which is terrible because you also dont get any indication what to expect in the next level where you can base your choices on.
- The game crashes randomly, which is very anoying for endless mode, you have to start all over again. outside the fact that this is also the case when you make a wrong purchase choice as adressed earlier.
-/+ The achievements are broken as well, you get 2 achievements while launching the game. 1 is for buying an archer and the other is for buying a couple of upgrades for your wall (lives). Then I get the meet the merchant achievement 1 level too earlie as well.
+ The game has a nice design though.
+ The sounds arent bad either.
+ It is entertaining if you can look past the poor design choices and the less then transparant  shop.

I enjoyed it. Keep in mind, this is Tomb Raider Lite. I'm still unsure if it's an improvement over Temple of Light; however, Temple of Osiris is a different beast in many other ways. The combat is still solid, and Crystal Dynamics introduced a mini loot system that continually refreshes the combat. That said, the game seems a bit easy (and gets easier as your arsenal increases). I really wish there was a hardcore mode or something to up the challenge or garner interest in a second playthrough. This is Tomb Raider, after all, so there are a fair amount of semi-challenging puzzles. The gunplay seems to outshine the puzzle solving, but that's ok given this title is not trying to be overly ambituous.
The game also times you on your completion of each tomb. Your time is uploaded to a master server where you can compare your completion times against your friends or the community's. Sadly, it seem there is cheating/hacking out there, so the system is effectively broken. I suppose its original intention was to get you to retry the same area over and over, but dangling that carrot from the stick fails here. Nice try though....
The single player story is paper thin, but there is a multiplayer co-op component to make up for it. The artwork is pretty damned good. Overall, I think Crystal Dynamics delivered and then some on the aesthetics. They always seem to do a good job keeping this franchise fresh an interesting. Value-wise? Totally worth the $15 or so spent.

TL;WR: Looks like a rip-off, but it's great and will be even better soon! DLC is reasonably priced if looked at in perspective of price per costume/movie included.
I pre-ordered this and was quite unhappy with the state the game was released in, especially in comparison to the console versions. However, as of today, 45 steam achievements have appeared, and although they are currently locked (just for now), they show that Team Ninja is moving to rectify any problems that they had upon initial release. Some of the achievements also reference online play and crimson stages, two of the biggest bits of content left out of the initial release.
Also, in terms of the 'extortionate price' of the DLC, even I thought the same when seeing it for the first time, but when you look at how much each DLC contains, the price seems a lot more reasonable. However, they really should have just split them up into a lot smaller packs, both to make the price to seem more fair upon first seeing it, and to give players better choice of what they want to buy (e.g. buying 81 skins for £40 only to want/use 10 of them is a bit silly).
Fun Set - 81 costumes. Roughly 50p/$0.78 per.
Halloween Set - 51 costumes. Roughly £1/$1.55 per.
Variety Set - 68 costumes. Roughly 80p/$1.24 per.
Tropical Paradise Set - 54 Costumes, 16 movies. I roughly averaged the price of the skins from the first 3 packs at 75p/$1.17 per. This leaves the movies at roughly 60p/$0.93 per.
Excuse the rough maths/currency conversion, but it puts things in perspective.
Provided upcoming patches go smoothly, I'll be well chuffed.

I didn't see any reviews of this game yet so after playing for an hour here is what I think of it:
It plays very similarly to Legend of Grimrock; grid-based dungeon crawling with monsters, loot and puzzles.
Things which set it apart for me in a positive way are:
a) your party slowly but continually recovers health (every 15-30 seconds you gain a little chunk back)
b) NO FOOD MANAGEMENT (thank god)
c) keyboard shortcuts for each party members' attack so you won't get carpal tunnel from clicking during battles
d) back row characters can melee attack and don't require special long range or ranged weapons
e) if a party member dies you just have to wait a short time for them to heal up, no travelling anywhere or using special items to revive them; only characters that are living when a monster dies get the exp from it so that is the downside
Some minor negatives:
a) main menu music is quite loud and you can only mute the volume of music not adjust it down (and you can't change that until you're playing the game after creating a party, at which point the minimal settings screen can be opened in the bottom left corner)
b) you have to exit game to change keyboard shortcuts in the config screen you cannot do it while the game is running (probably a limitation of the game engine)
c) some of the UI elements seem more designed for a touchscreen ("swiping" inventory left and right for example), and it isn't shown in-game in any fashion that you have to swipe left/right to see more inventory items, I honestly accidentally figured that out
I'm enjoying the game and while I don't know how long it will end up taking to beat, it seems like a good value for what you get.

This is one of those questions, similar to beer or brandy. Some will say they prefer beer because it's cheap and quenches the thirst. Others will swear by brandy because it's tasty and worth the price. So it goes between Metro 2033 and Metro 2033 Redux. We were all thinking it, so I thought I might as well get this comparison out of the way. There's no real way to compare redux to the original, since it's marketed as a flat upgrade. Is that really the case though?
What's leftover from the original, first of all. Well, the voice actors, locations, and moral point system are still there. The levels are all more or less the same, with only a few variations and extra secrets. The VAs are still stiff fake Russians, with the best dialogue coming from the one off conversations you hear in passing. The moral points are as secretive as ever, and they're all the same ones as were in the original, so veterans of 2033 won't have to relearn one of gaming's most secret features.
The differences then, and there are quite a few. It'd be easiest just to say that it's Last Light in 2033 form. Everything from the combat to the lighting is copy pasted straight from Last Light. The gunplay is more responsive, the colors are more vibrant, and guns can be customized at shops.
The question is "is this good for the game?". I would say no. The bulk of 2033s entertainment value came from it's incredibly depressing atmosphere, which is something Redux painfully lacks. 2033 was all gray in the tunnels, dirty white on the surface, and the only color came from fires that enemies were hanging around. There was also no ambiance, so you could here all creaking metal structures and mutants cries. 4A seem to have wanted to go for a more action movie feel, but the very core of 2033 contradicts their ambitions. You're supposed to be a single little man fighting to just not be killed by the world.
I have to say I'd recommend this game. You can turn the music off, which goes a long way to giving Redux a survival feel once again, and it's better optimized than 2033 was. However, I would say it's not as good a story game as 2033 was. If you have enough money or they're on sale, get both to appreciate the differences, but otherwise I'd say go for the original.

I wouldn't recommend this game at this time.
There are quite a few bugs left from the Beta, and some new ones to spice things up for you heh. For example I have had to give up playing the campaign due to a Fatal Error occuring frequently in mid-mission, which is when you can't save, the frustration can be felt quite strongly when you're doing one of the longer Story missions and just as you were about to win, Fatal Error. There is another frustrating bug that still occurs from Beta, where you get a UI option over a ship to Execute a captain that is routing from the battlefield, but the button is not clickable. This occurs so often that it feels like there is a dice roll to figure out if your allowed to click it. There is also another quite annoying bug in multiplayer, where you will spend Renown to get your ships back, but quite often the connection times out forcing you to force close the game, when you get back the Renown will be spent, but your ships will still be damaged, as if you hadn't spent it.
Speaking of UI, it is quite clunky, where you have to individually place each ship down while deploying, and if you want to redeploy, you can't just drag a box around them and select where you want them to shift over to, you have to click the UI button over each the ship to tell it you want to redeploy that individual ship. Which can be frustrating when your stuck using a majority of escort ships due to most of your fleet being stuck in the warp or too damaged to fight. There is also no way to lock fleet formations, so you'll likely have ships going at different speeds towards the enemy, even if you put them in a Selection Group (Ctrl+1, 2, 3, etc), as well as have them line up in a generic horizontal line if you do a group move order anywhere, which will lead to some ships deciding to cross into each other's path, causing crashes. It can also be quite frustrating since in the campaign, they suggest that you group your small fleet close together to cover one another, but it's quite difficult to do that without a lot of unnecessary micromanagement. If you're stuck doing a Transport Escort mission, good luck trying hide them in the center of your fleet, without your fleet abandoning them.
If your ships either get lost in the warp or destroyed, or even heavily damaged and kept out for several "Turns" (they basically 1:1 used the same mechanics as the turn based campaign for the multiplayer), you'll likely just enter missions with the minimum cruisers, and as many escort ships as you can get, just to warp out before you get hit too hard. Rinsing and repeating this same tactic until your other ships are ready to battle again for a real fight. I really feel like this was a bad idea and leads to you not wanting to bother actually playing missions until you have enough of your ships returned to service.
Another issue I have is the map, you can't really zoom out too far to see the full view of the area. You have a mini map, but it seems that unidentified ships don't show up in it, so you'll have to tilt your camera to a horizon position or scroll around to see where all the enemies are constantly.
The missions themselves that I have seen so far are not too engaging.
Which is just a deathmatch between your fleets, the most fun mission you'll enjoy playing in my opinion.
Which is you escorting or defending against these extremely slow and unwieldy transports, and due to not having any fleet formations, you will likely only use the same strategy of making it look like your defending your transports on one side, while you have your Transports use Running Silent to slowly move towards the end zone from the far opposite side of the map.
Where you must kill the enemy flagship or defend your own before they warp out, more often than not you'll be doing a Benny Hill chase (especially against Eldar and Chaos) and they'll warp out before you can get to them.
: It's basically boarding tag, board the defender's ship with the data, take it, then hope you can warp out before they take it back but it ends up being a chase the enemy ships and hope you can catch up, as well as have their shields down before they warp out of the area. Probably one of the more annoying missions, depending on which faction you are.
: You have go over these timed spots to bombard the planet, or stop the enemy from going there. Good luck if you're fighting Eldar or Chaos, since they'll likely get to those bombard spots before you can get over to them, and it'll take time to actually kill them, even if you catch up, so they'll just slide right in and move to the edge of the map until next bombardment time. As defender you also start off at the edge of the map, meaning you have to get to the middle area to try and slow down the enemy ships. It would be nice if defenders had an early indicator of where the bombard zone would be, so that they could place units near there or do a ruse by putting ships in locations to fake out the enemy.
I love the Warhammer 40k, as well as the tall ships in space theme and there are quite a few neat ideas but I just can't recommend it right now. It feels like it needs a lot of love to really shine, and I truly hope the devs can provide it.

I bought this game shortly after it released and beat the story on Normal. I quit and picked it up again 2 years later. I played it on Hard+ and am currently on the final mission to catch Rais. After this I'll probably just farm and get my Legendary points up. Once I get my one-handed to 20 legendary then I'll try Nightmare.
After all this, I'd say it's a really good game. There's something about it, all the sneaking around, all the head-on fighting, the dodging and counter-attacks makes close-combat really fun and tactical. Guns kinda feel weak but you can increase their damage with legendary skills. I prefer using bows so I'm putting all my points into bow damage. If you think bows are weak (I thought so when I first used it) don't ignore it just yet. With only 5 points in bow legendary skill, it added 160% additional damage for bows and I can kill zombies with one arrow to the head! There's still room for 15 more points in bows so it will get better as you play.
Anyway, I like collecting crafting materials and crafting things to survive. It makes the game relaxing in this way. I turned off the music so I could hear zombies easier... But when it was on, the score was pretty decent. You might like it.
Lots of areas to explore and things to do, I hope you enjoy it as much as I have so far.

Game is good but not amazing.
Brief description:
Game features capaign (Imperial Navy only), solo skirmish with AI and skirmish aginst other players (Orcs, Chaos, Eldars, Imperial Navy).
In campaign you are tasked with defending the Gothic sector while dealing with pirats as well. Every turn you get few deployements to missions. Combat missions are made very much like tabletop game with rectangular battle area. There are few mission types and sometimes some special mission will come up. You can also make some important decisions during the campaign.
Between missions you can visit harbor and build, upgrade, repair ships.
In skirmishes you just get to combat mission without story.
What's so good:
+ FINALLY WARHAMMER 40K SHIPS !!! for fans this is just enought to buy the game, ships are detailed and look gorgeous.
+ excellent warhammer 40k mood and Epic campaign
+ hilarious Orcs
+ Ships variety - every race has its way of building ships, so every race ships has strength and benefits compared to others, within one race there are few ships in each weigth class
+ Ship colisions - you can ram enemies on purpose or by accident ram your own ships.
What's not so good:
- Some small balancing issues.
For example: Orcs favour that allows to pull ships is way overpowered as it allows to pull enemy ship into the torpedo volley and then just ram it easly.
If in a mission you have to eliminate specific target, the target is visiable to you from start, completly eliminating needs for any sort of reacon skills or using environment (by placing my targeted ship I have to protect in a gas cloud I expect it to be hidden, but no, AI always knows where to look for it).
- Repetetive mission types, since missions are very short (5-10 min max), limited number of mission types becomes boring fast, sure playing an assassination vs some specific race is different that against other race, but after doign 10 of each you get just bored.
Conclusion:
Recommended for Warhammer 40k fans.
Review based on game about 1 month after release, without most recent patches and balancing.

This review is more for the creators of Meadow.
I love this game.
Searching for the crystals is very interesting when you have other animals come along. If you happen to be alone and you find a stone with the two diamonds on it, though, tough luck. You'll just have to go look for other people and bring them to the spot.
There are a few problems that need to be fixed soon. The main issue for me is that the game constantly freezes. I've waited for a few minutes for it to fix itself, but I end up having to just resart the game. This freezing problem happens about every five minutes or less, so it gets pretty annoying after a while. Especially when you are trying to lead or follow a pack.
I would like some things to be added in the future. Prey needs to be included in the game so that life in Meadow is a little more interesting. Hunting for cubs and for yourself would be very pleasing. Of course, rabbits, deer and frogs can't be included, but rodents and possibly birds can be. Carrying prey to the younger animals would be cute. For the prey animals in Meadow, there could be berries and grass to feed on. Including the ability to lap up water would be nice as well. Adding this would give meadow a more natural feel to it, though it still doesn't mean that any animal could die if they dont hunt or scavenge.
One more possible thing to add is small, narrow dens that have a tunnel leading in and a cavern large enough to hold a mother animal and her young, rather than big, open dens. I personally do not mind if they all have the same construction, they just need to be scattered along the seasons. Looking for a certain small den to return to with just a few other players or just by yourself would be nice.
(EDIT(s))
some characters I would love to see- Adult Wolf character and possibly a wolf pup. I would be so happy if wolves were added. I've found the perfect spot for a bunch of wolves to hang out :3

Trying out as a trial, and haven't played base SFV. Played a bit of SFIV and various other fighting games.
For anyone else looking at this from a gameplay perspective, it's pretty fun so far. I have the advantage of having a friend who is at about my skill level in fighting games so as long as I can do private lobbies that's generally all I need. There were some connection issues in game, expected as we're in different countries, and they generally resolved themselves pretty fast. Haven't ventured into online yet, but first impressions are alright.
There's one thing I don't understand though, and that's the lack of training mode availability in this beta. I understand the desire to keep the offline content on lock in order to not be practically giving away the game for days, but damn it's such a waste to have access to all of the characters but no ability to try them out. To be fair, does this really matter for a beta made to test online connections? Sort of, actually. Unless you're someone who's played SFV or fighting games in general you'll probably immediately get decimated online, that means you'll probably leave after a couple of frustrating matches, and the size of players working through the beta will probably drop like a rock.
A couple of days in training mode aren't going to make you into a top-tier fighter or anything, but at least you'll know a character's moves without having to use a phone or something.
Anyway, personal rant aside, it's pretty fun to play so long as you are going into it with some experience. It's a beta for people who care enough about SFV to commonly deal with the online mode, and want to see it improve. It's not going to be nice to you if you're new, and I suppose it's not above criticism, but please at least try to recognize that these server issues are going to happen on a beta specifically made to test network connections. Also, c'mon man, it's free! Grab a friend and make a lobby,♥♥♥♥♥♥around as much as you want, so long as you're ready to do it online. Hope more people pick up on this, and I hope for the best when it comes to the online connections improving for actual SFV players.

This is one of those questions, similar to beer or brandy. Some will say they prefer beer because it's cheap and quenches the thirst. Others will swear by brandy because it's tasty and worth the price. So it goes between Metro 2033 and Metro 2033 Redux. We were all thinking it, so I thought I might as well get this comparison out of the way. There's no real way to compare redux to the original, since it's marketed as a flat upgrade. Is that really the case though?
What's leftover from the original, first of all. Well, the voice actors, locations, and moral point system are still there. The levels are all more or less the same, with only a few variations and extra secrets. The VAs are still stiff fake Russians, with the best dialogue coming from the one off conversations you hear in passing. The moral points are as secretive as ever, and they're all the same ones as were in the original, so veterans of 2033 won't have to relearn one of gaming's most secret features.
The differences then, and there are quite a few. It'd be easiest just to say that it's Last Light in 2033 form. Everything from the combat to the lighting is copy pasted straight from Last Light. The gunplay is more responsive, the colors are more vibrant, and guns can be customized at shops.
The question is "is this good for the game?". I would say no. The bulk of 2033s entertainment value came from it's incredibly depressing atmosphere, which is something Redux painfully lacks. 2033 was all gray in the tunnels, dirty white on the surface, and the only color came from fires that enemies were hanging around. There was also no ambiance, so you could here all creaking metal structures and mutants cries. 4A seem to have wanted to go for a more action movie feel, but the very core of 2033 contradicts their ambitions. You're supposed to be a single little man fighting to just not be killed by the world.
I have to say I'd recommend this game. You can turn the music off, which goes a long way to giving Redux a survival feel once again, and it's better optimized than 2033 was. However, I would say it's not as good a story game as 2033 was. If you have enough money or they're on sale, get both to appreciate the differences, but otherwise I'd say go for the original.

As the store page for the vanilla game is still available (i.e. the Redux edition does not make the original disappear) I am only going to concentrate on the new aspects of the game. Should you be interested in what Metro 2033 is about feel free to read my review on the vanilla game's store page.
Initially, I thought this Redux edition was only a graphical enhancement to the game released back in 2010. Make no mistake: the creators have done a superb job! Redux sports better lighting effects, more detailed textures and, to be honest, we have so many bits and pieces here that it is simply better to use YouTube and look for some comparison videos.
But is this good for us? Well, yes! Remember when Last Light came out? It offered better graphics so much so that we can say it was as Metro 2033 was originally intended to be. So, the developers picked this upgraded, more refined engine and remade all the levels of Metro 2033. We have the ultimate Metro 2033 experience now!
And the upgrades do not stop there: some new elements introduced in Last Light were also borrowed. For instance, melee was not possible but finally, taking out enemies silently is possible not just from the distance. Also, diary pages are now hidden throughout this game. Since you explored everything for the extra ammo now you can find these and read more about Artyom's thoughts and emotions.
Some sections were expanded upon and there are new sections such as the hall in Polis where you can stop by and marvel at the establishment along with the bartender who you can drink with. Beside the diary pages there are many safes hidden, as well. Keys to them appear on dead bodies or simply on shelves and while they glow in red due to the cobwebs sometimes it is difficult to spot them. Oh, cobwebs! We now have these and setting them on fire with the lighter is as fun as it was in Last Light!
Redux is the definitive version of Metro 2033. A version that expresses that this is how it should have been all along back in 2010. You can dismiss the idea if you want due to the fact that money is - once again - asked for it. However, if you are a true fan of Metro and you liked its sequel I'm sure it will be an immediate purchase for you. :)

Deathstate is what you get when you take Binding of Isaac, add some "bullet hell" mechanics, and put it in a colorful 16-bit H.P. Lovecraft universe.   It's a relatively simple game:  Steer one of a growing cast of unlockable characters through a series of procedurally-generated worlds, gobbling up unlockable guts--monstrous hearts, eyes, brains, lungs, etc.--and equipping arcane tools that modify your stats and offensive capabilities.
And I quite literally mean "steer":  As a single stick shooter, you don't have direct control over when or where you shoot.  Instead, your character automatically targets and shoots enemies when they come into range, leaving you to focus entirely on movement and dodging.  This unusual choice may turn off some players because it sounds like a dumbed-down twin stick shooter.  It doesn't help that the first map (called a "layer") is frequently pretty easy, leaving many to assume you can simply sleepwalk through the game while your character does all the work.
However, it's not long before the difficulty ramps up and you realize that the game is built on maneuvering around the dozens of bizarre enemies and their various projectiles and attacks.  The single stick conceit doesn't make the game easier...just different.
Fortunately for those who descend a few layers and feel that the game is still a little too easy or light on the "bullet" aspect of a bullethell, the game gives you the opportunity to increase the difficulty.  This comes in the form of crystal skulls, which are located at the beginning of each run and then randomly throughout the middle of levels.  Approaching one gives you the option to "desecrate" it, upsetting the cosmos and upping the ante; enemies will be a lot nastier, projectiles will be more plentiful, and the player will die to fewer hits.  There appear to be differences between desecrating the skull at the beginning of the game (which activates an "Insanity" mode) and those that are periodically discovered within the Deathstate (which simply add "Desecration" levels to the run).  But once you start a run, you must die to undo the effects.
Nonetheless, Deathstate isn't exactly the most complex roguelite shooter.  You won't constantly stumble across novel item synergies (or contraindications) like you would in Binding of Isaac.  In fact, you're usually free to hoover up all of the stat-enhancing guts you come across.  But as of the v1.20 Beta, the developer has taken a lot of community feedback regarding item, organ, and character balance in an effort to significantly expand on the variety of item effects, combinations, and character classes.  The result is that there's a greater depth and range of options in Deathstate than ever before.
In sum, the game offers up enough unlockable characters, items, weapons, and dungeons--and more than a few weird gameply mechanics and secrets--to keep things fresh and interesting for anybody wanting a new roguelite-shooter in their lives.

The changes that were forced upon the free-to-play community are actually well worth the meager 10 bucks.  There are far more people playing now, the options have increased quite a lot.  It's a much better experience.

Absolutely terrible.
Where to start? Hm.
1. Extremely annoying and not-enjoyable gameplay modes like "assassinate the ship that's way faster than your fleet and you have 3 minutes". And "protect the paper cargo ships against a fleet 2x larger than your's who can insta-kill them just by ramming into them".
2. Unskippable cutscenes. This is a mortal sin in 2016. CALL THE GAME INQUISITION.
3. Ship AI. I've found on many occasions (usually at least once a mission) shouting at my ships WHAT ARE YOU DOING? This usually appears in the form of ship A assigned to attack ship B instead decides to just stop and do nothing mid-flight. Usually this manifests in the form of me assigning a ship to do something important while I'm off micro-managing another battle, only to find that the order was no carried out. Or ships turning AWAY (for some reason) from enemies whom they are assigned to protect, often at really pivotal moments like the enemy warping out.
4. Enemy AI cheats. You hid your ships in a nebula - which is supposed to cloak them. And yet somehow the enemy always knows exactly where you are. Funny, that.
5. Graphics. The graphics in general aren't that great. Sure there are fancy nebula skyboxes and really detailed ships, but you spend most of the time so zoomed out that it hardly matters. Also asteroid fields don't really animate. Particle effects are mediocre. And despite all this mediocrity, there are still graphical glitches. Texture flickering, weird poly and lighting artifacts.
6. Extremely annoying mandatory tutorial to start the campaign.
7. Despite aforementioned tutorial, a lot of really important stuff that users might like to know is left out. Apparently players must discover these on their own. Like - how many ways are there to cancel an enemy warp? What's the difference between the blue and purple bar above health? And the data-theft missions, would have been nice if it were written somewhere that they can steal the data back. Also 3 minutes is stupidly short amount of time with these big lumbering imperial ships.
8. I also noticed that ships do not lead their quarry when asked to attack. If the quarry is a faster ship, this means they will never catch up to them.
I can give more details, but if I were to sum it up more concisely: its just not a fun game. I find myself spending more time yelling at the AI for being stupid and/or glitchy, or facepalming at (literally) impossible missions, than I do actually enjoying the game.
Its really unfortunate. The game has a lot of potential, and it could be fun, except that all its potential is wasted in the really-bad mission types. Escort the paper ships, timed mission to assassinate a ship that's faster than your's. Chase ship that's faster than your's. So grindy. I wanted this game to be good. I was even a pre-order. I regret that now.

Purchased this game with my husband and father and have been playing as a trio on our LAN. We've enjoyed the world a lot so far and haven't even adventured too far from the safety of our little base camp. I cannot wait to see this game achieve its potential! For its early stage release, its in good shape so far and has a good amount of content to keep us occupied, despite the bugs we've run into.
Some things I hope are adjusted in the near future:
Level scaling vs enemy leveling
We started at the Dwarven fortress and found lots of easy to kill sheep and rabbits out of the entrance, but slightly down the road we started encountering a mix of level 1 all the way up to level 30 beasts all in the same area. We made it to level 10ish and found that level 1 panthers would murder us but we could easily kill a level 20 goblin. I would like to see a little more control of what level monsters are in one area or a way to see what level/difficulty it is before having to engage with it. Seems a little out of balance currently. We were basically kicked out of our base camp by a level 21 panther that was camping our corpses, had to cut our losses and move on after 6 deaths.
Rewards for exploration
Perhaps we havent adventured far enough, but i'd love to see rewards for exploring cool ruins/towns that are scattered around the world. Such as small caches of items or armor.
Minimap
Hopefully its planned, but the game is in desperate need of some kind of map feature, especially when playing with friends.
Interaction interface
Not a huge fan of the holding "E" to interact with items, especially when having to open a door in a hurry (to escape a monster). I would prefer an instant action button to open chest or doors.
Overall the world is BEAUTIFUL! I think most of the complaints we have will be ironed out in the future patches.

I want to preface this by saying, yes, DnL is very remeniscient of Ark. You could be excused for thinking this game looks kind of like a total conversion for Ark. And for good reason. Studio Wildcard, the developers of Ark were aquired by Snail Games, the developers of DnL, back in December 2015. So they've had access to the proprietary Unreal Engine dev kit used for Ark, and are using that to develop DnL. So, all the millenials that are crying "ARK CLONE" kind of missed the news I guess. Anyway, it's all but impossible to look at this game objectively because of it's parallels to Ark. So I'm not going to try, I'm just going to embrace it.
DnL is pretty much where Ark was when it came out on EA 2 years ago. It runs like a dog. I get around 20-25 FPS with my current rig, which isn't a slouch, but is by no means a beast either (I run Ark now at 45-60 FPS). But let's not forget, this is an early access title, and in a little over 2 years, could possibly be where Ark is today performance wise (which by no means says a lot, because Ark still needs a lot of work done in the optimisation department).
This is probably the weakest area in the game so far (besides it's optimisation). Combat is painful. Ranged combat (bows/crossbows) is woefully inadequate. Bow and crossbow hit for the same damage, regardless of player level. There are various elemental/magic arrows, but I'm yet to try them because they are incredibly expensive to make, and going by how much better iron hook arrows are over stone hook arrows (the arrows used to tame animals), I doubt they will be worth the time or effort spent harvesting the required ingredients (you'd probably use way more resources than you could get using these arrows).
Melee is extremely clunky due to the lack of a first person perspective option. You are locked into over the shoulder chase cam, and this makes it difficult to aim melee attacks. Also, the alternative attacks for weapons seem to go in random directions most of the time, and if you're weilding a shield, you can't do the alt attacks at all because shield blocking is bound to the same mouse button as alt attack. This could be by design though, for balance.
Now we got to spell casting. This is all but completely inviable as a combat option outside of very, very special occasions. The resource pools, and there are multiple, make it totally prohibitive. This may be an active design choice by the devs to make magic combat something really special, but it just feels like the time and resource investment isn't at all worth the payoff. For the amount of rersouces required to cast spells, they feel underpowered to the point if uselessness.
There's 2 types of magic in DnL. One is a consumable system. You craft X amounts of a particular spell, like a Rune of Light, and you get 1 use of that spell for each crafted item. These use no mana, and are basically a one shot cast. Pretty much like potions. Nice and simple, works perfectly well.
The other is a complex system of mana, focus and durability, and requires the use of a staff.
This magic has 3 resource pools (it's arguable you could say 4, but I'll explain that later).
First, you have the spell stones/scrolls/whatever they are (let's call them scrolls, because they look like pieces of paper). These need to be crafted, and higher level spells require a special crafting structure (magical work bench). They also have a durability, the higher the spell the lower that durability pool is. They need to be equipped in a special spell slot in your character sheet, and only one spell can be equipped at a time. Each time the spell is cast, the scroll loses a point of durability. Spell scrolls can be repaired, lower level ones in your inventory, higher level ones need to be placed in the magical work bench.

When cast, they also consume some of your mana. You need downtime to replinish this, at the cost of focus.
They also cost some focus, because mana is replinished from your focus pool. This can be replenished by consuming flowers, focus potions or by sleeping in a bedroll/bed.
The possible 4th pool I mentioned is the fact you really need to carry a large number of the same spell around with you so that when one breaks you have a backups in your inventory. So your inventory serves as the resource pool, as it's finite based on weight.
Each casting of a spell also reduces the durability of your staff, tying it into the first resource pool.
All this makes magic an extremely clunky and resource intensive system, not to mention the juggling act you need to do to keep your spell slot equipped with spells.
The entire conbat system needs to be rebalanced/overhauled.
Let's get to the meat of the issue though. I've noticed a number of red flags.
1) Lots of legacy stuff from Ark still exists in DnL.
(legacy keybinds have since been removed) As a matter of fact, the entire settings system, both in-game and the .ini files are basically lifted straight from Ark.
2) Lots of misinformation within the game itself. Like animals being named differently to their bestiary entries. In fact, the vast majority of the creature in the game don't match even the names given in the bestiary. There's other issues with items having misinformation in their descriptions too.
3) Bucket loads of "chinglish". So much badly translated text.
All these can realistically be forgiven, after all the game is in early access, and has only been out for a little under 2 weeks at the time of writing this. So only time will tell really.

I adored the original Lara Croft game Guardian of Light and was incredibly excited when they announced Temple of Osiris and I wasn't disappointed. Just like GOL, Temple of Osiris is a fun action packed arcade shooter with flourishes of puzzles and challenges. However, there are a few noticeable improvements from the first. First being Temple of Osiris is more open and works in hubs (rather than chapters) just like the Tomb Raider reboot which allows the game to implement the main pillar of exploration from the main series. Secondly, the game improves on its loots system giving more meaning to the gems scattered throughout the world as you can use them to open chests to gain access to new powerups and legendary weapons. On top of that you have the ability to change the time of day and the weather which also works alongside the loot system as certain weapons/powerups only work in certain conditions such as night-time.  The game also has a lot more post game content as these different weather/day-night cycles change the world around Lara and the other characters meaning in different conditions different challenges and puzzles will appear giving more for the player to do rather than just going through the tombs completing challenges just like the first game. The only real negative of Temple of Osiris is that the puzzles aren’t always as inventive or as challenge as the original. However, the game is still fun the nonetheless and I highly recommend it.

NEO Scavenger definitely attracts a wide range of people, and that's one of its most charming aspects. First and foremost, the ultimate genre is survival, so people who like survival games such as Don't Starve or even This War of Mine, a less well-known title, will enjoy NEO greatly because it doesn't fall off this path at any point. There's a storyline no doubt, but it isn't the key focus of the game and I easily played it without paying attention to what my character's goals actually were.
It's a text-based game which, I must say, is well-scripted. There are few typos or grammatical errors that I've noted, and, although white text on a black background is bound to wear the eyes out after a long enough session, the words themselves are very readable and humorous at times.
The gameplay is easy, but you won't start the game with much success. You begin by choosing the skills of your character, from benefits like 'Medic' to flaws like 'Feeble'. By adding more flaws, you can choose more skills. This is often where you'll fall at the first hurdle. It takes a bit of trial and error to find your perfect set-up, which gives you a bit more value for your money, though I must say the amount of scenarios one can find is limited, or at least from my experience. Certain instances reoccur quite a lot, and it can be hard to overcome that skill curve. The game doesn't tell you how to play it. You really are trying to survive.
In summary, NEO Scavenger is a decent game. It offers a nostalgic layout with a challenging premise with many interesting concepts and mysteries to delve into (or not). If you want to play it well, an element of strategy is required. There are also battle sequences for Pokemon fans, which is average in nature, and depends wholly on the skills and 'luck' of your current character. NEO is repeatable, but there is a limit on how many hours you can put into it. For £11, this is understandable, and it's an acceptable price, although waiting for a sale isn't a bad idea.
If you dislike losing, reading, repeating processes until perfection, playing a game without guidance, games without a lot of sound or mouse-based gameplay, it might be worth looking into another survival game, but, if not, NEO Scavenger is a solid purchase which you can play again and again without internet or a gaming computer.

You choose a server, select what animal you want to run around as (you unlock as you go) and enter the world. The mechanics are simple and easy to understand and you can decide if you want to play with others or strike out on your own. The map is large and you can find yourself in a different season depending on the area you are in.
I'd recommend this game to anyone looking at something easy, relaxing and fun to play.

I don't often write reviews, but I have rarely seen a more badly designed game.
Let's list off what's wrong here:
Let's go and assume that since major countries are backing you, you have access to the best soldiers of earth, since it is the only logical explanation.
Earths finest soldiers are prone to headshotting their teamnates when they are under fire.
Same earths finest soldiers have at most 25% chance to hit enemies unless they are 2 steps away.
Earths finest seem unaware that helmets exist.
Earths finest are unable to pick up one of the 3 medkits laying next to their dying blood brother.
Earths finest have to chose between shooting, or ducking for cover. Unable to shoot then duck, that would require too much brainpower.
Earths finest must forego intensive field training to understand how to use suppressing fire.
Earths finest are unable to move an inch while an enemy moves 1 kilometer accross the map, predictably position themselves right next to them, and headshot their asses (which have no helmets)
It is illegal to send more than one chopper with more than about 4 soldiers to tackle a vastly superior enemy force.
It is illegal to send more than one jet to fight off an heavily armored flying saucer.
Enemies shoot through walls, cargo trucks, cement, floor, and headshot you since you have no helmet.
Your soldiers look like they are farmers hand picked from their selected country in order to have the least chances possible to win a fight. Strategic choices don't matter. In effect, it becomes a luck game. Will your armed retard be lucky enough to shoot a crawling gremlin, or will he miss 7 shots and then proceed to shoot his friend in the♥♥♥♥♥ Find out in X-Com, Enemy Unknown!
Honestly, I have no idea how a game like that could have such an high rating. It is barely playable.
There are pros, though. The base management and loadout options are cool, along with soldier classes. But in the end it doesn't matter, since helmets were not invented. The story looks awesome too, I bet I would enjoy it if i could just watch the game instead.
For the record, I played on Classic Ironman. I understand Easy mode would help by making Earths finests not die to plasma beams to the face, but that's beside the point.
This game is probably the only one in my library i've regretted getting, and it was only 10$. Do not get this if you want a strategy game, it is an irrealist mess of luck based combat.
