To my knowledge this is the third game from the developers Tindalos Interactive. I would encourage people to look at Steam reviews of their two previous games Etherium and Stellar Impact.
Battfleet Gothic is well presented with excellent details in the cut-scenes, and the graphics are very good. The gameplay is different to typical strategy games and involves selecting ships for a fleet to undertake a variety of different mission types, which scale in diffucluty very sharply, depending on what faction you play as or against.
I really wanted to like this game after spending considerable time on the Beta. The game was originally supposed to be released on the 21st March but when the beta went live it was riddled with 'Fatal Error' bugs and crashes to desktop. The beta, which consisted of multiplayer 1 vs 1 and the first three missions of the campaign was extended to the new release date of 21st April. As things went on many of the bugs seemed to be ironed out.
However, once the game ws finally released it became apparent that it was still riddled with bugs. I would still encounter random 'Fatal Error' crashes while playing the campaign. In addition, when trying to play multiplayer 2 vs 2 with a friend practically every other game would result in a crash to the game's main menu, or back to desktop.
The problem is that all too often I don't get to play it due to all the bugs and crashes. Just getting a multiplayer 2v2 set up with my friend takes several tries as the invite system just doesn't work. Then once in the game the chances of finishing the match are far too slim. All in all a good concept but let down by poor coding.
After trying to play multiplayer with my friend we both decided to request Steam Support for a refund, which I hope they will honour as this is the only game I've ever requested a refund on. I would strongly suggest you save yourself the bother and avoid this game. Based on the history of Tindalos Interactive I cannot see anything changing as they never fixed the bugs on their previous two games either if you look at their reviews.

Okay, played some Battlefleet Gothic: Armada today and I have to say. It is a good game. Graphics are amazing and the UI is simple to use. The AI is brutal (typical for the WH40K series) and always outclasses you.
However, I do have some..misgivings.
Your own ship "AI" is about as intelligent as a rock. You MUST micromanage everything, even if you put the abilities to "auto-use". You also have to wrangle and drive your escorts or else they just become something else for your capital ships to knock out of the way causing massive damage to both ships. The AI of your ships should be smart enough to detect the velocities of your other ships and that of your allied ships and move out of the way and use skills and orders apporpriate for what it is doing at the time.
The multiplayer is inherently flawed in its implementation. Dont like playing against players? Oh well. Want to play with your buddy? Well the invite system MIGHT work. Its like they built the MP aspect of the game for Professional Bracket-based play, which is fine if the game wasnt based off a defunct table-top and catered to a niche market. Also it only supports up to 4 players at one time.
Single player, while interesting, is also flawed. There are three game modes for SP, Campaign (which is beautiful and lore friendly), Skirmish, and Custom mode.
I havent really played the Campaign past the Beta "tutorial". So I can't comment much on it. Skirmish is where you take random game modes and fight whomever the game wants you to, which defeats the purpose of the Skirmish mode IMHO. The custom mode lets you design any battle you want even picking a random admiral with or with out skills.
These last two modes pretty much come close to breaking the game for me. I believe the game would have better if FOCUS Entertainment had implemented both the SP and MP the same way they did their War Game series. In which you can create a lobby, invite your friends, await other players to play against, or do a comp stomp.
I understand why they did the things they did because of their leveling systems, dont want people to comp stomp till they get a Battleship then go into combat against other people. However, they have defeated this by having an Admiral needed for each mode.
All this being said, the game is beautiful and the designers spared no details to the ships and have each faction some plus and bonuses.
Overall, imma be busy for the next few months.

Shiny Gauntlet is a combination of a few very specific genres. It Is part dungeon hack’n’slash, bullet hell and rogue-lite. It has been developed by Spitewrench, a Jamaican developer, and remains their first and only game on Steam. The game has been inspired by the likes of The Binding of Isaac and Legend of Zelda.
My expectations entering the game were relatively low. As of writing the game only has three Steam reviews and has escaped any publicity. Essentially, the game is a little-known title that has not been picked up in the gaming press. Because of this although I had minor expectations for this I was still interested in playing it and giving it an opportunity. Consequently, you could suggest that I was hoping to discover a hidden gem.
Unfortunately, my first impressions of the game are that it is essentially a flash quality game. It is clear what the game is attempting to achieve but its production values fall far below the expectations of a game of its type. Games such as The Binding of Isaac where it draws its inspiration from are not necessarily known for their production values – more so their playability – yet they feel head and shoulders better than that available here. Consequently, the production quality is a bit of a let down.
The game does not load at full screen. There are no options to change the game’s resolution or sound. The only options that the player has is to customize the keys. However, I don’t see a reason why many players would want to change the game’s settings because you essentially used the WSAD keys to move and the arrow keys to attack in that direction. Further, the E key swaps weapons, Q performs an action and the spacebar enables you to use your ability.
I found the game to be difficult. This is in part because of the less than full screen resolution. Even as someone who has spent many hours playing similar games I struggled to find my bearings within the game. It also doesn't help that the game essentially throws you in at the deep and expects you to know what you are doing. Therefore, I would suggest that the addition of a tutorial would serve as a big boost to the game. Consequently, until then I cannot recommend the game to newcomers to these types of games.
Working in the game's favor is the fact that it has a number of different game modes. There is the fully fleshed out story mode. But for those of you seeking a different type of challenge beyond just a main campaign type deal you have access to an endless mode and a challenge mode. In endless mode you endeavor to get to the lowest possible dungeon level. Challenge level enables you to play for fabulous prizes.
The game has Steam achievements. However, it lacks Steam trading cards. The addition of trading cards will result in an increase of sales. As a result of a lack of features the game doesn't require any of the other features that Steam has to offer.
Although I believe that there is a market for this game I don’t believe that I or a sufficient number of Steamified users would fit within the niche to make it an easy recommendation. There are better games available to purchase on Steam that fit within the specific genres that Shiny Gauntlet fits within at about the same price point. However, if you’re a fan of those genres then you may consider checking this one out in an indie bundle or at a sale.

Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light was a memorably great game. It had a stupid plot and terrible voice acting, but the two-player mode really made that game shine - combat felt more intense and rewarding while the puzzles (which are modified when there are 2 human players) were very fun to solve. I loved playing the game in 2-player local mode with two Xbox controllers plugged in.
On the surface, that formula seems largely intact, and now you can have up to 4 human players. Sounds awesome, right?
Well, no. The level design has a disjointed feel, the combat just doesn't feel satisfying, and bosses are a joke with 4 human players all firing on them at the same time. The puzzles have become too simple, whether with 1 or 4 players. It looks like a different team was assigned to the game, and they tried to copy Guardian of Light without actually understanding what made that game good.
It's possible to have fun, especially with 4 human players on the same PC. It just can't compare to the previous game. It's also marred by technical issues like clipping bugs and random framerate drops.

text:
I've decided to write my thoughts after seeing a mixed public opinion on it. TL; DR version is at the bottom.
Temple of Osiris is the sequel to the action-adventure / puzzle game "Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light," which holds an
positive score on the Steam store. Both games are played from an isometric perspective and have a heavy emphasis on solving environmental puzzles with some action-shooting thrown in for good measure. Gameplay-wise, the two are very similar in controls and mechanics, such as the use of the grappling hook or rolling spheres to certain locations to advance. The big difference, however, is that Temple of Osiris can be played with up to 4 players in comparison to Guardian of Light's two-player experience, and Lara Croft now uses Osiris's object-altering staff to assist with puzzle-solving instead of Totec's spear.
Despite being very similar in its core aspects, it is very clear that the developers attempted to improve virtually every aspect of the game from the first, and one huge change from the first game to this one is the graphics and the aesthetics. Probably the most immediate and biggest contrast from the first game in terms of aesthetics is the menu screen:
In Guardian of Light, the menu screen is a still image of an open book with several comic panels serving as the "buttons," while some background music played softly in the distance.
In Temple of Osiris, the player is immediately shown a dramatic, fully-animated scene of Croft and her companions in an intense back-lit part of Osiris's kingdom, with very sharp contrasts in light and color. Lara Croft is standing in a pose that suggests a state of confidence that screams "My body is ready." All of this happens with incredibly dramatic, cinematic music playing in the background.
The list goes on:
The first boss of Guardian of Light is in a rigid isometric view that puts an emphasis on puzzle-solving.
In Temple of Osiris, the first boss features explosions, flames, particles, special effects, and general chaotic insanity galore. The screen shakes at every boom, at every quake of the ground. Even the camera is tilted at a lower angle to show the scene behind the objects in the foreground; a background that is blurred by the depth of field hints at the utter chaos and ancient horrors that lurk below. Unfortunately, I didn't get a good, long look at it because I was too busy dodging the missiles exploding on the ground.
The difference is as huge as Super Mario 64 and Super Mario Galaxy. I almost thought that somewhere in the development team of Temple of Osiris, people were seeking Michael Bay as a consultant.
The keyword here is "cinematic." The graphics and the aesthetics of Temple of Osiris are clearly intended to be much more cinematic in comparison to Guardian of Light. Depth of field is much more emphasized and commonplace. Ambient occlusion is everywhere. Overall, the graphics have been massively touched upon compared to Guardian of Light. All of these changes to the aesthetics serve to give the player the sense of wonder and adventure, to strike home the point that they are about to explore an unknown yet exciting danger. The chaos during the action sequences and the boss fights emphasize the desperation and insanity of the moment, that the player is literally fighting against the gods with barely anything more than guns. Not a single scene in Guardian of Light gave me that same sense as Temple of Osiris did.
But games are not all about the graphics, the sound, or the first-impression, and that leads us to the biggest factor: the gameplay.
As stated before, the two games play very similarly compared to each other, with the only big difference being the manner in which puzzles are solved. However, that difference in puzzle-solving is one of the biggest factors that is causing the divide on the public opinion towards this game.
I will go ahead and admit it:
This is the deal-breaker for many people; it is the biggest gameplay-related complaint that constantly keeps being mentioned in the reviews. Personally, I believe it to be so for one big reason.
First, the nature of the staff mechanic. When Lara (or Isis / Horus in multiplayer) activates the staff, all objects with the symbol of Osiris are "activated" and react accordingly. For example, floor tiles with the symbol will lift higher in height, allowing players to reach higher locations and advance, and time-bombs will have their timer slowed to be safely pushed across longer distances or even used as portable platforms. In Guaridan of Light, the spear is used primarly to ascend or cross terrain due to its nature as a temporary player-created platform.
What ends up happening is that the staff mechanic of Temple of Osiris forces the player to immediately look for objects marked with the symbol, which usually end up giving away the answer simply by their positioning and two-way function. More often than not, these objects are floor tiles that stay in one place in the world in which the player only has a limited amount of control over; up or down. In Guardian of Light, the spear mechanic teaches the player to look at the problem as a whole. Because the means to advance is directly in the player's hand, there is no obvious focal point in the puzzle for the player to look for. This in turn encourages players to analyze the situation and create a plan, making mental guesses on the outcomes of each possible plan before actually attempting it.
Looking at the design of the puzzles and the action sequences in both games, Temple of Osiris is clearly meant to have much more emphasis on the action-adventure aspects rather than the puzzles. There are many more "chase scenes" in Temple of Osiris than in Guardian of Light, and the boss battles are much more intense and engaging. Combined with the addition of 4-player co op instead of the duo team in Guardian of Light, it may have been a design choice in order to make the game more accessable and appealing to a larger audience, people who may or may not be avid puzzle-solvers or simply don't want puzzles to be the bigger aspect in the action-to-puzzle ratio. It's anyone's guess.
A very big complaint I do have to address is the control. The controls in Guardian of Light are absolutely fantastic; they are responsive, quick, and fit perfectly in the game. Unfortunately for Temple of Osiris, the movment controls were much more sluggish compared to Guardian of Light, for reasons unknown. I speculate that it may have to do with the turning that Lara does when changing directions, which can easily send the player into situations where he or she is exposed to taking damage or dying immediately. The sluggish movement can be a huge source of frustration for the player.
According to other reviews of this game, Temple of Orisis also has a rather sizable amount of bugs and glitches, some of which end up ruining the gaming experience completely. However, I have not experienced any of these bugs or glitches in the game so far, leading me to believe that the game has problems on specific graphic cards and/or computer setups.
With everything laid out on the table, it is time to answer the big question: "Is this game worth buying?"
Honestly, I think the game is pretty good. It may have some very noticable flaws, but the game as a whole is very playable, and more importantly, enjoyable. I still ended up having the same amount of fun with this title as I did with Guardian of Light, despite all of the reviews that say otherwise.
Players that really enjoyed the puzzles of the first game, or are avid Tomb Raider fans may end up disappointed with Temple of Orisis. But people like me that aren't extreme fans of the Tomb Raider franchise who are simply looking for interesting games can definitely find this game enjoyable.
TL; DR: 7 / 10

Short version:
Don't be fooled. The demo is heavily front-loaded, and comes from an earlier version of the game. I was intrigued by the demo's promise - the Choose Your Own Adventure-style mechanics, the sneaking around crumbling ruins looking for supplies, the scary combat that made encounters tense and meaningful.
However, this "final" version is a hot mess of a game that feels cheap and lazy in nearly all aspects of its design. It's flawed at the very core of its concept, and I can't recommend it at all. Bad/10, don't buy unless you like random coin tosses wiping your saves and making you start over.
Long version (includes playable demo):
In fact, we can play the game right now, for free, in the space of this review. That's how shallow it is. Are you ready? Okay. I'm flipping a coin. Heads? Tails? Good choice, let's see: oh, you lose. Here we go. Heads? Tails? Interesting tactics. Okay - oh, you lose again. Heads? Tails? Oh, neat, have some random loot. But you also hurt yourself getting the loot. Also, dogs. 20 dogs. They eat you. Oh, well, actually, you can flip a coin to see if you can get away. You want to do that? Okay... oh. Darn. You lose after all.
I'm not exaggerating. The game is almost entirely based on a flip of a virtual coin. Everything you do comes down to absolute random chance. Forget any notion of augmenting the luck of the draw with your virtual skillset - your skills themselves are nothing more than cards in a deck. You've got "Strong." You're good at melee, right? "Strong and Melee." Oh, too bad, your enemy drew "Strong" *and* "Tough." Whoops. You're dead. Delete your, say, 20 hour save file and start over from scratch.
That's really the depth of this game's design. Make the wrong choice in a CYOA event? Dead, save file deleted. And some of this stuff is out-there random, too. It would be amusing if, like in the real thing (good old paper-back CYOA books), you could bookmark at least some of your progress and fix your mistake eventually, but nope - the whole game is based on stupid, abject luck killing you and forcing you to start over. Over and over and over again. In a game this flimsy-floozy, ironman needs to be an *option.* "Hardcore" is a distinction you earn by being good enough to rate as a consequence-based experience. This is not that. This is a dozen feral dogs appearing one after another at the whims of RNJesus to arbitrarily kill you for laughs.
Combat is a death sentence if you don't take very specific traits. That is stupid. Even if you do take the token, all-but-required traits, it's still just a toss of a coin whether or not you get killed. There's no strategy. No planning. No real player input. It's all just stupid, basic numbers. It's the laziest type of junk non-game you can imagine. Think you're a maverick and you don't want to play as a Herculean beefcake? You want to try to get by on stealth, cunning, and guile? Maybe get some hits in with finesse? Forget it. Sneak up on a guy with Tough and the best you'll do with your crowbar is tickle his funny bone. He'll then Chris Redfield you, exploding your head with a single punch. If you try to use melee weapons, and you don't have the right traits, you're dead. The enemy will bump you, and you will fall apart. Combat against an enemy with Tough is functionally impossible if you are not similarly equipped - you could catch him completely by surprise, and it doesn't matter a whit.
The actions you can take are rarely based on logic or the flow of a fight, as you'd perceive it - instead, the game makes no bones about it, and literally tells you that they're randomly available to you. Sometimes you can attempt to dodge. Sometimes you can't. Sometimes you can attempt to kick a downed enemy. Sometimes you can't. And of course, any given action has a chance of failure, even after passing the "can I even try it" dice roll. It's just random chance on top of random chance. It's mindless.
There's nothing wrong with making combat meaningful and deadly - I'd love to see more games give the player reason to actually avoid looking at enemies like loot-and-XP-pinatas - but this isn't that. Enemy encounters are ridiculously random, and the player has scarce few tools to avoid it. More often than not, its Olympian sprinter dogs dodging a million attacks, causing your character to whine, cry, and generally give up on life the instant he's bitten or scratched.
I'm reminded of Unreal World, another "survival" game I was fixated on for a long time. After going through hours upon hours of painstaking hunting, building, and gathering, arming and armoring myself against the elements and my enemies, I fell victim to a wretched combat system that just shrugged and said, "meh, you lose." My character in that game was supposedly possessed of excellent skill with a blade. Despite this, I found myself staring in disbelief as my character flubbed every single strike, missed every attack, and ate every swing of a clumsy bandit's rusty handaxe as my only input as the player was "try to attack again, or just give up on life." That's this game in a nutshell, only this game has added "choices" that can wipe your progress instantly. Naturally, that means this game is "better," right?
It's a shame. People have been clamoring for real survival games for years, and this lazy schlocky junk is what we get. Amateurish garbage whose apparent mission in life is to cure us of that desire. It's nipping the genre at the bud, and that sucks.

Shelter = Adult Badger
Shelter 2 = Lynx
Paws = Lynx Cub
Owning all three = Bear Cub
Owning
of the content, OSTS and games = Eagle.

So I've completed both XCOM 2 and Enemy Within, and honestly, I'd recommend Enemy Within above XCOM 2. Sure, there may be more bugs, the graphics may not be quite as good, the interface might be a little less slick and there might not be much modding support for Within, but trust me, with Enemy Within, there's just that feeling of proper advancement that just feels lacking in XCOM 2.

The story is simple and not really important to the overall game which is fine for me because it has no effect on my gameplay other than bad guys are chasing me and I need to destroy their boss. The art style is like a 16-bit video game which makes me nostalgic for Super NES and Sega. It was easy for me to get started with an intuitive GUI and keyboard short cuts to operate the ship with little need for a mouse--I should try a gamepad.
The focus is entirely on optimizing the various ships during the game in order to survive and ultimately defeat the boss. The type of ship systems, weapons, and upgrades a player finds or buys can determine whether they make it to the end or die trying.
Before the game starts you are in the hanger which allows you to select one of the various ships to start your journey and there is information on how to unlock additional ships as well as ship layouts. But no opportunity while in the hanger to do some tweaks on your ship before you start your journey, which for me is disappointing, but I understand it could unbalance the game if not implemented carefully.
You have the option to choose one of three difficulty levels which also changes the gameplay and forces you to adapt your strategies. I tried at first playing normal thinking it would be difficult enough to challenge me but not too easy; I changed to easy mode pretty quick. I recommend new players to start with easy mode and disable advanced edition so you can get a feel for the game unless you like the sink or swim challenge of hard mode first.
There are 8 sectors for the player to traverse and within each one is tons of unvisited locations to explore. I really like how every new game will have an entirely new path for the sectors and differing numbers of locations and encounters which makes each play through feel unique. The challenge with exploration is fuel limitations.
I will admit that combat took me a while to comprehend because I was just point and shoot, but after several games, I learned targeting key ship systems like shields and weapons can make a huge difference.
Unlike other games where you have a save or checkpoint to return to when the player character dies, FTL starts you all over again from the beginning, which is frustrating but gives you a goal to work towards as you rethink your ship customization and strategies.
The game reminds me of an arcade game because once you achieve all the goals and achievements there is nothing else to do other than try to beat your highest score. A leaderboard would be nice so you can compete with other players or friends to be the best at FTL. Also, I would like to see a multiplayer version or expansion released whereby users can put their latest victorious ship to the test against another player’s ship.

I've been playing this game in a pre-release version, and now since its release. It's got tons of personality - great artwork, synth music, psychedelic visual effects - it's sort of like Stuart Gordon's FROM BEYOND movie as a Saturday morning kids' cartoon, mixed with a 16-bit dungeon crawl, re-animated as a roguelite bullet hell shooter.
It's instantly gratifying with pick-up-and-play arcade style action, but with some item collecting and tons of unlockables to keep you going. It's weird, Lovecraftian, funny, and addicting. My only complaint is that death sets you all the way back to Layer 1, and the game can get repetitive if you have to progress through the same few levels over and over again just to get back to where you died. This design choice does limit your moves - you're less likely to be daring and take a risk if you know the last twenty minutes of your game might be wiped out because you got cornered.
Overall, I've very excited to see how this game continues to shape up as the developer adds new content and works out the kinks. I'll be spending plenty of time with it.

Clicker mix tower defense game. In this game, you defend your house from an endless horde of undead skeletons.
Game consists of waves of enemies, each wave getting harder. Each wave lasts exactly 60 secounds, with no difficulty option available. You start with a normal bow, clicking on enemies will shoot arrows at them, depending on their hp, may require several arrows before they die. Skeletons are your enemies, and they come in various sizes, armors and weapons, and run at different speeds at your base, so there is some timing involved to land the arrows. At later waves, there are "kamikaze" bombers and catapults (wave 20 onwards, which can launch bombs onto your base from a distance) thrown into the mix.
At the end of each wave, you get to spend the money you get from killing enemies, on either upgrading your weapon (only crossbow and gun available, and shots represent how many times you can click before waiting for reload) or base (few choices like upgrading your tower level and the hp of your wall, recruiting archers and gunners to help defend, and buying tower gun).
The whole gaming area is confined to one screen, your base on the right, and your enemies attacking from the left. Once your base fall, you lose. There are some minor changes like weather and daylight / night, but these changes are only cosmetic, and the general background setting remained the same between waves and games. Music is soothing but repetitive.
Overall, not recommended. Game gets boring and repetitive really fast, with limited replayability. There are more games on Steam, some even free, that offers more entertainment than this game.
Cons:
- same background setting
- each wave last 60 seconds, restart at wave 1 after death, which gets repetitive and boring
- limited choices of upgrades
- expensive / overpriced upgrades - gun
- long reload time on upgraded weapons - crossbow
- no explanation of the upgrades - unsure what upgrading tower level actually means
Pros:
- clicker mix tower defense concept
- trading cards

The people giving this negative reviews are mostly veterans who didn't pay attention to anything SyncError and sponge have been saying for the past year. Here are some facts:
1) They have been telling us to switch to Steam for over a year. The people who already had the game on Steam didn't have to pay a single cent, even if they weren't subscribers. The subscribers who didn't switch even though they were told to do so can mail support and get the game for free.
2) The friends lists weren't saved because the accounts no longer exist. Just find your friends in-game and send them a friend request. We can do that in-game now through the Admin menu, something we couldn't do before.
3) The game works on Linux with Wine/playonlinux.
4) We have user-owned private servers and LAN now, something the fanbase has been begging for since the private Beta.
5) We still have stats. Just not the stats from before the switch, as again, the accounts no longer exist.
6) We can switch names now.
7) Delicious, delicious UTF-8 support finally lets us use Unicode letters in chat.
8) People are working on a replacement for QLRanks.
9) The one-time payment is about a 3rd of the price of a premium/pro account, and everyone can do everything the premium/pro users could.
10) We now have Valve Anti-Cheat. Cheaters who get banned now have to pay money for a new account.
11) The new UI and settings menu are far, far better than the old ones.
12) Watching demos is no longer a pain without 3rd party tools. We can now view our demos by pressing "Replays", there is a list of timestamps for each frag that happened in the game, and the new demo viewer itself is all kinds of awesome.
13) SyncError confirmed that we'll be getting gibs DLC.
The update was great. Stop whining.

I'm only a few hours in, and have lots more to do, but so far I'm pleased with this purchase.  I inevitably get frustrated somewhere around my fifth or sixth death, utter a loud expletive, and take a break. However, I keep coming back whenever there's a temporary lull in my day. Judging by the extensive list of items and features I have yet to unlock, I have a long way to go.
The controls are responsive and surprisingly simplistic. The etheric 'bullets' your character fires aren't aimed manually, but are instead fired automatically at the nearest enemies, making it your responsibility to put your astral explorer in the right place at the right time. The many swarms of weaker, projectile-less enemies can become a real problem, because they act as constant meat-shields to the more threatening enemies, prolonging every encounter and increasing your chances of losing precious hitpoints to your own incompetence.
Like most roguelike-likes,  the items you to pick up or don't pick up can make or break your run through the game, but you aren't entirely at the mercy of the Random Number Generator. Success always feels possible, if difficult, thanks to the bullet hell elements and the dodging mechanic. The many, many projectiles in the lower levels can be phased through or dodged by the directional arrow keys if you are fast enough, giving the game a high skill ceiling.
In short, the game is easy to learn and hard to master, and I give it extra points for the cool setting. I am very much enjoying this punishing fever dream of a game.

I really like the idea of this game, but they took any fun you could have had with it away when they force you to bum rush the objectives. There are a few different game modes where you have to capture data off a ship by boarding it, eliminate the flagship, or destroy the escort. Unfortunately, the game forces you to focus on nothing BUT the objective, totally ignoring the enemy fleet in a mad dash to win. The escort ships die very easily, so you can ignore the defenders and win. Focusing all fire on the flagship guarantees an easy victory, so again the defenders are worthless. This will be a 3-part review, first part dealing with the game in general, the second will cover the quality of the PC import, and finally in the third part I'll summarize my fnal impression.
<<<The game>>>
DoALR is a very decent and multi-layered fighting game, with a large number of fighters, each one with their distnictive fighting style and approach. Moreover, there is also quite a few fighting areas, a lot of them having some limited interaction possibilities (throwing the opponent off a cliff, breakable elements, traps etc.). Also, the triangle system seems to be working pretty well and make it possible for a newbie to start fighting even if they don't know any special moves or combos yet. Still, if you want to master a character, you need to invest some time and creativity. I think the game keeps a nice balance in this regard. The tag team is also worth prasing as it can bring you a lot of fun, especially when you learn how to perform switch juggles.
When it comes to visuals, the game is beautiful, even though it is based pretty much on the same engine as the original DoA 5. And of course there are also the female characters and their outfits. We all know that these are the main selling points of this franchise and that's perfectly fine. Unless you're some brick-headed prude or an insecure SJW hipster, you are in for a nice treat of some very high quality eye candy during your matches.
It is a little bit disappointing that Last Round is basically just a compilation of content from the previous installments in the franchise, with just little original content. However, minding that so far it's the only DoA game to be released on the PC, if you never have played these games before, everything is new to you anyway.
The only major downside of this game as far as I can tell is the frustrating enemy AI, especially in higher difficulty levels. The issue is not that it's too good, but that it blatantly cheats. A well-programmed AI would determine the high difficulty levels primarily by its ability to perform devastating combos and juggles; in this game, the difficulty is primarily determined by how much the system is bent in favor of the AI. Examples of the cheating include: AI always escaping your multi-throws, no chance for you to escape the AI's multi-throws and most annoyingly of all - turning your throw around and against you. By the latter I mean the instances when the AI exposes itself, you proceed to use the opportunity to do a throw, you see precisely that the throw is 100% going to land, but suddenly in some magical way, it turns out that it is the AI that ends up throwing you instead -and with a counter bonus. To be fair, though, it was much worse in the original DoA 5, and in comparison between the two installments, Last Round has much improved. Still, this "difficulty system" can frustrate to the point of throwing the controller at something in anger.
Also, the hitboxes tend to be crazy at times. There are instances in which either your or the opponent character lands a hit ,even though you can clearly see that there was no contact. It doesn't really happen that often, though.
<<<PC Import>>>
If I was to jusge this product solely by the way it has been adapted for the PC, I'd say it was a total failure. The way I see it, Tecmo did only the absolute minimum to make it work on this platform. There are no achievements, features are missing, Online play unavailable upon release, graphics inferior in comparison to the console version, and of course, the modding controversy.
If you sum it all up together, you'll inevitably come to the conclusion that Tecmo just wanted to open an additional fast income channel with this import:
- Half-baked conversion: check
- Missing key features: you bet
- Dumbed down graphics: absolutley
- Ridiculously expensive DLC content available almost from day one: hell yeah
- Pleas/ threats to the community not to mod the product, and thus override the necessity to buy the ridiculously expensive DLC to get new content: checkity-check-to-the-A
When pre-ordering Last Round for PC, I was really excited about the prospect of finally being able to play one of my favourite fighting games on a PC, just imagining how great it would look when handled by a machine with decent specs. You can imagine the disappointment after learning the hard way how much this product is lacking.
<<<Summary>>>
Don't get me wrong, Dead or Alive 5 Last Round is still a great fighting game and I really enjoy playing it, even though it's just against the AI at the moment and with DoA 5 for PS3 visual quality. That is why I find it very difficult to pass a verdict on whether or not it is worth getting. However, minding the fact that you pay pretty much the same for a PC version than what you'd have to spend for a PS4 one, and yet you get an inferior and cut product, it is evident that this is a rip off and a blatant money grab.
As much as I love the franchise, I simply can't recommend the PC version of DoA 5 Last Round. Maybe if they patch the game in the near future to make it at least match the quality of the console version, it will be worth your money. Right now I don't think the current state of the product is fitting the demanded price.

FTL:Faster Than Light is a Sci-Fi Rogue-like, where you take control of a ship and its crew running through the galaxy from rebels while trying to aid The Federation, whom the rebels are fighting. As for the game play, it is a mix of strategy, timing and RNG. Each run can take up from 3 minutes to 2 hours depending on how well you do. The different elements inside your ship make combat seem dynamic, but as you get better at the game you may find strategies to overcome every enemy. That being said there are many ships to unlock, each with their own variations each with unique strengths and weaknesses. My only complaint is that there aren't many events, so once you know what each event does you can quickly pick your options without even reading the event. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys rogue-likes or a quick strategy game.

Dead Or Alive 5 - Last Round is the latest version of the game and as far as I know, it is also the first Dead Or Alive fighting game released on PC. Based on forum talk the game has had its share of problems, so I consider myself lucky. But let's get to the actual review part.
I played the Story mode in one sitting and took a glimpse on the Arcade-modes as well, and I have to say that I am enjoying it so far. I think that the story was interesting and there are plenty of fighters involved in it. The number of fights is ok in my opinion, you get around 70 or so chapters in it (1 chapter=1 fight) so depending of how many times you lose you might end up spending quite a bit of time with it.
The fights are fun and fast paced. I chose to play the Casual mode because I don't have that much experience from Fighting games and because the characters have a great amount of move sets you usually manage to deliver stylish combos even with trial and error. There is a command practice mode where you can try to master all the 100 or so different moves for each character if that's what helps you learn more easily. Also, Breast Motion settings. <3
I was a bit sceptic whether or not there is any room for character customization at first because the game has a couple DLC bundles which are quite pricey on their own. Thankfully I was proven wrong and even though the base game might not give you for free all the most revealing outfits, there is still plenty of DOA-worthy cleavage. :) Some characters also have a few extra options in addition to the actual outfit like hairstyle or glasses which you can change. So unless you REALLY want all the towel outfits for the girls, it might be better wait for sales.
I will probably update this review when the Online game modes become available but so far it's been very enjoyable and the game looks good even on my machine which is already a few years old. But for now I highly recommend the game for all who like me decided that Mortal Kombat X is too pricey and well....I would cheat myself if I didn't admit that Sweat + Breast Motion settings = cool. :D

The game is pretty, and it has detailed mechanics. However, the game has always had problems. It was buggy on release, and periodically they'd release a patch that would break the game that you were currently playing.
So you turn off automatic updates in Steam, and you're able to play your game without it being interrupted by an update. But then they forced a patch despite having updates off, and yet again my game is ruined.
And for about a year, the multiplayer was broken, such that we couldn't finish the game until the next patch. Of course, that patch broke our game.
So despite the number of hours that I've played, it's been one game-breaking thing after another. Plus, the Ai lack sophistication, and I understand that the Civ6 Ai is even dumber.
And as much as we've tried to use the multiplayer, the implementation of multiplayer for this game is lazy. There really needs to be a PBEM mechanism, rather than force everyone to be playing at the same time.
Civ4 was problematic, as well, so I'm just not going to buy any more games in this series.

I have to admit - when I first came across Quake Live, it was kind of a turnoff. While this game might look like Nuclear Throne, the mechanics underneath these visuals feel more like The Binding of Isaac.
For example:
* Each level is procedurally generated
* Each "floor" has a boss
* You move deeper into the game and it gets much much harder
* As you progress you unlock more characters
* There are 140+ weapons/items to unlock
* Tons of passive and active items
* There are item/weapon shops
* There are lots of little different active events that you can encounter
I realize some of these things are also in Nuclear Throne but all of these games are quite similar in some aspects.
TL;DR:
* Nuclear throne doesn't have the amount of unlocks/progression that Dead State has.
* The Binding of Isaac doesn't have the bullet hell that Dead State has
* This game is worth picking up IMO if you like Rogue-lites

The game that I spent the most time on steam. Easily plus 200 hours to the 207 I played while I was playing offline back in the day. I think Civ 5 is a good game but I don't think it is perfect. Here is some reasons why
-Playing multiplayer, I realised that the start of a game is really important. However sometimes when I play at with people with full knowledge or even less knowledge than me, I found my Civ in a bad position because of my location. In order to compete with them equally we had to decide different maps which we didn't like. That's why we usually played on Earth map. Starting with useless desert tiles and rushing into building a Petra was less effective while my friends started with natural wonders. Usually ends in a reset because of how unfair it is. If the RNG aspect of the begginings gets eliminated, It would be great.
-Back in the day when I started the game, I found it very easy to play the game. I slowly became better at the game and learned how to actually WIN a game. However those little military, economic and science helpers are very annoying. I am aware that they could be closed but then I would not be able to learn the game. Instead of giving me 3 pharagraphs about moving a unit to another location or basically putting them to garrison mode, keep it short and clean. People with common game knowledge will easily understand how the mechanics work.
-It is very obivious that some nations are stronger then others no doubt. When I am playing with friends we usually put rules such as no ''Oda''. The unique ability of armie morale is too op and when Oda builds a really good army in mp, even the worst player can easily defeat one of us. Possibly destroy our civ and deleting us from the game.
-Wars. I know they changed wars in Civ 6 but in Civ 5 it is horrible. I had games where Shaka instantly puts 15 İmpi's on my border and I realize that he will attack me and a turn later he declares war. If it is a real person I am probably dead. If it is a bot then it gives me hard time and annoys me. Casus Belli system is required. No civ should be able to declare war on one another just because they felt like it. Strong peaking nations in early game as Shaka is just one example that causes you to hate the game at that moment because it just ruins everything.
-Biases. I know there is charts on the internet that show how bot civ's will lean towards certain actions. But biases are mostly wrong. The famous Gandhi backstab meme is the best example. One day you are trading with him, other day he nukes you and razes your lands.
-Alexander. Why this guy settles every piece of single land that he finds. I don't think it is historically accurate either. I mean shouldn't he conquer stuff instead of colonizing and settling it.
-Religion. I find using religion to overcome your enemies really useless. Also Isabella using 100 missionaries and 50 inquisitors to change my religion doesn't really bother me.
-Victory types. The only victory I saw in a multiplayer game was conquering everything. I saw culture and science in single's and that's it. In high thinking mp games It should be more competitive to win games. The one with the better start and the one alone in an island usually wins.(I guess it is realistic Ex:U.S.A)
Other than that I loved playing civ 5. The price is really cheap when you buy the all dlc bundle when discounts happen. Hopefully they will do the same in civ 6.

BoneBone is a simple game. Waves of skeletons will approach your castle, gradually increasing in duration and enemy toughness. Your job is to click to fire arrows from your bow and prevent them from breaching your defenses. There's not much to the game besides spamming arrows. You can purchase two additional weapons but their cost and slow reload times make them inadequate for general use. You can hire archers and gunners for your tower and upgrade its health. That covers all the upgrades this game has to offer.
My main gripe with this game and the reason I have given it a negative review is that the developer has destroyed any replay value it might have by failing to include a wave select option. I made it to wave 20 (which was more tedious than it was fun) at which point a catapult-manning skeleton showed up with no warning whatsoever and blew my tower to pieces. I would like the option to choose to start from wave 5, 10, 15, or 20 with either the upgrades and money I had at those times or better yet, with no upgrades and the average amount of money players would have earned by that time, free to spend on different upgrades to see what works.
This is a feature I would expect from other games of this type. I'm not wasting half an hour every time I lose at wave 20 just to get back to where I was and possibly get wrecked again. Additionally, this game could be a lot less repetitive. I understand it's only $2 but Steam shouldn't be a place for newbie developers to dump MyFirstGame.exe. Add some new upgrades...a campaign...anything.

This game, is easily one of the best Fps' there is and quite possibly my personal favorite. It does everything nearly flawlessly, the story engaging and original, the characters memorable and fully realized, the world feels incredibly real and rich with atmosphere. Each area giving it's own unique feel. The gameplay runs smooth, and although defintley floaty, it is made to adapt to any players style. The source engine gives way to beautiful set pieces and with it's physics makes everything interactive and once again, feel so real. The animations on characters still hold up to most multi-million dollar games sent out today and in some cases manages to surpass it in how natural it looks. As for the flaws, it definitley has some, mostly from the combat. Although taking out enemies is satisfying it's far from the best shooting mechanics there is, with little gun variation. Although they do serve their purpose well enough it isn't an issue of it being bad, but more of it being medicore, which can be upsetting when so much else is done so well. And a few segments that during the first run are interesting and important to the plot will drag on upon future playthrough because these are not cutscenes, so you have to sit through these sections or take the time to break up gameplay by loading a future chapter. Ultimately though these are are minor complaints, I would still call this game a masterpiece as it is just such a well made, polished game that has so much to offer it's players. You never feel like an area was rushed, or any small section recieved less overview than another. From start to finish it is a great experience and one that any fan of shooters NEEDS to play through, at least once.

Why am I recommending against buying? Well lets divide up your area of interest.
40K Fan?
Well in the very first mission you have a Navigator helping your ship to navigate in real space, make sense? Only if you are grossly unfamiliar with 40K. Navigators are hybrid mutants that assist ships in transit through the warp, they couldn't care less about what happens in realspace, except of course the politicing of the Navis Nobilite. Oh, and the Navigator has no third eye, just a glowy patch on their head (with no cloth blocking it! Don't look too closely or you'll die), and they look like a freak, when every lore instance of a navigator describes them as aritocratic humans. I could list more examples, but no-one wants to read a story. Did the devs even do any research on 40K lore?
Gameplay?
Unbalanced as hell. It's not just that each faction has different archetypes and all are ultimately unbalanced, but mission types are unbalanced as well. Are you the Attacker on a Breakthrough mission? You are at a disadvantage. Are you the attacker in a Cruiser Clash (basic kill all enemies) using Eldar while your oppenents are Orks? Hope they don't hide in a gas cloud! If they do you pretty much auto-lose! Are you the Ork attacker fighting Eldar in a cruiser clash? Good luck doing any damage, their engines will see them out of your range pretty much permanently.
In addition the game tends to be more about spamming abilities, kiting endlessly, and tons of micromanagement. If this game had been turnbased it would have worked perfectly, but in real time (even with the slow time abilities) it ends up being a click fest.
Advancement / RPG elements?
You start with 3 light cruiser slots, with 2 different types of Light Cruiser. Both are almost identical, the Imperial for instance has all the same armor and weapons, except one has torpedoes and the other has a forward facing Lance. The Chaos have one with broadside lances, and one with launch bays (fighters, bombers). They are almost identical, and it takes 3ish missions to get a Cruiser slot. I've done 15ish missions and haven't unlocked any bigger ships yet, so the Gods of the Warp alone know how long it will take to get Battleships. It is a huge grind, and you are punished for losing. If a ship is destroyed in battle you can't use it for the next two battles. Sounds fun right? You lose one mission and then are at a huge disadvantage for the next 2 missions, making it more likely to lose those missions, in turn punishing you further. So what ends up happening? People will go into missions with ships they don't care about, and immediately warp out, just to ignore this 'feature'. It ends up being super fun!
All-in-all:
The game is fun, but not $40 worth of fun. I'd suggest waiting until the Steam Summer Sale, get it for 50% off, with the benefit of a few balance patches evening things out.
Edit: After playing for a few more hours the game does get more fun. However, it is really only when you get access to Battlecruisers (the second to last ship tier, which takes many, many hours to achieve) does the game really expand. Additionally if you unlock Battlecruisers with one race that does nothing at all for your other races, you need to sink even more hours in to unlock it with the other races. Even with battlecruisers the races are still very limited, Chaos BCs don't get above 50 armor for any facing, Eldar never get shields, Orks are slow tanks with no range regardless of the ship class, Imperial ships are always jacks-of-all-trades. In addition the further in you get the more annoying the destroyed ship, lost in the warp, and heavily damaged modifers become. With a 700 point game you are often using more than 50% of your capital ships, if it goes very poorly and you cannot warp out injured ships you may have very few capital ships for your next 2 battles.
Even after more time my recommendation doesn't change, wait for it to go on sale, and wait for some patches.

I'm a casual gamer typically (unless there are zombies involved - then it's anything goes).  This is the game I go to after I've been eaten for the fourteenth time in one of the few games I'm very intense about.  It's calming, interesting, and I really like the storyline.  I like that I don't have to go insane during the fight sequences.  This game is by no means easy, but it doesn't induce the same stress levels that a first-person kill-fest does.  And for when I just need to bug out for a while, I don't have to pay attention to the story-line.  I can involve myself in it if I want to, or ignore it and just concentrate on not dying of pneumonia.
The one negative I have about it is that it feels unfinished.  I keep looking to see if there are updates, and there are, but usually they're minor bug fixes or else they're updates about the game going mobile.  I feel like there's a lot missing here that could be expanded upon.
Overall, I recommend this game and hope everyone who plays it enjoys it.

Right out the gate this runs better then ARK. I have 1.6k hours into ark and ill let you in on the good and the bad.
I was extremely skeptical to buy a game running the same engine and basically re skinning things as it seemed from videos and screenshots i saw.
This review is on a PVP official server.
So first off..
The talent/skill and crafting sytem..
- This really makes this game shine and makes you feel like you have a purpose and a reason to play and keep gathering things and crafting things. (new spells)(new structures)
-The skill tracking system is really a nice touch and great in this game, making you gather one more piece of wood to unlock a new skill or structure.
-The quest tracker is really nice to be able to get an idea of what you are doing and possibly to scout out some things to look forward too, when it works. (it bugged for me a few times)
The overall feel and combat sytem
- This really is the main difference between ark and this game. The way it feels in 3rd person and being able to dash side to side and cast spells feels really smooth. where in ark moving or accessing things was always slow clunky feeling.
- The hit boxes sometimes feel off and it prob has to do with optimization and servers atm.
- The way you fight has many options and you dont feel locked to a super powerful animal/dino that you and your mates spent 3 months breeding for 400 hours just to get top tier stats. right out the gate you feel like you are doing damage with spells and not struggling as hard against AI.
The leveling system
- does a feel bit grindy lv 1-10 but it doesnt feel like RNG just made all your things dissapear because you lag teleported to death.(ark)
- It feels very rewarding and immersive everytime you level and see new things you can cook,craft, enchant, and use for weapons.
PvP
-So far i havnt been KOS yet, i havnt seen much drama. chinese apparently are force feeding 1 character to max on our server. other than that friendly and chill community.
- another cool thing you get a shield around your base and the opposing house has to declare war against you. I am not 100 percewnt sure how it all works yet or if anyone is exploiting it yet but we havn't been offlined yet.
Some negatives as it has just been realeased and if you are not a patient gamer please wait to purchase or get some hair on that sack and be involved in something.
- Fps drop has happened 2 times in the first 3 hours ive played. one being a structure built between to caverns was lagging me out for whatever reason and the other was when i was in the starting city. Other than that i play medium, nothing on low. as ark i would do all low setings and still get terrible fps and major lag spikes to this day.
- Trying to traverse up cliffs or semi steep terrain can be really annoying.
-Having to lay foundations on almost perfectly flat terrain is pretty annoying.
- Quest tracker has bugged on me.
-Loading screen to get into the game feels like it takes 10 years.
(will update as i go on) Thanks for reading!

Crystal Dynamics’ considerable talent should have been fully devoted to the upcoming Rise of the Tomb Raider, rather than detoured on this stop-gap project. And I say that respectfully, as I loved Guardian of Light and Tomb Raider ‘13. The stellar design and art direction of GOL is missing here, however, dipping the Lara Croft franchise into generic adventure murk with such decidedly sloppy execution. And while a patch may rectify technical problems, this was phoned in as a whole; it’s clear the studio’s attention is elsewhere.
I Paid: $20
Worth: $5
Good:
• Exponentially more fun with more players.
• Mechanically sound enough to enjoy.
• Egyptian theme works.
Bad:
• Single player suffers due to co-op emphasis, with brain-dead puzzles.
• Enemies flash a bright white when hit, resembling a mid-90’s arcade shooter.
• Visual cues abound when your character’s power meter is full: the HUD animates annoyingly, your character emanates particle effects while idle, and your weapon’s effects change accordingly (as they should).
•Technically demanding, despite being decidedly last-gen. No single area feels like optimized code.
Worse:
• Environmental detail exceeds the limits of an isometric vantage point, and as a result breakables and hazards get lost in the intricacy. It’s as though the camera was ripped from a third-person view and perched high above, with no tweaking of the assets from the new distance.
• The world has no sense of location. You never quite know where you are or should be, despite being constantly told by the HUD and never feeling lost. The tombs feel like the overworld rather than a contained level, causing confusion as to what challenges or collectibles you should be pursuing. Progress and a sense of completion feel oddly disjointed, and then suddenly, you’re at the end. It never gels.
• Loot system is just terrible, and not worth the incentive.
Advice for buyers:
Turn off the ridiculous Depth of Field effect; it’s completely wrong for this style of game and hinders play – a classic example of the industry’s “filter over function” problem.

Meadow is a really fun game. I know it classifies itself as an MMO but I wouldn't really consider it one. If you've ever played the Shelter games, this is basically Shelter, with multiplayer, without hunting. In Meadow, you work together with others in packs to find stones which can unlock new skins for your animal, new emotes or even a whole new animal! Keep in mind there are no AI in this game at all. There is no competition between players and players simply communicate via simple emotes, no text chat or voice chat at all. This is one of the reasons why Meadow is such a cheerful game that can always make you happy and never upset you!
In addition, the community of Meadow is REALLY friendly, and one of the best I've seen.  They're always willing to lend a helping hand, and talk like civilized people. Meadow itself has beautiful starry night graphics, and after playing a couple of hours of it with my friend, I can say I have no complaints about the game.
It's perfect in every way, and its such a cheerful and happy game that can turn your gloomy day into one of the best days. One of the most memorable times I had was when I found a group of 8+ animals with my friend. It was fantastic just seeing other people and everyone was just so happy and glad that we had a huge pack now! The devs are really friendly and are always updating the game with features that players suggest!
Therefore, I can't see any reason to not recommend Meadow to anyone. If you haven't tried it already, you really should, as you're missing out on a ton! If you prefer a singleplayer experience, Shelter might be a better pick for you!

First time playing FTL was with this Advanced Edition, so this isn't a review of what the Advanced Edition adds to the base game, but what the whole package provides.
Gameplay is a mashup of roguelikes and RTS, with the ability to pause in order to make more strategic decisions when necessary. It *will* unfairly kill you at times. Once you understand the game, you'll find that you can make it tot he final battle more often than not due to good planning and a decent amount of luck, but the final battle is unfortunately where the success of your run due to the RNG elements comes into play. If you had decent RNG and great planning, you're still going to lose in the final battle because no matter how well you know the game, you won't have the power necessary to overcome the challenge.
Cool concept, decent art style, soundtrack is outstanding, took about 4 hours for me to get my first victory, did a few additional runs afterwards for kicks, beat it three times over the course of 10 hours, and that was enough for me. Not a must-play by any means, but if you're looking for something to play to kill time while waiting for a bigger release, then this is a viable option.

It doesn't mean that the Meadow isn't worth playing - quite the opposite! TEF came out over 10 years ago and featured pretty much the same idea: you are playing with other people as forest animals, with no other way of communication than emotes. In TEF there was body language, here we've got 2D emotes popping above our heads.
This time though we can choose from several animals to play as (unlocked through gathering puzzle pieces or buying other Shelter games). It is quite sad that you have to spend a lot of money just to play as a lynx or an adult badger (not mentoning the eagle issue) but on the other hand it is a nice reward for the current fans (aka owners of previous games). My only hope is that some day in future those unlockable animals will be available for all.
The world is big and the graphics unique. It's a pleasure to wander the forest. And as always with this kind of social experiments in games, it is amusing how much you can actually interact with people without words. The encounters can be funny or even touching. It's easy to bond with a goat who patiently helps you get your first skins and emotes, and sad when either of you has to go.
I played 4 hours on my first session and I'm not bored yet. I guess I missed the "gameplay" of The Endless Forest too, since I've spent months and months in the freaky looped forest (still rocking that first generation pictogram!).
All in all I'm quite happy that this kind of game has been made again, with a fresh concept and design (although I'm not sure anything will ever beat human-faced deer). For the 3€ it's definitely worth its price, of course as long as you like casual exploration games and/or forest life. You should try the other Shelter games too, not to unlock anything, but for the sake of experiencing them. And if you're looking for even more - give TEF a try. It's free. Very old, but still quite original and interesting.

One of greatest touring car race simulations.
Pitstop strategies can be used to great effect in longer races and when race regulations demand to have a pitstop during race (STCC rules). Plenty of setup choices to tune pace for your driving style and durability of tires etc.
Car physics are good and realistic, engine and tire modeling are properly done.
Visually it's starting to show the age and some controller settings are limited and awkward by today's standards.
Also you may need to edit some configuration files manually to get it use your VRAM properly and so on.
It's still a good simulation of touring car racing with some open-wheel racers as well.
If only there was a sequel or update coming.

I owned the original Fighting Fantasy book "Appointment with F.E.A.R" way back when, and enjoyed it a great deal, especially as it departed from the usual sword-and-sorcery settings. I was always impressed with how cleverly it was composed, with your ability to choose from no less than 4 super-powers and having to take quite a different path through the story to succeed in each case - despite its tounge-in-cheek superhero approach it was one of the most cleverly woven together FF books.
Fast forward, and I was pleased to try out this version which runs very well on my potato of a laptop. The graphics are mostly the illustrations lifted from the original novel with a little added colour - no bad thing, as they are quality artwork. There are a few additions there too. However, the developers seem to have used the computer to have expanded the options even further - three times I played as the Flying/Super Strength hero and each time was given a different set of starter clues which completely changed the path of success through the game. And it isn't too easy - I still haven't managed to succeed in beating it yet after about 8 playthroughs.
Recommended if you fancy something a little different in the VN line or if you were a fan of the original book.

Appointment with FEAR is a stylish comic adventure, where you pick the hero you want to be and choose which crimes to fight in the city. You progress in the game automatically, but you have some choice that will have impact on further progress and results in the game.
The story is a simple comic book one - you are the hero of the city that has to save it from the villains. At the start of the game you get to know, that you have 3 days to get enough clues about the big bad guys called FEAR and save the city. The clues you gather through investigating crimes, fighting smaller bad guys and using your super powers to get something more or less special. Some quests you encounter are not connected to the main story and are there just to keep you busy, but since you lose time to find the clues for the big thing, it means the smaller quests are still somewhat related to the main story. The dialogs are nicely written, some are funny, others are more typical for comis books but they all feel well integrated.
You fight the villains in this game by simply selecting which attack to use in a fight. There are always 3 choice and they have different hit chances and do different damage to your opponent. Basically, you just press on one and hope to hit, so far I was never even close to lose a fight, so it seems they are made the way you always win. The game does not feel challenging at all, its more for casual fun gameplay.
The graphic has a nice style and feels absolutely comic-like which is the goal of the game. Surely fans of older comic magazines will enjoy playing with this graphic. There are not many visual effects, but the existing ones fit the game nicely. The interface is simple but again fitting the game style.
The progress is rather quick, especially if you are a quick reader. Most of the game you only read what is happening in the city and rarely choose which action to pick next. There are no mini-games in Appointment with FEAR, so after few playthroughs the game feels a bit repetative since the choices remain the same and are not reandomised. Overall the progress is fine though, since the dialogs and texts are not bad and quite often you will lauph or at least smile a bit.
The music is pretty cool electronic and definetely serves the comic game with science plays a big role. The sound feedback in fighting and small animations was fitting the game really well and the stay in menus or the game was made enjoyable by the fine tracks playing in the background.
Appointment with FEAR is a nice comic-style adventure, which will offer you some fun moments and replayability. Players enjoying being a hero with super powers in a pick your adventure games, will definetely have some fun with this title. Most other players will enjoy few hours of gameplay, but most likely will figure out how to save the city once and after that, the game is quite done.
I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. Rate and leave a comment if you enjoyed reading it.

is a lot more fun than I first anticipated.  Having seen a lot of footage and information beforehand, I didn't see myself playing it for more than an hour.  Once I started playing yesterday though, I couldn't put it down.
I'm going to do something unorthodox and break down the game based on its own description.
is a...
1)
- this means that you use your controls to move, and the game aims and shoots for you.  My first thought was that this would be annoying, but it's actually quite a positive thing.  You target and fire at the closest enemy, which leaves you with the remaining responsibility to dodge and use items.  And you'll need all the concentration you can get for those two things, especially later in the game when it gets hard.  On top of this you still feel in control because the movement is so fluid and responsive.
2)
- There is permadeath.  Game runs are quick and brutal when you first play.  The game's progression through levels is linear (for the most part), but the content of each area is procedurally generated, meaning it's different every time.  This includes the physical shape of the level as well as enemies and items.  It makes each run feel fairly unique.
3)
- This descriptor may be a bit misleading for some.  On the game's default easy difficulty setting, you'll be spammed with enemy bullets, sometimes in patterned formations, and in large quantities in the later levels.  But it's not nearly as much as a classic "Bullet Hell" shmup like the TouHou games, so it may give a bad first impression to bullet-hell enthusiasts.  HOWEVER: If you want a higher difficulty you will quickly unlock "Planar Altars" which start showing up in the early areas, and allow you to crank up the difficulty via the game's "Desecration" level.  This shows promise in satisfying more hardcore gamers.

I really enjoy this game.
Very simple at first, with the "one stick system" being a fairly intuitive movement. Bullets shoot out of the character, attacking only the closest character, and tyou progress through the levels.
The wrinkle comes from the second stick, providing a short dash that allows the player to avoid bullets, as well as two abilities that can be activated. Several passive abilities, such as bombs, rockets or flamethrowers, round out the characters attacks.
What starts as a fairly simple, easy system quickly becomes more complex, the difficultly ramping smoothly to provide a surprisngly engrossing experience. It is much closer to games like Touhou or vertical bullet hells than to the immediate cousins of Nuclear Throne or Binding of Isaac. This works to the games benifet, providing a tense, methodical experience where foresight and planning pay off.
I would definitely recomend this to many people, though with the ceveat it's closer to a true bullet hell than other games that are visually similar in gameplay. The patterns get tough, and careful use of your dash and a bit of luck make for an excellent experience.
Also, I love the pixel art, and the music isvery fitting. The neon effect goes a long way to turn what could have been a boring visual design into something memorable!

Braid is a beautifully realised platformer featuring mechanics largely based on time manipulation, use of these mechanics allow you to interact with the enemy and environment according to rules that shift as you continue into the rabbit hole.
I won't lie this game is sometimes going to tax your brain, but it's well worth playing and beating at least once (if you want all the trophies you'll need at least twice).
If you're scared of puzzles it probably isn't for you but you don't have to be a genius to work it out, eventually you'll have your eureka moment, just hopefully not while in the bath tub and then running outside screaming.
Technically it works well and is fully playable even on a single core P4 so no one should have to miss out.
Is it difficult? Yes, frequently to the point of hair pulling.
Is it strange? Somewhat, though it makes more sense once you can read the story in order.
Is it worth playing? Definitely, at least if you can stand puzzles, platforming, and a story that makes little or no sense immediately.

I'm just doing this review to help me track how much I actually do enjoy the games I play and I found it made sense to start with Half Life 2 considering it's on sale at an absurd price and because you probably need a spoiler free review so here it goes.
Half life 2 has forever made his place into my list of the best games I have ever played. The amount of fun you have playing it is immense and the story of the game grabs you and makes you play it until you complete it. Half life 2 is forever seen as one of the best games if not the best game ever to be made and here are some pros and cons of it.
Pros:
- One of the best gaming stories out there, if you have not played Half life 1 don't worry, you don't really need it, I do recommend it and you might want to buy that too or just get the bundle, trust me. The story, like I said, catches you and never lets go, you are forever holding your place in this game and playing it makes you want to know more about what's going on and why are you here, the overall interesting arc and details will make you stay and complete it.
- Characters are very well done, from the silent Gordon Freeman to the annoying enemies, to the usual whimpy bad guy and mysterious G-Man, every single character in this game has something to offer
- The gameplay feels just right and it's nothing more than basic and fun which makes this experience even better if you combine it with the story
- The graphics while not great will do just enough for you to enjoy this game 100%
- The overall feeling of Half Life 2 is...complete. You will feel a rush while you play, you will feel scared a lot more than you think, Half Life 2 is pretty dark tbh, you will feel relieved, you will feel satisfied, confused, energetic, well...you will feel, that's for sure.
CONS
- You will need half life episodes (epi1/2) to continue on with this game, and while that's not bad considering the price, you will not get to understand Half life to a full 100% because...well...there's not Half Life 3, VALVE doesn't make games anymore, they completely sold out and you have to deal with it
- Literally nothing else
Final Verdict: 10/10

As of right now I have 125 hours and counting into Dark and Light.  I have experienced alot that the game has to offer, working my way up the tier of animals to tame and gotten up to griffin so far.  It has a few bugs, from dinos getting stuck under other dinos while attacking, a few graphical glitches and the occasional stuck dino on some random part of the landscape.  Overall however, the pros vastly outweigh the cons for me.  I do not feel like I would enjoy the official servers as I think that the rates for harvesting and taming are a bit too low for it to be a fun experience for me.  However as an admin of my own server I can tell you it is a great game.  It is like ark, yes, however, in ark you are forced to have to tame dinos to accomplish anything.  In DnL you can literally go through and play as long as you like without ever taming anything if that is your goal.  The player is plenty powerful enough to take down most if not all creatures in the game and tames are only used to further enhance or expand that experience.  This is definately worth 25 dollars, but do not go into it expecting a game that has no bugs.  There are bugs, and some of them will annoy you.  Enjoy it for what it is and learn how to manipulate or workaround any bugs you find.  Btw I have an i7 7700 with a 1070 vid card and I run just fine at high/epic on all settings at 40+ frames.  So no graphics issues for me.
